en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā:
The Commencement of the Work.
Having paid homage to that Great Seer who possesses constant knowledge— a knowledge that does not exist apart from the one who knows— and who is endowed with every excellence;
and having likewise taken up the essence of all teachings from other teachers, [I compose this work].
The commentary on the meaning of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* shall now be composed. Regarding the commentary on the salutation and so forth:
here, at the outset, this author of the treatise accumulates a store of merit for the sake of accomplishing the true welfare of both himself and others.

“By the words ‘the Tathāgata,’ etc.: therein, the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, who is the source of compassion—that is, the locus for the arising of great compassion—having relinquished (*osajja*) and abandoned (*cajitvā*) the state of bliss (*sukhapada*), which has come into his own hands, which is the foundation of bliss, the cause of bliss, or the giver of bliss, namely Nibbāna;
[he did so] in existence (*bhave*), which arises from the Kali age and is the cause of suffering.”
[I bow] to such a Tathāgata as he, who, performing in the cycle of existence deeds that are exclusively difficult— unmixed with what is easy and exceedingly hard to do,
such as the fivefold renunciation— acted solely for the welfare and benefit of others.

[Kha] And to that Dhamma, which the elephant-like sages, the best of men, the Blessed Ones— who are liberated from old age, disease, and so forth, being free from aging, illness, and the like— [have realized].
They honored [it], having paid homage; likewise, on that further, supreme raft of Dhamma—
capable of crossing over from the great flood of saṃsāra for those beings who have plunged into it— standing upon which, by way of practicing rightly,
men and non-men, both humans and gods, [crossed] the ocean of the three realms consisting of the rounds of defilements, karma, and kamma-vipāka.
I pay homage to that Dhamma which has enabled them to cross over and reach the further shore of the great ocean-like mass of saṃsāra, which is agitated by the three rounds;
and I pay homage to that Dhamma which destroys evil, abandons the defilements, or brings about the abandonment of the suffering of saṃsāra.
[Ga] Because of the Blessed One’s status as the son of the Lord of Sages, and because he attained the state of an Arahant through the teaching of the Dhamma arising from his breast.
The Pātimokkha restraint is that which has become the status of a heart-born son of the Lord of Sages; it is attained, praised, and a field for the removal of defilements.

It is a fertile field for those seeking merit, a place where the seeds of merit grow, and a well-prepared soil renowned and celebrated throughout the world. Or, as one who upholds what is heard, it is "unheard" (*assuta*) because of its absence of hearing defilements;
it is called "made living" (*pāṇīkata*) because even one who is not yet a living being is made into a living being [by it]. It is the Pātimokkha restraint.

Because he possesses this restraint, he is one who has "restraint made manifest" (*pāṇīkatasaṃvara*); that *pāṇīkatasaṃvara* is excellent, being desirable by the world including the devas through its qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
For it is said in the Udāna (27): "Even the devas envy such a one.
At all times, throughout every moment, his mind is continuous and uninterrupted by the flood of qualities, that is, the multitude of virtues such as virtue.
"Or even a group with perfected minds"—that is, even a multitude of the eight types of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*)—to them too I bow.
Thus, here the application of the meaning for all three [verses] should be seen in brief.
[Gha-ṅa] Having thus accumulated an abundance of merit, he states what it is he intends to accomplish: "I shall elucidate the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*."

I shall expound this treatise named *Abhidhānappadīpikā*—so called because it illuminates (*paridīpanato*) and makes manifest (*pakāsanato*) the designations for the Buddha and others by way of their forms and their grammatical genders.

I shall expound that which is established internally [as a latent potential] by making it manifest externally. For the internal state is developed and brought forth in dependence upon the external state.
Now, do there not already exist among the ancient masters various treatises on designations that expound names and genders, such as the *Amarakosa*, the *Tikaṇḍa*, the *Uppalini*, and others?
There are also treatises on gender (liṅga-sattha) composed by Pāṇini, Vyāḍi, Vararuci, Candragomin, Rudra, Vāmana, and others.
To this, he says: "Thus, displaying the essence of what was spoken by the Buddha, [this work] sets forth names and genders.

By this, he means that although the treatises of the ancient masters exist, the names and genders therein do not conform to the Buddha’s word; therefore, [this work] provides those that do conform to it.
He elucidates this meaning with the words: "I shall expound the science of naming (abhidhānasattha), demonstrating the names and genders.

A *nāma* is so called because "by means of it, the meaning is named (*namyate*) or expressed," according to the verbal root *nam* in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). A *liṅga* is so called because "it is characterized (*liṅgayate*)"—that is, analyzed—by rules such as "from this [stem], the suffix *āp* occurs when it denotes a female," and so forth;
or alternatively, it is a *liṅga* because "by means of it, the gender-markers (*liṅgin*), such as 'female' and so on, are indicated (*liṅgīyante*) or manifested."

Feminine, masculine, and neuter. To the question, "What is the purpose (*payojana*) in composing this treatise on terminology (*abhidhāna-sattha*?"—in order to show that which, when it exists, enables listeners to apply themselves to hearing it—he said: "In names and genders," and so forth.

Since proficiency (*pāṭava*) is the state of being skilled in the Buddha’s word, that itself is the meaning, the purpose; those who desire that are "those who seek proficiency" (*pāṭavatthino*). For them...
For listeners who possess proficiency, skill, and expertise regarding names and grammatical genders, there exists a powerful cause for determining the meaning within the Buddha’s word;
therefore, for that reason, the connection [of the text] is as follows:
they shall expound the treatise *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, demonstrating the names and genders essential to what was spoken by the Buddha.
Now, in order to show the ease and brevity of the formulation, he says "moreover" (*bhiyyo*), and so forth. "Moreover" means generally;
by way of the distinction of forms—that is, through the performance of grammatical functions such as femininity, masculinity, and so on—the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders are to be known.

And that [gender] is to be understood as belonging to nouns (*nāma*), to noun-adjectives (*nāma-visesana*), and to all-pronouns (*sabba-nāma-sadda*) which refer to nouns, because there is no other mode [of application]. Among these, the distinction of forms for nouns is as follows:
For example: *churikā*, *sattha*, and *asiputti* are synonyms (verse 392). *Asi*, *khagga*, and *sāyaka* are synonyms (verse 391).
*Pānīyaṃ*, *salilaṃ*, and *dakaṃ* are synonyms (verse 661). As for a specific name:
*nisītha* means "the middle of the night" (verse 70). As for the word *sabba-nāma* used as a reference to a name: *ākaṅkhā*.
*Ruci* has been explained; however, *lālasā* is feminine according to Abhidhāna 163.
Due to association, fixed gender, and inseparability, it should be known as feminine, masculine, or neuter. "In some cases" refers to where there is no difference in form, such as:
*marīci*, *migataṇhikā* (Abhidhāna 65); *raṃsimā*, *bhākara*, *bhānu* (Abhidhāna 63); *āpo*, *payo*, *jalaṃ*, *vāri*.
Abhidhāna, verse 661: For words such as *marīci* (mirage), because their form is not distinct [from others], they might be suspected of belonging to other genders;
however, through association with words like *migataṇhikā* (deer-thirst), *bhākara* (sun), and *jala* (water)—which have fixed genders—they are determined to be of that same gender.

By means of "direct prescription" (*āhacca-vidhāna*), which involves stating [the word] specifically for each of the feminine, masculine, and neuter, one should know whether it is feminine, masculine, or neuter. "In some cases" (*kvaci*) means where [it is so prescribed].
A difference in gender is not the cause for determining the meaning; nor is co-occurrence (sāhacariya) intended as a distinction of gender, nor does one accept that there is only a single gender.
For example: *vallarī*, *mañjarī*, and *nārī* [are feminine] according to Abhidhāna verse 550; *viṭapo* [is masculine], while *viṭabhī* [is feminine] according to Abhidhāna verse 547;

*bhīti* [is feminine], while *itthī* [is feminine], *bhayaṃ* [is neuter], and *uttāso* [is masculine] according to Abhidhāna verse 166; *vajiraṃ* [is neuter] according to "punnapuṃsakeccādi" in Abhidhāna verse 24.
[Cha] Now, regarding the "distinction of gender" (*rūpabheda*):

since a compound (*dvanda*) of words with different genders would otherwise arise due to the application of the rules for determining gender, the author begins by formulating a maxim (*paribhāsa*)—starting with the words "of those with non-different gender"—to prohibit that and ensure that only compounds of words with identical gender are formed.
A compound is made only of names with non-different gender, not of those with different gender; for example: *vimutti-asaṅkhata-dhātu*.

The phrase "may there be purity and liberation" (suddhinibbutiyo siyuṃ) is an example from Abhidhāna, verse 9. It is not only the case that the dual number is used here; rather, the single-remainder (ekasesa) construction is also employed for words of identical gender, as in:
"the naked one and those clad in sky-clothing" (naggo digambarāvatthā), Abhidhāna, verse 734. However, in the work of Sabbadharā, it is stated: "jīmūta means cloud and mountain.
But is it not also the case that the single-remainder construction is made even for words of different genders, as in: "mother and father" (mātā pitā)?
"Parents," "sons," and "sons and daughters" are the designations in verse 249. "Fathers-in-law," "mothers-in-law," "fathers-in-law," "brother," and "sister" are the designations in verse 250.
For here, "parents" (*pitaro*) refers to both mother and father; "sons" (*puttā*) refers to both son and daughter;

"fathers-in-law" (*sasurā*) refers to both mother-in-law and father-in-law; and "brother" (*bhātā*) refers to both brother and sister—thus, even for those of different genders [the same term is used].
It is shown that this is a single-remainder compound (*ekasesa*). There is no fault because their different genders are demonstrated in their respective places.
"Tāta" means father, progenitor; see Abhidhāna 243. "Ammā," "ambā," "jananī," and "mātā" mean mother; see Abhidhāna 244.
"Apaccaṃ," "putto," "orajo," and "suto" mean child, offspring; see Abhidhāna 240. "Nāriyaṃ," "duhitā," and "dhītā" mean daughter; see Abhidhāna 241. [She is] the mother of the husband and wife.

"Mother-in-law" (*sassu*) means "spoken to" (*vuttā*) and "honored" (*tappitā*). For their designations include such terms as "father-in-law" (*sasura*), and so forth; this is the twenty-fourth verse concerning the "place" (*ṭhānantara*).
Likewise, here no confusion has been made—unlike the enumeration of words with different genders that lack a sequential order.

For in that [previous list], meanings such as "heaven" (*sagga*) and "direction" (*disā*) appear in their respective order, while meanings such as "Sakka" and "direction" appear together with their respective relations.
Just as the application of the *sarūpa* rule applies to all names that denote the same meaning as the term being stated, so too do those names associated with its synonyms;

since all these must be denoted at the occasion of stating that [term], this sequence is accepted for the purpose of ensuring that the entire application of the *nāma* rule and the *sarūpa* rule may occur easily in one place. And such being the case, necessarily...

In the section on synonyms such as *sagga* (heaven), words like *diva* are the designata; in the occasion of [synonyms for] *hara* (the moon), words like *kumāra* are the designata. Thus, a confusion of genders according to the sequence [of the list] could not be avoided.
However, no such confusion has been made here except where the aforementioned sequence [dictates it].
This is because they are expressed according to their possibility through synonyms and in accordance with the sequence of the feminine section and so forth—for example: *īti*.
“...and *tvitthī* and *ajañña*, as well as *upasagga* and *upaddava*,” is the title of verse 401.

For here, those [words] which possess three genders have been recorded only in their respective sections on the three genders, not by way of mere recitation as in the numerical lists (*gaṇanapāṭha*). Thus, in all cases, the arrangement is applied according to what is possible.
And it has been said: “There is no *dvanda* compound for the sake of expressing a distinction, nor is there an *ekasesa* (elliptical) compound, nor any confusion.”
"Where, for those of different genders used without a specific sequence? (Amarakośa 1.4).
Now, in order to show the application of gender-denoting words according to their position within meanings, he says "liṅgavācake," etc.

Gender-denoting words situated at the end or middle of the quarters of verses, as well as gender-denoting words with multiple meanings such as *ñāṇadassana* (knowledge and vision), etc., [are to be understood accordingly].
The gender-markers (*liṅga*) proceed toward, that is, reach, the primary meaning by way of denoting it.
Other lines of verse beginning with [the word] *ādi* proceed toward, that is, reach, the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) by way of denoting gender. For example:
"In the fruit, in insight, in the divine eye, and in omniscience..."
In the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) and in the path (*magga*), there is the designation "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*); verse 794.
Resonance (*ṇāda*) is a condition for the causes and supports such as faith and robes;
play (*kīḷā*) and so forth are found in various dwellings (*vihāra*), while "dwelling" (*vihāra*) refers to the abode of the Sugata; verse 857.
*Khagga*, *kurūra*, and *nettiṃsa*—these are three synonyms for "sword" (verse 1089);
*kusala*, *sukata*, and *suṭṭhu-kata*—these are three synonyms for "well-done" (verse 938).
*Samaya* [is used] in the sense of "conjunction," "multitude," "cause," and "moment."
Regarding penetration (*paṭivedha*), there may be [an occasion] at the right time; regarding abandonment (*pahāna*) and views of gain (*lābhaditthi*), there is the verse numbered 778.
Regarding the wilderness (*kantāra*) and forest difficulties (*vanadugga*), there is the verse numbered 1107.
And herein—
In the cases of "majority" (*yebhuyyatā*), "mixture" (*byāmissa*), "disjunction" (*visaṃyoga*), and "exclusive" (*kevala*);
in the sense of "firmness" (*daḷha*), "excess" (*atireka*), and "without remainder" (*anavasesa*)—that [term] is a designation (*abhidhāna*) in these three [contexts].

(Verse 786) In the case of "concentration" (*samādhi*), it belongs to the masculine singular; in the case of "confusion" (*ākula*), it follows the gender of the word being expressed (*vāccaliṅgika*). (Verse 1035)

In the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* (verse 1066), beginning with "Jaḷe thūlo mahatyapi," and in other such instances, it should be understood that the statement "it goes first" (*pubbaṃ yantī*) is made on account of the majority of cases;

for the middle position of a verse and the middle position of a line are both occupied by words expressing gender, even when they appear before or after [other words]. Alternatively, it refers to the middle position of verses...

The application [of words] should be understood according to their occurrence: those that occur at the beginning of a verse, those that occur in the middle of a verse, and those that occur at the end or in the middle of a foot, as well as those occurring both before and after.
[Ja] Now, regarding the specific rules, he provides a mnemonic summary (*paribhāsa*) for the sake of ease of learning, beginning with "pumitthiyaṃ.

In the case of "pumitthiyaṃ," the word "dvīsū" (in two) is to be understood; for example, in the 24th verse, *asani* is a designation for two genders. This applies to all genders—that is, to all three genders.
The word "in three" (*tīsu*) is to be understood as denoting completion, as in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* verse 942: "the seventh among the seven, the best among the good.
Furthermore, in this context, a name whose gender has been excluded is to be understood as having the remaining gender by way of elimination, according to the *Amarakosa* (1.5):
"a name whose gender is excluded has the sense of the remaining gender," as in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* verse 81: "the year (*vassa*) is feminine. Here...

By the commentary on the prohibition of the singular number (*ekaliṅganisedhabyākhyāna*), there is the prescription of two genders; that is, under the pretext of prohibiting the singular, two genders are expressed (as stated in the *Amarakośacintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).

Having explained the section on synonyms (*abhidhānalāhava*), he now states the section on usage (*paṭipattilāhava*) with the words beginning "At the commencement of another synonym" (*abhidhānantarārambhe*), etc. Of the other synonym...
When there is the commencement of another designation, one must understand these two designations: "that which ends in *tu*" (*tu-anta*) and "that which begins with *atha*" (*atha-ādi*).
The meaning is that a word such as *nāma* (name), ending in *tu* or beginning with *atha*, does not connect with what precedes it. In this regard, an example of a word ending in *nāma* is:
*Jino Sakko tu Siddhattho abhidhānaṃ gāthā Kesavo*. (The Victor, Sakka, Siddhattha, the name, the verse, Kesava.)
The section on synonyms for *cakkapāṇi* consists of 16 verses. The section on synonyms for *mahissaro*, *sivo*, and *sūlī* consists of 16 verses.
Regarding gender: the synonyms for *paṇhi* and *pāsaṇi* in the masculine consist of 277 verses. The synonyms for *rajo* and *pupphaṃ* in the masculine consist of 238 verses.
The synonyms for *tirokaraṇī* and *sā* consist of 298 verses. The synonyms for *ullocaṃ* are both masculine and neuter.
299 verses. For example, as in *atthapadaṃ*: “In the stomach, likewise in the digestive fire (*pācānala*), and in the woman of the intestines (*gahaṇītthī*)” — 973 verses.
*Paṇīta* means "sweet" in three [senses], and also "excellent" when prescribed. *Añjasā* means "straightway," "in a row," "in a line," and "a street" — 940 verses.
Here, by the word *atha*, in the sense of immediate succession (*anantariyattha*), there is a characterization of its own specific method (*sakapariyāya*).

Furthermore, in the case of words such as *sadda*, it is not connected with what precedes it. Also, regarding the term *pāṇaka*, there is the definition in verse 623: "A *pāṇaka* is a creature that moves upward and has hairy limbs.
[Jha] Now, from among those expressions corresponding to the Buddha’s words, I shall provide an account of some of them that are of frequent usage.
In order to show the absence of ego-centeredness (*ahaṃkāra*) by way of not being struck down by other teachers, he said: "Excessive application" (*bhiyyo payoga*), and so forth.

Regarding the *Saugata*—the tradition consisting of the word of the Sugata, namely the Three Baskets (*piṭakattaya*)—it is called "tradition" (*āgama*) because the threefold excellences come (*āgacchanti*) through it.
In that [tradition], "excessive application" means that which is applied with abundance; that [is what is meant].

Having approached and taken [these meanings], and having brought together both the etymological logic found in certain sections of the *Araññavagga* and other parts, as well as the logic appearing in the treatise named *Nighaṇṭu* which conforms to the Buddha’s word, the gender and noun-forms are explained; that which was established internally is now made manifest externally.
For indeed, the state of being made clear is itself the state of being known by those who perform their duties properly. This is the benediction.
Or rather, even for a word whose occurrence is certain, there is a state of being "present" (vattamānatta) through the desire to express it as present;
for thus in the world, intending the accomplishment of what is certain to happen, one desires to speak of what is yet to come—whether as present or as past.
For example, when someone is addressed by another saying, "May this [curse] fall upon me," that person, being certain [of the outcome], [speaks accordingly].
Thinking "it will be so," one wishes to speak of something becoming worse;

for that very reason, Pāṇini 3.3.132, which is a statement of extended application (*atidesa*) regarding the rule "this is a blessing, as if it were already become" (*āsīsāyaṃ bhūtamiva ca*), is refuted.
The commentary on *paṇāma* and so forth is finished.
1. Commentary on the Section on Heaven (Saggakaṇḍa) 1.

Now, since the meaning of what is expressed (abhidheyyattha) is twofold—namely, the conventional meaning (paññatti) and the ultimate meaning (paramattha)—and among these, for the most part, the ultimate meaning is superior to the conventional meaning;
and even among those [ultimate meanings], because it specifically effects the eradication and subsiding of the defilements (kilesas), [it is the most excellent].
In due order, eight qualities are supreme, yet even among those, Nibbāna alone is supreme;

and of all these qualities, the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) alone is supreme. For it was said by the Blessed One: “Dispassion is the supreme among qualities, and the Visionary is the supreme among bipeds” (Dhammapada 273;
Nettippakaraṇa 125). For here [it is said]: “To whatever extent, monks, there are conditioned phenomena...”
"Whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost of those phenomena" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34; 5.32;
Itivuttaka 90). According to this statement, among all phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—only Nibbāna, which is synonymous with dispassion, is the most excellent.
Furthermore, the All-Seeing One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, [is the foremost] among all those phenomena and among bipeds, such as gods and humans.

The Blessed One has stated that the state of wisdom (*paññā*) is the best; therefore, in order to first show at the beginning of the *Saggakaṇḍa*—by way of aspiration and by way of praise—the very name of the Buddha, which expresses the meaning of being the best in all things, he says "Buddho," and so forth.
Therein, the names ending with the word "Jina" are the names of every Buddha. He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to everything.
*Buddho*: when there is an object of action (*sakammaka*), the suffix *tap* occurs for the agent (*kattari*). One whose awakening (*buddhi*) is distinguished is *buddho*;

here, the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule beginning with "yada" (*yadādi*) in the sense of praise (*pasaṃsāyaṃ*). *Dasabalo*: one who possesses the ten powers (*dasabalāni*), such as the aggregates of giving and virtue (*dānasīlakkhandhādayo*), or the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇādayo*).
*Satthā*: one who instructs (*sāsati*) and disciplines (*vinayati*) beings (*satta*). *Sabbaññū*: one whose nature is to know all phenomena (*sabbadhamma*). *Dvipadānaṃ...* [of two-footed beings...]
"Among two-footed beings, the best is the 'best of two-footed beings' (dvipaduttama).

In the *Buddhavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā* (*BuA* 8.37), because the use of the genitive case characterized by selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is prohibited in compounds, it is understood that this is not such a genitive characterized by selection.
But why is it prohibited there? Because in a compound, the three characteristics of selection generally do not apply.

Because of the absence of deficiency. For although the sixth case is indeed prohibited there, since the seventh case exists as having the characteristic of specification (*niddhāraṇa*), that [prohibition] must likewise be negated for it as well.
The Lord of the Munis is the King of the Munis (*munindo*). Merit, knowledge, fortune, and so forth are called *bhaga*;
because he is endowed with these, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). He protects (*nāthati*) by seeking the welfare of beings, or he torments (*upatāpeti*) the defilements.
He is the *nātha* (Protector) because he exercises sovereignty over beings or because he aspires for their welfare.

He is the *cakkhumā* (Possessor of Vision) because he is endowed with the five eyes, namely: the eye of the Buddha, the Dhamma-eye, the Samantacakkhu (Universal Eye), the wisdom-eye (*paññā-cakkhu*), and the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*). He is the *Aṅgīrasa* because a fathom-wide radiance constantly issues forth from his body.
He is the *muni* because he has measured (*munana*) all phenomena in every aspect, or because he maintains silence (*mona*) when preaching the Dhamma.
2. A *lokanātha* is a protector (*nātha*) of worlds (*loka*) or of those within the worlds. He is called *anadhivara* because there is no other superior person (*uttamapuggala*) greater than himself;
or, because his own existence has reached the ultimate limit, there is no other superior state of existence (*attabhāva*) beyond this that could be aspired to.
He is so called because he seeks and searches for the great aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.

Mahesi: he is a great sage (*mahesi*), or one who possesses great sovereignty (*īsa*) and majesty (*vibhūti*). Vināyaka: he leads (*vinayati*) beings toward their welfare (*hita*) by instructing them;
or, he leads beings to the distinguished state of *nibbāna*, thus he is a leader (*vināyaka*). Samantacakkhu:

because he is endowed with omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*)—which has acquired the name "all-seeing" due to its nature of perceiving all phenomena—he is the All-Seeing One. His knowledge has gone to perfection (*sobhanaṃ gataṃ ñāṇamassa*).

He is the Sugata because he has gone well, or because he has gone such that there is no returning again to saṃsāra; or alternatively, he is the Sugata because he has gone rightly for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of himself and others.
He is the Bhūripañña (of vast wisdom) because his wisdom is broad and extensive, or because his wisdom is equal to the infinite earth;
the meaning is that his wisdom is like the boundless great earth. He is the Mārajit because he has conquered the fivefold Māra, beginning with the defilements.
3. Among men, the lion is the best. Alternatively, he is a man (*nara*) and he is a lion (*sīha*), thus a "man-lion" (*narasīha*).
He is called a "lion" (*sīha*) because he endures; according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*), the initial vowel *a* of the prefix is replaced by *i*.
Or, because he resembles a lion, he is a man and he is a lion, thus a "man-lion. For just as the lion, the king of beasts, harms and overcomes all creatures with his four fangs, [so too does he].
Likewise, the Blessed One also harms and overcomes the entire world by means of four qualities consisting of virtue, wisdom, merit, and supernormal power;

this is the application of the simile. He is the "best of men" (*naravara*) because he is the most excellent among all persons, or because he is the most excellent among men—that is, among gods and humans—as in the passage from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (1.23):
"A wise man, established in virtue... where the word *nara* is used.
All gods and humans are gathered [under his protection]. He is the Dhamma-King (Dhammarāja) because he causes the Dhamma to proceed as a king;

or, he is born as the king of the world including the gods by means of the Dhamma, not by means of non-Dhamma, thus he is the Dhamma-King; or, he is the Dhamma-King because he rules according to the Dhamma; or, he is the Dhamma-King because he is a king who protects the Dhamma.
He is the Great Sage (Mahāmuni) because of his excellence among sages. He is the God of Gods (Devadeva) because he is the god beyond all other gods. Among the gods...
Or he is the superior deity, the God of Gods. He is the world-honored one, the teacher of the worlds;
or, because he is the object of veneration for the worlds, he is the world-honored one. He is the Lord of Dhamma according to the manner already described.
He is the Tathāgata because, just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones attained omniscience, so too has he attained it; or because his knowledge has gone rightly (tathā) and truly (sammā).
The detailed exposition of the meaning of the word *tathāgata* by means of the passage beginning with "the Tathāgata," etc., is found in various places:
*Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 1.7; *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 1.12; *Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 2.3.78; *Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 1.1.70;
*Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* 18; *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā* 38; *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* 1.3; *Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā* 2, Nidānakathā; and *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*.
14; Paṭisambhidāmagga Aṭṭhakathā 1.1.37; Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.7; Dīghanikāya-abhinava-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.7; Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.12; Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.1.170:
This should be understood according to the method stated therein. 4.
He is "Self-Become" (sayambhū) because he becomes a Fully Enlightened One by himself, without being awakened by another. "Rightly" means by his own self, in an unerring manner.

He is the *Sammāsambuddha* because he awakens, has awakened, and will awaken to all phenomena (*sabbadhamma*). He is possessed of excellent wisdom (*varapañña*) because he is endowed with the highest insight.
He is the *Nāyaka* (Leader) because he leads sentient beings from the ocean of *saṃsāra* to the further shore of *nibbāna*. He is the *Jina* (Victor) because he has conquered the five Māras.
And here [he is called] Samantabhadra, Lokaji, Chaḷabhiñña, Advayavādī, Sirīghana, Akaniṭṭhaga, and Akaniṭṭhaka.
(ka.), the Wheel of Dhamma; the thunderbolt of passion, the enemy of passion (ka.); the Three Refuges; equal to space, equal to the moment (ka.);
he whose virtues are equal to space (from *Tikaṇḍasesa-ṭīkā* 1.1.8); the mine of virtues; great bliss; the diamond; the power of loving-kindness;

the peerless; the conqueror of enemies; great enlightenment; the element of Dhamma; the white banner; the destroyer of space; liberation through the destruction of the three [fetters]; liberation through the destruction of the three.
By means of his own meditative absorption on space—namely, the state of the cultivation of emptiness—he who conquers the state of saṃsāra; [the word *ji* with the suffix *kvip*];
because he has conquered the state of saṃsāra through the cultivation of the mode of perception held by the proponents of emptiness and the Buddhas, namely, "all is indeed empty," he is thus:

the Lord of the Ten Stages (*dasabhūmissara*), possessed of the Five Knowledges (*pañcañāṇa*), the One of Great Renunciation (*bahukkhama*), the Fully Awakened One (*sambuddha*), and the All-Seeing One (*sabbadassī*).
Mahābala, Sabbabodha, Sambodhadhamma, Dhammakāya, Saṅgutta, Arahā, Dvādasakkha, and many others such as Vītarāga—these are names of the Buddha;
these synonyms have been taken mostly from the Amarakosa and the Tikaṇḍasesa Abhidhāna.
[He is so called] because of his complete accumulation of merit and his complete accumulation of knowledge.
Etymological explanations such as "Bhadra" (the Auspicious One) and "Seththa" (the Best One), as well as "Samantabhadra" (the All-Auspicious One), should be understood.
And it is said: "The names of the Great Seer are incalculable according to his qualities;

even from among the thousand names, a name may be designated by way of a specific quality. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā 1313; Udāna-aṭṭhakathā 53; Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā 1.1.76; Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā 38).
In this context, *uddheyya* means that which is to be extracted. *Api nāmasahassato* means by many thousands of names; this is a discourse on the names of all Buddhas.
The group of seven beginning with Sakka is the name of our Buddha. He is called *Sakka* because he is capable (*sakkoti*) of conquering the five Māras;

or alternatively, they are called *Sakkas* because they were capable of breaking the worldly boundaries (*lokamariyāda*) due to their cohabitation with their sisters. [This refers to] the Sākiya kings.
Because he belongs to the lineage of those former kings, the Blessed One is called "Sakka.
Immediately upon his birth, treasures and jewels appeared, and thus he was given the name Siddhattha;
or, because all goals (attha) were accomplished by him as their cause, he is Siddhattha. He whose food (odana) was pure (suddha) was Suddhodana; his descendant is...

Suddhodana. Because the sage Kapila of the Gotama lineage was their teacher, the Śākyas are called Gotamas; however, because the Blessed One was born in the Gotama lineage, he is a descendant of the sage Gotama. 5.
Having descended into the Śākya lineage, having emerged from the Śākya lineage (ka.), the Śākyamuni who is the Buddha is the Lion of the Śākyas.
He is the "Lion of the Sakyans" because of the excellence of the Sakyans. The Sage born from the Sakyan clan is the "Sakyamuni.

Because the son of the deity Suriya was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the Blessed One is called "Kinsman of the Sun" (*Ādiccabandhu*); this is based on the etymology "the kinsman or relative of the Ādicca [clan].
Here too, in the Kali age, there are such things as the *Māyādevīsutta*, the *Mahāsamaṇa*, and the *Kalisāsana*. (Note: *kulisāsanādīni* is a variant reading for *kalisāsanādīni*.)

He whose teaching (*sāsana*) is an instruction (*anusāsana*); or alternatively, he whose teaching is the means for achieving welfare (*hitasādhana*) amidst strife (*kali*), evil, or dispute—these are to be understood as the synonyms for Gotama (*Tikaṇḍasesa-ṭīkā* 1.1.11). 6.
The forty-six names beginning with "liberation" (*mokkha*) and ending with "extinction" (*nibbuti*) are the names of *nibbāna*. They are liberated...
In this context, it is "liberation" (mokkha) because one is released from passion and the other defilements by means of it. It is "cessation" (nirodha) because passion and the rest cease therein;

or else, it is "obstruction" (rodha) because it obstructs the defilement known as craving (vāna), and since that [defilement] is absent therein, it is "cessation. It is "Nirvana" (nibbāna) because it has emerged from craving, which is termed "desire" (vāna);
or else, it is "Nirvana" because the fire of passion and the rest is extinguished by means of it. Just as a natural lamp [is to those being carried away] by the current of a river...
It is a "resting place" (*dīpa*); likewise, this *nibbāna* is a "resting place" because it serves as a support for those being swept away by the great flood of *saṃsāra*, just like an island.
Or, it is a "resting place" because it acts like a lamp for those free from defilements; for it is said: "The wise go out like this lamp.
Or else, it is a "resting place" because it shines forth, being made manifest solely to the noble ones' eye of knowledge.

It is an island (*dīpo*). It is the destruction of craving (*taṇhakkhayo*) because it is the cause for the exhaustion of cravings. It is supreme (*paraṃ*) because it is the antidote to lust and the other defilements, or in the sense of being unsurpassed.
It is a refuge (*tāṇaṃ*) because it protects and guards one from the states of woe and so forth. It is a shelter (*leṇaṃ*) because those who fear the terrors of *saṃsāra* take shelter therein.

It is formless (*arūpaṃ*) because it has no shape such as long or short; or it is formless because it is devoid of conditioned phenomena (*paccaya*). [It is free] from lust and the other defilements...

It is "peaceful" (*santa*) because it makes [the mind] peaceful. It is "truth" (*sacca*) because it is non-erroneous by virtue of being the cause for the destruction of lust, or because it is included within the Four Noble Truths.
It is "without attachment" (*anālaya*) because there is no attachment—that is, craving—therein.
It is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) because it is not mixed with conditions. It is "auspicious" (*siva*) because it brings about a state of security; [it is so called] by those who fear *saṃsāra*.
It is "auspicious" (*siva*) because it is to be cultivated; the suffix *-vap* is used here with the prefix *adi*.

It is "deathless" (*amata*) because there is no death (*mata*)—that is, no dying—in this, or because death has ceased for the person who has attained it. It is "very difficult to see" (*sududdasa*) because of its extreme difficulty to perceive.

It is the "supreme goal" (*parāyaṇa*) because it is to be gone to, to be reached, by others—the supreme noble persons (*ariyapuggala*); or alternatively, it is the supreme goal because it is to be gone to from beyond.

The meaning is that it is to be understood as having a nature other than the nature of *saṃsāra*. Alternatively, it is the "refuge" (*parāyaṇa*) because it is the place where other noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) are established.
That Dhamma by which the four paths specifically remember (*saranti*) and destroy (*hiṃsanti*) the defilements is the "refuge" (*saraṇa*);
or it is the "refuge" because it is the dwelling-place of the noble ones. Where there is no calamity (*īti*), affliction (*upaddava*), or wandering away (*pavāsa*), [that is the refuge].

It is "without calamity" (*anītika*) because it lacks craving—which has acquired the name "calamity" (*nīti*) because it leads beings through the cycle of existence—or because it is free from that craving.

It is "taintless" (*anāsava*) because the taints (*āsava*) have no object within it. It is "steadfast" (*dhuvam*) in the sense of being permanent; or it is "steadfast" because it moves toward, or becomes the object of, the paths.
For the root *dhu* is listed in the Kaccāyana grammar as meaning "to go" or "to move. It is so called because of the non-existence of any intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) to be perceived.
It is "non-indicative" (anidassana). It is "unmade" (akata) because it is not produced by conditions. Because it exists at all times, it goes toward a nature that does not decay;
or, it is known by that [nature], thus it is "clearly seen" (apalokita). For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "When it has gone thus, it is known.
Or, it is "looked upon" (lokita) because it is known by way of its worldly nature; it is "clearly seen" (apalokita) because of the departure from that state. In the sense of being subtle...
It is *nipuṇa* (subtle), because by means of it the four paths thoroughly (*odhiso*) cleanse and purify defilements without remainder;
that is *nipuṇa*. That which never has destruction within it is *ananta* (infinite). They are called *khara* because they perish (*vinassanti*); they are the conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
That in which these do not exist is *akkhara* (the imperishable). Alternatively, it is *akkhara* because it is the opposite of the conditioned things termed *khara*.
And here, the verses beginning with "asaṅkhataṃ" (the unconditioned) are called "Rucirā" (The Beautiful). 8.
It is the "destruction of suffering" (dukkhakkhayo) because it is the cause for the exhaustion of all suffering. That which afflicts is "affliction" (byābādho);

that very thing is "affliction" (byābādo), namely the truth of suffering (dukkhasaccaṃ). The state of that is "afflictedness" (byābajjaṃ), meaning the state of being oppressed by suffering; where that does not exist—
"Unafflicted" (*abyābajjha*); there is also the reading *abyāpajjha*. In this context, "afflictions" (*byāpādā*) are conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*) because they afflict—that is, they perish.

Their state is "affliction-ness" (*byāpajjha*), which is the state of perishing of conditioned phenomena. That in which this does not exist is "unafflicted" (*abyāpajjha*). This is how the meaning should be understood;
furthermore, according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*), the letter *dy* becomes *jjh*. [It is so called] because of the absence of the rounds of defilements, kamma, and kamma-results.
It is the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*). It is secure (*khema*) in the sense of being fearless, or it is secure because by means of it the fires of passion and so forth are exhausted (*khaya*).

It is absolute (*kevala*) due to its unmixed nature with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and its state of dissociation. It is the "departure" (*apavagga*) because conditioned phenomena depart from it.

It is "dispassion" (*virāga*) because passion has departed from it. It is sublime (*paṇīta*) because it has been brought to a state of preeminence. When this is attained, there is nothing [further] remaining.
It is *accuta* because it has passed away from the passing away (*cuta*) of the noble ones (*ariya*). It is a *pada* because it is to be attained and reached by the noble ones.
It is *yogakkhema* because by means of this, the four bonds (*yoga*) are destroyed (*khaya*).

It is *pāra* because one is able to fulfill and pacify the torment of the suffering of *saṃsāra*; for it is said: "It is sufficient for the one scorched by the torment of the suffering of *saṃsāra* to be pacified. It is *pagata*.
Or, it is "the further shore" (pāra) because the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have reached their end there. It is "liberation" (mutti) because of being freed from the defilements;

however, those of other schools say it is "liberation" because of being freed from the self [conceived] through the body and the faculties. It is "peace" (santi) because of the calming of the defilements.

It is "purification" (visuddhi) because beings are purified by it from the stains of lust and so forth. It is "deliverance" (vimutti) because of the deliverance from all conditioned phenomena. It is the unconditioned alone.
It is the "unconditioned element" (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) because it is devoid of a being and a soul, or because it maintains the characteristic of peace.

It is "purity" (*suddhi*) because beings are purified by means of it from the stains of lust and so forth. It is called "extinction" (*nibbāna*) because it is a "weaving out" (*āvuṇoti*)—in the sense of not providing [fuel] for emergence from the cycle of existence—which is craving;
and because one has emerged from that, it is extinction.
10. The Tetrad on those with Taints Destroyed and so forth refers to the Arahants. One whose taints (āsava) have been destroyed is "one with taints destroyed" (khīṇāsava).

Because there is nothing further to be done beyond that, one for whom there is no more training is "one beyond training" (asekha). One from whom lust (rāga) has departed is "one free from lust" (vītarāga).
One who is worthy of the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra being struck [down] is an "Arahant" (arahā); the reading "arahaṃ" is also found.
The "fivefold beginning with the world of the gods" (devalokādipañcaka) is a name for heaven (*sagga*). The world or abode of the gods is the "world of the gods" (*devaloka*).

They sport (*dibbanti*) here, thus it is *divo*. [From the root] *aja* in the sense of going; because it has multiple meanings, it is used in the sense of standing. It is called *agga* because they stand there for a long time; it is a place. A beautiful *agga* is *sagga*;
or, it is well-attained (*suṭṭhu ajīyati*) by means of merit, thus it is *sagga*. The three gods sport here, thus it is *tidiva*. Primarily...
Indeed, it is designated by the three names Hari, Hara, and Brahmā. It is called *tidasālaya* because it is the abode (*ālaya*) or place (*ṭhāna*) of the *tidasā* gods.
However, some say that "the triad beginning with Devaloka is the name for heaven in general, while the pair beginning with Tidiva refers specifically to the Tāvatiṃsa realm";
this should not be accepted as authoritative, since in works such as the *Amarakośa*, both terms are included under the general category.
Here too, the well-performed ones enter into the *nāka*, the *suraloka*, and the *piṭṭhapa*; thus it is called *piṭṭhapa* according to the *pisodarādi* rule.
It is the abode of the *tidasas* (the thirty-three gods); the word *dasa* is elided [according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*].

It is the *avaroha*, the *phalodaya*—the arising (*udaya*) of the fruit, namely the fruit of karma, which is a place worthy of being seen (according to the *Tikaṇḍa-ṭīkā*)—*mandara*, *serika*, and *sakkabhavana*.
"Space," "sky," and so forth—terms common to the divine realms (*devaloka*)—should also be understood here as included. 11–12.
The group of fourteen beginning with "Tidasa" is a collective name for the deities. Regarding the phrase *jātīsu jātijātīsu* (in the lineages, in the lineages of lineages):

since it is said that "a wise person (*byatti*) is also called [a lineage]," and because there is a plurality of such wise persons, this is expressed in the plural number. There are three [categories] consisting of birth-beings and destruction.
They have ten as their measure; thus they are the *Tidasas*. For these beings do not undergo changes of intellect, decay, or death like humans and others;
rather, they arise, exist, and perish at exactly twenty-five years of age. Death is *mara*; those who have no such death are *amaras*.
They play (*dibbanti*), meaning they sport with the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth; thus they are *devas*. They awaken (*vibujjhanti*).
They are called *vibudha* because they do not sleep, or because they awaken to past and future births. They are *sudhāsina* because of their habit of consuming the food of nectar (*sudhā*).
They are *surā* because they possess liquor produced from the ocean during the churning for the nectar (*amṛta-mathanodtha*;

according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*), or because they sport (*suranti*), or because they delight in happiness (*sukhena ramanti*). Although they are long-lived, [they live] according to their fixed limit.
They are *marū* because they die by means of their virtue (*sīla*) at the time of their attainment. They are *divokā* because heaven, the world of the gods, is their home and dwelling place.

They are *amatapā* because they drink the deathless (*amata*), as it is possible for them to consume even ambrosial food; or alternatively, they are *amatapā* because they drink the medicine of immortality (*amatosadha*).
They are *saggavāsino* because of their habit of dwelling in heaven. They are [called] those for whom old age has been cast off, because they always appear as if twenty-five years of age.
*Nijjarā* (wearing away). *Animisā*: they do not blink, thus they are "unblinking"; the meaning is that they keep their eyebrows motionless.

*Dibbā*: they dwell in heaven, thus they are "divine. *Devatā*: gods themselves are *devatā*; the suffix *-tā* is added to the word *deva* in its own sense (*sakatthe*). *Devatāni*: gods themselves are *devatāni*; the suffix *-i* is added in its own sense (*sakatthe*).

In the phrase "apume," the feminine gender is used according to the first instance of the same-sense suffix (*sakatthika*), while [the neuter] is according to the second instance of the same-sense suffix.
The neuter gender is to be understood; or, according to the second view—that it possesses its own inherent meaning—it may have two genders.

In that regard, on the side of the feminine gender, there is the substitution of *nikāra* for [the suffix] beginning with *ya*. However, in the *Amarakośa*, it is stated at 1.9: *“devatāni pume vā”* (the word *devatāni* is masculine or [neuter]). Its meaning is:
the word *devatāni* is optionally masculine, while it is invariably neuter. And in the commentary (*ṭīkā*), it says: *“Sakatthikā pakatito”*... [and so forth].

"Gender and number are transcended" means "masculinity and neuter-ness. *Devo* itself is *devatā*; here, the suffix *tā* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). Even suffixes used in the sense of identity transcend the gender, number, and so forth of the base word.
Regarding the word *api*, it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*: "Femininity [is also transcended]; *devatā* itself is *devataṃ* because of the suffix *aṇ* [which denotes identity].
In this context, the term *sakatthikā* refers to the second type of suffix used in the sense of identity.
“By nature” (*pakati-to*) refers to the first *sakatthika* suffix. Therefore, it is stated as “masculine and neuter gender” (*puṃnapuṃsakattaṃ*);
otherwise, since a word ending in the *tāpaccaya* suffix would always have a feminine gender, one would have had to say only “feminine gender.

[Examples include: *supabbā*, *sumanā*, *tidivesā*, *āditeyyā*, *divisadā*, *lekhā*, *aditinandanā*, *ādiccā*, *ribhavā*, *vibhavā* (variant reading), and *rikāro* may be the mother of the gods (*devamātā*).
Thus, in the *Tikaṇḍa*, it says: "Then they become" (*tato bhavanti*); [in the] *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*: "They are not subject to death (*asoppā*); 'death' (*maccu*) is the act of dying (*mati*);
those who exist in death are 'the dead' (*maccā*); not dead are 'the immortal' (*amaccā*)" (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*). Also [terms such as]:

"seated in the immortal" (*amatāsana*), "those whose mouth is fire" (*aggimukha*), "those who eat the sacrificial oblation" (*havibhojana*), "those with long life" (*girabbāṇa*), "givers of gifts" (*dānavārayo*), "those who are radiant" (*bindāraka*), "those worthy of worship" (*pūjiya*), "those of long life" (*cirāyuka*), "those destined for heaven" (*saggina*), "those who feed on the sky" (*nabhosada*), "the sun" (*āditya*), and so forth.

These are merely the common names for deities. 13. These—Siddhas and the rest—are classes of deities, origins of deities, and lineages of deities, because in their arising, the deities alone are the primary cause.
Because they are endowed with qualities such as *aṇiman* (minuteness) and so forth, and because "the desired objects are accomplished (*sijjhanti*) by means of this," one is a *siddha*. Of whom...
A *bhūta* is that which expands its discourse through speech; it is classified as a *pisāca* and includes those such as the *adhomukha*. As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*):
it is called a *bhūta* because they expand (*brūhanti*) their discourse within it. A *gandhabba* is one who inhales (*abbati*) and partakes of fragrance (*gandha*);
these include the celestial singers such as Hāhā and Hūhū. A *guhyaka* is one who hides (*guyhati*); the suffix *-ka* is used here to form a noun, referring to those such as Maṇibhadra.
A follower of Kuvera. Regarding "yakkha": it is called a *yakkha* because he is worshipped (*pūjīyate*) in the worship of the *yakkhas*;

[this refers to] Kuvera and others. A *rakkhasa* is so called because they protect themselves (*rakkhanti attānaṃ*) from it; [this refers to] Vibhīṣaṇa and others. A *kumbhaṇḍa* is so called because of his testicles being the size of jars (*kumbha*).

A *pisāca* is so called because he eats (*asati*) or devours flesh (*pisitaṃ maṃsaṃ*); [this refers to] Sakuni, Sakunti, and others who are followers of Kuvera. By means of the *yadādi* suffixes, there is the substitution of *pi* for *pisi*.

The state of being a *sācāda* (a type of celestial musician) for an *asura* is established by Pāṇini 6.3.109 and Moggallāna-pañcikā 1.47. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), it includes the *vidyādhara*, the *apasara*, and the *kinnara*.
One who possesses (*dharati*) knowledge (*vijjā*)—such as spells for pills, ointments, and mantras—is a *vidyādhara*.

They drive away (*apasārenti*) and crush (*khalayanti*) [enemies], thus they are *apasaras*; these are the celestial courtesans (*suravesī*) such as Ubbasī, according to Amara 1.55. This is the meaning of the term *apasara*.
The plurality belongs either to the genus (*jāti*) itself, or to the individual (*vyakti*) itself, or likewise to the plurality [of parts] within that [individual].

The word "forest" (*vana*), for instance, is sometimes employed with reference to the genus and sometimes with reference to the individual. In that case, when it refers to the genus, it functions by taking on the number belonging to the individuals.
When it is employed with reference to the individual, [it takes the number of] the parts of that individual, such as the hands, feet, and so forth.

It functions by taking a plural number. However, because the word *vana* denotes a substance qualified by a genus and a singular number—either by denoting the genus residing in individual entities such as *dhava* trees, or because it is a genus-word—it is in the singular. According to the opinion of Vāmana and others, the word *apasara* is used in the feminine plural;

according to the opinion of others, however, it should be seen as occurring in both genders (masculine and feminine) and in both numbers (singular and plural). This is because [the *vanaspati*] possesses a body that is neither horse-faced nor human.
A "kinnara" is one who is contemptible, or simply a man, or one who resembles a man because of his human-like form. These are classes of deities.

As for the group-deities (*gaṇadevatā*), they are as follows: “The Ādiccas, the Visus, the Vasus, the Tusitas, the Ābhassaras, the Anilas, the Mahārājikas, the Sādhyas, and the Rudras—these are the group-deities. (Amara 1.10)
It is stated in the *Amarakośa*:
"In that [realm], there are twelve Ādityas, ten Viśvedevas established,
the Vasus are numbered as eight, and thirty-six Tusitas are recognized."
The Ābhassara deities number sixty-four;
the Vāta deities are forty-nine; those named Mahārājika are two hundred and twenty.
The Sādhyas are renowned as twelve, and the Rudras are established as eleven.
These Gaṇadevatās are to be understood from their respective contexts. 14.
Regarding the fourfold group beginning with the *pubbadevā* (former gods) among the asuras: *pubbadevā* means "the gods who were formerly [there]";

this is a *dutiya-samāsa* (second-case compound). Alternatively, *pubbadevā* means "the gods of former times," for these were previously situated in the city of the gods (*devapura*), and subsequently they were displaced from there by Sakka and others. They are the enemies of the *surā* (gods).
The beings are the enemies of the *suras*. They are called *asuras* because they are the adversaries of the *suras*, or because, unlike the *devas*, they do not rejoice (*suranti*) or play;
or because the liquor (*surā*) arising from the ocean was accepted by the *devas* but not by these, and thus they are called *asuras* because they have no *surā*—so say those of other schools.
They are the *dānavas* because they are the offspring of the mother named Danu. Danu is one of the thirteen daughters of the *rakkhasas*.
The name of one daughter. These terms—*pubbadeva* and so forth—always function in the masculine gender (*puma*, *pulliṅga*).

*Deccā*, *deteyyā*, *danujā*, *indārī*, *suradisā*, *sukkasissā*, *ditisutā*, *pubbajā*, and so on, are also general names for an *asura*. The specific types of *asuras* are its particular designations.
For the purpose of battle with the *suras*, [he gave] the striking of his own military forces and weapons.
He gives (*dadāti*) [booty], thus he is *pahārado*; he is *pahārādo* for that very reason. He whose excellent (*saṃ*) and praiseworthy (*pasattha*) son-in-law (*varo*) is *jāmātā* is *sambaro*.

For his son-in-law is Sakka (as stated in *Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 1.1.256). Alternatively, he is *sambaro* because he protects (*saṃvuṇoti*) the faculties (*indriyāni*) among those who carry merit (*puññāharīsu*).
He possesses strength (*bala*), thus he is *balī*; or he is *balī* because of his preeminent body of strength; he is *bali* for that very reason, according to the rule "bali-ādayo."

This indicates that there is no *sandhi* (euphonic combination) even in a compound. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes fish, birds, and so forth, as well as the *kuñca* group and various types of *asuras*.

15. The eight [terms] beginning with *pitāmaha* [are used] in the sense of Brahmā. The father (*pitā*) of the *pajāpati*s (lords of progeny), who are themselves the fathers of the world, is the grandfather (*pitāmaha*).
The suffix *-āma* is prescribed by Moggallāna 4.38. He is called "father" because he occupies the position of a father to all worlds, or because he protects (*pāti*) the entire world.
He protects, thus he is a father (*pitā*); the suffix *ita* is applied. Because of his vast body, he is Brahmā; from the root *braha* meaning "growth," the suffix *mapaccaya* is added.

He is the lord (*īsa*) of the worlds, thus the Lord of the World (*lokesa*). Because he arose from a lotus, he is a lotus (*kamala*), which is a *padma*. That lotus is his seat (*āsana*) or place of origin;
thus he is the Lotus-Seated One (*kamalāsana*). Gold is a golden egg (*hirañña-aṇḍa*); its interior (*gabbha*), its embryo (*bhūṇa*), its quality (*guṇa*), is the Golden-Womb One (*hiraññagabbha*).
He is the "Elder of the Gods" (*surajeṭṭha*) because he is the eldest among the gods due to his qualities such as the *jhānas*.
He is the "Lord of Creatures" (*pajāpati*) because he is the master and lord of creatures (*pajā*, i.e., sentient beings), or because he protects the creatures.
Other names for Brahmā include: Attabhū, Parameṭṭhi, Sayambhū, Caturānana, Dhātā, Kamalayoni, Duhiṇa, Viriñci, Sajitā, Vedhā, Vidhātā, Vidhi, Haṃsaratha, Viriñca, and Papitāmaha.

16–17. The pentad beginning with Vāsudeva [is explained] in reference to Kaṇha. He is Vāsudeva because he is the offspring (apacca) of Vasudeva. He is Hari because he seizes (harati) the life of mortals by his nature.
He is Kaṇha because of his association with the qualities of Kaṇha. He is Kesava because he has slain the asura named Kesi;
here the vowel *i* becomes *a*, and the root *han* becomes *va*. And it is said:
“Since Kesī was slain by you,
therefore listen to my instruction;
he was known by the name Kesava.”
“You will become superior in the world”—thus it is also stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.
He who has a discus (*cakra*) in his hand is *Cakrapāṇi*. [He is] *Viṣṇu*, *Piṇhu* (variant:
*Ka.*), *Nārāyaṇa*, *Vekuṇṭha*, *Dāmodara*, *Mādhava*, *Sambhu*, *Devāri*, *Puṇḍarīkākṣa*, *Govinda*, *Garuḷaddhaja*, *Pītambara*, and *Accuta*.
Maṅgala, Siṅgī, Janārdana, Upendra, Indāvaraja, Catubhuja, Padmanābha, Madhuripu, Tivikkama,
Devakīnandana, Śauri, Śrīpati, Purisottama, Vanamālī, Balidhaṃsī, Kaṃsārāti, Adhokkhaja, Sabbambhara,
Keṭabhaji (the conqueror of Keṭabha; *Cintāmaṇiṭīkā*), Vidhu, Sasabindu.
Śrīkara, Śrīvarāha, Ajita, Parapuruṣa, Śrīgaṛbha, Ṣaḍbindu, Ananta, Naraka-jit,
Keśara, Jāti-kīla, Nara-siṃha, Purāṇa-puruṣa, Nalini-śaya, Vāsudeva, Narāyaṇa,
Punarvasu, Sarva-rūpa, Dharaṇīdhara, Vāmana, Eka-śṛṅga, Soma-garbha, Ādi-deva, Ādi-varāha, Suvarṇa-bindu.
Sadāyogī, Sanātana, Rāhumuddhabhida, Kālanemi, Paṇḍava, Vaḍḍhamāna, Satānanda, Pajānātha, Suyāmunu, and so forth, are the names of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, the names of his father are Vasudeva, Ānakadundubhi, Amara, and so forth.
His charioteer was named Dāruka (according to Tikaṇḍasesa 1.1.34). His counselor, however, was Pavanavyādhi.
The wise ones say: "Pavanabyāmi Uddhava" (*Tikaṇḍasesa* 1.1.35); both Pavanabyādhi and Uddhava are names for the minister of Piṇhu (*Kaṭṭhīkā*).
Regarding the group of six beginning with *Mahissara*: *Hare*.
One who possesses great lordship and majesty (*vibhūti*) is a *mahissara*. [He is] devoid of the state of possessing qualities (*guṇavatthāra*).

He is *siva* because he is now, by virtue of having the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), free from agitation and becomes tranquil; according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*), the vowel *a* becomes *i*, and the consonant *m* becomes *v*.
Thus, in all cases, the derivation of words should be understood either through the use of pronouns such as "that" (*yadādi*) or by means of etymological analysis.

He is *sūlī* because he possesses a spear (*sūla*) in his hand. He is *issara* because he originates in what is desirable (*iṭṭha*); or alternatively, he is *issara* because he rules (*issati*) or overcomes (*abhibhavati*). Of animals...
He is the Lord of creatures (*paśupati*). According to Rudda and Rabhasa: "The word *pasu* refers to deer and goats;
it also denotes a creature (*pamu*) and a male. [Note: *guṇe* and *ka.* are glosses. Because he possesses the most excellent quality of darkness (*tamas*), he takes away everything;
thus he is Hara. *Vutta* is a verb. Sambhu, Īsa, Sabba, Īsāna, Saṅkara, Candasekhara, Bhūteśa, Khaṇḍaparasu, Girīsa.
Maccuñjaya, Pinākin, Pamathādhipa, Uggā, Kapardin, Sirīkaṇṭha, Kāḷakaṇṭha, Kapālabhara,
Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Virūpakkha, Tilocana, Sabbaññū, Nīlalohita, Māra-hara, Bhagga, Tyambaka,
Tipurāntaka, Gaṅgādhara, Andhakari-pu, Byomakesa, Bhava, Bhīma, Rudra, Umāpati.
Bhagālī, Kapisañjana, Hīra, Pañcānana, Khakuntala, Gopālaka, Piṅgakkho Vibhaṅga, Kūṭakara, Candāpīḷa,
Mahānaṭa, Samīra, Ho, Nandivaḍḍhana, Guḷākeso Migūha, Mihirāṇa, Meghavāhana, Suppatāpa Suppasāda, U, Thāṇu Upāṇḍa, Sipiviṭṭha.
*Kīlo*, *dhammavāhana*, and so forth are also names of Hari.
The triad beginning with *kumāra* refers to the sons of Hari. *Kumāra* is used in the sense of playing; one who plays is a *kumāra*.
He is sixteen years old, and this [deity] is also sixteen years old. For it is said: "The fool shall be sixteen. He destroys the power of the demons (*dānava*).
*Khanda*, *ṇḍassa*, *ndo*. One who bears a particular weapon called a spear is a *sattidhara*;
or, one who bears the threefold power (*sattitta*) consisting of majesty, energy, and incantations is a *sattidhara*. In the *Amarakosa*, however, it says:
"Kattikeyya, Mahāsena..."
Sarajāta, Chaḷānana,
Pabbatīnandana, Khanda, Senānī, Aggibhū, and Guha.
Bāhuleyya, Tārakaji,
Visākho, Sikhivāhana,
Chamāturo, and Sattidhara.
“The youth who rends the mountain peak”—thus it is said in the *Amarakosa* (1.41–2).

18–21. The twenty names beginning with Sakka are the names of Sakka. He is called Sakka because he is able (*sakkuṇāti*) to conquer the asuras. He is called Purindada because he gives (*dadāti*) a city (*pura*) or is the giver of cities.

He is called Devarāja because he is the king of the gods. He is called Vajirapāṇi because the thunderbolt (*vajira*) is in his hand (*pāṇi*). [He is called] Sujā... because of his beautiful birth (*sujā*).
He is the husband of the Asura maiden, Sujampati. He is Sahassakkha (the Thousand-Eyed) because of his capacity to see the intended purpose of many gods and humans.
He is Mahinda, the lord and king of the great gods; or Mahinda is the lord and king who is to be honored by the gods (*mahitabbo*);

or he is Mahinda because he is both great and a lord (*mahā ca so indo ca*). He is Vajirāvudha (the One Whose Weapon is the Thunderbolt), for whose weapon is the thunderbolt (*vajiram āvudham yassa*); he is also called *Vajirāyudha*.
*Pāṭha*: He who possesses the treasures (*vasu*) and jewels (*ratana*) is *Vāsava*. He who has a thousand eyes is *Dasasatanayana*.
Because he is the sovereign over two divine worlds, he is *Tidivādhibhū*. The lord of the *suras* is *Suranātha*. He who holds a thunderbolt (*vajira*) in his hand is *Vajirahattha*.
The master of beings (*bhūta*, i.e., sentient beings) is *Bhūtapati*. Because he is worthy of honor, he is *Maghavā*.
In the Great Worship (Mahāpūjā), O Laughing Hero (Hassaghava): one who possesses wealth designated as "treasure" (kosa) is a Kosiya;

they also say he is a Kosiya "by virtue of belonging to the Kosiya clan. He rules (indati) through supreme sovereignty, thus he is Indra. He overcomes the asura named Vatra, thus he is Vatrabhū. Pāka was the name of the asura Vatra’s brother;
because of his instruction (sāsana) or subduing (niggaha), he is Pākasāsana. Viḍaṃ...
Its pervasive vitality is its "fecund vigor" (*viḍ-oja*). [He is] Sunāsīra, Purandara, the Bull of the *lekhās* (the gods), the highest among the gods, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*),
the Lord of Heaven, the Lord of the Suras, the Enemy of Bala, the Lord of Sacī, the Crusher of Jambha, the One with Bay Horses,
the Destroyer of Namuci, the Shatterer, the One who rides upon the clouds, Ākhaṇḍala— he is so called because he shatters the enemy forces through his brilliance.
*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*, *Kosika*, *Suragāmaṇī*, *Nākanātha*, *Harī*, and so forth, are also names of Sakka. His wife, Sakka’s consort, was named Sujātā;
she is called Sujātā because she was born with ease (*sukhena jātā*) or because her birth was beautiful (*sundarā jāti*). *Pulomajā*, *Sacī*, *Indānī*, and so forth, are also names of Sakka’s wife.
Sakka had three cities: Masakkasāra and the others. *Masakkā* refers to both Maya and Sakka; they remember [these cities].

Regarding *Masakkasāra*: it is said in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* that they go there for the sake of sport, and thus it is the place where the retinues of Mahissara and others, as well as Sakka, experience their play;
hence the meaning. However, in the *Saṅgaha-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Either *Masakka* or *Vasoka* is the name of the city of the Asuras;
but because this [city] is their most excellent [abode], it is called *Masakkasāra* and *Vasokasāra*. [The term] *Amarā*...
Its city is Amaravatī; that itself is Amarāvatī, [the lengthening of the short vowel] being according to Pāṇini 6.3.119.
That Sakka’s palace is named Vejayanta. It is called Vejayanta because the banner (paṭākā) called Vijayanti is praised, or because victory (vijaya) exists therein.
That Sakka’s assembly hall is considered Sudhammā. It is called Sudhammā because its dhamma is beautiful; it is a pavilion for the gods.
22. That Sakka’s chariot is named Vejayanta. It is called Vejayanta because it is joined with a banner named Vejayantī.
That Sakka’s charioteer and driver is named Mātali. He is called Mātali because he is the offspring (*apacca*) of Mātala.
That Sakka’s elephant is named Erāvaṇa; Irāvaṇa is the ocean, and because he was born there in the Irāvati ocean, he is Erāvaṇa.
*Jāto* [refers to] Erāvata; for the remainder, *aṇa...* [is used]. According to the *Piṅgala-sūtra*, in the sense of "belonging to Erāvaṇa," it becomes *Erāvaṇo* (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).

His stone throne of Sakka is named Paṇḍukambala. It is called Paṇḍukambala because it resembles a white-colored blanket (*paṇḍu-vaṇṇa-kambala*). A stone is simply a rock (*pāsāṇa*), and that which is a seat is a "stone-throne" (*silāsana*).
23. That Sakka’s sons were Suvīra, Jayanta, and so forth. He is called Suvīra because he is exceedingly heroic (*sūra*).
He is called Jayanta because he conquers the asuras. That Sakka would have a lotus pond named Nandā. It is called Nandā because it causes delight (*nandīyati*).
"Pokkhara" refers to both the lotus and water; it is called a "lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*) because it leads (*nayati*) the minds and selves of sentient beings toward those [lotuses and waters].
It is called a *pokkharaṇī* because it is provided with beautiful, clear water; that very thing is a *pokkharaṇī*.
That Sakka has four groves and parks, such as Nandana and others. It is called *Nandana* because it gladdens (*nandati*).
It is called *Missaka* because it is interspersed with various celestial trees. It is called *Cittalatā* because it is variegated by various creepers and vines, being diverse in color and hue.

Or, because it is endowed with a creeper (*latā*) of the mind, it is a "mind-creeper" (*cittalatā*). Alternatively, it is "mindful" (*cittā*) because the longings (*āsā*) of the deities exist therein;

there is a creeper named *āsāvatī*, and that which possesses this is a "mind-creeper. Or, they "take" (*lanti*) the minds of the deities, thus they are "mind-takers" (*cittalā*), namely the celestial trees;
the collection of these is a "mind-creeper" (*cittalatā*). This is the name of that forest in the feminine gender, just as [the name] "Khuddasikkhā" [is used].
Phārusaka is that place where *phārusaka* trees exist. 24.
The three types of *asani* are the weapon of that Sakka. It is called *asani* because by means of this weapon, the world-system is struck (*assate*) and consumed (*bhujjate*).
This word *asani* occurs in two genders, masculine and feminine. It rests in the hand of Sakka in the *kuli* [palace].
It is called *kuliśa* because it "stands" (*tiṭṭhati*). For the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.6.26) states: "The word *kuli* means 'hand' or 'arm'.
Alternatively, it is *kuliśa* because it "becomes thin" (*lisati*) upon the earth (*kuyaṃ*, i.e., the ground). Regarding *vajira*:

from the root *vaj* in the sense of "going," it is *vajira* because its movement "goes forth" (*vajateva*) and is not struck back by anything; the suffix *-ira* is applied. Because it is associated with *vajira*, the word *kuliśa* is also used in the masculine and neuter genders.
*Bhidura*, *pavi*, *satakoṭi*, *suru*, *sambo*, *dambholi*, and so forth, are also names for the thunderbolt (*vajira*).
Among these, *bhidura* is both masculine and neuter, while *pavi* and the others are masculine.
*Rambhā*, *Alambusā*, and so forth, are called the celestial nymphs (*accharā*) among the female deities. For they are indeed a specific class of *accharās*.
*Etā*. They are called *accharāyo* because they possess (*atthi*) a clear, stainless complexion (*accha-nimmala-vaṇṇa*). "Apasarā" is also a common designation for them.

They are called *rambhā* because they produce and increase the delight (*rati*) of the sons of the gods; or alternatively, they are called *rambhā* because they cause the fire of desire (*raṃ kāmaggiṃ*) to shine, blaze, and burn—here, the nasalization (*niggahīta*) is elided.
By means of their delight in sensual pleasures, they are capable (*alaṃ*) and able to make the sons of the gods dwell within themselves.
*Alambusā*, *Assukārā*. Female deities who have become goddesses among the gods and sons of gods are "female deities" (*devitthiyo*).
Those such as Pañcasikha, Hāhā, Hūhū, and others are called "gandhabbas. He who has five crests or tufts of hair is Pañcasikha.
One who abandons the joyful sound of the lute known as Nindibhaddhanī is Hāhā. One who [utters] the specific sound of song "Hū" is Hūhū.

They are called *hūhū* because they are summoned (*hūyate*). They are called *gandhabba* because they smell (*abbanti*) or consume (*bhuñjanti*) fragrance (*gandha*); or else, singing (*gāyana*) is their nature (*dhamma*), thus they are *gandhabba*, with the suffix *-bb-*.

25. Regarding the two terms beginning with *vimāna*: they belong to the section on celestial mansions (*vimāna*). That by which the gods travel through the sky is a *vimāna*; it is a *vimāna* because its measure (*māna*) has departed (*vigata*) or is absent (*vinā*).
It is called *byamha* because it moves in the sky (*vihe*); the suffix *-am-* is applied before the letter *h*.
And here, both the words *vimāna* and *vyamha* function as non-feminine, that is, masculine or neuter.
The triad beginning with *pīyusa* refers to the deathless (*amata*). It is called *pīyusa* because it is drunk (*pīyate*); for it is said, "the drinkers of the deathless" (*amatapā*).
The suffix *-usa* appears in the *Uṇādi* 4.76 and *Ṇvādi* 215 rules as *pīyūsa*. Its name is also *peyusa*. It is so called because by means of it, death (*mata*)—that is, dying—is not [experienced].
It is the deathless (*amata*). It is called *sudhā* (ambrosia) because they suckle and drink it with ease.

Furthermore, in this context, the term *amata* applies to three genders: it is neuter when referring to sacrificial remains, nectar, water, jars, and so forth; masculine when referring to the deity Dhanvantari and others; and feminine when referring to the *gaḷoñhā*, *abhaya*, *malakya*, and so forth. Thus:
"The deathless" refers to sacrificial remains, nectar, water, jars, that which is unasked for, and liberation; as a masculine noun, it refers to the deity Dhanvantari and others.

According to the *Medinīkośa* (16.77–8), the words *amatā*, *māgadhī*, *pathyā*, *guḍūcī*, and *āmalakī* are feminine; however, because it is used as a companion term (*tamsahacaraṇato*), the word *pīyusa* also occurs in all three genders.
Furthermore, the word *sudhā*—referring to nectar, plaster, and so forth—is always feminine, as in the *Amarakośa* (23.101): "Plaster is *sudhā*;
[it is] nectar, *nuhī*..."

The group of five beginning with Sineru refers to the kings of mountains. *Sineru*: from the root *si*, meaning "to purify" (*soceyye*), it is called *sineru* because it purifies, causes others to purify, and shines;
the suffix is *-eru*. From the root *mī*, meaning "to harm" (*hiṃsāyaṃ*), it is called *meru* because it harms all other mountains by virtue of its own superior height;
the suffix is *-ru*. *Tidivādhāra*: it is the support and foundation for the three heavens, namely the two celestial worlds. *Neru*: it leads (*nayati*) the gods.
The name *Sumeru* has its designation expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). *Hemaddi*, *Ratana-sānu*, *Surālaya*, and others are also names for the king of mountains.
26. *Yugandhara* and the others are the names of the seven circular mountain ranges (*paribhaṇḍapabbata*) that surround Sineru.
It is called *Yugandhara* because it supports the pair (*yuga*) consisting of the moon and sun, traveling upon its summit at their height. *Īsa* means a great lord.
It is called *īsadhara* because it is the dwelling place of the *īsa*. It is called *karavīra* because many *karavīra* trees (*assamāraka*) are found there;
or, it is called *karavīra* because peacocks (*ke*) cry out (*ravanti*) there. There is also a reading *karavīka*;
here too, only the latter sense applies, or it is called *karavīka* because many *karavīka* birds are found there. Many excellent medicinal herbs (*sudassanā osadhi*) are found there.
It is called Sudassana because it is beautiful; or, it is Sudassana because it is to be seen with ease; or, it is Sudassana because there is a beautiful sight therein.
It is called Nemindhara because it supports itself by making itself like the rim of the five circular mountain ranges;
or, it is Nemindhara because it is to be maintained or characterized by its state as a rim; or, it supports the "chariot-tree" (rathadduma), which is the rim.
"By the majority" refers to Nemindhara. Vinatā is the mother of the Supaṇṇas; because it is her dwelling place, it is called Vinataka—so states the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.
Alternatively, it is Vinataka because broad rivers (*natā nadī*) flow there.

It is Assakaṇṇa because many *assakaṇṇa* trees are found there, or because its peaks resemble the ears of a horse (*assakaṇṇa*). These, beginning with Sineru, are the "principal mountain ranges" (*kulācala*).
There are eight mountains that are the families, sources, and origins of the mountains known as the immovables (*acala*);
these, beginning with Sineru, rise up in successive tiers, and among them, Assakaṇṇa is the outermost. However, in the *Nimi-jātaka*, it says:
"Sudassana, Karavīka, Īsadhara, and Yugandhara..."
“Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the great mountain Giri.
(Jātaka 2.22.568) Having spoken thus, it is stated that after Sineru is surrounded, the mountain named Assakaṇṇa is established, and surrounding that, the mountain named Vinataka;
thus another sequence has been described. Although it has been so stated, it is merely a difference in names.
In this context, it should be understood that there is a distinction, not a distinction in meaning. 27.

Regarding the Ganges flowing through the sky, which originates from the peak of Mount Meru, it has three names: Mandākinī, Ākāsa-Gaṅgā, and Sura-Nadī. It is called *Mandākinī* because its nature (*sīla*) is to flow slowly (*mandaṃ akituṃ*).
It is called *Ākāsa-Gaṅgā* because it is the Ganges flowing in the sky. It is called *Sura-Nadī* because it is the river of the *surā*, the gods. *Suradīghikā* is also a name for it.

28. The Triad of Koviḷāra, etc.: Regarding the *pāricchattaka* tree, which is known as the "bearer of fruit": it is called *koviḷāra* because it tears the earth (*kuṃ*) with its roots; the *ḷo* is a suffix.
It stands like an umbrella (*chatta*) all around (*pari*), thus it is a *pāricchattaka*.

Born from the ocean (*pāri*), it is a *pārijātaka*, being the offspring of the sea; the suffix *-ka* is used here for the sake of emphasis. There are also other names such as *pāribhadda*, *nimbataru*, *mandāra*, and so forth.
The names of the *pāricchattaka* tree:

the *kapparukkha*, the *santāna*, the *mandāra*, the *pārijātaka*, and the *haricandana*—these five divine trees (*devadduma*) are called the "trees of the immortals" (*amara-devataru*) because they grow only in the celestial realms (*devabhūmi*).
A *kappa* is a desired object; the tree of that [object] is the *kapparukkha*.

The relationship [between the tree and its fruit] is by way of the state of producer and produced; or, a tree that stands for an eon (*kappa*) is a *kapparukkha*. *Tāna* means stretching out; the suffix *-ṇa* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

That which possesses a complete stretching out (*sammā tāno*) of fragrance is a *santāna*, namely the *sirīsa* tree. It is called *mandāra* because gods rejoice (*mandante modante*) by means of it; the suffix *-āra* is applied.
It is called *haricandana* because it delights (*cadayati*) and gladdens (*sukhayati*) the Lord of the Monkeys (*hariminda*); the suffix *-ana* is applied. These are the five divine trees.
These are stated according to the method of the *Amarakośa*; however, according to the Buddhist method, there are seven divine trees. And it is said:

“The *pāṭalī*, the *simbalī*, the *jambū*, the *pārichattaka* of the gods, the *kadamba*, the *kapparukkha*, and the *sirīsa* is the seventh. (*Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* 584; *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā* 1.1, commentary on the Verañjakaṇḍa).
In that regard, the *pāṭalī* is the variegated *pāṭalī*, which stands in the world of the asuras.
Likewise, the *simbalī* among the garuḷas, the *jambū* in Jambudīpa, the *pāricchattaka* in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and the *kadamba* in Aparagoyāna.
The *kapparukkha* is in Uttarakuru, and the *sirīsa* in Pubbavideha. Because these seven arise only in the established grounds of the devas, they are called "divine trees" (*devataru*).
The description of the heavens is complete.
29. The eastern, western, and northern directions are respectively called *pācī*, *pacī*, and *udīcī*. That direction in which the sun moves first in the morning is *pācī*;
here, the letter *na* has been elided. That direction in which the sun moves later at the close of day—
That is the *patīcī*. That direction toward which the sun rises is the *udīcī*; or, that direction toward which [the sun] moves after giving cold is the *udīcī*.

Here, the vowel *u* expresses the sense of separation (*viyoga*), while the syllable *da* has the sense of giving (*dāna*). Alternatively, it is *pācī* because it "goes forward" (*pañcati*), that is, attains the eastern state (*pubbabhāva*).

It is *patīcī* because it "goes back" (*patincati*), that is, attains the western state (*pacchābhāva*). It is *udīcī* because it "goes upward" (*udañcati*), that is, attains the state of giving cold.
"Udīcī. And here, it should be understood that by association with *udīcī*, *patīcī* occurs in the feminine, and by association with *patīcī*, *pācī* occurs in the feminine.
