Thus, one should apply the respective genders of each [term] through their mutual association.
In the case of the pronouns *pubba*, *pacchima*, and *uttara*, the masculine gender applies merely by being stated.

The pair beginning with *dakkhiṇā* refers to the southern direction. That direction in which the sun turns toward the center is *apācī*. Here, the prefix *apa-* has the sense of "middle," as in the word *apadisa*;
there is also a reading *avācī*. [In this case], the prefix *ava-* is used in the sense of bending downward.

That direction in which the sun bends downward—that is, becomes downward-facing—is *avācī*. Alternatively, when expressing separation from heat and so forth, [the term] in which the sun [is absent]...

It inclines; thus it is "avācī" (downward). The pair beginning with "vidisā" (intermediate directions) is in the middle of the directions. They are called "vidisā" because they have emerged from the cardinal directions (*disā*).

Alternatively, they are "anudisā" because they correspond to or follow after the cardinal directions. It is also said that *apadisaṃ* is a name for the intermediate direction (*vidisā*), an indeclinable neuter noun, as in the verse: "But *apadisaṃ* [is used] for the intermediate direction" (*Amarakośa* 3.6). 30.
The eight elephants beginning with Erāvaṇa are called "direction-elephants" (*disāgaja*) because they protect the cardinal directions such as the East. Puṇḍarīka...

It is called *sītamba-ja* because its color resembles that; it is a *puṇḍarīka* because of its similarity to that [lotus]. It is *vāmana* because of its short stature. It is *kumuda* because it rejoices (*modate*) in the earth (*ku*).
It is *añjana* because of its dark, ointment-like (*añjana*) color. Its teeth are like blossoming flowers, thus he is *puṣpadanta*. He moves upon all grounds, thus he is *sabbabhūmī*;
or, because he is a universal monarch (*cakkavattī*) who ranges over all grounds, he is *sabbabhūmī* by virtue of being worthy of that title.
"Because his teeth and limbs are beautiful, he is Suppatīka; his beautiful teeth and limbs are his, thus he is Suppatīka" (as stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī).
For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "Suppatīka is the name for the elephant of the Īsāna direction who possesses beautiful limbs.

The mention of the connection with Erāvaṇa and the other elephants of the directions is for the purpose of indicating the names of their respective offspring, such as Pācī and Vāraṇa; however, their female elephants are as follows—
Abbhamu, Kapilā, Piṅgalā, Anupamā, Tambakaṇṇī,
Subhadantī, Aṅganā, Añjanāvatī, and Amara— these are considered the two pairs of deities presiding over the eastern direction,
beginning with Dhatarattha. One by whom the kingdom (raṭṭha) is supported is Dhatarattha.
*Rassa* means short. The lord (*adhipo*) or leader (*nāyako*) of the *gandhabbas*, such as Pañcasikha and others, is the *Gandhabbādhipa*.
Regarding the pair beginning with Kumbhaṇḍasāmi, these are the deities who are lords of the southern direction. The lord or leader of the *kumbhaṇḍas* is the *Kumbhaṇḍasāmi*.

They are called *Virūḷhaka* because the *kumbhaṇḍas* grow (*viruhanti*), attain increase (*vuḍḍhiṃ*), and reach expansion (*virūḷhimāpajjanti*) within him; or alternatively, it is because he possesses (*kaṃ*) happiness (*sukhaṃ*) that has grown (*virūḷhaṃ*) and reached maturity (*vuḍḍhippattaṃ*).
Virūḷhaka. The pair beginning with Virūpakkha refers to the deities presiding over the western direction.
One whose eyes are disfigured is Virūpakkha; or, one whose eyes are of various shapes is Virūpakkha. The lord of the *nāgas* is the *Nāgādhipati*. 32.
The tetrad beginning with the Lord of the *Yakkhas* refers to Kuvera. The lord of the *yakkhas* such as Āḷavaka and others is the *Yakkhādhipa*. [The lord] of Vissavaṇa...
Vessavaṇa has offspring. Kuvera is so called because his body (*vera*) is wretched (*kucchi*) due to his standing with three feet and eight fearsome fangs.
Nara-vāhana means that men (*nara*) are his vehicle (*vāhana*), as he is drawn by men in palanquins and chariots through his anger.
He is the friend of Tyambaka, the king of the *yakkhas*, Guyhakesara, one who possesses human qualities, the giver of wealth, the king of kings, the lord of riches, and the king of the *kinnaras*.
Yakkho, Ekapiṅgalo, Sirido, Puññajanessaro, and so forth, are also names of Kuvera.
The city of this Kuvera is called "Aḷakā" or "Aḷakamandā. *Alaṃ* means adornment (*vibhūsana*); because it performs adornment, it is *alakā*, which is the same as *aḷakā*.
Because it causes delight (*modakaraṇa*), it is *aḷakamandā*; here, the letter *u* has been changed to *a*.
And there is no arrival. *Kelāsa* is also its name: *keli* is its purpose, hence it is *kelo*; one sits upon this, hence it is *āsa*;
thus it is *kelāsa*, being a permanent *kammadhāraya* compound like "black snake" (*kaṇhasappa*). Its weapon, the armament of Kuvera, is the *gadā*.
"Ga" refers to the thunderbolt (*vajira*); it gives pain like that, hence it is called *gadā*. These four are as previously described.
The deities beginning with Dhatarattha are known as the presiding lords (adhipati) of the four directions, starting from the east in order. However, in the *Amarakosa*, it is stated:
“Inda, Aggi, Pitupati, Neru, Varuṇa, Anila, Kuvera, and Īsa are, in this order, the lords of the directions beginning with the east.”

“Ravi (the Sun), Sukka (Venus), Mahīsūnu (Mars), Tamo (Saturn), Bhānuja (Mercury), Vidhu (the Moon), Budho (Jupiter), and Suraguru (Venus)—these are the lords of the directions, as well as the planets. (Amarakosa 3.3–4) Different lords of the directions have been mentioned [here].

The statement regarding Indra, Ravi, and the others as lords of the directions serves the purpose of indicating the names of the cardinal and intermediate directions according to the Pāñjika and other sources, such as “Inda,” “Disā,” “Ravi,” and “Disāra.”

33–34. The eighteenfold [set] beginning with Jātaveda pertains to fire. It is called *jātavedo* because it finds (*vindati*) and consumes (*ghātayati*) what has been born (*jāte*) or arisen (*uppanne*).
Alternatively, it is *jātavedo* because it finds (*vindati*), obtains (*labhati*), or knows (*vidati*) what is born or existing in the darkness.

Or, it is *jātavedo* because its knowledge (*vedo*) regarding what is born (*jātaṃ*)—that is, its manifestation—is manifest (*pākaṭo*). A "crest" (*sikhā*) refers to a flame; from its connection with that, it is called *sikhī*. It shines (*jotati*).

It shines, thus it is *joti* (light/fire). It purifies, thus it is *pāvaka*; [the suffix] *ṇvu*. It burns, thus it is *dahana*. They breathe or protect by means of this, thus it is *anala*; [the suffix] *ala*.
It carries or causes the offering (*huta*) to go to the Vedas, or it itself receives it, thus it is *hutāvaha*.
A flame is called *acci*; because of its connection with that, it is *accimā* (flaming). Smoke is its banner or sign, thus it is *dhūmaketu*. It moves, burning crookedly.
It goes, thus it is *aggi* (fire). It has rays (*raṃsi*), thus it is *gini*; the suffix *-ini* is used in the sense of possession (*assatthi*).

There is also a reading *agginī*, which means "one who is like fire. He has radiance (*bhānu*), thus he is *bhānumā*. It kindles (*tejeti*) the remaining primary elements and derived matter, thus it is *tejo* (heat/fire).
Its crest (*sikhā*) is smoke (*dhūma*), thus it is *dhūmasikho*. It has wind as its companion (*sakha*), thus it is *vāyusakho*. Having burned, it burns (*dahati*). (ka.)
One whose path has a black furrow is *kaṇhavattanī*. A descendant of the seer Vessāṇara is a *Vessāṇara*.
One who eats the oblation (*huta*) offered as a sacrificial gift (*havi*) is *hutāsa*.
*Dhanañjaya*, *jalana*, *āsayāsa*, *rohitassa*, *sattācci*, *sukka*, *citrabhānu*, *vibhāvasu*, *suci*, and so forth, are also names for fire.

The triad beginning with *sikhā* [is formed] from *aggijālā* (flame). It is called *sikhā* because it binds (*sinoti*) or becomes sharp (*nisānī*); the root *si* in the sense of "sharpening" (*nisāne*) takes the suffix *kā*, and the suffix *khap*.

It burns, thus it is *jālā*. That by which one reaches (*accati*) or is honored (*pujjate*) is *acci*. *Sikhā*, *jālā*, and other forms exceeding these exist as feminine; however, *acci* is not masculine.
35. Regarding *dvayaṃ aggikaṇe*: *tīsu phuliṅgo’ggikaṇo* (Amarakośa 1.60). *Phuliṅgāni* means sparks of fire.
It is called *vipphuliṅgaṃ* because it goes forth (*phullaṃ*) scattering in various directions; likewise for *phuliṅgaṃ*. However, in the *Sabbadharakata*, it is stated:
"It is called *phuliṅgo* because it goes forth (*phuliṃ gacchati*). This triad refers to ashes. It [removes] the luster of soiled bronze, cloth, and so forth.

It is called *bhasma* because it causes [impurities] to fall away; the suffix *-ma* is applied here. Alternatively, it is *bhasma* because by means of it the dirt (*mala*) of cloth and other items falls down or is cast off.

It is called *seṭṭhi* because he possesses a desire (*icchā*) for the state of whiteness in bronze vessels and the like—which is thus a wish (*abhilāsa*) or a beautiful thing (*sobhana*)—and because the word *sa-* has the sense of "possessing" (as in the examples "having wings," "having hair," etc.). [The following refers to] the dirt...
It is called *sārikā* because it makes a sound (*sarati*);

that very thing is *chārikā*, as in the case of terms such as "six sense bases" (*saḷāyatana*). 36. There are two types of hot ashes. Because it takes away (*lāti*) what is wretched (*kukku*) due to its heat, it is called *kukkula*;

for it is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "The word *kukku* [is used] for a span, for a hand, for a hollow, and also for what is wretched. Alternatively, it cuts (*lunāti*) the hand, which is wretched (*kukku*).
It is called *kukkula* because it cuts and burns; that itself is *kukkula*. Hot ashes are *uṇhabhasma*; [the phrase refers to] being in that. The triad [refers to] blazing wood as fuel.
It is called *aṅgāra* because it goes to destruction (*aṅgati* = *hāniṃ gacchati*); the suffix *-āra* is applied, and this word is both masculine and neuter.
For it is stated in the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (3.329): "The word *alāta* is not feminine; *kuje* (in a pit) is *aṅgāra*. It takes destruction itself.
It does not have stability or distinction; thus, it is *alāta*. It emits smoke upwards; thus, it is *ummata*, and that itself is *ummuka*. The group of five [refers to] fuel such as wood.
It nourishes—that is, increases—the existing fire; thus, it is *samidhā*. That which nourishes is *idhuma* or *umo*.
That which nourishes is *idho*. It is taken up by the fire; thus, it is *upādāna*. It nourishes; thus, it is *indhana*.
37. The group of five begins with *āloka*. It shines and illuminates, thus it is *obhāsa*.

It is clear and bright, thus it is *pakāsa*. One looks (*ālocayati*) or sees by means of it, thus it is *āloka*; or, one looks out (*āloketi*) by means of it, thus it is *āloka*, according to the reading of the two verbal roots:
*loka* and *loca* in the sense of "seeing. It shines forth, thus it is *ujjota*; or, it shines while destroying darkness, thus it is *ujjota*. It heats or radiates all around, thus it is *ātapo*.
It shines (*dippati*), thus it is *ātapa* (heat). "Equal" (*samā*) means these five have the same meaning;

this is the sense. In the case of the ten [wind-derivatives]: it kills living beings just as food [can kill], thus it is *māruto*; that itself is *māluto*. It cleanses (*punāti*) rubbish and so forth, thus it is *pavano*.
It blows (*vāyati*) and goes, thus it is *vāyu*; or else, it is *vāyu* because by it the fragrance of flowers and such is carried away.

*So* means wind (*vāyu*). Likewise, *vāto*. It is called *anilo* because by it beings breathe (*ananti pāṇanti*); [the suffix] *ilo*. It moves (*īrayati*) that which is still (*santaṃ*) and motionless, causing it to shake, thus it is *samīraṇo*;
or, it is *samīraṇo* because its nature is to move (*samīrituṃ*) or to shake. It carries fragrance (*gandhaṃ*), thus it is *gandhavāho*;
[the suffix] *ṇo*. *Vāyo* is like wind; in both cases, there is the augment *yā*. It moves and scatters trees and such on all sides, thus it is *samīro*.

"Sadā," "sabbadā," and "gati" are [etymological components] of *sadāgati*. Furthermore, *sasana*, *gandhavaha*, *āsuga*, *maruta*, *jagatipāṇa*, *pavamāna*, and *pabhañjana* are also names for the wind (*vāta*).
38. These six types of wind (*vāyu*) to be explained hereafter are specific varieties of wind:
that which goes upward is called *uddhaṅgama*; [the winds] of feces, urine, and so forth...
It moves downward by way of being expelled, thus it is "downward-moving" (*adhogama*). It stays in the belly, in the abdomen, thus it is "staying in the belly" (*kucchiṭṭha*).
It lies and remains in the hollow of the interior, thus it is "the receptacle" (*koṭṭhāsa*). That by which one breathes repeatedly is "in-breath" (*assāsa*), the air that has gone outside.
Out-breath (*passāsa*)—even the air entering inside—is included under the term "in-breath" (*assāsa*) because of their association. [This applies] to all parts of the body.

It is called *aṅgānusārī* because it follows along with the limbs by producing sweat, blood, and so forth. In the *Amarakośa*, however, this wind is described as fivefold according to its location and function:
"The vital breaths (*vāyu*) residing in the body are *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. And regarding this, the commentary states:
"The *prāṇa* is in the heart, the *apāna* in the rectum, and the *samāna* is situated in the middle of the navel."

The *udāna* wind is located in the region of the throat; the *byāna* wind is in all the joints; the *pāṇa* wind is in the heart; the *apāna* wind is in the anus; and the *samāna* wind is situated at the navel. The *udāna* resides in the region of the throat, while the *byāna* pervades the entire body—such is the determination of their locations (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).

Among them: the *pāṇa* wind causes the entry of food and so forth; the *apāna* wind causes the discharge of urine, feces, semen, and bile; the *samāna* wind performs the digestion of food in the middle [of the body] and so forth; the *udāna* wind produces speech, song, and so forth;
and the *byāna* wind causes perspiration, blood-flow, opening and closing of the eyes, movement, and so forth—the activities of exertion, opening and closing of the eyes, and locomotion.

(ka. It is *pāṇa* because it enters [the body] through the mouth and so forth by way of being manifest (*pakaṭṭha*) and endless (*anantya*). It is *apāna* because it expels urine and so forth by way of being endless.

It is *samāna* because it properly carries along (*saman-ti*) what has been eaten and digests it by way of being endless. It is *udāna* because it generates the capacity for speech and so forth by way of ascending (*uddham-anantya*).
It is *byāna* because it specifically circulates sweat, tears, phlegm, and the like, as well as the activities of exertion and thought (according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*), by way of being endless.
"Vāyo is [the wind] because of its carrying out [of functions]"—and as for those functions, they are stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* as follows:
the entry of food, the discharge of urine and so forth, the digestion of food, speaking and so on, and the closing of the eyes and so forth;
these are the functions in order. 39. "The pair" refers to the wind entering within. *Āna* is said to be the wind exiting outward; that which is departed from that is *apāna*.

Exhalation (*passāsa*) is that which is removed from inhalation (*assāsa*). These two refer to the wind exiting externally. Inhalation (*assāsa*) is the breath (*sāsa*) occurring at the beginning [of the respiratory cycle].
"Āna" is so called because one breathes (*ānanti*) by means of it; the "āna" occurring at the beginning is simply "āna," with the elision of one *ā* sound. 40.
Terms such as "impetus" (*vega*) and "speed" (*khippa*) occur constantly due to their nature as wind-phenomena; thus, they proceed in that sequence, by that progression, and by that method.
(ka. It is said: therein, *rayanta* means speed (*vega*). In all instances, it is derived as an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). Speed is that by which one goes to and reaches the desired place.
"In order to express the meaning of the verbal root, a single instance has been shown."
"Roots have many meanings and should be understood according to their usage," as stated in the *Candradhātupāṭha*. Because of this, the root *vaj* (to go) also functions in the sense of "attaining.

This applies everywhere [in the case of roots]. The substitution of *e* for the vowel *a* occurs as follows: that by which they speed is *java* (speed); that by which they move swiftly is *raya* (velocity).

The group of nine beginning with "quick" (*khippa*) refers to swiftness. Now, what is the difference between *java*, *sīgha*, and so on? Terms such as *java* denote movement characterized by momentum (*savega*), whereas *sīgha* and the others denote mere swiftness.

However, it is a word denoting a state (*dhamma-vacana*); likewise, there are such usages as “it cooks quickly” (*sīghaṃ pacati*) or “he sees” (*passati*), and “it goes quickly” (*sīghaṃ gacchati*), but not such usages as “it cooks with speed” (*javaṃ pacati*) or “it goes with speed” (*javaṃ gacchati*).
How then is it in cases such as “he goes with velocity” (*vegena gacchati*) or “he goes with speed” (*javena gacchati*)?

In those instances, there is no fault, because a distinction (*bheda*) is intended to be expressed. [The root] *khip* means “to throw” or “to pass”; thus, *khippaṃ*. *khipa*... [text fragment] ... *khippaṃ* (quickly).
*Peraṇe*: "It moves quickly" (*sayati*) thus it is *sīgha*. [The root] *si* with the suffix *gha*. For etymological derivation (*byuppatti*) occurs in whatever manner possible;

however, conventional usage (*saññā*) must be understood from common worldly practice, and this is the case everywhere. "It crosses over" (*tarati*) thus it is *turita*. "It leaps" (*laṅghati*) thus it is *lahu*. [The root] *laṅgha* is used in the senses of going and drying;
there is the substitution of *ha* for *gha*, elision of the nasal (*niggahīta*), and the suffix *u*. There is also the word *laghu* as a synonym for *lahu*.
It flies quickly (*āsū*): from *khepatīti āsu*. It crosses over (*taratīti tuṇṇaṃ*): the short vowel becomes *ṇa*. It moves swiftly (*arati gacchatīti araṃ*).

It does not linger, it does not delay (*na vilambīyati na ohīyatīti avilambitaṃ*): the root *labi* means to hang down or delay. It turns quickly, it lies down (*tuvaṭṭati sayatīti tuvaṭṭaṃ*), or it proceeds with a sense of haste (*turitabhāvena vattatīti vā tuvaṭṭaṃ*):
there is the elision of the syllable *ri*.

41. The first half of the noble ascetic life is continuous (*santata*). Here, among the eight groups [of syllables], the sixth is the lightest of all; the six following groups are *sa*, *bha*, *sa*, *bha*, *bha*, *bhā*;

and the eighth is *go*. It is called *satata* because it extends (*tanoti*) on all sides. It is *nicca* because it is not to be gone away from (*na iccaṃ na gantabbaṃ*) by way of destruction (*nāsabhāvena*);
or, it is *nicca* because it does not go to destruction (*nāsaṃ vā na gacchati*). This applies in cases such as "the elephant" (*nāgo*), and so forth.
There is no fault even here in the sense of "it goes away" (*viyāti*). *Avirataṃ* means it does not cease. *Anārataṃ* means it does not take delight.
*Santataṃ* means it extends all around or repeatedly. *Anavarataṃ* means it does not stop. *Dhuvaṃ* means it constantly runs or moves;
the root *dhu* is found in the Kaccāyana Dhātupāṭha as meaning "to go" or "to move."
*Vipulā* (the expanded) refers to the excellence [of syllables]. Herein, in the *ayuga-pāda* (non-even feet), there are twelve syllables;
in the *yuga* (even feet), eighteen. In all *ariyā* (noble) meters, there are twelve syllables in the first foot, eighteen in the second, twelve in the third, and fifteen in the fourth.
However, when [the syllables] decrease in the first and third feet, they become increased in the even feet; this is the characteristic of *vipulā*.
Now, what is the difference between *satata* (constant) and *atisaya* (excessive)? *Satata* means continuity, being uninterrupted by other intervening moments;

*atisaya*, however, means repetition (*ponopuñña*) and excellence (*pakaṭṭha*). Among these, repetition is the recurrence of an action, while excellence is the intensification of the components of that action.

*Bhusaṃ* [means] "he speaks intensely" (*sabbesaṃ bhāsati*), from the root *bhās* with the suffix *u*. Alternatively, *bhusaṃ* [means] that which falls downward (*adho patati*), from the root *bhass*. [The root is] *bhas*.
In *adhopatane*, it is *assa u*. *Atisaya* means exceeding; *atisaya* is the act of dwelling beyond or proceeding beyond. It is *daḷha* because it burns everything (*dahati sabbaṃ*);
the *pu* becomes *ḷo* due to the previous [rule], or it is *daḷha* because it breaks or tears apart (*dalati vidārayati*), with the suffix *hapaccayo*;
or it is *daḷha* because it brings what is burning (*dahanto lāti*), with a change of phoneme (*vaṇṇavipariyayo*). *Abhisaya* and *daḷha* together form *atisayadaḷhā*. It crosses (*tarati*).
*Atikkamati* means "intense" (*tibba*); [the *o*] becomes *vo*, and [the *a*] becomes *i*. It goes or proceeds, thus it is "one" (*eko*); that very thing is "exclusive" (*ekanta*).
Or, it crosses over or transcends the one, thus it is "exclusive" (*ekanta*). That which exceeds the measure is "excessive" (*atimatta*). It takes much, thus it is "strong" (*bāḷha*);
there is the elision of the *u* and a change of the phoneme, with the sound *ha* [added]. *Ativelaṃ*, *accatthaṃ*, *nibbharaṃ*, *nitantaṃ*, *gāḷhaṃ*, and so forth, also [denote] intensity.

The substance (*dabba*) exists; while the mere qualities (*dhammamatta*) contrary to that are present, the terms *khippa* (swift) and so forth—though lacking a specific suffix for excellence (*atisaya*)—are used in the sense of the neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
The two words "khippaṃ bhavati" and "khippaṃ bhavabhī" appear as if they were redundant;
the excellence (*atisaya*) is masculine, as in "the excellence of this quality" (*assa guṇassātisayo*) or "the excellence of this substance" (*assa dabbassātisayo*). "Khippaṃ... [and so on].

"He eats," "he constantly offers oblations," and "he is constantly delightful"—in these cases, it is precisely because they are adverbs of action (*kriyāvisesana*) that the state of being a paṇḍaka [is indicated].
Among those [terms] such as *khippa* (quick), etc., those which denote substances (*dabba*) are found in all three genders (*liṅga*). This is shown immediately after [the rule stating]:

"The gender is the property of the substance. For example: *khippā jarā* (old age is quick), *khippo maccu* (death is quick), *khippaṃ gamanaṃ* (going is quick). *Santatā* (continuity) is craving; *santataṃ*...
"Suffering," "space as peace," "excessive action," "excessive man," "excessive state," and so forth. 42–43. The group of twelve [verses] concerning Māra.

Because he was burnt by the fire from the eye of Hara (Śiva), and because he was burnt by the fire from the eye of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva), there is no conflict; his body is without conflict (*aviggaha*).
He desires, that is, he arouses the longing for pleasure, thus he is *kāma*; the suffix *-anta* is applied to the root *kā* to form this word.

He is called *Manobhū* because he exists in the minds of beings through his amorous form. He is called *Madana* because he intoxicates [beings] with the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
He is called *Antaka* because he brings about the end and destruction of the worlds. He is called *Vasavattī* because he exercises mastery by his own nature.

He is called *Pāpimā* because he desires evil, or because he is joined with it. He is called *Pajāpati* because he is the lord (*pati*) of those who are born (*pajā*), that is, of those who lack self-control.
Those who are negligent regarding wholesome states are the "kinsmen of negligence. He is called *Kaṇha* because he is associated with dark qualities.
He is called *Māra* because he slays wholesome states. He is called *Namuci* because he does not release one from unwholesome states.
He is also known as Mīnaketana, Kandappa, Dappaka, Anaṅga, Pañcasara, Sambarāri, Manasija, Kusumesu, Anaññaja, and Pupphadhanvā.
*Raṭṭhipati*, *makaraddhaja*, *iccādi*, and so forth, are also names for Kāma, the son of Viṣṇu.
*Taṇhā*, *aratī*, and *ragā*: these three are the daughters of that Māra. She is called *taṇhā* because she causes one who sees her to thirst;

there is the elision of the *l* and the substitution of *ṇhā*. She is called *aratī* because she creates aversion toward the wholesome qualities (*kusaladhamma*) of others. They are called *ragā* because they cause passion...
"Herein" means among the defilements (*rāga*). That elephant of Māra is named Girimekhala. Because its body is so vast that it resembles a mountain, it is like a mountain (*giri*);
and because it was given the name "Mekhala" by Māra through the act of claiming ownership—thinking, "Let this elephant of mine be named Mekhala"—it is like a girdle (*mekhalā*).
Thus, he refers to a single elephant by a combined pair of names, just as one might say "Vajirāsani" or "Sītuṇha."
44. *Tikaṃ yame*. Because he restrains (*saṃyamana*) living beings, he is a *yama*; death and the like are his servants, and he reigns over them, thus he is the King of Death (*yamarāja*).
Since he exercises authority even over the three realms (*tedhātuka*), his domain is vast; he is the possessor of that domain (*visayī*).

Where [the suffix] does not succeed by way of grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), there it is everywhere [to be understood] by means of the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) beginning with "ya" and so forth.

For it was stated previously: "Or the derivation of the word should be understood thus. Alternatively, they are *vesā* because they go to disagreeable places (*visadisa-ṭṭhāna*) due to producing suffering;
*vesāyī* means that which moves (*ayati*) or proceeds by way of presiding over those *vesā*, i.e., the denizens of hell (*nerayikā*). *Yama* is the king of the *yamāna* (those who go).
Other names for Yama include Dhammarāja, Katanta, Samavatti, Kāla, Daṇḍadhara, Antaka, and so forth.
His weapon is his very eye; for it is said that by the mere glance of that wrathful mind, the bodies of beings melt away like lumps of ghee thrown into the heat of the sun.
These two belong to the division of the *asuras*. For although they possess the status of gods, because they share the commonality of dwelling below, they are included here.
The speech [of Vepacitti] is [so called] because it shares with Māra the common quality of causing harm to sentient beings; and because he acts together with Yama, his speech is [called] *vacana*.
His mind is trembling (*vepita*) or shaken in battles and the like, thus he is *Vepacitti* (Sammohavinodanī Aṭṭhakathā 1.1.256). He whose hair is full is *Puloma*;

alternatively, he is *Puloma* because his great fame (*umā*) is *pulā*, or because his fame or beauty (*kanti*) is *umā*. As it is said: "In the words *umā*, *atasī*, *hemavatī*, *haliddā*, *kitti*, and *kanti* [the suffix -a denotes 'fame']."
For this is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*. This, however, was the father of Sujātā, the wife of Sakka.

[The term] *kinnara* consists of two parts: a "wretched man" (*kucchito puriso*) because he has the face of a horse and the body of a human, or "some kind of man" (*kiñci puriso*), or "one resembling a man" (*purisasadiso*);
thus, *kinnara*. *Turaṅgavadana*, *assamukha*, and so forth are also names for the *kinnara*.
45–46. Synonyms for space (*ākāsa*). It is called *antalikkha* because the world perceives therein the diversity and interval between various objects;

or, it is *antalikkha* because one perceives (*ikkhati*) by means of it—here the long vowel *ī* becomes short *i*. Alternatively, *ikkhā* is the act of seeing or perceiving; the interval or cause thereof is *antalikkha*.
It is called *kha* because it pierces (*khanati*) obstructions—the suffix *kvip* is applied. [It is the sphere] of Ādicca, the leader of all the hosts of planets.
*Patha* means a road; *ādiccapatha* is the path of the sun. It is called *abbha* because it does not exist [as a solid obstruction]. They go by means of this, O gods, thus it is *gagana*;
*yu*, *massa*, and *go*. It resounds there, thus it is *ambara*; *ro*. *Haya* means to move; it moves or goes everywhere in a special way, thus it is *vehāsa*;
that which has this [quality], or where there is no laughter (*hāsa*) of the mind due to the non-attainment of an object, is *vehāsa*.
The path of the wind is the *anilapatha*. It is called *ākāsa* because by means of it the meanings of words (*padattha*) shine forth intensely;
or alternatively, *ākāsa* is that which is not filled (*na kassati*) or not scratched (*na vilekhiyati*). It is called *nabha* because no substance whatsoever exists therein;
or *nabha* because there is no ground (*bhūmi*) there; or *nabha* because birds do not fear it, or because they are therein. *Vina* means birds.
It is called *vehāyasa* because beings (*vaya*) go (*gacchanti*) there; thus, O friend, it is so named. The stars and such are called *tārā*; their path is the *tārāpatha*.
The path of the *surā*, that is, the gods, is the *surapatha*. It is called *agha* because it cannot be struck (*na haññati*); here, *han* becomes *gha*.
*Ananta*, *visaṇupada*, and so forth, are also names for space (*ākāsa*).
47–48. The group of eleven beginning with *megha* pertains to the cloud (*megha*). It is called a *megha* because it mists (*mehati*), flows (*gharati*), and sprinkles (*secati*).

It is called a *valāhaka* because it carries water (*vāriṃ vahati*); according to Pāṇini 6.3.109, Moggallānapañcikā 1.47, and Nīti-sutta 1340, 1343, the *vā* of the word *vāri* becomes *vo*, and the *ss* becomes *l*.

It is called a *deva* because by means of it the worlds (*loka*) rejoice (*dibbanti*), that is, they attain growth and increase (*vuḍḍhi-virūḷhi*). It is the food (*anna*) for the people and the worlds.
He is called *Pajjunna* because by him food (*pajja*) comes into being; here, the letter *a* becomes *u*. He is called *ambudhara* because he bears (*dhāreti*) water (*ambu*).
He is called *ghana* because he destroys (*hanti*) the heat (*santāpa*) of the worlds; here, *ha* becomes *gha*. He is called *dhārādhara* because he bears a stream of rain (*jaladhāra*).

He is called *jīmūta* because by him life (*jīvana*)—that is, water—is bound (*mūta*, meaning "bound"); here the syllable *vana* is elided, or alternatively, because he measures (*munāti*) or binds (*bandhati*) the life of the worlds.
In *jīmūta*, there is the substitution of *jī* for *jīvita* (life), according to Pāṇini 6.3.109; Moggallāna-pañcikā 1.47; and Nīti-sutta 1340, 1343.
It is the same elsewhere. That which carries water is *vārivāha*. That which gives water is *ambuda*. That which bears water is *abbha* (cloud), with the suffix *kvi*;
see Bo [Moggallāna].
The triad concerns rain (*vutthi*). It rains, it sprinkles, thus it is *vassa*; from the root *vassa* (to sprinkle). Thus, *vassa* and *vutthi* are synonyms.
The pentad concerns lightning (*vijju*). It moves constantly, it trembles, thus it is *satero*; there is the elision of the suffix *-ta*, and that itself is *sateritā*.
It does not stand still even for a moment, thus it is *akkhaṇā*. It moves crookedly, having become deformed because it does not remain for long, thus it is *vijju*. It flashes forth, thus...
Lightning. *Acirappabhā*: that whose radiance is not long-lasting is "acirappabhā. 49.
The tetrad [of terms] regarding the roar of clouds (*meghanāda*). The roar of clouds is *meghanāda*. *Dhanita*: it is sounded;
from the root *dhana*, meaning "sound. *Gajjita*: the act of roaring; from the root *gajja*, meaning "sound. *Rasita*: it resounds. By this [method], *harādādi* and so forth apply everywhere.

The suffix *to* is used in the neuter sense of abstract state (*bhāva*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the forms] *svanita*, *ghanita*, and so forth are included (according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*), and by "etc.," [the forms] *ghanita*, *harādarāsa*, and so forth are included (according to the *Byākhyāsudhā-ṭīkā*).
Both [terms] refer to Indra’s bow. *Indāvudha* is both *indassa āvudhaṃ* (Indra’s weapon) and *dhanu* (bow);
it is also *indadhanu*. *Vātakkhittambu* is water cast by the wind; it is a drop (*bindu*). It is called *sīkara* because it makes cold (*sītaṃ karoti*) or because it sprinkles (*siñcati*).

*Sīkara*: *sa* plus *ī*, with *ra* and *ca*; or, because it flows here and there by the force of the wind, it is *sīkara*; *assa* plus *ī*, with the insertion (*kāgama*) of *ka* in the middle. 50. A triad [of terms] for a stream of water. *Āsāra*:
the intense (*bhusaṃ*) falling together (*saṃ*) of streams of water due to their velocity; it flows again and again, thus it is *āsāra*.
It maintains its velocity, thus it is *dhārā*. It falls downward, thus it is *sampāta*; the sound *saṃ* is used for the downward direction.
The falling together of streams of water with force is *dhārāsampāta*; *āsāra* is [the term for] the movement of a torrent (*sara*), as stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*:

"In the sense of movement, *ghau* is *āsāra*. Both terms refer to *vassopala* (hailstones). They are called *karakā* because they are grasped by the hand (*kara*), or because they form a mass of water;
thus Rudra says: "But *vassopala* is *karakā*, and *karakā* is also seen [as a synonym]," where the word *kara* [is used]. "The word *kara* [is used] for hailstones."
"From the hand, from the trunk, and from the sun"—this is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*.

"Solid stone" (*ghanopala*) means a stone (*upala*) or rock that has arisen from a mass (*ghana*) or at a time of density. "Bad weather" (*duddina*) means poorly given; this word *duddina* refers to a sky covered by clouds.
There is also a word *duddina* with the sense of "unbeautiful," which, being a term for what lacks quality, follows the gender of the word it qualifies.

51–52. *Chakkaṃ tirodhāne* (The group of six [terms] regarding concealment). *Dhara* [is used] in the sense of covering (*āvaraṇe*), preceded by *api*, etc. It covers or wraps around, thus it is *pidhāna*;
there is no elision [of the initial *p-*]. It holds away, thus it is *apadhāraṇa*. It holds across or conceals, thus it is *tirodhāna*. It holds between, thus it is *antaradhāna*;
there is the elision of the *niggahīta* [nasal]. It covers over, thus it is *apidhāna*. And here, the prefixes such as *apa* and others [modify] the verbal root.
These [terms] indicate the sense of an obstruction. It covers, thus it is *chādana* (a covering). *Byavadhā*, *antaradhī*, and so forth, also mean concealment.
These are synonyms for the moon by way of its successful attainment. It exercises supreme sovereignty over the constellations, thus it is *indu*.
It shines, gladdens, brings happiness, and moves, thus it is *canda*. The king of the constellations is *nakkhattarājā*. *Umā*...
It is *soma* because it exists together with beauty (*kānti*); or, it is *soma* because it flows forth as happiness (*sukha*), with the suffix *-map*. It makes the night (*nisā*);
or, its rays (*kara*) are there at night, thus it is the "night-maker" (*nisākara*). They rise up (*usanti*), burn, or destroy darkness; they are rays (*osā*).
Because these rays are held (*dhiyanti*) or established therein, it is *osadhi*, a particular star, the lord (*īsa*) of which is the moon.
*Osadhīso*. He whose rays are cool like frost is *himaraṃsi*. That which has a hare as its mark (*aṅka*) is *sasaṅko*.

It is called *candimā* because it leads to what is similar to the moon (*canda*) and camphor (*kappūra*). There is the substitution of the vowel *i*. Here, that which possesses the mark of a hare is *sasī*.

Alternatively, it is *sasī* because it "consumes" (*sasati*) or destroys the quality of heat; the suffix *ī* is applied, and the term is metaphorically used for that which is characterized by it. Its rays are cool.
"Yassatthi" means "possessing cool rays. Because he is the lord (*nātha*) of the night (*nisā*), he is called "the Lord of Night" (*nisānātha*).
He is the king of the *uḷūs* (moons) and the stars, thus the "King of Moons" (*uḷurājā*). He is called "Mā" because he makes himself like camphor;
this word "mā" is masculine, and by association with it, terms such as "King of Moons" are also masculine. [He is also known as] Himāṃśu, Kumudabandhu, Vidhu, Sudhaṃśu, and Subbhaṃśu.
*Nisāpati*, *migaṅka*, *kalānidhi*, *dvijarāja*, *sasadhara*, *nakkhattesa*, and so forth, are also names for the moon.
53–54. A *kalā* (digit) of the moon is the sixteenth part that completes the sixteen portions. [The root] *kala* means "to count"; it is called a *kalā* because it is counted as one and so on.
There are two [parts] in the body of the moon. That by which something is conceived or known is called a *bimba*.
The suffix *vappaccaya* is applied after *manas*; by means of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*), *massa*, *bo*, *assi*, *nassa*, *mo*, and *vassa* are substituted for it.

The word *bimba* is not feminine. It is called *maṇḍala* because it adorns (*maṇḍayati*); the suffix *alo*. In the feminine, it is *maṇḍalī*. This [word] *bimba* is not feminine in all three genders; *maṇḍala* applies to all three genders (*Amarakośa* 3.15). A half-part is that which is deficient by one quarter.
It is called *aḍḍha* because it consumes or exhausts the whole; the suffix *to*. Likewise, *addho*. *Upaḍḍho* means "half."
A word is augmented by a prefix; these three [terms] are masculine. It breaks or divides a whole, thus it is *khaṇḍa*.

Because it can be carried in small quantities during transport and so forth, it is *sakala*; [with the suffix] *-alo*, both *khaṇḍa* and *sakala* are masculine, though according to the grammatical treatise (*sattha*), due to a difference in form, they are neuter.
These three, beginning with *aḍḍha*, are masculine when referring to an unequal portion, but neuter when equal; thus he says, "half" (*addhaṃ*), indicating the distinction by form.
It is said: "The word *addha* is used for an equal portion. However, the pair beginning with *khaṇḍa* (fragment), even when occurring for an unequal [portion], functions as both masculine and neuter.
Therefore, in the rule "the word *addha* is used for an equal portion," both of these—namely *aḍḍha* and *upaḍḍha*—are included.

When applied to an unequal portion, it is masculine; when applied to an equal part, it is neuter by way of difference in form. Or, through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it takes the gender of the object that possesses that portion.
—"Half a garment, half a cloth, half a blanket" (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).

Since clarity (*pasāda*) and the other qualities are necessarily present in the moon, whereas they are merely incidental elsewhere, they are mentioned here in the context of the moon. It specifically causes one to settle or causes one to become clear; thus it is "clarity" (*pasāda*). One who is thus clear, that itself is "clarity" (*pasannatā*).
This triad [of terms] refers to the moon's radiance. The expansion or transformation of the *kumuda* lily is *komudī*. It explains or establishes the moon; thus...

*Candikā* [is derived from *canda* with the suffix *-ika*. It is called *juṇhā* because it possesses radiance (*juti*); here, the suffix *-ṇa* is applied, and the suffix *-ap* is elided. Alternatively, it is called *juṇhā* because it leads to or binds (*nayhati*) the radiance and beauty of the moon.

The group of four [suffixes] is used in the sense of mere beauty. It is called *kanti* because it shines or gleams; the root *kana* means "to shine," or alternatively, it is called *kanti* because it is desired (*kāmīyati*).

*Sobhā* (splendor) is so called because it shines beautifully and radiates. *Juti* (luster) is so called because it illuminates. *Chavi* (skin/surface) is so called because it covers; from the root *chad*, meaning "to cover," with the suffix *-i* and the elision of the letter *d*.

55. The group of seven [terms] refers to characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). *Kalaṅka* (a mark/stain): it is so called because it "marks" (*laṅkayati*) or makes one's self inferior. *Lañchana* (a brand/mark): that by which one is "branded" (*lañchate*) or "characterized" (*lakkhate*).

*Lakkha* (a target/number): that by which one is "characterized" (*lakkhyate*). Likewise, *lakkhaṇa* (a characteristic/sign). *Aṅka* (a sign/mark): that by which one is "marked" (*aṅkīyate*) or "characterized" (*lakkhyate*).
*Ankena*: by means of this, it is a mark (*aṅka*). *Abhiññāṇaṃ*: that by which one knows a specific distinction; thus, it is a sign of recognition. *Cihanaṃ*:
that by which one is marked or characterized; thus, it is a characteristic.

[The root] *ciha* is used in the sense of marking. Among all beauties, the supreme beauty is called "well-proportioned" (*susamā*); all its beauties are perfectly even, hence it is "well-proportioned," the most excellent beauty.
56. Regarding the quality (*guṇa*) of a specific tactile sensation (*phoṭṭhabba-visesa*), the word *sīta* is neuter: "Devadatta’s cold [feeling] prevails.
The three qualities beginning with *sīta* take the gender of the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*); for example: "cool ground," "cool water," "cool wind.
It is called *sīta* because it is resorted to by those afflicted by heat; that which is associated with this is *sīta*. [The root] *sas* is in the sense of moving.
*Īra*, *itta*, and that which flows (*sarati*) for the sake of cold is *sisira*. That which takes (*lāti*) the quality of cold is *sītala*.
*Mahikā* refers to mist. *Hima*: that which harms (*hiṃsati*) is *hima*; [here] *ssa* becomes *mo* and there is the elision of the *niggahīta*.

*Tuhina*: from *tuha* (to eat), that which consumes or harms is *tuhina*; [the suffix] *ina*. That which flows upward is *ussāva*. That by which they are led out or exhaled is *nīhāra*; [there is no further suffix].
*Īhā* (endeavor) is the cause for this, hence it is *nīhāra*; [the suffix] *āro*. Or, because one who is passionate (*rāgī*) is honored (*mahīyate*) by means of words, it is *mahikā*;
[the suffix] *ṇvu*. 57. The group of six [terms] refers to a constellation (*nakkhatta*). It is called a *nakkhatta* because it does not perish (*na khīyate*) due to its repeated rising;

or, it is called a *nakkhatta* because it does not wear away (*na kharati*) or destroy its own place of movement; or alternatively, from the root *nakkha* meaning "to go," that which goes is a *nakkhatta*.

It is called *joti* because it illuminates and makes manifest the signs of the beautiful and the ugly; it is neuter due to its association with the terms *nakkhatta* (constellation) and *bhaṃsa* (star).
It is called *bhaṃ* because it shines and makes manifest the aforementioned sign. It is called *tārā* because by means of it people cross over (*taranti*) what is to be done;
or because it protects (*tāyati*) its own path and moves there; or because it saves (*tāreti*) the world from harm. And this...
*Tārakā* and *ulu*: these three are neuter. *Tārā* itself takes the suffix *ṇvu*, becoming *tārakā*; *tārā* itself becomes *tārakā* by means of the suffix *ṇvu* (according to the *Ka*).
That which rises high (*uccaṃ*)—it leaps (*lavati*), moves (*ulayati*) [according to the *Ka*], or goes—is *ulu*. That very thing is *uḷu*.
The meaning of the word *ca* ("and") is that not only *tārakā* is neuter, but also *ulu*. Because of its association with *ulu*, it is also neuter in the alternative sense.
58–60. The twenty-seven constellations (*nakkhatta*), beginning with Assayuja and ending with Revatī, are so called.

These constellations have been described here according to their actual positions in the sky, and not in reverse order. As it will be stated: "The twenty-seven constellations in their proper sequence.
Because of its association with the form of a horse, it is *Assayuja* (Horse-yoked). Because of its similarity to Yama, [it is] everywhere... [the rest of the passage is missing].

It is called *Bharaṇī* because it supports (*bharaṇī*). *Kattikā*: because it is like fire (*aggi*), it cuts or cleaves; or because it acts, it is *Kattikā*. Together with *Kattikā*, it is *Sakattikā*.
[It may also refer to] *Bharaṇī* or *Rohiṇī*. It is *Rohiṇī* because, arising from the lotus (*kamala*), it grows or increases in the lotus.
*Migasira*: because the cluster of stars has the shape of a deer's head (*migasīsa*), it is *Migasira*; this is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) because the latter member is predominant.
Neutrality (*napuṃsakatta*). Because it resembles Rudra, who is established in wrath and is fierce, it sometimes eats and devours;

thus it is *addā*. It rains repeatedly for the benefit of beings; thus it is *punabbasu* (the "re-rain"), from the root *vassa*, meaning "to sprinkle. It nourishes beings, or that in which they are nourished; thus it is *pusso*.
Because it is like a serpent, it does not cling or embrace; thus it is *asileso*.

It is honored (*mahīyate*) by those seeking its fruit; thus it is *Maghā*. By the substitution of *gha* for *ha*, it becomes *Māghā*. It causes one to receive fruit; thus it is *Phaggunī*, with the suffixes *yu* and *ī*.
There are two: *Pubbaphaggunī* and *Uttaraphaggunī*. Because of its hand-like shape, it is called *Hattha*. Because it bestows variegated fruit like a carpenter (*tacchaka*), it is called *Cittā*.
It makes the beautiful and the ugly subtle; thus it is *Sāti*. Alternatively, it is *Sāti* because it makes the body beautiful or because it is beautiful itself.

*Svāti* (abbreviation for *svāti*), or *sāti*, because it bestows both auspicious and inauspicious fruits; for it is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: “*Sāti* [is used] at the conclusion of giving. This [term] occurs in two [meanings].
It is *visākhā* because it cuts (*khaṇati*) diverse fruits (*visada-phala*); or, she whose friends (*sakha*) are manifold (*vividha*) is *visākhā*.
It is *anurādhā* because auspicious and inauspicious fruits are acquired (*anurādhayati*) or gathered (*saṃsijjhati*) by means of her. By virtue of her qualities, she [surpasses] all others...
*Vuddhattā* means "because of being grown" (*jeṭṭhā*). It is called *mūla* because the root (*mūlati*) establishes itself; it is the "root" because good and bad fruits are established therein.
*Āsāḷha* is the name for the punishment of servants; because they have that shape, the two constellations are called *Āsāḷhā*, by way of *Pubbāsāḷhā* and *Uttarāsāḷhā*.
It is called *Savaṇa* because one hears (*savati*) good and bad fruits through it, or it is hearing (*savaṇaṃ*). They seek wealth (*dhana*) therein, thus it is *Dhaniṭṭhā*.

It is called *Dhaniṭṭhā* because it possesses (*dhanati*) an abundance of treasures (*vibhūti-nidhāna*). It is *Satabhisaja* because it is the lord (*adhipati*) of the hundred physicians (*sata-bhisaja*), or of those who possess a hundred medicines.
*Bhadra* means a bull; its tracks (*padāni*) are its feet (*pādā*), hence *bhadrapadā*. There are two *pubba-bhadrapadā* and two *uttara-bhadrapadā*;
since this is a collection numbering four, the plural form is used. *Rā* is said to mean wealth (*dhana*).
*Revatī* is so called because she is the daughter (*tabbantatāya*) of *Revata*; or else, *Revata* is a type of sage (*isibheda*), and his offspring is *Revatī*.

61. Regarding the pair concerning the planet Rāhu: that is called *sagga* (the sky/heaven); he shines there, thus he is *Sobhānu*. He causes the splendor (*sobha*) of the moon and other bodies to vanish, thus he is *Rāhu*. *Tamo*, *Vidhuntudo*, *Candādo*, and *Sehikeyo* are also names for Rāhu.
*Sūra*, *Canda*, *Aṅgāraka*, *Budha*, *Jīva*, *Sukka*, *Asita*, *Rāhu*, and *Ketū*—these nine, beginning with Sūra, are known as the nine planets (*navaggaha*).

A heap consisting of twelve parts, beginning with Aries, is called a *rāsi* (sign). By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), it includes Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.
Two [names] are for the *bhaddapada* constellations. *Poṭṭho*, *go*, *pāṭho*, and *bhaddo go*—these are its parts or feet, thus they are *poṭṭhapadā*.
62–63. By two verses, the names of the Sun are given. It shines intensely (*ābhuso dippati*), thus it is *ādicco*; the suffix *-cc-* is added to *āpa*. Of the worlds...
He is called *sūriya* because he generates brilliance (*sūra-bhāva*). Likewise, he is *sūra*. He is *sataraṃsi* because he possesses many rays (*raṃsi*) for the virtuous (*sataṃ*).
He is *divākara* because he makes the day (*divā*) or because his light (*kara*) exists during the day; this word *divā* expresses all grammatical cases and not merely the locative case.
He is *verocana* because he shines or blazes especially. He makes the day (*dinaṃ*), [and] of the night-lilies (*kumudānaṃ*)...

He makes the day (*dina*) free from clouds (*mākulya*), thus he is the Day-maker (*dinakara*). He whose rays are hot is the Hot-rayed One (*uṇharaṃsi*). He makes light (*pabha*), thus he is the Light-maker (*pabhaṅkara*).

A garland (*mālā*) of rays (*aṃsu*); where that exists, he is the Ray-garlanded One (*aṃsumālī*). Lord of days (*dinānaṃ pati*) is the Lord of Days (*dinapati*). He burns, thus he is the Burner (*tapano*).

By him beings are made to cry out (*ravanti*) because they are tormented, thus he is the Roarer (*ravi*). He who possesses radiance (*bhānu*) is the Radiant One (*bhānumā*). He who possesses rays (*raṃsi*) is the Ray-possessor (*raṃsimā*).

*Bhāṃ* and *ābhāṃ* he makes; or, the source (*ākara*), the place of origin, for those [lights] is *bhākara*. He shines and glows, thus *bhānu*. He is surpassed even by the gods and is worthy of worship, thus *akko*.
He whose rays (*raṃsi*) are many, numbering a thousand, is *sahassaraṃsi*. Twelve qualities:

the maker of light (*pabhākara*), the maker of manifestation (*vibhākara*), the cutter-apart (*vikattana*), and that which was cut-apart by Vissakamma; [the suffix] *-yu* is used in the sense of action (*kammani*). (From the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).

*Mattaṇḍo*, *divamaṇi*, *taraṇi*, *mitto*, *citrabhānu*, *vibhāvasu*, *gahappati*, *haṃso*, *savitā*, and so forth, are also names for the sun. 64. *Pajja* refers to the names for the rays and effulgences of the sun and others.
It is called *raṃsi* because beings delight (*rasanti*) in it. It is called *ābhā* because it shines intensely (*ā-bhāti*). It is called *pabhā* because it shines forth (*pakārena bhāti*).
It is called *ditti* because it illuminates (*dippati*). It is called *ruci* because it shines brightly (*rocati*). It is called *dīdhi* because it shines steadily (*dīdhyati*).
It shines, thus it is *dīdhiti*. Or, it shines, thus it is *dīdhiti*; look at the *dha*, there is the insertion of the vowel *i*.
By this, small creatures perish, thus it is *marīci*; [the suffix] *īci*. It does not exist, it goes to the quarters, thus it is *aṃsu*; there is the insertion of *ussa*.
Because they accompany the *marīci*, *dīdhiti* and the others are indeed a corrupted reading; however, Savarasāmī says: *aṅguli, kākali, sāri, sarāri, tumbiari, susi*.

The *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* states: "The [suffix] *dī* occurs in the sense of 'gone' (*atta*) for both feminine and masculine; *bhānu* and *aṃsu* occur in both genders. The root *maya* has the sense of "going" (*gamana*).
The term *daṇḍaka* refers to a root that appears in the *Daṇḍaka-prakaraṇa*; this should be seen on pages 253 and 413 of the *Niruttisāramañjusā-ṭīkā*. The suffix *kh* involves the augment *ū*.
Alternatively, *mā* is the root in the sense of "measuring" (*māna*), and *ukha* is a *daṇḍaka* root in the sense of "going" (*gati*).
The meaning is "the element" (*dhātu*) as it appears in the *Daṇḍakappakaraṇa*; this should be seen on pages 253 and 413 of the *Niruttisāramañjusā-ṭīkā*.

Regarding *mayūkha*: it is derived from *māyā* and *ukhati*, thus *mayūkha*; or, according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*, it is derived from *māpa* (measure) and *gagana* (sky), meaning that which measures the sky and moves upward, following the *pisodarādi* rule.
*Kiraṇa* is so called because it scatters (*kirati*) darkness; *kara* is so called because it scatters darkness.
65. There are two [halos] renowned as the solar disc (*ādiccamaṇḍala*), which arise from portents and the like within the circle of rays.

That which is placed (*dhīyate*) all around (*pari*) the sun is called a *paridhi*; that which extends all around (*pari*) it is called a *parivesa*; or, that which encircles (*pariveṭhayati*) the sun is called a *parivesa*.
*Ṭhassa so* [is a grammatical note]. *Upasūriyaka* and *maṇḍala*—these two are also names for the *paridhi*.

There is a pair [of terms] regarding a mirage (*marīcikā*). It is called a "mirage" (*marīci*) because it resembles a mirage. That which contains the thirst and craving of deer due to its appearance as water is called "deer-thirst" (*migataṇhikā*).
Before the rising of the sun, the ray that has arisen and ascended is called the dawn (*aruṇa*).

It is called "dawn" because it moves with the color of dawn (*arati gacchati*). Dawn is also known as the offspring of the Sun, the legless one (*anūru*), the son of Kaśyapa, the descendant of Kaśyapa, and the fire of Garuḍa’s crest.
"Names. Explanation of Space (Ākāsa).
66–67. The Tetrad on Time (Kāla). Time (kāla) is that by which the measure of lifespan and so forth are reckoned or counted;

alternatively, *kāra* means "making," with the suffix *-na* used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), thus it is simply *kāla*. Indeed, there is no such thing as time apart from activity (*kriyā*), for [the Buddha] said: "Great time..."

However, because it is eternal in nature, the conventional designations such as "past" and so forth do not exist [in it]; nevertheless, because it is a collection of temporal parts (*avayava-kāla*), that too is called "time" (*kāla*).
It is called *addhā* because it exhausts the life of sentient beings; this word *addhā*, ending in the vowel *ā*, is masculine. It is called *samaya* because it arrives again and again.
It is called *velā* because it takes (*lāti*) destruction (*vināsa*); here there is a dropping of the syllable *va*. *Diṭṭha* and *aneha* are also names for time.
The "moments" (khaṇa) and so forth, however, are its specific qualities—the distinctions or divisions of that time. To the question, "What are they, and what is their measure?", he says:
"A moment," and so on. Time marked by ten finger-snapshots (*accharā*) is called a *khaṇa*. [The root] *khaṇ* means to injure; it is a *khaṇa* because it injures [time].
[The suffix] *a* [is added]. Ten *khaṇas* constitute a *laya*. By this statement, even those who expect the number of *vīka* [to be mentioned]— [End of excerpt]
It is understood that there are such designators [for time]. *Laya* means it goes; or, cutting away the life of beings, it goes, thus it is *laya*.
There are ten *layas*, which is called a "momentary *laya*" (*khaṇalaya*) because it is a collection of momentary *layas*. Those ten momentary *layas* may be a "muhutta";
this word is not feminine. [The root] *huccha* means crookedness; it is so called because it makes the day and night crooked by showing what is beautiful and what is ugly.

In *muhutto*, there is the insertion of the letter *m* at the beginning of the root, and the elision of the *cch*. Those ten *muhuttas* are called a *khaṇamuhutta*. [The following] triad concerns the day (*dina*).
It is called *divaso* because they play (*dibbanti*) and sport therein. It is called *ahaṃ* because it does not abandon its return [to the night].

It is called *dinaṃ* because it takes up (*ādādeti*) inactivity; [the suffix] *ina* is added and the [root vowel] is elided. Or, it is called *dinaṃ* because they play therein; [the suffix] *na* is added to *vassa*. *Ghasaro* devours.
*Andhakāra*, *ro*, *cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*, and *vāsara* are synonyms for day. 68. *Kallantaṃ* means at dawn.
It is called *pabhātaṃ* because "light shines" (*pabhāti*) in this world; likewise, it is *vibhātaṃ*. [The root] *usa* means "to afflict.
It is *paccūso* because it destroys the darkness (*timira*). It is *kallaṃ* because by means of it, the numbers and so forth are counted (*kalyante saṅkhyāyante*).
*Ahomukhaṃ* and *ūsos* are synonyms for dawn (*paccūsa*).
There are two terms for evening (*padosa*): the beginning of the night is *abhidoso*; the further part of the night is *padoso*.

In terms of derivation, the prefix *abhi-* is placed first before the word *dussa*, and it carries a secondary accent; alternatively, it is so called because they "become hostile" (*abhidussanti*) or "become corrupt" (*padussanti*) therein.
All actions [are performed] at *abhidoso* and *padoso*.

This is a triad referring to evening (*sāyanha*). It is called *sāya* because one tastes (*sāyati*) the end of the day (*dina*), or because one brings the day to its conclusion; or else, it is called *sāya* because one goes (*ayati*) while making the end of the day.
It is a masculine or neuter noun. They meditate together upon it, thus it is *sañjhā* (twilight), as in: “The body of Brahmā, the father of the world, the mother of the world.”
For this is the tradition of other schools. In this context, the reading appears as if it were an interpolation.
*Dinaccaya* means the passing away, the elapsing, or the end of the day. *Dinantam* is also a name for that same thing.
Twilight (*sañjhā*) is threefold by way of morning, afternoon, and midday. *Pubbaṇha*: "that which is both the former (*pubba*) and the day (*ahaṃ*)" is *pubbaṇha*.

Furthermore, "aparañca taṃ majjhañca taṃ ahañca" means "the afternoon (aparaṇhaṃ), the midday (majjhanhaṃ), and the day (ahaṃ). By metaphorically applying the whole to its parts (*samudāyopacāra*), the word "day" (*aha*) refers to a portion of the day;
thus, it is a *kammadhāraya* compound. The term *sañjham* refers to the combination (*samāhāra*) of those three junctions (*sañjhā*).

"Combination" (*samāhāra*) means bringing together or unification; and since that does not occur for things existing at different times, it is [so called] because they are grasped by the intellect as being simultaneous.

Because they occur at the same time, there is a *digu* compound regarding that referent. For the teacher, considering that "samāhāra" means a collection (*samūha*) and that in relation to it there must be only the genitive case, does not apply the designation of a *aññapada* (relative) compound.
Furthermore, according to the rule "the vowel *ā* becomes short when it is non-predominant," [the form is established].
Since *samāhāra* is a state (*bhāva*), it takes the singular number because of its unity; however, when *samāhāra* is used in the sense of an object (*kamma*), there are three designations.

In the compound *samāhaṭā*, the plural number and the absence of the short vowel occur because, according to the first rule of compounds, the primary meaning of the individual words (*padatthapādhānya*) is emphasized.

69. The group of five [terms] concerns "night" (*ratti*). *Nisā*: It makes the body thin (*tanuṃ karoti*) by ceasing all activity; hence it is *nisā*. *Rajanī*: Those who are impassioned (*rāgino*) delight (*rajanti*) therein; the suffixes *yu* and *ī* are applied.

*Ratti*: It takes up (*gaṇhāti*) non-activity; hence it is *ratti*. Alternatively, they delight (*rajanti*) therein, thus it is *ratti*. This is according to the divisions of the first, middle, and last watches of the night.
That which has three watches (*yāma*) or periods (*pahāra*) is *tiyāmā*. It covers the day, thus it is *saṃvarī*.
*Nisīthinī*, *khaṇadā*, *khapā*, *vibhāvarī*, *tamassinī*, *yāminī*, *tamī*, and so forth, are also names for the night.

A night joined with the moon, endowed with the radiance of the moon, is called *juṇhā*; it is *juṇhā* because of its connection with the moonlight (*juṇhā*). That night in which darkness (*tama*) is predominant is called *tamussannā* or *timisikā*; it is *timisikā* because dense darkness (*timisa*) is abundant therein, according to the rule that the suffix *-ika* is added after a word ending in *-a*.
70. The Triplet on Midnight. The middle watch of the night, which constitutes the time for activity, is called *nisītha*, *aḍḍharatta*, and *mahānisā*.
It is *nisītha* because one sits (*nisīdati*) and lies down (*sayati*) therein. It is *aḍḍharatta* because it is half (*aḍḍha*) and it is night (*ratti*);

the word *ratti* here refers to a portion of the night, or alternatively, it is *aḍḍharatta* because it is half of the night (*rattiyā aḍḍha*). It is *mahānisā* because it is both great (*mahatī*) and night (*nisā*).
The tetrad concerns darkness (*andhakāra*). It is called "darkness" because it makes the world blind, struck, and devoid of vision.

It is "gloom" (*tama*) because one passes through it; or alternatively, "gloom" is so called because people here long for pleasure (*rati*); the root *tam* means "to long for. The word *tamas* is not feminine;
by association with that [root], *andhakāra* is also [masculine/neuter]. *Timisaṃ* is an island; or alternatively, from the root *tim* meaning "to moisten," they are moistened there.
*Atimisa* means "very dark. *Timira* is the same; it is derived from the prefix *ati*. 71.

Darkness possessing these four factors is called "fourfold darkness" (*caturaṅgatama*): that which completes fourteen nights, the dark fortnight known as the fourteenth day, a dense forest thicket, a mass of clouds, and midnight.
72. That which is both blind and dark is "blind-darkness" (*andhatama*); it is that which makes the world shrouded in gloom. This term *andhatama* refers to thick darkness or intense darkness.

*Dvayaṃ pahāre* (The word *pahāra* has two genders). It is called *pahāra* because the drum (*bheri*) and other instruments are struck (*paharīyate*) therein; the suffix *ap* is added in the masculine for the purpose of naming. By the rule *yā pāpuṇe mo*, or by *upayama*, [the word] *ahoratta* (day and night) becomes *yāma*; from *yamita* (that which is restrained), the suffix *ṇo* is added. That which is a *pahāra* itself is designated as a *yāma*;

thus it is known as *yāma*. The second lunar day is called *pāṭipada*. It is called *pāṭipada* because the moon (*canda*) enters (*paṭipajjate*) into its waning or waxing on that day. The third and subsequent days are simply *tithi*, not *pāṭipada*. It is called *tithi* because it extends (*tanoti*); or else, *tā* means "protection" and *ithi* is the suffix. The word *tithi* occurs in two genders.
73. *Dvayaṃ pannarasiyaṃ*: The fifteenth day is that which completes the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*); there is also a reading *paṇṇarasī*. *Dvayaṃ puṇṇamāyaṃ tithiyaṃ*:
[The two terms refer] to the lunar day of the full moon. By means of this, the waning and waxing of the lunar days is measured;

it is the moon, and it is the month (*māsa*) when it is full—thus it is the "full-moon month" (*puṇṇamāsa*). This is the lunar day of that month, or it is called *puṇṇamāsī* because the full-moon month belongs to it.
“Puṇṇo” means the moon; or “puṇṇamā” refers to that lunar day (tithi) when the moon is full. However, if the reading is “puṇṇimā,” then “puṇṇo” is the state of the moon being full.
From that [word] is derived the abstract suffix (bhāvapaccaya), and this [suffix] is seen in the sense of what is produced by that.
Because the gender follows worldly convention, it takes the feminine gender. When that full moon occurs with the moon lacking even a single digit, it is called “anumati.”
That which is consented to and followed along with the deities and ancestors is *anumati*. When the moon is full, it is called *puṇṇamā* or *rākā*;
"rākā" refers to the night providing the opportunity for seeing [the full moon]. As it is said: "When the moon is deficient in its digits it is *anumati*, when full it is *rākā*" (*Amarakośa* 4.8).
Another, occurring on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, is *amāvasī*, also called *amāvāsī*. They dwell together (*amā saha vasanti*) [with the sun].
The conjunction (*amāvasī*) of the sun and moon; *amāvāsī* is formed by lengthening the vowel, where the word *amā* is a prefix (*sahattha*) and an indeclinable (*abyaya*).

It is called *dassalā* (from *dassa*, as in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*), because the sun and moon are seen (*dissante*) there [by the reckoners], according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*. "By the reckoners" (*gaṇakehi*) is supplied from the *Gha*-commentary; its other names are *sūriyindusaṅgama* (the meeting of sun and moon). 74.
Time marked by sixty *ghaṭikās* is called a day-and-night (*ahoratta*). They are called *ghaṭikā* because they bring together (*ghaṭenti*) the day and night. *Aho*...
*Ca ratti ca ahoratto*, [meaning] day and night, is masculine. *Ahoratta* is also neuter when used as *adigutta*. Those fifteen days and nights are called a *pakkha* (fortnight).
It is called *pakkha* because by it beings (*bhūta*) "cook" or undergo transformation (*pacanti pariṇamanti*).

These two fortnights, consisting of the prior and posterior halves, are respectively known as the bright half (*sukkakāḷa*) and the dark half (*sukkakāḷapakkha*). According to the sequence of the science of astronomy (*jotisattha*), the bright fortnight is designated as the first.

The dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*) is designated as "the other" (*apara*). For that very reason, in the world, regarding specific months, there is the conventional usage (*rūḷhī*) of *sakapakka* and *parapakkha*, and even *aparapakkha*.
It is *sukka* because one grieves (*socanti*) here; it is so called because those who delight in darkness grieve therein, or because it indicates (*sūceti*) or makes manifest (*pakāseti*).

It is *kāra* because it scatters (*kirati*) what is bright (*sukka*); or it is *kāla* because of that very [darkness], or because of the light (*joti*) by which one delights (*arati*) therein. That very [light] is [the opposite].
The dark [fortnight]. Those two, the bright and the dark fortnights, combined, are called a month (*māsa*). [The root] *mas* means "measuring"; it takes the suffix *-ana*. 75–76.

The names of the twelve months according to the lunar asterisms (*nakkhatta*). A month joined with or characterized by the asterism Citrā, when the moon is full, is called Citta. Because it ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no lengthening of the vowel; this applies everywhere in the same way.
The state of being joined with the full moon is determined by the name of whichever asterism is present at that time.
The names of the twelve months should be understood. The twelve divisions beginning with Citta and ending with Phagguṇa are to be known as "months" (*māsa*) in their respective order.
Because it is praised (*pasattha*), it is *Jeṭṭha*; because of its connection with that [praise], it is *Jeṭṭha*. The sun (*ravi*) is not endurable (*asayha*) here, thus it is *Āsāḷha*.

In this [month] there is flowing (*savanti*), thus it is *Sāvaṇa* (by the suffix *yu*). Here fruits ripen (*phalanti*), thus it is *Phagguṇa* (by the suffix *yu*, with the substitution of *ḷa* for *la*).
Go, horse, and [return] in the month of Kattika. The month of Kattika is called *pacchimakattiko* (the latter Kattika); the month of Assayuja is called *pubbakattiko* (the former Kattika).

77. There are two [months] in the month of Sāvaṇa. Here, the sun goes out from within the street (*antovīthi*); the suffix *-anīya* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). There are two [months] in the month of Citta. It makes the worlds delightful (*ramma*) through the variety of various flowers and fruits; or, it is called *rammaka* because people delight (*ramanti*) therein. 78.
From the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika—that is, starting from *pacchimakattika*—four months each follow in succession.

The seasons are known as *hemanta* (winter), *gimha* (summer), and *vassāna* (the rains). *Hemanta*: It is called *hemanta* because cold (*hima*) exists therein; thus it is *hemanta*, just as *suttanta* and *vananta* [are formed].
Alternatively, it is *hemanta* because everything there undergoes decline (*hinoti*); the suffix *-anta* is added and the augment *m* is inserted. *Gimhāna*:
It is called *gimhāna* because it oppresses or torments (*girati pīḷayati*); the suffix *-māna* is added, the vowel *i* is shortened to *u*, and there is a change of phonemes. *Vassāna*: It rains...

Here, "the rains" refers to the rainy season (*vassa*). Regarding the phrase "the climate in two," it is the word *utu* itself that applies to the two [seasons], not the winter (*hemanta*) and so forth;
however, in the *Amarakosa*, the word *utu* is stated to be masculine (*pume*), as in *Amarakośa* 4.20.79.
Furthermore, in order to show the divisions of the climate, he states "winter," etc., which expresses the common usage of the noble ones (*ariya-sāmañña*). Or else, according to what has been said:
This is according to the statement explained in the classification of the three seasons (*utu*). However, this was said with reference to the phrase "starting from the dark fortnight of Kattika.

Therefore, beginning from the dark fortnight of Kattika, there are six seasons (*utu*)—Winter (*hemanta*), Cool Season (*sīsira*), Spring (*vasanta*), Summer (*gimha*), Rains (*vassāna*), and Autumn (*sarada*)—each consisting of two months in successive order. [The term *utu* is so called] because it returns again and again.

Having made [the word *sisira*], it is called *issa u*. *Sisira* means cool; because of its connection with that, it is *sisira*. There is no lengthening due to the rule of vowel combination (*vā-vidhānato*), and the letter *m* serves for euphonic junction (*padasaṃdhikaro*).

*Vasa* is used in the sense of shining. That which is inhabited is *vasanta* (spring). Because of the presence of flowers (*pupphadhannuttā*) or because of being possessed of flowers (*pupphavantattā*), desire dwells here, thus it is *vasanta*.
That in which one remembers (*sarati*) or is oppressed (*pīḷayati*) is *sarada* (autumn); there is the substitution of *do* for it. *Sā*...
Or, it is called *sarado* because dogs (*sunakhā*) delight (*ramanti*) there;

[the suffix] *do* is added after the root *sara*. 80–81. A triad concerning summer (*gimha*). It is called *uṇho* because it heats (*usati*) and burns (*dahati*); [the suffix] *ṇho* is added, and there is the elision of the letter *sa*.

It is called *nidāgho* because they lie down (*nidahante*) in it; [the suffix] *gho* is substituted for *ha*. It is called *gimho* because it oppresses (*girati*) and torments (*pīḷayati*); [the suffix] *mo* is added, *ho* is substituted for *ra*, and there is a change of phonemes (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*). A triad concerning the rainy season (*vassānu*).

It rains (*vassati*), it rains continuously (*pavassati*) there; thus it is *vasso*, *vassāno*, and *pāvuso*. [The suffix] *-u* is added to *assa*, and there is the elision of the conjunct (*saṃyogalopa*).
By means of the three seasons beginning with *vassāna* (the rainy season), the sun’s southern course (*dakkhiṇāyana*), its movement toward the southern direction, occurs;

by means of the other three—*sisira* (winter), *vasanta* (spring), and *gimha* (summer)—its northern course (*uttarāyana*), its movement toward the northern direction, occurs. [The root] *i* is used in the sense of motion (*gati*), in the abstract state (*bhāve*).
*Yū*, *ayana*. Beginning from the transition into Puṣya until Āṣāḍhā, during which the sun moves northward, is the northern course (*uttarāyana*).
Beginning from the transition into Āṣāḍhā until Puṣya, during which the sun moves southward, is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).

"The two rainy courses" (*vassoyanadvaya*): these two courses combined are called the "rainy season" (*vassa*). It is called *vassa* because [beings] grow (*vassanti*) therein, or because it is characterized by the rainy season (*vassakāla*).
*Vassa* is like *citta* and *cakkhudasaka*.
*Pajjaddha* means half-year. *Saṃvaccharo*, *saṃcharo*, and *sassa co*—*vaccharo* is also a name for that same thing. These do not possess the feminine gender;
they are not feminine (*anitthī*). *Paccāsatyā* is autumn (*sarad*); *paccāsatyā* is also [a term for] a year (*hāyana*).
*Sarada* is characterized by the autumn season, as in the expressions "the month of Sotadassa" or "Vesākha. *Hāyana* means one who abandons or develops;

or, in terms of its literal meaning, it is *hāyana* because it moves (*ayati*) while abandoning (*jahanto*). *Samā* means it brings together (*samayati*), differentiates (*vikalayati*), or develops (*bhāveti*); the root *sam-* is used in the sense of completeness (*vekalpe*).
According to Rudda: "In the sense of a year, *samā* is feminine; *samaṃ* is used for all things that are equal."

For the sake of skill in all conventional expressions regarding all beings, for the sake of all assemblies and all modes of practice, and because it pertains to time and its divisions, even the measure of a celestial year mentioned in the systems of others (*parasamaya*) should be cited and explained here. For indeed, one month of human beings is a day and night for the Pitṛs;
likewise, one year of human beings is a day and night for the gods. Therein, the period of the sun’s northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)...
A day for the gods is a night, while the southern course of the sun is their night.
For the deities, twelve thousand years constitute a *yuga*, measured by a period of three hundred and sixty-one days and nights per year. Thus it is said:
“This twelve-thousand-year span is proclaimed as a *yuga*.”
“Ah, this which has been proclaimed as the Brahma [lifespan] is multiplied a thousandfold,” according to the *Vedadīpaka* treatise.
And that four-yuga period of humans is two thousand divine [years], which constitutes two days for Brahmā.
The four yugas are by way of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. Among them, the measure of the Kṛta-yuga, in terms of human reckoning, is twenty-eight thousand [years].
Seventeen million years for the Kṛta age; twelve million and ninety-six thousand years for the Tretā;
eight million and sixty-four thousand years for the Dvāpara; and four million and thirty-two thousand years for the Kali. And it is said:
“Empty, empty, space—these are for the Nāgas; for the Karamuni-sāsanas, pride and intoxication;
for the Yuganaddha, *māna* and *mada*; for the Tretā, *khaṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *suñña*.
Six, nine, and twelve are the established numbers of years.”
"Suñña, suñña, kha, and vedā; rasabhujaga—this is the number of years in the Dvāpara age. Suñña, ākāsa, saṅkha, and netta;
guṇa and jalanidhi—this is the number of years in the Kali age."

This aggregate [of years] is forty-three lakhs and twenty thousand years. And it is said: “The sky, space, emptiness, cloth, teeth, and oceans—this is the collection of measures for the four yugas. By one day and night of Brahmā, two *kappas* of humans pass.
Within that period, there are eight *nāgas*, two *karas*, seven *munis*, one moon, six tastes, twelve suns, the four Vedas, and the oceans;
two eyes, three qualities, thirty-two teeth—[all these] established by their respective numerical values.
The number should be grasped. The words *khā*, *kāsa*, and *ambara* are synonyms for "zero" (*suñña*). And zero is included within the calculation by means of the dot (*bindu*).
All of this should be expanded in pairs, in reverse order. Therein, the expansion of the Kṛta-yuga is as follows:
1,728,000. Of the Tretā as follows: 1,296,000. Of the Dvāpara as follows: 864,000. Of the Kali as follows: 432,000. [This is] the aggregate of the four yugas.
And as follows: 4,320,000. Taking the final digit of the sequence of the yugas and the sum respectively, one should count in reverse order. It is as follows:
“One, ten, a hundred, and likewise a thousand, ten thousand;”
"A hundred thousand (lakkha) and a million (niyuta), each ten times greater than the preceding.

Among these, ten thousand is an *ayuta*; ten hundred thousand is a *niyuta*. Since those [higher numbers] do not exist in the *kali* and *dvāpara* ages, one should calculate there only up to the limit of a hundred thousand (*lakkha*).
Thus, by means of the figures for the *yugas* and their total sum, the number of years previously stated becomes known.
Therein, a day of Brahmā is an eon of arising for humans, while his night is an eon of destruction.
During one day of Brahmā, fourteen human ages (manvantaras) occur. The measure of one such human age is seventy-one divine yugas;
that [human age] is equivalent to two hundred and eighty-four yugas, plus fourteen more, according to the human reckoning.
Thus, by means of fourteen *manvantaras*, there are nine hundred ninety-four *yuga* periods. However, the human measure consists of four sets of twenty-four thousand *yugas*.

And within these ninety-nine hundred and seventy-six *yugas* of the *manvantaras*, the number of human years is seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand; this is the measure of the *yugas* as they have been calculated.
There are five junctures (*sandhi*). Therefore it is said in the *Sūryasiddhānta* (1.18–19):
“Seventy-one cycles of the ages (*yuga*) are here called an intermediate period of Manu (*manvantara*).
At its end, the number of those [ages] is completed; the juncture (*sandhi*) is said to be a deluge of water.”
“O Mānava, those with their junctions (sandhi) are to be known as fourteen in an aeon (kappa);
the measure of the aeons from Kṛta onwards is established as fifteen with their junctions.
The measure of the Kali age is by one quarter; that of Dvāpara by two quarters; and that of Tretā by three quarters.
This cycle of four ages (catuyuga) revolves like a wheel; through fifteen conjunctions (sandhi), there are twenty-four ages of men.

But for the gods, it is a wheel of ages. When these fourteen manvantaras, together with their conjunctions, are combined as one, they constitute a thousand ages of the gods, which is a thousand four-age cycles of men; and that is one day of Brahmā.
Another person is a *manu* during this *manvantara*; indeed, the sons of Brahmā are the *manus*. 82.
The pentad on the aeon of destruction (*khayakappa*). It is called an *kappa* because the world is destroyed (*kappati*) within it. They perish therein, thus it is a "destruction" (*khaya*).
An *kappa* and a destruction are therefore *kappakkhayā*. The world contracts, ceases, or is destroyed within this [aeon].
*Saṃvaṭṭa*. That which is born at the end of the four *yugas* is the *yuganta* (end of the age). That wherein the world dissolves and wastes away is *palaya*;

it is masculine; the suffix *-ṇo* is used for the sake of forming a noun. However, some here, having cited the reading "the destruction of the *kappa*," assume that two words have a single designation;
this does not accord with the *Amarakośa* or its commentary. For it is said therein: "*Saṃvaṭṭo*, *palayo*..."
“*Kappa*, *khaya*, and *kappanta-micca-pi*” (Amarakośa 4.22), and “the group of five [terms] ending in *khaya* and *kappa*” (Amara 4.22).
The pair refers to *kāḷakaṇṇī*. Because it is to be censured, it is not marked with auspicious signs; thus it is *alakkhī*. It makes its own support appear black-colored because it does not shine;
