thus it is *kāḷakaṇṇī*—from the root *kar*, the suffix *ṇo*, the short vowel *a* becomes *ṇo*, and the vowel *ī*. The pair refers to *siri*. Because it is to be praised...
*Lakkhī* means "she who is perceived. *Sirī* means "she who is resorted to by those who have performed merit," or "she who resorts to them";

[the suffixes] *ro* and *ī* are added. 83. Two [names] for the mother of the Danus. From the root *dā*, meaning "to cut" (*avakhaṇḍane*), she who cuts is *danu*. Two [names] for the mother of the Devas. She who is called *ditī* is the stepmother of the Asuras;

because she is their adversary, she is *aditi*. 84. *Āguntaṃ* refers to evil. Because one protects (*pānti*) oneself from it, it is *pāpa*; there is the addition of the letter *pa*, and it leads to a miserable rebirth (*duggatiṃ*).

It is "evil" (*pāpa*) because it is blameworthy. It is "misdeed" (*kibbisa*) because by it one is made to waver or become lax; or alternatively, it is *kibbisa* because the suffix *-issa* (from *karoti*) denotes that which produces undesirable fruit, thus making it *ibbisa*.
It is "enmity" (*vera*) because one proceeds with what is deformed. It is "misfortune" (*agha*) because it does not destroy grain;
here *hana* becomes *gha*, or else it is *agha* because it is a place not to be approached by the virtuous (*sādhu*). The root *hana* means "to go. It is "wicked conduct" (*kuccharita*).
*Duṣcaritaṃ*: Its performance is censured (*du*), thus it is *dukkaṭa*. It does not purify, thus it is *apuñña*. It is the opposite of the wholesome, thus it is *akusala*.
It destroys (*hanati*) happiness (*kaṃ*), thus it is *kaṇha*; this is a reversal of the color (*vaṇṇa*). By means of it, turbidity (*kalusa*) is stirred up;
or, cutting away (*lunanto*) happiness (*kaṃ*), it lies there, thus it is *kalusa*. Its movement (*itaṃ*) is censured (*du*), thus it is *durita*. It is not to be gone toward.
*Āgu*: that by which one goes is *āgu*; or, it is *āgu* because one goes while afflicting (*āpīḷayaṃ*). For it is said in the *Ekakkharakosa*:

“*Ā* [is used] in the sense of ‘anger’ (*kodha*) and ‘arrogance’ (*udāṭṭi*)” (85–86). The group of six [terms] refers to *dhamma*. They are called *kusā* because they dwell (*senti*) in the continuum (*santāna*) in a contemptible manner; these are lust (*rāga*) and so forth. That which cuts (*lunāti*) or severs these is *kusala*.
It makes happiness (*sukhaṃ*), or its performance (*karaṇa*) is beautiful (*sobhana*), thus it is *sukata*. It makes happiness, thus...
It is bright (*sukka*). It purifies, thus it is merit (*puñña*). It sustains everything, thus it is the Dhamma.

However, others say that "meritorious Dhamma" (*puññadhamma*) is a single compound word; this should not be accepted, as it contradicts the *Amarakosa* (4.24). His conduct is beautiful, thus it is well-conducted (*sucarita*).

The triad refers to that which pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). "Present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) means the manifest personal existence; that which is produced therein is "pertaining to the present life."
"Born in this world" means pertaining to this world (*ihalokika*). "Born in the visible, immediate personal existence" means visible and immediate (*sandidṭṭhika*).
Two [terms] refer to the future life (*samparāyika*); their meaning is easily understood from the literal sense of the words. Two [terms] refer to that very time (*takkāla*);
it is "that-time" because it is born at that very moment, not at a proximate time or the like. At that [time], it is precisely then...
"Born in time" (*kāle jātaṃ*) means "the present" (*tadātvaṃ*); *tadāttam* is also a reading for this. "The two" refers to the future time (*āyatikāle*).
"Subsequent time" (*uttarakālo*) is the later time. It is called "future" (*āyati*) because it will come; the prefix *ā-* is used here with the root *i* meaning "to go.

And herein, whatever is distant or near within this present existence is "pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikaṃ*). But whatever is even more distant, whether in this present existence or in the next world, that is the "future" (*āyati*).
87–88. *Pāmodante* means "they rejoice. That by which one laughs is "laughter" (*hāsa*). One whose self (*attā*)—that is, the mind (*mano*)—is [joyful] is "glad-minded" (*attamana*).
For the mind of one who is corrupted is not called "self"; the state of that [mind] is "gladness of mind" (*attamanatā*), which is joy (*pāmojja*).

It refreshes and satisfies, thus it is "rapture" (*pīti*). One finds happiness by means of this, thus it is "well-being" (*vitti*). One is satisfied by means of this, thus it is "contentment" (*tuṭṭhi*); because it accompanies that [rapture], it is well-being (*vitti*), due to its concomitance with that.
*Pīti* is joy; *attamanatā*, however, is a distinct category of form according to the detailed exposition (*niddesa*).
It is called *ānanda* because it intensely gladdens (*ā-nandati*). *Muda* means laughter; hence *pamuda* and *āmoda*. *Santussana* is contentment (*santosā*). *Nandana* is delight (*nandi*).
*Sammada*—as well as *sammadā* and *sammuda* (or *sammada*)—is so called because the vowel *u* becomes *a*. *Pāmojja* is the state of a person or of the mind that has become delighted (*pamodita*).

The triad refers to happiness (*sukha*). It is called *sukha* because it digs well (*suṭṭhu khaṇati*); [the suffix] *kvi* is applied. It is called *sāta* because it is tasted or relished (*sādīyati assādīyati*). It is called *phāsu* because it touches with affection (*sinehati*);
or, it is called *phāsu* because it touches upon or removes (*bādhati*) suffering (*dukkha*). The heptad refers to what is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*). The root *bhadi* means "to be auspicious";

it is called *bhadda* because it makes things auspicious. It is called *seyyo* because it is more excellent due to being highly praised. It is called *sobhaṃ* because it shines. The root *khī* means "to destroy" (*khaye*); it is called *khema* because it destroys what is unhappy (*asukha*).

*Khema* means secure (*mo*). *Kalyāṇa* means that which moves toward or goes to what is wholesome (*kalya*) and free from disease; or, it brings about and leads to what is wholesome and beneficial (*hita*), thus it is *kalyāṇa*.

The intention is that the suffix *-ṇa* is applied when the root is *kaḷ* (to move) and the word *kalya* is the accompanying term (*upapada*). *Maṅgala* means prosperity (*maṅga*); it is that which moves toward or brings forth fortune (*dhañña*), thus it is *maṅgala*, according to the *alo* rule.
*Siva* means that which pacifies suffering (*sameti dukkhaṃ*), according to the *vo* rule.
89. *Chakkaṃ dukkhe*. Here, endurance is difficult; thus, it is *dukkha*. [The root] *kas* means to go; that which is scraped away (*kasati*) is non-merit, hence it is *kasiraṃ*.
Alternatively, one who lies down in a contemptible manner (*kucchitena ākārena seti*) is *kasiraṃ*. [The root] *kir* means to scatter; that which scatters happiness is *kicchaṃ*.
Or, that by which a desire to perform merit has been made is *kicchaṃ*, for it is said: “Faith has suffering as its proximate cause.”
"Nīgha" means that here there is no striving (*īhā*) for the sake of attainment; *gha* is substituted for *ha*.
Alternatively, it is "nīgha" because it destroys merit (*puñña*), harms, or goes away; or it is "nīgha" because it does not destroy or go toward merit.

That by which one falls into misfortune is "byasana"; or it is "byasana" because it specifically exhausts or wastes away. That which does not destroy prosperity is "agha. These are the evils and so forth.

In the case of a quality (*guṇa*), the gender is as previously stated. Words denoting evil, merit, happiness, and so forth—as well as *ākiccha* (distress) and *kiccha* (difficulty)—when used in reference to a substance (*dabba*) that possesses those qualities, function in all three genders. For example:
*A pāpā utumatī kaññā*, "An evil girl in her menses," *A pāpo rājāpyarakkhako*, "An evil king who does not protect."
Pāpa is a clan of hunters, violent; Pāpa is a brahmin and a servant.
Puñña is this ford, Puñña is the river, Puñña is this mountain.
Sukha is a clan of sensualists, [all] soft; happy is the dwelling with one’s mother and with one’s kin.
Happy is the pursuit of a young woman, happy indeed is the seizing of Maghavā, happy is the seizing of a young woman (ka.).

However, when one wishes to express only the quality—such as happiness and so forth—as the qualifier (*visesya*), and not the substance (*dabbam*) [as was previously the qualifier], then, as it is not seen in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*, the gender is determined solely by the distinction of the form (*rūpabheda*).
For example: "Whether in poverty, in strength, or in wealth, one’s own retinue is happy."
“Happy is dwelling with the virtuous, and happy is supreme peace.

Now, one might ask: since the three modes of conduct—“This action was ill-done,” “This is well-done karma,” and “This action of mine is defiled”—exist for others as well, why is there a mention of only evil and merit?
It is said in reply: “Ill-done is *dukkaṭa* (ill-performed).”
The usage [of the term] in the three genders occurs even when based on action (*kriyā*), as in "well done" (*suṭṭhu kataṃ*) or "beautifully made" (*sukataṃ*);

it is not necessarily based on quality (*guṇa*) alone. When even the word *kalusa* (turbid/evil) is observed to have a specific usage in refined applications across the three genders, then the inclusion of the word *pāpa* (evil/bad) should be explained as having the primary sense of "matter" (*attha*). 90.
The group of five [words] refers merely to wholesome and unwholesome karma (*subhāsubhakamma*). That which possesses a portion of desirable or undesirable fruition is "fortune" (*bhāgya*).
It is *niyati* because it leads to beautiful and ugly results. It is *bhāga* because it distributes beautiful and ugly results.

It is *bhāgadheyya* because the distribution (*bhāga*) of desirable and undesirable things (*dheyya*) is deposited (*dhīyati*) therein. It is *vidhi* because it ordains (*vidadhāti*) beautiful and ugly results.
*Aya*, *subhāvaha*, *deva*, *diṭṭha*, and so forth, are also names for the mere state of beautiful and ugly kamma. The pentad [of terms] refers to birth (*jāti*). Arising is *uppatti*.
*Nippajjana* means arising; [the root] *pada* means "going," preceded by *ni*. See this, O wise one! *Janana* means birth (*jāti*). It is called *janana* because it is produced (*janīyate*).
*Ubbhava* means arising upwards. 91. *Pajja* [is used] in the sense of cause.
That which brings about its own fruit is a *nimitta*; [the root] *mā* means "measure," preceded by *ni*. [The suffix] *ka* forms the word.

They bear fruit as their cause. It is called a *ṭhāna* (basis) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein. It is called a *pada* (foot/track) because by means of it the fruit goes (*pajjati*) or lies down (*nipajjati*).
It is called a *bīja* (seed) because from it [the fruit] is specifically born (*visesena jāyati*), with the short vowel becoming long.

It is called a *nibandhana* (bond) because it binds and sets in motion its own fruit without remainder (*nissesena*). It is called a *nidāna* (source) because by means of it something is led forth (*nidīyate*) or extracted (*nicchīyate*); [it is formed with the suffix] *yu*, for it lays down (*nidadāti*) the fruit.

Or it is the *nidāna* (source). It is called *pabhava* because the fruit originates (*pabhavati*) from it. It is called *hetu* because it impels (*hinoti*), goes toward, and transforms the continuity of the form of the effect;
or else, it is *hetu* because the fruit is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) therein—*hi* meaning "establishment. It is called *sambhava* because the fruit arises (*sambhavati*) by means of it.
It is called *setu* because it binds (*sinoti*) the fruit. It is called *paccaya* because the fruit comes (*eti*) depending upon (*paṭicca*) it.

92. That cause which is proximate, or more proximate than others with respect to its fruit, is considered the *padaṭṭhāna* (proximate cause). It is the station (*ṭhāna*) of the terms (*padānaṃ*), that is, of the causes;

thus it is called *padaṭṭhāna*, just as one says "king of kings" (*rājarājā*). There are three kinds of causes: the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), the cooperative cause (*sahakārīkāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*kāraṇakāraṇa*).
For example, the seed is the *padaṭṭhāna* of the sprout in the sense of being its material cause, while the earth, water, and so forth are [its other causes].
The cooperative cause (*sahakārī-kāraṇa*) is as follows: "Fever is the cause of the trembling of karma; phlegm is the cause of that [fever].
Thus, phlegm is the causal cause (*kāraṇakāraṇa*) of the trembling of karma.
This triad concerns the body, the dominant influence, and the deity. That by which sentient beings live is the life-force (*jīva*). One who fulfills the desire for a support is a person (*purisa*).

*Ātman*: That by which beings constantly go (*atanti*) or proceed is the *ātman*. The pair [of terms] refers to the states of being characterized by passion (*rajas*), purity (*sattva*), and darkness (*tamas*). *Pradhāna*:

That in which qualities (*guṇa*), namely passion, purity, and darkness, as well as form (*rūpa*), are placed (*padhīyante*) or dissolved (*palīyante*) is the *pradhāna*; [the suffix] *yu* is added. *Prakṛti*:

That which produces (*pakaroti*) effects such as sound and so forth for the sake of human enjoyment is *prakṛti*; [the suffix] *ti* is added. The designations "passion," "purity," and "darkness" refer respectively to delusion (*moha*), attachment (*rāga*), and aversion (*dveṣa*).

Existence (*bhāva*) with mindfulness is *sattaṃ*; it is the state of being established. That in which beings are attached is *rajo*; it is the state of being bound. That in which beings perish is *tamo*;
it is the state of fleeing. 93. By way of their course, there are names for living beings. That by which beings breathe and live is *pāṇo* (breath); one who possesses that is a *pāṇo*.
One who possesses a body, reckoned as a physical frame, is a *sarīrī*. That which comes into being through karma is *bhūtaṃ*; [this term is used] in the neuter, and also in the masculine.

The word *vāsa* has the sense of "meaning. It is called a *satta* because it is attached (*sañjati*) to form and so forth; even those devoid of desire and lust are called *satta* by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*).

A *dehī* is one who possesses a body (*deha*), that is, a physical frame (*kāya*). It is called *pūti* because it fills (*pūreti*); a *puggala* is one who swallows—that is, consumes—food known as putrid (*pūti*), with the elision of the suffix *ta*.
Alternatively, it is called *pugga* because it goes filling the life-span of beings; a *puggala* is one who takes (*lāti*) or eats (*bhakkhati*) that [life-span].
That by which they live is "life" (*jīva*); one who possesses that is a "living being" (*jīva*). One who possesses the aforementioned "breath" (*pāṇa*) is a "sentient being" (*pāṇin*).

Because it is born in various ways, it is "progeny" (*pajā*). It is called "creature" (*jantu*) because it is born. It is called "person" (*jana*) because it generates wholesome and unwholesome [kamma].

It is called "world" (*loka*) because it breaks up; from the root *luja*, meaning destruction, with the suffix *ko*. He is called the "Tathāgata" because he goes in the same way as previous beings go toward birth, aging, and death.

94. The phenomena beginning with visible form (*rūpa*), which are apprehended by the eye and so forth, are called "objects" (*gocara*), "supporting objects" (*ālamba*), "spheres" (*visaya*), "objects of cognition" (*ārammaṇa*), and "bases" (*ālambaṇa*).
It is called *rūpa* because it manifests and makes known its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). It is called *sadda* (sound) because it is uttered;

or, from the root *sapp* meaning "to go," it is *sadda* because it is understood (*sappate*) by means of it. *Gandha* (odor) is derived from the root *add*, for *addana* means "striking" or "afflicting."

It is called *gandha* because it is sought after (*yācana*), or because it is desired (*abhilasīyate*), or because it indicates and reveals its own basis as "there is this here," like one who slanders;
thus it is *gandha*. It is called *rasa* because beings taste (*rasanti*) and relish it; thus it is *rasa*. It is called *phassa* because it is touched (*phusīyati*); thus it is *phassa*.
They are called *gocara* because the senses (*gāva*) move within them. They are called *ārammaṇa* because they are apprehended by mind and mental factors (*cittacetasika*).

*Ālambā*. If preceded by *vi*, [the root *bandh*] means "they bind"; thus, they bind the faculties (*indriya*), hence they are called *visaya*. They are called *ārammaṇa* because the mind and mental factors (*cittacetasika*) come and take delight (*ramanti*) therein; [the suffix] *yu* is added.
These are also called *indriyattha* (objects of the faculties), because they are desired or longed for (*atthyante*) by the faculties.

95. Regarding *sukka* at the end of a verse: *suc* means sorrow; they grieve (*socanti*) because of it, and those who desire that [state] are called *sukka*; [the suffix] *a*. *Gu* means sound; it is sounded (*guyate*).
*Kittīyati* means it is praised; thus *goro*. In the *Ro* and *Si* [recensions], it is *sevīyati*, thus *sito*; or, it binds the mind, thus *sito*. It cleanses all colors, thus *odāto*.
The root *dā* in the sense of breaking apart, preceded by *ava-*. One runs toward or is purified by this, thus *dhavalo*; the suffix *alo*.

The root *sita* in the sense of color, with the suffix *ṇo*, thus *seto*. The root *paḍi* in the sense of motion; it shines forth or makes manifest, thus *paṇḍaro*; the suffix *aro*. *Suci*, *visado*.
*Ajjuṇa* and *sukka* are names for white. The group of six [terms] refers to red.
*Soṇa* means "in color"; *ṇo* [is a suffix]; *rattuppalavaṇṇo* means "the color of a red lotus. *Ruha* means "to produce," from which *latte* [is derived], meaning "red.

That by which they are colored is *ratto*; the root *ranja* means "to dye. *Tambo* is a specific type of metal known as copper (*udumbara*); it is called *tambo* because of its copper-colored nature. *Mañjeṭṭhā*...
The *rattavalli* is the name of a plant by which ivory and other such objects are dyed red; because of its color, it is called *mañjeṭṭha*. *Rohita* means "red-like";
the only distinction is that it is lac (*alakta*).

96. Up to *sāmala*, [the colors] are black. *Nīla* means "in the color. It is *kaṇha* because it "scrapes" (*kassati*); from the root *kas* meaning "to scrape," with the suffix *ṇho*. It is not white (*sito*).
*Asita*: "As" means to be fit; by virtue of being a single portion among colors, it is fit, thus it is *kāla*.

That very thing is *kāḷa*. *Mac*, *maci* mean to grind (*kakkana*); grinding is pulverizing. That which grinds white and other colors is *mecaka*; the suffix *ṇvu* [is applied], and this is its state. *Sā* means to make thin;
that which is made thin, or is diminished by opposing colors, is *sāma*. *Sāmala* is like *sāma*; the only difference is the suffix *mala*.
The word *paṇḍu* is used for white and yellow; the meaning is that the word *paṇḍu* is stated for a color that is a mixture of white and yellow.

And it is said in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (5.13): "A pale color (*paṇḍuvaṇṇa*) is described as being joined with white and yellow. It is called *paṇḍu* because it goes (*gacchati*) into a single reckoning (*ekagaṇana*);
[the root] *paḍi* is in the sense of going, with the suffix *u*. *Hariṇo*, *paṇḍuro*, and *paṇḍuvaṇṇa* are also names for this color. *Īsapaṇḍu* means slightly pale.
*Abhyattapaṇḍuvaṇṇo* is called *dhūsara*, meaning the color of dust; [the root] *dhūs* is used in the sense of making grey (*kantikaraṇe*), belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, with the suffix *ara*. 97.
*Kiñciratto* is the slightly reddish color called *aruṇa*, such as the eye of a fish or the redness of the eyes of one intoxicated by passion (*Cintāmaṇiṭīkā* 5.15);

it is said to be the young sun. *Setalohito* is the color mixed with white and red, called *pāṭala*, such as the *pāṭala* flower. It is *pāṭala* because it causes to split (*pāṭayati*); [the suffix] *ala*, from the root *paṭ* in the sense of dividing (*vibhājane*).

The suffix *ka* occurs after the root *pī* (to drink) with the addition of *ta*, *ī*, and *tta*. That which has a luster like turmeric is *haliddābha*. The triad [of suffixes] applies to a color found on grass, leaves, and so forth.

From the root *las* (to shine), *palāsa* is derived in the sense of shining intensely; in the reading *pālāsa*, however, there is the lengthening of the short vowel. From the root *hṛ* (to take away), *harita* is derived in the sense of "taking the mind," hence it is green (*ito*).

*I* and *hari* [are also used]. 98. The words *kaḷāra* and *kapila* are used for a color mixed with blue and yellow. From the root *kala* (to count), *kaḷāra* is formed by changing *la* to *ḷa*. From the root *kaba* (to color), *kapila* is formed with the suffix *ila* and the change of *ba* to *pa*.

*Piṅga* refers to one whose radiance is like that of yellow orpiment (*rocanā*), having a glow similar to yellow orpiment; *piśaṅga* is also used. The word *prabhā* (radiance) possesses both genders. The root *pij* has the sense of shining; thus, *piṅga*. When the letter *s* is added subsequently, it becomes *piśaṅga*.

Having shown that the four terms beginning with *kaḷāra* express specific types of tawny-brown (*piṅgala*), he says "beginning with *kaḷāra*" etc., in order to show that they also express the general meaning of *piṅgala*.
This is its meaning: not only do *kaḷāra* and the others denote specific types of tawny-brown...
They occur [in these senses], yet they also occur in the sense of "Piṅgalasāmaññattha" (the general meaning of Piṅgala). For it is said in the Amarakosa:

"Kaḷāra, Kapila, Piṅga, Pisaṅga, Kaḍḍu, and Piṅgala" (Amarakośa 5.16). However, some maintain that the four words beginning with *kaḷāra* and ending with *pisaṅga*, when denoting the quality (*guṇa*) of being tawny (*piṅgala*), function in the masculine;
but when denoting the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), they follow the gender of the word used to describe them. Thus...
They speak by connecting it with what follows; however, because that contradicts the *Amarakośa* and because here all [colors] beginning with white (*sukka*) are included, it should not be accepted.

99. The triad [of terms] refers to something similar to the throat of a cuckoo when it is weak. In *kalyate*, *kala* means "time" (*kāla*); in *masi*, the suffix *ṇo* is applied in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*) and action (*karman*). It is *kala*.

*Kammāsa* is [derived from] *māsa* (month) and *kamma* (work); *lassa* is a suffix, and *kala* means time. Because one measures (*masati*) that [time], it is *kammāsa*, just as in the case of "potter" (*kumbhakāra*).

*Saba* is in the sense of going; because it goes (*sabatī*), it is *sabala*—the suffix is *ala*. It is called *citto* because it is thought (*ciyyate*); the suffix is *ta*. With the *traṇa* suffix, it becomes *citro*.
*Kammīro* and *kabburo* are also names for *sabalo*.
When mixed with black and yellow, it is called *sāva*. It is *sāva* because it flows (*sayati*) in its course; [the suffix] *-ava* is used. *Kapisota* is also a name for *sāva*.

When mixed with black and red, however, they are called *dhūma* and *dhūmala* when they have a smoky appearance. It is *dhūma* because it is like smoke (*dhūmo viya*). It is *dhūmala* because it takes on (*lāti*) smoke.

When these—beginning with *sukka* (white)—which possess the quality of flowing (*sāvantā*), are applied to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) by way of non-differentiation (*abhedopacāra*), [they denote the substance itself].

In that case, it takes the gender of the word it qualifies (*vāccaliṅga*); for example, *sukko haṃso* (a white swan), *sukkā haṃsī* (a white female swan), *sukkaṃ haṃsakulaṃ* (a white flock of swans), and so forth—this should be applied accordingly.

When they denote a quality (*guṇa*) or the mere state of being a quality (*guṇamatta*), then they are masculine; for example, *haṃsassa sukko* (the whiteness of the swan), *mayūrassa citto* (the variegation of the peacock), and so forth—this should be applied accordingly.

100. That which ends in the suffix *-lāsa* denotes dancing. From the root *nata*, meaning "bending of the limbs," there is the substitution of *nacca* due to the rules beginning with *pabbajjā*. Dancing is the act of *natanaṃ*.
*Naṭanaṃ* or *naccaṃ*; in all cases, these are nouns derived from verbal roots (*bhāvasādhana*). It is danced, thus *nattanam*. It is performed with grace (*lasati*), thus *lāsanaṃ*;
the root *lasa* means "to shine" (*kānti*), or alternatively, it is that which ought to be performed gracefully, thus *lāsanaṃ*.
*Naccaṃ*, *vāditaṃ*, and *gītaṃ*—this triad of arts is called *nāṭya* (dramatic performance), according to Amara 7.10. *Tura*.
*Tur* is used in the sense of "hurting. That by which one is hurt is *tūriya*, such as a drum (*muraja*) and so forth. The sound produced from that is *tūriya*; [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied.

A triad characterized by that is the *tūriyat-tika*. This belongs to a dancer, thus it is *nāṭya*. Because of the commonality with the third [category], *tūriya*, there are also dramatic plays (*nāṭaka*).
101. A place for dancing, such as a royal courtyard and the like, is called a *raṅga*. [It is so called because] "they go there while delighting; they take pleasure (*rajjanti*) there."
Or, taking it as "ettha" (here). *Sūjhasūcanaṃ* is the indication by means of the hands and so forth;

it is the pointing out or manifestation of that which is to be indicated or manifested, such as a sword-stroke and the like, and is called *abhinaya*. This is because "naya" means leading (*nayanaṃ*), and it is "leading toward those who are looking.
*Byañjaka* is also a name for that same thing.

The detailed exposition of thirty-two types of *aṅgahāra*—such as *bharata-sārthavāha*, *aṣṭottaraśataka-karaṇa-niṣpanna-sthirahasta-parivartaka*, and so forth—is to be seen in the fourth chapter of the *Nāṭya-śāstra* composed by the sage Bharata. *Aṅgahāra* is a specific kind of dance consisting of the movement of the limbs;
it is called *aṅgahāra* because it is "the carrying (*hāra*) or movement (*vikkhepa*) of the limbs. [The term] *tīka* refers to an actor. Everywhere.
The means of accomplishing the action [is shown] by such examples as, "one who dances is a dancer. 102.
The nine aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), beginning with the erotic (*siṅgāra*), are the sentiments of drama because they are to be relished.

For just as people of refined mind, while eating food prepared with various condiments, relish the flavors and experience joy, so too [do they experience joy] when [the performance] is embellished by various dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*).

In the commentary on verse 352 of the *Mahāsāmi-ṭīkā* to the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, it is stated: "They take pleasure in the state of being well-endowed with the [eighteen] factors, thinking 'it is beautiful' (*sumanā*).
103. Among those [styles], in order to show the essential nature and the divisions of the *siṅgāra* (erotic) style alone, he says:

"Of the man," and so forth. Based upon—that is, making as the cause—the union with a woman, that longing or desire which belongs to the man, the person, a particular modification of the mind, [arises] toward the woman and the man.

Depending upon and making contact with union, that longing, desire, or particular modification of the mind which belongs to a woman—and which serves as the cause for amorous play and the like, or which is accompanied by the causes of amorous play and the like—is called the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment (*rasa*).
Furthermore, in this context, that longing which has arisen through seeing, hearing, or touching a woman or a man, or through their separation, is what is termed "sentiment" (*rasa*). That which...
However, the song that proceeds by taking that [union] as its cause is called "flavor" (*rasa*) because it produces enjoyment for the world.
But in all cases, "desire" (*pihā*) is said to be the flavor by way of metaphorical designation for the fruit. 104.
The nature of excellent men and women is the state of union and separation; this is the predominant feature here in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment.

The highest method of development is as follows: for the most part, that which consists of songs concerning the union and separation of superior persons is what is called *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment).

Because women and men are the cause of this, it is "caused by women and men" (*itthipurisahetuka*). That *śṛṅgāra* is considered to be twofold through this classification: enjoyment (*sambhoga*) and separation (*viyoga*). And therein—
The garden, house, grove, garlands, sandalwood, and so forth;
these, as well as others that produce graceful gestures, are the determinants (*vibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*sambhoga*).
However, the determinant of separation (*viyoga*) is the sight of the beloved, which generates the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And it has been said:
That by which the aesthetic flavors (rasas) are produced is proclaimed as the determinants (vibhāva);
this is their very manifestation (anubhāva).
"He is renowned among poets as the 'expresser' (byañjaka).

Enjoyment (sambhoga) is the experiencing that occurs together with eating. Separation (viyoga) is the parting, the state of being apart. *Siṅga* is a noun-derivative (*nāmadhātu*); it is "siṅga" in the sense of piercing (*vijjhana*).
This is the name for the "horn" (*siṅga*) of the defilements, which is designated as the state of being urbane (*nāgarika*); he performs that [action].
*Siṅga* means "horn"; that which produces it in those possessed of passion is *siṅgāra* (the erotic). It is called *vilāsa* because it is the manifestation of the horn of the defilements (*kilesa*).
*Suci* and *ujjala* are also names for the erotic.
*Karuṇa* (the pathetic) has the nature of an accumulation of sorrow.
To one who has abandoned attachment to the desirable and the means of attaining desirable wealth,
[there is] killing, binding, and beating, along with the afflictions and torments of defilements.
The sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) arises.

The heroic (*vīra*) [sentiment] increases enthusiasm. Its determinants (*vibhāva*) are discipline, fortitude, strength, and valor. And this [heroic sentiment] is threefold: the hero in generosity (*dāna-vīra*), the hero in righteousness (*dhamma-vīra*), and the hero in battle (*yuddha-vīra*).
The marvelous (*abbhuta*) has the nature of an accumulation of wonder.
The going to palaces, gardens, mountains, and so forth; the seeing of divine beings;
the seeing of assemblies, celestial mansions (*vimāna*), illusions, magic, arts, and so forth;
and the seeing of the science of nets (*jāla-vidyā*) and the like—these arise for him through the attainment of what is desired by the heart.
Laughter is that which has the nature of an accumulation of mirth.
It is accompanied by merriment and artifice, consisting of costumes, the display of limbs, and disconnected speech;
such is the laughter of deceivers and the like.
The terrifying has the nature of an accumulation of fear.
It consists of seeing high and dreadful shrieks, yakkhas, petas, and the like;
and of seeing empty houses, great forests, slaughter, and imprisonment.
The agitation caused by those [women] is terrifying due to their lack of restraint, their shaven heads,
and their cruelty; yet, when considered through such contemplations, the nature of women— and of low people—
is peaceful and like that of a recluse’s accumulation.
The seeing of those who are peaceful, whose senses are calmed, who are steadfast,
and whose nature is the Dhamma that causes peace— this indeed shall be the "peaceful" flavor.
That which has the inherent nature of accumulation through loathing is "loathsome."
But from the sight, hearing, or description of putrid flesh and the like,
the flavor of repulsiveness arises through the contemplations of the loathsome.
That which has the nature of accumulating anger is the "fierce" (rudda).
And that [fear] arises from battle, from the affliction of fierce kamma, and from harsh speech such as lying and so forth.

Among these, the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) and *raudra* (the furious) are neuter (*napuṃsaka*), while the others are masculine (*puṃsa*) according to their formal distinctions. These nine dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*) are stated according to the system of the *Ratnakosa*. For it is said therein:
“The erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrible, the pathetic,
the marvelous, and the peaceful— these are the nine dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa).
However, in the *Amarakośa*—
“The erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, the terrible, the loathsome, and the furious—these are the rasas. (Amarakosa 7.17).
Thus, eight rasas have been mentioned. Now, why has the ninth rasa, which exists, not been mentioned here? It is said in reply:
Laughter, pleasure, and compassion,
anger, envy, and fear, as well as disgust and wonder— these are [the eight].
The stable states (*ṭhāyībhāva*) have been enumerated.
However, because the *rasa* (flavour) itself becomes the stable state, and because the number eight belongs to the primary [flavours], it was not stated that "only those eight" were mentioned.

Furthermore, this *santa-rasa* (the flavour of peace), due to its aesthetic charm (*dhammasiṅgāratta*), is included within the *siṅgāra-rasa* (the erotic flavour) by virtue of its desire for a righteous battle.

For the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is indeed threefold. Some, however, say that there is a supreme rasa called "affection" (*vātsalya*), which arises from such conditions as the meeting with a beloved.
Rabhasa also said:
"The erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, and the terrifying..."
“Compassion, the marvelous, and serenity, along with affection—these are the ten aesthetic flavors (rasas).
Others, however, say:
“Laughter is accompanied by the erotic;”
“Karuna is born from cruel deeds;
Virata is born from the marvelous;
and Bibhatsa is born from the terrifying.”
They say there are four aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*).

"Bībhaccha" refers to killing and binding; the vowel is long due to the rule of *abbhāsikāra*. By the rule "the *dh* of *vassa* becomes *ch*, and [the following *v*] becomes *bībhaccha*," it is formed. That which has Rudra as its deity is called *rudda*. And it is said:
"The erotic sentiment (*siṅgāra*) has Hari as its deity; the comic (*hāsa*) has Prahasta as its deity."
"Karuṇa is Yamadeva, while Rudra is the presiding deity of Rudra"—thus it is stated in the *Saddakappadduma* regarding the term *rodra*.

In this context, *bhāva* (emotional state) refers to a transformation of the mind arising from desire, anger, laughter, and so forth, because it "causes [the poet’s] intention to be cultivated and manifested. This is threefold: stable (*ṭhāyī*), transitory (*byabhicārī*), and sattvic (*sāttiko*).
Among these: "Laughter, joy, compassion... [and so on].
Anger, fear, as well as disgust and wonder—
these are enumerated as the states of standing still.
The deviant [mental state] has thirty-three divisions, as follows:
suspicion, illness, and despondency;
likewise envy, intoxication, and pride.
Laziness, dejection, anxiety, delusion,
mindfulness, intelligence, fortitude,
restlessness, joy, and oppression.
Agitation, dullness, and mental excitation;
drowsiness, discursive thought, and fear;
longing for a womb, and despondency.
Excessive sleep, indolence,
and anger, death and likewise disease,
lack of health, and insanity—
Vibodha has thirty [subdivisions].
The sattvika is eightfold, as follows:
stiffness, perspiration, and horripilation;
Trembling of the body,
change of color, and perspiration—
these are the eight sattvikas.
It is *sthāyin* (permanent) because of its purity and exclusivity; it is *vyabhicārin* (transitory) because of its variability.

Just as in a drama the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the *sthāyin*, while laughter and the rest are the *vyabhicārins* that assist it; so too, in the language of enumeration, greed, hatred, and delusion alone are called the "seven luminaries.
Therein, that which is produced from the *sattva* disposition is the *sāttvika*. The performance that makes the emotion known is the *anubhāva*; "anu" means subsequently.

Having considered that he "cultivates" and "manifests" it, therein the nature of enjoyment (*sambhoga-svabhāva*) is the state called *rati* (delight); its *anubhāva* (consequent manifestation) consists of the casting of glances with the cleverness of the eyes, the playful gestures of the brows, and speech that captivates the mind through its charm.
And it is said: "The playful charm of his casting glances with the cleverness of his eyes..."
"Speech that captivates the heart and other such qualities are proclaimed as the manifestation of union.
But the manifestation of separation is:
"Longing and likewise anxious thought,"
For him there is the chanting of refuge,
agitation and lamentation,
as well as madness and even disease.
Stupefaction consists of death itself;
these ten are enumerated here.
The power of laughter, however, is its transformation of time and so forth; that which is compassionate is as follows.
Through sighs, discoloration,
the breaking of the joints of the limbs,
and through lamentations and sorrows.

The *abhinaya* (dramatic representation) is performed by the wise masters. The terrifying *abhinaya* is constant, characterized by trembling of the hands, feet, and face; stiffness of the limbs; and a parched palate and throat due to the agitation of the heart.
However, for Rudra, the knitting of the brows and so forth constitutes his *anubhāva* (consequent emotion).
Likewise, the Hero is manifested through generosity,
fearlessness, and so forth, as well as by means of gestures, hints, and the like.
The first [of the theras] should be placed at the beginning. But for the hideous one—
this is the concealment of the skilled one.
Pressing with the feet, arms, or elbows,
causing terror and so forth— by such means,
one should always employ the method of intimidation.
But the marvelous [qualities] are:
the extent of his tamed eyes,
and his serene confidence and tranquility.
One should display horripilation and tears through words of praise. Of the eight types of sattvika-bhāvas—
stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, weeping, paleness, and fainting— they should be manifested in their respective order.

The acting [expressions] for *nikriyatā* (destruction), *vāta* (wind), *ccāsīta* (exhaustion), *dobhagga* (ugliness), *apāṅgapūraṇa* (filling the corners of the eyes), *mukhacchāyāvipallāsa* (distortion of facial complexion), *locanamajjana* (closing of the eyes), and *mahipāta* (falling prostrate) are as follows.

Likewise, for the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as *nibbeda* (despair), *gilāni* (sickness), *saṅkissa* (apprehension), *mada* (intoxication), *samā* (tranquility), and *ālasya* (laziness), the acting expressions are, respectively: *sāsa* (sighing), *santāpa* (feverish distress), *disāvalokana* (looking around), *guṇamacchera* (concealment of virtues), *bhīta* (fear), *ṅgamaddana* (rubbing of the limbs), *samā* (tranquility), and so forth.

Suspicion (*saṅkā*) among those who are unfaithful is a state of mind characterized by apprehension. Sickness (*gilāni*) is the condition of being ill. Despair (*nibbeda*) is self-contempt. Arrogance (*mado*) is excessive negligence.
Weariness (*samo*) is exhaustion. Dejection (*dīnatā*) is mental suffering. Fortitude (*dhiti*) is contentment. Joy (*hariso*) is clarity of mind.

Oppression (*pīḷā*) is a distortion of the facial expression caused by cruel conduct and the like. Agitation (*āvego*) is confusion. Stupidity (*jaḷatā*) is a lack of comprehension; ferocity (*uggatā*) is cruelty.
Sutta means sleep. Tāsa is agitation of the mind. Ussāha is exertion. Visāda is despondency. Abahittha is the concealment of one's outward appearance. Amarisa is intolerance. Vibodha is wakefulness.
The remaining terms have not been explained in detail for fear of prolixity. This concludes the commentary on the *rasa* (flavors).
105. The names for speech are given by way of a verse. That which is to be spoken is "bhāsita" (spoken). From the root *lap* (to speak), "lapita" (uttered). It is that which is spoken (*bhāsīyate*).
*Vohāra*: It is called *vohāra* because it is to be used (*voharīyati*). The root *hara* (to take) is preceded by the prefix *vi*. Alternatively, there is a verbal root *vohāra* meaning "speech.

*Vacana*: It is called *vacana* because it is spoken (*vuccati*). The root *vac* belongs to the *manu*-class. *Utti*: It is called *utti* because it is uttered (*uccati*). *Vācā*: It is called *vācā* because it is spoken (*vuccati*). *Girā*: They swallow it or it makes sound, thus it is *girā*. The root *gi* means "sound," with the suffix *ira*.

Alternatively, it is *girā* because it is to be sung (*gāyitabbā*). *Vāṇī*: It is called *vāṇī* because it is sounded (*vāyate*) or it makes sound. The suffix *yu* is applied, and the vowel is changed to *ī*.

It is called *vāṇī* because it is like an arrow (*vāṇa*) in the sense of piercing the vital spots of others; the suffix *-ī* is added. The seer named Bharata was a composer of scriptures, and this [speech] belongs to him, thus it is *bhāratī*.

It is called *kathitā* because it is spoken (*kathīyati*); the suffix *-tā* is added. It is called *vacī* because it is uttered (*vuccati*); the suffix *-ī* is added. *Brahmī*, *sarasvatī*, and *vacas* are also names for speech. 106.
Where there is a single verb (*ākhyāta*), that which possesses one verb is "with a case-factor" (*sakāraka*) due to being accompanied by a case-factor word together with its qualifiers.
A collection of words whose purpose is to convey a relationship—a grouping of words—is what is called a sentence (*vākya*).
For example: "King Vessantara performs karma that has a happy result," or "The man goes. Here, the mention of a verb (*ākhyāta*) is intended as an illustration for any word expressing an action;
therefore, such expressions as "Devadatta, having made a mat" would also be considered sentences. However, in the *Amarakosa*, it is stated: "A collection ending in *tiṣya* and so forth..."

"A sentence (*vākya*) is either a collection [of words] ending in *ti* and so forth, or an action associated with its factors (*kāraka*)" (Amarakośa 6.2). He states the definition of a sentence by means of these two characteristics.
Its meaning is as follows: a sentence is a collection or aggregate of words ending in *ti* and so forth, whose purpose is to express a relationship;

for example: "He reads loudly" (*uccaṃ paṭhati*), "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*). Likewise, a verb (*ākhyāta*) expressing a state of being (*bhāva*), when accompanied by indeclinables (*avyaya*), factors (*kāraka*), and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), [is also a sentence].
A sentence (*vākya*): A verb ending in *tya*, etc., whether accompanied by indeclinables (*avyaya*), or by objects (*kāraka*), or by qualifiers (*visesana*), is called a sentence.
The mention of "ending in *tya*, etc. is an indicator for verbal roots (*kriyāśabda*); therefore, expressions such as "Devadatta, having made a mat" (*devadatto kaṭaṃ katavā*) are also sentences.
He states another definition of a sentence, independent of that indicator: "Or a verb (*kriyā*) connected with its factors (*kāraka*). [This refers to] a verbal form.
Or, a sentence is a construction involving a factor of action (*kāraka*), such as "the king goes" (*rājā gacchati*) or "the king has gone" (*rājā gato*).

According to this view, it asserts that the status of being a sentence belongs to every collection of words consisting of actions and factors of action, whether they include indeclinables (*avyaya*) or not.
When there is a repetition or a statement two or three times due to fear and so forth—such as "snake, snake! pierce [it]!"—[this is also considered a sentence].

The phrase beginning with "vijjhā" should be understood as *āmeḍita* (repetition). The root *meḍi* means "madness," and when preceded by the prefix *ā*, it is used in the sense of uttering something two or three times.
As it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* on the *Harivaṃsa*: "When Vāsava repeats this very sentence, he *āmeḍayati*.
Even in the expression "an *āmeḍa* was made by Devadatta," the meaning is the same; for due to grief or other causes, one utters "brother, brother" repeatedly.
The [suffix] *to* occurs in the sense of the agent (*bhāve*) and the object (*kammani*). And the word [ending in *to*] functions as a sentence (*vākya*). 107.
To show the scope of the emphatic repetition (*āmaddita*), he says: "In fear," and so forth. In cases such as "A snake! A snake! A thief! A thief! it is used in fear. In cases such as "Pierce!
Pierce! Strike! Strike! it is used in anger. In cases such as "Excellent! Excellent! it is used in praise.
In such instances as “Go, go! Cut it, cut it! and so forth, [the repetition] is used for haste. In such instances as “Come, come! and so forth, it is used for curiosity.

In such instances as “Thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha’” and so forth, it is used for wonder. In such instances as “Come forward, venerable sirs; come forward, venerable sirs! and so forth, it is used for laughter.
In such instances as “Where is my only son? Where is my only son? and so forth, it is used for sorrow. In such instances as “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! and so forth...

Regarding *pasāde*: the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated; by this, the inclusion of censure (*garahā*), disrespect (*asammāna*), and so forth, should be understood.
Among these, it occurs in the sense of censure in such cases as "a wicked man, a wicked man," and in the sense of disrespect in such cases as "you handsome one, you handsome one.
Thus, in these nine instances and others, a wise person—a learned one—should employ, or apply, reduplication (*āmeḍita-vacana*); reduplication means uttering [a word] repeatedly.
It is called *āmeḍita* because it is repeated or uttered again and again (*punaḥ-punaḥ uccāriyati*).
108. *Iru*, *yaju*, and *sāma* are the three Vedas. Among them, the word *iru* is feminine (*nārī*) and has the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*).

The root *ic* means "to praise" (*thuti*); since the gods desire (*icchanti*) this, it is *iru*. [The suffix] *u* is added, and the *c* becomes *r*. That by which they sacrifice is *yaju*; [the suffix] *u* is added. It [denotes] the final ritual action (*antakamma*), in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

*Mo*: It is *sāmaṃ* because one pacifies (*soyanti*) evil with it; the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is "to pacify" (*ossā*), as in the phrase "it [is used] at the end of the thinning [of defilements].

They know the Dhamma by means of these, thus they are the *vedas*. These three *vedas* together are called *tayī*; it is *tayī* because it has three parts (*tayo avayavā*). This word *tayī* is feminine (*nārī*) and of the feminine gender (*itthiliṅgo*).

*Tikaṃ* [means] "in the Veda. *Manta*: that by which one measures (*munāti*) or knows the Dhamma; [the suffixes] *-to*, *-ussa*, and *-a*. *Suti*: that by which the Dhamma is heard (*suyyate*); the word *suti* is used in the feminine. 109.
To show the ten seers (*isi*) who composed the Vedic treatises, he says "Aṭṭhaka," and so forth. *Atthaṃ*: welfare (*hita*); or, in the sense of *attha*...
He makes a weapon (*sattha*); thus he is Aṭṭhaka. He performs pleasant speech (*vāma-kalyāṇavacana*);
thus he is Vāmaka—or, because of his short stature, he is Vāmana—and he is the same as Vāmaka, with the letter *k* substituted for *m*. "Vāma" means Hara; that deity is his, thus he is Vāmadeva.
"Vāma" refers to what is on the left, to the contrary, and to the repulsive; it refers to the right, to wealth, and to that which is exceedingly beautiful.
"In *payodhara* [there is] *kāma*, one should know that *vāma* is also at the back"—thus it is in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*.
The offspring of the seer Aṅgīrasa is an *Aṅgirasa*; Citrasikhaṇḍin’s offspring is his son. Or else, in *aṅgi*...
He whose bodily essence (*rasa*) has attained perfection as mercury (*pārada*) is Aṅgirasa. For that very reason, he calls his son, the teacher of the *surās*, "Jīva.

He is called "Jīva" because he causes the gods to live when they have been struck down by the *asuras* in battle; thus he is immortal. (3.24) The commentary on the *Cintāmaṇi* should be consulted. He is "Bhagu" because he supports (*bharati*);
or, he goes to and knows the lunar mansion (*bhānakkhatta*) called Bhaga, thus he is Bhagu. He bestows restraint (*saṃyama*) upon Yama.
Because he was like Yama and because he was a fire worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), he is called Yamadaggi;
he was the father of Rāma, the father of Paraśurāma (*Saddakappadduma*). The offspring of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭha.
The offspring of Bhāradvāja is Bhāradvāja. The offspring of Kassapa is Kassapa. The offspring of Vessāmitta is Vessāmitta. Thus, these are the ten seers (*isayo*).
The authors and makers of the *Mantāna* Vedas.
(110) Having shown the Vedas, he says "Kappa," etc., in order to show its six ancillaries (*chaḷaṅga*).
*Kappa* is the instructor of sacrificial rites, because it is considered that "it is fashioned" (*kappate*) or "it originates. *Vyākaraṇa* is the explanatory grammar of correct words, specifically...

It is called *yu* because by means of it sounds are made manifest (*ākarīyante*) or brought into activity through the rules of phonetics (*pakaticcādi*). The science of light (*jotisattha*) is the science of calculation (*gaṇanasattha*), which demonstrates the results of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
It is called *sikkhā* because by means of it one trains (*sikkhyante*), practices (*abbhasyante*), and studies (*ajjhayante*);
it is the guide to the places, organs of articulation, and efforts of the letters beginning with *a*. It is called *utti* in the sense of certainty or completeness.

Etymology (*nirutti*) consists of the addition of phonemes (*vaṇṇāgama*), the substitution of phonemes (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*), and so forth. Prosody (*chandoviciti*) is that which establishes the sequence of the *anuṭṭhubhā* and other meters as taught in the Vedic tradition.
They say these six are the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Vedas.

111. "Ancient" (*purāvutta*) refers to that which has the nature of being composed in the past; its "composition" (*pabandha*) is its detailed expansion or continuous succession, such as the *Bhārata* and other works.
A work such as the narrative of the *Bhārata* war, composed by Vyāsa and others, is called *itihāsa*. The term *iti-hāsa* is a noun derived from the indeclinable *iti-hā*, meaning "thus it was said";
thus, *itihāsa* means "that which exists as 'thus it was'.
A treatise that elucidates the names of trees and other things through their synonyms, such as the *Ratnamālā*, is called *nighaṇṭu*.
By means of the suffix *imin*, [the author] indicates that the word *nighaṇṭu* is masculine; it is thus everywhere.

In this regard, it is called *nighaṇṭu* because names (*nāmāni*) that have arrived there are gathered (*ghaṭenti*) and made into a heap (*rāsīkaronti*) therein—thus there is the addition of the vowel *i*.

Alternatively, it is *nikhaṇṭu* because it digs up (*nikhaṇati*), breaks apart (*bhindati*), and shows by way of analysis (*vibhajja*) both the meaning and the word through the relationship between the signified and the signifier—thus there is the substitution of *kha* for *ṭa*. It is precisely that.
Having formed the syllable *gha*, it is called *nighaṇṭu*.
By this [term], it is stated that it is an elucidator of the names of trees and so forth, because it elucidates many synonyms for each individual meaning.

This is merely an illustration, for that treatise also proceeds by way of elucidating how many meanings are expressed by a single word (Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.256; Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.22; Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 2.3.59).
Sārattha-Ṭīkā 1. Commentary on the Account of the Third Council. 112.

That which is the treatise of the cavillers (*vitaṇḍavādin*) in the world is to be understood as *lokāyata*. [The root] *tan* means extension; it is called *vitaṇḍa* because they extend (*tanoti*) here that which is mutually contradictory, or that which is opposed to heaven and liberation (*saggamokkha*).
The suffix *-ḍa* is added, and the nasalization (*ṇatta*) occurs; or alternatively, by means of the staff of argumentation (*vādadaṇḍa*) that is contradictory.
It is called *vitaṇḍa* because "they strike" (*tāḷenti*) the disputants (*vādino*) therein; the root *taḍi* means "to strike.

Furthermore, even that place depending upon which the disputants' debate proceeds is spoken of by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) as their "place," just as it is said in the *Dīgha Nikāya*: "The eye is a lovely form, a pleasant form in the world;
herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases."

*Ni.* 2.401; *Ma.* Ni. 1.134; *Vibha.* 204. "Loka" refers to the world of fools. Because they resort (*āyatanti*), strive, or exert themselves for the sake of the pleasure of debate (*vādassāda*) therein, it is called *lokāyata*.
Alternatively, it is called *lokāyata* because by means of it the world does not strive (*na yatati*) or exert itself (*na īhati*) for future welfare (*āyatiṃ hitaṃ*).
For, relying on that treatise, sentient beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds.

That which is beneficial for poets and scholars, which produces the attainment of poetic composition, enjoyment, and so forth, and which establishes the rules and methods for the construction of poetic meters known as *kriyā*—namely, works such as the *Subodhālaṅkāra*—is called *keṭubha*.
It is called *keṭubha* because by means of it (*etena*), poets proceed (*kiṭanti*) or attain skill (*kosallaṃ*) in their compositions; from the root *kiṭ*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *-abha*.
*Assukāra*: Alternatively, it is *kiṭubha* because it causes (*kiṭati*) or brings about (*gameti*) the classification of actions and so forth;
or, because it goes through (*gamento*) and fulfills (*pūreti*) that [classification] without remainder, it is *keṭubha*. [The roots] *ubha* and *umbha* mean "to fill.

That which is called *kriyākappa* is that by means of which action—characterized by the differentiation of speech and so forth—is fashioned (*kappīyati*) and analyzed (*vikappīyati*). Furthermore, it is [so called] because of the classification of phonemes, word-connections, word-meanings, and so on.
Because it contains an exceedingly great variety [of topics], he says: "the classification of ritual action" (*kriyākappavikappa*). And this is said with reference to the *Mūlakriyākappa* treatise.

For that has a vast scope, measuring one hundred thousand [verses], and consists of treatises such as the *Nayacarita* and the *Nalacarita*. 113. That in which some matter has been apprehended is "one in which the matter is apprehended" (*upaladdhatthā*);

thus it is called an *ākhyāyikā* (tale/narrative), because the conduct of the protagonist and the instructor is related therein (*ākhyāyate*). The suffix *-ṇvu* is used here for the purpose of forming a noun.

That which is a composition (*pabandha*) by way of its very structure and is elaborated in detail is "composition-plot" (*pabandhakappanā*), such as the *Kādambarī* and others. It is called a "tale" (*kathā*) because it is told (*kathīyati*).
Wealth (*attha*) refers to land, gold, and so forth; among these, land is primary because the others originate from it.

The science that serves as the means for their acquisition (*ajjana*) and protection (*pālana*) is the "science of wealth" (*atthasattha*). This includes works composed by Payānaka and others, as well as those composed by Bāhusvāti, Cāṇakya, and Ābbīki.

(Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 6.5): Regarding that, the term *daṇḍanīti* (the art of government) is employed. Punishment (*daṇḍa*) characterized by execution, imprisonment, and so forth, is the fourth means among the [four] beginning with conciliation (*sāma*).

The application (*nīti*) of that [punishment] is *daṇḍanīti*. Generally, the term *nīti* is designated by *daṇḍa* because, due to the abundance of the fault of killing, it is mostly an application of punishment;
and since its meaning is *daṇḍanīti*, the treatise (*sattha*) is also called *daṇḍanīti*.

In this discourse, there are two [types of] *vutta*. That which is called *vutta* is so termed because it causes its own grammatical operation (*kāriya*) to reach completion within the context of the sentence.
That in which an operation proceeds while it is occurring is called *pavatti*. By the letter *ca*, those ending in *-ud* and so forth are included.
The suffix *ṇo* is used here in the sense of "possessing" (*assatthi*), meaning that the operation exists therein. That which has risen to completion within the context is called *udanta*.

114. *Adhivacanantaṃ* means "name" (*nāma*). It is called *saññā* because one perceives (*sañjānanti*) by means of it. It is called *ākhyā* because it is described (*ākhyāyate*) by means of it. It is called *avhā* because one calls out (*ahvayate*) by means of it; the root *hu* means "sound," or alternatively, the root *vhe* means "calling.
It is called *samaññā* because one understands correctly (*sammā ājānāti*) by means of it, or because one knows equally (*samaṃ jānāti*) by means of it.

It is called *nāma* because that by which something is designated (*abhidhīyate*) is *yu* (a suffix); it is called *nāma* because one bows down (*namati*) or inclines toward (*nāmayati*) it. It is called *abbhassate* because one approaches (*abbhassate*) it. It is called *nāma* because one bows down (*namati*) or causes to bow down (*nāmayati*).
Or "name" (*nāma*). "That which is called" (*ahvāyati*) is *avhāya*; here the suffix *-ya* is used in the sense of the object. "Name itself" is *nāmadheyya*.

It is *nāmadheyya* because it is "to be borne" (*dheyya*) by names—that is, by the sounds of names (*nāmasadda*), or by the forms and names (*bhāgarūpanāma*)—according to Pāṇini 5.4.36 (*vā*); or, using the suffix *-dheyya* in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*) via the rule beginning with *yadādi*;
or, it is *dheyya* because "meaning stands here" (*tiṭṭhati ettha attho*); or, it is *dheyya* because it is "borne"—that is, uttered—thus *nāmadheyya* is name itself as that which is to be borne.
*Adhīnaṃ vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ*: a word that is dependent; dependent on what? On the meaning (*attha*). *Paṭivacanaṃ paṭivākyaṃ*: a reply to one who has been questioned.
A word that has gone back, or come after, is a *paṭivākya*. *Uttaraṃ*: that by which one is answered or surpassed. 115.
Regarding the triad [of terms] concerning questioning: it is to be asked, thus it is a *pañha* (question). For an object desired to be known is called a *pañha*. Questioning...
In the case of *pucchana*, there is the suffix *ña*; for *cha*, there is *ha*; and for *us*, there is *a*. The verbal root (*dhātu*) is also *pañh* in the sense of "inquiring. *Yuja* means "to join";

that which is to be joined with, or to be inquired about, is *anuyoga*. Inquiring, or that which is to be inquired about, is *pucchā*. By this same method, the formation of both as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*) should also be understood.
The tetrad [is used] in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). It is called *nidassana* because by means of it one illustrates (*nidasseti*) something as being similar to the original (*pakata*);

it is a statement that provides a corroboration of the original. It is called *upogghāta* because by means of it one is led to (*paṭipādīyate*), brought near to, or established in [the meaning]. The root *han* preceded by the prefix *upa* has the sense of leading to or establishing. It is called *diṭṭhanta* because by means of it something is shown (*dassīyate*);
or else, *anta* refers to the end, and *diṭṭha* refers to the end or the completion of the original.

*Yena* means "by which"; this is the illustrative example (*diṭṭhanta*). Alternatively, in all cases, it should also be treated as an instrument (*kammasādhana*). It is called an *udāharaṇa* (example) because that which is primary is cited for the purpose of providing an illustration (*upapādana*).

116. *Saṅkhepa* (abbreviation) consists of four [components] in brief. *Samā* means having an equal sense. It is called *saṅkhepa* because it is abbreviated—that is, it is stated by way of a single part; the root *khip* means "to throw" or "to cast.

It is called *saṃhāra* because by means of it, things are brought together and explained in an abbreviated manner; the root *hṛ* means "to take away. It is called [an abbreviation] because it is combined and abbreviated.
*Samāsa*: [from] *asu*, meaning "to cast down. That by which something is grasped in brief is a *saṅgaha* (compendium).

"You possess a hundred pieces of gold," and so forth—such empty speech, speaking of what is not real, is called *abbhakkhāna* (false accusation). Speaking or declaring that which is untrue is *abbhakkhāna*. 117.
The pair [of terms] regarding dispute, in the context of division and the subject matter of debt-claims and so forth (*Cintāmaṇiṭīkā* 6.9): "contrary" (*viruddha*).

The conventional expression is that one "commits" (*karoti*) [an offense] and then "takes it away" (*avaharati*), or "speaks" (*vadati*). When one speaks after having committed something contrary [to the truth], it is called a "dispute" (*vivāda*).
In all these cases, the formation of the abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) is appropriate. "Sapana" refers to the form such as: "Speaking false speech, you shall go to terrible hells," and so forth.
The verbal root *sap* means "to revile"; with the suffix *-tha*, it becomes *sapatha*.
The triad is well known. It is *yaśa* because one attains fame (*yaśas*) by means of it; or, that which travels everywhere (*sarvatra yāti*) is *yaśas*;

or, that which is renowned and celebrated is *yaśas*. It is *siloka* because it spreads (*pattharati*); *siloka* is used in the sense of accumulation (*saṅghāta*). It is *kitti* because it is praised (*kittiyate*) or spoken of;
*kitta* is used in the sense of sound (*saddana*). It is also *samaññā*, which is well known; the prefix *sam-* is added to the root *jānāti* (to know) in the sense of being renowned. Likewise.
For it is said in the *Ratanakosa*: “Known, well-known, reckoned, famous, renowned.
*Ghossanā* means sounding with a loud voice; from the root *ghusa*, meaning sound, *ghossanaṃ* is sounding, which is *ghossanā*. 118–119. The pair [of terms] refers to an echo. *Ghossanaṃ* is sound;
that which has gone toward (*paṭigata*) it is a compound in the accusative case (*dutiyā-samāsa*). Thus, *ravaṃ*...
*Paṭirava* means an echo. Alternatively, it is a counterpart to sound (*ghosa*), thus *paṭighosa*; it is a counterpart to shouting (*rava*), thus *paṭirava*.
*Paṭisuti* and *paṭiddhani* are also names for an echo. *Vācīmukha*, *vacanopakkama*, and *upaññāsa* are synonyms.
The prefix *upa-ni* in *upavesana* means "to sit down near. *Upa* signifies "first" or "near," referring to the placing or setting down of a word in proximity to a preceding statement.

The suffix *upa* becomes *nya*. The group of seven [suffixes] occurs in the sense of praise (*thuti*). *Kath* is used in the sense of praise; *yu* is the suffix. Alternatively, *katthanā* is derived from the verbal root *kath* according to the rule for dissimilar dual forms (*vā-āsarūpa-dvibhāva*).

From the root *silāgh* in the sense of praising, we have *silāghā*. Alternatively, *sīlāghā* is the striking (*āhanana*) of virtue (*sīla*), that is, of qualities similar to it; this same word is shortened [to *silāghā*].
*Silāghā* means praise. *Vaṇṇanā* means that which is to be praised; it is used in the sense of praise (*vaṇṇa-pasaṃsā*). *Nu* is used in the sense of praise (*thu-tiyaṃ*), thus *nuti*.

*Thu* is used in the sense of extolling (*abhitthave*), thus *thuti*. *Thoma* is used in the sense of praise (*silāghāyaṃ*), thus *thomanaṃ*. The root *saṃsa*, preceded by *pa*, means to praise (*pasaṃsane*).

The cry of crested peacocks (*sikhaṇḍīnaṃ*)—the sound of their calling—is called *kekā*. [It is derived from] *kā* in the sense of sound; *kekā* is that which makes the sound "ke" (*ke iti kāyati*), in the sense of an action (*kammani*).
Alternatively, *kā* means "to sound" or "the act of sounding. *Kekā* is the cry (*kā*) occurring in peacocks (*ke*); this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*).
The roar of elephants is called the "koñca-roar" (*koñcanāda*), a roar resembling the cry of the *koñca* bird. The sound or noise of horses—that is, of steeds—is called "hesā";
*hesā* is derived from the root *hes*, meaning "to neigh. It is *hesā* because it is the act of neighing (*hesana*), or because it proceeds as the sound "he."
120–121. *Dvayaṃ pariyāye*. That by which one goes toward, reaches, or understands a clearly manifest meaning is *pariyāya* (a method or way).
That by which a single meaning is stated again and again is *vevacana* (a synonym). *Dvayaṃ sākacchāyaṃ*.

Discussion (*sākacchā*) is speech that is either together with others or correct and non-contradictory; it is also called *saṃkathā*. [In this context, the following phonetic rules apply: *to* becomes *co*, and *tassa* becomes *cho*.
The following are synonyms for censure (*garaha*): speaking with the expression of hatred is *upavāda*. Regarding *kusa*, it refers to calling out and splitting;
in some places the reading is *apakkosa*, which is incorrect. *Vaṇṇa* means praise; speaking against that is *avaṇṇavāda*.
Speaking with contempt is *anuvāda*. The speech of people, which is censure, is *janavāda*. Speech by way of censure is *apavāda*. *Parivādana* is [the same].

*Parivāda* (censure), *rassassa dīghatā* (the lengthening of a short vowel). These, beginning with *upavāda*, are synonymous (*tulyattha*) and have the same meaning (*samānattha*). This is the rule regarding the various divisions of irregularly formed words (*visamavuttappabheda*).

The root *khipa* means "to throw"; *khipana* is the act of throwing, that is, casting out—hence *khepa*. The root *nidi* means "contempt" (*kucchāyaṃ*); with the suffix *a*, it becomes *nindā* (blame).

Just as *upavāda* and the others have the sense of reproach (*garahattha*), so too do *kuccha* and the others; thus they have that same meaning. The root *kuccha* means "to cast down," belonging to the *curādi* class.
From the roots *kus* and *akkos*, with the suffix *it*, and from the root *gup*—in the sense of "to despise" (*kucchanesu*)—the form *goppa* arises;
here, by the rule "after *tij*, *gup*, and *kitamāna*, there is optionally *cha*, *kha*, or *sa*," the suffix *cha* is applied. The root *garah* also means "to despise.

In this regard, some say that "insults" (*upavāda*) and so forth have the sense of false accusation (*abbhakkhāna*), while "reproaches" (*khepa*) and so forth have the sense of censure (*ninda*); however, that contradicts the *Amarakośa*, as the sense of false accusation [is distinct].
And because it has been stated [thus], it should not be accepted. These seven, beginning with "upavāda," apply even in the case of false accusation (*abbhakkhāna*).
For one who desires to dispute, there is first a "bad speech" (*dubbāda*), which is a reproach (*upārambha*) such as:

"What kind of action is this appropriate for the Blessed One, who was born in the Śākya clan, the crest-jewel of the entire world?"—this being preceded by the disclosure of his virtues—and then: "This is indeed appropriate for you, the son of a harlot."
Reproach preceded by censure is also [a form of] upārambha (reproach). Among these, that reproach which is preceded by censure and accompanied by blame is called *paribhāsana* (reviling).
Approaching others and attacking or disturbing their mind is *upārambha*. Speaking with the expression of hatred is *paribhāsana*.

It is called "ignoble speech" (*anariyavohāra*) because it is the mode of expression of ignoble and base people, or because it is not the mode of expression of noble and superior persons. 122. [End of section].
That speech which is uttered by base people— by way of the eight modes of discourse such as claiming to have seen what was not seen among things that have been investigated—

is said to be "abusive" (*abhivākya*); it is so called because, being a means for transgressing and manifesting overstepping, it exceeds the bounds of propriety (*ariyā*) that ought to be observed by noble persons (*ariya*).
123. *Anulāpa* means speaking repeatedly or frequent utterance; it is called *anulāpa* because it is a repeated (*anu*) speaking (*lāpa*).

*Palāpa* is speech that is useless or purposeless, such as the talk of the insane and so forth; it is a speaking devoid of purpose (*palāpa*), where the prefix *pa-* indicates the sense of separation.

*Ālāpa* is pleasant speech spoken at the beginning of occasions such as coming and going; it is a speaking (*lāpa*) at the beginning (*ādi*), and the word *āpuccha* (requesting leave) is also used here.
Lamentation (*paridevana*) is that which is established through hatred; it is called *anusocana* (sorrowing), *atikkamalāpa* (excessive wailing), and *vilāpa* (lamentation).
*Vilāpa* means various talk (*vividhena*), or talk in various ways (*vividhaṃ vā lāpo*). Lamentation (*paridevana*) is *parideva*; that very thing is *pariddava*.
[The root] *dev* is used in the sense of lamentation. 124. Contradictory speech is *virodha*. Contradictory babble is *vippalāpa*. That which is sent is a *sandesa* (message).

"Sandissamāno attho tassā" means "the meaning being seen by her. That by which the meaning seen is expressed is called *sandesa*; or rather, it is called *vācika*. [The root] *vac* is used in the sense of "sending a message";
with the suffix *-ika* in its own sense (*sakatthe*), the meaning is: "that which is a message consisting of speech," hence *vācika*.

Speech that is mutually consistent and free from contradiction is called "conversation" (*sambhāsana*) or "dialogue" (*sallāpa*). For example, as one says, "Today is an auspicious constellation," the other also says, "So it is."
125. Harsh speech and rough words are called *pharusaṃ*. It is called *parusaṃ* because it causes another person to swell up (*ussāpeti*) or burn;

that very same word, by changing the letter *pa* to *pha*, becomes *pharusaṃ*. It is called *niṭṭhuraṃ* because, due to its unpleasantness, it is not desirable—just as in the case of "chest" (*uro*), as in the word "elephant" (*nāgo*).
Both [terms] refer to speech that is pleasing to the ear. It is called *manuññaṃ* because it thoroughly (*ābhusaṃ*) makes known (*ñāpeti*) and satisfies the mind (*manaṃ*).
*Ñā* is used in the senses of measure, counting, and consideration. *Assukāra* means "causing tears. *Hadayaṅgamaṃ* means that which goes to or enters the heart (the mind).
The pair beginning with *saṃkula* refers to two statements that are contradictory from beginning to end, or mutually opposed sentences, such as:
"As long as I live I shall be silent, yet my father is a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārī*)."
My mother was barren, and my grandfather was childless. "Saṃkula" means that which becomes turbid or agitated by this; "kiliṭṭha" means that in which things become soiled. 126.
A sentence such as "ten pomegranates," etc., which lacks a collective meaning, is: ten pomegranates, cakes on a platter, and a goat-skin.
*Palālapiṇḍā* (Nyāyabhāṣya 5.2.10; Moggallānapañcikāṭīkā 1.1): Because it is unconnected, it is designated and called "unbound" (*abaddha*).
It is "unbound" because the heart is not bound therein.
It is "false" (*vitatha*) because there is no such truth (*tatha*) or reality therein. Harsh words and so forth are [included] under the term "false" up to those possessing the three genders.
127. *Pajjaddhaṃ* means in true speech. This word *samma* is an indeclinable (*abyaya*), remaining the same across all genders, cases, and numbers.

*Avitathaṃ* means not false. That which exists among the good and virtuous is *saccaṃ*. Alternatively, from the root *sat* (to exist) or *sāta* (to endure), with the suffix *-ya* according to the rule beginning with *vaja*, it becomes *saccaṃ*.
The word *tatha* is a synonym for "real" (*bhūta*); as in, "by the real path, by him who speaks things as they truly are," thus [he is] the *Tathāgata*.
The usage is *jināti* (from the Kaśyapa school). Likewise, *sādhu* and *tacchaṃ* [are used] in the sense of "good" (*sādhutthe*).

The words *yathā* and *tathā* also signify truth (*sacca*) and are without gender (*aliṅga*). Words ending in those [suffixes] express "truthful speech" (*saccavacana*) and "possessing reality" (*vantavācaka*).

With the exception of the words *sammā*, *saccaṃ*, and *yathātathaṃ*, the remaining terms such as *avitatha* and so forth function in all three genders. However, the word *saccaṃ* itself is without gender. In the *Amarakosa*, however, both the words *sammā* and *sacca*...
The state of being three genders (*tilliṅgatta*) has been stated for *tabba*, as follows: "Truth (*sacca*), reality (*taccha*), rightness (*rita*), and correctness (*sammā*);
these [four] are in the three genders" (Amara 6.22). For example: "the truthful Brahmin," "the truthful woman," "the truthful brahmin family.

However, here, because there is no difference in form across all genders, numbers, and case endings, the word *sammā* is an indeclinable (*abyaya*); likewise, because there is no difference in form even among the three genders, the word *sacca* is an indeclinable.
And it has been stated that they are without gender (*aliṅga*). For example: *sammā-vācā*, *sammā-vohāro*, *sammā-vacanaṃ*;
*saccaṃ brāhmaṇo*, *saccaṃ nārī*, *saccaṃ vippakulaṃ*. However, the words *micchā-musā* are indeclinables (*abyaya*) in all instances.
For example: *micchā-vācā*, *micchā-vohāro*, *micchā-vacanaṃ*; *musā-vācā*, *musā-vohāro*, *musā-vacanaṃ*.
128. To demonstrate sixteen synonyms for sound (*sadda*), he spoke the *upajāti* verse beginning with “*ravo*.
It is called *ravo* because it is sounded or made to resound; the root *ru* means “to sound. *Nāda* is shouting; *nināda* is a meaningless sound; the root *nada* means “inarticulate sound.

*Ninada* is the same, with the only difference being the short vowel. It is called *sadda* because it is uttered or expressed; the root *ghus* means “to sound,” and thus *ghosa* is manifestation or resonance. *Nigghosa* is the same.
*Naḍanaṃ* means sounding. From the root *dhan*, meaning "to sound," that which is sounded is *dhani*. Thus, *nigghosa*, *nāda*, and *dhani* form the compound *nigghosanādadhaniyo*.
*Rava* itself is *rāva*. *Ārāva* is a word expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). Likewise, there are *saṃrāva*, *virāva*, and *ārava*. *Ghusanaṃ* means resonance (*ghoso*).
*Ārāva*, *saṃrāva*, *virāva*, *ghoso*, and *ārava* constitute a *dvanda* (copulative) compound. From the root *su*, meaning "to hear," that which is heard is [suta].

*Suti*. It flows (*sarati*) or goes toward the state of being heard (*suyyamāna-taṃ*), thus it is *sara*. That by which one breathes out (*nissanati*) is *nissana*; the prefix *ni-* is used here in the sense of "breathing" (*sambhattiya*).
*Sara* and *nissana* form a *dvanda* compound. 129.

That which is released (*visajjīyate*) and does not stick (*na laggīyate*) due to phlegm (*semha*) and so forth is *visaṭṭha*. It is to be thought of (*manitabba*) as *mañju*; [the suffix] *ju* is added to the root *mana*.

It is *mañju* because it delights the minds of those who hear it when they know it; [the suffix] *u* is used here, and there is no elision of *ra*. It is *viññeyya* because it is to be understood with ease.
It is *savanīya* because it is to be heard since it brings about welfare and happiness. It is *avisārī* because it does not stray or go even a finger’s breadth outside the assembly;
[the suffix] *ṇī* is used in the sense of its nature (*sīla*). Alternatively, it is *avisārī* because it does not wander in various directions.

The meaning is that it does not split into two, like a severed sound (*chinnassara*). It is called a *bindu* because it is found or obtained (*vindyate labbhati*); here *va* is substituted for *vi*, there is the insertion of the *niggahīta*, and *u* is added.

Alternatively, it is a *bindu* because of its circular shape; in this latter case, the form is established through [the rules of] *pabbajjā* and so forth. It is profound (*gambhīra*) because it arises from a distant place relative to the five locations of articulation (*ṭhānagati*).
It is a "resounding roar" (*ninnāda*) because of repeated sound; the doubling of the consonant occurs because it is a frequent action (*kriyābhikkhañña*).
*Assa i*: there is the insertion of *niggahīta* (*anusvāra*); because that exists here, it is *ninnādī*. Thus, in this way, the Blessed One’s voice possesses eight qualities (*aṭṭhaṅgika*).
130. The cry of animals such as rhinoceroses and the like is called *vassita*. The root *ru* means sound; thus, *ruta*. The root *vassa* means sound; the act of sounding or crying out is *vassita*.
The pair beginning with *kolāhala* refers to indistinct sounds produced by many people gathering together. The root *kula* means aggregation or counting. (Ka.)

*Kolanaṃ* is *kolo*, meaning "unification"; that which seizes (*āharati*) or finds (*vindati*) this is *kolāhala*. *Kalo* means it performs or harms what is sweet; that which seizes this is *kalahalo*.
The root *hala* is used in the sense of "scratching. The triad refers to singing. The root *ge* means "sound":
that which is to be sung is *gītaṃ*, *gānaṃ*, and *gītikā*. In all these cases, the derivation is based on the abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*).
131. The seven tones beginning with *usabha* arise from the *tanta*, *kaṇṭha*, and *uṭṭhita* [registers], O Immortal One (Amara).
The three beginning with *chajja* are *gāmas*; the meaning is that they are collections (*samūha*). And it is said: “A *gāma* is the conjunction of a collection of tones.

According to the method of playing in the human world, having performed three intonations (*mucchanā*) for each individual tone, there are twenty-one intonations; according to the method of playing in the divine world...
However, they say there are fifty-five notes (*mucchanā*). For in that regard, seven notes are assigned to each individual string, and one to the innermost string;
thus, fifty-five notes are recorded. It is for this very reason that in the commentary on the *Sakkapañha Sutta*, it says:
"Having played fifty-five notes" (*Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 2.345), referring to Pañcasikha’s playing of the lute.
This was stated by the author. *Muccha* occurs among the synonyms for delusion (*moha*); it means "fainting" (*mucchanā*).
Just as a lute can be played according to a sequence, so too there are forty-nine places of fainting (*mucchanaṭṭhāna*) for the virtuous.
For each vowel (*sara*), there are seven places. Since there is a determination of the vowels' softness and loudness, there are thus forty-nine places.
