This is the group of words beginning with *sara* (lake), a collection of [words] starting with *sara*. To show the classification of names similar in form to *sara* and others, he says "usabho" and so forth.

The root *isa* means "to go. It is called *usabho* because it enters the mind (*cittaṃ pavisati*); thus there are *abho* and *issu* as well. Alternatively, the meaning of the verbal root is "to burn" (*usa dāhe*). Furthermore, because he...
It roars like a bull (usabha), therefore it is called "usabha. It is sung by the wise (*dhīmanta*), thus it is *dheyya*; this is a modification of the vowel, a metrical convention (*vatta*).
It is supported by the nose, the throat, the chest, the palate, the tongue, and the teeth.
Because it arises in six ways, it is therefore called "sixfold" (chajja) in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (7.1).

It is a *gandhara* because it seizes (*arati*) scent (*gandha*) and subtle essence (*lesa*); others say it is *gandhāra* due to the lengthening of the short vowel, according to the rule "of others also."
(Pāṇini 3.1.137) *Dīgho* (Cintāmaṇi-Ṭīkā 7.1). The country named Gandhāra; because this [note] is sung by them, it is called *gandhāra*, with the suffix *ṇo*.
That which exists in the middle of the specific musical intervals (*laya*) is the *majjhima* (middle). That which completes the five, beginning with the *devarāja* [scale], is the *pañcama* (fifth);
(alternatively, that which completes the five great elements is the *pañcama*). Here, the reading appears as if it were an interpolation.
In the ultimate sense, it is that in which the *saras* sink; as for the word *yasmim*: according to the rule *sadato adhikaraṇe gho* (Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.1), the suffix *ṇo* is applied.
For it is said: "That in which the *saras* sit down (*nisīdanti*) is *nisāda*; by reason of that [it is so called]. These seven *saras* have been declared—that is, spoken of. 133–135.
To show those which roar, such as the *usabha* and others, he says "they roar," etc. The *sara* named *Usabha*...
Cows low; likewise, swift horses neigh; crested peacocks cry out "chajja"; goats bleat "gandhāra";
the special birds known as *koñcas* cry "majjhima"; cuckoos and the like cry "pañcama"; and elephants roar "nisāda.
And it was said by the sage Nārada:
“The peacock cries out in *chaḍḍa*; the cows low toward the bull;
the goat bleats toward *aja*, and the goats and sheep toward *gandhāra*; the curlews cry out in *majjhima*.
In the season when flowers abound, the cuckoo calls out in *pañcama*.”
“The donkey brays for the deity; the elephant brays for the Nisāda.
All these beings, such as peacocks and others, being intoxicated with joy (*samada*), sing the fifth [note] and cry out the fifth.
There are three types of villages: the *chajja* village, the *majjhima* village, and the *sādhāraṇa* village. In that regard, the division of the lute-neck...
Having designated the lower portion as "Chajjagāma," the middle portion as "Majjhimagāma," and the upper portion as "Sādhāraṇagāma.
But what is the reason for this division of villages? Because there is a division within a single stream across the village boundaries;
when that [stream] is divided, the villages are also divided. However, in the *Māghaṭīkā*, at the place where "Sādhāraṇagāma" occurs, it is "Gandhāragāma."

It was stated that there are seven *mucchanās* for each individual village; however, here, with respect to the seven *saras* beginning with *Usabha*, three *mucchanās* are stated for each one. Why is this?

Because here it is explained according to the method of recitation used in the human world, whereas there it is explained according to the method of recitation used in the deva world; therefore, exactly seven places are obtained in each case.

Just as there might be three modes of intonation (*mucchanā*) for each of those aforementioned notes (*sara*), such as the *usabha* and others, so too seven places (*ṭhāna*) are to be found for each; this is the meaning.

(136) To show that the notes (*sara*) differ in their pitch-intervals (*sutitta*) within the scales (*gāma*), he says "three," and so forth. Regarding the *usabha* note, by way of its *tāra*, *kala*, and *manda* [qualities]...
There are three scales (*sutiyo*). For the *dhevatā* scale, there are two [notes] by way of the sharp (*tāra*) and the soft (*manda*).

For the *chañña* scale, there are four by way of the sharp, the soft, and the *kākalī*. For the *gandhāra* scale, it is the same. For the *majjhima* scale, there are three by way of the sharp, the soft, and the *kākalī*.
For the *pañcama* scale, there are two by way of the soft and the *kākalī*. For the *nisāda* scale, there are four scales by way of the sharp and so forth. Thus it is.
In the seven lakes, twenty-two suttas may be found combined in sequence. However, in the *Māghaṭīkā*, a different classification of the suttas is stated.
For it is said there: "The four suttas are easy to understand;
the middle one is established in the middle sense."
Gandhāra is known as having two notes, and likewise Usabha has three.
Chajja should be known as having four notes, and Nisāda likewise has two.
Dhevatā, however, has four notes, while the fifth is considered to have three.
All of this should be understood from the treatises on drama (*nāṭaka-śāstra*). 137.

By the phrase beginning with "in a higher [pitch]" (*uccatare*), he demonstrates the various types of sound according to their essential nature. In a higher sound, that is, one of very high intensity, it is *tāra*;
it is called *tāra* because it causes one to cross over or awakens the mind. In an indistinct, yet sweet sound that is pleasant to hear, it is *kala*; [it is called] *kala*...

[The word] *manda* is formed [from the root *mad*]. It occurs in the sense of being intoxicated (*madi*), praise (*thuṭi*), joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), delusion (*moha*), and sleep (*supana*).

One who becomes dull or sluggish by means of this is called *manda*. The three words beginning with *tāra* take all three genders because they are adjectival (*vāccaliṅga*). For example: *tāro dhani* (a high-pitched voice), *tārā vāṇī* (a high-pitched speech), *tāraṃ rutaṃ* (a high-pitched sound), and so forth.

A sound that is indistinct and sweet is *kala*. Within that, a subtle *kala* sound is called *kākalī*; it ends in the suffix *-ī*. Alternatively, a voice that is slightly *kala* is called *kākalī*. Here, the word *kā-* has the meaning of "slightly" (*īsa*).
*Samatā* (evenness) in *kriyādi* refers to the evenness of actions such as singing, instrumental music, and the placement of feet, as well as the evenness of time;
this is called *laya*. [The root] *lī* is used in the sense of "going evenly" (*sāmyagati*); the suffix *-a* is added in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*).

Some say that *laya* is the evenness of all dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) as well. 138. There are two [types] of lute (*vīṇā*). [The root] *vi* means "to produce" (*janana*); with the suffix *-to*, it becomes *īṇatta*; or else, the root is *vīṇa* in the sense of "encircling" (*veṭhana*); with the suffix *-ā*, it becomes *vīṇā*. *Valla*...
From the root *val* (to cover), with the suffix *ṇvu*, we have *vallakī*; it belongs to the *nadādi* group. *Vipañcī* is also a name for the lute (*vīṇā*).
It is called *vipañcī* because it "unfolds" (*vipañcayati*), meaning it expands sound; it belongs to the *nadādi* group (as stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 7.3).
That lute, distinguished by seven strings (*sattatantī*), is called *parivādinī*, for it "speaks all around" (*parito vadati*).
Regarding *inī*: some maintain that all four terms beginning with *vīṇā* are general designations for the lute (*vīṇā-sāmañña-vācaka*).
In their view, the suffix *-sā* should be understood as indicating the feminine gender for all four; however, because this contradicts the *Amarakośa* (7.3), their opinion is not to be accepted.

A musical instrument made of wood and other materials in the shape of a trough (*doṇi*) is called the "bellows" (*pokkhara*) of a lute. It is called *pokkhara* because it nourishes, increases, or produces sound;

[the suffixes] *-ra*, *-ra*, increase, and vowel modification [apply here]. The root *du* means "to go"; with the suffix *-ṇi*, it becomes *doṇi*. *Kakubha* and *pasevaka* are also names for the bellows.
It is called *kakubha* because it obstructs or binds the wind (*kaṃ* = wind). It is called *pasevaka* because one sews (*pasibbati*) it together.
In the *pokkharaveṭhaka* and the *camma*, it attains the state of a lute (*vīṇā*); thus it is called *upavīṇa*. It encircles the *pokkhara*; thus it is a *veṭhaka*, with the suffix *ṇvu*. 139.
The pentad beginning with *ātatā* are the names for the fivefold musical ensemble (*pañcaṅgikatūriya*). 140.
Among the instruments covered with leather—such as the *bheri* drum and others—which are to be bound with leather, each one is joined to a single surface in the middle.

Instruments such as the *kumbha*, *thuṇa*, and *daddarika*, which are joined with a membrane (*tala*), are called *ātata* (stretched). It is called *ātata* because it stretches; the root *tan* means to expand.

Even specific types of lutes such as the *mahatī* are indeed *ātata*; for instance, Nārada’s lute is called the "Great One" (*Mahatī*). Because they are covered with leather, the qualification "covered with skin" (*cammāvanaddhesu*) was applied.
Furthermore, because it has the shape of a jar (*kumbha*), it is called a *kumbha*. And because it originated from the city of *Thuna*, [it is called *thuṇa*].
*Thunañca* means a jar-pillar (*kumbhathuṇa*). That itself is a jar-pillar; or else, the root *thu* means "to praise," with the suffix *-no* in the sense of an object.

It is a jar-pillar because it is both a jar (*kumbha*) and a pillar (*thuṇa*); or alternatively, the meaning of the verbal root is "to fill" (*thuṇa pūraṇe*). The root *dara* means "tearing apart" and "burning.
Through reduplication (*dvebhāva*), the substitution of *kāp* for the initial, and the addition of the suffix *-ika*, one who makes the sound *daddara* is called a *daddarikā*.
141. Instruments such as the *muraja* drum, which have two surfaces, are called "stretched" (*vitata*). They are called "stretched" because they specifically extend sound.

All types of "bound" instruments (*vinaddha*)—such as the *paṇava* drum and others—which are covered on all sides and on both the front and back parts, as well as the four-cornered *ālambara*, the *gomukhī*, and so forth, are called "stretched-and-bound" (*ātatavitata*), being bound with leather and strung with cords.

For it is said: “stretched and unstretched. Regarding *paṇa*, it is used in the senses of conventional usage and praise; it is called *paṇava* because it is praised (*paṇīyati*), with the suffix *-avo*.
(142) That which has a hollow, such as a bamboo flute, is called *susira*; a hole is a hollow, and by association with that, it is *susira*.

The root *vana* and *sana* are used in the sense of acquisition; the suffix *-so* gives *vaṃso*. The root *sama* is used in the senses of tranquility and weariness; with the suffix *-kho*, it becomes *saṅkho*. [Instruments] such as the *sammatāḷa* are absolutely...

That which has become liquefied through pressure or contact with fire is called "ghanā" because it becomes solid again; [the derivation is as follows]: *hana* means to strike; with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of an action, the *h* is changed to *gh*.
That which becomes equal (*sama*) by means of its solidity (*ghanabhāva*) is "samma"; that which is to be struck with sticks and so forth is "tāḷa"—from the root *taḷ* meaning to strike;
thus, being both *samma* and *tāḷa*, it is "sammatāḷa. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the inclusion of] bronze cymbals (*kaṃsatāḷa*), stone cymbals (*silātāḷa*), and so forth is intended.

[The section on] Instruments (*gahaṇa*). In this context, a "wooden cymbal" (*sammatāḷa*) is one made of wood. A "bronze cymbal" (*kaṃsatāḷa*) is one made of metal. A "stone cymbal" (*silātāḷa*) is a cymbal played with a stone and a metal plate.

These four are the names for the *ātatā* and so forth. It is called *ātojjam* because it is struck (*tujjati*) and beaten (*tāḷīyati*) all around (*ā*). [It is also produced] by the breath from the mouth in the case of flutes and similar instruments.
*Āto* [is used] only in the sense of a person. They play or they sound it; thus *vādittaṃ* (instrumental music) and *vāditaṃ* (played/sounded), from *ito* and *to*.

They play it as a musical instrument; thus *vajjaṃ*, which is *yo*. 143. Two [forms] for *bheri* (drum). It is called *bheri* because by it (*etena*) beings (*sattujanā*) are made to fear (*bhāyanti*);

[the suffix] *ri*. *Ubha* is used in the sense of filling; *ubhanaṃ* and *ubhi*. Where there is the sound "dunda," that is *dundubhi*. These two, *serī* and *thī*, are feminine; *dundubhi* is masculine.

*Pumā* (Amara 7.6). Regarding the two types of *mudiṅga*: it is called *mudiṅga* because one moves (*iṅgati*) or goes (*gacchati*) toward joy (*mudaṃ*, *modaṃ*). The *muraja* is so named because it was born from the *murā* demon.
The various types or distinctions of this *muraja* are the *āliṅga*, *aṅkya*, and *uddhaka*.
And it is said: "The *haritakyākṛti*, the *tvakya*..."
"Yavamajjhaka, Tatha, Uddhaka,
Āliṅgya, and Gopuccha— these are fully described according to their shapes," as stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* as well.
*Āliṅgyate* (is embraced) thus *āliṅgo*, with the suffix *ṇo*. That which exists in the lap (*ucchaṅka*) is *ucchaṅkhyo*. Because it sounds by being held upward with one mouth, it is *uddho*;
being *uddho*, it "sounds" (*kāyati*), meaning it makes a noise, thus it is *uddhako*. This word *uddha* possesses all three genders. That which rises is *uddho*, with the suffix *to*;
[here] *do* is substituted for the root *gam*. Etymologically, however, the word *uddhaṃ* used in the sense of "above" is strictly an indeclinable (*abyaya*).

*Tiṇavādīni* are four names for a drum (*paṇava*). From the root *tanu* (to expand), with the suffixes *avo*, *itta*, and *ṇatta*, we have *tiṇava*. From the roots *mā* (to measure) and *śabd* (to sound), with the suffix *ṇo*, we have *ḍiṇḍima*, as it resounds or makes a noise like "ḍiṇḍi.

144. It resounds as "ālamba," thus it is *ālambara*. For it is said in the *Amarakośa*, in the section on the collection of various meanings (23.167): "The *ālambara* is the sound of musical instruments and the trumpeting of lordly elephants.
The curved wooden stick used for playing the lute and other instruments is called *koṇa*. It is *koṇa* because one strikes or makes a sound with it; the suffix is *ṇo*. *Dadda*... [text ends]
It makes a sound, thus it is a *daddari*; or, it transforms through a particular sound, thus it is a *daddari* (from the root *ri*).
It abandons the sound "paṭa," thus it is a *paṭaha*; or, it strikes the skin (*paṭa*), thus it is a *paṭaha*. [The root] *hana* is used in the senses of harming and going; [the suffix] *kvi*.

Others, such as the *maddala*, are varieties of the *bheri* drum. It takes the sound "madda," thus it is a *maddala*; [the root] *lā* means to take; [the suffix] *a*. There is also a reading *mandala*.

It is called *mandalā* because it produces a soft sound (*mandaṃ saddaṃ lāti*). By this [method], other types of drums such as the *ḍamaru* and so forth should also be understood as varieties of the *bherī*.

145. *Janappiya*: that which is dear to people, to be loved by people; *vimadda*: the rubbing together of unguents such as saffron and various fragrant substances; from this rubbing arises *parimalo*, meaning "fragrance.

It is derived etymologically (*nerutto*) from the sense of "that which is rubbed" (*parimajjati*), "that which is spread" (*pavattayati*), or "that which is applied" (*āsayaṃti*). *Mala* is the suffix.

Or, it means "bearing" (*dhāraṇe*) as in *malla* (a wrestler). It is called *parimala* because it is "perfumed" (*parimalyate*) or "borne" (*dhārīyate*), with the suffix *ṇo*. Alternatively, by the inclusion of the term "crushing" (*vimadda*), there is the exclusion of things such as ponds and wells, which possess a scent of crushing;

and by the inclusion of the term "people" (*jana*), there is the exclusion of things such as flies. That fragrance (*gandha*) which travels far, is exceedingly pervasive, and reaches very great distances is called *āmoda*;

it is so called because people rejoice (*āmodante*) by means of it, with the suffix *ṇo*. From here onwards, [the terms] beginning with "pleasant scent" (*iṭṭhagandha*) and ending with the word "fame" (*vissa*) [are explained].
Occurring in the three genders. 146.
The tetrad on pleasant odor (*iṭṭhagandha*). A pleasant odor is *iṭṭhagandha*; alternatively, that which has a pleasant odor is *iṭṭhagandha*.
One by means of which they thoroughly delight or are satisfied is *surabhi*; thus, that which has a beautiful odor is *sugandha* or *sugandhi*.
And [the suffix] *ca* [is applied], with the substitution of *i* for the internal vowel.
The word *dvaya* is used in the sense of "bad odor. Since it possesses a putrid odor (*pūti gandho assa*), there is a substitution of *i* as before;

they wish to form a *kammadhāraya* compound even in the sense of "possessing" (*assatthi*), yet the *bahubbīhi* alone is the logical rule for the sake of brevity in grammatical operation. Thus, "it has a bad odor" is *duggandha*.
Therefore, it was stated by Kaccāyana: “The *bahubbīhi* is lighter than the *kammadhāraya* ending in suffixes expressing the sense of the final member.

Others, however, disregarding this brevity (*lāghava*), desire [the compound] to end in suffixes expressing the sense of the final member. Alternatively, the property to be expressed is of two kinds: light and heavy;

therein, the *bahubbīhi* is light, while the *kammadhāraya* ending in suffixes expressing the sense of the final member is heavy. Furthermore, what purpose is served by the *bahubbīhi*? It serves the purpose of expressing excellence (*atisāya*) and so forth.
Since it cannot be understood [otherwise], for the sake of establishing that meaning, it must necessarily be regarded as a *kammadhāraya* compound preceded by a *mantatthi* (suffix).

"Dvayaṃ" refers to the two: the smoke of the funeral pyre and so forth, and the scent. "Visa" means separation; [the suffix] *so*. The scent of raw substances such as fat and the like—due to its connection with that [substance], [the suffix] *i*, and the word *yaṃ* indicates its neuter gender.

147. The four beginning with saffron (*kuṅkuma*) are called the "fourfold aromatic blend" (*catujjātigandha*). [The root] *kuka*, *vaka* [means] taking up; [the suffix] *umo*; there is the elision of the *niggahīta*.
And *kuṅkuma* (saffron), red sandalwood—which is called "Kasmīraja"—or else *kuṅkuma* is a substitution for *kamiṣsa*;

[the suffix] *yu* occurs after the root *yu*, meaning to mix; its flower is *yavanapuppha*, or "divine flower" (*devakusuma*), or it is called *yavanapuppha* because it is a flower born in the land of Yavana.
That which is also called "lavanga" (cloves) is a flower similar to the *nuhī* flower.
The root *tagi* has the sense of "going" (*gati*); it is a *daṇḍaka* root. It is *arō*, *tagaraṃ*, and *kuṭilaṃ*. That which is born from *taru* is *turukkha*;
indeed, the resin of the *sallakī* tree is called "*turukkha*. 148.

[Now follow] the names of the six tastes according to their sequence. It nourishes water (*kaṃ pānīyaṃ sevate*), thus it is *kasāva*; it is *ava*. Alternatively, it causes one to relish (*savāpeti*) water, thus...

*Kasāva* means astringent. *Tuvara* and *kasāya* are synonyms for astringent. The root *tij* means to sharpen; [from it come] *titta* (pungent) and *kaṭu* (bitter). *Madhu* means sweetness; because of its connection with that, it is *madhura* (sweet).
It cuts off dullness (*jaḷatta*), thus it is *lavaṇa* (salty); [the suffix] *yu*. In the word *amba*, there is the suffix *ara*, the substitution of *i* for *a*, and the substitution of *la* for *a*.
*Kaṭa* means motion; [with the suffix] *ṇvu*, there is the substitution of *u* for *a*. These six are called "flavors" (*rasā*). They exist in substances (*dabba*) possessing them.
The words *kasāva* and so forth function in all three genders.
149. Two [terms] regarding tangibles (*phoṭṭhabba*). That which is to be touched is *phassa*, *phoṭṭhabba*, *tabba*, *sassa ṭo*, and *tassa ṭho*.

Three [terms] regarding that which possesses an object (*visayin*). That which has an object (*visaya*) in the sense of being grasped is *visayin*. It is called *ukhati* because it goes toward the object.
"Akkha" [is so called] because it is "ussatta" (elevated) and "dvitta" (doubled), or because there is no "kha" (void) or feeling (*vedanā*) therein.

For pleasant feelings and the like do not arise in the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) by way of association; rather, they arise only in the impulsion-moments (*javana*) and so forth—thus it is said.
Furthermore, it is "akkha" because of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) upon the mind-faculty (*manindriya*); "indo" means the self (*attā*), and its mark is the *indriya*.

[The term] *indriya* has two [meanings]. Other schools (nikāyantarika) maintain that the eye and so forth do not function without an immediate motivator; therefore, there exists a self (*atta*) which is the motivator of the eye and other faculties, and thus the eye and so forth serve as the mere mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the self.

Alternatively, it is called *indriya* because it exercises supreme sovereignty (*paramissariya*) over them, since the sharpness, dullness, and other qualities of visual consciousness and the rest arise from the sharpness, dullness, and other qualities of the eye itself.
*Chakkaṃ* means eyes (*nayane*). It is called *nayana* because it leads (*neti*) the person dependent upon it; [the suffix] *yu* is added. *Asu* means to pervade (*byāpane*);
it is called *akkhi* because it exists as if pervasive (*byāpī*) toward sense objects (*visayeṣu*); [the suffix] *ko* is added to *as*. Alternatively, *akkha* refers to pervading and seeing;

it is called *akkhi* because it pervades (*akkhati*) toward sense objects, or because one sees (*akkhati*) by means of it. *Nettaṃ* means that which leads (*neti*). *Locanaṃ* means that by which one looks (*locati*) or sees (*passati*).
*Locanaṃ*. [The term] *acchi* is used in the sense of clear vision and pervading; it is *accha*. It is called *cakkhu* because it sees (*cakkhati*) and relishes form (*rūpa*), with the suffix *-u*;
or alternatively, it is *cakkhu* because it sees (*cakkhati*).
150. The pentad refers to the channel (*sota*). It is called *sota* because one hears by means of it. It is called *saddaggaha* because sound is apprehended by it. *Kara*... [text fragment].
*Karaṇe*, *ṇo*, *kaṇṇo*, *kaṇṇati*: it is called *kaṇṇo* because one hears by means of it; *kaṇṇa* is in the sense of hearing. *Savana* is that by which one hears; it is both *suti* and *yu*.

The tetrad [of terms] refers to the nose. *Nasanti etāyāti natthu*: *thu*, *ā*, *nāsā*. With the suffix *ṇvu* and the addition of *aka* and the letter *i*, it becomes *nāsikā*. *Ghā* is in the sense of grasping odor; it is called *ghāna* because it performs the grasping of odor;

with the suffix *yu*, or because they smell by means of it, it is *ghāna*. The dyad refers to the tongue. *Jīvati etāyāti jivhā*, *ho*: *jīva* is in the sense of maintaining life. Taste is the cause for maintaining life.

That which is called *jīvita* (life); it is called *jivhā* (tongue) because it calls out to that [life], with the elision of the vowel (*vaṇṇalopa*). It is called *rasanā* (tongue) because one tastes by means of it;
the root *ras* means to taste, or it is called *rasanā* because it knows taste.

For *ñā*, there is *nā*; or for *nī* (to lead), there is *a*. (A 151). *Pajja* refers to the body. It is called *sarīra* because it moves or goes, or because they move toward and harm it; thus it is *sarīra*, with the suffix *īra*. *Vapa*...

In the continuity of seeds (*bījasantāne*). It is called *vapu* because one sows the seed of the wholesome and unwholesome here; from the root *vap*, "to sow. It is called *gatta* because by means of this one goes (*gacchati*) or grasps (*gaṇhāti*) the wholesome and unwholesome;
from *gamu* in the sense of going, or *gaha* in the sense of grasping. It is called *attabhāva* because the designation "self" (*attā*) and the corresponding cognition arise from it.

It is called *bondi* because one restrains (*saṃvarati*) therein; from the root *vu* in the sense of restraining, with the suffix *di* and the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta*. It is "diverse" (*vividhaṃ*).
The analysis is: *gaṇhāti ettha* (it grasps here). From the root *dih* in the sense of accumulation (*upacaya*), that wherein the wholesome and unwholesome accumulate and increase is the *deha*.
This word *deha* is used in the masculine gender for a male person. *Kāya* means the source (*āya*) or place of origin of things that are contemptible (*kucchita*).

From the root *tan* in the sense of extension (*vitthāra*), with the suffix *u*, we have *tanu*; this word *tanu* is feminine. Here too, the particle *vā* (or) should be connected [to the preceding]. "Limb by limb... [etc.]
"Let the thin [body] be united with the thin [one], and the afflicted with the afflicted"—this is stated in the *Uttaramegha* (verse 42) of the *Meghadūta*.
"Kaḷe-retasi varaṃ kaḷevaraṃ": this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). 152–154.

The group of six [terms] refers to the mind (*citta*). It is called "mind" (*citta*) because it thinks (*cinteti*). It is also "heart" (*ceto*), with the elision of the letter *na*. It is called "intellect" (*mano*) because it knows (*manati*) or understands.

It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (*viññāṇa*); [this is] *yu*. It carries its own support, thus it is the heart (*hadaya*); [this is] *yo*, with the short vowel *do* [also applied]. The mind itself is the mental (*mānasa*);
[the suffix] *saṇa* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
These are the names for the fourteen qualities known as "Buddha. It meditates, thus it is wisdom (*dhī*); [the root] *jhi* means to think; *jha* becomes *dha*; [it belongs to] the *nadādi* group.

*Dhī*: it is called *dhī* because it "holds" (*dhāreti*); [the suffix] *kvi*, [belonging to] the *nadādi* group; *dhī*. Or else, *dhī* is so called because "by means of this, the state of being wise (*dhīkāra*) arises regarding mental formations (*saṅkhāresu*)," [the suffix] *a*, [belonging to] the *nadādi* group.

It is called *paññā* because "by means of this, one understands" (*paññāyate*); [the suffix] *a*. It is called *buddhi* because "by means of that, one awakens" (*bujjhate*); [the suffix] *ti*. It is called *medhā* because "it destroys" (*hiṃsati*) amidst the entanglements (*sāsaṅgamesu*);

[the suffix] *a* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), or [the root] *mi* in the sense of "destroying" (*hiṃsāyaṃ*), with the prefix *dho*; thus, *medhā*. It is called *mati* and *muti* because "it thinks" (*manati*) or "it knows" (*jānāti*); as it is said: "it understands" (*munāti*).

*Muti*: from the root *mū* in the sense of "knowing" (*ñāṇe*), with the suffix *ti*, thus *muti*. *Bhūrī*: from the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattāyaṃ*), with the suffix *ri*, belonging to the *nadādi* group; or, it is *bhūrī* because it delights (*ramati*) in the meaning known as "vastness" (*bhūsaṅkhāte atthe*), with the suffix *kvi*, belonging to the *nadādi* group.

*Mantā*: from the root *man* in the sense of "to know" (*jānāti*), with the suffix *anta*, and the vowel *ā*. *Vijjā*: from the root *vid* in the sense of "to know" (*jānāti*), established by the rule beginning with *pabbajjā*.

*Yoni*: from the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (*missane*). It is *yoni* because it mixes (*yamati*) or becomes blended (*missībhavati*) with objects of knowledge (*ñeyyesu*). *Paṭibhāna*: they shine forth (*bhanti*) or present themselves (*upaṭṭhahanti*) facing toward (*paṭimukhaṃ*).
*Paṭibhānaṃ*: that by which one is able to respond; [the suffix] *yu*. *Amoho*: that by which one does not become deluded.
*Vīmaṃsā*, *vicayo*, *samupekkhā*, *upaladdhi*, *paṭipatti*, *utti*, *cetana*, and so forth, are also names for intelligence (*buddhi*).

Terms such as *vipassanā* and others are synonyms for the various types of wisdom (*paññā*) when they have reached maturity; they are distinctions within wisdom. Among these, [wisdom] regarding the manifold aspects of impermanence and so forth...
"Seeing formations" is insight (*vipassanā*), friend. Right view has the characteristic of right seeing; it is twofold, by way of the mundane and the supramundane.
Therein, the former is obtained at the time of the occurrence of the six purifications, while the latter is obtained at the time of the purification by knowledge and vision.
By the phrase "beginning with," the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) and the others are included. In various places...

Investigation (*vicāraṇā*) among tasks. It is the mental application (*cittābhoga*) and so forth in this [context of] applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). It is called investigation (*vicāraṇā*) because one investigates (*vicārayati*) by means of it; the root *car* means "to accumulate," belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, with the suffix *yu*.
One who is fully aware is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*), whether referring to a person or a collection of phenomena (*dhammasamūha*).

From the verb *jānāti*, the suffix *ña* is applied to form *jā*; the state of that is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*). By applying the suffix *ña* to *sampajañña*, the doubling of the consonant occurs. This [clear comprehension] functions by way of clear comprehension regarding purposefulness (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) and so forth.
It is fourfold. One who brings wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) to their completion is "wise" (*nipaka*); he is a person possessing knowledge (*ñāṇī*). His state is "wisdom" (*nepakka*).

There are two [derivations] for "feeling" (*vedanā*). That which feels is "the felt" (*vedayita*); from the root *vida* in the sense of experiencing, with the suffix *-ṇa* due to its belonging to the *curādi* class, followed by the suffix *-ta* and the insertion of the vowel *i*.
That which feels is "feeling" (*vedanā*), with the suffix *-yu*.
155. Regarding the group of five [terms], there is *vitakka* and *takka*. *Takka* means *vitakka*. It is called *takka* because it directs associated states toward an object (*ārammaṇa*).
*Vitakka* differs from it only by the prefix (*upasagga*). It is called *saṅkappa* because one intends (*saṅkappanti*) by means of it;

the suffix *-a* is added to the root *kappa* in the sense of *vitakka*, or to the root *kappa* in the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*), belonging to the *bhūvādi* class. Thus, they intend—that is, they originate—by means of it.

*Vā* means intention (*saṅkappa*); *kappa* means thought (*vitakka*), belonging to the *curādi* class. *Apa* means reaching; it reaches the object, causing the associated states to reach it, thus it is *appanā*.
The suffix *yu* becomes *ā*. *Ūha* means thought (*vitakka*). That by which one thinks is *ūha*. Here, the words *takka* and *ūha* also signify "interpolation" (*ajjhāhāra*).
Interpolation (*ajjhāhāra*) is defined as the bringing in of an additional distinction to fill a deficiency, that is, the taking up of something extra (from the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).
“*Ajjhāhāra*, *takka*, and *ūha*” is stated in the *Amarakosa* (5.3). Two [terms] refer to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
The root *aya* has the sense of going; it is a *daṇḍaka* root. That by which one goes along the course of time is *āyu*; [the suffix] *ṇu*. Or, that by which one goes is *āyu*;
[the root] *i* in the sense of going, with [the suffix] *ṇu*, *isse*, and *e aya*. That by which they live is *jīvita*; [the root] *jīva* in the sense of sustaining life.

The tetrad concerns concentration (*samādhi*). It is "one-pointed" (*ekagga*) because it has a single peak (*eka-agga*), that is, an object (*ārammaṇa*), due to the absence of wandering toward various objects.
For it is said in the *Saddhammaṭīkā*: "In this context, the word 'peak' (*agga*) denotes the object. The state of that is one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).
Alternatively, it is "one-pointed" because it moves toward (*ajati*) or goes to a single object; the state of that is one-pointedness. [It abandons] sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

It is *samatha* because it comes together (*sameti*). The root *sam-ū* means to pacify. As stated in the *Pārāyaṇa*: "Concentration (*samādhi*) is the antidote to sensual desire. (Dharmasaṅgraha 160).
Distraction (*vikkhepa*) is the scattering [of the mind] toward various objects;

that which is devoid of this is non-distraction (*avikkhepa*). Concentration (*samādhi*) is the firm placing [of the mind] upon a single object. In this context, it refers to that which proceeds by way of the distraction toward various objects within perception.
Alternatively, it is *samādhi* etymologically (*nerutto*) because one attains (*sameti*) the piercing of the mind through volitional effort (*adhisaṅkhāta*).
156. Here follow synonyms for energy (*vīriya*). It is *ussāha* because it endures (*sahati*) or bears up against (*khamati*) suffering;
[the suffix] *ṇo*. It is *ātappa* (or *ātāpa*) because it intensely heats (*tāpeti*) both body and mind; [the suffix] *ā*. (Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā 1135).
In this verse, *tap* means to heat or torment. It is called *paggaha* because it uplifts and raises the sluggish mind;
or, it is called *paggaha* because it causes one’s own basis to grasp the ultimate truth (*paramattha*). For it is stated in the *Ekakkharakosa*: "The prefix *pa-* also refers to the ultimate.
It is called *vāyāma* because they strive by means of it; the root *vāyama* means exertion. Alternatively, *vaya* is a verbal root meaning "to go."

*Dhātu* (element). Or, *vāyāma* (exertion) is so called because it "strives" (*vayati*) at all times; or, it is *vāyāma* because it "always moves" (*amati*) like the wind (*vāyu*). It is *parakkama* (perseverance) because it "treads upon" (*akkamati*) successive stages;
or, it is *parakkama* because it "treads upon" (*akkamati*) laziness (*kosajja*), which stands as its adversary.

It is *padhāna* (effort) because one "strives by means of it" (*padahati yena*); [the suffix] *-yu* is added. For the root *daha* (to burn), there is the substitution of *dha* for *da*; *daha* means to reduce to ashes, and with the prefix *pa-* attached to the root *dhā*, [it forms *padhāna*].
It should be accomplished, so it seems. *Vīriya* means that which is good for the brave (*vīra*), or the action of the brave, or that which is to be set forth or put into motion according to method;

[the root] *īr* means "to go. *Īhā* is that by which one strives (*īhati*) or goes toward the fruit of the beautiful and the ugly; *īh* means "striving," with the suffix *hap* added to the final syllable.
*Uyyāma* is that by which one exerts oneself upward; [the root] *yam* with the suffix *amo*. It is called *thāma* because the fruit of the beautiful and the ugly stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein.
*Dhiti* (fortitude), *ti* (stability), and *ṭhā* (standing) refer to the cessation of movement.
(157) This shows the four factors of energy (*vīriya*) as described by the method of exposition.

The "remaining" of the three, beginning with the skin, refers to their state of being left over once the flesh and blood have served as the limit; the "drying up" of the flesh and blood, however, refers to their state of being parched.
These four, proceeding by way of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), are the factors and causes of energy (*vīriya*).

The root *aṅg* has the sense of "going. Because the fruit of energy goes to success (*siddhi*) by means of these, they are called "factors" (*aṅgāni*). The root *tṛc* means "to protect"; with the suffix *ṇa*, it becomes *taco*. The root *nah* means "to bind";
with the prefix *ā*, it becomes *nhāru*—this is also a reading. In that case, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*). The root *sis* is used in non-standard applications.
*Yu*, *dvitta*. That which exists not and is exhausted over a journey is *aṭṭhi*; this is a neuter form according to etymological derivation (*nerutto*).

Alternatively, *aṭṭhi* is that by which one stands firmly (*ābhuso tiṭṭhati*); thus, *i*. *Man* means knowledge; with the suffix *so*, the nasalization (*niggahīta*) is dropped, resulting in *maṃsaṃ*.

*Ruh* means to be born; with the suffix *ito*, it becomes *lohitaṃ*. 158. Even when there is no immediate accomplishment, that effort by virtue of which one exerts oneself is *ussoḷhī*: an intense striving (*adhimattehā*), an effort endowed with superior power (*adhikasattiyuttā īhā*).

*Ussolhi*: that by which one endures powerful, difficult tasks; it is derived from *saḷha* (to endure) with the prefix *us-*, belonging to the *nadādi* class. Alternatively, it is the bringing together (*ūhā*) of various efforts (*ussāhānaṃ*);

like the term "paccaya" or "padaṭṭhāna," there is the substitution of *ḷ* for *r*, the elision of *ū*, and the *nadādi* suffix. It applies even to mere exertion. The pair [of terms] refers to mindfulness (*sati*).

It is called *sati* because one remembers (*sarati*) by means of it, or they remember by means of it, or because it is merely the act of remembering (*saraṇa-matta*). It is the opposite of negligence (*pamāda*).
It is *sati* because it remembers (*sarati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*). *Anussati* is repeated mindfulness (*anu-punappunaṃ sati*); or rather, the prefix alone constitutes the distinction.

Both [terms] are feminine. The pair refers to modesty (*lajjā*). The root *laji* means "to oppress" (*pīḷe*); this is a *kātantadhātu*. The root *lajja* means "modesty" (*lajjane*); this is a *moggallānadhātu*. One is modest (*lajjati*) regarding evil, thus it is *lajjā*, with the suffix *a*.
*Hirī* is that which is to be modest about; it has the suffix *i*. One is ashamed (*hiriyati*) of evil, thus it is *hirī*. These two have the same meaning and are synonymous. This is the pair.
*Ottappa*. It is *ottappa* because one is afraid (*bhāyati*) of evil; the root *tap* (to fear) is preceded by the prefix *ava*.
One who fears evil due to virtue is *pāpabhīru*, whether referring to a person or the mind; its state is likewise [called] so. 159.

These are synonyms for equanimity (*upekkhā*) as a feeling, according to the latter half [of the verse]. It is *majjhattikā* because it occurs in a state of neutrality (*majjhatta*) or with a neutral nature (*majjhattasabhāva*).
*Upekkhā* is so called because it is an "looking" (*ikkhā*) that occurs in proximity to two types of feeling; "looking" (*ikkhā*) means seeing.
It is "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhā*) because it is neither painful nor pleasant; the letter *m* is used for metrical or euphonic connection (*padasandhikara*).
It is "mental application" (*cittābhoga*) because it bends (*ābhujana*) and turns toward (*āvaṭṭāpana*) the mind as it proceeds by way of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
And here, the verbal root *bhuj* has the sense of "maintaining" (*pālana*) and "taking in" (*ajjhohāra*), while with the prefix *ā-*, it has the sense of "turning toward" (*āvaṭṭana*).

This, however, is said with reference to that which leads [the mind] into the cognitive process (*vīthi-javana*). Mental application (*cittābhoga*) is the bending of the mind toward the object or its occurrence there;

this, moreover, is stated by way of the leading of the mind toward the object. It is called mental attention (*manasikāra*) because it makes the mind dissimilar from the state of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), or because "making" (*kāra*) is the act of making, and it occurs in the mind (*manasmiṃ*).
*Kāra* means making (*manakkāra*). Here, by the first alternative, two types of practitioners are described; by the latter, however, the other [type] is meant.
The dyad refers to resolve (*adhimokkha*). The root *muc* means releasing. Resolve (*adhimokkha*) is the act of resolving, the making of a definitive determination that "this alone is so.
*Nicchaya* means deciding or determining. The root *ci* has the sense of going; it is a *daṇḍaka* root, and there is doubling of the consonant, as in *chatta*.
*Nibbhusaṃ* is the intensive prefix for *chedana* (cutting), expressing certainty. The root *chidi* means "to divide into two. [In *nicchaya*,] *ni* is the prefix and *ssa* is the suffix;

this is an irregular (*asarūpa*) doubling. 160. *Pajjaddhaṃ* is used in the sense of compassion (*dayā*). The root *daya* signifies giving, going, harming, and protecting. *Dayā* is so called because it feels the suffering of others and harms one's own happiness; it has the suffix *a*. The root *kapi* means "to move.
*Anukampā* is so called because it repeatedly causes the mind, which is supported by the self, to tremble; it has the suffix *a*.

*Karunā* (compassion) is so called because it obstructs (*rundhati*) happiness; the root *rudh* means "to obstruct," and the *dh* is changed to *ṇ*. Alternatively, it is *karuṇā* because by means of it, one makes oneself dependent (*adhīna*);

the suffix *yu* and the vowel *ā* [form the word]. That very same thing is *kāruñña* (pity). *Anuddayā* (tenderness) is a word formed by adding a prefix. The latter half [of the term] refers to abstinence (*virati*).

The root *ram* with the prefix *vi-* means "to cease. Abstinence is *veramaṇī*; the suffix *yu* is applied, and since it belongs to the *nadādi* class, it takes the feminine suffix *ī*. Alternatively, it is *veramaṇī* because it destroys (*maṇati*) or dispels (*vināseti*) what is opposed (*vera*). Abstinence is *virati*. Abstinence from afar is *ārati*.
161. A tetrad concerning patience (*khanti*). Enduring, bearing, is *titikkhā*; [the root] *tij* means patience. *Kha* is a pair; [it is] the agent, etc., and *ā*. Bearing, enduring, is *khanti*;

[the root] *kham* means to endure. One endures, thus it is *khamana*, and also *khamā*; [the root] *khamu* means to endure. A dyad concerning loving-kindness (*mettī*). [The root] *mid* means moisture;
one becomes moistened, one feels affection, thus it is *mettā*; [the suffixes] *ta* and *ā*. Also *metti*. Or else, in friends...
*Bhava* (existence) has the forms *mettā* and *metti*.

In the latter half [of the verse], it concerns *diṭṭhi* (view). *Dassana* (seeing) is that which is seen; from the root *disa* in the sense of looking, with the suffix *yu*, we have *dassana*, which is *diṭṭhi*.

From the root *labha* in the sense of obtaining, we have *laddhi*; this refers specifically to wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). The remaining [forms] apply to both. A settled position is a tenet (*siddhanta*); it is established.
*Pakkha* means a tenet (*siddhanta*). The meaning is "the establishment of the proven position after having refuted the opposing position" (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that by which the end is established. *Samaya* is a movement or course that proceeds everywhere.
162. *Dohaḷa* is used in the sense of craving (*taṇhā*). *Tasa* is used in the sense of thirst; that by which beings tremble is craving, with the suffix *-ṇha*. In the sense of debt, it is *tasiṇā*.
*Ejā*: from *ej*, meaning "to shake" or "to move. *Jālinī*: because it is like a net (*jāla*) in its inability to provide an escape from *saṃsāra*;

the suffix *-inī* is used here as a simile. *Visattikā*: from *vis*, meaning "to enter"; it is called *visattikā* because it has spread (*visatā*) everywhere; the suffix *-ika* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). *Chando*: in the sense of desire (*icchā*);
*chandanaṃ* is *chando*, which also refers to the wish to act (*kattukamyatā*). *Jaṭā*: because it is like a tangle (*jaṭā*) due to being entangled (*ākulībhūta*) with various objects (*ārammaṇa*).
*Kamu* is in the sense of desire; it is *nikanti*. *Isu* is in the sense of desire; with the suffix *a*, *issa* becomes *āsā*. *Sivu* is in the sense of weaving;
because it weaves (*sibbatī*) existence and so forth, it is *sibbinī*; with the suffixes *a* and *inī*. Because it leads beings to existence, it is *bhavanetti*.
163. *Jhe* is in the sense of thinking; because it meditates (*jhāyati*) directed toward an object, it is *abhijjhā*; with the suffix *ā*. *Vana* is in the sense of longing; it longs (*vanati*).
That by which one is entangled is *vana*. Or, in the sense of moving (*gati*), it moves toward an object; thus it is *vāna*, with the suffix *yu*. *Lubh* means desire;
the state of being greedy is *lobha*, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Rañj* means passion; the act of coloring, or that by which they are colored, is *rāga*, with the suffix *ṇo*.

*Laya* means moving; it repeatedly adheres (*layati*) to objects, thus it is *ālaya*; or, that by which one repeatedly adheres—that is, clings—is *ālaya*. "Adherence (*laya*) [is used] in the sense of destruction."

In the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*, it is said: “*Saṃsilese*, *sāmye*, and *turiyattikassa*. *Pihā*: [The root] *pih* is used in the sense of desire (*icchā*); it belongs to the *curādigaṇa*. With the suffix *a*, it becomes *pihayati*. That by which one desires is *pihā*. *Manoratha*:
Because it causes the mind to wander among various objects, it is like a chariot for the mind; thus it is a *manoratha*. Or, it is a *manoratha* because the mind itself is like a chariot.
[The root] *is* is used in the sense of desire; with the suffix *a*, there is the substitution of *cch* for *s*. *Lasa*: [The root] *las* is used in the sense of longing (*kanti*).

*Abhilāsa*: that by which one shines having made [an object] present before oneself; the suffix *ṇo*. The root *kam* means desire; with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *kāma*. *Dohaḷa*: from the root *duh* in the sense of filling, *duhanaṃ* is "the act of filling"; that which takes (*lāti*) this is *dohaḷa*.
Alternatively, *dohaḷa* is that by which the heart (*hadaya*) is afflicted (*duṭṭha*). Or, *haḷa* is a substitute for *hadaya*;

from the root *hal* meaning "to shake," with the prefix *dvi-*, it is *dohaḷa* because it shakes or trembles (*kampati*) by means of two [factors]. The suffix *a* is applied, *dvi* becomes *do*, and *la* becomes *ḷa*.

*Ḷo*: Alternatively, *dohaḷo* means "two hearts for that ultimate reality" (*paramattha*). [The derivation is as follows: *do* replaces *dvi*; *haḷo* replaces *hadaya*; *ḷo* optionally replaces *da*; there is the elision of *ya*.
Although *dohaḷa* is a specific kind of desire, it is designated here by the general term "desire" (*icchā*) because it possesses the common characteristic of being a wish.

Even though it is by nature free from craving (*taṇhā*), he says "let him long for" (*ākaṅkhātu*) and so forth, using this very context to describe it through its commonality with the nature of wishing for an object.
*Kaṅkhā* is desire (*icchā*). *Rucī* is delight (*ruca*); delight is the wish to act. Or, from *ruca* in the sense of radiance, it is *ruci*.
It is simply the wish to act. That *ruci* which is excessive is called *lālasā*. From the root *lasa* in the sense of shining; it shines again and again or excessively, thus it is *lālasā*.
[The doubling of the consonant occurs] by rule (*assā*). [It is used] in the sense of begging, in great desire, and in the excess of craving. [Cited from the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.]
7.28) *Ussukka* means longing or desire; *rudda* means hostility. (164) This triad refers to opposition.

*Vera* generally arises among the brave, but it also occurs in those who are hostile or wicked. From the root *rudh* meaning "to obstruct," *virodha* is the act of being obstructed. From *dis* meaning "dislike," *viddesa* is the act of disliking.
From *rus* meaning "anger," *roṣa* is anger. From *dus* meaning "dislike," *dosa* is the act of disliking. That which strikes against an object (*ārammaṇa*) is called *paṭigha*; from the root *han*.
*Hiṃsā* (violence) and *paṭigha* (aversion) occur in the masculine gender. *Kudh* means anger; the act of being angry is *kodha*. That which comes and strikes is *āghāta*. *Kup* means to be agitated;
that which is agitated is *kopa*, or it agitates the mind, thus it is *kopa*. *Rus* means to be resentful;
the act of being resentful or feeling ill-will is *rosa*.

Two [states] are in the thinking of harm toward others. It is *vyāpāda* because the mind is “vitiated” (*byāpajjati*) or destroyed by it; it also refers to resentment (*paṭigha*). The root *pada* means “going. It is *anabhirati* because one does not delight (*na abhiramati*) in the prosperity of others;

the root *ram* means “to delight. 165. Two [states] are in enmity (*upanāha*). The root *naha* means “binding”; it is *upanāha* because the mind binds itself repeatedly or binds itself having approached [the object]. It is *baddhavaira* because one is bound by enmity. Two [states] are in sorrow (*soka*). The root *suc* means “sorrow”; with the suffix *-ṇo*, it becomes *soka*. *Socana* is the act of grieving. *Sucate* is the act of grieving.
The triad refers to weeping. *Rudi* means the shedding of tears; in all these cases, the suffix *-to* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). *Kadi* means calling out and weeping;

with the substitution of *aṇṇ* for the suffix *-tap*, it becomes *ruṇṇaṃ*. The dyad refers to lamentation. *Devanaṃ* is wailing due to grief. Lamentation (*paridevo*) is crying again and again, or crying on all sides; it is also called *pariddavo*.

166. *Tikaṃ* (the triad) refers to fear (*bhaya*), which is defined as the agitation of the mind. In all these cases, the formation is by means of the abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*). From the root *bhī*, meaning "to fear": *bhāyanam* is *bhīti*;
thus, *bhayaṃ* [is formed] with the suffix *ṇo*. From the root *tasa*, meaning "to be terrified": *uttasate* is *uttāso*; [this is formed] with the suffix *ṇo*.

The dyad refers to great fear. This belongs to those who are fearful (*bhīru*); thus, *bheravaṃ* [is formed] with the suffix *ṇo*. It is "great" (*mahanta*) and it is "fear" (*bhaya*) because it generates fear; thus, it is *mahabbhayaṃ*. The reading *mahābhayaṃ* is also found.
167. *Pajja* is used in the sense of that which is to be feared. This word *bherava* exists as a term denoting a general quality;

hence it is specified here. That from which one fears is *bhiṃsana*; [the suffix] *yu* is added, with the augment *bind*. That from which one fears is *bhīma*; [the suffix] *mo* is added. *Dara* means "to tear apart";
that which is torn apart is *dāruṇa*; [the suffix] *uṇo* is added. That from which one fears is *bhayānaka*; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is added, with the substitution of *anakā*. *Ghura* means "terrible."
It is *ghora* because it roars (*ghurati*) and terrifies (*bhisati*). It is *paṭibhaya* because fear and mental terror (*cittutrāsa*) turn back from it.
It is *bhesma* because one fears from it; here the suffix *sma* is used. It is *bhayaṅkara* because it produces fear; this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*).
These nine terms, beginning with *bhaira*, function as qualifiers for a substance that serves as the cause of fear, terror, and so forth; at that time, they apply to all three genders.
In terms of gender, it is neuter in its general sense.
(168) The pair [of terms] refers to the inability to endure the prosperity of others. *Issa* means "in the sense of envy" (*issattha*); alternatively, the root-meaning is "to envy" (*issāyanti*).
It is called *issā* because one verbally or mentally attributes faults even when virtues exist. [The suffix] *a* is applied. *Ussuya* is a variant of *usūya*.
*Dosāvikaraṇe*: A triad concerning stinginess (*macchera*). *Masu* [is the root] for touching; from the suffixes *cchera* and *cchara*, *macchara* itself becomes *macchariya*.
The suffix *iya* is used in the sense of the same word (*sakatthe*). Alternatively, in this primary form *masu*, when the *s* is replaced by *ṇam*, there are the suffixes *cchera* and *cchara*;

*masu* is also a verbal root meaning stinginess (*macchera*). A triad concerning ignorance (*aññāṇa*). *Mūha* means mental confusion; by means of it, associated states become deluded, or it itself becomes deluded; it is merely the state of being deluded.
Or *tanti* is delusion (*moha*). *Vida* means knowledge; that which does not know is ignorance (*avijjā*). That which does not discern is non-knowing (*aññāṇa*).

The triad [of terms] refers to conceit (*māna*). Conceit is the inflation of the mind by exalting oneself above others, whether based on what is real or unreal—such as thinking, "I am a hero, a wealthy man, virtuous, and endowed with wisdom," or "I am a leader, virtuous, and possessed of intelligence" (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*).
7.22) *Māna* (pride) belongs to the *curādi* class, [ending in] *-a*. The root *dhā* has the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*);

with the prefix *vi-* and in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*), that by which one establishes (*vidadhāti*) oneself in states such as superiority and so forth is *vidhā*; it occurs in three genders. That by which one inclines upwards is *unnati*; it is feminine. 169.
There are two [terms] for restlessness (*uddhacca*). The root *han* means "to go"; that which goes (*hanati*) higher and higher is *uddhata*; [it ends in] *-ta*.
*Hanassa dho*: the substitution of *dha* for *hana*. *Asarūpadvittaṃ*, *cittaṃ*. *Uddhaccam* is the state (*bhāva*) of one who is agitated (*uddhata*).
From the root *dhāva* in the sense of "going," it is called *uddhavaṃ* because the mind runs upward (*uddhaṃ dhāvati*) by means of this;

[the suffix] *a* is short. The pentad beginning with *tāpa* refers to remorse (*kukkucca*). From *tapa* and *dhupa* in the sense of "tormenting" (*santāpe*), it is called *tāpo* because the mind is tormented by this; [the suffix] *ṇo*. It is contemptible (*kucchitaṃ*).
It is called *kukku* because it acts (*karoti*); this refers to the mind (*citta*) or one who possesses that mind. The state of that is *kukkucca*.

It is called *pacchātāpa* because one is tormented by it afterwards (*pacchā*). That by which one is tormented subsequently is *anutāpa*. The root *sar* means "to go" or "to move"; it is called *vippaṭisāra* because the mind repeatedly moves about (*pati punappunaṃ sarati*) in an ugly way (*virūpena*) by means of it; the suffix *-to* is added to that.

170. *Pajjaṃ* refers to doubt (*vicikicchā*). From the root *likh*, meaning "to scratch" or "to write": it scratches the mind by way of making it twofold; thus, it is *manovilekho*. From the root *diha*, meaning "to accumulate";
however, here, because it is preceded by the prefix *saṃ*, it means "to doubt," with the suffix *-ṇo* in the sense of an instrument. From the root *sī*, meaning "to lie down";

here, because it is preceded by the prefix *saṃ*, it means "perplexity" (*kaṅkhā*), and this applies in all cases. That by which one says, "How is this? is *kathaṃkathā*. From the root *kit*, meaning "to remove disease."

*Vicikicchā*: The suffix *cha* is added; *dvitta* (doubling) and so forth. It is called *vicikicchā* because by means of it there is an absence of healing (*vigatā cikicchā*) or a counteraction of knowledge (*ñāṇappaṭikāra*).

*Dveḷhaka*: From the roots *ila* in the sense of "going" and "shaking. It is *dveḷhaka* because the mind wavers in two ways (*dvidhā ilati*) by means of this. The suffix *hap* is added, and the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). *Kaṅkhā*: [The root] *kaṅkh* is in the sense of doubt (*vicikicchā*);

the suffix *a* is added in the feminine. *Saṅkā*: [The root] *saṅk* is in the sense of suspicion. *Vimati*: Because one conceives (*maññati*) in various ways (*vividhena ākārena*), it is *vimati*. [The root] *man* is in the sense of knowing; the suffix *i* is added in the feminine.
171. *Tikaṃ*: This triad refers to intoxication (*mado*) characterized by physical beauty, wealth, and so forth, which arises from the fault of low-natured pride (*nīcapakatidosasambhūta*).

When this exists, a person becomes averse to giving precedence, showing respect, or looking upon others. Regarding the word *mada*, the lexicon *Rabhasa* states: "In the sense of 'where' (*kattha*), it is used for *urīgabbaretesu* (the secret parts of women); in the sense of 'intoxication' (*mado*), it is used for *hassebhadānesu* (the gifts of horses and elephants);

and in the sense of 'pride' (*mado*), it is used for *purisamānesu* (men who are proud). [The root] *gabba* means 'to be proud' (*māne*), belonging to the *curādi* class, with the suffix *a*; or alternatively, [it comes from] *gara*, meaning 'to sprinkle' (*secane*).

*Bo*: Regarding *māna*, it is pride (*mānā*). Specifically, that which honors excessively is overweening pride (*abhimāna*). In the term *ahaṅkāra*, the word *ahaṃ* is a particle; the word *amha* is also used here.
That by which one makes oneself (*attānaṃ*) "I" is egoism (*ahaṅkāra*). Both [terms] are derived from the root *cint*. *Cinta* is in the sense of thinking.

From the root *jhā* in the sense of thinking, that which is meditated upon is meditation (*jhāna*). In both cases, the formation expresses the state (*bhāva*), with the suffix *a*. What is the difference between applied thought (*vitakka*) and thinking (*cintā*)? Applied thought...
The former occurs prior to speech; for it is said in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (4.348): “Householder, having first thought and reflected, one subsequently breaks forth into speech.
The latter, however, does not occur prior to that [speech]. This is the distinction between them.
Alternatively, *vitakka* is a single mental factor included among the miscellaneous [mental states], whereas the other...

However, the distinction between these two is that [the latter] is a single mental factor (cetasika-dhamma) named attention (manasikāra), which is included in the category common to all [mental states].

The pair [of roots] *ni* and *cha* is used in the sense of determination (*nicchaya*). The root *naya* has the meaning of "going" (*gamana*); it is a verbal stem (*daṇḍaka*). That which determines the object (*ārammaṇa*) is "determination" (*niṇṇaya*); here, the *n* of the prefix becomes *ṇ*.
Now, what is the difference between resolve (*adhimokkha*) and determination (*niṇṇaya*)? Resolve (*adhimokkha*) plunges deeply into the object...
"It remains; the decision is merely the act of determining"—this is the distinction between these two.
Alternatively, resolution (*adhimokkha*) can also occur in relation to serene confidence (*pasāda*), whereas the other cannot; this too is a difference between them.
In that context, since the word "decision" (*nicchaya*) applies here as well, it is mentioned for both.
The synonyms for *abhyupagama* (acceptance/assent) are as follows: the root *jñā* preceded by *pati-* means "to accept"; with the feminine suffix *-a*, it becomes *paṭiññā*.
Likewise, from *śru* with *-a*, it becomes *paṭissava*; both of these are nouns denoting the state (*bhāvasādhana*).
*Saṃvidā*, *agū*, *paṭiññānaṃ*, *niyama*, *assava*, *saṃsava*, *aṅgīkāra*, *abhyupagama*, *samādhi*, and so forth, are also names for acceptance (*abhyupagama*). (Amara-kosha 5.5).

172. Six synonyms for disrespect (*anādara*): *Mana* belongs to the *curādi* class in the sense of honoring; or, *mana* means knowledge. Knowing while placing [the other] below is *avamāna* (disrespect);

the suffix *-yu* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Whoever is treated with disrespect must necessarily be disregarded by that person through one or another of the three—body, speech, or mind.

Thus, even in the context of disrespect, because there is no intervention [between the agent and the object], the word *tiras*—which signifies disappearance—is connected [to the action] as the cause of concealment (*tirodhānakaraṇa*).

*Tirakkāro* (disrespect). The root *bhū*, preceded by *pari* and *parā*, means contempt; *jānāti* (to know), preceded by *ava*, also [means contempt]. In all these cases, the suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and the vowel *a* is substituted.

*Dara* means respect (*ādara*); respect is honor (*sakkāra*). Its opposite is disrespect (*anādara*). *Parābhavanaṃ* is *parābhava* (ruin); *avajānanaṃ* is *avaññā* (contempt). The pair [of terms] refers to insanity (*ummāda*).
The derangement of the mind is *bhanti* (insanity). The root *mada* means insanity; it is *ummāda* because of its intensity or because of the faults that are established on a wrong path (*ummagga*).
173. *Snehantaṃ* means in affection. *Pemaṃ* is the state of being dear; this is it. Or, it is a pond (*āpo*) because it causes one to swell (*pīnati*); the state of swelling is *pemaṃ*, this is it.

From the roots *siniha* and *snih* in the sense of affection, the suffix *ṇo* is applied to form the abstract noun. Two terms refer to infatuation (*mucchā*). *Pīḷa* is in the sense of oppression; the oppression of the mind is *cittapīḷā*.
One who has lost the perception characterized by the discerning of blue and so forth is *visaññī*; the state of such a person is *visaññitā*.

In the case of *pamāda*, there is a pair [of meanings]. That by which one, though being capable, does not do what ought to be done oneself—that is *pamāda*. The prefix *pra-* is used in the sense of intoxication (*mada*).

*Pramajjana* (the act of neglecting) is *pamāda*; it is derived from the root *ma* with the suffix *ṇo*. In the case of *saja*, there are the senses of relinquishing (*visajjana*), embracing (*āliṅgana*), and fashioning (*nimmāna*). The relinquishing of mindfulness (*sati*) is *sativossagga*; it is derived from the root *sañj* with the suffix *o*.
The pair beginning with "curiosity" (*kotūhala*) refers to the excellence of investigating previously unknown objects. *Tuja* is used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*).
*Kuṃ* means evil; that which drives away (*tojeti*) evil is *kotūhalaṃ*. Here, *alo* is a phonetic modification. *Tula* means to weigh; that which weighs (*tulayati*) evil is *kutūhalaṃ*.
Here, *a* is the suffix and there is the addition of the letter *ha*. *Kotukaṃ* and *kutukaṃ* are synonyms for these. 174.
*Vilāsa* and so forth are activities and gestures. Of what kind are they? That activity arises from the state of feminine charm (*siṅgāra-bhāva*) and the state of passion (*rati-bhāva*) in women.

That which is called by the sound "hāva. It is called *hāva* because those possessed by passion (*rāgin*) are summoned (*hūyante*) therein; from the root *hu*, meaning "to summon," with the suffix *-ṇo*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of *vicchitti* and the rest;
for it is thus stated in the *Nāṭakaratanakosa*:
"Grace (*līlā*), charm (*vilāsa*), coquetry (*vicchitti*), affectation (*vibbhama*), and affected indifference (*kilakiñcita*)."
Moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭamita, vibboka, lalita, and likewise vikata—
these ten should be understood as the natural modes of behavior (ceṭṭhā) arising from the feminine nature (thīna).
Furthermore, there are hāva, helā, vikkhepa, sammūḷha, mada, and kapaṇya.

In that context, *vilāsa* (coquetry) is the change in one’s standing, sitting, walking, or looking when approaching a beloved; it is also the sudden manifestation of anger, surprise, or the contortion of the face.

It is derived from the verbal root *vilas*, meaning "to sport. *Lalita* (graceful movement) is the arrangement of the hands, feet, limbs, eyebrows, eyes, and other features, accompanied by actions performed with delicate refinement.

It is derived from the verbal root *lal*, meaning "to sport. *Vibhrama* (bewilderment) is the imitation of a beloved’s dress, gait, glance, smile, and speech for the sake of diverting the mind when one has not yet attained union with that beloved.

That which is performed is *līlā*. The root-meaning is from *lala* in the sense of play (*vilāsa*), or *lala* in the sense of service (*upasevā*). *Heḷā* or *helā* is the increase of desire during sexual union;
it is derived from *hila* in the sense of making a gesture (*hāvākaraṇa*). *Vibbhamo* (confusion) is a reversal produced by intoxication, passion, or laughter.

*Vicchitti* is the warding off [of a lover] by means of ornaments, ointments, and so forth, due to some offense by the beloved, out of jealousy, indifference, or through the exertion of one's female friends.
*Chidi* means "cutting" or "dividing into two. Others say that even a small ornament given out of affection is called *vicchitti* because it is a bond of joy (*pītinibandhana*).
The terms *kilakiñcita* and so forth should be understood according to the *Byākhyāsudhā-ṭīkā-ṭīppaṇa*, following the authority of the dramaturgical treatises (*nāṭaka-sattha*).
175. The triad refers to laughter (*hasita*). *Hasa* means "laughing"; in all instances, it is derived from the abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*). That laugh, when mild, is called *mihita*.
And "sita" is said [to mean] smiling. The root *mih* means "slight laughter. There is also a reading *mandasitaṃ mhitam*; there is also a verbal root *mhi* meaning "slight laughter.
It is a substitution (*syādeso*) for either *mhi* or *mih*. "Sitaṃ" [is formed with] the suffix *-ta* in all cases denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*).
"With slightly blossomed teeth, with side-long glances, and with smiles..."
The wise desire the smile (*sita*) as the door to the unobserved twice-born (*alakkhitadvijadvāraṃ*), according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (7.34).

There are two types of loud laughter (*mahāhasita*). The root *aṭ* means "to go"; thus, laughter that goes far is *aṭahāsa*, or laughter that has transcended is *aṭahāsa*. Its *ṭ* becomes *ṭh*, and the vowel *i* becomes *a*. *Vihasita* is that which lies between the smile (*sita*) and the laugh (*hasita*).
With cheeks contracted and eyes [wide open], it is accompanied by sound (*sassana*) and likewise by sighing (*nissana*).
The wise have called a smile that is accompanied by passion and directed toward a desired object "vihasita" (a playful smile), according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (7.35).

Regarding the two terms for the bristling of hair: *romañca* is the rising (*añcana*) of the body hairs; the root *añc* means "to go," with the suffix *-ṇo*. *Lomahaṃsana* is the bristling of the body hairs (*lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ*), meaning their state of being turned upward.

176. The group of six beginning with *parihāsa* refers to the joking of those who are dear and so forth. It is called *parihāsa* because they joke (*parihasanti*) therein; the suffix *-ṇo* is used here in the sense of one who desires to overcome (*paribhavitukāmena*).

*Hāsa* means laughter or jesting. *Du* is a root meaning jesting or disrespect; *a* is a root meaning to give or to cause to give. *Khiḍa* means play; thus there is *khiḍḍā*, and *khiddā* is also a reading.
Alternatively, *khaṃ* means empty and *iḍḍā* means speech; that which exists here [involving] that is *khiḍḍā*.

*Kīḷa* is used in the senses of delight and playing, or as a root for dwelling. *Kīḷanaṃ*, *keḷi*, *kīḷā*, and *kīḷitaṃ* all mean play. This also applies to the group of six beginning with jesting (*parihāsa*).
The teachers also state that [the word *middha*] is formed by means of the locative case (*adhikaraṇasādhana*).

It belongs to the group of three (*tika*) in the section on sleep. The root *dā* preceded by *ni* means "to sleep"; it ends in *a*. The root *sup* means "to lie down"; it ends in *ino*, forming *supinaṃ*. With the suffix *a*, it becomes *soppaṃ*.

*Middha* is the closing of all the limbs caused by extreme fatigue and other such factors. *Middha* is the state of fainting. The root *mid* means "to endure the effects of action" (*kāriyakkhamana*); it ends in *to*. It causes one to become dull (*medhayati*).

Or *middha* (drowsiness); the meaning is that it afflicts by way of unworkability (*akammaññabhāva*). The root *cal* has the sense of shaking; with the prefix *pa-* and the suffix *-ppa*, it refers to the state of fainting (*mucchāpāya*).

It is called *pacalāyikā* because it proceeds (*ayati*) or occurs through the closing of the eyelids (*akkhidala-pacalabhāvena*); [the suffix] *-ṇvu* is added, and the vowel is shortened (*assittaṃ*). 177–178.
With the prefix *ku-*, [the root] *ta* means "deceitful" (*ketavantam*). *Karaṇaṃ* becomes *kati*; when *kati* is censured, it is *nikati*. *Aṭa* means "to go"; in a contemptible manner...
It is called *kūṭa* because it wanders (*aṭati*). Alternatively, the root is *kuṭa* in the sense of "cutting," though in the *Dhātumālā*, it is derived from the root *kūṭa* in the sense of "deceit.
*Rabhi* means "fraud" (*byāja*); fraud is indeed cheating (*ketava*). *Saṭha* means "cheating";
it is *saṭha* because one deceives (*saṭhayati*), or because by it one does not speak correctly. *Ketavaṃ* is the practice of a cheat (*kitava*); a cheat is one who practices gambling (*jūtakāra*).
A thief (*coro*), or a place for insects (*kita-nivāse*), is *avo*. Deceit (*kapaṭo*), fraud (*byājo*), hypocrisy (*upadhi*), and guile (*kusati*)—these are also names for cheating.

The group of seven [refers] to intrinsic nature (*sabhāve*). Being (*bhavanaṃ*) is *bhāvo*; its own (*sassa*) being, or the being that exists (*santo vā saṃvijjamāno bhāvo*), is intrinsic nature (*sabhāvo*).

In the sense of placing (*saja*), releasing (*visajjana*), embracing (*āliṅgana*), and fashioning (*nimmāna*): there is no releasing of this, thus it is *nissaggo*. In the sense of manifesting (*pakāsane*), *rūpa*.
Visible form that exists is "with-form" (*sarūpa*). "Making" (*karaṇa*) is "becoming" (*bhavana*); how many? The first [category] has how many bases? The meaning is:
just as it arose at the first moment, so it is at all times. Morality (*sīla*) is in concentration (*samādhimhi*); concentration is restraint (*niyama*).

In the senses of characteristic, seeing, and mark—likewise, that which is to be characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*), with the suffix *yu*. Likewise, that which comes into being is "existence" (*bhāva*).

*Dvayaṃ ussave*: [The word] *ussava* [is derived as follows]. From the root *usa* (to burn), with the suffix *ka*. It is called *ussava* because they "emit" (*usavanti*) [joy] here, or because various prosperities "flow forth" (*savanti*) here.

From the root *chi* (to cut). With the suffix *chaṇa*, it means that one cuts away sorrow here; thus, it is a *chaṇa*. [Regarding the derivation of *chaṇa*: From the root *yu*, there is the elision of *issa*.

Or, it is called *chaṇa* because those who cut away sorrow and evil "move about" (*aṇanti*) or "make sound" (*saddāyanti*) here. *Chi* (to cut) is the root. *Aṇa* is a *daṇḍaka* (extended) root meaning "to sound."

179. Just as a person carrying a lamp—a light provided with oil such as pressed sesame oil—clearly perceives, with ease, even small objects and various collections of extremely subtle materials situated within deep darkness, inner chambers, and the like;
so too does one perceive this [Dhamma], which is "provided with oil," being accompanied by the manifold oils of the many discourses of the Buddha, such as those in the *Pariyāya* collection.

The construction is as follows: a person who maintains the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* text through learning, memorizing, and so forth, and who is a listener, will easily perceive the minor categories of meaning as well as the extremely profound categories of meaning found in various treatises.

Thus ends the commentary on the section on Heaven in this *Abhidhānappadīpikā-vaṇṇanā*, composed by the Great Minister Sirimahācaturaṅgabala, who was a lion among the elephants of poets and whose wisdom roamed the great forest of the entire field of grammar (*byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the Section on the Heavens is finished.
2. The Section on the World-Spheres. 1. Commentary on the Chapter on the Grounds.
180. Here, in this section on the earth (bhūkaṇḍa), the chapters—namely the "Earth Chapter" and so forth—are explained in sequence by means of eleven sections:

the ten [sections] beginning with the earth together with their primary and secondary members (aṅga-upāṅga), and the netherworld (pātāla). The primary members (aṅga) that assist [the earth] are salt and so forth;
the secondary members (upāṅga) that assist those members are distance and so forth.
181. Synonyms for the earth (*bhūmi*). It is called *vasundharā* because it holds (*dhārayati*) treasures (*vasūni*) and jewels (*ratnāni*). Regarding *khamu*: the root *khama* means to endure;
with the substitution of *cha* for *kha*, it becomes *chamā*. Alternatively, from the root *chi* meaning to cut: it cuts off (*chindati*) the downward falling of beings, thus it is *chamā*;

*ma* is the suffix, and *ā* is used for the feminine. It is called *bhūmi* because beings (*bhūtāni*) exist (*bhavanti*) upon it. The root *bhū* means to exist, and *mi* is the suffix. It is called *pāṭipadikā* because it extends far (*puthāti*).

When the suffix *nadādi* is applied, followed by the feminine marker *ī*, and after the substitution of *puthu* for *puṭha*, and the formation of the vowel-increment (*vuddhi*), the form is *pathavī*. When the substitution of *ussu* occurs, it becomes *puthuvī*. However, when the substitution of *patha* occurs, it is *pathavī*;
in this alternative, there is the insertion of the augment *ava*. Alternatively, from the root *thava* in the sense of "going" (*gati*), because it "extends" (*pathavati*) here, it is *pathavī*;
it belongs to the *nadādi* class. Or else, it is *pathavī* because it "spreads everywhere" (*sabbattha pattharati*); [the root] *thara* means "to spread," preceded by *pa-*, with the vowel shortened.
“[The earth] is water, rivers, etc., the earth, and tears.
‘Because it is overflowing with the fat and flesh even of the honey-beetle (madhukeṭabha),
this goddess is called Medinī by those who proclaim the Brahman,’ so says the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 11.3.”

From the verbal root *vac* (to speak), with the suffix *-in*, we have *vacanī*; with the suffix *-meda*, *medinī*; and also *ī*. Or, from *mida* (to moisten), with the suffix *-yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* class, and the substitution of *i* for *e*, we have *medinī*.
From *maha* (veneration), belonging to the *nadādi* class, we have *mahī*. Because it is extensive, it is *ubbī*; or, because beings dwell (*avanti*) upon it, it is *ubbī*, [ending] in *-assu*.
It is *vasumatī* because *vasūni* (riches) exist in it. That in which the worlds move is *go*, used for both masculine and feminine. From *kā* (sound), *kāyati*...

Herein: *kāyati* (it sounds) at the time of conquering Māra, thus *ku*. It holds treasures (*vasūni*), thus *vasudhā*. It supports the entire world, thus *dharaṇī* (with the suffix *yu*, belonging to the *nada*-class).
It supports, thus *dharā* (with the feminine suffix *ā*). *Gam* in the sense of going; it goes, thus *jagatī* (with the suffix *anta*, doubling of *ga*, change to *ja*, and elision of *na*;
belonging to the *nada*-class). *Bhū* in the sense of existence; with the suffix *ri*, belonging to the *nada*-class.
The root *bhū* is used here in the sense of "to be. One who supports (*dharati*) beings (*bhūta*, i.e., sentient beings) is a *bhūtara*. The root *ava* means "to protect";

with the suffix *yu*, belonging to the class beginning with *nada*, it becomes *avanī*. 182. *Khārā* refers to alkaline earth (*mattikā*) that has a salty taste; it is called *ūsa*. That which eats (*khādati*) is *khārā*; the letter *da* is replaced by *ra*.

Because it is a partial agent (*padesakattā*), the earth (*mattikā*) is associated with the measure (*matta*). The root *ūsa* means "to afflict" (*rujāyaṃ*); thus, *ūsa*. From the connection with *ūsa*, we have *ūsavā*, with the suffix *vantu*. With the suffix *rapaccaya*: [it forms *ūsarā*].
*Ūsaro*. Two [terms] occur among three.
*Thala* occurs in the sense of a place and as a locative base (*adhikaraṇe*). A *thala* is artificial; a *thalī* is natural, such as a riverbank and so forth.
The word *jaṅgala* applies to a portion of land or a region of earth that is hard and parched. Therein, it is "hard" because of its lack of moisture and its hardness.
It should be understood as "rough" (*lūkha*) because it is accompanied by sharp gravel and the like, cows and the like that tear [the ground], hooves, clods of earth, excrement, and so forth.

Regarding the root *gal* in the sense of "falling," "dropping," or "flowing down": *jaṅgala* is so called because water (*jala*) falls (*galati*) there, or because things fall there by means of water;
thus it is a waterless region. For the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (3.3.393) states: "The word *jaṅgala* refers to a waterless region; it has three genders, but in the feminine it means 'minced meat'."
There is elision of the suffix *lassa* and the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). 183.
Because they strive (*īhanti*) here by means of knowledge (*veda*) and wisdom (*paññā*), it is called *Vedeha*. That very same [place] is also *Videha*;

and because it lies in the eastern direction from Sineru relative to this island, it is both "eastern" (*pubba*) and "Videha," hence *Pubbavideha*. The same applies to the other [continents]. Because they go (*yanti*) there by means of cattle (*gava*), it is...

*Goyāna*. And because it is another *goyāna*, it is called *Aparagoyāna*. It is *Jambudīpa* because it is marked by the *jambu* tree, or because it is a continent (*dīpa*) where that [tree] predominates due to its enduring for an eon (*kappa*) and other qualities.

It is *Kuru* because happiness (*kaṃ*) is vast (*uru*) and great (*mahanta*) there through the power of the five precepts established by the nature of things (*dhammatā*), or because they obstruct evil (*kuṃ*) there; thus, "Kuru" (*kvi*). *Dīpa* is used in the senses of shining, illuminating, and a lamp.
They shine in the midst of water, thus they are called *dīpa*s; or, the True Dhamma shines therein, thus they are *dīpa*s. Great islands by measure are *mahādīpa*s. 184.
There are twenty-one specific districts among the intermediate regions, such as Kuru and others;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Suramaha, Paccuggata, Talakuṭa, Asmāka, and others may occur in the masculine gender in the plural when referring to many males. The *Kuru*s were royal princes belonging to that district.

The dwelling place of those people, even though it is but a single province, is called "the Kurus" by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhisadda*) using the plural; thus it is everywhere. It is called *kuru* because it restrains (*rundhati*) evil (*kuṃ*);
these are the Kuru princes. Their dwelling place is the Kurus. Due to the elision of the causal suffix (*paccayalopa*), there is no *vṛddhi* [strengthening of the vowel];
this should be seen in all cases according to the Pāṇini Sūtras 1.2.52 and 4.2.81. [The term applies] in such contexts as victory over enemies and the transgression of worldly boundaries.
They are capable (*sakkonti*), thus they are *sakkā*. They take or seize a treasury (*kosaṃ*), or they inquire about what is wholesome (*kusalaṃ*), thus they are *kosalā*.

They run along with the path (*magena*), thus they are *Magadhā*; or, they long for meats (*maṃsesu*), thus they are *Magadhā*. The root *gidha* means to desire. They serve by means of this, thus they are *Sivi*;

the root *si* means to serve, and *vi* is the suffix. Or, they bring about welfare (*sivaṃ*), thus they are *Sivī*; the suffix *i* is used in other senses. The root *kala* means sound; the suffix *iṅga* is applied.
