The Kaliṅgas; their dwelling place is Kaliṅga. Regarding Uttarāpatha, it is stated in the *Thomanidhi* that "formerly, in the region of Jagannātha, the area between the banks of the Kṛṣṇā became the country of Kaliṅga.
Alternatively, they are called Kaliṅgas because they "take up strife" (*kaliṃ gaṇhanti*), with the suffix *kvi*.

Or, they are called Kaliṅgas because they "sing sweet sounds" (*kalaṃ madhurasaddaṃ gāyanti*). Or, it is a derivative form (*assittaṃ*); or, they are so called because they "mark [themselves] with happiness" (*kena sukhena liṅganti*).

*Kaliṅgā*: *liṅga* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) with the sense of "going. They are called *Kaliṅgas* because they do not vomit out again the bribe (*lañja*) they have eaten themselves, even when requested by those they have defeated.
*Avantī*: sons of Pañcāla are *Pañcālā*. *Vajjī*: they are to be avoided (*vajjetabbā*);
based on the expression used [in the scriptures] such as "these are to be avoided," the kings acquired the name *Vajjī*, or they are the kings of the kingdom of Vajjī.
The Vajjis. Alternatively, that name of the kingdom should be understood by way of the princes who dwell there. They are Gandhāras because they "bear" (dhārenti) the earth (gaṃ);

or alternatively, they are Gandhāras because they "move about" (aranti) with the fragrance (gandha) of their fame. The root *ci* means "to incite"; they are Cetayas because they "incite" (cetanti), that is, they exert themselves in deeds such as warfare.
185. *Vaṅga* is a verbal root meaning "to go. *Videha* refers to those who possess distinguished bodies;
alternatively, they are called *videha* because they have come from the island of Pubbavideha. *Oja* means "splendor.

They are *kamboja* because they perform their transactions (*vohārakaraṇa*) by means of a conch (*kambu*) or a shell (*sambuka*), or because their strength (*oja*) is born from a conch (*kambukaja*). *Mada* means "crushing"; they are *madda* because they crush.
Alternatively, they are called *maddā* because they grant me bliss (*siva*); or they are called *maddā* because they rejoice (*modanti*) through the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth;

[the root] *mada* means "laughter. [The root] *bhañja* means "crushing," thus they are *bhaggā*. *Aṅga* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) meaning "to go"; it is a staff-like [suffix]. They are called *Sīhaḷā* because they lick (*lanti*) a lion (*sīha*). [The root] *kāsa* means "splendor" (*ditti*);

they are called *Kasmīrā* because they shine (*kāsanti*) with prosperity (*sampatti*); [the suffix] *mīra*. [The root] *kāsa* means "splendor," with the suffix *i*, thus *Kāsī*. [The root] *paḍi* means "going," thus *Paṇḍu*.

Alternatively, *kuru* means that which obstructs (*rundhati*) evil (*kuṃ*) here; thus, even though it is a single country, it is expressed in the plural because of the great number of those who depend upon it.
It is the same in all cases. 186. *Dvayaṃ bhuvane*.
From the root *luja* in the sense of "not seeing," that which is destroyed (*lujjati*) is the world (*loka*); *ga* becomes *ka*, and *ja* becomes *va*. They exist (*bhavanti*).
"Ettha" means the world (*bhuvana*), O youth. *Jagati*, *viṭṭha*, and so forth are also synonyms for the world. The pair [of terms] refers to a commonality of location.
From the root *dis* in the sense of "pointing out" (*atisajjana*); pointing out is making known. One who points out or designates [someone] as "this one is such-and-such" is a *desa*.
From the root *si* in the sense of service; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *sisa*, meaning "object" (*visaya*).

A borderland (*milakkhadesa*) devoid of the conduct of the civilized is called a frontier region such as Kāmarūpa and so forth. They are "barbarians" (*milakkha*) because they speak an unintelligible tongue;

that is, they speak an unintelligible speech (*abyattavācaṃ*), thus they are barbarians. Alternatively, they are barbarians because they have no eye of wisdom to show them the path of civilized conduct, and thus stains such as passion (*rāga*) are in their eyes.
Or, they are barbarians because they are unrefined (*assitta*); the dwelling place of those [barbarians] is a barbarian land.
A "border region" (paccanta) is that which is born outside the Middle Country.
That country where the four castes are not found is called a land of barbarians (milakkha);
beyond that is the Central Land (majjhabhūmi). (Cintāmaṇi-Ṭīkā 11.7)

Because it is the middle region from the standpoint of the Noble One’s conduct (*ariyācāra*), it is called the Middle Country (*majjhadesa*); the Middle Country has a circumference of nine hundred *yojanas*.

(187) A region with little water and much moisture is called a marshy place (*anūpa*); it is "marshy" (*anūpa*) because water (*āpa*) follows after (*anu*) it, or because it is the beginning (*ādina*) of water, or because there is a destruction of what is beyond (*paralopa*).
[The root] *kac* means to bind; with the suffix *cho*, it becomes *kaccha*. And there is the term "marshy region" (*anūpadesa*). By its newly rising...

*Tiṇena lakkhite harite dese saddalo*: *dala* means "splendor" (*ditti*), with the suffix *-a* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). A place where splendor exists is "verdant" (*saddala*). 188.
A region where people live by water brought from a river is called *nadyambujīvana*;
one whose mother is a river is called *nadīmātika*, using the suffix *-ka* in a *bahubbīhi* compound. A place where crops (*sassa*) ripen through rain (*vassana*) is [called *vassasassika*].

A region where the harvest succeeds through rain is called "one whose mother is the rain-god" (*devamātiko*); in this bahubbīhi compound, the suffix *ko* is applied, and here the word *devo* refers to the rain.
189. Words beginning with *anūpo* and ending with *devamātiko* occur in all three genders. [The following list begins: *candasūro*, etc., referring to the moon, the sun, Mount Sineru, and so forth.
The word *sassati* is uttered and explained. They remember and go everywhere, thus they are *sassatiyo*; from the root *sara* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *so* for the word *sara*.
From the root *raṭha* in the sense of "going," they go there, such as cities and so forth, thus it is *raṭṭhaṃ*, with the suffix *to*. That which is to be conquered by the citizens is *vijitaṃ*.

A bridge (*setu*) existing upon a bank (*āḷi*) functions in the masculine gender (*pulliṅge*). From the root *si* in the sense of "binding," with the suffix *tu*. From the root *ala* in the sense of "adornment."
*i*, *āḷi*, and *tassaṃ āḷiyaṃ*.

A *parisara* is a territory or ground situated near the vicinity of a city, mountain, or the like; it is so called because things flow (*saranti*) all around (*parito*) there. [The suffix] *ṇa* [is used]. In the group of three [suffixes], *va* is excluded.
A *goṭṭha* is a place where cows (*gāvo*) stand. From the root *kula* in the sense of counting: a *gokula* is a place where cows form a herd (*kulanti*) there.
*Gokula* means a herd of cattle (*gunna*) or a cow-pen (*ghara*). *Vaja* means "going" (*gatiyaṃ*); it is called *vaja* because cows go there for the purpose of dwelling.
*Goṭṭhānaka* and *goṭṭhāna* are also names for a *vaja*. 190.
By this verse, the names of the path (*magga*) are given. It is called *magga* because travelers (*pathika*) delight (*majjate*) in it, making it free from distress (*nittiṇaṃ karīyati*). *Majja*...
In the sense of purification (*suddhiyaṃ*); no; that whose body (*gattaṃ*) is sought by travelers (*pathikehi*), or it is a path (*maggo*); in the sense of seeking a path (*magga-anvesane*);

or it is a path (*maggo*) because one goes to what is auspicious (*sivaṃ*) therein, or by means of this; for in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe* it says, “*mo* [is used] in the sense of ‘auspicious’ (*sive*) and ‘assembly’ (*parisāyañce*)”;

the meaning is “it makes going (*gamanaṃ*) auspicious,” and this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāvisesanam*). In the sense of going on a road (*pathi-gatiyaṃ*), belonging to the *curādi* class, with the augment *nā*. They cause to go on the road (*panthayanti*).

*Pantho*: that by which one goes is a path (*pantho*); [the suffix] *a* is used, with the elision of the *kṛt*-affix marker. *Patho*: that by which one reads or goes is a road (*patho*). From the root *ad* (to go), *addhā* is where one goes;
[the suffix] *dha* is added, thus *addhā* means a path. This word *addhā* is also used for time; however, when expressing an equal portion, it is *addhaṃ*.
Therefore, the word *addha* has two genders, masculine and neuter: it is *addhā* when following words beginning with *rāja*, and *addhaṃ* when not following such words.

Añj- in the sense of "going": *añjo*. Vaj- in the sense of "going": *vajo*, and with *umo* [suffix], *vajumo*; when followed by *ṭo*, *vajato*. Pada- in the sense of "going": *pado*; when followed by *a*, *dassa jo* [substitution occurs] and there is doubling (*dvittaṃ*), thus *pajjo*.

Ay- in the sense of "going": *ayo*; in the sense of "going," with *yu* suffix: *ayyu*; in the sense of "going," with *avo* suffix: *avvo*, belonging to the *nadādi* group. Vatt- in the sense of "turning" (*vattane*); turning means going and so forth;

with *ani* suffix, belonging to the *nadādi* group: *vattanī*. Kantana- in the sense of "a staff" is masculine and neuter. It is called *paddhati* because it is struck (*haññate*) by the feet (*pādehi*) of travelers (*pathikehi*).
By virtue of its identical meaning with the word *pada*, the term *padasadda* is established through its conventional usage as a fixed application;

thus, the verbal root *han* is preceded by the word *pada*. Here, *han* becomes *dha*, and the vowel *a* is elided. Because it is associated with *paddhati* (a path), it is *vattanī*; and because it is associated with that, *padavī* is used in the feminine. 191–192.

Its subdivisions are the specific types of that path, such as the paths for pedestrians (*jaṅghamagga*) and so forth, excluding those that are not paths. A path traversed by feet is a *jaṅghamagga*; a path traversed by carts is a *sakaṭamagga*. These paths for pedestrians and carts are included within the category of great roads (*mahāmaggā*).
And here, the word *atha* should not be used in the phrase “*tethā*”; rather, it should be “*te cā*.

However, if the reading is “*matāddhanī*,” then “*tethā*” must indeed be used; in that case, the construction should be made thus: “a one-footed path (*ekapadī*) on a road (*addhani*) consisting of a single track (*ekapadika*).
A “one-footed path” is so called because it has only one foot for those walking along it, being without a companion, and not because it is a pair [of paths] for one who is sitting.
At the end of a compound, the suffix *ī* is always applied; when followed by the suffix *ka*, it becomes a single-word form (*ekapadika*), and the vowel *ī* is shortened.

A "desert" (*kantāra*) is a difficult path characterized by faults such as thieves and thorns. It is both masculine and neuter. It is called a "desert" because one crosses over (*taranti*), transcends, or goes through it by means of water (*kena pānīyena*).
The root *tara* means "to cross. However, this term is used here in its conventional sense (*rūḷhi-vasena*) with respect to the "thief-desert" and so forth. Alternatively, *kati*...
Because it is dangerous, one cuts through it; because there is constant coming and going here, it is a *kantāra* (wilderness), with the addition of *ā* and *n*.
Because one goes with difficulty here, it is *duggama* (difficult to traverse).
193. The pair [of terms] refers to the opposite road. A road (*magga*) that must be gone toward is a *paṭimagga*; a path (*patha*) that is the opposite road is a *paṭipatha*.
Furthermore: a road that is long, straight, and very far is called *addhāna*. It is a journey (*ayana*) over a distance (*addhā*); it is a road that extends for a long time.

Just as in the term "basis" (*padaṭṭhāna*), there is the elision of the letter *ya*. [The compound] *dvayaṃ pasattheddhani* is analyzed as: "a beautiful path" (*sobhano patho*) and "a way" (*pantho*). Because it has departed from being a path to be traveled, it is *uppatha* (by-path) and *apatha* (no-path); this is an *abyayībhāva* compound, where the prefix *a-* is used here as a particle.

194–196. Thirty-six atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one *aṇu*. It is called *paramāṇu* because it is the most subtle (*parama*) among all that is subtle (*aṇu*), or because it is the limit (*parama*) of the subtle.
The word *aṇu* has the sense of a staff; it is a verbal root (*dhātu*). Those thirty-six *aṇus* are called a *tajjārī*.
It is called *tajjārī* because it causes its respective support (*nissaya*) to decay (*jarāpeti*) by making it impure. The root *jara* means to grow old.
*Jara* refers to the decline of age, or *a*, such as a river and so forth. Thirty-six of those *jarāyu* are called a *rathareṇu*;
*rathareṇu* is the dust raised by the movement of chariots. Thirty-six of those *rathareṇus* are called a *likkhā*. [The root] *lakkh* means to see;
it is called a *likkhā* because it is visible even to the naked eye (*pakaticakkhu*). It is a derivative form (*assittaṃ*).
Seven *likkhā*s are called a *ūkā*; a *ūkā* is said to be a head-turning worm (*sirovattakimi*), and it is so called because of its size. Seven of those *ūkā*s are called a *dhaññamāsa*;
a *dhaññamāsa* is a grain of rice (*vīhi*) itself, which is measured as a *māsa*, hence "grain-measure" (*dhaññamāsa*).
The root *mas* means to measure. Seven of those *dhaññamāsa*s are called an *aṅgula*. The root *aṅg* has the sense of "going"; with the suffix *-ula*, it becomes *aṅgula*, meaning a measure.
With the *ul* suffix, it becomes *aṅguli*, meaning a finger or a finger-joint. Regarding *amudviccheti*: that which measures twelve fingers is called a *vidatthi*.

It is so named because it is measured (*vitthāriyate*) or established (*vidhīyate*) by the thumb together with the little finger; or, it is derived from the prefix *vi-* combined with the root *tanu* in the sense of expansion (*vitthāre*).

The root *dhā* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*). In both cases, according to the first alternative, there is *tha* for *t*, *ta* for *na*, and *da* for *t*. In the latter case, there is *da* for *dh*, *tha* for *t*, and a dissimilar doubling (*asarūpadvibhāvo*).
Now, two *vidatthis* may be one *ratana*. (*Ram* means play; *tan* is a suffix; *lopa* is elision. Those seven *ratanas* are called a *yaṭṭhi*. (*Ya* is from *payatana*;
*tassa ṭho*, *tassa ṭo* [grammatical rules]). Twenty *yaṭṭhis* are called an *usabha*. (*Usa* is from *dāha*; *abho* is a suffix).
Here, however, the interval between two *usabhas* is an *usabha*. Eighty *usabhas* in measure is a *gāvuta*.

*Gāvuta* is that which is joined (*yuta*) with names, oxen, or cows. The root *yuja* means "to join" (*samādhimhi*). Its meaning is the joining of a measure grasped by the intervals between the oxen's teeth;

that is what is called a *catugāvuta-yojana*. The root *yuja* means "to join" (*samādhimhi*); *yu* has the sense of joining [a distance] by means of four *gāvutas*, thinking, "Let this much be called a *yojana*."

197. Regarding strung master-archers' bows, five hundred [fingers] are called a *kosa*; others say it is for those not yet strung. In the word *kusana*, the suffix *ṇo* is applied; the name of the *kusana* is *kosa*.
However, here it is a *kosa* because it is the measure of a *kosa*, measuring two thousand finger-breadths (*karas*).
But elsewhere it is said: "Twenty-four finger-breadths make a *kara*."
It is said: “By eight thousand renowned [men], measuring with a *kos*, by one who discerns. Regarding the term *caturambana*:
a plot of land suitable for sowing seeds of the four kinds of grain is called *karīsa*. It is called *karīsa* because they perform plowing, sowing, and so forth there;
it is a field (*īsa*). A *caturambana* is that wherein they sow the seeds of the four kinds of grain.
An *ambaṇa* measures eleven *doṇas*. However, others say that "a place four *ambaṇas* and four *yaṭṭhis* in size is called a *karīsa*";
this should not be accepted, as it would entail the consequence of being a synonym for what is within a *karīsa*.
In terms of measurement, a space measuring twenty-eight *hatthas* is called an *abbhantara*; within that, in its inner portion—

What has arisen does not exclude the interior. For wherever anyone stands or sits, the space extending twenty-eight cubits all around that person is called their "interior space. It is the "Earth Chapter" because it begins with the earth;
or alternatively, the earth itself is primary in view of its role as a constituent factor (*aṅga*), and the designation is made according to what is primary.
"Bhavati" is a designation for the *Bhūmivagga*.
The commentary on the *Bhūmivagga* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Puravagga*.
198. The Hexad on the City:
“A port (paṭṭana), a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna), a city (nagara), a market town (puṭabhedana);
a woman (thī), a city (pū), a full one (pūriyo), a site (ṭhānīyaṃ), Kabbaṭa, and a heap (puṭa).”
It is protected by means of verses of praise:
“The wise man should show the city, with its various divine abodes, palaces, shops, and mansions, adorned with royal highways. (Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 1.2.1)

The Characteristics of a City (*Nagaralakkhaṇa*). The root *pu* means "to protect" (*pālane*); *pura* also means "to protect. It is called *pura* because it purifies (*punāti*), leads forward (*pureti*), and protects against foreign armies and misfortune.

The suffixes *-ro* and *-a* [are added]. Alternatively, the meaning of the verbal root is "going at the front" (*agga-gamana*). A city (*nagara*) is so called because it possesses "mountains" (*naga*), such as palaces and the like;
the suffix *-ra* is added. By the particle *vā*, the masculine gender of the word *nagara* is included, or else it may be *nagarī* (feminine) or *pattana* (neuter).
(Amara 1.2.1) The neuter gender [of *puṭabhedanam*] is due to its association with *paṭṭana* (port/city). (Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā 1.2.1) Some teachers maintain that this applies to the word *pura* as well.

Because there is no fear from any quarter (*akutobhaya*), that which is beneficial for standing is *ṭhānīya*; [the suffix] *īya* is used. It is called *puṭabhedana* because the bundles of merchandise are opened (*bhijjante*) here.
Having shown the place of permanent residence, he says "thiya" and so forth to show the other [type of city]: "The king stands (*tiṭṭhati*) here," thus...

*Rājaṭhānī* (royal capital), *yu*, *nadādi* (belonging to the class beginning with *nada*). It also refers to a place of permanent residence, as in such passages as: “There were eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.263). *Khandhāvāra*:
That wherein people are surrounded (*varenti*) or enclosed on all sides (*āsamantato*) by timber trunks (*dārukkhandha*) and so forth is a *khandhāvāra*.

Because the verbal root *var* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has the sense of surrounding, it here carries the meaning of enclosing. This group of five [terms] refers to a city; thus, it is called a *khandhāvāra*.
However, there is only one name for a place where one has resided for a short time.

199. *Mūlapura*: excluding the primary city (*mūlapura*), any other city that is surrounded by walls and so forth measuring a *yojana* in extent is called a "branch-city" (*sākhānagara*) because it resembles a branch, being subordinate to the primary city which stands like a trunk.
200–201. By means of two synonymous terms, these are the names of the primary city: *Vānarasīsa*, or a rock shaped like that [head].

In this context, regarding what should have been called “Vānarasīsa,” the word “Bārāṇasī” is stated by substituting *va* for *vā*, changing the vowel, lengthening it, nasalizing it, and eliding the final *s*.
It is called Sāvatthī because it is the dwelling place of the sage Savattha;
or alternatively, it is Sāvatthī because all wealth (*sabbadha*) exists there (MAṬṬHA 1.14). Here, *sāva* is a synonym for wealth.

The word *attha* [is used here]. Because it has become threefold (*tikkhattum visālībhūtattā*), it is *Vesālī*. From the root *ass* in the sense of "to be satisfied" (*assatthutthe*), with the suffix *ī*, [it becomes] *Assatthā*.

From the root *math* in the sense of "injury" (*mathi hiṃsāyaṃ*), with the suffix *ilo*, [it becomes] *Assittaṃ*; from that, *Mithilā*. Because there is ornamentation (*alaṃ bhūsanam*) here, it is *Āḷavī*, with the suffix *vī* and the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*.

From the root *kusa* in the sense of "calling out" (*avhāne*), because they call out (*kosanti*) here with the ten sounds beginning with "Eat! Drink!", it is *Kosambī*, with the suffix *bo*, belonging to the *nada*-class, due to being filled with *kusamba* trees.
Some say it is called Kosambī because it was built not far from the hermitage of the seer Kusamba. (Aṭṭha. 35; Ma. Ni. Ṭī. 1.14; 2.284).
It is Ujjenī because it conquers fierce enemies; [the suffix] *yu* is applied according to the rule beginning with "nadādi.
It is Takkasīlā because reasoning (*takka*)—where *ūha* means filling what is deficient—is its custom (*sīla*) or nature; for it is by human effort that...
"Deficient" (*ūna*); having gone there, he fulfills that deficiency. *Cam* means "to eat"; with the suffix *po*, it becomes *campā*.
A mine (*sākara*) is a source or place of origin for those riches; that itself is *Sāgala*. A mountain shaped like a jackal (*saṃsumāra*) is here [called] *Saṃsumāragiraṃ*;
or, *Saṃsumāragiraṃ* is so called because a jackal sings at the time this was built. *Ge* means "sound," and *iro* [is the suffix]. Of kings alone...
It is Rājagaha because it is to be grasped as a sovereign capital (*ādhipacca*). It is Kapilavatthu because it was the dwelling place of the seer named Kapila;
the word *vatthu* is used here in the masculine or neuter gender.
It is Sāketa because the power (*sāka*)—meaning the might—of kings in battle and so forth arose there. [As it is said: "The word *sāka* refers to a king possessing power, or to trees and islands."
In the *Nānatthasaṅgahe* (Compendium of Various Meanings): *Sañjāta* means "arisen from this"; thus, there was a king named Sāka, or because a tree arose here in ancient times, it is called Sāketa.
*Indapatta*: they attain (*pāpuṇanti*) sovereignty (*inda*), the state of supreme lordship, in this place;
or, Sakka, the king of the gods, is the *inda*, and he has attained (*patto*) this place, hence *Indapatta*. *Ukkaṭṭhā*: it maintains a torch (*ukka*) at the time it was built, hence *Ukkaṭṭhā*.
*Vaṇṇavikāra* (phonetic modification). Because there was a young tree named *pāṭalī* in the place where it was built, it is called *Pāṭaliputtaka*;
or else, because a village headman named Paṭali lived here in ancient times with his son, it is called *Pāṭaliputtaka*.

It is *Cetuttara* because it is supreme (*uttama*) in the kingdom of Ceti; however, in the reading "Jetuttara," it is a phonetic modification (*vaṇṇavikāra*), because it is a place for conquering enemies (*verijaya*).
And that which is called *Jetuttara* because it is the most excellent (*jetta*) and the highest (*uttara*). That which shines (*dippati*) when it is being laid out is *Saṅkassa*;

[the root] *kas* means "to shine," with the suffix *-tta*. Alternatively, it is *Saṅkassa* because Brahmins, while looking for the boundary marks while it is being laid out, see a man with a sickle in his hand and lay it out there;
[the root] *kas* means "to scratch" (*vilekhana*). That [place]— [End of fragment]
Kusinārā. By this [term], many specific towns such as Mathurā, Madhurā, Mādhurā (according to Ka.), Pāsaṇapura, Soṇikā, and others are included.
202. The tetrad refers to the path leading to an inner village. A *racchā* is a road suitable for a chariot; it is [the term for] renunciation (*pabbajjā*) and so forth.

That in which goods are displayed for sale at the edge of a district is a *visikhā*; the prefix *vi-* here is used in the sense of "serving" (*sevā*), or alternatively, it is that "where people enter" (*visanti*).
*Visikhā*: from *vis*, meaning "to enter. *Rathikā*: that which is beneficial for a chariot (*ratha*); the suffix *-ika*. *Vīthi*:
from *vī*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *-thi*. A road that is not pierced through the middle by another road is called a *byūha*.

It is a *byūha* because it "crowds together" (*byūheti*) people, in the sense of not allowing them to pass elsewhere; from *ūha*, meaning "to crowd together," due to its being a massing. It is not pierced through (*na nibbijjhate*).

"Not pierced by a cross-road" means unbroken; *vidha* is used in the sense of striking. A road that has been pierced by a cross-road is called a "cross-road" (*raccha*), a "path" (*patha*), or "way" (*addhi*).
*Patha* is derived from the root *path* (to go); *patho* is the nominative. *Addhi* is derived from the root *ad* (to go). 203.
A "quadrangle" (*catukka*) is at a crossroads. The combination of four paths is a quadrangle. *Cara* is used in the senses of going and eating.
*Caro*, *rassa co*, and *caccaraṃ* are terms denoting a courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*). A "junction of roads" (*maggasandhi*) is the meeting point of two or four roads.
*Siṅgha* means smelling; it is a term for a hawk (*āṭaka*).
The pair [of terms] refers to a covering made of bricks and the like over a field or a slope. A "field" (*vappa*) is the mud of a moat surrounding a difficult-to-access city.
Having made a mound or a hut with earth, and having had it trampled by oxen and elephants, one should have the base of the wall made thirty cubits in measure;
likewise, having raised it a hundred cubits from there, one should have it covered with earth and built upon that.
It is called a *pākāra* because they build (*pakubbanti*) it, or because it is made all around (*samantato karīyati*). [The suffix] *-a* is used here in the sense of the agent other than the object.

In *saññā* (the suffix), there is the lengthening of the short vowel. From the root *vu* in the sense of "covering," *varaṇa* is derived from *vuṇoti*; the suffix *yu* is applied and *rāgama* (the augment *ra*) occurs. "Sāla" is also a name for a rampart. The pair [of terms] refers generally to a royal residence.
Because it specifically illuminates all the houses, it is called *uddāpa*; from the root *dīp* in the sense of "illuminating," the form *ī* is used.

Because they come together and construct a boundary, it is *upakārikā*; the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. In the case of the suffix *ke*, when followed by a feminine form ending in *tā*, the preceding [vowel] is long.

The vowel *a* becomes long when followed by *kānta* (Pāṇini 6.1.65). Indeed, even with the substitution of *a*, it is called "ko," just as Devadatta is called "Datta. Alternatively, there is the suffix *kap*.

(204) The pair [of terms] refers to a wall made of clay or bricks and so forth belonging to a house and the like. From the root *kuṭ* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*), that which cuts or divides the path is *kuṭṭa*.
From the root *bhid* in the sense of making two (*dvidhākaraṇe*), one is *bhitti*. A city-gate (*gopura*) is the gate (*pura*) for the speech of cattle (*gu*). Near the door—
*Koṭṭhaka* means a gatehouse; *akkuṭṭha* (from the root *kus*) means to revile; *ṭhaka* and *koṭṭhaka* refer to a specific type of dwelling.
There are two [terms] for the threshold (*indakhīla*). *Isa* means desire; *esa* means seeking; thus, *ika*. The *khīla* or thorn of the Lord (*inda*), that is, Sakka, is the *indakhīla*.
There are two [terms] for the side-wing of a gatehouse, the eaves of a mansion, and a wind-hut. *Aḍḍa* means to transcend or to harm.

a. A watchtower (*aṭṭālaka*) is a structure for the purpose of observation (*ālokapaṭicchanatthāya*). 205. Having driven two beautiful pillars, adorned with garlands and the like, into the ground on both sides above [the gate], that which is fashioned as the outer door is called a *toraṇa*.

[The root] *tura* means "to ward off" (*vāraṇe*); with the suffix *-yu*, or because they resound (*raṇanti*) at the end, it is a *toraṇa*. [The root] *tu* means "to praise" (*abhitthave*). [The root] *raṇa*...

The meaning of the word [is as follows]: a change in syllables (*vaṇṇavikāra*). "Outside the gate" means *bahidvāraṃ*. It is called a moat (*parikhā*) because it is dug (*khaññati*) all around (*pari*).
It is called a long one (*dīghikā*) because it is endowed with length.

206–207. [The suffix] *-manta* is used for a house (*gehe*). [The root] *mand* is used in the senses of delight, praise, and brilliance. It is called a palace (*mandiraṃ*) because they rejoice (*mandante*) therein.

*iro*. "Sīdanti tattha" means "they sink there," hence *sadanaṃ* (a dwelling), with the suffix *yu*. The root *sada* is used in the senses of dispersing, going, and ending. "Na gacchanti" means "they do not go," hence *agā*, referring to pillars and so forth;
that which receives (*rāti*) them is *agāraṃ*. When the short vowel is lengthened, it becomes *āgāraṃ*. "Ci" in the sense of piling up: that which is piled up or covered over is *nikāyo*;
here, by way of grammatical convention (*nipātanā*), the syllable *ci* undergoes the substitution of *ka*. "Lī" in the sense of clinging: with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *nilayo* and *ālayo*.
*Vasa* means dwelling; because they dwell here, it is *āvāsa* (abode), with the suffix *ṇo*. *Bhū* means existence; because beings exist here, it is *bhavana* (dwelling). *Vis* means to enter;
that which is entered is *vesma* (house), with the suffix *mo*. *Kit* means dwelling; with the suffix *yu* in the sense of a location, it is *niketana* (home).

That wherein they settle or reside is *nivesana* (residence). *Ghara* means to sprinkle; because one sprinkles away defilements (*kilesa*) here, it is *ghara* (house), or else it is called *ghara* because it is seized (*gahyati*).

No. *Gaha* is a substitute for *ghara*. It is called *gaha* because it "takes" (*gaṇhāti*) the wealth brought by men; the suffix *-tha* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), thus *āvasatha*.

*Sara* is used in the senses of going, thinking, and harming; it is a *saraṇa* (refuge) because good and bad karmas "go" (*saranti*) or "are thought of" (*cintenti*) therein, or because one "remembers" (*sarati*) the heat of the sun and so forth.

*Si* in the sense of service, with the suffix *-ṇa*, becomes *patiṭṭhāya*. *Uca* in the sense of gathering, becomes *oka*. *Sala* in the sense of going: [the suffix] *-tiyava* is applied to form *itthi*.

Or “vā”: thus, in the case of the root *sāl* (to collect), when there is the suffix *dhātu*, the specific distinction is simply *lattam*. From the root *ci* (to accumulate), with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of an action, we have *cayo*.

From the root *kuṭ* (to cut), with the suffix *i*. From the root *vas* (to dwell), [with the suffix *ti*]. In the sense of a dwelling, from the root *upadha* with the suffix *ette*, we have *geham*. From the root *sad* (to sit), with the suffix *umo*, we have *sadumaṃ*.

Both refer to a sacrificial ground (*yaññāyatana*) resembling a temple (*devakula*) that is devoid of noise. From the root *cit* (to honor), with the suffix *iyo* in the sense of an action, [we have *ceyya*]. From the root *yat* (to strive), [with the suffix *ana*, we have *yatanaṃ*].

It is called an *āyatana* because those desiring fruit strive (*āyatanti*) and exert themselves (*vāyamanti*) therein; or else, it is called an *āyatana* because it extends (*tanoti*) those things that come (*āyanti*), thus meaning "that which extends the arrival [of results].
Here, the particle *tu* has the sense of connecting two preceding and succeeding movements.
There is also a reading: "and shrines (*cetiyāyatanāni*)."

208. There are two types [of buildings]: those of the gods and of kings, which are made of bricks and the like. It is also similar to other [buildings]. Because the eyes and the mind find delight (*pasīdanti*) therein, it is called a *pāsāda*. [The root] *yu* means to mix; with the suffix *po*, there is lengthening due to the power of the rule for long vowels, and the substitution of *o* for *au*.

This type [of building] belongs to others besides kings—namely, wealthy people, merchants, and so forth. Its roof is shaven (*muṇḍa*), not like that of a palace (*pāsāda*); thus it is a *muṇḍacchada*. [The root] *hara* means to take away; with the suffix *yo*, there is the augment *mi* before *yam*.
At the gate of Duggapura, or wherever else, a pillar or a palace established upon an elephant’s frontal globe made of clay and other materials is called *hatthinakha*.
It is named *hatthinakha* because it is the "nail (*nakha*) of the elephant" (*hatthissa eva nakho yassa*), or alternatively,
by the word "nail," the palace together with the nail is intended.

209. A house with a roof resembling the curved wing of a *supaṇṇa* or *garuḷa* is a "golden-curved-roofed" (*suvaṇṇavaṅkacchadana*) house. The root *vaṅka* means "to go. Because it has a roof on only one side, it is called an *aḍḍhayoga*.

A particular type of dwelling with many corners joined by a single peak is called a *māḷa*; some say it is a bedchamber constructed in a circular shape. [The derivation is: *mā* in the sense of measuring, with the suffix *ḷo*, thus *māḷo*.
A square-shaped particular type of dwelling is called a *pāsāda*; some say it is a long, rectangular *pāsāda*.

210. It shines and glows with those who are peaceful (*santehi bhāti dibbatīti sabhāyaṃ*); thus it is *sabhā*. The suffix *ya* occurs as before, and in both cases there is the substitution of *sa* for *santa*.
"Maṇḍa" refers to the rays of the sun; that which drinks or destroys them is a *maṇḍapa*. By the word *vā*, the masculine gender of the term *maṇḍapa* is included.
A place of assembly or gathering for people is a *janālaya*. It is constructed for the purpose of seating.
*Sālā* means a hall. *Paṭikkamana* is that where they retreat; from the root *kamu*, meaning "to step," with the suffix *-yu* in the sense of location (adhikaraṇa).
(211) A dwelling that has become the residence of the Victor is called a *gandhakuṭi*; a hut perfumed with divine fragrances is a *gandhakuṭi*.

The triad [of terms] refers to the place of cooking. *Rasāvatī*: it possesses flavors (*rasa*); *pāka* is cooking, and the place of that is the *pākāṭṭhāna*. *Mahānasa*: there are many great things to be eaten here; from the root *asa*, meaning "to eat," with the suffix *-yu* and a change of vowel grade (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*).
212. *Āvesana*: the workshop or studio of craftsmen such as goldsmiths. It is called *āvesana* because they enter (*āvisanti*) into it;

the suffix *-ana* is used here. *A soṇḍā*: a drinking hall built for the purpose of drinking liquor. They are called *soṇḍā* because, having deliberated on what should and should not be done, they consume (*sanonti*) all goods to be given for the sake of whatever object they themselves desire;
from the root *sana* (to give), belonging to the *tanādi* class. The suffix *-ḍa* is applied, and there is a change in the vowel (*vaṇṇavikāra*).
And this trunk of theirs dwells there. Because of the proximity of the word "drinking" (*pāna*), the term *surā-śoṇḍa* (drunkard) here includes those addicted to liquor as well.
A place for the discharge of feces—that is, excrement—is a "latrine" (*vaccaṭṭhāna*). A hut for the discharge of feces is a "latrine-hut" (*vaccakuṭi*).

A dwelling place for sages (*muni*) or seers (*isi*) is called an "hermitage" (*assama*); it is called an *assama* because they thoroughly (*ā*) pacify their anger (*krodha*) therein; [the prefix] *ā* signifies "intensely."
Alternatively, it is called an *assama* because passion (*rāga*) and the other [defilements] meet (*sameti*) there.
213. The triad [of terms] refers to a shop for the sale of merchandise. In the sense of "commercial transaction" (*byavahāra*), the root *paṇ* [is used];

things such as clothing that are to be sold are *paṇyā*. Because they sell these here, it is a *paṇyavikkaya*; and since *ki* [in this context] means "exchange of goods," the word *sālā* means a house; thus, it is a *paṇyavikkayasālā*.
*Āpaṇo*: that in which they trade and deal is a marketplace (*āpaṇo*), [formed with] the suffix *ṇo*. *Paṇyavīthikā*: a street or path for goods being brought for sale. *Udosito*:
from the root *vas* (to cover), with the suffix *to*; that by which water is covered or sheltered is a warehouse (*udosito*), a rain-cover.
*Bhaṇḍasālā*: a hall for the storage of goods. *Caṅkama*: from the root *kam* (to step), meaning "one walks here."
*Caṅkamanaṃ*, *caṅkamo*, and *dvittādi*. 214. It is called *jantā* because they burn therein;
from the root *jala* (to shine), with the suffix *anta*. According to the rule “*itthiyamatiyavo vā*,” there is the substitution of *a*, *ā*, and the elision of *la*.

Alternatively, *jantā* means "the flame" (*aggi*) in the word *janeti*; from the root *jana* (to produce), with the suffix *anta*. That very thing is the house (*gharaṃ*); thus, it is *jantāgharaṃ*. [The suffix] *i* [is added] after *aggi*.
*Sālā* means a hall (*aggisālā*). *Pā* is to drink; those who drink there are *papivanta*, and their place is a *papā*. A hall for drinking water is a *pānīyasālā*;

that itself is a *pānīyasālikā*. *Gas* means to go; *bho* becomes *bo*. That which protects (*avati*) is an *ovaraka* (room); *aro* [is the suffix], with *ko* in the sense of identity, and the elision of *s*.

Dwelling is *vāsa*; a house for that purpose is a *vāsāgāra*. One sleeps in it, thus it is a *sayanī*; [the suffix] *yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* class; that itself as a dwelling is a *sayaniggaha*.

215. The tetrad [applies] to the king’s harem (*itthāgāra*); by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it also applies to royal women because they serve that purpose or exist for that purpose (according to Ka).

The "harem" (*itthāgāra*) is the non-house (*agāra*) of royal women. It is called a "harem" (*orodha*) because royal women are confined (*avarundhīyante*) therein; from the root *rudh*, meaning "to obstruct" or "to enclose.

It is "pure-limbed" (*suddhanta*) because its guards are pure (*parisuddha*) due to their total absence of sensual desire, and because they are at the end (*ante*), that is, in close proximity. "At the end" (*ante*) means within.
The city, the house, and the inner apartment (*antepura*); or, that which is at the end of the city is the inner apartment. There is also a reading, "the interior apartment" (*antopura*).

That place which is not a domain for vulgar matters for kings and rulers, a place not shared by anyone else, is considered and called the "inner recess" (*kacchantara*), which is also termed the "pleasure garden" (*pamadavana*).
What is called a pleasure garden is either situated near the auxiliary buildings or adjacent to the city.
Or, "the inner palace" (*antepura*) refers to that place where the king dwells together with his harem, and no other people may enter.

"Pamadānaṃ vanaṃ" means "pleasure grove" (*pamadavana*). By the rule of euphonic substitution (*nipātana*), the vowel *ā* becomes *ī*; thus, from the word *ākāra*, the meaning is "of women. In some instances, the long vowel becomes short.
The space between the thigh (*kaccha*) and the groin (*pakoṭṭha*) is the "interior of the thigh" (*kacchantara*). The groin (*pakoṭṭha*)...

The term *abbhantaradvāraṃ* means "inner door. 216. There are two terms for a staircase constructed of bricks and the like. It is called *sopānaṃ* because it exists together with a foothold (*upāna*); alternatively, *sopānaṃ* may also be used as a neuter noun. That by which one ascends is *ārohanaṃ*; the root *ruha* (with the prefix *ā-*) signifies "to grow" or "to arise. There are two terms for a ladder made of wood and similar materials.

It is called *nisseṇī* because one sleeps upon it firmly after reaching a wall or other structure; the root *si* means "to serve," and *ṇī* is a suffix belonging to the *nadādi* class. It is called *adhirohiṇī* because one ascends upwards by means of it; the suffix *-sā* indicates that both of these terms are feminine in gender.
217. The group of five [terms] relates to the lattice (*jālaka*). It is called a *vātapāna* (wind-drinker) because it drinks the wind. A "cow's eye" (*gavakkha*) is the eye of cows;

due to the elision of the final vowel in the compound, it becomes *a*. Because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), it takes the masculine gender; alternatively, in the word *akkhi*, the analysis is: "the eye of cows is *gavakkhī*. *Jāla* means "splendor" (*ditti*), thus *jāla*.
A cage (*pañjara*) joined with the form of a lion is a *sīhapañjara*. It is the place where light and sunlight enter.
*Sandhi*: it pierces the junction; *āloka* means that by which one looks out, or it is itself the junction, thus *ālokasandhi*.

Two [terms] are to be understood as derived from the root *lagi*. The root *lagi* has the sense of "going," with the suffix *a*, belonging to the *nadādi* class. It strikes repeatedly by way of going and coming, thus *paligha*; [the suffix] *ṇo*.
Because its form is like that of a monkey (*kapi*), it is *kapisīsa*. That which is called *aggaḷa* is the door-leaf, that which holds the door-leaf in place.
(ka. Its pillar is the door-pillar (*aggaḷatthambha*). According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "The word *aggaḷa* has three meanings: wave, staff, and door-bolt.

From the feminine form [of the stem], the suffix *-ā* is applied, resulting in *aggaḷā*. It is called *nibbaṃ* because it causes rainwater to flow out completely; [the root] *abb* is used in the sense of moving or harming.
The lower end or final limit of the roof-covering (*chadda*) is the "roof-end" (*chaddakoṭi*); [it refers to] that [place].

218. A triad [of terms] for the roof of a house. It is a *chadana* because one covers (*chādeti*) with it; from the root *chada*, meaning "to cover" or "to conceal," belonging to the *curādi* class. By the rule "in *paṭagamana*, etc., *ala* is added," the suffix *ala* is applied. It is a *chadda* because one covers with it; beginning with the doubling of the consonant, etc.

A triad [of terms] for the courtyard of a house. From the root *aja*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *ira*, we have *ajira*. From the root *cara*, meaning "to move" or "to eat," we have *cara*. From the root *aṅga*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *yu* in the sense of instrument or location, there is a change of vowel and the substitution of *ṇa*.
A pentad [of terms] for the outer porch outside the door of a house, for the walkway, and for the door-pillar. However, *alinda* is also desired for other types of pillars.
*Paghāṇa* (and *paghaṇa*) is so called because they are struck (*hananti*) first (*paṭhamaṃ*) and people go there (*gacchanti ettha*); here, *ghaṇa* is the substitute for *hana*.

*Alinda* is so called because the friend (*ali*, i.e., Indra) is there; "alinda is a part of a house; it may also be *paghāṇa* or *paghaṇa*"—thus it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (12.12) and the *Amaramālā*.
*Ālinda* begins with a long vowel. *Padhāna* means the front (*mukha*), as in *pamukha*; for [it refers to] the four fronts of a house.
That very place is called *padhāna* where virtuous people and even visitors sit down. It is called a *dvārabandhana* (door-fastening) because the door is fastened and closed there.
219. There are two [parts] on the door-posts.
It is called a *pīṭhasaṅghāṭaka* (bench-junction) because benches are joined together there by means of wrought iron and other materials.
It is called a *pīṭhasaṅghāṭaka* because it is joined together by frames (*pīṭha*); the root *ghaṭ* means "to join.

Because it has two parts and resembles an arm (*bāhā*), it is called a "door-arm" (*dvārabāhā*). "Door-leaf" (*kapāṭa*) and "panel" (*kavāṭa*) are also names for the door-arm; it is so called because it splits (*pāṭayati*) or encloses (*vāṭayati*) the wind (*kaṃ*);
the suffix *-ṇo* is added in the sense of the object, and in the feminine it becomes *kapāṭī*.

Two [terms] for the peak of houses and so forth: *kuṭa* means "cutting"; with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *kuṭo*. *Naya* has the sense of "going. That which leads (*nayati*) on the head (*ke/sīse*) is *kaṇṇīkā*; [the suffix] *ṇvu*, the change to *it*, and the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*.
(220) Two [terms] for a door: *dvāraṃ* is that where two go (*aranti*);

or, it is *dvāraṃ* because guards ward off (*vārayanti*) evil people from it—the elision of *u*. It is *paṭiharo* because guards ward off (*paṭiharanti*) or remove those unknown to them; it carries away (*harati*) adversaries.
Or, *paṭihara* means "counteracting"; it is the counteracting of the short vowel by lengthening it.

The tetrad [of roots] begins with *ummāra*, which is called the "door-sill. *Ura* is in the sense of "going," and *māra* is in the sense of "doing. It leads (*neti*) the body (*deha*) into [the house] by way of entry, thus it is *dehanī*;
"dehalī" is also a reading, as it takes (*lāti*) the body into [the house] by way of entry, thus it is *dehalī*. *Ila* is in the sense of "going."
*Ṇvu*. It is called *indakhīlo* because one throws a foot (*pāda*) there; the root *khip* means "to throw.

There is the elision of the suffix *passa*, or alternatively, it is called *indo* because it gives (*dadāti*) passage (*iṃ*); that is, the door. A stake (*khīlo*) placed there is like a thorn (*kaṇṭako*), for by its forceful impact, it is like a stake.

*Thambha*: from *paṭibandhana* (binding); *thambho*. Or, it is *thambho* because it supports (*dhāreti*); from the root *dhṛ* (to support), with the suffix *rambha* and a change of vowel. *Thūṇo*: from *thu* (to praise), with the suffix *uṇo*, or optionally *yu*;

or, it is *thūṇo* because it supports; with the suffix *yu*, elision of *ra*, and the addition of *assū*. Regarding *aḍḍhendupāsāṇe*: the word *paṭika* applies to stones shaped like the half-moon. From *paṭa* (motion), with the suffix *ṇvu*. When followed by the feminine suffix *itthi*, the form becomes *katā*. *Gajī*: from *gaja* (sound), with the suffix *ṇvu*, the feminine suffix *itthi*, and the addition of the nasal *bindu*. *Isī*: from *isa* (desire), with the suffix *ṭhaka*.

221. *Valabhī* means a crest (*cūḷā*). According to Rudra, it is used in the sense of a crest: “*valabhī* is a crest on the top-knot” (*sikhāyaṃ valabhī cūḷe*), and Rudra also states that it ends in a short vowel:
“on the crest, on the *vaḷabhi*, on the crest” (*sikhāyaṃ vaḷabhiyaṃ cūḷe*; *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 12.15). In the context of roofing, *gopānasī* is considered to mean a wooden beam or timber.
*Vaṅka* is a specific term for wood. They are called *gaṃ* because they drink—that is, they destroy—rainwater and the rays of the sun and other sources by way of preventing them from entering inside.
*Gopānasī*: that by which the rafters (*gopāna*) and bricks (*iṭṭhakā*) and so forth are bound or fastened there. *Viṭaṅka*:

that portion of wood which, having been placed outside in houses such as those with square halls, is set up for the sake of providing a dwelling for clever birds. *Kapotapālikā*: "that which protects pigeons" (*kapota*);
the suffix *-ika* is used in the sense of the object of the action. From the root *ṭaki*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go," birds (*vinaḥ pakkhino*) "settle" (*ṭaṅkanti*) [there].

*Ettha* means *viṭaṅka*. *Ṇo*. 222. Two terms refer to the keyhole. The opening for a key is a hole; thus, it is a "key-hole" (*kuñcikāvivara*). The cavity that serves as the place for inserting the bolt is a hole; thus, it is a "bolt-hole" (*tālacchiggaḷa*). This triad refers to the key. [The root] *kuñc* is used in the sense of bending (*koṭilye*);
with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *kuñcikā*. That which protects (*tāyati*) is a *tāla*. With the suffix *alo*, from the root *tal* (meaning "to stand" or "remain"), it is *tāla*.
*Etena* means "by this," or *tāla* [is derived from] *tala*, meaning "to stand upon. *Avāpuraṇaṃ* means "that by which one opens" or "unveils";

it is derived from the root *vara* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *yu*. The substitution of *po* for *va* and the lengthening of the vowel in the prefix (*upasaggassa*) are established by the statement:
"The doors of the Deathless were opened for them" (Dīghanikāya 2.71; Majjhimanikāya 1.283). Some also recite the verbal root as *pāra* in the sense of "covering. It is preceded by the prefix *ava*.
In the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇa*), when there is the root-meaning of *vassa*, the vowel lengthening of the prefix occurs;

however, in cases such as "opened" (*apārutā*) and "having put on the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā*), it is established through the addition of the letter *p*. The root *vid* means "to obtain"; with the suffix *ika*, it becomes *vedikā*, and with the suffix *ka* in its own sense, it remains the same.
In other instances, it is simply *iy*.
223. *Saṅghāṭa* and so forth are specific parts of a building. It is called a *saṅghāṭa* because the rafters (*gopānasya*) and other members join together properly therein;
it is a specific type of timber situated above the pillars according to the east-west and south-north axes.
Furthermore, there are three timbers for the east-west axis, while those for the south-north axis extend from the lower limit—
There are three types of sticks; however, according to the maximum limit, there may also be five, seven, nine, and so forth.

It is called a "wing-rope" (*pakkhapāsa*) because it is like a snare (*pāsa*) used for binding in order to prevent the two wings from falling apart. It is called a "balance-beam" (*tulā*) because it balances and remains steady upon the shoulder-cloths (*saṅghāṭa*);

the root *tala* means "to stand firm," and this is a non-derived form. Alternatively, it is a balance-beam because by means of it one balances or measures the state of equilibrium of the wings; the root *tula* means "to measure."
A triad concerning the broom. *Muj* (to clean), with the suffix *yu*. *Majj* (to cleanse), with the suffix *yu*. *Sudh* (to purify); in all cases, the suffix *yu* is used in the instrumental sense.
224. A triad concerning the place for discarding rubbish. *Kaṭ* (to discard or wipe away). It is called *saṅkaṭīraṃ* because they discard (*saṅkaṭanti*) [rubbish] there;
the suffix is *īra*. Alternatively, *saṅkaṭo* refers to rubbish (*saṅkāro*); it is called *saṅkaṭīraṃ* because they move (*īranti*) or throw that [rubbish] there; the suffix is *īra*.

*Khepe*. A place for refuse is a *saṅkāraṭṭhāna* (refuse-place). It is called a *saṅkārakūṭa* (heap of refuse) because refuse (*saṅkāra*) is piled up or discarded there; the suffix *-ko* is used here in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
[The word] *catukka* refers to a broom, used for sweeping away or removing chaff and the like. That by which various kinds of refuse are gathered into a heap and bound together is called *kaca*;
since that is desired (*icchitabbo*) here, it is *kacavara*; the suffix *-vara* is used in the sense of desire (*icchāyaṃ*). *Ucchiṭṭha* means leftover.
*Kalāpa* means a collection (*samūha*); there is the elision of the letter *ka*. It is called *saṅkāra* because it is mixed (*saṅkarīyati*) or made impure with various kinds of grass and so forth;

the suffix *ṇa* is used. *Avakara* is also used here. It is called *avakara* because it is scattered away (*avakarīyati*) or cast out; the suffix *a* is used. Halāyudha says: "Sammajja, majjanī, saṅkāra, and avakara are considered synonyms.
The root *kas* is used in the sense of scratching (*vilekhana*); the suffix *ambu* is added.
225. *Gharādibhūmi*: That portion of ground belonging to houses, fields, monasteries (*vihāra*), and so forth, which is called *vatthu*, is used in the neuter gender.

It is *vatthu* because they dwell (*vasanti*) upon it; [the root] *rat* means to dwell. *Gasa* means to intoxicate or delight; it is *gāmo* because they are delighted (*gasanti*) there; [the suffix] *mo*. They dwell together (*saṃvasanti*) here, thus it is *saṃvasatho*;

[the suffix] *atho*. A village that is well-known or famous is called *nigama*. A *nigama* is a village that is superior (*atireka*). The prefix *ni* has the sense of "excessively" (*bhusa*). Because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), the vowel is shortened.

A village that has increased (*vaḍḍhita*) through people who enjoy wealth and so forth, being superior even to a market town (*nigama*) because it is greater than it, is called or described as "adhibhū"; it is called *adhibhū* because it becomes superior (*adhiko bhavati*). 226. The pair [of terms] refers to the boundary portion of a village and so forth.

The root *si* means "to bind" (*bandhane*). That which is taken after having been delimited is a *mariyādā* (boundary); see *mo*. The pair [of terms] refers to a cowherd hut; there may be a *ghosa* or an *ābhīrapallī* (Amara 12.20).

The root *ghu* means "sound" (*sadde*). It is a *ghosa* because they cry out (*ghosanti*) here. A village of cowherds is *gopālagāmaka*; the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*).
The commentary on the section on cities is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Men (Naravagga): 227–228.

These are names for human beings (*porisanta*) belonging to the human race. A "human" (*manusso*) is so called because his mind (*mano*) is preeminent (*ussanna*); this is by virtue of qualities such as mindfulness, courage, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Those whose minds are cultivated and whose hearts possess sublime qualities—whom are they? They are the distinguished beings dwelling in Jambudīpa.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, in three respects the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and even the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
What are these three? They are brave, they are mindful, and they live here the holy life. (Aṅguttara Nikāya).
9.21. For in that very place arise the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Paccekabuddhas, the Chief Disciples, the Great Disciples, the Wheel-turning Monarchs, and other beings of great power.

However, some say that because they possess similar forms and so forth, those dwelling on the other great continents were recognized as being merely human, just like the inhabitants of the minor islands. Others, however, say: "By means of greed and the rest..."
And because of the predominance (*ussadatā*) of the mind accompanied by non-greed and the other [wholesome roots], they are "human beings" (*manussa*).

For among those beings who belong to the human species, greed and the like predominate in some, while non-greed and the like predominate in others. Due to the predominance of greed and the like, they fulfill the path to the states of misery;

due to the predominance of non-greed and the like, they fulfill the path to the happy destinies and the path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore, [it is said] "by greed and the like," and "by non-greed and the like."

"And because of the preeminence of the mind (manas) when it is accompanied [by its functions], those distinguished beings dwelling in the four great continents are called 'human' (manussa) along with those dwelling on the minor islands.
However, the worldly say they are "human" (manussa) by virtue of being descendants of Manu;

for "Manu" was the first person of the first aeon, the founder of the world's social order, the provider of what is beneficial and harmful, who stood in the place of a father to sentient beings. He...

In the Teaching (sāsana), he is called "Mahāsammata" (the Great Elect). Because they abide by his exhortations and instructions—both directly and through tradition—human beings are said to be like his children.
For this very reason, they are designated as "mānavā" and "manujā," using the suffix *usa*.
The offspring of Manu is "mānusa," with the suffix *usa*. [The root] *mar* means to abandon life; with the suffix *ca*, it becomes "macca."

Alternatively, by means of *pabbajjā* and other such suffixes, the suffix *-tya* is applied, and there is the elision of the final portion of the verbal root. From that, by means of the rule beginning with *“yavata,”* the suffix *-ca* is added, and there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*).
The offspring of *manu* is a *māṇava*; here, *māṇava* also [occurs], with the suffix *-ṇava*. Born from *manu* is a *manuja*. *Nī* in the sense of leading:

he leads, thus *nara*, with the suffix *-ara*. *Pus* in the sense of nourishing: the suffix *-ṇa*; or, he fills (*pureti*), thus *posa*. *Pur* in the sense of filling: the suffix *-sa*; there is the elision of *r* after the vowel *u*. He purifies, thus...
The [root] *pu* means "to purify" (*pavane*); with the suffixes *ma*, *si*, and *sā*, it forms *purisa*. Because he goes before (*pureti*), he is called *purisa*; also *porisa*.

And because of the lengthening of the short vowel, it is also *pūrisa*. Herein, the pentad beginning with *manussa* applies to females as well; however, *nara* and the others apply only to males because they are distinguished by the masculine gender.
In that regard, from *manussa*, *mānusa*, *manuja*, and *māṇava*, the suffix *ī* is added according to the *nadādi* group, and there is the elision of one *sa*: thus, *manusī* and *mānusī*.
*Manujī*, *māṇavī*: [These are feminine forms derived from] *maccā*. The suffix *-ī* is applied after a word ending in *-a*. Regarding *paṇḍita*: up to the limit of *vidvasu*.
One who has produced (*sañjāta*) wisdom (*paṇḍā*) is a *paṇḍita*; [this is formed by the root] *tṛ* and so forth. Or, from the root *paḍi* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *-ta*.

One who awakens (*bujjhati*) is a *budha*. One who knows (*vidati*) or understands is a *vidvā*; from the root *vida* in the sense of "knowledge," with the suffix *-vasu* and the elision of *-s*. From the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*).

One who makes things manifest (*vibhāveti*) or reveals them through virtue (*sīlena*) is *vibhāvī*; this is a derivative from the suffix *-ṇī*. Those in whom passion and the like have subsided (*sameti*) are *santo* (peaceful);

alternatively, one whose end or conclusion (*anta*) is beautiful (*sundara*) is *santo*. One who possesses beautiful wisdom (*paññā*) is *sappañño*. One who knows what [is] called "what" (*kiṃ*) is *kovido* (learned/expert);
this is an etymological derivation (*nerutto*), or alternatively, one who finds (*vindati*) evil (*kuṃ*) is *kovido*. One who has wisdom (*dhī*) is *dhīmā* (wise); it is beautiful...

One who meditates (*jhāyati*) is a *sudhī*. The root *jhi* means "to think. By changing *jha* to *dha*, we get *dhī*; one whose intellect (*dhī*) is beautiful is a *sudhī*. Alternatively, *sudhī* is one whose intellect is excellent.

*Kavi* (in the sense of "to praise") with the suffix *i* forms *kavī* in the feminine; or from *ku* (in the sense of "sound") with *i*, we get *kavi*. One who manifests (*byañjayati*) is *byatto*. The root *añja* means "to go," with the suffix *to*.

For roots beginning with *bhuj* and others, the final consonant becomes *n* and the root reduplicates. Alternatively, one whose self (*attā*) is distinguished is *byatto*. *Cakkhu* (in the sense of "seeing") with the suffix *yu* [forms *cakkhu*].

*Vicakkhaṇo*: he discerns (*vicāreti*), thus he is "discerning" (*vicakkhaṇo*); this is according to etymology (*nerutto*). *Visārado*: that from which timidity (*sārada*) has departed, thus it is "confident" (*visārado*). 229. *Medhāvī*:

one whose intelligence (*medhā*), retentive memory (*dhāraṇā*), thought (*mati*), and wisdom (*paññā*) exist, is "intelligent" (*medhāvī*); [this is] according to the *vī* suffix. *Matimā*: by virtue of being endowed with pre-eminent intelligence, he is "possessed of intellect" (*matimā*). *Pañño*: through association with wisdom (*paññā*), he is "wise" (*pañño*). *Viññū*:

by nature he knows distinctions (*visesa*), thus he is "discerning" (*viññū*); [this is] according to the *rū* suffix. [The root] *vida* means "to know"; [with the suffix] *uro*, [it becomes] *viduro* or *vidūo* (according to the *Kaśikā*).

The suffix *vidū* is applied after the verbal root *rūp*. One who possesses wisdom (*dhī*) through yoga is a *dhīra*; the suffix *ro* is applied. Because of his habit of distinguished vision, he is *Vipassī*;

the suffix *ṇī* is applied. One who knows aversion (*dosa*) is *dosaññū*; the suffix *rū* is applied. He awakens, thus he is *Buddho*; the suffix *to* is applied. The root *du* means "going"; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *dava* (foam). *Dava* means "going" and *abbā* (needle) means "going"; thus, *dabba*. The root *vida* means "knowledge," with the suffix *dasu*.
230–231. *Mahilā* [is formed] with the suffix *anta*, signifying "woman" in general. *Isu* [is used] in the sense of "desire"; [it belongs to] the *nadādi* group, and the suffix *to* is applied.

The end (*anta*) of a boundary (*sīmā*) is *sīmanta*; this refers to the parting of the hair. Because she is connected with that, she is called *sīmantinī*, with the suffix *inī*. This [suffix] *nārī* belongs to a man (*nara*); here the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of "belonging to this.

She in whom the fetus (*gabbha*) remains is a *thī* (woman). [The root] *dhā* means "to hold"; there is a modification of the vowel (*vaṇṇavikāra*), and the suffix *ī* is applied. [The root] *bandh* means "to bind"; the suffix *ū* is applied, and for *bandha*, the substitution *vadhā* occurs.

And by the rule beginning with *ṇvu* (Pāṇini 3.1.141), the word *vadhū* denotes both a daughter-in-law and a wife. The root *vana* means "to associate"; with the suffix *to*, there is the augment *ikāra*.
The root *aṅga* has the sense of "going"; with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *aṅganā*. *Aṅganā* also refers to an excellent woman;

thus, because she possesses limbs (*aṅga*) such as hands and feet that are praiseworthy and endowed with the characteristics of an auspicious noble woman, the suffix *nap* is applied in the sense of "possessing" according to Moggallāna. Therefore, it is *aṅganā*.
4.92. *Pamadā*: she who possesses intoxication (*mada*) even toward those who are not beautiful is a *pamadā*. Here, *pamadā* refers specifically to an excellent woman;

thus, a *pamadā* is one whose mental transformation is produced by an intense intoxication born of physical beauty. She is *sundarī* (beautiful) because she is endowed with physical form and grace, even if she is already distinguished.

She is *kantā* (lovely) because her way of being is desirable; the root *kam* means "desire," and the suffix *-ta* is added. Alternatively, she is so called due to her connection with loveliness (*kanti*).

*Kantā* means beloved; it is also used in the sense of "distinguished. She who delights and gladdens the hero is a *ramaṇī*; [the suffix] *-yu* is added after roots beginning with *nand*, such as *nad*.
*Day* in the sense of protecting takes the suffix *-to* in the passive sense (*kammani*). One whose strength is small is *abalā*; here the vowel *a* has the sense of diminution (*appattha*).
One whose village is like that of a mother is a *mātugāmo*; or alternatively, one who goes like a mother is a *mātugāmo*.
*Gam* means going; *ṇo*: she swallows like a mother, thus *mātugāma*; *gas* means eating, *mo*.
Or, she sings like a mother, thus *mātugāma*; *gā* means sound, *mo*. She takes both the pure and the impure like the earth (*mahī*), thus *mahilā*;
or, she moves among great and numerous lustful minds, thus *mahilā*; *ila* means moving, *maha* means honor, *iro*, *lattaṃ*.
"Ā," [refers to] a woman (*mahilā*). *Mahelā* is also used here.

The triad [of terms] refers specifically to an excellent woman. Regarding "lala" in the sense of playfulness (*vilāsa*), the suffix *yu* is added after roots beginning with *nand*. Alternatively, from the *curādigaṇa*, *yu* is added to "lala" in the sense of desire (*icchā*).

"Bhīru" has the nature of fear; from the root *bhī* (to fear) and the suffix *ru*: "The word *bhīru* refers to a timid person," according to the *Rabhasa* lexicon. She is one whose passion is excessive.
*Kāminī*: one who possesses *kāma* (desire) in the form of passion (*siṅgāra*) and intoxication (*mada*). The suffix *-inī* is applied in this manner in all such cases.
*Vāmalocanā*, *bhāvinī*, *nitambinī*, *rāmā*, and so forth, are also names for distinguished women.
The [first] two [terms] refer to a woman who is in the prime of her youth.
An eight-year-old girl is called *gorī*, while a ten-year-old is a *kaññakā*;
when she has reached her twelfth year, she is designated as a *kumārī*—according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.8).

However, in this context, they are treated as a single entity through the metaphorical application of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). Others, however, say that this word *kaññā* [is used] when preceded by a connection with a masculine term.

"...he causes [them] to cease in conjunction. Regarding "kumārī": from the root *kumāra* (beginning with *cur*), in the sense of playing, it means "she plays" (*kumārayati*). The suffix *a* is applied according to the *nadādi* class; the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), or it is established by the suffix *ṇvu*.
Regarding "kaññā": it means "desirable" (*kamanīyatā*). From the root *kana* (in the senses of shining, beauty, and movement), the suffix *yo* is applied;

the *ny* of *nya* becomes *ña*; then the suffixes *a* and *ā*. Regarding "yuvati": it is a primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) derived from the word *yuvan*. Although the word *yuvati* is used as a general term for a young woman (*varitthi*), there exists another base (*pakatyantara*) for the word *yuvati*. Regarding "taraṇī": from the root *tara* (in the sense of crossing over), the suffix *yu* is applied, followed by *utta*, and the vowel *ī*.

232. *Sābhisekā* means one who has received consecration; a royal woman who is a chief queen is called a *mahesī*. In the context of great worship (*maha-pūjā*), the suffix *iso* is used for the action. From *issa*, the suffix *ī* follows.
Alternatively, she is a *mahesī* because she rules over or surpasses (*īsati abhibhavati*) the other great royal women. The root *īsa* means sovereignty (*issariye*). The suffix *ī* is applied.
Other royal wives, being enjoyers (*bhoginī*) through their connection with enjoyment (*bhoga-yogā*), take the suffix *ī* and *inī*. A woman who goes to a man’s rendezvous (*saṅketa*) is a *yānārī*.
She is called a *dhavatthinī* and an *abhisārikā*. She is a *dhavatthinī* because she desires (*atthayati*) or seeks a husband (*dhava*);

the root *attha* is used in the senses of seeking and desiring, with the suffix *-inī*, denoting a particular type of unchaste woman (*asatī*). The root *sara* means "to go"; she goes to an appointment (*saṅketa*), hence the suffix *-ṇvu*.

233. The group of six [terms] refers to a courtesan (*vesiyā*). She is reckoned and taken up [as such] due to her skill in the sixty-four arts and her possession of beauty, virtue, and other qualities.
*Gaṇikā*: from the root *gaṇ*, meaning "to count," with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Vesa* means "dress" or "appearance"; she shines exceedingly by means of that, or she is desired for her various costumes.
The suffix *ya* is used in the sense of "shining exceedingly" or "desiring. A female slave endowed with beauty is a *vaṇṇadāsī*;
for some masters, out of greed for wealth, turn even a beautiful female slave into a courtesan. She who beautifies the city is a *nagarasobhinī*. [By] form...
"Upajīvinī" means one who lives off [others]. "Vesī" refers to one endowed with excessive seductive charms (*vesa*).
Both terms are used in the sense of "unfaithful. "Kulaṭā" means one who wanders through or ruins families. "Bandhakī" means one who practices binding or following after [men];

it belongs to the *nadādi* group. 234. The set of four refers to the most excellent noble woman. "Varārohā" means one whose hips (*āroha*) are excellent (*vara*). She is called "Uttamā" because of her possession of supreme qualities.

Like a rutting elephant through fear of the goad, or like a lustful woman heading toward her bonds, [she goes] by way of the whip. She is called *varavaṇṇinī* because of her possession of excellent beauty (*varavaṇṇa*); the suffix *-inī* [is used here].
As it is said: “That woman who is pleasant in all her limbs in the cold, who is pleasant and cool in the heat, and who is devoted to her husband—she shall be *varavaṇṇinī*. [The word] *ruddo*;

Two [terms] refer to one whose conduct is unbroken. A woman for whom the husband alone is desirable is *patibbatā*; alternatively, she is *patibbatā* because her vow (*vata*) is directed toward the husband. [Etymologically: *asa* (to exist) + *anto* (suffix) + *ī*, with the elision of the initial vowel. Or, she is *satī* because she is composed; from the root *samu* (to calm), with *anto* and *ī*.

Two [terms] refer to a woman who has a fixed husband within a family such as that of a prince addicted to sensual pleasures. A woman corresponding to her family is *kulitthī*; she is a *kulapālikā* because she protects and guards the family, formed with the suffix *ṇvu*.
235. Two [terms] refer to a widow. She whose husband (*dhava*) has departed is *vidhavā*. She whose husband is empty or lost is *patisuññā*.

The two [terms] refer to a maiden who seeks a husband. She chooses (*varati*) or searches for a husband, thus she is *patimbarā*; here there is the elision of the second vowel. She herself chooses a husband, thus she is *sayambarā*; here there is the elision of the first vowel; the root *vara* means "longing. The four [terms] refer to one who has given birth. *Vijanī* means "in the releasing from the womb";

with the suffix *-to*, she is *vijātā* because she has given birth (*vijāyittha*). With the root *sū* meaning "to bring forth," with the suffix *-to*, she is *jātā*. She whose offspring (*apacca*) born is a son (*putta*) is *jātāpaccā*. She who has brought forth is *pasūtikā*; here the suffix *-ka* is added and the final vowel is changed to *-i*.

236. *Dvayaṃ* (the dyad) refers to the female messenger (*dūtī*). That which is sent forth is a messenger; from the root *du* (to go), with the suffix *īm*, it becomes *dūtī*. She conveys [messages] according to what is desired, hence the suffix *ṇvu*.

*Tikaṃ* (the triad) refers to the female servant (*dāsī*). She who exists in a base state or eats poorly is a *dāsī*; the suffix *ī* is applied. Alternatively, she by whom [tasks] are given is a *dāsī*; from the root *dā* (to give), with the suffixes *so* and *ī*. From the root *ciṭ* (in the sense of sending), with the suffix *ṇo* in the passive sense, and the suffix *ī*. She who carries a water-jar (*kuṭa*) is a *kuṭadhārikā*; the suffix *ṇvu* is applied.

The two [terms] *saṃvarikā* and so forth are used in the sense of one who discerns the beautiful and the ugly. *Varā* is used in the sense of a state (*gati*), while *inī* is used in the sense of an agent (*kattari*). That which possesses the discernment (*ikkhaṇa*) or investigation (*nirūpana*) of the beautiful and the ugly is called *nirūpinī*; here, the suffix *i* is applied, and the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*sakatthe*). These two words have the same meaning.

A woman of the Kṣatriya caste who is the wife of anyone is called *khattiyānī* or simply *khattiyā*. *Khattiyānī* is derived from *khattiya* with the suffix *āno*, where *ī* is substituted for *ā*. With the suffix *ṇa*, it becomes *khattiyā*. 237.
*Pajjā* refers to a wife who has taken the hand [of her husband] in the presence of fire as a witness; otherwise, it is used figuratively (*upacārā*). They cause separation (*dārayante*).

*Yena* means "by which. *Dara*, in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*), takes the suffix *ṇo* when not denoting the agent but forming a technical term (*saññāyaṃ*). That by whom a son is born is a *jāyā*; from the root *jana* (to beget), with the suffix *yo*, there is the substitution of *jā* for *janissa*, and *ā* is added:
thus *jāyā*. Alternatively, she is a *jāyā* because she conquers (*jayatīti*); from the root *ji* (to conquer), with the suffix *yo*, there is the substitution of *jā* for *jissa*, and *ā* is added:

thus *jāyā*. *Kala* (in the sense of counting) has the suffix *atto*. She who leads to the house (*gharaṃ netīti*) is a *gharaṇī*; the suffix *ṇa* is applied. She is a *bhariyā* because she is to be supported (*bharitabbato*); from the root *bhara*...

*Bharaṇe* (in the sense of supporting), *yo*. *Piyā*, because she is to be loved; *pī* in the sense of pleasing and desiring, *yo*. One who protects (*pāleti*) the offspring (*pajaṃ*), that is, the son, is called *pajāpati*;

from the root *pā* in the sense of protecting, with the suffix *ātta* and shortening of the vowel. She who completes two [persons] is the second (*dutiyā*). The first is the husband, the second is the wife.
One who serves (*paricarati*) at the feet of the master is a *pādaparicārikā*, with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Patinī*, *pāṇigahitā*, and *sahadhamminī* are also names for her alone.

238. The triad on *sakhī*. In various duties, she appears together with [others] and makes herself manifest; thus she is a *sakhī*. The root *khā*, preceded by *saha*, is used in the senses of making manifest and speaking.

The suffix *ī* follows. The root *ala* is used in the sense of ornamenting, preceded by *ā*; the suffix *i* follows. Regarding "equal in age," the suffix *ya* is seen in the Pāṇinian rule 4.4.91 (*vayasi tulye saññāyaṃ so*) for the purpose of forming a designation of equality in age.

*Jārī* refers to the wife of a paramour (*jāra-sāmikā*); she belongs to him, hence *jārī*. The suffix *ṇo* (which becomes *ī*) is used here. Because she wanders elsewhere, having transgressed her husband, the suffix *inī* is applied. Regarding the rule "In the masculine, however" (*pume tu*):
the word *tu*, being a gender-indicative particle (*liṅganta*), does not connect with what precedes it. From the root *ara* (to go), with the suffix *tu*, the vowel *a* is elided, resulting in *aru*.

That which is born from passion (*rati*) is *rajo* (dust/passion); here, the syllable *ti* is elided. From the root *puppha* (to blossom), we have *pupphaṃ*. This triad refers to a woman who possesses dust (*rajassalā*). Due to connection with her season (*utu*), she is *autunī*; the suffix *inī* is applied. Due to connection with dust (*raja*), she is *rajassalā*; the suffix *sala* is applied. Because of the state of possessing flowers (*pupphavantatā*), she is *pupphavatī*. *Thīdhamminī*, *avī*, *atteyī*, *malinī*, *utumatī*, *udakī*, and so forth, are also names for her.

A triad concerning the pregnant woman (*gabbhinī*). One whose womb contains a fetus that is heavy or light is called *garugabbhā*. One by whom a being has entered (*āpanna*) or reached the state of a fetus is called *āpannasattā*.

One who is joined with a fetus is *gabbhinī*. A triad: that by which the fetus is enveloped and remains in the womb is known as the *khyā* (the womb). It is called *khyā* because the fetus rests (*āsayati*) or stays there;
[the suffix] *ṇo* is added. That which goes to decay (*jarā*) is *jalābu*. [The derivation is: *u*, with *r* becoming *l*, and *y* becoming *b*; the root *i* preceded by *jarā* means "to go."
It is called *kalala* because it takes on (*lāti*) blackness (*kalaṃ*) and decay (*jarataṃ*); or else, from the root *kala* meaning "to count" (*saṅkhyāne*), with the suffix *alo*.
240–241. [The word] *satta* [is derived as follows]: *dhū* means "to shake" (*kampane*); one who shakes fear (*santāsaṃ*) is a *dhava*, with the suffix *a*. One who has this [quality] is a *sāmika*;
with the suffix *āmi*, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), or the suffix *i*; the *niggahīta* becomes *mo*, and there is lengthening of the vowel *a*, thus *sāmiko*.

*Bhara* means to support; one who supports is a *bhattā* (husband), a term of respect. *Kama* is in the sense of desire; the suffix *-ta* is applied according to the rule "after *pakka* and others, *-nta*.
*Pā* is in the sense of protecting; with the prefix *ati*, it becomes *pati*. *Vara* is in the sense of desiring; the suffix *-a* gives *vara*.

*Pī* is in the senses of satisfying and longing; the suffix *-ya* gives *piya*. Because he is the cause of pleasure (*ratikāraṇattā*), he is the *upapati* (lover) of the wife (*patino*). When the compound is formed, by conventional usage (*abhidhānato*) he is placed first, or else the husband (*pati*), being subordinate, is called the *upapati*. *Jara* is in the sense of the decline of age; that by which one is worn out is a *jāra* (paramour), as is a *dāra* (wife).
*Sattakaṃ putte*: "Offspring" (*apacca*) is so called because by being born, one does not fall into hell through it; *pata* means "to go.
Or, "offspring" (*apacca*) is that by which the lineage (*vaṃsa*) does not fall—that is, does not perish—therefore it is "offspring. This term refers to both son and daughter, and is always neuter.

*Pū* means "to purify. One is a "son" (*putta*) because he purifies his ancestors; the suffix *-tana* is applied here according to the rule "after *chada* and others, *-tana*. Or, he is a "son" (*putta*) because he fills [the lineage].
*Attaja*: born from oneself; there is also a reading *atrāja*. *Suyata*: heard (*suta*). [The root] *su* means to press out; or, one who hears is *suta*, with the suffix *ta*;

*su* is used in the sense of hearing. *Tanuja*: born from the body; also *tanaya*. [The suffix] *ya* is added; or, that which extends (*tanoti*) or gladdens (*mudati*) is *tanaya*, with the suffix *aya*.
*Sūyata*: son (*sūnu*); the suffix *nu* is added in the sense of the object; [the root] *sū* means to procreate.
The words *putta* and so forth, ending with *sūnu*, when applied to a daughter, function as feminine terms. *Duhitā* and *dhītā* always refer only to a female. [Etymologically:

from the root *duh* in the sense of "filling," with the suffix *-rātu*, the substitution of *ottā* for the vowel, and the addition of the letter *i*. From the root *dhā* in the sense of "holding," with the suffix *-rātu* and the suffix *-āssī*. Furthermore, *putta* and the others denote *kuṇḍa-golaka* and similar types by way of their general meaning;
however, when born of a woman of equal caste who has been duly wedded— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the definition of a son born of a wife of equal caste.)
A son begotten by oneself is called "legitimate" (*orasa*). By the word *sajāta* ("born together"), there is the exclusion of the *kuṇḍaka*, *golaka*, *khattā*, and others.

A son born of a paramour while the husband is alive is named *kuṇḍaka*; when the husband is dead, one born of a paramour is named *golaka*. A son born of a noble woman and a non-noble man is called a *khattā*; for it is said:
"The *khattā* is the offspring of noble women and non-nobles" (*Amara-kośa* 2.30.3). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Māgadha and others are included. For it has been stated:
“One born from a lover while [the husband] is alive is a *kuṇḍa*;
one born when the husband is dead is a *golaka*. This is the Amara-kośa (16.36).
And there is the verse from the Abhidhāna (503): “A *māgadha* is one born from a *śūdra* woman and a *kṣatriya* man.”

*Urasā* and *manasā* are [used] in the sense of "produced" (*nimmita*). From the word *uras*, with the third case ending, the suffix *ṇo* is applied in the sense of being produced; because it is established [therein], it is called "produced by that" (*tena nimmito*).
