Alternatively, *oraso* means "born from the chest" (*urasi bhavo*). 242. Regarding the pair of words for those who have four husbands: according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.38) and the *Amaramālā*, "the word *dārā* is masculine in the plural, and neuter when referring to a wife.
The indeclinable word *jaṃ* is a synonym for *dāra*. Therefore, there are also the forms *jampati* and *dampatī*.

It ought to be so; however, here they are cited according to the opinion of Kaccāyana. *Jāyā* (wife) and *pati* (husband) form *jāyāpati*. This is an *itarītarayoga* (mutual connection) *dvanda* compound.
Similarly, there are *jānipati*, *jāyampati*, and so forth; when the word *jāyā* is followed by *pati*, it becomes *jāni* by means of the rule beginning with "when *pati* follows.

The triad [of forms] is neuter. *Vigata* (gone away) is the *rāgāsava* (taint of lust) from which he has departed; thus he is *vassavaro*. *Su* is in the sense of hearing (*savane*), [forming] *aro*. *Paṇa* is in the sense of transaction (*byavahāre*).

*Ḍo*, *paḍi*, *liṅgavekalye*, or *bhūvādi*. It is neither female (*itthī*), nor male (*pumā*), nor neuter (*napuṃsaka*); according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), it is the state of being neuter for both female and male, and its root form (*pakati*) is *na*.
Its root form is the third (*tatiyāpakati*); *saṇḍa* and *kalībanta* are also its names. "The third root form" means the third kind;
its status as the third arises in relation to similar females and males. First.
For the first nature is female, the second nature is male, and the third nature is the other.
243. The group of six [terms] refers to relatives in general: *bandhu* means a kinsman; *a*, *ussāva*. It is called *bandhu* because it binds (*bandhati*), with the suffix *u*.

One's own people are *sajana*. One who has a common lineage (*gotta*) or family (*kula*) is *sagotta*; this is the inherent state (*sabhāva*) of being common. *Ñā* is used in the sense of "knowing" (*avabodhana*).

*Kamma* means "kinsman"; *ñātaka* is simply *ñāti*. The suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). The word *su-* also has the meaning of "one's own" (*sva*) [according to Amarakośa 16.36].

The pair [of terms] refers to close relatives within seven generations of men. One who is connected by blood is a *sālohita*; here, the syllable *sa-* is substituted for the connection (*sambandha*), and there is a change in the order of words (*pubbanipāta*).
One to whom the offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is common is a *sapiṇḍa*; *sanābha* is also used here, where *nābhi* refers to the family line extending up to seven generations.

(Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.33). The triad refers to the father. The root *tā* is used in the sense of protecting; *to* is used in the sense of an agent. One who generates (*janayati*) is a "father" (*janaka*), with the suffix *ṇvu*. The root *pā* is used in the sense of guarding;

with the suffix *ritu*, it becomes *pitā*. 244. The hexad refers to the mother. The root *ama* is used in the sense of honoring; with the suffix *mo* in the objective case, and with the addition of *bo*, it becomes *ammā* and *ambā*. One who generates (*janayati*) is a "mother" (*jananī*).
*Yu*, *nadādi*. *Māna* means "to honor. One who honors a son is a mother (*mātā*); or, one who protects (*rātu*) or nourishes (*pātīti*) is a mother;
for *pāti* has the suffix *mo*. One who gives birth is a progenitor (*janetti*); from the root *jan* with the suffix *ṇvu*, there is the form *janikā*.

A mother who is not the primary [biological] mother is a stepmother (*upamātā*). One who carries a child is a nurse (*dhāti*). From the root *dhā* meaning "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*), [the suffix *ti* is applied]. Of the wife, that is, the spouse...
The younger brother and the elder brother are both named Sāla; she is his own wife. Her brother is Sāla;

[the term] *alo* refers to the brother of one’s wife (*jāyā*). The root *sar* is used in the senses of movement, thought, and injury; *ṇo* is the suffix; *sāla* is derived from the sense of reflection (*vitakka*), belonging to the *cur*-class (curādi).

245. The sister of the master or husband is called *nanandā*. She is called *nanandā* because she does not rejoice (*na nandati*); the absence of the prefix *āt-* occurs due to the rule of optionality (*vibhāsā*) regarding the elision of *na*. The root *nand* is used in the sense of prosperity (*samiddhi*), belonging to the *bhū*-class (*bhūvādi*).

There are two [terms] for *ayyikā*. The mother of one’s mother is *mātāmahī* (grandmother). For the father’s father and the father’s mother, there is *āmaha*, etc., beginning with *na*; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is applied in the sense of worship (*araha pūjāyaṃ*), [with] *raha* becoming *ya*, and from the root *aya* in the sense of going (*aya gatimhi*), with the suffix *ṇvu*, [we get] *ayyikā*.
The brother of one’s mother is called *mātula* (maternal uncle); "the brother of the mother is *mātula*"; the suffix *ula* is applied to the mother’s brother.
His wife, the spouse of that *mātula*, is called *mātulānī*; "the wife of the *mātula* is *mātulānī*"; the suffix *ānī* is applied to the wife of the *mātula*, beginning with *na*.
Alternatively, this [term] for the mother-in-law (*mātulānī*) is derived from *mātula* with the suffixes *ī* and *ānī*.
246. The mother who gives birth to the two, husband and wife, is called *sassu*; [the root] *sas* is used in the senses of going and harming.
Their father, however, is called *sasura*; from the verbal root *sas*, the suffix *uro* is added. And the son of a sister is *bhāgineyyo*.
The word *nāma* refers to the offspring of a sister, namely a nephew (*bhāgineyyo*); the suffix *-eyya-* is applied here.

(Verse 247) Regarding the children of a son and a daughter, the suffix *-ita-* is applied after the root *su-*. The root *nah-* means "to bind," while *ritu* and *nī* mean "to lead" or "to carry. The term *paputta* means "the son of a son";

here, there is the elision of the *-tt-* and the substitution of *ussa-* for *putta-*. The term *sāmibhātā* means a brother-in-law (*devaro*); alternatively, it refers to a younger brother of the husband.

The brother of the husband is called *devara*. However, the elder [brother-in-law] is called *sasura*. [The root] *div* is used in the sense of play; [the suffix] *ara*. There are two [terms] for the husband of a daughter. [The root] *jan* means birth;

[the suffixes] *itu*, *assāttaṃ*, and the substitution of *na* for *mā*. There are two [terms] for the father of a father. The father of a father is the *pitāmaha*. 248. Nouns ending in *hus* [are formed] with each respective suffix.

The sister of a mother is *mātucchā*; [the suffix] *ccha*. The sister of a father is *pitucchā*; the meaning is that she is the sister of the father (*pitubhaginī*). *Pitucchā* is the same as *pitubhaginī*.
The word *pitāmaha* does not denote only the biological father, but also the father’s father and so forth; thus, the term *papitāmaha* is also mentioned here.

*Pitu* (father) becomes *ayyaka* or *payyaka*; this is a phonetic substitution (*tulopa*). From the root *su* (to hear), with the suffix *ṇha*, we have *suṇhā*. With the suffix *ṇisa*, we have *suṇisā*.

With the suffix *sa*, we have *husā*, where *ha* is substituted for *ta*. In all these cases, the suffix *ā* is applied according to the rule: "In the feminine, the suffix *ā* follows [the base ending in] *m*."

249. A set of four [terms] regarding a brother born of the same womb (*ekodara*). One who stands in the same womb is *sodariya*; it belongs to one who is *samāna* (the same). A womb that is the same is *samānagabbha*;
that which exists therein is *sagabbha*, with the suffix *-ṇa*. One born of the same womb is *sodara*. One born of the same womb is *sahaja*.
The word *saha* signifies "equal" (*tulya*).

Your mother and father—these two people are called "parents. Because both are designated by the term "progenitor," when there is a desire for non-differentiation, the singular form "father" (*pitā*) is used even in the sense of the highest [collective] fatherhood.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "birth" (*jāti*) is non-differentiated, and because that birth exists in both [parents], there is oneness? Furthermore, gender and number do not belong to a genus (*jāti*), so since it is not a substance (*adabbatthā*), should there not be an absence of the plural number?
[Response: This is not a fault. For one who holds that the word-meaning is the genus (*jātipadatthika*), it is not...
"Substance" (*dabba*) or "the individual instance of substance" (*dabbapadatthika*) is not the genus (*jāti*). However, for both [terms], the referent of both words here is a specific meaning.
For one who takes the genus as the referent, the genus is primary and the substance is secondary; for one who takes the substance as the referent, it is the reverse.
In that case, when there is a desire to express the genus, the gender and number should be stated according to the substance; and because that [substance] is plural, the plural number is used.
In the desire for non-distinctive speech, both son and daughter are called "sons" (*puttā*), for the designation "son" is applicable to daughters as well because they are known [to be such].
However, in the opposite case, it does not occur because of the lack of conventional expression. In the desire for distinctive speech, the form "sons and daughters" (*puttadhītaro*) occurs. 250.
Both mother-in-law and father-in-law are called "parents-in-law" (*sasurā*). For this designation is based on the connection with their offspring and their kin.
It remains even when applied to a mother-in-law (*sassu*). However, when there is a desire for a term expressing distinction, the application of the sound [suffix] is contrary to the previous case.
Both a brother and a sister are called "brothers" (*bhātaro*). The state of having resided in the same womb is restricted to the designation of a brother, yet it also exists in the case of a sister.
Therefore, when there is a desire for a term expressing non-distinction regarding that state of having resided in the same womb, both are called "brothers. And here, in all these instances:

The "remainder of one" (*ekasesa*) should be understood as twofold, according to whether the forms are identical (*sarūpa*) or different (*asarūpa*). In that regard, in the case of the remainder of identical forms, only the plural is used;
however, in the other case, the dual is used, as for example: *puriso ca puriso ca* (a man and a man) becomes *purisā*;
*nāmañca rūpañca* (name and form) becomes *nāmarūpañca*, which is *nāmarūpaṃ*; and *mātā ca pitā ca* (mother and father) becomes *pitaro*.

There are three stages of life: childhood (*bālya*), youth (*yobbanam*), and old age (*vuḍḍhattam*). Among these, three [terms] refer to childhood; two refer to youth. The state of being a child is *bālattam*;

with the suffix *-ttam*, it is *bālatā*. With the suffix *-ṇya*, it is *bālyam*. Alternatively, from the root *bal* (to breathe), they are called *bālā* because they "breathe" (*balanti*) merely by means of inhalation and exhalation;
or they are called *bālā* because they are "restrained" (*balyante*) or "concealed" (*saṃvarīyanti*), from the root *bal* (to restrain/conceal). The state of these is *bālattādi*.

The state of youth (*yuvan*) is *yobbañña*; [the suffix] *ṇya* is applied to the noun *yobbañña*, and *ṇa* is also used. Alternatively, from the root *yu* (to mix), there is the substitution of *ussa* for *yu*, and the vowel increase (*vuddhi*).
The state of those [qualities] beginning with youth is *yobbaññādi*. 251.

Those hairs and so forth that have become white due to old age are called *palita*; or rather, that which is the whiteness of those [hairs] is called *palita*. From the root *pac* (to cook/mature), the suffix *ita* is applied, and the letter *c* is replaced by *l*.

The dyad [of aging] refers to the maturation of the body, characterized by wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth. *Jarā*: The aged (*vuḍḍhā*) become worn out; thus it is *jarā*. It is the decline of vitality (*vayohāni*).
*Jaratā* is simply aging (*jarā*), with the suffix *-tā* added in the sense of the thing itself (*sakatthe*). *Vissasā* is also a name for aging.

It is called *vissasā* because it specifically causes one to sink down or fall away (*saṃsati*). The root *saṃs-* here has the sense of "to hasten" (*raya*) and "to be negligent" (*pamāda*), but in this context, it has the sense of "not sinking" (*avasaṃsana*).
There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and doubling of the consonant.
Childhood, youth, and old age have been explained previously. Now he states the names derived from them. Among those, *addhaṃ* [is used] in the sense of "half.

From the root *puth*, meaning "to expand," with the suffix *uka*, we get *puthuko*. From *pal* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *ṇvu*, the vowel *i* is substituted, there is doubling of the consonant, and thus *pillako*.

*Chupa* means "to touch" (*samphasse*); *ussāttaṃ* means "a young animal" (*chāpo*). *Kumāra* is used in the sense of "playing" (*kīḷāyaṃ*); *kumāro* means "a boy. *Bala* is used in the sense of "living being" (*pāṇane*);

with the suffix *-ṇo*, it becomes *bālo*. *Pū* is used in the sense of "blowing" (*pavane*); with the suffix *-to*, it becomes *pūto*. With the suffix *-ko* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), it becomes *potako*; in the feminine (*itthiyaṃ*), it is *potakī*.
*Poto*, *sāvo*, *sāvako*, *abbhako*, *ḍimbho*, *susuko*, *susu*, and so forth, are also synonyms for *chāpa* (a young animal).
252. Having shown terms that denote a child in general, he says "atha," etc., to show specific names for children.
One who lies on his back, or lies supine, is *uttānasaya*. With the suffix *kap*, it becomes *uttānaseyyaka*. One who drinks from the breast is *thanapa*; the word *ḍimbha* is also used here. 253.
A group of seven [terms] refers to a youth (*taruṇa*).
A fool remains such until sixteen years of age;
thereafter he becomes young;
and at seventy years of age, he becomes old.

One should observe the three stages of life (*vaya*). From the root *tṛ* (to cross), with the suffix *uṇ*. One who stands in the stage of youth is called *vayaṭṭha*; thus [it is formed]. Regarding this, the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.42) and *Rudda* state:

"The word *vaya* refers to childhood and so forth, as well as birds; however, in some cases, *vaya* means youth. From the root *dah* (to reduce to ashes), with the suffix *aro*. From the root *yu* (to mix).
*Sa* is a substitute for *a*, having the form of a student (*sissa*). *Sa* occurs in the sense of leaping; *u* is a suffix that does not elide its vowel.

*Susu* is the substitute for *su* when it means "young" or "one who has just begun" (*pāṭipadika*). The offspring of a *manu* is a *mānava*; there is a modification of the phoneme (*vaṇṇavikāra*), and *na* becomes *ṇa*, thus *māṇava*.
With the suffix *ka* added in the sense of contempt, *māṇavaka* is established. And it is said:
“*Apacce kucchite mūḷhe, manutossaggiko mato*” (Mhv 4.1.161). [The root] *dara* means to split; with the suffix *ṇvu*, [it forms *daraka*].

There are two terms for a boy who has been raised in comfort: *sukumāra*—a pleasant (*sukha*) boy—and *sukhedhita*. [In *sukhedhita*,] there is the elision of the suffix *kha*. He grows or increases easily (*sukhena*), thus he is *sukhedhita*. There is also the reading *sukhocita*; it is *sukhocita* because comfort (*sukha*) is gathered or accumulated (*ucita*) therein, from the root *uca* meaning to collect.
254–255. Synonyms for one who has grown old by means of two feet: *mahallaka*. He takes (*lāti*) great age (*mahatta*), thus *mahallaka*; with the suffix *ṇvu*, there is reduplication (*dvitta*).
*Vaḍḍha*: from the root *vaḍḍh* (to increase), with the suffix *to*; its *ḍha* becomes *ḍha*, and the *ḍha* becomes *ḍa*. The vowel *a* is elided; *dhā* (in the sense of moving or returning);

the suffix *iro*; the *dha* becomes *tha*; and the *i* becomes *e*. Thus: *vaḍḍha*. *Jara*: in the sense of the decline of age, with the suffix *to*; its replacement by *in*, the elision of the final portion of the root, and the substitution of *ṇa* for *n*.

Thus: *jiṇṇa*. With the suffix *ka* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), it becomes *jiṇṇaka*. One whose natural age (*pakataṃ vaya*) or youth has passed is called *pavayā*; this is also a name for an elder (*vuḍḍha*).

The names [ending in] *-ant* are declined with the *pād*-case suffixes. Therein, the triplet [of terms] refers to the elder brother (*jeṭṭhabhātari*). One who is born first (*agge*), earlier (*pure*), or at an earlier time (*pubbe*) is called *aggaja* (born first) and *pubbaja* (born earlier).
This one is old, this one is old, and this one is especially old among these; thus he is the *jeṭṭha* (eldest). From the word *vuḍḍha*, the suffix *iṭṭha* is applied.

According to the rule “*vuḍḍhassa jo iyiṭṭhesu*” (the *j* of *vuḍḍha* is substituted [for *ḍh*] before *i* and *iṭṭha*), the *j* replaces *vuḍḍha*. When there is no elision (*alopa*), the following vowel becomes long (*parassāsavaṇṇattaṃ*).
The triad [of terms] refers to a younger brother born later. This one is young and this one is young; because this one is especially young among these, he is the *kaniṭṭha*.
[The forms] *kaniyo*, *kaṇiṭṭho*, and *kaṇiyo* occur. Among those ending in *-iṭṭha*, there is a substitution of *kan-* for the word *yuvan* and a substitution of *kaṇ-* [for *yuvan*].
Born at a later time is *anuja*. Born at a subsequent time is *jaghaññajo*. In the latter, subsequent time...
"Jāto aparajoti dvepyatra" (two [words] are used here).

"Vali sithilaṃ taco cammaṃ yassa valittaco" means "one whose skin and hide are wrinkled is 'valittaco'"; this is a dvanda compound. Alternatively, "valino" means "one who has wrinkles as his hide," using the suffix *-ina*.
Since words beginning with *uttānasaya* and ending with *valina* are adjectival in gender (*vāccaliṅga*), they function in all three genders, just like *uttānasaya*.
A child, a girl lying on her back, a neuter person lying on his back.

(256) The group of five [is placed] at the head. *Si* means "he lies down"; *so* is the nominative; and it is long. Because it is the most excellent among the limbs (*aṅga*), it is called the "supreme limb" (*uttamaṅga*);

alternatively, because it is both supreme and a limb, it is also called the "supreme limb. Both "head" (*sīsa*) and "supreme limb" (*uttamaṅga*) together form the compound "head and supreme limb" (*sīsottamaṅgāni*). *Si* here signifies service (*sevā*); *ro* is the vocative.

It is called *sira* because one serves (*sevanti*) by means of it. *Muda* means joy or satisfaction; the suffix *dho* is applied. It is a form of address. *Masa* is used in the sense of touching, with the suffix *ttha*; the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity, or *masi* is used in the sense of measure. It refers to the hair on the head.

It is called *kesa* because it lies (*seti*) or stands (*tiṭṭhati*) upon the head (*matthaka*); there is an elision of the locative case ending. *Kati* is used in the sense of cutting, with the suffix *alo*.

It is *assutta* (unstrung). From the root *vala*, meaning "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of an object, we have *vālo*. That which grows on the head, the highest limb (*uttamaṅga*), is *uttamaṅgaruho*. That which is born on the crown of the head (*muddha*) is *muddhajo*.
The compound *vālo ca uttamaṅgaruho ca muddhajo ca* is a *itarītarayoga-dvanda* (mutual conjunction) of two terms. *Cikuro* and *kaco* are also used here. [The roots are:

*ci* in the sense of "accumulating" (*cayane*), *kura* in the sense of "sound" (*sadde*), and because it has multiple meanings, [the root] *chid* in the sense of "cutting. It is called *cikurīyate* because it grows thickly.
*Cikura* means hair; *kaca-bandhana*, [Aṭṭhakathā] 257.
Hair with flowers inside, hair tied up with pearls and so forth on the outside and arranged [into a shape], is called a *dhammilla*.

It is called a *dhammilla* because it is held and bound together on one side; the suffix *-ila* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). By way of custom (*dhammena*), [it refers to] the people of various regions.
Or, it is called *dhammila* because it is adorned (*ilatī*) by its arrangement; the root *ila* means "to go.
Some say there are two types among the five topknots of youths, namely the three small ones (*cūḷattaya*). It is called *kākapakkha* because its shape resembles the wing of a crow.
*Sikhaṇḍaka* is simply *sikhā* with the suffix *-ka* added for emphasis. For precisely because the words *sikhā* and *sikhaṇḍa* are synonymous, one speaks of a "crested one" (*sikhaṇḍī*).
"Śikhī" refers to a peacock.

Both "pāsa" (tress) and "hasta" (hand)—these two—occur following the term *kesa* (hair) as part of a compound expression for a mass of hair (*kesapariyāya*), and not as standalone terms, such as in "a tress of hair" (*kesapāsa*) or "a hand of hair" (*kesahasta*).
[The root] *pā* is used in the sense of protecting; thus, *pāti* means it protects or encompasses.

*Pāsa*: some say it means "to bind" (*pasa bandhaneti*), but that is not correct. *Hana* is in the sense of "going"; that wherein the limbs (*avayava*) are bent down (*nihananti*) is called *hattha*, with the suffix *-tha*;

*pakka* is also used here. Regarding the matted hair (*kesacaya*) of ascetics (*tāpasānaṃ vatīnaṃ*), the word *jaṭā* is used there; *jaṭa* is in the sense of "twisting" (*jaṭane*) or "interlacing" (*saṅghāte*). According to Aṭṭhakathā 258: "In the feminine, it takes the suffix *-ati* or *-ava*.

That which is bound by food for the journey (*positabhatta*) and so forth is *veṇī* and *paveṇī*. *Vī* is in the sense of "procreation" (*pajane*); procreation is the release of the embryo (*gabbhavimokkho*); or *vī* is in the sense of "weaving a thread" (*tantasantāne*), with the suffix *-ṇī*. In the alternative sense, it is *paveṇī*.
The pair [of terms] refers to the crest situated in the middle of the head. *Cūḷā* is used in the sense of inciting (*sañcodana*) or making a gesture of contempt (*hāvakaraṇa*).

*Sikhā* has already been mentioned. *Kesapāsī* (the braid of hair) is included here under the *nada*-group. Among women, the straight path in the middle of the hair is considered and called *sīmanta*. It is *sīmanta* because it is within the boundary (*sīma*), or because the boundary lies there;

the letter *m* is inserted in the middle. 259. The triad refers to body hair (*loma*). From the root *lū* (to cut), that which grows continuously is cut away, thus it is *loma*; the suffix *ma* is added. That which grows on the body is *tanuruha*.
*a.* From the root *ruha* in the sense of "growing" or *rūha* in the sense of "manifesting," with the suffix *mo*, there is elision of *ha* and the substitution of *o*;

from *lū* in the sense of "cutting," with the suffix *mo*, there is the substitution of *ra* for *la*: thus, *roma*. Hair grown on the eye is called *pamha* and *pakhuma*. It is *pamha* because one measures (*paminoti*) by means of it;

the prefix *pa-* is used in the sense of measuring, with the suffix *ha*. That which is grown on both eyelids of the eye is *pakhuma*; [from *pakhu* with] the suffix *uma* and the elision of the consonant cluster.

The hair (*loma*) that has grown or emerged on the face of men—that is, on the mouth—is called *massu*. [The root] *mas* means "to touch"; with the suffix *su*, it becomes *massu*. There is a triad for the eyebrow.

[The root] *bham* means "to be unstable"; with the suffix *ū*, there is the elision of *m*, resulting in *bhū*. With the suffix *um*, it becomes *bhamu*; with the suffix *kap*, it becomes *bhamuka*. Because it is associated with *bhamuka*, *bhamu* is used in the masculine gender. 260. There is a triad for the tears of the eyes. [The root] *khip* means "to cast";

with the suffix *po*, there is the substitution of *issatta*. Water produced in the eyes is *nettajala*. [The root] *as* means "to fall downward"; with the suffix *su*, it becomes *assu*. *Nettajala* and *assu* form a *dvanda* compound. *Assu* is neuter.

There are two [meanings] for *akkhiputtalikā* (the pupil of the eye). When the star (*tārā*) is seen in the eye, it is called *nettatārā*. From the word *kaññā*, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *ap* is applied;

the word *kaññā* undergoes the substitution of *kanīna*; and according to Kātanta 2.2.65—"when followed by a feminine suffix beginning with *t* or *k*, the preceding vowel *a* becomes *i*"—it becomes *kanīnikā*.
The word *tārakā* is also used here.
The word *chakkaṃ* [is derived from] *mukhavivare*; however, poets apply it even to a collective term characterized by that.

The root *vada* means "distinct speech," with the suffix *yu* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). The root *mu* means "binding"; the absence of the vowel *o* is due to a grammatical rule (*nipātanā*), thus forming *mukhaṃ*.

According to those who follow the *Sabbadharakata* school, however, *mukhaṃ* is a conventional term (*nipātita*) based on the root *khan*, as in "it is dug out" (*khaññati*); the root *khanu* means "digging. The root *tuḍi* means "tearing apart," with the suffix *a*; the root *tanu*...

Or, in detail: *ḍo* is without a suffix (*assutta*). It is called *vattaṃ* because one speaks by means of it (*tena vadati*), or it is called *vattaṃ* because it is spoken by means of it (*anena vuccate*).

[The root] *vada* is used in the sense of distinct speech; the suffix *to* is added. [The root] *lapa* is used in the sense of speaking; the suffix *yu* is added in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*). It is called *ānanaṃ* because breathing (*āna*) exists by means of it; [the root] *ana* is used in the sense of living; the suffix *yu* is added. *Assaṃ* is also used here.
[The root] *asa* is used in the sense of eating; the suffix *so* is added in the instrumental sense.
261. *Aḍḍhaṃ* means "half. One who is born twice in two places is a *dvija*. One who is born in the mouth (*lapana*) is *lapanaja*. Regarding *danta*:

from the root *dā* in the sense of "cutting," one cuts food with it, thus *danta*; the suffix *-anta* is added, or alternatively, from *das* in the sense of "eating," they eat food with it, thus *danta*;
the final vowel of the root is elided. Or, from *dam* in the sense of "taming," the suffix *-ta* is added. From *daṃs* in the sense of "biting," *daṃsate*.
It is called *daṃsana* because it bites (*vilikhyate*); from the root *yu*, with the suffix *ran*, it becomes *rada*. From the root *rad* (to bite), with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *radana*.

The word *dāṭhā* refers to a specific type of tooth, a division of teeth; it is feminine in gender. From the verbal root *daṃs*, the suffix *ṭha* is applied, and for *daṃsin*, the substitution *dā* occurs, resulting in *dāṭhā*;
this is a term where the letter *ja* follows *muddha*. The term *apāṅga* applies to the outer corners of the left and right eyes, at the ends of the sockets.
*Apāṅga* means near (*apa*) to the ear (*aṅga*), which is reckoned as the body.

262. The group of four [terms] refers to the lip (*oṭṭha*). It is called *dantāvaraṇa* because it covers or conceals the teeth (*danta*). Regarding the word *oṭṭha*: from the root *usa* (to burn), with the suffix *ṭha*—according to the rule "after *sa*, *da*, *sa*, *ta*, *pu*, *cha*, *bha*, *ja*, *haṃsa*, etc., there is *ṭha"—and with the consonants *sa* and so forth, we have *ṭṭha*.
Thus, by the doubling of the *t* and *ṭh*, we get *oṭṭha*. This term also applies to a donkey. Alternatively, from the root *usa* (to burn) [the same derivation follows].
*Ṭṭha*, *ottaddhitta*, etc.; in both cases, *muddhaja* is the companion [term]. *Adhara* means that food is held (*dhāreti*) here for a short while (*īsaṃ kiñci kālaṃ*);
for here the letter *a* has the sense of "slight" (*īsattha*).
"In the masculine, it should be known as [the month] Mādhava..."
“That indeclinable [‘na’] is used in the sense of negation,
in the sense of slightness, in the sense of opposition,
and in the sense of similarity, according to its application.”
This is stated in the *Ekakkharakosa*. It is called *dasanacchada* because it covers (*chādayati*) the teeth (*dantā*) when they are bared (*dasane*).

Here, some say that by the word *adhara* only the lower lip is meant; however, their statement should not be accepted, as it does not accord with the usage of the great poets (*mahākavi*) in such passages as "with the pair consisting of the eyes, the lower lip, the hands, and the feet."

*Tikaṃ* means "on the cheek. *Gaḍi* refers to a part of the face; [the suffix] *-a* is used here because the statement in the *Dhātupāṭha* concerns the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātu*), and this applies everywhere in that manner.

Why is it called *kapola*? Because it is filled (*pūriyate*) with water (*jala*), thus *kapola*; [the suffix] *-alo*. Or, from the root *kapa* in the sense of covering (*acchādane*), [with the suffix] *-olo*, thus *kapolo*, belonging to the *nada*-class.

*Gaṇḍī*. The lower part below is called the chin (*cubuka*); *cibuka* is also used here. From the root *cibu* in the sense of hanging down (*olambake*), [with the suffix] *-ṇvu*; the vowel *a* is elided.

263. Two [terms] for the front part of the neck: *gala* and *kaṇṭha*. *Gala*: from the root *gad*, meaning "to eat," with the suffix *a*; or from *gil*, meaning "to swallow. It is called *gala* because one swallows by means of it; it signifies the throat. *Kaṇṭha*: the root *kaṇ* has the sense of sound; it is a *daṇḍaka* root.

With the suffix *ṭha*, it becomes *kaṇṭha*. This [term] has the letter *d* as its second [consonant]. These three [terms—*gala*, *kaṇṭha*, and *kaṇṭha*—] have the same meaning. *Kandharā*: from the root *gā*, meaning "sound," with the suffix *īva*. It is called *kandharā* because it bears (*dharati*) the head (*kaṃ*). *Sirodharā*: it is called *sirodharā* because it bears the head (*siraṃ dharati*). Or alternatively, *sirodharā* refers to those things upon which the head is placed (*dhīyate*).

From the root *dhā*, in the sense of "stopping motion" (*gatinivatti*), with the suffix *ara*. *Kambugīvā*: a golden *āliṅga* is a type of drum (*muraja*); that neck which resembles or is similar to that is considered *kambugīvā*.

This is a mark of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*). Alternatively, that neck which is marked and characterized by three lines is considered a "conch-like neck" (*kambugīvā*), and this too is a mark of a Great Man.
"Conch" (*kambu*) means gold; a neck resembling a collar made of conch is a "conch-like neck. [The root] *kamb* means to cover; with the suffix *u*, it becomes *kambu*.
264. A triplet on the aggregates (*khandha*). In the sense of "going," *ana*. The head of the arms is *bhujasira*. That which bears the head (*kaṃ*) is a shoulder (*kandho*);
by the substitution of the letter *kha* for the letter *ka*, it becomes *khandho*. Alternatively, it is called *khandho* because it "bears" (*khamati*) the burden;
from the root *khamu* (to endure/bear), with the suffix *to*, and *dha* substituted for *ta*, and *na* for *ma*, or [the nasal] is elided. Its connection is its...
*Jattu*: that which is called the middle of the trunk (*khandha*), which stands in the midst of the trunks. *Jan* means "to be born," and *jar* means "decay of age";
thus *jattu* is neuter. *Dvayaṃ bāhumūle*: the two [terms] refer to the base of the arms.

The base of the arms—that is, of the *bāhu*s or *bhujā*s—is *bāhumūla*. *Kaca* means "binding" (with the suffix *-cho*). The lower part of this *kaccha* is called *passa*. *Disa* means "to look"; with the suffix *-ap*, there is a substitution of *passa* for *disa*.
265. A triplet on *bāhu* (arm). That by which one carries is *vāhu*; *vāhu* itself becomes *bāhu* [by the rule] *ku-ṇv-ādi* (Pāṇini 7.3.59).

That by which one enjoys is *bhujo*. The root *bhuj* is used in the senses of protecting and eating. *Bāhu* and *bhujo* form a *dvanda* compound; these two [words] are in the dual number, and in the feminine they become *bhujā*.
That which carries or moves is *bāhā*. Here too, the suffix *apara* occurs; here too, the suffix *pāra* occurs (according to Ka.); here too, the suffix *paveṭṭha* occurs (?).

*Tikaṃ* (the triad) refers to the hand. *Hasa* is in the sense of laughing (*hasane*), with the suffix *tho*. *Hara* is in the sense of taking away (*haraṇe*) or alternatively, it means a constellation (*nakkhatte*). *Kara* is in the sense of doing (*karaṇe*), with the suffix *a*. *Paṇa* is in the senses of trade (*byavahāra*) and praise (*thuti*), with the suffix *i*. *Pā* is in the sense of protecting (*rakkhane*), with the suffix *ṇi*. *Karapāṇayo* is a dual compound meaning both the hand (*karo*) and the arm (*pāṇi*).

*Pañcasākho* (five-fingered) is also used here for the same thing. *Pakoṭṭhanto* is the wrist-joint; it is called the *maṇibandho* (wrist). *Pakoṭṭho* is the part below the elbow (*kappara*) up to the wrist (*āmaṇibandhaṃ*). It is called *maṇibandho* because gems (*maṇi*) are bound (*bandhati*) there. *Kusa* is in the sense of reviling (*akkose*), with the suffix *ṭho*; thus, *pakoṭṭho*.

The term *dvayaṃ* (a pair) refers to the two parts at the middle joint of the arm. The root *kapu* means "to injure" (*hiṃsā*), with the suffix *-aro*. There is also a reading *kupparo*; in that case, there is no vowel *u*. The root *kapu* means "to injure," with the suffixes *-oṇi* and *-i*, forming *kapoṇi*, which denotes a woman.

*Kaphoṇī* is also used here; see the word *phattaṃ* in that context. 266. The external space between the two—the wrist (*maṇibandha*) and the little finger (*kaniṭṭha*)—which belongs to the hand (*pāṇi*) and the palm (*pāṇitala*), is called *karabha*.
It is that by which children, having fashioned weapons, strike one another. The root *kara* means "to injure."

*Abho* means "hand" or "the act of doing. There are two [types] when referring to the mere finger. *Kara* and *pāṇi* mean hand; *karasākhā* means a branch of the hand. *Agi* has the sense of motion (*gati*), or *aṅga* has the sense of motion, and *uli*. This is a feminine noun (belonging to the *nadādi* class), thus:

*aṅguli*. These fingers are of five varieties, namely: the thumb (*aṅguṭṭha*), the forefinger (*tajjanī*), the middle finger (*majjhimā*), the ring finger (*anāmikā*), and the little finger (*kaniṭṭhā*).
They may be [derived] from *ka*. *Aṅga* has the sense of "going. Alternatively, it is called *aṅguṭṭha* because it stands at the tip (*agge*) or in front (*pure*);

there is the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta* and the elision of the vowel *a*. *Tajja* is in the sense of harming; that by which one threatens is *tajjanī*; [the suffix] *yu* is added, belonging to the *nadādi* class.

It stands in the middle, thus it is *majjhimā*. There is no name for it, thus it is *anāmikā*; the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). They are exceedingly small, thus they are *kaniṭṭhā*.
The suffixes *kana* or *kaṇa* are used after the root *iyiṭṭha*. 267.

When the thumb (*aṅguṭṭha*) is joined with *tajjanya* and so forth, and is extended (*tata*) or stretched out (*pasārita*), four designations (*saññā*) beginning with *padesa* occur in sequence, as follows:
when the thumb is joined with *tajjanya* and extended, it is *padesa*. [The root] *disa* means "to look. When the thumb is joined with *majjhima*...

*Tate* means extended; *talapatiṭṭhāyaṃ* means resting on the palm. When the thumb is joined with the ring finger, it is *gokaṇṇo*: either because it resembles an ox’s ear (*gokaṇṇa*), or because it is the measure of an ox’s ear;
or else, there is a certain specific animal called an *okapiṇḍaka* (ox-eared deer), and because its ear-like measure resembles that [of the hand-span], it is called *gokaṇṇo*.
*Tālo* and *gokaṇṇo* together are *tālagokaṇṇā*. Due to the difference in gender, it was not stated as "*tālagokaṇṇavidatthī*."

When the little finger and the thumb are extended, it is a *vidatthi*. It is called *vitatthi* because one stretches (*vitanoti*); *vitatthi* itself is *vidatthi*, as the root *tanu* means "to extend," and its *tha* is substituted for *ta*.
*Vidatthi*. There is also a reading: "From that, [the cubit] by measure.

The hand, when bent and contracted, is called a *pasata*; the prefix *pa-* is used with the root *sara* meaning "to go," with the suffix *-to*. Because this is a section on measurements, this refers specifically to the *vitatañjali* (the outstretched palms).
This is desired by poets: "The hands with palms joined in añjali, whose fingers are extended and well-aligned because they are extended and well-aligned;
and when the thumb is bent, it is considered 'with banners' (sapatāka)."
With hands like banners, the añjali joined together is desired.
It was desired by deities, elders, and parents in former times;
the distinctions [of its types] should be understood here and there from the *Atthappakaraṇa* and other works.

Just as one gives a handful of water (*jalañjali*), or drinks with the hollowed palms (*añjalinā*), or as it is said, "this deity has joined his palms" (*katañjali*). Alternatively, since the *puṭañjali* (folded palms) will be explained later, here it refers specifically to the *vitatañjali* (outstretched palms).

268. The triad [of terms] refers to a snake’s hood with outstretched hands. From the root *ramu* (in the sense of playing), with the suffix *tano*, there is elision of the *malo* (the nasal), resulting in *ratana*;

it also refers to gems, Buddhas, and so forth. From the root *kuka* (in the sense of taking), with the suffix *u*, there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*), resulting in *kukku*. From the root *hasa*, with the suffix *tho* or *to*, we have *hattha*; or, because it is accompanied by a hand (*hattha*), the snake’s hood (*pakoṭṭha*) is called a "hand."

The pair *sampuṭa* and *añjali* refer to the hollowed palms. *Karapuṭa* means a fold or cavity made of the hands; *añja* is used in the senses of distinction, movement, and beauty; *ali* is a synonym for *añjali*. Thus, *karapuṭa* and *añjali* together form the compound *karapuṭañjali*.

The pair [of terms] refers to the fingernail. It is called *karaja* because it is born or grows on the hand (*kare*). It is called *nakha* because there is no sense-faculty (*kha*) therein; this is due to its being a conventional term (*saññā-sadda*), or because it is not a domain of the senses (*avisayatta*). Furthermore, *punabbhava*, *kararuha*, and *nakharo* are also names for the fingernail.

The word *dvayaṃ* refers to what is known as the two fingers held together in a fist (*puṭaṅgulika*). [The root] *khaṭ* means desire; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *khada*, or from *khaḍ* meaning injury, the *d* is replaced by *ṭ*. [The root] *mu* means binding;

with the suffix *ti*, its *u* is replaced by *ṭh*, and there is doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ*). 269. *Byāma* is the name for the two arms, including the hands, when they are extended across the two shoulders—that is, stretched out.

It is called *byāma* because one is measured (*byāmīyate*) by it. It is derived from the prefix *vi-* and the root *yāma* (to stretch). *Uddhaṃ* means above; *tatā* means stretched out; thus, the arms are stretched upward.

And the person (*pōso*) is that which has a measurement equal to the measurement of those [limbs] taken together; the term *porisa* applies to that [height] measured by an uplifted arm and a forearm (*uddhantatabhuja-posappamāṇe*). By the word *bhuja*, both the upper arm (*sahakara*) and the forearm (*bhujā*) are included, with the elision of one of the two words for "measurement" (*pamāṇa*). The measure of a man (*purisa*) is *porisa*. And here, the word *purisa* refers to a man together with his own arms. As in the three [verses], for example:

*Porisam piṭṭhito katvā, porisam ubhato kare;* *Porisam ubhato hatthe, porisam ubhato pāde;* *Porisam ubhato akkhi, porisam ubhato kaṇṇe;* *Porisam ubhato nāsam, porisam ubhato dante;* *Porisam ubhato bhamu, porisam ubhato ūru;* *Porisam ubhato jaṅgham, porisam ubhato aṅguṭṭhe;* *Porisam ubhato kese, porisam ubhato sīse;* *Porisam ubhato hadayam, porisam ubhato udaram;* *Porisam ubhato pāṇim, porisam ubhato pādam;* *Porisam ubhato akkhikūṭam, porisam ubhato kaṇṇacūḷikam;* *Porisam ubhato nāsikaggaṃ, porisam ubhato dantamūlam;* *Porisam ubhato bhamukantaram, porisam ubhato ūrukūṭam;* *Porisam ubhato jaṅghamūlam, porisam ubhato aṅguṭṭhapabbam;* *Porisam ubhato kesantam, porisam ubhato sīsantam;* *Porisam ubhato hadayantaram, porisam ubhato udarantaram;* *Porisam ubhato pāṇimūlam, porisam ubhato pādantam;* *Porisam ubhato akkhikūṭantaram, porisam ubhato kaṇṇacūḷikantaram;* *Porisam ubhato nāsikaggantaram, porisam ubhato dantamūlantaram;* *Porisam ubhato bhamukantantarantaram, porisam ubhato ūrukūṭantaram;* *Porisam ubhato jaṅghamūlantaram, porisam ubhato aṅguṭṭhapabbantaram;* *Porisam ubhato kesantantaram, porisam ubhato sīsantantaram;* *Porisam ubhato hadayantantarantaram, porisam ubhato udarantantarantaram;* *Porisam ubhato pāṇimūlantaram, porisam ubhato pādantantaram.* [The Buddha said: "He who stands a man's height behind, a man's height on both sides, a man's height with both hands, a man's height with both feet; a man's height with both eye-sockets, a man's height with both ears; a man's height with both nostrils, a man's height with both teeth; a man's height with both eyebrows, a man's height with both thighs;

a man's height with both shanks, a man's height with both big toes; a man's height with both hair-tips, a man's height with both head-tips; a man's height with both heart-regions, a man's height with both belly-regions; a man's height with both hand-roots, a man's height with both foot-ends; a man's height with both eye-socket-ends, a man's height with both ear-lobes; a man's height with both nose-tips, a man's height with both tooth-roots; a man's height with both eyebrow-interiors, a man's height with both thigh-tops; a man's height with both shank-roots, a man's height with both big-toe-joints; a man's height with both hair-end-interiors, a man's height with both head-end-interiors; a man's height with both heart-interior-regions, a man's height with both belly-interior-regions; a man's height with both hand-root-interiors, a man's height with both foot-end-interiors. In these three [verses], as follows:
— *porisaṃ jalaṃ*, *poriso hatthī*, *porisī yaṭṭhi*. 270. Two [words] for the chest (*urasi*).
From the root *usa* (to burn), with the suffix *ro* and the elision of the *salopa*, or from *ara* (in the sense of going) with the suffix *assukāra*.

From *hara* (in the sense of taking away), with the suffix *yo* and the substitution of *do* for the *ra*. *Koḷaṃ* (from *koṭṭha*), *bhujantaraṃ*, and *vakkho* are also names for the chest. Three [words] for the breast (*uroje*). From *tanu*...
In detail: *tanoti* (it stretches) and they desire it, thus *thana*; its [root] is *tha*. *Thana* is used in the sense of a divine being (*devasadda*) or in the sense of theft (*coriya*).
*Kuca* means contraction; thus, *kuca*. That which bears milk (*payo*) is a *payodhara*. "The *kuca* and the *payodhara*" is a *dvanda* compound.
At the tip of the breast, at the very top of the breast, is the *cūcuka*, in the neuter gender. "The *cūcuka* is the face of the breasts," according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.

16.77 *Ratanakoso*: [The following words undergo specific changes: *cu*, *cavane*, *uko*, *dvittaṃ*, *dīgho ca*, *cūcukaṃ*, *cancu* in the sense of "going" (*gatiyaṃ*), *uko*, elision of *na* (*nalopo*), and the substitution of *assūkāro*.

Thus, *cūcukaṃ*. *Dvayaṃ* refers to the two parts at the back of the body (*kāyassa pacchābhāge*). [The root] *piṭ* is used in the sense of "piling up" (*saṅghātesu*) with the suffix *to*. In the other case, it is from *pisu* in the sense of "moistening" (*secane*).

271. *Tikaṃ* (the triad) refers to the middle part of the body. That which exists in the middle is *majjha*. From the root *lag* (to cling), with the suffix *a*, we have *majjha*; that which exists in the middle is *majjhima*. *Catukkaṃ* (the tetrad) refers to the belly (*udara*).

From the root *kus* (to revile), with the suffixes *chi* and *sa* changed to *co*, we derive [the term for the digestive fire]. From the root *gah* (to seize), with the suffixes *ani* and *īm*, we have *gahaṇī*.

Alternatively, it is called *gahaṇī* because it seizes—that is, it holds—the fetus. It is the region within the mother’s womb known as the seat of the fetus; however, in the context of the element of heat (*tejodhātu*), it refers to the digestive fire.

It is called *gahaṇī* because it receives food according to how it has been eaten by means of digesting it, and because it does not discard it. The prefix *ud-* is used in the sense of moving upward (*dara-gamane*).
It is *udara* because wind moves upward (*uddhaṃ gacchati*) within it. The root *gu* is used in the sense of sound; with the suffix *-abha*, and by doubling the consonants, etc., it becomes *gabbha*.
*Picaṇḍa*, *jaṭhara*, and *tunda* are also used in this sense.

In the sense of "arising in the womb" (*kucchisambhave*) and "situated in the womb" (*kucchiṭṭhe*), the two terms *koṭṭha* and *anta* are used. From the root *kusa* in the sense of "reviling," the suffixes *to* or *ṭho* are applied. The root *ama* has the meaning of "going"; the suffix *to* is added. 272.

Regarding the fourfold group beginning with *kaṭi*: from the verbal root *han*, the suffix *yu* is added; the *h* becomes double (*dvitta*); the *h* becomes *j*; and the *han* becomes *gha*, resulting in *jaghana*.

From the root *tam* with the prefix *ni*, in the sense of "it definitely transcends that," the suffix *bo* is added, forming *nitamba*. From the root *sū* in the sense of "procreation," the suffix *ṇi* is added. From the root *kaṭa* in the senses of "rain" and "covering," [the suffix *i* is added].
*Kaṭi* is so called because it is covered or clothed with garments and the like; the suffix *i* is added. These two [terms] refer to the female.

Here, it should be understood that by the word *jaghana*, the upper part of the female hip is meant; by the word *nitamba*, the posterior part of the female hip; and by the remaining two, the hip in its general sense is expressed. And it has been said:
"The *nitamba* is the rear of the female hip, while the *jaghana* is the front" (Amara-kośa 16.74).

273. *Liṅga* [is used] in the sense of gender. It is called *aṅgajāta* because it is born from a limb (*aṅga*), that is, from the body; the word *aṅga* here denotes the body, [the compound being formed] by taking it to mean "that which has this as its limb.
*Rahassaṅga* is a limb born in a secret place (*rahasi*); there is the elision of the locative case-ending, the substitution of *issa* for *aṅga*, and the doubling of the *s* in *issa*.
*Vatthaguyha* means that which is to be concealed by a cloth (*vatthena*). [The root] *miha* means to sprinkle; with the suffix *yu* in the instrumental sense, it becomes *mihayi*.

*Retomuttāni yenāti mehanam*: that by which urine and semen are discharged is the *mehana*. The root *miha*, preceded by the prefix *ni-*, means "to sprinkle"; *to* is a suffix indicating the instrumental case. It is a superior limb (*varaṅga*) because it is a principal part of the body.
*Vaja gatiyaṃ*, with the suffix *-assīkāra*, or because it arises without external conditions, it is called *bīja* (seed);

here the modification (*vikāra*) indicates its state of being devoid [of moisture]. *Phala nipphattiyaṃ*: it bears fruit (*phalati*) by means of this, namely a son; thus it is called *phala* (fruit). *Lingati “itthī, puriso”ti*: it characterizes [the body] as "woman" or "man."
It is called *liṅga* because it goes (*gacchati*) by means of it; or *liṅga* is that which moves (*gamane*), or that which is hidden (*līnaṃ*) and not manifest, or a limb (*aṅga*).
Among these, the words *bīja* and *phala* also apply to the testicles.

The two [words] refer to the male organ and the scrotum. From the root *ama* in the sense of moving, with the suffix *ḍo*; or the meaning of the word *aṇa*, with the suffix *ḍo*; or from *aḍi* in the sense of a testicle, with the suffix *ḍo*.
Regarding "to": *Kusa* means to revile; it does not [mean to praise]. Here, the word *aṇḍa* refers to a seed as well; furthermore, *aṇḍakosa* is the name for the sheath (*kosa*) taken as a compound.
For it is said in the *Pārājika* (13, 14): “from the egg-sheath (*aṇḍakosa*) of a hen’s chick,” and in the *Amarakośa* (16.76), the name *aṇḍakosa* is likewise stated as a compound.
And here, the analysis (*viggaha*) should be made as: the sheath (*kosa*) of the egg (*aṇḍa*), which is the seed (*bīja*), is the “egg-sheath” (*aṇḍakosa*).

The word *dvayaṃ* refers to the two organs of a woman. *Yu* [is used] in the sense of mixing (*missane*), in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), for the womb (*yoni*), and for both the female and the male; thus *itthipumaṃ* means "female and male," and [the term applies] therein. That which they resort to (*bhajanti*) is called *bhagaṃ*; here it refers to the abode of Māra (*māramandira*) and the pit of Māra (*mārakūpa*).

274–275. The triad [of terms] pertains to the origin (*sambhave*) of women and men. *Asuci* (impure) is the opposite of *suci* (pure); it ends in the vowel *i*, is used in the dual number, or has the gender of its source (*sambhavaliṅga*).

From the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *a* is added. *Saka* means "one's own power" (*sāmatthiya*); [from this] the suffix *to* is added, and for that [suffix], *ko* is substituted. [In the case of] *asu*, *so* is substituted, or *ko* is substituted for *su* in the sense of sorrow (*soke*).

Two [terms] for the path of excrement (*vaccamagga*). It is called *pāyu* because one purifies by means of it; from the root *pū*, meaning "to purify," with the suffix *u* (which is a substitute for *ūsāya*), or alternatively, from the root *pay*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *u*—it is *pāyu* because one goes to excrement by means of it. This word is used in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*) when referring to a person. *Guda* is used in the sense of play (*kīḷā*). *Apāna* is also used here. Eight [terms] for excrement (*vacca*).
From the root *gūtha*, meaning "to discharge," or from *gup*, meaning "to protect," with the suffix *tha*. From the root *kira*, meaning "to scatter," with the suffix *īsa*, we have *karīsa*.

From the roots *vara* and *varaṇa*, meaning "obstruction" or "collection," with the suffix *ca*, we have *varca*. The compound *gūtha-karīsa-vacca* is a copulative compound (*dvanda*); these are used optionally.
They occur in the masculine; they are always neuter, though their masculine gender occurs only in some instances, while their neuter gender applies everywhere—this is the general sense.
*Mala* means "to move" (with the suffix *a*), or "to hold. *Saka* means "power"; [here] *sa* becomes *cha*. That which is uttered or abandoned is *uccāra*;
the root *car* preceded by *upa* signifies "abandoning" and also "lifting up. *Miha* means "to sprinkle"; [the suffix] *lo*.

The reversal of the vowel-color (*vaṇṇa*) and the state of *ḷ*. "It is scattered" (*avakarīyati*): the syllable *uk* [is added], with the obligatory suffix (*avassutta*); it is said (*kira*) that [the root] is in the sense of dispersing. "It is smeared" (*samalaṃpyatra*). The root *samu* is in the sense of pacifying; the suffix *alo*. Two [forms] occur in the sense of releasing.

*Su* is in the sense of hearing; hearing is flowing; it belongs to the *cur*-class, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Muca* is in the sense of releasing; the suffix *to*; or *mutta* is in the sense of urination. It is called (*uccate*), i.e., it is spoken of.
In the compound *gomutte*, the word *pūtimutta* (stale urine) is used in the sense of urine belonging to cows (*gavaṃ sambandhini mutte*). Today (*ajja*).

For even when it is functioning, it is called "putrid urine" (pūtimutta) because of its foul odor, just as one says "putrid body" (pūtikāya). The word *chakaṇa* refers to the excrement of horses and the like;
[the suffix] *yu* is added after the root *sak*, and the *s* is changed to *ch*.
276. The lower part of the navel is called the *vatthi*; it has two parts. *Vatthi* is the bladder (*muttapuṭa*). As it is said: "The *vatthi* is the bladder that holds the urine."
*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 16.73: *Ratnamālā*. It is called *vatthi* because "it dwells (*vasati*) here"; from the root *vas* (to dwell), with the suffix *-tha*, or it is established by the suffix *-tthi*.
Both these two words, *ucchaṅga* and *aṅka*, are used in the masculine gender. It is called *ucchaṅga* because "one rests (*ussajjati*) upon it";
from the root *saj* (to cling/attach), with the substitution of *ch* for *s*, and doubling of the consonant. The root *aṅk* has the sense of "going. *A*.
*Aṅka*: Alternatively, *aṅka* means a mark (*lakkhaṇa*). According to the *Amarakośa*, "in the sense of the lap or a sign, it is *aṅka*" (Amara 23.4).

This pair refers to the region above the knees. *Ara*: in the sense of going (*gamana*), with the suffix *u*. The vowel *a* is elided. *Satthi*: from the root *sañj* in the sense of clinging (*saṅga*); that which clings to the cloth is *satthi*, with the suffix *thi*. *Ūrusatthi*:

a copulative compound (*dvanda*) consisting of *ūru* and *satthi*; it may also be used as a neuter. *Jaṇṇu*: this triad refers to the knee. From the root *jan* in the sense of being born (*janana*), with the suffix *ṇu*. When doubled, it becomes *jaṇṇu*.

277. There are two terms for the ankle (*pādagaṇṭhi*). The root *gup* (meaning "to protect") is masculine; with the suffix *ka* used in the sense of identity, we have *goppha*. The "knot of the foot" (*pādassa gaṇṭhi*) is *pādagaṇṭhi*. *Ghuṭikā* is also used here. From the root *ghuṭ* (meaning "to turn"), *ghuṭikā* is derived by adding the suffix *ṇvu* in the sense that "by this it is turned.

There are two terms for the hind part of the foot, the portion below the ankle. The word ending in *-tu* is a masculine noun. From the root *pas* (meaning "to press" or "to touch"), the suffix *ti* is applied;
its *t* becomes *ṇ*, the *s* becomes *h*, there is a change of phonemes, or it is established by the addition of the suffix *ṇi*. Thus, *paṇhi* is formed.
With the addition of the letter *s* and the vowel increment (*vuddhi*), [the form] is *pāsaṇhi*. In the case of *ilipya*, from the root *ila* meaning "to go," there is the elision of the suffix *ta*.
The two [terms] refer to the tip of the foot. The tip of the foot is *pādagga*. It is a *kammadhāraya* compound:

the foot that has gone far (*pakattha*) is *papada*. There is also a reading of “*papado*. The three [terms] refer to the foot. From the root *pada* meaning "to go," with the suffix *ṇo*, it is *pādo*. Because one goes (*pajjate*) or moves, it is *pādo*. From the root *cara*.

The suffix *yu* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), forming *caraṇam*; this is optional in the masculine, but obligatory in the neuter. Here, in the sense of "foot" (*aṅghi*), the root *ahi* means "to go. The vowel *i* is substituted for *ha*, and *gho* is substituted for *has*.

278. There are two [forms] for a limb beginning with the hand (*hattha*). The root *aṅg* has the meaning of "going," with the suffix *a*. With the prefix *ava*, the suffix *yu* is applied in the sense of "mixing," with the suffix *a*. *Patiko* and *apaghano* are also used here. After the root *im* preceded by *pati*, the suffix *ko* is applied. After the root *han* preceded by *apa*, the suffix *a* is applied, and there is a substitution of *ghana*.

*Dvayaṃ passaṭṭhimhi*: *pā* in the sense of protecting (*rakkhaṇe*), with the augment *su*, the addition of the letter *ḷi*, the suffix *ko* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), and *passa* becomes *pho*. With the addition of *aḷ*, there is *phāsukā*. There is also a reading as *pāsuḷikā* and *pāsukā*. *Phusa* is a root in the sense of touching (*samphasse*); in that case, there are the prefixes and suffixes. *Dvayaṃ aṭṭhimatte*:
*asu* in the sense of throwing away (*khepane*), with the suffix *i*, and *sa* becoming *ṭṭha*, thus *aṭṭhi*;

this refers to the neuter (*paṇḍaka*) gender. *Dhā* in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇe*), with the suffix *tu*, thus *itthī*. *Kīkasaṃ* and *kullaṃ* are also used here. It is the bone produced at the lower end of the throat (*galassa kaṇṭhassa*).
*Galantaṭṭhi*. [The root] *ga* means "to go"; here, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*).
279–280. There are two [terms] for a fragment of a skull bone. When combined, however, it is *karoṭi*, feminine; [according to] Amara 16.69. [The root] *kapu* means "capability";

with the suffix *aro*, it is *kapparo*. Alternatively, it protects the head (*kaṃ*), hence *kapparo*; [the vowel] is shortened, and the *l* becomes *r*. It protects the head (*kaṃ*), thus [it is called *kapāla*]; [this applies] to the category beginning with *kamma*.
No. Regarding the statement, “*Sirotthimhi kapālo’tthī, ghaṭādisakalepice*,” from the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.68): the phrase “*kapālo’tthī*” means that it is not feminine (*anitthī*).
The word *kapāla* is optionally masculine (*pulliṅga*) by way of alternative usage. [The root] *kaḍi* means to cut (*chede*); the suffix *aro* is applied.
*Mahatī sirā* is *mahāsirā*; it is also called *sirā*. [The root] *si* means to bind (*bandhane*); the suffix *ro* is applied.

The triad concerning the "hollow-possessing" [vessels] refers to the vessels that carry the wind. For the vessels of the body are threefold: one carries the wind; another binds the bones like a thread;
and the other is known as the "intestinal," which carries food. Therein, the first is illustrated by the third [term], and the second by the first and second;

however, the third will be explained further on. *Naha* means binding (*bandhane*), with the suffix *aru*. *Si* means binding (*bandhane*), with the suffix *ro*. *Dhama* means sound (*sadde*), with the suffix *yu*.
*Nadādi*, *ani* or *dhamanī*. To show the third [term], he says "rasaggasā," etc.

It swallows (*gasati*) the essence (*rasa*), thus it is *rasaggasā*; the root *gas* means to eat. It carries (*harati*) or leads (*neti*) the essence, thus it is *rasaharaṇī*; with the suffix *yu*, it belongs to the *nadādi* class.

These three [terms] refer to muscle. *Mana* means to know; the suffix *so*. *Misa* means sound, or with the prefix *ā*, to touch. *Pisa* means a part, with the suffix *to*. *Palala* is also a poetic synonym (*kabba*) here.

The pair [of terms] refers to dried meat by means of heat (*ātapa*) and so forth. *Tiliṅgakantu* is a word ending in *-tu* where *liṅga* is the base. From the roots *vala* and *valla*, meaning "to cover," with the suffix *ūro*—which is *ā* when applied to the feminine according to the rule "the suffix *āp* occurs after the feminine"—we have *vallūrā*. *Uddhaṃ tattaṃ* means "heated thoroughly. From the root *tapa*, meaning "to heat," with the suffix *to*. 281. The group of four [terms] refers to blood (*lohita*). From the root *ruha*, meaning "to produce," with the suffix *to* or *ito*.

It is called *rudhiraṃ* because it flows (*runjhate*) through the skin; thus, *iro* is the suffix. From the root *soṇa*, meaning "color," with the suffix *to*. From the root *rañja*, meaning "to color," with the suffix *to*. *Asaṃ* means "born from a wound" (*khataja*); here, it is said that "thought (*cintā*) is born from a wound" (*khatā jāyate*), according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.64).

The group of three [roots] relates to *kheḷa*. *Lā* in the sense of taking; with the suffix *alo*, it becomes feminine (*itthiyam*). Or, *lala* in the sense of desire; it is feminine. *Khela* in the sense of movement;
with the suffix *a*. *Khala* in the sense of moving or accumulation; with the suffix *ṇo*, the vowel is changed to *ḷ*, or alternatively, that which moves toward the void (*khaṃ*) is *kheḷo*.
*Ila* in the sense of movement; with the suffix *kammani ṇo*, or *ila* in the sense of movement; with the suffix *a*, it is feminine (*isse*).

There are two [words] for *pitta* (bile). *Mā* in the sense of measure, with the suffix *dhu*. *Mada* in the sense of intoxication or madness, with the suffix *ṇu*; the *da* becomes *dha*. In the reading *māyū*, *maya* in the sense of going, with the suffix *ṇu*.

The two words *mādu* and *māyu* are masculine (*pulliṅga*). It is called *pitta* because it "covers over" (*apidadhāti*). The root *dhā* preceded by *api* in the sense of covering, with the suffix *to*;
there is elision of the *a*, and it belongs to the *bhujādi* group; thus *pitta* is neuter (*napuṃsaka*).

*Semha* (phlegm) has two [derivations]. From the root *siliṣ*, meaning "to adhere" (*silesane*), belonging to the *curādi* class: that in which one adheres is *semha*. [The suffix] *mana* is applied; *li* becomes *ha*, and there is a change of phonemes (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*).
In the other sense, [the suffix] *umo* is applied, resulting in *silesuma*. Phlegm is also [derived here]: that which increases (*phāti*) by means of water (*kena*) is *kapha*;

this is an etymological derivation (*nerutta*). 282–283. That whose oiliness (*sneha*) has dissolved (*vilīna*) or disappeared (*vibhūta*) is called *vasā*. From the root *vas*, meaning "to dwell" (*nivāse*), with the suffix *ā*. There are two [terms] for that whose oiliness has not dissolved.

*Mid* means to liquefy (*snehane*), [the suffix] *ṇo*. *Vap* means the continuity of seeds (*bījasantāne*), with the suffix *a*, [forming] *vapā*. In the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*, it is stated: “*Vapā* means an opening (*vivara*) or a fissure (*meda*)”;
however, in the *Amarakośa*, the identity of meaning for *meda* and so forth is illustrated, for it is said there: “*Medas*, *vapā*, and *vasā* [are synonyms]” (Amara 16.64).
The triad [of terms] refers to the bodily splendor produced by ornaments such as sandalwood paste and gold. *Kapu* means capability (*sāmatthiye*); the act of arranging (*ākappanaṃ*) is *ākappa*.

"No. [The *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.99) states: "In *nepaccha*, it refers to the house and its contents; and *vesa* [refers] to a brothel (*vesyāgaha*) or a merchant's house (*vessagaha*). [This is from] Rabhasa. [Etymological derivation:

From the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*kantiya*), or from *visi* in the sense of "pervading" (*byāpana*), with the suffix *ṇo*. *Nepaccha* means "complete narration" (*ni-sesato pathanaṃ pakkhyānaṃ*).
[The suffix] *ghyaṇ* is applied to the root *path* in the sense of "narration" (*pakkhyāne*). It also means "remedy" (*paṭikamma*) or "adornment" (*pasādhana*).

*Chakka* refers to ornaments such as necklaces (*hāra*) and the like. *Maḍi* means to adorn; with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *maṇḍiya*. *Sādha* means to accomplish; with *yu*, it becomes *sādhuya*. Alternatively, *sāṭha* refers to the movement of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*); *pasāṭhana* (unfolding) is used here with *muddha* as a secondary term. *Bhūsa* means to decorate;
with *yu* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), it becomes *bhūsiya*. That which is worn (*ābhariyyate*) is an ornament (*ābharaṇa*);

from *bhara* meaning "to support" or "to wear," with *yu* in the sense of the object (*kamman*). *Alaṅkāra* is that by which decoration (*alaṃ vibhūsanaṃ*) is performed; with the suffix *ṇo*, it forms *alaṅkāro*.
The suffix *yu* is used after the roots *piḷandha* (to adorn) and *bhūsana* (to decorate). *Parikkhāra* and *parikara* (according to Ka. both mean "ornament.

The pair [of terms] refers to a crown (*makuṭa*). From the root *kira* (to scatter), with the suffix *īṭ*; from the root *maki* (to adorn), with the suffix *uṭ*. *Mukuṭa* is also a reading; these two [terms] are not feminine.

The pair [of terms] refers to the central gem (*nāyakamaṇi*) at the top of the crown. A gem that kisses the crest of the crown is a *cūḷāmaṇi*; a gem that kisses the head of the crown is a *siromaṇi*.
284. There are two [types] on the turban (*uṇhīsapaṭṭa*). A head-wrapping is a *siroveṭhana*. The prefix *upa-* is used in the sense of binding;
*īsa* is a phonetic modification (*vaṇṇavikāra*). That which exists for a long time even among gods and humans—therein, regarding ear-ornaments, there are two types beginning with the *kuṇḍala*.
[The root] *kuḍi* means to burn, [forming *kuṇḍala*] with the suffix *-alo*. *Veṭha* means to wrap; wrapping of the ear is *kaṇṇaveṭhana*; this is accompanied by the word *muddha* (head).

The triad [of terms] refers to the ornament known as the *tāḷaka*. *Kaṇṇikā* is an ornament for the ears; the suffix *-ika* is applied to "ear" (*kaṇṇa*) when it denotes an ornament characterized by many features.
That which fills the covering of the ear is *kaṇṇapūra*. An ornament for the ear is *kaṇṇavibhūsana*; the suffix *-yu* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
The palm-leaf ornament (*tālapatta*) is also included herein.

285. There are two [terms] for a neck ornament (*gīvābharaṇa*). *Kaṇṭhabhūsā* (neck-adornment) is a feminine noun; it means the decoration of the throat (*kaṇṭha*). *Gīveyya* is that which exists on the neck (*gīvā*); the suffix *-eyya* is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavattha*). Alternatively, *gīveyya* is an ornament (*ābharaṇa*) of the neck; the suffix *-eyya* is used in the sense of an ornament belonging to the neck.

There are two [terms] for a pearl necklace (*muttāvali*). A *hāra* is that by which the mind is captivated (*harīyate*). A *muttāvali* is a row (*āvali*) or series of pearls. The word *hāra* is also used here.

There are four [terms] for an ear-ornament (*pakoṭṭhābharaṇa*). A *pakoṭṭha* is the lower part of the temple (*kappara*). From the root *nī* (to lead), with the prefix *u-* and the substitution of *iy*. [The other forms are: *pakoṭṭhaka*, *pakoṭṭhika*, and *pakoṭṭhiya*. These are the four. [Note: The text implies the derivation of *pakoṭṭhaka* from *pakoṭṭha* with the suffix *-ka*, *pakoṭṭhika* with *-ika*, and *pakoṭṭhiya* with *-iya*.]
*Vala* means covering or concealment; *ayo* is not feminine and is also used in the sense of "to join. *Kaṭa* is used in the senses of covering and going;
with the suffix *ṇvu*, it forms *parihāraka*, meaning that which carries or moves the mind all around (*pari-samantato*). *Avāpaka* is also used here. 286–287.
There are two [terms] for an ornament consisting of bracelets fashioned from pearls and other materials. *Kā* is a sound; with the suffix *kaṇa*, and *kaṇa* being a sound...

Alternatively, *dvittaṃ* (a pair), *kaṅkaṇaṃ* (an anklet): from the root *kaki* in the sense of "going" (*gatyatthe*) with the suffix *yu*, or from *kaki* in the sense of "restlessness" (*lolye*). It is called *kaṅkaṇaṃ* because one moves (*kaṅkati*) by means of it; the suffix *yu* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
*Karassa bhūsā* (ornament of the hand) is a feminine compound. The pair refers to a small bell (*khuddaghaṇṭikā*).

It is called *kiṅkaṇī* because it sounds (*kaṇati*) in a bad way (*kiṃ*); it belongs to the *nadādi* group. *Kiṅkiṇī* is also a variant reading, in which case it belongs to the *yadādi* group. A small bell is simply a "small bell" (*khuddaghaṇṭikā*); the suffix *ko* is used here in its own sense (*sakatthe*), derived from the root *ghaṭa* in the sense of "moving" (*calane*).

The term *dvayaṃ* (a pair) refers to *aṅgulyābharaṇa* (finger ornament). That which exists on the finger (*aṅguli*) is *aṅgulīyaka*; [it is derived from] *aṅguli* with the suffix *īya*, and *ka* in the sense of identity.

An ornament for the fingers is *aṅgulyābharaṇa*. *Ummikā* (ring) is also used here. That same *aṅgulīyaka*, when it possesses letters (*akkhara*) or engraved characters (*sākkhara*), is called *muddikā* or *aṅgulimuddā*.
[The root] *muda* means "to rejoice"; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *muddikā*. This term also applies to a particular kind of fruit. [It is used] on the finger.
*Bhava* means a ring; *muddā* means a finger-ring.

Both [terms] refer to an ornament for a woman’s waist. *Rasa* means sound. With the suffix *yu*, [the form] *rasanā* is derived in the sense of an agent; thus, *rasanā*. That same word, with the suffix *inī*, becomes *rasanī*. Rudra states:
“*Rasanaṃ* is used in the sense of ‘essence’ or ‘wealth,’ while *rasanā* is not [used] for the tongue. A garland for the *khā* [orifice] of the male organ is called *mekhalā*.
Regarding etymology, *mehana* is the meaning of the male organ (*mehanindriya*). A girdle (*kāñcī*) consists of seven [bones], as does the waist-band (*sārasana*).
A girdle may consist of a single bone, while a belt (*mekhalā*) consists of eight bones.
It should be known that a chain (*rasanā*) consists of sixteen [bones], and a cluster (*kalāpa*) consists of twenty-five; a cluster is composed of twenty-five [bones] (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 16.108).

The triad refers to golden ornaments for the *pagaṇḍa*. *Pagaṇḍa* means the upper part of the forearm. [The suffix] *ke* has the sense of "sound"; [the prefix] *uro* indicates the addition of the letter *y*. [The root] *aṅga* means "to go. [The suffix] *do* [indicates location]. An ornament existing at the base of the arm, or an ornament for the base of the arm, is called *bāhumūlavibhūsana*.

288. The tetrad refers to ornaments for the feet of women. An ankle-ornament (*pādabhūsana*) shaped like an armlet (*aṅgada*) is a *pādaṅgada*. [The root] *maji* has the sense of "sound"; [the suffix] *īro* [forms the word]. An anklet on the foot is a *pādakaṭaka*.
It is called *nūpura* because it fills out the deficient foot; [this is an example of] a change in phonetic form (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*). A *pādakaṭaka*...
And because the word *kaṭaka* occurs in the masculine gender as well—as in *nūpura*—it forms a *dvanda* compound.
*Tulākoṭi* and *haṃsaka* are also used here. From the root *tula*, meaning "to go" or "crookedness": it is called *tulākoṭi* because its tip (*koṭi*) is curved; this is masculine.
It is called *haṃsaka* because its gait is like that of a swan (*haṃsa*). 289. *Mukhaphulla* and others are varieties of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). *Mukhaphulla* is a golden facial ornament.
It is called *mukhaphulla* because it "blooms" (*phullati*) at the mouth; the root *phulla* means to blossom. Even golden ornaments for the teeth and so forth are indeed *mukhaphulla*.
An *unnata* is a forehead ornament fashioned from gold and other materials; the prefix *upa-* is used with the root *nam* in the sense of bending.

Furthermore, they say that the distinction between *mukhaphulla* and *unnata* can also be understood by reversing [the definitions]. It is called *gosthana* because it has the shape of a cow's udder; it is *ossatta*, which is that very same thing.
*Uttamatta* is the *uggatthana* [ornament]; it is a type of necklace (*hārabheda*) consisting of four sets of eight beads. *Gamū* means "to go"; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *gama*;

with the doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*), the insertion of *assitta*, and the addition of *giṅ*, it becomes *gamaka*. This is a type of necklace consisting of thirty-two beads. By this and other such examples, types of necklaces such as the *addhahāra*, *māṇavaka*, *ekāvalī*, and *nakkhattamālā* are included;
thus it is stated in *Amarakosa* 16.106.

290. *Pajja* means merely cloth (*vattha*). From the root *cil*, meaning "to rain" or "to cover"—it is that which is covered—there is the suffix *ṇo*; thus, with the feminine suffix *thi*, it becomes *celī*.

From the root *chad*, meaning "to cover," preceded by *ā* in the sense of the instrument, there is the suffix *yu*. From the root *vas*, meaning "to cover"—it is that which is covered—there is *vattha*, with the suffix *tho*.

With the suffix *ṇam*, it is *vāso*. With the suffix *yum*, it is *vasanaṃ*. From the root *ama*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *yu* in the sense of the instrument, it is *aṃsukaṃ*; this is also a synonym for *raṃsi* (ray). *Amba*... [text ends]

In the root *sad* (to sit), the suffix *aro* is applied in the agentive sense (*kattari*). In *paṭa* (to go), the suffix *a* is applied in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*), and this [word] refers to a beautiful garment (*sobhanacelepi*). In *du* (to go), the suffix *so* is applied in the instrumental sense; there is doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ*).
It is called *dussaṃ* because it "casts away" (*khepati*) what is ill-formed (*durūpaṃ*), or it is called *dussaṃ* because it "illuminates" (*dīpeti*) what is ill-formed;

the prefix *du-* is used here in the sense of "splendor" (*dittiyaṃ*). In *cala* (to wear/garment), the suffix *asso* is applied, and there is the substitution of *ḷ* for *t*. In *saṭa* (in the senses of breaking, spreading, going, and ending), the suffix *ṇvu* is applied.

291. *Pajja* refers to varieties of cloth. Among these, the first two refer to the cloth known as *dukūla*. *Khu* is a root meaning "sound"; with the suffix *mo*, it becomes *khumasadda*. With the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*), *khuma* becomes *khoma*;

thus, *khoma* is a derivative of *khuma*. *Khuma* is the name for the flax plant (*atasī*); the cloth produced from its husks is called *khoma*. This term is used according to the gender of the object it describes (*vāccaliṅga*).
*Kūla* means "to cover"; that which is woven (*kulyati*) with difficulty is *dukūla*. Alternatively, it is so called because it is produced from trees (*dumehi*) and covers (*kūla*).
*Dukūla*. However, some say that *dukūla* is another kind of cloth and not what is called *khoma*.

That should not be accepted, because it is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha* (3.3.295) within the *Kaṇḍasesa* commentary on the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: “*Khoma* refers to smooth *dukūla* and also to *atasī* cloth,” and “*Khoma* refers to smooth *dukūla*.
A *kosa* is the cocoon of a silkworm; [the term is used] because it is produced from that.
*Koseyya* means "silk" (*kimikosa-uttha*), as stated in the *Amara-kośa* (16.111). *Koseyya* itself, when washed, is called *paṭṭuṇṇa*;
it is said, "*Paṭṭuṇṇa* is washed silk," as stated in the *Amara-kośa* (16.113). *Pattuṇṇa* is also an alternative reading.
They also say it is called *paṭṭuṇṇa* because it was produced in the kingdom of *Paṭṭuṇṇa*. [The root] *kam* is used in the sense of desiring; [it is so called] because of its desirability.
*Kambala* is a cloth produced from the hair of a specific kind of deer named *raṅku*; it is called *rāṅkava*, meaning "hairless" (*vigaromaja*).
[The suffix] *-a* is added, and there is an augment (*āgama*) of *v* in the middle. The word *vā* indicates that the word *kambala* is neuter.
*Rallaka* (Amarakośa 16.116) is also a synonym for *kambala*. From the root *saṇ* (to sound), with the suffix *-a* in the sense of the agent, we have *saṇa*, which refers to a strong, firm bark.
One is the tree-source (*rukkhayoni*), from whose bark the weavers (*kevaṭṭā*) and others make nets and such. *Sāṇa* is a derivative of *saṇa*;
it is cloth. *Koṭumbara* is a garment made from deer-hair that has been pounded and refined;

[it is called] *koṭumbara* because of the root *kuṭ*, meaning "to cut," with the suffixes *-usso* and *-assu*, or because it is produced in the region of Koṭumbara. *Bhaṅga* refers to all [fibers] together, such as *khoma* and the rest.
Having washed it, [it becomes] "washed-cloth" (*katavattha*). In the case of *bhanja*, it means "to crush" or "to trample. Alternatively, *bhaṅga* refers to the hemp plant;
because the cloth is a product of that, the cloth is called *bhaṅga*. And it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "Hemp is also known as *bhaṅga*.

Furthermore, by the word "crop" (*sassa*) here, the fruit is meant, according to the statement in the *Amara-kośa* (14.15): "The fruit of trees and so forth is 'crop' (*sassa*). Thus, the cloth made of hemp is also [called] *bhaṅga*.
Some say it is made of bark. "Another cloth" (*vatthantara*) refers to a specific type of cloth; by the word "etcetera," cotton and other materials are also included.
292–293. The set of four [terms] refers to the lower garment worn beneath. It is called *nivāsana* because one wears it on the lower part of the body; the prefix *ni-* indicates the lower part.
The root *vas* means "to cover," and the suffix *-ana* is used in the sense of the object. Generally, that which exists within or in the middle is called *antarīya*.

*Īyo*. Because they share the same gender (*samānaliṅgattā*), it is a *dvanda* compound. That which exists within (*antare*) is "internal" (*antaraṃ*); [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied. Or, that which is a dwelling (*vāsa*) existing in the middle (*majjhe*) is "an undergarment" (*antaravāsako*);
[the suffix] *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). Here, even though there is a prefix (*upasaṃbyānaṃ*), [the rule applies];

see Amarakosa 16.117. The group of five [terms] refers to the upper garment. From the root *vara* meaning "to cover," preceded by *pa*, with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the object (*kammani*), there is a vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) in both cases; thus, *pāvāro* ("cloak").
It is called *uttarāsaṅga* because it is fastened (*āsajjati*) on the upper part of the body; the root *sañj* (with prefix *ā-*) means to attach.

It is so called because it is mostly wrapped around or covered over (*upari saṃvīyate pidhīyate*); the suffix *yu* is used here. The root *vī* (with prefixes *upa-* and *sam-*) means to weave or extend.
That which exists or is found on the upper part of the body is *uttara*; thus we have *uttarīya*, with the suffixes *ṇa* and *īya*. *Saṃvyāna* is also used in this sense.
"New cloth" (*navaṃ vatthaṃ*) is considered and described as "unbeaten" (*ahata*); it is called "unbeaten" because it has not been struck by stones or other such objects.
It is cloth that has been recently brought from the loom. "Unbeaten" (*anāhata*), "without a weaver's comb" (*nippavāṇi*), and "woven from the threads" (*tantaka*) are synonyms here. And it is said:
"Unbeaten, without a weaver's comb, and woven from the threads—these are new cloths in the autumn" (Amara-kosa 16.112).
The pair [of terms] refers to worn-out clothing because of their long duration. That which has no end (*anta*) is *anantaka*; the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (as a pleonastic).
A wretched cloth is a *kappaṭa*; *kappa* means "thought" (*vitakka*), and *aṭa* is the suffix.

The pair [of terms] refers to unstable clothing; worn-out clothing is unstable clothing. It is called *paṭaccara* because it moves (*carati*) or flutters (*phoṭati*); *paṭaccara* itself becomes *paḷaccara*, due to the substitution of *ḷ* for *r*.

294. [The word *vāra* occurs] in *dvayaṃ-koṭika-ādi-sannāhe* (the armor consisting of two ends, etc. and in *coḷe* (a rag). [In *vāra*: *kaca* means binding; there is the augment *uko* and the elision of the *niggahīta*.

Because it wards off (*vāreti*) an arrow (*vāṇaṃ*), it is called *vāravāṇo*; the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the object (*kammani*). Due to conventional usage (*abhidhānato*), the word *vāra* is placed first [in the compound].

These [words] are not feminine. The word *dasā* refers to a part of a garment (*vatthassa avayave*) and is feminine. "The word *dasā* [is used] for a garment (*vatthaṃ*), for a state (*avatthāyaṃ*), for a portion of a garment (*vatthaṃse*), and in the plural."
*The Cintāmaṇi-Ṭīkā*, 16.114, by Rabhasa: The root *dā* means "to cut" (*chedane*); when used in the sense of an object (*kammani*), it becomes short (*rasso*).
