That which is a covering (*kañcuko*) made of gold or other materials for the head (*uttamaṅga*), the top of the body, is called a "helmet" (*nāḷipatta*). A cloth of gold or other materials shaped like that [helmet] is a "helmet-cloth" (*nāḷipatta*). Its synonyms are *sīsaka*, *siriya*, and *sirohanta*. [Verse 295: The triad [of terms] refers to length (*dīghatte*).

The prefix *ā-* combined with the root *yam* (meaning "to cease," *uparame*) with the suffix *ṇo* forms *āyāma*. Alternatively, *ā* (meaning "intensely") combined with *yā* (meaning "to go" or "to reach," *gati-pāpuṇesu*) with the suffix *mo* forms *āyāma*. The state of being long is "length" (*dīghatā*). The root *ruha* (meaning "to grow," *janane*) with the suffix *ṇo* [forms *rohaṇa*].

The dyad is explained in detail. Regarding the object that is the basis [of the robe], the term *osāra* is a conventional usage (*rūḷhi*). It is called *pariṇāha* because it encompasses (*pariṇahati*) on all sides; the root *naha* means "to bind," with the suffix *-ṇo*. Extensive spreading (*visāra*) is *visāla*;
that itself is vastness. 296. The tetrad concerns the robe (*cīvara*). It is the "banner of the Arahants" (*arahaddhaja*);

by conventional usage, this refers to robes other than those [of the Arahants]. Dyed with *kasāya* or *kasāva*, it is *kāsāya* or *kāsāva*; because they share the same grammatical gender, they form a *dvanda* compound. From the root *ci* (to accumulate), we have *īvara*. It is called *cīvara* because it is accumulated (*cīyate*) from pieces of cloth.
The circles and so forth are its members; they are the constituent parts of the robe as a whole. The root *maḍi* means "adornment," with the suffix *-ala*, thus *maṇḍala*.
This edge of the robe stands all around it, like the Cakkavāḷa mountain range surrounding the great earth.
What is called the "swirl" (*vivaṭṭa*) is the seam located at the center of the robe; for it is said to be a "swirl" because it rolls separately from each side.

*Vaṭṭa* means in a whirlpool. *Kusi* is the name for a piece of cloth situated in the middle of paths; from the root *kusa*, meaning "to cut," with the suffix *i* added in the sense of action, it becomes *kusi*, denoting both male and female. 297.
Those which are the four [types] of fruits and so forth are the origins—that is, the causes—of cloth, because it arises from them.
*Kappāsika* cloth is called *phāla* because it is a derivative of the fruit (*phala*); the suffix *-ṇo* is used for derivatives, according to rule III.
For example: *phālo paṭo*, *phālā celī*, *phālaṃ vatthaṃ*. However, *khome* and other types of cloth are *paṭas* because they originate from the bark;
they are produced from the bark (*taca*). 298. Silk cloth is called *kimija*. That which is made of animal hair is *kambala*. These two [terms] refer to the inner lining cloth.

Some say it is *kaṇḍapaṭa*. These two [words] have the same meaning; they are synonyms. [The root] *ju* is in the sense of "going" (*gati*), belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, or in the sense of "binding" (*bandhana*).
With the suffix *yu*, there is the substitution of *ana*; that which ends in *sā* is feminine. That by which one is made invisible or covered is *tirokaraṇī*;
[the suffix here is] *yu*. *Patisīra* is also used here. [The root] *si* preceded by *pati* is in the sense of "binding," with the suffix *ro*.

299. Both [terms] refer to a canopy (*ulloca*) depicted on an upper cloth; here, the word *atha* indicates gender and so forth. It is called *ulloca* because it is "bound above" (*uddhaṃ locate bandhīyati*); the root *luca* means "to see.
It is called *vitāna* because it is "spread out" (*vitanyati*) in the moonlight; the root *tanu* means "to expand," with the suffix *-ṇa*, belonging to the *curādi* class.
Both are stated—that is, declared—to be masculine and neuter.
“*Sināne*”: two [meanings]. *Naha* [is used] in the sense of sorrow; *yu* [is used] in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in *sinā* [meaning] sorrow, [used] in the sense of an instrument.
“*Sināne*” is a word ending in the locative case. Two [meanings]: by means of water and so forth, or by means of a hut and so forth (*ka.*); by means of cleansing and so forth (*nissaya*);

or by means of saffron, turmeric, and so forth (*Cintāmaṇiṭīkā* 16.121)—[all these are used] for the purpose of making the body clean. That by which impurity is scraped off or removed is called *ubbattanaṃ*.
*Vat* in the sense of "turning" belongs to the *bhū-ādi* class. *Majj* in the sense of "purity" takes the suffix *-yu*. *Sama* and *tila*—these two have the same meaning.
(Verse 300) *Tilakākati* means a *tilaka* (mole/freckle). *Cittakākati* means a *cittaka* (spot/mark). By the letter *ca*, *tamālapattākati* means a *tamālapatta* (mark made with tamāla leaves).
In their general sense, they mean a *visesaka* (ornamental mark). Both *visesaka* and *tilaka* are not feminine; the remaining two [forms] are [gender-neutral].
The neuter form is *amara* (16.123). The triad refers to *candana*. The root *cad* means to delight;
*hilādana* means to cause happiness. [The suffix] *yu* is applied. It is the essence (*sāra*) of fragrances and the highest among them, thus it is *gandhasāra*;

or, it is the essence joined with fragrance, or its firm parts, thus it is *gandhasāra*. It is called *malayaja* because it is born on the mountain of the Malaya island. *Bhaddasirī* is also used here.
301. The triad on yellow sandalwood (*pītacandana*). Regarding "gosīsa": it is *gosīsa* because it is produced in a region of Mount Malaya;
or, it is *gosīta* because it is cool like a cow's [udder], and by adding the suffix *-sa*, it becomes *gosīsa*. It is called *telapaṇṇika* because its leaves are the size of sesame leaves.
It is called *haricandana* because it "takes away" (*harati*) the mind; that very thing is sandalwood, hence *haricandana*. *Pītasāru* is also used here, as is *susīta*.
The three beginning with *gosīsa* function as masculine and also as neuter.

The group of four refers to red sandalwood (*rattacandana*). It is called *tilapaṇṇī* because it possesses leaves the size of sesame leaves; there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) here for the sake of distinguishing it from the preceding term.
*Pattaṅga* means "having leaves as its limbs" (*pattamaṅgamassa*), which signifies that its leaves are secondary due to their smallness.
For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: “*Aṅga* and *gatta* refer primarily to the limbs of the body. The root *rañj* means ‘to color’; with the suffix *yu*, it denotes the agent as the cause.
Because of its red color, it is both ‘red’ (*ratta*) and ‘sandalwood’ (*candana*), hence ‘red sandalwood’ (*rattacandana*). However, in the *Amarakosa* (16.131), it is stated:
“The [names] beginning with *gosīsa* and ending with *rattacandana* are used in a specific sense. Among those, the meaning of *gosīsa* is exactly as previously described.
*Dhavala* (white) and *susītala* (very cool) refer to sandalwood produced specifically in the region of the Malay Mountains, known as *telapaṇṇika*.
*Haricandana* is sandalwood grown on a mountain shaped like a green frog; it has the fragrance of jackfruit and is yellow in color.
*Tilapaṇṇī* and *pattaṅga* are names for a certain red-scented sandalwood that resembles red sandalwood in its essence.
“Dvayaṃ rattacandane. Alternatively, the four beginning with *tilapaṇṇa* are names for a single specific type of sandalwood, a red heartwood similar to *lohitacandana*.
*Kucandana* is also included here; as stated in the *Ratnamālā*: “*Pattaṅga*, *rañjana*, and *ratta*;
and *patraṅga* and *kucandana*.”
302. *Dvayaṃ* refers to two things: for merchants and others, it is the yellow wood known by the conventional term “kāḷeya”;

and that which follows the nature of black color is *kāḷānusārī*, meaning it produces black color. That which generates black is *kāḷiyaṃ*. Regarding *kāḷīyakaṃ*—as in the phrase “*kāḷeyaṃ* is *kāḷīyakaṃ*;
it bestows color and produces luster”—the commentator Byāḍi states that *jāsakaṃ* means that which gives luster (*kantidāyakaṃ*) (Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā 16.126).

The triad [of terms] is a general designation for *agaru*. The root *lū* means "to cut," and *ho* [is a suffix]. Because it is light (*lahu*) by nature, it is *agaru*; when its final vowel is shortened, it becomes *agalu*. Both forms are masculine.

*Vaṃsikaṃ*, *rājārahaṃ*, *kimijaṃ*, and *joṅgakaṃ* are also used here. When this *agaru* is black, it is called "black *agaru*. However, the *agaru* that has the fragrance of jasmine flowers is called auspicious (*maṅgalya*).
The pair [of terms] refers to the *sallakī* tree; it is called *turukkha*. From the root *piḍi* meaning "to compress" with the suffix *ṇvu*, we have *sihala* and *yāvaṇa* as well.

303. Two [terms] for musk: *miganābhi*. Where? In the sense of praise (*silāghāyaṃ*), the chest (*ūro*), and rivers etc. (*nadādi*). The suffix *ko* is used in its own sense (*sakatthe*). The rut of a deer is *migamada*; or, that by which a deer dies is *migamara*, and that very thing is *migamada*. Two [terms] for leprosy (*kuṭṭha*):

from the root *kuṭ* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*), with the suffix *ṭho* or *to*. By the rule “*ṭho* after *kuṭa* etc.,” the suffix *ṭho* is applied; thus *kuṭṭhaṃ*, which also refers to a specific disease.
That which protects goats when they have entered their own shade is *ajapālakaṃ*, with the suffix *ṇvu*. Also *pāribhābyaṃ*, *pākalaṃ*, and *phālakī* (variant: *phālako*).

*Uppala* and *vāppa* are also [names for this]. Two names for *piḷaṅga*: it is called *lavaṅga* because it moves (*aṅgati*) while cutting through disease (*roga*). *Devakusuma* is the flower of the gods;

*sirisa* is also known here. Two names for *kuṅkuma*: born in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, it is *kasmīraja*. *Agnisikha*, *vara*, *vallīka*, *pītana*, *rattasaṅkoca*, *pisuna*, *dhīra*, and *lohitacandana* are also [names] for it.
304. He shakes off the pair. *Yakkhadhūpa* is incense made by *yakkhas*; a *yakkha* is a deity.

*Sajjulaso* is the resin (*sileso*) of the *sajja* tree. [The derivation is: *assu*, with the elision of *si* (*silopo*), and the substitution of *e* for *a* (*essattaṃ*); thus, the juice (*raso*) of the *sajja* is *dava*, making it *sajjulaso*.
[The suffix] *assu* and the substitution of *la* for *ra* (*lattaṃ*). There is also a reading *sajjaraso*. Herein, *rālo* (the elision of *ra* and *la*), *sabbaraso*, and *bahurūpo* also apply.

*Tikaṃ* refers to *takkola*. *Takka* [is derived from] the root *tak* in the sense of "to reflect" (*vitakke*), with the suffix *o*. *Kula* [is derived from] the root *kul* in the sense of "reckoning" (*saṅkhyāne*), with the suffix *ṇvu*.
That which has a fruit joined with a sheath (*kosa*) is *kosaphala*. *Dvayaṃ* refers to *jātiphala*. That which has a *jāti*-fruit accompanied by a sheath is *jātikosa*.
Its *jāti*-fruit is not merely its reputation; it is the actual *jāti*-fruit.

305. *Pajjaddha* refers to camphor (*kappūra*). Because it becomes solid (*ghana*) and then melts (*sarati*), it is called *ghanasāra*. Like a cloud (*abbha*), it is white; thus it is *sitabbha*, with the prior member placed first according to grammatical convention. *Kappa* is used in the sense of capability; *ūru* means "capable. It is designated as *canda*, *himavāluka*, and also *himāvhaya* (called snow). *Pajjaddha* refers to lac (*lākhā*). Because it makes something intensely red (*ābhuso rattaṃ karoti*), it is *alattaka*;

[it is also] *latta*. [The suffix] *kvi* is applied. [The root] *yu* is used in the sense of mixing, with the suffix *ṇvu*. [The root] *lākha* is used in the sense of drying, with the suffix *a*; or [the root] *lā* is used in the sense of taking, with the suffix *kho*. [The root] *jana* is used in the sense of producing, with the suffix *tu*, and the *na* is elided. *Dumāmaya* is also used here.
306. Two [meanings] for *saraladdava*: *sirivāsa* is the abode (*āvāsa*) of *siri*, that is, of *lakkhī*. *Saraladdava* is the resin (*dava*) of the tree named *sarala*.
*Pāyasa*, *vakadhūpa*, and *siriveṭṭha* also apply here. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (16.129): “*Sirivāsa* refers to excellent food, while *pāyasa* is considered masculine.
*Rudda* [is another term]. Two [meanings] for *añjana*: the root *añju* is used in the senses of clarity, anointing, movement, and beauty.
*Yu*: in the sense of "action" (*kajja*) and "calamity" (*byasana*). It is called *kajjala* because it is afflicted (*kajjati*) by disease;

thus it is *alo*. There are two [meanings] for *gandhagāhāpanacuṇṇa*: *vasa* has the sense of "to harm"; or, it is *vāsa* because it dwells upon bad odors (*duggandha*); the suffix *ṇo* is added. Or, *vāsa* is used in the sense of "service" (*upasevā*), or in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*).
That very thing is the powder (*cuṇṇa*). *Yuja* means "to join" (*yoga*); with the suffix *ṇo* in the objective sense, *vāsa* itself as the "joining" is *vāsayoga*.
The pair [of terms] refers to the act of smearing. *Vaṇṇa* occurs in the senses of color, coloring, expansion, and quality; it belongs to the *curādi* class. That which colors is *vaṇṇaka*;
the suffix *ṇvu* is added. *Lipa* means to smear. That which is smeared is *vilepana*;

the suffix *yu* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*). 307. That preparation of clothing, betel, and so forth, by means of perfumes, garlands, incense, and the like, is called "perfuming" (*vāsana*). *Vāsa* means service or application; that which is perfumed—that is, prepared—is *vāsana*; the suffix *yu* is added.

A triad concerning *pupphadāma* (flower-garland). *Mā* [is used] in the sense of measuring (*māne*), and *lo* [is used] in the sense of bearing dust (*mala-dhāraṇe*). Thus, like *māla*, it is *mālya*. *Dama* is in the sense of going (*gatiyaṃ*).
Since flowers are bound (*damanti*) here, it is *pupphadāma*; the meaning is "the place for making a heap of flowers. Alternatively, *dā* is in the sense of cutting (*lavane*), with the suffix *mo*.
However, in the *Amarakośa*, verse 16.135, it states: "The terms *mālā* and *mālya* are names for a garland worn on the head."
The terms *mālā* and *mālya* refer to flowers as well; for it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: “*Mālā* and *mālya* [refer to] flowers and beasts.

The pair [of terms] refers to cloth and so forth when they have acquired fragrance. The root *bhū* means "to exist"; with the suffix *-ta*, it forms *buddhādi* (awakened, etc.). That which causes fragrance to dwell [in something], that is, causes it to be acquired, is called *vāsita*.

The root *vas* means "to dwell"; with the suffix *-ta* in the passive sense, it applies to all three genders—as in: *bhāvito paṭo* (the cloth is perfumed), *bhāvitā celī* (the garment is perfumed), *bhāvitaṃ vatthaṃ* (the cloth is perfumed).
*Vāsito*, *vāsitā*, *vāsitaṃ vatthaṃ*. (308) The group of five [terms] begins with *muddhamālā*.
[The root] *tas* is used in the sense of ornamenting; it belongs to the *bhūvādi* class. That which is worn above (*uddhaṃ*) is called *uttaṃsa*.

That which is born upon the crest (*sikhā*) is *sekharo*; [the suffix] *ra* is added. That which protects (*avati*) the head (*muddhaṃ*) is *aveḷā*; [the root] *ava* means "to protect," and the suffix *elo* is added, with the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*. It is also called *āveḷā*.
The reading is *dīghattaṃ* (lengthening). *Sekhara* and *āveḷā* form a *dvanda* compound. A garland (*mālya*) adorned upon the head is *muddhamālya*; [it is used] in that sense.

With the prefix *ava-* in the sense of adorning, it is called *avataṃsa*, because it is placed (*tasiyati*) above (*uddhaṃ*); that very thing is a *vaṭaṃsaka*. The suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
Here, the letter *ṭ* is substituted for that [suffix]. Since prefixes and particles have multiple meanings, the word *ava-* here indicates the sense of "above"; thus it has been stated.

The triad concerning the bed (*seyyā*). That upon which one lies is a *seyyā*; [it is derived from] the root *si* (to lie). That wherein one lies is a *sayana*, and also a *sena*. In both cases, the suffix *yu* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); [with the suffix] *isse*, there is the substitution of *aya* for *e*; in the other case, there is the substitution of *etta*; and by the rule "or the following [suffix] is elided when dissimilar," there is also elision [of the suffix], thus *sayanī* is also used here.

The dyad concerning the couch (*mañca*). The prefix *pari-* is combined with the root *aki* in the sense of a characteristic mark; the suffix *ṇo* is applied, with elision of *i* and the substitution of *la* for *ra*.

The root *maci* is used in the senses of holding, splendor, and worship; it belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and takes the suffix *a*; the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakattha*). *Khaṭā* is also used here. It is called *khaṭā* because it is desired (*khaṭyate*) by those seeking a place to lie down; the root *khaṭa* is used in the sense of longing (*ākaṅkhā*).
309. *Dvayaṃ mañcādhāre*. The support of a bed is *mañcādhāra*. That by which one lies down or moves about is *paṭipāda* (the leg).

Regarding the parts or members of a bed (*mañcaṅga*), the word *aṭani* is feminine; [it is derived from] the root *aṭ* meaning "to go," with the suffixes *ani* or *yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* group, with the vowel shortened.
310. These four types of beds beginning with *kuḷīrapāda* (crab-legged) are varieties of beds. Among them, *kuḷīra* is a crab (*kakkhaṭaka*).

Because its feet are shaped like those of a crab, it has "crab-feet" (*kuḷīrapāda*). Regarding the term *āhaccapāda*: it is one whose foot stands having struck (*āhacca*) against the edge of the opening;
thus it is called *āhaccapāda*. In the former sense, the word *āhacca* ends in the suffix *-icca* through the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) “*riccā*”;
in the latter sense, however, it ends in the suffix *-tvā*. That [animal] whose foot enters and stands within the opening of the edge is *āhaccapāda*. *Masa*...
In the words *āmasane*, *āro*, and *sakatthe*, the suffix *ko* is applied. That in which the crossbar (*aṭanī*) enters and remains within the foot-opening is a *masāraka*.
That whose crossbar is joined as one with the frame and the foot is a *bundikābaddha*; here the vowel *e* is substituted for *ai*.
Furthermore, in this context, they also state that the characteristics of the two middle couches may be reversed.

311. Two [terms] refer to the head-support (*sīsādhāra*). That which especially bears the head is called *bibbohana* (pillow); [the suffix] *yu*, *batta*, and *assotta*. That upon which one reclines, by which the head-seat is made, is called *upadhāna* (cushion); [the suffix] *yu*, from the root *dhā* in the sense of "holding. Three [terms] refer generally to a seat (*pīṭha*).

The root *pīṭh* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class in the senses of "injury" and "defilement"; [the suffix] *ṇvu*, [with the augment] *ā*. By the rule beginning with "when *ya* etc.," when the suffix *ka* follows a feminine form ending in *tā*, the preceding vowel *a* becomes *i*;

what is the purpose of the word "*ka*" here? [It is to indicate: "volition" (*cetanā*). What is the purpose of the word "*paccaye*" (in the suffix)? [To exclude cases where the suffix is not a *paccaya*.]

*Bakā*. What is the meaning of *itthī*? *Pācakā*. What is the meaning of *kata*? *Vuttakammā*; this is a *kamma*-suffix (*kammapaccaya*), and one should also look at the Moggallāna Sutta 4.142 regarding the *ta*-suffix:
*pīṭhaṃ*. *Āsanaṃ* means that which they sit upon. There are two [meanings] for the word *pīṭha*: an excellent seat or a stool.
The root *kuca* is used in the senses of rubbing together, bending, stiffening, and scratching; it takes the suffix *cho*. *Bhaddaṃ*.
*Kalyāṇa-pīṭha* and *bhadda-pīṭha* refer to a seat made of ivory and the like, which they call these two types of hair-combs (*kesamajjani*).

At that time, it is also called a *pasādhanī* or a *kaṅkatikā*. Among other types of seats, the long seat is considered an *āsandī*. [The word *sadana*] is derived from the roots *sad*, *visar*, and *gam*, with the addition of the suffix *-na* and the augment *-d-*.
312. A great variety of seats, by way of length and breadth, is considered a *kojava*. [The root] *ku* means "to steal," with the suffix *ṇo*;
or alternatively, it is a *kojava* because it moves (*javati*) upon the earth (*kuyaṃ*), where *ju* means "to go. A variety of seat joined with long wool is considered a *gonaka*.
[The root] *gu* means "sound," with the suffix *yu*, the suffix *ko* in the sense of identity, and *ussa* meaning "upward" or "elevated."

Two [terms] for a rug (*attharaṇa*): *migaloma-puṇṇatāya jātaṃ uṇṇāmayaṃ*. [The root] *thara* means "to spread" (*santharaṇe*); preceded by *pādi-* (i.e., *pa-*) it is never used without that prefix. It is called *attharaṇa* because it is "spread thoroughly" (*ā bhuso tharīyati*); the suffix *-yu* is added. Two [terms] for a woven cloth (*saṃsibbanacittaka*):

*cittarūpam assa atthīti cittakaṃ*. [The suffix] *-ika* is generally not subject to the augment *i*. *Vānacittakaṃ* means "that which has a woven design" (*vānena saṃsibbanena sañjātaṃ cittarūpam assa*); the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (*sakatthe*). 313.
Two [terms] for a dense flower-patterned cloth (*nirantarapupphapaṭa*): *ghanasandhibhūtaṃ puppharūpam etthāti ghanapupphaṃ*. "A dense, joined flower-design is found here," thus it is *ghanapuppha*.

*Paṭalikā*: that which has a fringe (*paṭala*) is *paṭalikā*; the suffix *ika* is used here. *Dvayaṃ bahumudulome setavatthe*: there are two [terms] for a white cloth with many soft fringes. *Seto*: this is derived from the root *si* (to serve);
it is called *seta* because it is served by those who desire welfare (*siva*). The suffix *to* is applied. *Paṭikā*: from the root *paṭa* (to go), with the suffix *ṇvu*, we get *paṭikā*;
it also refers to a crescent moon or a stone. *Uddalomī*: that which has fringes (*dasā*) on both ends is *uddalomī*; its fringes (*loma*) extend upward (*udita*) on both sides.
It is *uddalomī* (upward-haired), *issattaṃ* (manliness), and *dvittaṃ* (duality). Regarding *ekantalomī*: that which has fringes (*dasā*) on only one edge is *ekantalomī*;
that which has hair (*loma*) as its fringe on one side or edge is *ekantalomī*. Thus, *uddalomī* and *ekantalomī* become *uddalomiekantalomino*.

Although it is stated that "the conjunction of words occurs according to the speaker's desire, not within other compounds," [this form is used] because it is a verse and for fear of losing the meter (*chandohāni*).
Regarding *visandhi*: But where there is a hiatus (*visandhi*) both in verse and in prose—as in the phrase "dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāya" and so forth—how is that to be explained?

Because the rule "not within the members of a compound" is not universal (*anicca*), there is no fault even in those cases; for it is stated in the Paribhāsa: "That which is not joined with 'na' is non-universal" (Paribhāsendusekhara 97).
314. That very same pair already mentioned is called *kuttaka* when it is suitable for dancing—that is, fit to be the place for dancing—among sixteen women.

The particle *hi* is used for filling out the meter. There is also a reading, *naccayogyamhi*; in that case, it is a locative absolute expressing state (*bhāvasattamī*). They perform dancing there; thus it is *kuttaka*. [The derivation is as follows:
from the root *kṛ* (to do), with the suffix *to*, followed by *assu*, belonging to the *bhujādi* class; then the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
A cloth or seat variegated with forms such as lions and so forth is called a *vikati* (modification).

For there is a duality based on the states designated as the "natural" (*pakati*) and the "modified" (*vikati*) belonging to a single agent; furthermore, according to one's desire, there occurs a distinction in gender, number, and case-ending, as for example:
"human beings became the food of the *yakkhas*" (*manussā yakkhabhattaṃ ahesuṃ*), or "the seven treatises are called the Abhidhamma" (*sattappakaraṇāni abhidhammo nāma bhavanti*).

"Devadatta attains the kingdom. For where there might be a mention of both the base (*pakati*) and the derivative (*vikati*), the expressive word takes the number of the base alone, not that of the other, because the latter is subordinate by virtue of being dependent upon it;
this is to be seen in verses 6–7 of the *Kaccāyanasāra*. However, when one wishes to express the state of being related to the base and so forth, [the derivative takes its own number].
In that case, because there is no other thing to be predicated by the speaker, it is expressed as a transformation (*vikati*), as in: "Devadatta attains kingship.

However, here it is stated specifically through a change of gender: "The mind would be a transformation" (*cittaṃ vikatikā bhave*). It is called a *vikati* because it is transformed (*vikarīyati*). 315.
To show the manner of making the two kinds of rugs known as the *kaṭṭissa* and *koseyya*, he speaks of the common practice of the Noble Ones (*ariyasāmañña*).
"Kaṭṭissa," etc. A rug made from silk threads and silk wool is called *kaṭṭissa*;
by the rule of "single remainder" (*virūpekasesa*), both silk (*kosiya*) and *kaṭṭissa* are referred to as *kaṭṭissāni*, and a rug made from those is a *kaṭṭissa*.
A rug made from silk thread is called *koseyya*. "Sewn with jewels" means...
This is a qualification for both [terms]. Following the sequence, the word "in existence" (*bhave*) should be supplied after each in turn.
Because the word *attharaṇa* (spreading/cloth) is used even for things made of wool, it is stated here as "*attharaṇa*" just as one says "the cloth is the ritual act" (*suttaṃ kamma*).
And here, the letter *c* should be understood as representing the *gaṇa* of heavy syllables because it stands at the end of a foot; for by that very [rule], there are fifty-seven [syllables].
They are complete: for in the first noble path there are twelve [factors], likewise in the third;

in the second there are eighteen, and in the fourth fifteen. When added together, they amount to fifty-seven. 316. The triad on *dīpa*. *Dīpa* is in the sense of shining (*ditti*), belonging to the *div-ādi* group.

It is called *dīpa* because it shines (*dippati*); the suffix *-no* is applied. The prefix is added to the word for the sake of excluding other meanings, as in the term "lamp" (*padīpa*). *Juti* is in the sense of shining, belonging to the *bhū-ādi* group; the suffix *-no* is applied.

Two [terms] for a mirror: *ādāsa*. The word *liṅga* ends in *-tu*, as in the phrase “*pume tu*” (in the masculine, however). It is called *ādāsa* because it is looked at (*ādissate*) in this; it is formed with the suffix *ṇo*, from the root *dis* preceded by *ā-* in the sense of seeing, with the suffix *issa*. It is called *dappaṇa* because one shines (*dippati*) in it; it is formed with the suffix *yu*, meaning the state of shining.
*Makura* is also used here. Two [terms] for a ball made of leather used for play: [these are to be known] because play occurs together with young women in the pleasure-palaces (*vāsabhavana*);

the naming of the object follows that sequence. From the root *guḍ* in the sense of piercing, with the suffix *ṇuka* and the suffix *usse*, [we get *gullā*]. Or, from *guḍ* in the sense of playing itself, then the substitution of *ṇḍa* for *da* occurs. From the roots *kad* in the sense of calling out or weeping...
And *ca*, *ṇuka*, *kudda*, or even in the sense of playing (*kīḷāya*); *ussattaṃ*; not for one who has seen before. Two [meanings] in the sense of fanning (*bījanīmatte*).

*Vaṭi* in the sense of dividing (*vibhājane*); it is called *tālavaṇṭa* because it is made from palm leaves (*tālapaṇṇa*). *Vaṇṭa* means a portion of a palm leaf that has been separately divided for the purpose of making a fan or similar object;
even though the word *tālavaṇṭa* possesses the aforementioned verbal meaning, [it is used in this specific sense].
Because it possesses the word "saññā" (name/designation), its application should be understood as being common to all types of fans.
However, when one wishes to speak specifically of a fan made of palm leaves, then it should be specified by the word "tāla" [palm] as "tālatālavaṇṭa" (a palm-leaf fan). Just as in the cases:
"the oil of sesame" (tilassa telaṃ) and "the robe of the Sugata" (sugatassa sugatacīvaraṃ). Or, it is called "bījanī" because it is that by which they join [objects] with the wind (yojayanti).
*Yu*, *nadādi*; *yuja* in the sense of joining (*yoge*); *yassa* is *vo*; *ussī*; *vaja* in the sense of going (*gatiyaṃ*) or *assī*. *Byañjanaṃ* is also used here. 317. *Dvayaṃ caṅkoṭake*.
*Kuṭa* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*); with the suffix *ko* in its own sense (*sakatthe*). *Karaḍi* in the sense of a vessel (*bhājanatthe*), with *ko*.

Two [words] for a casket (*sampuṭa*) of camphor and so forth, or a casket of *sarūpaka* and so forth (according to *ka.*). It is called *samugga* because it "rises up together" (*samuggacchati*); [formed with] *kvi*. *Puṭa* in the sense of joining together (*saṃsilesane*); belonging to the *bhūvādi* class; [with] *a*.
*Pajjaddhaṃ methune*: Sexual intercourse. *Gāmadhamma* is the nature or conduct of village-dwellers;
here, by the word "village" (*gāma*), the village-dwellers themselves are meant, just as one says, "the village has arrived. It is the nature of the wicked, that is, of bad persons (*asappurisa*);

or, because it is the opposite of the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), it is called "untrue Dhamma" (*asaddhamma*). *Byaya* means destruction; it is called *byavāya* because strength (*bala*) is destroyed (*byayati*) by it, or else there is an insertion of the letter *v* in the middle. Alternatively:
*Avāya*: because increase (*vuḍḍhi*) has departed from it, it is *avāya*; *byavāya* is an intensive form of *avāya*. *Methuna*:

the conduct (*ācāra*) of pairs consisting of women and men who share the same desire; its figurative application (*upacāra*) extends to others. *Ramu*: in the sense of "to delight" (*ramane*), used either in the abstract state (*bhāve*) or as the instrument (*karaṇe*).

318. The group of four [terms] relates to marriage (*vivāha*). *Vaha*: in the sense of "to reach" (*pāpuṇe*), with the suffix *ṇo*. *Upayama*: preceded by *upa*, in the sense of "to cease" (*uparame*), with the suffix *a*. *Pāṇiggaha*: the grasping of the hand (*pāṇi*) by one living being (*pāṇin*) of the other. *Ubbāha*: derived from *nī* in the sense of "to lead" (*naye*), with the suffix *a*; here *pāṇipīḷana* (the pressing of hands) is also included.
The three groups of things desired for their own sake (dhamma-kāmattha) are spoken of. Conduct manifested through tradition is *dhamma*.

Pleasure born from the conjunction of sense object and sense faculty is *kāma*. All requisites are *attha*. When liberation is included, these things desired for their own sake—*dhamma*, *kāma*, and *attha*—are called the four groups.
Liberation (*mokkha*), which is dissociated from the three groups, is *nibbāna*. However, by means of the four factors beginning with *dhamma*, which possess equal power...
Through the fourfold exertions, the noble one is released from death (17.57).

319–320. *Khujja* has two [meanings]. One who avoids what is contemptible (*kucchita*) is a *khujja*; here, there is a substitution of *ka* for *kho*, and the suffix *ṇo*. *Gaḍi* is used in the sense of censure; the suffix *ulo* is added.

Three [terms] refer to a person with a short body. *Rasa* means sound; the suffix *so* is added. Or, one who does not attain the measure of a fathom (*byāma*) is a *vāmana*; this is an etymological derivation (*nerutta*).

*Rassa* and *vāmana* form a *dvanda* compound. Regarding *lakuḍi* in the sense of "dwarf": the suffix *a* is used in the sense of the base word itself, and the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of "one who is like that";
thus, one who moves (*ḍeti*) like a staff (*laku*), or like a small jar (*ghaṭikā*), is called a *lakuṇḍaka*.

The group of five [terms] refers to people who are lame. One who goes (*aṅgati*) by means of another is a *paṅguḷo*; the suffix is *ulo*. One who creeps (*sappati*) by means of a chair (*pīṭha*) as his habit is a *pīṭhasappī*.

Regarding "sappa-gamane" (snake-like gait) and "pakkho" (lame): [these occur] in two conditions. One whose modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*), such as walking and so forth, are severed is called "one whose deportments are severed" (*chinniriyāpatha*).
One whose shanks (*jaṅghā*) are gone, being like the axle (*akkha*) [of a chariot], is called "lame" (*pakkho*).
For just as movement cannot be accomplished when the axle of a chariot is broken, so too it is for him when his "axle-shank" is broken; this is the application of the simile.

Two [terms] for one who is lame (*khañja*). From the root *khaj* in the sense of "deficiency of movement," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class: *khañjatīti*, with the suffix *a*. From the root *khoḍ* in the sense of "obstruction of movement":
*khoḍī*. Two [terms] for one who is mute (*mūga*). Because he is unable to speak, he is like a deer; thus, he is *mūga*. With the suffix *issu*. He whose speech is empty is *suññavaca*.
A person who is crooked in his hands and so forth is called *kuṇī*. *Kuṇanaṃ* is *kuṇo*, meaning deficiency of the hands and so forth; he who possesses that is [called *kuṇī*].

*Kuṇī*: either from *kuṇa* (to contract) with the suffix *ī*, or from "it leads in a deformed way" (*kucchitaṃ nayati*), thus *kuṇī*; the nasalization (*ṇattaṃ*) is as in such usages as "crippled in hand" (*hatthena kuṇī*) or "crippled in foot" (*pādena kuṇī*).
[The following] two terms refer to people who look askance. From *vala* (to conceal) with the suffix *iro*.
It makes something deformed, thus *kekaro*, with the suffix *usse*.

321. *Dvayaṃ nikkesasīse*: "Nikkesa" means head (*sīsa*). [The root] *khal* is used in the sense of moving about (*khalana*) and accumulation (*sañcaya*); with the suffix *āṭ*, it becomes *nikkesa*. Because he possesses a head that is empty (*kha*), he is called *khallāṭa*;

the suffix is *ṭa*. Three terms refer to a shaven head (*khuramuṇḍasīsa*): *Muṇḍa* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; it means to break or cut (*khaṇḍana*), with the suffix *a*. *Bhaṇḍa* means to revile (*paribhāsana*); with the suffix *u* and the pleonastic suffix *ka*, it becomes *bhaṇḍaka*.

*Muṇḍaka* is also used here, as is *muṇḍika*. One who is empty of one eye in the middle of the eyes is called *kāṇa*. [The root] *kaṇa* is used in the senses of sound, movement, and closing the eyes; with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *kāṇa*. He "makes a sound" (*kaṇati*).
"One who has an eye that is closed is called *kāṇa* (one-eyed). However, regarding that closing of the eye, it occurs with only one eye.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries, it is stated: "One-eyed (*kāṇa*) means one whose one eye is blind, or one whose both eyes are blind" (*Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 1.1.132).
One who is empty of both eyes is called *andha* (blind); this is in the context of applying the term "blindness" to the act of seeing.

322. Two [terms] refer to one whose sense-faculties have perished. *Bandha* means "binding"; with the suffix *iro*, there is elision of the nasal (*na*). One whose hearing (*suti*)—that is, the ear—is deficient or impaired is *sutihīna*.

*Eḷa* is also used here. Three [terms] denote a state of illness in general. From the root *gila* (in the sense of "wasting away"), with the suffix *yu*, one in whom disease or sickness has arisen is *byādhita*.

From *ata* (in the sense of "going continuously"), with the suffix *uro* in the locative or agentive sense, one is *āturo* (beginning with a long vowel). *Āmayāvī*, *vikato*, *apaṭu*, *abbhamito*; *abbhānto* is also used here.
*Ummāda* is a specific disease consisting of the agitation of the *vāta* and other humors; one who possesses that is "insane" (*ummatta*). The suffix *-mada* occurs in the sense of insanity.

It is called *ummāda* because it intoxicates (*madayati*) by means of the aggravated *vāta* and other defects; this is the derivation (*ṇo*). From "hunchbacked" (*khujja*) up to "insane" (*ummatta*), these terms take the gender of the object they qualify (*vāccaliṅga*) due to their connection with the gender of the referent.

For example: a hunchbacked man (*khujjo puriso*), a hunchbacked woman (*khujjā itthī*), a hunchbacked neuter (*khujjaṃ napuṃsakaṃ*). An insane man (*ummatto puriso*), an insane woman (*ummattā itthī*).
A mad person; a neuter. 323. *Navaka* refers to one who is ill.
From the root *taki* (to live with difficulty), belonging to the *bhūvādi* class: that which intensely (*ā*) causes such [difficulty] is *ātaṅka*;

the suffix *a*. From the root *ama* (disease) with the suffix *yo*: or from *maya* (in the sense of going), or alternatively, from *ama* (disease) belonging to the *curādi* class: that which causes illness (*āmayati*), i.e., is afflicted, is *āmaya*.
*a.* There is no elision of the *kārita* suffix. *Vidha* means piercing; that which pierces is *byādhi*. [The suffix] *i* is added, and there is the insertion of the vowel *a*.
Or, it is *bādha*, meaning affliction; in that case, the augment *y* is inserted. Alternatively, *byādhi* is that in which there are various *ādhayaḥ*, which are mental torments.
For it is stated in the *Amarakośa* (8.28): "In the masculine, *ādhi* is mental anguish. *Roga* is disease; *gadā* is the weapon of Kuvera; *gada* is the name of Bhr̥tar̥ṣṇa’s son.
For in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha* it is said: “*Āmaya*, *āyudha*, and *gadā*. The root *ruj* means “disease”; with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the agent, *rujā* is feminine.
The state of being ill is *gelañña*. The roots *kal* and *gal* mean “to go” and “to count”; that by which one does not count (*na kalati*) is *akala*, which is the same as *akalla* (lo).
The root *bādh* means “affliction,” belonging to the *bhūvādi* class; the suffix *a*. Herein, *upatāpa* (torment) is also included.

Two [terms] for a disease of the throat: *sosa*. It is called *sosa* because it dries up (*soseti*) the seven elements, such as the nutrient essence (*rasa*), etc.; from the root *sus*, meaning "to dry," belonging to the *divādi* class, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Khi* means "destruction"; that which destroys is *khayo*; from the root *khi*, meaning "to destroy," with the suffix *a*. *Yakkhā* and *rājayakkhā* are also included here. *Yakkha* means "worship" (or "demon"), belonging to the *curādi* class.
324. Two [terms] for a disease of the nose: *pīnāsa*. That by which the nose is blocked is *pīnāsa*; it is also *pīnasa*.

According to Pāṇini 5.4.119, when forming a *bahubbīhi* compound with the prefix and the word "nose" (*nāsā*), they substitute *nasā* for *nāsā*. Furthermore, there is the elision of the letter *a* and the lengthening of the short vowel. "Drying up" (*soso*).
“Yakkhā and rājayakkhā; *patissāya* is cough (*pīnasa*), and *āpīnasa* is *patissāya*,” says Rabhasa. *Patissaya* is also found here.
In medical treatises (*vejjagantha*), the distinction between these two—*pīnasa* and *patissāya*—is stated as follows: “That which is constricted and dries up...”
The nose is indeed irritated by the smoke;
the person does not perceive odors or tastes.
One should know that this is the corrupted state caused by apīnasa.
The nose is blocked and congested,
with a thin discharge trickling from it;
there is a dripping, oozing, and trickling of phlegm.
Nittoda is in the pair of conch-shells;
in the state of existence (bhava),
there is sound and striking, characterized as "patissāya."
But here it is stated without distinction: the verbal root *sidh* preceded by *pati* has the meaning "to be afflicted. A disease born in the nose is "nasal disease" (*nāsikāroga*).
That which flows from the nostril is called "mucus" (*siṅghānikā*): [the root] *siṅgh* means "to sniff," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class;

that which sniffs is *siṅghānaṃ*, with the suffix *yu*; that which is born therein is *siṅghānikā*. It flows, i.e., trickles repeatedly, thus it is "flowing" (*assava*); [the root] *sū* means "to flow. Both [meanings apply].

*Vaṇa* means merely a wound. *Ara* occurs in the sense of going; *u*, *aru*, and *napuṃsaka* (neuter) are used only in this sense. *Vaṇa* means the crushing of a limb; it belongs to the *curādi* class, takes the suffix *a*, and thus forms *vaṇo*, which is not feminine.

There are two terms for a boil (*phoṭa*). *Phuṭa* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class in the sense of bursting open; *phoṭo* is formed with the suffix *ṇo*. *Pīḷa* means affliction; it belongs to the *curādi* class and takes the suffix *ṇvu*.
According to the rule "for a feminine [noun] ending in *a*, the suffix *ā* is added," one has *pīḷakā*; however, *pīḷaka*, *pīḷakā*, and *pīḷakaṃ* all occur in all three genders, as does *phoṭo*.

325. *Dvayaṃ* (two terms) refer to specific foul odors produced in wounds and the like. *Pubba* (pus): from the root *pū*, belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, with the suffix *a*. It means filling. *Pūya*: from the root *pū*, belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, meaning to spread or to have a foul odor.
*Dvayaṃ* (two terms) refer to the disease of the discharge of blood. *Rattātisāra*: the flowing (*saraṇa*) or going (*gamana*) beyond the normal state (*saṇṭhāna*) of red blood (*ratta-lohita*).
*Pakkhandikā*: that which leaps forth (*pakkhandati*) or discharges. From the root *kam*, meaning to step or move. [The suffix] *atiyava* is applied in the feminine.

Regarding “vātiti”: in the phrase “pakkamādīhinto ce,” the word *tissā* is included by the particle *ca*; there is elision of the final vowel of the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
In the case of the reduplication (*dvitte*), the following *k* is replaced by *kh* according to the rule beginning with *yadādi*, resulting in *pakkhandikā*.

In the pair [of terms] concerning *apamāra*: *saraṇa* means essence (*sāra*). That from which the essence has departed is *apamāra*; here, *sa* is replaced by *ma*. In the other case, there is the insertion of the letter *m*.
The term *dvayaṃ* refers to the division of the foot. A *pādaphoṭo* is the cracking, splitting, or bursting of the foot;

[the root] *phuṭ* means to split. It is called *vipādikā* because the foot becomes deformed (*virūpa*) due to this condition acting as its cause. At the end of the compound, the suffix *-ka* is added, with the preceding vowel remaining as it was; or alternatively, it is called *vipādikā* because the foot is afflicted (*vipajjamāna*) by being torn apart (*vidārīyamāna*).
326. Two [terms] regarding the disease of the swollen scrotum (*vaṅkhaṇaroga*): a disease that has reached growth is a "grown disease" (*vuḍḍhiroga*).

A scrotum filled with wind is a "wind-scrotum" (*vātaṇḍa*). Two [terms] regarding the disease of elephantiasis (*sīpada*): because it lacks firmness, the foot is loose; this is "elephantiasis" (*sīpada*), with the loss of color and so forth.
That which has a heavy foot—its state is "heaviness of foot" (*bhārapādatā*).

The word *kaṇḍuya* consists of five syllables. From the root *kaṇḍ*, meaning "to scratch," with the suffix *u*, there is lengthening (*dīgha*), resulting in *kaṇḍū*; it is like the word *vadhū*. With the feminine suffix *tī*, it becomes *kaṇḍūtī*, which is like *assū*.

Because it belongs to the *curādi* group, with the suffix *ya*, it becomes *kaṇḍūyā*, where there is no elision of the *ya*. From the root *khajj*, meaning "to eat," "to steal," or "to torment," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, with the suffix *u*, there is the suffix *yuṃ*, resulting in *kaṇḍūvanaṃ*, which is like *assū*.
There is a substitution for *u* (*uvādeso*) and lengthening (*dīgho*).
327. A triad concerning *kacchu*. That which is called “the skin disease” (*khasuroga*). Regarding *pātyattāna*: *pāma*, *mana*; it possesses *pāmā* [as its suffix];
it is masculine, belonging to the *rājādi* group. Specifically, it scrapes or licks; thus, *vitacchikā*. From the root *taccha* in the sense of making thin, with the suffix *ṇvu*.
There is also a reading *vivacchikā* or *viccaccikā* (Amara 16.53). From *vaccha* in the senses of reviling and threatening, belonging to the *bhūvādi* class. *Kaca* in the sense of binding.
*U*, and its *chatta* [substitute], *dvitta*, etc. A pair ending in *tila* and *kāla* is capable [of being combined]. Among them, the pair [is applied] in the sense of swelling (*sotha*).

The root *su* is in the sense of motion and increase (*bhūvādi*), with the suffix *tha*. In the suffix *tha*, as in *sayathu*, there is the addition of *us* and the elision of the final vowel (*ussatta*), and the augment *y*.

*Sopho* is also included here. *Sopho* is that which causes swelling (*phāyati*) extensively; *phāya* is in the sense of increase. For *phāya*, there is the substitution of *pho*; this is etymological (*nerutto*).

Two [terms] for a disease caused by enemies (*arisaroga*). *Dunnāma*: because of its inauspiciousness, its name is "ill-famed" (*dunnāma*); here the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base itself, or in the sense of contempt (*kucchā*).
*Dunnāmā* is a woman with a long girth. *Arisaṃ*: it hisses (*sasati*) like an enemy (*ari*); *sasa* is in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*), with the suffix *kvip*;

or *ara* is in the sense of going, and *isa*. Two [terms] for the disease of vomiting (*vamanaroga*). *Chadda*: to vomit; from the *cur*-class, with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Vamu*: in the sense of ejecting upward.
*Thu*. *Vamidhupyatra*. *Chaddikā*, *vami*—these two are feminine; *vamathu* is masculine. (328–329) Two terms refer to torment (*paritāpa*).
From the root *du* in the sense of torment, with the suffix *thu* from the *tanādi* group: *paritapanaṃ*, *santāpanaṃ*, *paritāpo*. Two terms refer to a mole or dark spot (*tilakāḷaka*).
It is called *tilaka* because it arises in the shape of a sesame seed (*tila*). It is called *tilakāḷaka* because it arises having become black like a sesame seed.

“Mahāvireko” is called “visūcikā. It is *sūcikā* because it completely (*nissesa*) purges (*suca*) or goes away (*gacchati*). The root *suca* (or *suca*) belongs to the *bhūvādi* class, meaning "to go.
Alternatively, from the root *suca* meaning "to purify" (*soceyya*), it is *visūcikā* because it purifies completely. Or, it is *visūcikā* because it pierces specifically like a needle (*sūci*).
Because it involves a great evacuation of mucus, it is a "great purge" (*mahāvireko*). The root *rica* means "separation" and "cleansing," with the suffix *ṇo*.

There are seven types of internal diseases, beginning with hemorrhoids (*bhagaṇḍala*). Among them, *bhagaṇḍala* is a specific kind of ulcer arising near the anus; it is feminine. [The term] "bhaga" means the female organ (*yoni*);
it is derived from the root *dṛ*, meaning "to split," with the suffix *-anta* applied according to conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), and the form *bhagaṇḍala* is established.

The root *dṛ* (in the sense of splitting) belongs to the *bhū-vādi* class; with the suffix *lat* (present participle), it becomes *bhagaṇḍala*. *Bhagaṇḍara* is also used here. *Meha* refers to urinary disease (*mutta-meha*), and that is characterized by excessive urination.
Diabetes is of many kinds: *madhumeha*, *rattameha*, *sukkameha*, and so forth. The root *miha* (meaning "to sprinkle") belongs to the *bhūvādi* class;

that which sprinkles urine is *meha*, with the suffix *ṇa*. *Jara* means "disease. It belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; that which decays is *jara*, with the suffix *a*; this is the well-known term for old age. *Kāsa* means "coughing" and also "splendor," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class;

that which coughs is *kāsa*, with the suffix *ṇa*, or alternatively, *kāsa* is that which exists badly (*kucchitaṃ asati*), with the prefix *ku-* added. *Sasa* means "breathing"; the act of breathing is *sasanaṃ*.
*Sāsa*: "Sāsa" means one who has a cough (*sāsana*); or, it is *sāsa* because he possesses that cough. *Kuṭa* means to cut; with the suffix *ṭha*, it becomes *kuṭṭha*.

By general rule, [the suffix] applies to changes in the skin. However, when applied to what is moistened, it is *sitta*. *Sūla* means pain; it belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; thus, *sūla*. *Viddadhi*, *asmarī*, *muttakicchā*, and so forth, are many different types of diseases. *Pajjaddhaṃ* refers to a physician (*vejja*).

One who knows the knowledge (*vijjā*) known as life-span measurement (*āyubbeda*) is a physician (*vejjo*). [The suffix] *ṇa* is applied here according to the rule "after *rāgā*, this [suffix] occurs in other meanings."
And [the suffix] *ṇa* [is applied]; or, in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), one who finds (*vindati*) is a physician (*vejjo*); [the suffix] *ṇya*, with *dy* becoming *j*.

One who heals (*bhisajjati*) or treats (*cikicchati*) is a healer (*bhisakko*); [the suffix] *a*, with *j* becoming *k*. One who removes disease by habit is a disease-remover (*rogahārī*); [the suffix] *ṇī*.

This word *hara* also functions in the senses of bringing and taking away—as in "pleasing" (*manoharo*) or "removing suffering" (*dukkhaharo*)—but here it means taking away. The root *kit* is used in the sense of removing disease.

The root *bhū* and so forth. One who treats (*tikicchati*) is a physician (*tikicchaka*); the suffixes *cha*, *ṇvu*, and the doubling of the initial syllable are applied. A healer of disease (*agadakara*) is also included here;
one who makes (*karoti*) beings free from disease (*agada*) is a healer of disease (*agadakara*), with the suffix *ṇa* applied in the sense of the object and so forth.
330. There are two terms for a physician who extracts arrows: a physician who extracts (*nīharaṇa*) arrows such as shafts that have entered the body is a surgeon (*sallavejja*).
It is called a *sallakatta* (surgeon) because it cuts or removes the aforementioned dart; the root *kat* means to cut, with the suffix *to*. The pair [of terms] refers to medical treatment.

*Tikicchā* is the act of healing (*tikicchana*), with the suffix *a* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The prefix *pati-* is used with the verb *karoti* in the sense of healing; for the root *kṛ*, there is the suffix *riyā*. The tetrad refers to medicinal herbs.
This belongs to physicians, hence it is *bhesajja*; the suffix *ṇya* is applied. That in which no disease (*gada*) exists is *agada*. This belongs to physicians.

Medicine (*bhesaja*), no. Regarding *usa* (heat/burning): it is called *osadha* because it causes the curing of disease; [the suffix] *dha*. Alternatively, *osadhī* refers to a substance that is not yet compounded; that which is compounded with those is *osadha*.
[The term] *jāyuppa*: from the root *ji* (to conquer), [suffix] *ṇu*. 331. The triad [of terms] relates to health.
Because they act harmfully, they "lie" (*sentī*) in the body in a contemptible manner; thus they are *kusā*, i.e., diseases. They...

It is *kusala* because it reaps (*lunāti*) and cuts away (*chindati*). *Anāmaya* is the absence of illness (*āmaya*); this is an *abyayībhāva* compound. *Ārogya* is the state of being healthy (*aroga*).

"The wholesome, the healthy, and health" (*kusalānāmayārogya*) is a collective *dvanda* compound. These two [terms] refer to people who are free from illness. The root *kal* is used in the senses of moving and counting.

One is called *kalla* (fit) because one moves at ease (*yathāsukha*) in all postures; thus *kalla*. "That which is suitable for the time" (*kālaṃ khamati*) is *kalya*, meaning healthiness; in that state...
"Appointed and fit," according to the *Aṅguttara-nikāya-ṭīkā*. That in which there is no illness (*āmaya*) is "free from illness" (*nirāmaya*).

This is also stated here. "Conduct" (*vutti*) refers to a praiseworthy mode of living; it is called "consolation" (*assatthī*). However, regarding a person who has emerged from disease, the term is "recovered" (*ullāgho*);

for "lāgha" means capability, and this prefix (*usaddo*) signifies freedom from disease. It is called the "Human Chapter" (*naravaggo*) because humans are its subject matter and because humans are its primary focus.
The commentary on the Naravagga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Catubbaṇṇavagga. 332.
Regarding *vaṃsa* as the limit of continuity (*santati*): from the root *kula* (in the sense of lineage) with the suffix *ṇa*, we have *kula*; and from *vana* (in the sense of association).

*Saṃtanu* means expansion; hence *saṃtati*. *Abhimukhaṃ janeti* (produces facing toward) thus *abhijano*. *Go* refers to a name (*abhidhāna*) and also to intellect (*buddhi*); that which protects these is *gotta*. *Gotra* is the same.
Alternatively, *gotta* is that which protects (*tāyati*) the sound (*sadda*) of the *go*; *tā* [is used] in the sense of protecting.

*Anu-* prefixed to *i* in the sense of going, with the suffix *a* in the instrumental sense. From the root *tanoti*, *saṃtati* [is formed]; there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), and it is feminine.
The poets consider *santati* (continuity) to refer to lineage (*panti*), extension (*vitthāra*), and clan (*gotta*);
it also refers to succession in existence (*bhava*) and to sons and daughters.

The four castes—Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—are the families (*kulāni*). For these are called "castes" (*vaṇṇa*) because they are to be praised (*vaṇṇetabbato*) and established (*ṭhapetabbato*) due to their mutual lack of intermixture. The word *vaṇṇa* [is used] in the sense of establishing.

333–334. *Chakkaṃ* refers to the group of six [terms] concerning the noble (*kulīna*). One who is descended from a family is a *kulina*; *ina* means "descendant. A beautiful person is a *sajjana*. One who accomplishes the welfare of others (*saparattha*) is a *sādhu*;

[this is derived from] the root *sādha*, meaning "to accomplish," with the suffix *u*. One who is good in an assembly (*sabhā*) is a *sabhyo*; [this is formed by] the suffix *yo* after the word *sādhu*. The root *aya* means "to go.

One who is to be approached or drawn near (*ayitabbo*) is an *ayyo*; [this is formed by] the suffix *yo* in the sense of the object (*kammani*). One who is descended from a great family is a *mahākulo*; [this is formed by] the suffix *ṇo*.
The term *bhūbhuj* is used as a general designation for a king. Because he shines (*rājate*) with extraordinary splendor, he is a *rājā*; the root *rāj* means "to shine.

One who rules over the earth (*bhū*), which is abundant (*bhūya*), is a *bhūpati*; alternatively, one who protects (*pāleti*) the earth is a *bhūpati*, from the root *pā* meaning "to protect," with the vowel shortened.

One who is the lord (*issara*) of the earth is a *patthiva*; the suffix *-ṇa* is applied, with the doubling of the consonant and the change of the vowel to *i*. One who protects the world (*jagati*), that is, the earth, is a *jagatipāla*, in the sense of the object of the action.
No. He is a lord of the quarters (*disānaṃ pati*), thus a *disampati*. Or, he protects the quarters or the meaning of the quarters, thus a *disampati*;

[this form arises] from shortening [the vowel] and the insertion of the *niggahīta* [anusvāra]. He enjoys the earth (*bhūmiṃ bhuñjati*), thus a *bhūbhujo*; [the root] *bhuja* is used in the senses of protecting and eating; here it means protecting, belonging to the *rudhādi* class. *Mahikhitopi* is also used here.
[The root] *khi* is used in the senses of dwelling and going; having gone to the earth (*mahiṃ akhi*), he is a *mahīkhito*.

335. Regarding the term *pajjaddha* (half-born) applied to one consecrated on the head (*muddhābhisitta*) who is of kṣatriya birth: this is because of the statement, “the royal offspring (*rājañña*) and the kṣatriya.
A son of a king who is a kṣatriya is a *rājañña*; the suffix *-añña* is used for offspring. According to the *Rabhasa*, “A kṣatriya has the lineage (*khatta*) of the *viras*;

he bears the marks of both the *rājañña* and the twice-born (*dvija*),” as these are synonyms found in the *Ratana-kośa*. A son of a *khatta* is a *khattiya*; the suffix *-iya* is seen after the word *khatta* when denoting offspring.
He is called a *khattiya* because he is the lord (*adhipati*) of the fields; thus, a king who conforms to the traditional conventions is so designated.

Furthermore, that designation applies even to those consecrated on the head (*muddhābhisitta*) because they originate from him—this is the sense of the suffix *-essatta*. The word *khatta* is derived from *khattha* with the suffix *-a*, and then the suffix *-ṇo*.

He is "consecrated on the head" (*muddhābhisitta*) because at the time of the investiture of sovereignty, he is sprinkled on the head by kṣatriya maidens and others with water from the Gaṅgā, which is pure, fragrant, and turned to the right.

First is the *khattiya*. However, due to his preeminence (*tappabhavatā*), those who are not formally consecrated are also designated as *muddhābhisitta* (anointed on the head), just as one born in the lineage of Brahmabāhu is called a "Brahmabāhuja.
For the followers of other schools hold the view that he is called "Bāhuja" because he was born from Brahmabāhu.
That king to whom all neighboring vassals bow down without exception is called an *adhissara*. [End of section 18.2. A sentient being (*satta*).

That which is adjacent (*lagga*) to another is *samantā*; the territory immediately bordering one's own domain is [called] *samantā*. Those who belong to that immediate vicinity are *sāmantā*, namely the neighboring kings.
Regarding the two [types of] universal monarchs (*cakkavattin*): one who is the lord of all lands is *sabbabhūmī*, with the suffix *-ṇya*.

One is called a *cakkavattī* because he turns (*vattate*) the conduct of a king—such as the taming of the unruly and so forth—by means of the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) brought forth by his merit; or, he causes the wheel-treasure to turn (*vatteti*). Thus ends the section on the Wheel-turning Monarch.

He is called a *cakkavattī* because he moves through the sky before himself; or because he causes the wheel of merit (*puññacakkam*), or the fourfold wheel, to turn among beings, or because those [beings] turn toward him;
or because he possesses the conduct practiced for twelve years and the ten royal virtues (*dasarājadhamma*) for the purpose of producing the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*).
In that regard, there is righteous protection, defense, and security for his household and his army.

The tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch consists of: making arrangements among the khattiyas, those devoted to them, the brahmins and householders, the people of the towns and countryside, the ascetics and brahmins, and the beasts and birds;
the prohibition of unrighteous acts; the provision of wealth for the poor; and approaching ascetics and brahmins to pose questions.
This very same duty applies to householders and those born as birds.
Or, having distinguished them separately, he is a *cakkavattin* because he sets in motion the wheels of command and Dhamma among beings in all twelve kinds of islands.

Alternatively, he is a *cakkavattin* because he sets in motion the wheels of command and Dhamma among beings in all four continents. Any other king who does not rule over all the earth—such as a neighboring ruler (*sāmanta*), a local lord (*bhūpa*), or a master of a single province (*maṇḍalissara*)—is not a *cakkavattin*.
This is because such a person is the master only of a delimited province (*maṇḍala*) defined by the extent of his own dominion, and not of the entire circle of the earth.
Also "lord of the circle" (maṇḍalissara). Here, by the two names "ruler of all lands" (sabbabhūma) and "wheel-turner" (cakkavatti), the king who is lord of the four continents is indicated;

furthermore, by the term "supreme lord" (adhissara)—which is spoken here including those yet to come—the king who is lord of one continent is indicated, and by the term "lord of the circle," the regional king (padesissa) is indicated.
Alternatively, by the term "lord of the circle," the lord of one continent [is indicated].
The king is described as a ruler of a province, together with the remaining kings, royal ministers, and so forth, down to the common people.
336. Two [terms] regarding divisions of kings. Those whose skins are delicate, smooth, and unexposed are the Licchavis.
"Licchavis and Vajjis" is a *dvanda* compound. Two [terms] regarding the queen in the family of the Perfectly Enlightened One; [she was born] in the Sakya clan, which arose earlier.

They are called *Sakyas* because they are born [there]. *Sakya* is also [a term for them]. That which exists among the *Sakyas* is *Sākiya*; [the suffix] *iya* is used, with the elision of *ya* and the lengthening of the vowel.
This group of five [names] refers to the mother of the Venerable Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha. *Bhaddā* means auspicious (*kalyāṇa*) and happy (*sokhya*).

She is called *Bhaddā* because she is auspicious by virtue of her family conduct, physical form, and so forth. *Kaccānā* is the feminine form of *Kacca*; this word *apacca* is always neuter when it means "son."
"And he becomes a son. Having reflected, "Just as Rāhu [seizes] the moon, this son of mine desires to seize my departure;

therefore, he must have the name Rāhula," the Venerable Rāhula—who was addressed by his father as "Rāhu is born, a bond is born"—being desirous of training, is the one here referred to as Rāhula. His mother is Rāhulamātā. A "bimba" is so called...
*Śarīram*: because it is endowed with a body of extraordinary beauty, it is like a *bimba* (an image); or, from the root *vam*, *bo*; for *va*, there is *batta*.
*Yaśas* means retinue and fame; she who bears (*dhāreti*) these is *Yaśodharā*. *Manādittā* means a horse. 337–339.
Of those Kṣatriyas whose wealth (*dhanam*) is a hundred—of what sort is that wealth? It is stored away (*nidhānagam*) in the earth and so forth.
The activity proceeded by way of deposits; of those hundred pieces of wealth, how great was their measure?
A hundred crores. By what limit? At the very least, by the lowest portion or the lowest limit, there were a hundred crores.
Furthermore, the daily allowance—the kahāpaṇa to be used day by day—was merely twenty ambaṇas.
Those kṣatriyas who possess such wealth are called “great kṣatriya householders” (*khattiyamahāsālā*). Those whose great wealth consists of vast riches are “great householders” (*mahāsālā*);
for instance, even a single *ambaṇa* measure of rice is worth eleven *doṇa*.

Those twice-born Brāhmaṇas who possess eighty crores of wealth in the form of hoarded treasures, while their daily expenditure is only ten *ambaṇa* measures of *kahāpaṇa* coins, those twice-born are called “great twice-born householders” (*dvijamahāsālā*).

Regarding "Nidhānage vaḷañje ca": when there is half of the wealth of those great brahmin householders—that is, when there is a portion equal to half of their wealth—they would be called "great householder householders" (gahapatimahāsālā). In both cases, the limit of wealth is defined by the lower boundary. 340.

One who is neither inferior nor superior, but established in the middle grade of authority—such as a prince, a general, or a chief minister—is a "high official" (mahāmatta). He is a "high official" because his measure (mattā) or status is great.
This is a declension based on the distinction of form (rūpabheda), following the neuter pattern. [As in: "In a high official by nature, in supreme wisdom..."
“*Padhāna* is neuter; however, when it signifies unity (*ekatta*), it is always masculine.

So says Rabhasa. Furthermore, Vopālita states in the section on masculines: “*Mahāmatta* and *paṭṭhāna* [are masculine]. That which stands out (*pakaṭṭha*) is *paṭṭhāna*; this may also be seen in verses 983 and 1123 of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*. The group of five [terms] refers to a counselor.

A minister (*saciva*) is one whose primary quality is wisdom (*mati-padhāna*), a companion. *Manta* is the determination of what ought to be done (*itikattabbatā-vadhāraṇa*); because of its connection with that, [the term is applied].
*Mantinī*. The suffix *-inī* is used in the sense of "possessing" (*assatthi-atthe*). Alternatively, she is *mantinī* because she leads by means of counsel (*mantena nayati*).
Or, *manti* refers to one who possesses counsel (*mantayogā*), and *nī* means "she leads" (*netī*); thus, she is *mantinī*, being both *manti* and *nī*. There is also a reading, *matisacivamantinī*;
in that case, it is a *dvanda* compound of two or three words. She lives together with the king, hence *sajīvo*. She is associated or united, hence *sacivo*. *Saca*...
In *samavāya*, there is the augment *i* after *va*. One who exists together (*amā*) with the king through counsel in all affairs is an *amacca* (minister);
here, *amā* is a particle used in the sense of "together," and the suffix *ccap* is applied. The word *amacca* applies to one who possesses the status of a co-liver.
There are two terms for a commander-in-chief: one who leads an army (*sena*) is a *senānī*; the lord of armies (*camū*) is a *camūpati*.

341. One who provides instruction (*upadaṭṭhari*) for legal disputes (*vivādānaṃ*) and transactions (*vohārānaṃ*), such as deposits (*nyāsādīnaṃ*), loans (*iṇādāna*), and the division of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*);

one who sees transactions through dice (*akkhe vohāre passati*) is called *akkhadasso*, [formed with] the suffix *ṇo*. These are the judges of the law (*dhammādhikaraṇiyo*). Here too, there is the term *pucchāvivāko* (one who decides questions) and *pañhavivāko* (one who decides problems).
*Pajjaḍḍhaṃ* means at the gate. One appointed at the door is a *dovāriko*, [formed with] the suffix *ṇiko* and the augment *okāra*. He wards off (*paṭiharati*) or makes known (*viññāyati*).

*Tena* means "by that," [forming] *paṭihāro*. *Ṇo* is a suffix. One who stands at the gate is *dvāraṭṭho*; here, the suffix *ko* is used in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*). Thus, it means a gatekeeper. *Dvāraṭṭhito* is also used here in the sense of a gatekeeper.

342. The group of bodyguards for kings is considered *anīkaṭṭho*. And in the *Amaramālā*: "That which is the protective class of kings is designated as *anīkaṭṭho*. One who stands with the *anīka*, meaning a multitude, is *anīkaṭṭho*;

the suffix *ṇo* is applied. Two terms refer to an old man: *kañcukaṃ* (cloak) and *coḷaṃ* (garment); because of his association with these, he is called *kañcukī*. One who finds (*vindati*) sorrow (*soka*) is *sovidallo*. The root *vida-*...
In *lobha*, there is *lo* [as a substitute], which is a group of consonants (*kalopa*). *Thāpeti* and *sovidhī* also occur here. There are two [terms] for a servant (*sevaka*).

One who lives after the master is called an *anujīvī*; [the suffix] *ṇī*. *Seva* means "to serve"; [the root] *bhū*, [suffix] *ṇvu*. *Atthī* also occurs here. *Attha* is used in the sense of "requesting. *Attha* is what is requested; it is a blessing (*āsīsa*);
because of its connection with that, it is *atthī*.
343. *Dvayaṃ adhikamatte*. Because of being superior (*adhikattā*) in villages, there is superiority; this "superiority" (*adhika*) is his oversight, his lordship (*issatta*).
He acts as one who is superior, thus he is "the superior one" (*adhikato*). These two are names for both the *thāyuka* and the *gopa*.
Among them, the *thāyuka* is the superior one in a single village, while the *gopa* is the superior one in many villages. And it is said in the *Amarakosa*: "The *thāyuka* is the superior one..."
"In the village, the cowherd [is master] among villages; he is the lord even over the wealth of cattle. Thus it was said by Rudda. "In the villages, the cowherd is the overseer;
he is the beloved even amidst the herds of cattle. This is from the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.
The pair [of terms] is the name for both types of wealth: gold and silver. "Hirañña" refers to unworked gold and so forth.

In this context, one who is engaged in that [work] is a *heraññika* (money-changer). Regarding the words *kana*, *ditti*, *gati*, and *kantī*: the prefix *ni-* becomes *nikkha*, which refers to a transformation of gold and so forth;
engagement (*niyoga*) in that [work] is *nikkhika*. Specifically, however, one who deals with gold is a *bhorika*.

The word *bhūri* means "gold," and because of its connection with that, one is a *bhorika*. One who deals with silver is a *nikkhika*; therefore, in both cases, the term *heraññika* applies to the general category alone. And it has been said:
“A *bhorika* has gold as its outer casing;
a *nikkha*, however, has silver as its outer casing”—thus it is said in the *Amarakośa*.
A neighboring king who surrounds one’s own territory on all sides in a circular fashion, being intent on conquest, is called an enemy (*sattu*).

Because of their adherence to a single purpose. Beyond that, a friend who is one interval away from the territory of the seeker of victory (*vijigīsu*) is [a neutral] because of performing a single task and providing assistance.

However, one situated outside the circle (*maṇḍala*) of the enemy, the seeker of victory, and the friend—standing in a distant circle and completely separated from the territory of the seeker of victory—who, despite having superior power, neither harms nor assists, is a neutral (*udāsīna*), because of being situated in a distant circle and providing assistance. In the distant circle...
*Āsatīti udāsīno*: the prefix *upa-* [in *upāsa*] means "to serve"; [the suffix] *yu*, [the ending] *assi*, and the augment *dāgama*.
One who takes the heel (*paṇhi*) and follows behind one who is attacking the enemy and desiring victory for the sake of the enemy’s welfare is a *paṇhiggāha*.
“The heel (*paṇhi*) is the rear foot of the victor,” according to the *Ratanakosa*. “The heel (*paṇhi*) is on the foot and on the back of the array (*byūha*),” according to *Tikaṇḍasesa* 3.3.134.
*Tikaṇḍasesa*: “*Paṇhi*, *pacchima-bhāge*, *pāda-mūla*, *oma-diṭṭhi-su*, *senā-piṭṭhe*, and *kumbhiyañca*”—thus [it is stated] in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*.
344–345. *Diṭṭhantaṃ* means an enemy (*ripu*). Because he is the opposite of a friend (*mitra*), he is an *amitta*. He is a *ripu* because he causes harm (*rapati*);

[the suffixes] *u*, *ittaṃ*, *rapa*, *lapa*, *japa*, and *jappa* are used in the sense of speaking. One who possesses enmity (*vera*) or opposition is a *verī*; [the suffix] *ī* is used because he is a cause of suffering.
In the sense of "like" (*iva*), the suffix *akāra* is applied [to form] *sapatta*. [The root] *ara* means "going," and because it belongs to the *bhū-vādi* class, the augment (*āgama*) is added.

*Sada* means "sitting," and as it belongs to the *bhū-vādi* class, it forms *sattu*, which also refers to barley flour. *Ara* means "going"; one who goes against (*vera*) or causes distress (*mara*) is an *ari* (enemy), ending in a short vowel *i*.

The compound of the four terms beginning with *sapatta* is a *dvanda*; according to the rule "a consonant followed by a disjunction [is doubled]," by the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*) in the sutta, the single letter *t* [is doubled].
And there is elision [of the suffix]. *Paccattha* means standing against; one who is connected with that is a *paccatthika* (adversary), meaning one who moves in opposition.
*Pantha* means going; it belongs to the *curādi* class. *Paripantha* is a place of leakage (a danger); one who is connected with that is a *paripanthī* (ambusher).

A side that is opposed is a *paṭipakkha* (opponent) or a companion in opposition; likewise, a *vipakkha* (adversary). That which is not beneficial is *ahita* (unwholesome). One who delights in harming is called *paratī*.

*Paro*, *kvi*. One who moves (*amati*) or goes (*gacchati*) by way of being an adversary is a *paccāmitto* (enemy); from the root *ama* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *to*, and doubling of the consonant.
That from which no calamity (*īti*) or misfortune exists is *anīto*; [from that] an *amitto* (friend). Its opposite is *paccanīto*;

that very same thing is *paccanīko*. Its *ko* suffix is like that of *niyako*. One who possesses hostility is a *virodhī*; [the suffix] *ī*. The roots *disa* and *dusa* are in the sense of "displeasure" (*appīti*), belonging to the *divādi* class.

Because of the habit of hating (*vidussana-sīlatā*), one is called *viddesī* (one who hates). *Dvittaṃ* and *issettaṃ* [are derived similarly]. The word *diso* means "one who hates. It is formed from the root *du* with the suffix *a*. With the suffix *tap*, it becomes *diṭṭho*;
here, there is a substitution of *ṭṭh* for the end of the verbal root. *Dvesaṇo*, *duhadayo*, *dassu*, *sāttavo*, and *abhighātī* are also used in this sense.

The pair [of terms] refers to compliance (*anukūlana*). *Anurodho* is the act of following along; it ends in the suffix *ṇo*. The root *rudha* means "obstructing. *Anuvattanaṃ* is the proceeding in accordance with what is suitable; it is formed from the roots *vatu* and *vatta* meaning "to proceed," as well as *bhū* and *yu*.
346. *Pañcakaṃ mittasāmaññe*. [The root] *mida* (to be moist) belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; with the suffix *to*, it becomes *mitta*. [The term] *vayaso* means "equal in age" (*vayasā tulyo*).
One should consult the Pāṇinian rule 4.4.91 regarding the suffix *ya* added to the words *mūla* and *vayas* to form a name.

Alternatively, one who moves together through all duties is a *vayasa*; from the root *vaya* (to go), with the substitution of the letter *sa* for *saha*. [One who] goes together in duties is a *vayasa*.

*Sahāyo* means "one who has a companion in going" (*aya-gamane*); it is the state of having a companion (*sahassa sābhāvo*), as in *sahadhammiko*. Alternatively, *saha* means loss (*hāni*) and *ayo* means gain (*vuḍḍhi*);
that which possesses these is *sahāyo*, a three-word *bahubbīhi* compound, as in *parakkamādhigatasampadā*. Or else, loss and gain are *hāyā*;
with the elision of the *n* (*nilopo*), that which possesses them is *sahāyo*, just as in the case of *sasadda* in examples such as *sapakkhako* and *salomako*.
Because its meaning is present. "One who has a beautiful heart" is *suhadayo*; [here] there is elision (*alopa*), and the *dy* becomes *j*, thus it is *suhajjo*.

It occurs with the prefix *sa-* in the sense of enduring. Endurance is non-resentment; here there is elision of *ha*, and it means a friend, a king, and so forth. Being equal (*samāna*), he is known or esteemed as a friend;

here there is elision of *ya*, and the nature of *samāna* becomes *sabhāva*. *Siniddho* and *sniddho* also occur here in the sense of a companion. This is according to the rule for the seven cases of the word *sakhi*.

But they behave with Mettiyā. "Sakhimhi bhavaṃ sakhyaṃ" means "friendship exists in a friend. It is called *sattapadīna* because it is understood through seven steps (*sattahi padehi avagamyati*), according to Amarakośa 18.12;
hence the suffix *-ino*. The pair [of terms] refers to inseparable friends.
One who associates at all times is *sambhatto*; the root *bhaj* is used in the sense of "service," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class. It is firm (*daḷho*).

A steadfast friend (*thiro mitto*) is a firm friend (*daḷhamitto*). The two terms [“*sanditthiko*” and “*diṭṭhamattasanto*”] refer to a friend seen for a short time. He is “seen” (*sandittho*) because he is to be looked upon for some time;

the prefix *sam-* here is devoid of meaning. The root *dis-* means to see; seeing is “seen” (*diṭṭha*). That which has this as its measure (*matta*) is “measured by what is seen” (*diṭṭhamattako*); the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). 347.

The two terms refer to a wandering person (*carapuriso*) who wanders merely in the form of an ascetic (*tāpasa*) and so forth. One who “wanders” (*carati*), that is, knows the enemy’s realm (*paracakkam*), is a “spy” (*caro*).

*a*, *cāropi*, *ṇo*. A hidden man (*guḷhapurisa*), a guarded man (*guttapurisa*). Of appropriate appearance (*yathārahavaṇṇa*), with a vow (*paṇidhi*), eating little (*appasapa*), and contact (*phassa*) is also here.

Among these, the first two [terms] refer to standing and walking by way of the merchant’s, the Sibali’s, the monk’s, and the Kaccāyana’s dress, etc. The others refer to those who have come here as if they were members of the army.
Appearance (*vaṇṇa*) means mode; "of appropriate appearance" means of appropriate mode. By means of which one is able to recognize the enemy's army, possessing that mode.

*Itthattha* (this meaning). That in which the knowable (*ñeyya*) is desired is *paṇidhi*; thus it is derived from *paṇidhīyate*. *Apasappa*: that which creeps away (*apa-sappati*) or moves away; thus it is *apasappa*. *Phassa*:
from the roots *phusa* in the sense of "to touch" or "to afflict";

thus it is *phassa*. The triad refers to travelers. One who goes on a road (*pathe*) is a *pathāvī*; [the suffix] *vī* is added, and the vowel is lengthened. With the suffix *ika*, it becomes *pathika*. One who goes by habit on a journey or road (*addhani magge*) is an *addhagū*. *Addhaga* is also used here.

Two [terms] for a messenger (*dūta*): *du* (in the sense of "to burn") and *to*. He carries a message or verbal communication by means of this; thus he is a "carrier" (*harati*). Two [terms] for an astrologer (*jotisika*):
one who calculates is a calculator (*gaṇaka*), with the suffix *ṇvu*. One who knows a specific time, a moment (*muhutta*), is a "moment-knower" (*muhuttika*);
there is no vowel lengthening due to the inclusion of the suffix *vāg*. Here too are included: *saṃvacchara*, *jotisika*, *devaññū*, *mohutta*, *ñāṇika*, and *kātantika*.
One who knows that which ends in *kānta* (the suffix *kta*) is a *kātantika*. (348) Regarding the two terms for a scribe:

from the root *likh* in the sense of "writing," with the suffixes *bhū* and *ṇvu*, [we have *lekhaka*]. That which comes into being through *lipi*—that is, by means of instruction regarding ink—is *lipi*;

it refers to the configuration of letters. One who makes that is a *lipikāra*. Regarding *akkharacaṇo* and *akkharacuñcu*: here, *cana* is in the sense of giving, with the suffix *bhū*; *cañcu* is in the sense of movement.
*Melānandā* is ink-stone; *melandhu* is an ink-well;
*melā* is ink-water; and *pattañjana* is ink for both [types of writing].
A pen is a brush for ink; it is also called a brush for ink-characters.
The messenger of praise, one with a safe journey, the letter,
and the bearer of the oral message; the golden tablet, the gold for its binding,
the place for writing, the book-chamber, and the seal which serves as the means of authentication.
Two [terms] refer to *vaṇṇa*. That by which meaning (*attha*) is praised (*vaṇṇīyati*) or made manifest is *vaṇṇa*; [the root] *vaṇṇ* means "to make manifest.
It is called *akkhara* because it does not harden (*na kharati*) nor perish (*na khīyati*); [the roots] *khara* mean "destruction" and *khi* means "decay," and in that case, *ara* is the suffix.
*Likhana*, *lipi*, and *likhi*—these refer to the arrangement of letters (*vaṇṇasaṇṭhāna*). *Lipi* and *likhi* are feminine.

These four—sowing dissension and the others—are the means for the purpose of conquering enemies. They are called "means" (*upāya*) because one attains the conquest of enemies by means of them. Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the alienation from another.
