According to the *Kāmandakīyanītisāra* (17.8), this sowing of dissension is considered by the wise to be threefold: the removal of affection and attachment, the production of mutual laughter [or rivalry], and intimidation.
In this regard, when the suspicion arises that "this one, having grown up under your protection like a tree in a palace, will cut off his own [life]," it removes both affection and devotion.
It also brings about overcoming (*abhibhavana*) and bringing low (*paddhana*).
Overcoming is a form of intimidation, such as [the thought]: "For another who aids an enemy, death itself shall be the end. It is a means of terrifying.
"Seizure arising from killing, and likewise affliction;
thus, by those who know the methods of punishment, punishment is considered to be threefold.
(Kāmandakīya-nītisāra 17.9) Affliction consists of binding, beating, and so forth.
The mutual assistance [of the couple], the seeing [of each other], the praising of virtues,
the full explanation of their relationship, and the manifestation of the future;
sweet and excellent speech, and the humble prostration saying, "I am yours."
Thus, by those who know the *sāman*, the *sāman* is considered to be fivefold (*Kāmandakīyanītisāra* 17.4–5):
“When this has been done, this will be for us”—this is the vision of hope, which clarifies the future. The giving of the limb of the *appaṇa* is the gift.
And the gift is fivefold: the handing over of a substance that is substantial or unsubstantial and has been received; likewise, the rejoicing in what has been so received.
Likewise, there is the giving of what has not been given before; likewise, the instigation by oneself to take from others with the words, “Take this object of his, for it will be exactly so”;
and likewise, the release from debt. As it is said:
“The relinquishing of wealth when it has arrived—whether superior, middling, or inferior;”
"Returning [a gift], likewise rejoicing in what has been received,
the gift of material objects, that which is unprecedented, causing one to take [the gift] oneself,
and the relinquishing of what is to be given— this is considered the fivefold gift. (Kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.6–7)

These four means are included within deceit (*māyā*) and the others; for indeed, deceit and indifference (*upekkhā*) are included within punishment (*daṇḍa*), while the "net of Indra" (*indajāla*) is included within dissension (*bheda*). However, some say:
“Personal gift, dissension, and punishment—this is the tetrad;
deceit, indifference, and the net of Indra: these are proclaimed as the seven means. (Kāmandakīya-nītisāra 17.3)

349. Now he states the synonyms for *bheda* and the others mentioned merely by name. Among them, there are two for *bheda*: *japa*, which occurs in both the mental and vocal senses (*japa* means "mental" and "speech," *Dhātvatthasaṅgaha*, verse 135); and *bhū*, *ṇo*. *Bhidi* means "to split," *ṇo*. There are three for *daṇḍa*: *daṇḍa* is in the sense of "striking," belonging to the *curādi* group.
*Saha* is said to mean "force"; that which arises from it is *sāhasa*. *Damana* is *dama*; [here] the long vowel is prohibited. 350.

*Sāma* belongs to the *suddavagga* (the *su*-group), while *dāna* will be discussed in the *brāhmaṇavagga*. According to the opinion of the teacher Sattar, *sāmya* and the others belong to the *evācariya* school.

The constituent parts of a kingdom are called *rajjasaṅga* because they provide mutual assistance. They are termed *prakṛti* (constituents) because they perform excellent service (*pakkaṭṭham upakubbanti*).
And it is said in the *Kāmandakīya*:
"The king, the ministers, the realm, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally..."
This sevenfold sovereignty, which provides mutual assistance, is called *rājya* (kingdom); this is the essence of the *Kāmandakīya-nītisāra* (4.1).
Ministers, the realm, the fortresses, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—these are declared to be the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of a king who desires victory.
“Thus these five, as well as a friend and the lord of the earth as the seventh—
this is a kingdom consisting of seven factors,” so said he who is honored by heroes. In that context,
although the *poraseṇī* (the foremost of the army) exists, its inclusion is established by the mention of the “realm” (*raṭṭha*) or the mention of the “force” (*bala*).

A separate mention is not made here; however, although it is established by the two [terms] in the *Amarakosa*, they are mentioned separately there for the purpose of indicating their preeminence. For it is said therein:
"The minister (*amacca*), the friend (*sakhā*), the treasury (*kosa*), and the kingdom, the fortress, and the army."
"The factors of kingship are the constituents; so too for the ancient Seniya"—thus [it is said in] the *Amarakośa* 18.17.
And regarding these—sovereignty, ministers, the realm, the fortress, the treasury, the army, and allies—one should understand that greater importance belongs to each preceding one.

However, here in this work on names and genders (*nāmaliṅgānusāsana*), since they are not employed in the science of terminology (*abhidhānasattha*), the author does not intend to state their relative importance according to that sequence.
Fifty [types of power] have been explained by way of their classification.

A treasury (*kosa*) consists of storehouses made of gold and other precious materials; a fortress (*dugga*) is a stronghold difficult to access due to mountains, water, trees, and so forth; a realm (*vijita*) is the territory consisting of inhabited districts;
and power (*bala*) is the wheel (*cakka*), which is sixfold according to the divisions of hereditary, purchased, hired, allied, forest-dwelling, and enemy forces.
In that context, there is the principal (*mūla*) arrived through desire; the wage (*bhata*) connected with remuneration; the army (*senī*) consisting of the populace (*paura*);

the ally (*sahāya*) who has become a companion; the enemy (*amitta*) who has become an adversary; and the forest-dweller (*aṭavika*), who is a friend assisting in the forest. That [ally] is also threefold: innate (*sahajja*), natural (*pākata*), and artificial (*kittima*).

Regarding this, the *Byākhyāsudhā* (on *Rudda* 1.4.29) states: "The term *liṅga* refers to gender, intrinsic nature, and natural state; it applies to the origins such as ministers and so forth; and the three genders also apply when qualities are equal."
351. By virtue of power (*pabhāva*) and so forth, there are three kinds of power (*satti*). Regarding "in one's own power":

therein, the establishment of joints and so forth, as well as of disintegration and so forth, exactly as they are, is the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), which is the power of counsel (*mantasatti*).

In the arising of one's own success, the treasury and the army constitute the power of abundance (*pabhūsatti*), because of their capacity for accomplishing that very abundance. And it has been said: "The power of treasury and army..."
“[He is] powerful,” it is said even in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*. The power of exertion (*ussāhasatti*) is a strong state of effort.
And it is stated in the *Byākhyāsudhā* (2.8.19) and also in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*:

“The strength of valor is the power of exertion. To show the nature and cause of majesty (*pabhāva*) and the other qualities, he says: “Majesty,” and so forth. Punishment (*daṇḍa*) means taming; for that purpose...

Power (*bala*) is also a form of force (*daṇḍa*). The radiance (*tejo*) born from that is "majesty" (*pabhāva*). That radiance born from it may also be construed in the masculine as "majesty" (*pabhāvo*).

It is called "majesty" (*pabhāvo*) because by means of it those possessing radiance shine forth (*pabhavanti*); [the suffix] *ṇo* is added. Alternatively, majesty is an eminent state (*pakaṭṭho bhāvo*).
A treasury (*kosa*) is wealth; the radiance born from that is what is called "majesty. Likewise, the radiance born from a treasury is by means of wealth.
It is an accessory for those who have prepared the meal. *Patāpa* means that by means of it, those possessing heat (*tejas*) cause others to tremble;

the suffix *ṇo* is used. 352. *Manta* refers to a pair. *Mantā* is said to be wisdom (*paññā*); because it exists in this [pair] and is to be accomplished by means of it, it is called *manta*. Alternatively, the root *mant* is used in the sense of "guarded speech"; in the abstract sense (*bhāve*), the suffix *ṇo* is applied. In the other case, the suffix *yu* is used in the abstract sense.
That *manta* has two spheres of operation (*dvigocara*), being the object of two persons, and is thus called *catukkaṇṇo* ("four-eared"). There are four ears (*kaṇṇā*) in this regard.
"Catukkaṇṇo" means that which has four corners. "So manto tigocaro" means that the mantra is the domain of three persons; thus it is called "chakkaṇṇo.
A mantra should be made either four-cornered or six-cornered, but not beyond that; therefore, only two [types] are included here.
However, in the *Amarakośa*, even the six-cornered type is rejected, for it is stated there: "It is 'achakkaṇṇo,' which is the domain of the third person and so forth" (*Amarakośa* 18.22).

Because it contains all the assemblies (*pārisada*) and all the opening lines (*pāṭipada*), even though they have not come here [to this specific recitation], the six qualities and so forth should be brought forward and explained for the purpose of generating proficiency among the listeners even in other traditions. For it has been said: "This [Abhidhamma] contains all the assemblies and all the opening lines;

it is considered the best of all treatises. Nothing whatsoever is excluded from anywhere; herein, all disputants find their end."* *(Note: The term "sabbapārisada" refers to the various groups of deities and humans present at the Buddha's teachings, while "sabbapāṭipada" refers to the introductory verses that open each book of the Abhidhamma.)*

Just as there are six strings [to a lute], so too are there six policies: alliance (*saṃdhi*), war (*viggaḥa*), marching (*yāna*), encamping (*āsana*), bifurcation (*dvaidhībhāva*), and seeking protection (*saraṇagamana*).

(18.18–19) Among these, alliance is characterized by giving (*upahāra*) and is threefold, having its cause in the granting of treasure, troops, or territory. War is characterized by taking away (*apahāra*), and it is also threefold:
open battle (*pakāsayuddha*), treacherous battle (*kūṭayuddha*), and silent battle (*tuṇhiyuddha*).

In the *Kāmandakīya-nītisāra*, the expedition (*yāna*) of a conqueror who is devoted to the virtues of those he has treated well—undertaken when others are beset by calamity, have fallen into misfortune, or when the place and time are favorable—is described as being of five kinds:

the expedition of assault (*viggayhayāna*), the expedition of alliance (*sandhāyayāna*), the expedition of coalition (*sambhūyayāna*), the expedition of opportunity (*pasaṅgayāna*), and the expedition of indifference (*upekkhiyayāna*). This should be observed in Chapter 11. [This concerns] the recipients.
"Viggayhayāna" and so forth refers to traveling after having suppressed, concealed, or disregarded [the offense].
"Sambhūyayāna" is traveling together with neighbors when one is unable [to travel alone]. "Pasaṅgayāna" is traveling elsewhere on account of some incidental occasion when one ought to go elsewhere.

“Neither is another able to kill me, nor am I [able to kill] another”—having thus surrounded oneself with considerations of time and other factors, the persistence of one desiring victory while increasing fortifications and the like is the *āsana* (posture).
That too is fivefold, distinguished as *viggaṇhāsana*, *sandhāyāsana*, and so forth.
In the midst of powerful enemies, the surrendering of oneself by means of words that are unobserved like the eye of a crow is the *ubhatovacanena* (by means of words on both sides).
"Dvedhaṃ" means twofold. It is "twofold" because there is reconciliation with one [party] who is stronger, and conflict with another who is weaker.
Or, it refers to the conflict with an enemy based on his inherent nature;
or the activity of a person of wicked disposition, which is caused by a combination of both reconciliation and conflict with that very enemy (Byākhyāsudhā 1.8.18).
That [dualism] is also twofold. The occurrence of both types of feeling within another's continuum is also called dualism.

Regarding the verse: “Being destroyed by an enemy, lacking means of resistance, and devoid of power, one is subdued” (Byākhyāsudhā 1.8.18), this refers to the subduing of one who is being destroyed by a powerful enemy, by someone inferior who has been conquered through righteousness (*dharma*).

The "resort" (*āsayana*) refers to the resorting to a weak enemy by means of the power of one's own qualities, or the resorting to a powerful enemy by providing him with resources such as his treasury; this is called a "resort.

These are the six qualities. Furthermore, whichever quality the conqueror (*vijigīsu*) abides in and by which he is able to carry out his own eightfold set of actions and to thwart those of the enemy—that quality he should resolve upon; that is "progress" (*vuḍḍhi*).

Trade in Kāsi, difficult roads, bridges, the binding of elephants, mining, the granting of wealth, and the settling of uninhabited lands—this is the eighth section from the *Kāmandakīyanītisāra*. 5.78.
Thus ends this group of eight.
Alternatively, that state in which one established in a certain quality does not perceive the increase or the exhaustion of one’s own kamma is a "state" (*ṭhāna*);
or, that quality in which one established perceives the destruction of one’s own kamma—one should not remain in that, for it is "exhaustion" (*khaya*).
This is the triad for those who know the definitive meaning (*nītivedī*). For others, there is the triad of *dhamma*, *attha*, and *kāma*.

*Dvayaṃ guyhe* (Two terms for "in secret"). *Rahassaṃ* means that which exists in a secluded place (*rahasi*), or that which exists in seclusion (*rahe*). The root *guh* is used in the sense of concealing; it takes the suffix *-ya*. These two [terms] apply to the three genders. An example is: *rahasso manto* (a secret counsel), *rahassā vācā* (secret speech), *rahassaṃ mantanaṃ* (secret deliberation).

353. *Pañcakaṃ vijane* (A group of five terms for "in a lonely place"). The root *vij* is used in the sense of being separate (*puthabhāve*), with the suffixes *-u* and *-to*. Alternatively, the root *vic* is used in the sense of separating (*vivecane*) or being separate. Rudda states:

"*Vivittaṃ* applies to the three genders in the sense of 'lonely' (*vijane*), meaning those who have not come together. That from which people have departed is *vijano*. It covers (*chādeti*)... [text ends].

*Channa*: from the root *chad*, meaning "to cover. It is called *raho* because it is worthy of being covered (*vittam arahati*); or from the root *rah*, meaning "to abandon" (*cāge*), or "they delight in this" (*ramante asmin*), hence *raho*.

There is a modification of the vowel (*vaṇṇavikāro*). According to the *Byākhyāsudhā* (2.8.22) and *Rabhasa*: "The word *raha* is used for secret lovemaking (*nidhuvana*) and for a secret place (*guyha*);
[the latter] is neuter. The second word *raho* is an indeclinable (*abyaya*). *Nissalākā*: here, the suffix *upāsu* is applied. *Nissalākā* is feminine; *upāsu* is an indeclinable.

The two [roots] *viś* and *sraṃbh* mean trust. *Sas* means protection; it takes the suffix *ṇo*. *Sambha* means trust. In the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*, Rūda also states: “*Vissambha* occurs in the sense of playful quarrel, as well as in trust and affection.
The two [roots] mean justice (*nyāya*). *Yuj* means concentration (*samādhi*); *samādhi* is acceptance (*abhyupagama*), [ending in] *to*. Because it is to be approached, it is *upāyika*.

From *upāya*, the suffix *iko* is added in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*), making it *opāyika*; *opayika* is also found in Pāṇini 5.4.34 (in the *gaṇa*). It means that which is obtainable (*labbha*) or that which is suitable (*bhajamāna*).

It is well-conducted, logical, and reasonable here. 354. *Sīlaka* [is used] in the sense of advice (*ovāda*). The root *vad*, preceded by *ava*, [denotes] distinct speech; with the suffix *ṇo*, it refers to the state [of that action].

*Sāsa* [is used] in the sense of instruction (*anusiṭṭhi*), as in *āssi* and *anusiṭṭhi*. From *anusāsati* comes *anusāsana*. It occurs in the feminine (excluding masculine forms) and in the neuter. And here:

The explanation of a single meaning by means of three names with different genders is for the purpose of demonstrating that not only is there a word whose gender corresponds to the object (*vāccaliṅga*), but there is also a word whose gender corresponds to the expressive agent (*vācakaliṅga*). "Two [meanings] in the sense of commanding":

from the root *āṇ* in the sense of sending, with the suffix *a* in the abstract sense (*bhāve*), we have *āṇā*; it is feminine. Herein, "instruction," "explanation," and "advice" are also included. "Two [meanings] in the sense of binding": from the root *dā* in the sense of giving, with the suffix *yu* in the abstract sense, we have *uddāna*. Alternatively, from the root *dā* in the sense of cutting, it is called *uddāna* because it gives separation [from suffering].
355–356. *Dvayaṃ aparādhe*: "It goes away by means of this" is *āgu*; [the suffix] *ṇu* is applied, there is elision (*palopa*), and the short vowel becomes long;
thus, in the neuter, it is *āgu*. That by which success (*rādha*) has departed is *aparādha*; *rādha* is used in the sense of accomplishment. *Dvayaṃ rājagahe*:

from the root *kṛ* (in the sense of scattering), with the suffix *a* in the agentive sense, it is *attaṃ*. From the root *bal* (in the sense of life-force), with the suffix *i*, it is *bali*; due to its association with *kara*, *bali* is masculine.

*Bhāgadheyyo* is also [included] here. According to Pāṇini 5.4.36 (vā.), *dheyya* has the sense of "a portion" (*bhāga*); or, it is called *bhāgadheyyo* because it stands as a portion (*bhāgatthena*), hence the suffix *-iyo*.

The pair [of terms] refers to a "gift of satisfaction. Because it fulfills one's desires, the portion that is to be obtained is called *puṇṇapatto*. *Tussanaṃ* means "satisfaction" (*tuṭṭho*); the abstract noun from that is *tuṭṭhī* (by adding *-ī*). That which is to be given by means of that satisfaction is the "gift of satisfaction" (*tuṭṭhidāyo*); this is formed by adding *-āya* to words ending in long vowels.
The group of six [terms] relates to "gifts" (pābhata).

For it is said: "Gold, a lion-throne, clothing, likewise what is called a 'fortunate seat' (bhaddāsana), a present, a gift to be received, and 'that which has been brought'—these are the words for a gift."
*Amaramālā* is called *silokāddha*. *Upadā*: that which is to be taken after approaching;
[the suffix] *a*, feminine gender. *Pābhataṃ*: that which is brought or carried by those desiring various objects;
this prefix *pa-* indicates the sense of longing (*patthana*). *Upāyanaṃ*: that which is to be offered; [the suffix] *yu* after this [root]. It approaches.
*Yena* means "by which" or "means. *Kuc* means "contraction"; with the suffix *ṇo*, *vigata-koca* becomes *ukkoca*.
That which is brought or conveyed together with a leaf—specifically a betel leaf—is called *paṇṇākāra*, except as a figurative usage. That by which they send is *paheṇaka*;
from the root *hi* meaning "to go," with the suffix *yu* and the pleonastic *ko*. *Padesanaṃ*, *upaggayhaṃ*, and *upahāra* are also used here.

*Gumbādideyya* refers to the tax (*deyya-suṅka*) levied from a caravan leader (*gumba-ghaṭādika*) or one who leads a caravan (*gumba-ghaṭādita*). It is not feminine. *Gumbo* means a share obtained on waterways, land routes, and so forth;
likewise for *ghaṭṭa*. These two have the same meaning. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), merchandise brought for sale (*pābhata*) is also included.

*Suṅka*: the root *suṅk* means to go; that by which one goes is *suṅka*. *Gam* means to go; with the suffixes *-bo* and *-assu*, it becomes *gumbo*. The pair [of terms] refers to what is obtained from villages, districts, and so forth.
In the sense of "to be obtained," *āya* is [the term]. Without a suffix, it is *ayo*. At the time when wealth is acquired, there is the arrival of wealth, which is *dhanāgamo*.
357. There are two [meanings] for *chatta* in its general sense. It protects from heat—that is, from the light of the sun—thus it is *ātapattaṃ*, with the suffix *to*.

It covers, thus it is *chattaṃ*, from the root *chada* in the sense of "covering," with the suffix *to*. With the protective suffix *traṇa*, it is *chattraṃ*; [this refers to] a golden one, inlaid with gold, belonging to kings.
The seat of kings is called the *siṃhāsana* (lion-throne). The analysis of the compound is: "a seat whose primary form is that of a lion" (*sīhākati-padhānaṃ āsanaṃ*).
There are two types of *cāmara* (yak-tail whisks). A fan made of hair is a *vāla-bījanī*. It belongs to the yak (*camaro*) animal, hence it is *cāmarī*.
According to the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.8.406): "The word *cāmara* refers to hair, a cluster, and a fringe. This is also treated in the *Pakiṇṇaka* section.
That which is scattered or dispersed is *pakiṇṇaka*; the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (to form an adjective). 358.

These five items, such as the sword and so forth, are the *kakudhabhaṇḍa* (regal insignia) of kings. [The root] *kuk* means "to take up"; with the suffix *-dha*, there is a change in the phonetic color (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*).
Because they must always be taken up at the time of the king’s departure, and because they are royal property, they are called *kakudha* and, being wealth, *bhaṇḍa*; thus they are *kakudhabhaṇḍa*.
359. Two terms refer to the *puṇṇaghaṭa* (auspicious jar). Because it is filled with water, it is called *bhaddakumbha*, meaning an auspicious or beautiful jar.

Two terms refer to the golden vessel (*hemabhājana*). From the root *bhar* (to bear, to support), *bharaṇa* means supporting, maintaining, and nourishing; for the sense of "supporting," there is the substitution of *bhiṅga* for *bharati*.
It is called *bhiṅgāra* because it bears or holds water; [the suffix] *āro* is added. *Karaka* and *kuṇḍikā* also apply here.
An elephant, a horse, a chariot, and a foot soldier—their collective group is called an "elephant-horse-chariot-foot-soldier" army (*hatthissa-ratha-patti caturaṅginī senā*).
This is a compound of aggregation (*samāhāra-dvanda*) because they are constituent parts of an army (*senaṅga*). That in which four parts (*aṅga*) are found is "fourfold" (*caturaṅginī*);
the suffix *inī* is added after *catu*.

360. *Hatthinī* ends in a dental (*dantyanta*). *Kuñja* means the jaw and the tusk; because of that [tusk], he is a *kuñjara*. Or, in the sense of excellence (*atisaye*), he is a *kuñjara* because he causes the earth (*kuṃ*) to decay (*jarāpeti*).
This is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). Alternatively, he delights (*ramati*) in a thicket (*kuñje*) or on a mountain peak (*girikūṭe*);

or he wanders while uttering a trumpeting sound (*koñcanādaṃ nadanto*); or he causes the earth (*kuṃ*) to decay by the impact of his trampling—thus he is a *kuñjara*. He wards off the enemy forces (*vārayati parabalaṃ*).
An elephant (*vāraṇa*) is so called because it wards off (*vārayati*) Nanda and the others. A "hand-yoked" one is a *hatthī*. A *mātaṅga* is the offspring of the seer Mataṅga;

or, it is a *mātaṅga* because its body (*aṅga*) is large (*mahanta*), with the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) and the substitution of the vowel *ā*. A *dvirada* is one that has two tusks (*rada*); for in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*, it is said:

"The root *rada* [is used] in the sense of scratching and in the sense of tusks. A *gaja* is so called from the root *gaj* meaning "to sound," as in "it sounds" (*gajati*); the suffix *a* is added. A *naga* is a mountain.
He is called a *nāga* because he appears like one; [the suffix] *-ṇo* is added. Because he drinks with both his trunk and his mouth, he is a *dvipa*.

[The root] *i* means "to go," O venerable sir. Because of his association with tusks, he is a *dantī*. He is also known as a sixty-year-old (*saṭṭhihāyana*), a possessor of tusks (*dantāvala*), one who has many feet (*anekapa*), a descendant of Matanga (*mataṅgaja*), a trunk-bearer (*karī*), a pillar-elephant (*thambherama*), a lotus-possessor (*padmī*), a great beast (*mahāmiga*), a *pīlu*, a lord of the Sindhu (*sindhura*), one with long breath (*dīghamāruta*), one with streaks (*rājīva*), one with watery eyes (*jalakakkha*), one who destroys pride (*nillura*), and a tusked one (*karaṭī*).

*Varaṅga*, *suppakaṇṇa*, and so forth are also names for elephants. Because he is sixty years old, or because his strength declines at the age of sixty, he is called a "sixty-year-old" (*saṭṭhihāyana*).

He who is the senior among the forest herds is called the "herd-leader" (*yūthajeṭṭha*) because of his seniority over his own herd. He is called the "herd-guardian" (*yūthapati*) because he protects and guards his own herd.
361. These are the lineages of elephant kings, beginning with the Kālāvaka. It is called *kālāvaka* because it utters sounds (*sadda*) in the forest (*kāla*);
the suffix *-vuka* is applied, and the vowel *a* is elided. That which is born in the Ganges is *gaṅgeyya*; this designation is based on its place of origin.

It is *paṇḍara* due to its white color. It is *tamba* due to its copper-colored hue. It is *piṅgala* due to its tawny color. It is *gandha* because it is endowed with fragrance. The root *maṅg* has the sense of "going."
He is *Maṅgala* because he is endowed with beautiful movement; [the suffix] *-a* is used in the sense of excellence or praise according to the *loka* (worldly usage).

He is *Hema* because of his golden color. He is *Uposatha* because he was born in the *uposatha* lineage; or alternatively, he is *uposatha* because he approaches (*upa*) and destroys (*usati*) his enemies—where *tha* comes from the root *tho*, *usa* from the root *dāha* (to burn), and *vasa* from the root *vasa* preceded by *upa* in the sense of dwelling (*nivāsa*)—thus he is *vassa*; [the term] *uposatha* also refers to a specific lunar day (*tithi*). He is *Chaddanta* because of his six-tusked teeth.
The strength of those ten *kāḷāvaka* elephants is borne by one *gaṅgeyya*;
likewise, it should be carried on up to the *chaddanta*. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, bears the strength of ten *chaddanta* elephants.
For that reason, the Blessed One possesses the strength of a thousand million according to the calculation of *kāḷāvaka* elephants, and according to the calculation of men, [the strength of] ten...
The strength of a thousand million men. 362. *Pāda* [refers to] a young elephant (*karipota*).
Up to five years of age it is a *kalabha*; *kala* means counting, *abha* means to nourish; thus, *kalabha*. In the *ḷatta* dialect it is *kaḷabha*.
Because it must be supported by its parents, it is a *bhiṅka*; because it is to be nourished (*bharati*), it is a *bhiṅka*. *Karisāvaka* is also used here. *Pāda*.

In *mattamātaṅge*: "pabhinno" refers to one whose rut has burst forth (*dānaṃ pabhinnaṃ yassa pabhinno*). "Mattā" means intoxicated; the root *mad* signifies madness. That which is produced in an elephant is "gajja," with the suffix *-ṇya*, meaning rut.
One in whom that has arisen is "gajjita. Both terms refer to a herd of elephants.
A collection of elephants is *hatthighaṭā*; a collection of *gajas* is *gajatā*, [formed] by the rule beginning with *gāma-jana-bandhu-sahāya*.

*Tā*. A foot [is found] on a female elephant (*hatthinī*). She is called *hatthinī* because she is joined with a trunk (*hasta*); the suffixes *ī* and *inī* are applied. From the root *kaṇ* (to sound), with the suffixes *iru* and *ko* in the sense of the word itself, we have *kareṇukā*.
Alternatively, it is *kareṇukā* because she is joined with a trunk (*kara*); the suffix *iṇu* is applied. Here, *kariṇī*, *dhenukā*, *vasā*, and *kareṇu* also refer to a female elephant. 363.
Two masses on the head of the elephant—the two masses on the elephant’s head known as *kumbha*s. It is called a *kumbha* because it exists on the head (*siras*); the suffix *o* is applied.

There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). "Vidu" refers to the middle part between two pots (18.37). It is called *vidu* because one finds (*vindati*) what is gathered like a hook (*aṅkusasaṅghāta*);
it is masculine, according to the *u*-sutta. Two [terms] are at the base of the ear. "Cūḷikā" is derived from the root *cūḷ* in the sense of immersion, with the suffix *ṇvu*;
or from *cuda* in the sense of urging (*sañcodana*). It is called *cūḷikā* because the untamed [elephant] is urged there by hooks and other means; *da* becomes *ḷa*, with the suffix *ṇvu*.

*Āsanaṃ* (seat) is that wherein one sits; it refers to the region of the trunk (*khandha*). *Khandhadeso* means the trunk itself which is the region; [it refers] to that. *Dvayaṃ* (the pair) refers to the root of the trunk. The root of the trunk is its lower part. 364.
*Tikaṃ* (the triad) refers to the pillar for tying an elephant. *Ālānaṃ*: in this [pillar] they tie, or by means of this they tie, hence *ālānaṃ*;

[the suffix] *yu*. The root *lā* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has the meaning of binding. *Āḷhako*: in this or by means of this they strike or bind; [the suffix] *ka*, from the root *han*. [The form] *nassa*...
*ḷo*, with the transposition of the letters (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*) and the suffix *ṇvu*. *Thambha* means to obstruct; *bandha* is also used here. The triad refers to a chain.
*Anitthī* means that a word ending in *tu* is a term for gender. *Gala* means to sprinkle. It is called *nigaḷo* because one is bound by it;

the suffix *a* is used, or it is an agentive derivation (*kattusādhana*). *Adi* means to bind; it binds, thus it is *anduko*. With the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *assu*. By this, one stumbles greatly (*bhusaṃ khalati*).

*Saṅkhalaṃ* refers to a chain; it also refers to a waist-cloth (*kaṭi-vattha-bandhana*). Regarding this, the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (18.41) states: "The word *saṅkhalaṃ* is used for a tight waist-cloth and for a shackle.
*Saṅkhalikā* is also used here. The pair [of terms] refers to an elephant's temple (*gaṇḍa*).
*Gaṇḍa* means a part of the face. Although it is not among the primary elements (*adhātu*), it is listed among the elements (*dhātu*) because its meaning is that of an action (*kriyārtha*).

*Gaṇḍo* is used for the cheek in general. *Kaṭa* means rain or covering; *a* is the suffix. There are two [terms] for the ichor of an elephant. That which is given is *dānaṃ*. *Mada* means intoxication;
*a* is the suffix in the sense of the instrument. 365.

There are two [terms] for the trunk of an elephant. *Soṇa* means color or going; *ḍo*, or *soḍa* in the sense of concealing (*gabbe*), with the insertion of the nasal (*niggahītāgamo*) and the substitution of *ṇo*. Both [terms] apply to both [meanings].

*Dvayaṃ* means on the tip of the trunk. *Soṇḍa* refers to the trunk; its *aggaṃ* (tip). *Pusa* is used in the sense of nourishing (*posane*). *Khara*—here *ssa* becomes *ko*—means a swelling (*ussottaṃ*). Alternatively, *puṣa* is used in the sense of growth (*vuḍḍhimhi*); *bhū*, *puṣa* is used in the senses of moistening, sprinkling, or filling (*snehasecanapūraṇesu*); it belongs to the *kiyādi* group.

Alternatively, *puṣa* is used in the sense of supporting (*dhāraṇe*), belonging to the *curādi* group. *Kacchā* is the name for the binding rope around the middle of an elephant's body. *Kaca* is used in the sense of binding (*bandhane*); the suffix *cho*. *Dūsā* here also means a leather thong (*varatrā*).
*Kutho* is a variegated blanket spread over the back of an elephant; those beginning with this are called *kuthādayo*. *Kuthādayo*.

Thus, there are those called *kappana*. [The root] *kapp* is used in the senses of capability (*sāmatthiya*) and arranging (*sajjanā*), with the suffix *-yu* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
There is also *kappanā*. [The root] *kac* is used in the sense of arranging; [the noun] *kutha* occurs in three genders. For Vopālita states in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (18.42):
"The neuter is *attharaṇa*, the feminine is *paveṇī*, and *kutha* in three [genders]. *Paveṇī*, *attharaṇa*, *vaṇṇo*, and *paritthoma*—these are synonyms for *kutha*.

366. There are two terms for a state elephant (*rājārahahatthin*). It is called *opavayha* because it is fit (*arahati*) to carry the king; the suffix *-ṇya* is used in the sense of being fit (*araha-atthe*).
It is called *rājavayha* because it is fit to carry the king; the suffix *-ṇya* is used. There are two terms for a trained elephant (*kappitahatthin*).

That in which readiness (*sajjā*)—meaning preparedness (*sajjanā*)—has arisen is called *sajjita*. That in which arrangement (*kappā*)—meaning preparation (*kappanā*)—has arisen is called *kappita*. From this very reading, the terms *sajja* and *kappa* [are derived].
These should be understood as synonyms for the ornaments of the virtuous.

A thorn that pierces the feet of an elephant is called a *tomara*. It is a *tomara* because one is struck (*tujjati*) by it; from the root *tuda* (to strike/pain), with the suffix *-ara*, changing *da* to *ma*, and adding the prefix *o*.
Regarding *veṇuka*: here it refers to a bamboo staff (*koṭṭha*), according to the *Amara-kośa* (18.41) on the garlands of bamboo; in some places, the reading *veḷuka* is also found.
367. The piercing thorn at the base of an elephant’s ear is called a *tutta*. It is a *tutta* because one strikes (*tujjati*) with it;

thus, the suffix *to*. The piercing thorn on the elephant’s head is called an *aṅkusa*. It is an *aṅkusa* because one marks (*aṅkate*) with it; from the root *aṅka* in the sense of marking, with the suffix *so*, and the vowel change to *assu*.
*Pajjaddhaṃ* means "on the elephant. *Maḍi* is used in the sense of ornamentation; one who adorns (*maṇḍayati*) or protects the elephant is a *hatthimaṇḍo*.

[The suffix] *ḍa* is added after *maḍi*, and there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). One who protects (*pāti*) the elephant is a *hatthipo*; the suffix *ṇa* is added in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
One who guards (*gopayati*) or protects the elephant is a *hatthigopako*. The root *gup* is used in the sense of protecting; the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*sakatthe*).
An elephant driver (*ādhoraṇa*) and a rider (*nisādī*) are also included here.
A teacher who trains elephants, horses, and so forth in actions such as walking is called a "leader" (*gāmaṇīya*).

Walking is "the village" (*gāma*), with the suffix *-no* used in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*). The act of walking by elephants and other animals is the "village"; one who leads—that is, trains—in that [act] is a "leader" (*gāmaṇīya*). This is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) for one who trains them in other actions as well.

One who leads a village (*gāma*) or a herd of elephants and so forth is a *gāmaṇī*; or, one who teaches the way of going (*gamana*) is a *gāmaṇī*. In all these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs.
*Turaṅga*: "Haya" is in the sense of motion, with the suffix *a*. One who goes quickly (*turaṃ*) is a *turaṅga*; with the suffix *kvin*, there is the elision of the nasal (*bindu*).

When that elision occurs, it becomes *turaga*. *Vāha*: "Vāha" is in the sense of exertion, with the suffix *a*. *Asa*: "Asa" is in the sense of eating, with the suffix *a*. A region situated not far from the Indus (*sindhu*) is also [called] *Sindhava*.
*Sindhava*: that which exists there (*tatra bhavaḥ*) is *sindhava*; due to the rule regarding a final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogantattā*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening.

*Ghoṭaka*, *pīti*, *turaṅgama*, *vājī*, *gandhabba*, *satti*, *ricca*, and others are also names for a horse. [The derivation of *ghoṭaka*: from the root *ghuṭ* in the sense of "turning about" (*parivartane*), with the suffix *ṇvu*. [The derivation of *pīti*: from the root *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (*pāne*).

Rudra states: "In the sense of drinking, *thī* is *pīti*; it is [also] a horse. [The derivation of *vājī*: because of its connection with speed (*vāja*), it is *vājī*, with the suffix *ī*. "This was formerly a winged creature (*pakkha*), but he became a god (*deva*) through his extreme steadfastness."
"Having employed Sakka, he was cut by the thunderbolt," so say those of other schools (*nikāyantariya*). The root *sap* means "to assemble";
it also means "power" or "capability. 369.
The breaking or distinction of that horse is *assatara*; one who surpasses the horse is *assatara*. [The suffix] *-tara* is used in the sense of "surpassing."
It is also established by means of the *tarap* suffix. A horse that possesses the essential nature of a thoroughbred, being well-born, unchanging, and of noble lineage, is called an *ājānīya*.
It is an *ājānīya* because it thoroughly (*ā*) knows what is a cause and what is not a cause; or it is established by the *ṇya* suffix.
In that case, the augment *nā* and the augment *ī* are added according to the rule "from *kiyādi*, [the suffix] *nā*," as can also be seen in verse 18.44 of the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*.
One born in a noble family is "kulīnaka"; the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

Even when struck by a heavy weapon in battle, a beloved horse does not abandon its master; one who is thus capable of enduring hardship is called *vinīta* because he is trained by the sound [of the whip].
Furthermore, he leads [the rider] toward excellence through his tamed nature; thus they say he is *vinīta*.

There are two terms for a young horse (*assapota*): *kiśora*, derived from the root *kas* (to go), with the suffix *oro*; or alternatively, it means "one who remembers something," with the elision of the nasal (*bindulopa*), thus becoming *asso*.

A *hayapotaka* is simply a *hayo* (horse) due to its youth; the suffix *ko* is used here in a diminutive sense. Next, there are two terms for a horse: *ghoṭaka*, derived from the root *ghuṭ* (to turn/roll) with the suffix *ṇvu*;

this term applies generally to any horse. *Khaluṅga*: one who goes harshly (*kharaṃ gacchati*); that very same word becomes *khaḷuṅko* by changing the letter *g* to *k*, shortening the vowel, and substituting *ḷ* for *l*.
*Khaḷuka* also [is used]. *Javana* is a horse superior to all others in speed; it is masculine (*yu*).

The pair [of terms] *kavi* and *mukhabandhana* are known as "bit. It is called *mukhāṭhāna* because it stands in the mouth. *Khalīna* is that which is fixed (*līna*) in the mouth (*khe*), i.e., the opening of the mouth.
Regarding this, the *Rabhasa* lexicon states: "The word *kavika* refers to a bit (*khalīna*); it is also said to mean 'speaking' (*kathana*) in the sense of *kavi*."
*Kavi* and *kavikā* also occur here. The root *ku* means "to sound. By the rule "i, ī, and ko [are added] in the sense of the word itself," the suffix *ka* is applied.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the neuter gender is included. And it is stated in the *Amarakośa*: "But *kavikā* is a bitron; it is not feminine" (Amara 18.49).
A whip made of cane, rattan, and so forth is called *kasa*. The root *kas* means "to move"; with the suffix *a*, it is derived instrumentally (*karaṇasādhana*).
371. *Kusā* refers to the reins reaching the horse’s nose; *kusa* refers to the bit. These two belong to the horse. *Vala* means to restrain;

with the suffix *vo*, there is the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*, and the vowel *ā*, thus forming *vaḷavā*. It is called *assā* because it possesses [the quality of] a horse (*asati iti assā*); according to the rule “*itthiyamatiyavo vā*,” the suffixes *a* and *ā* are applied, resulting in *assā*.

*Vāmī* is also used here. There are two terms for the hoof: *khura*. *Khura* means to cut. *Saphaṃ* is derived etymologically (*nerutto*) from the sense that by it one attains (*pharati*) ease (*saṃ*). “*Saphaṃ* is neuter.”
"Khura" means "male," according to the *Amarakośa* (18.49).

Two terms refer to the mere act of questioning; "puccha" means "negligence. It is called "naṅguṭṭha" because it does not move (*na gacchati*); the root "aṅg" means "to go," with the suffixes "ṭha" and "assu.
Both [terms] apply to non-females. "Lūma" is also used here. Two terms refer to the tail of one possessing hair, but not exclusively that of an elephant.

A "hair-hand" (*vālahattha*) is so called because of its connection with a collection of hairs, just as a "hand of hair" (*kesahattha*) refers to a mass [of hair]; it is the same here as well. Alternatively, a "tail" (*vāladhi*) is that in which a hair (*vāla*) is fastened (*dhīyati*).
Here, even though they have not yet arrived, the five gaits of the horse—known as *dhārā* and *dhāva* (variant: *dhāvā*)—should be described. As follows:
The five gaits are considered by the wise to be the streams of horses, O immortal one (18.48–49).
Therein, *vitthambhā* is *samāvagati*, which is *akkanditaṃ*; the root *kandi* is used in the sense of going and drying up (*to*). Beyond that is *caturāgati*, which is *dhoritakaṃ*;
from the root *dhora* in the sense of cleverness of gait (*to*), with the suffix *ko* added in its own sense (*sakatthe*). Moving by means of a circular carriage is *recitaṃ*.
In the context of "richa" (speed) and "viyojana-sambajjhana" (joining while separated), *sambajjhana* means mixing. *Vegena parikkhitto* (surrounded by speed) is *paricaraṇa*, which is *vaggita*;
the root *vagga* has the sense of going. *Turaṃ* is going evenly; *pluta* comes from the root *plu* meaning motion. Regarding this, it is said in the *Assasattha*:
"The even, the superior, the relaxed, the speedy, and the hurried are the [five] gaits in order."

372. *Dvayaṃ* refers to two types of vehicles equipped with wheels for the purpose of war. *Sanda*: [it means] going; it is called *sandana* because one goes by means of it, from the root *sadi* (to go), with the suffix *yu*. *Ratha*:
[it means] that by which one delights (*ramati*), with the suffix *tha*, and the elision of the letter *ma*. *Sataṅga* is also used here; it is that which has a hundred parts (*satam aṅgāni assa*).

That vehicle which is equipped with wheels for the purpose of war—that is, for battle—and not for the sake of sport, pleasure, or travel, is a *pussaratha*. And it is said in the *Amarakośa*: "This *pussaratha* is a wheeled vehicle, not for battle" (*amara* 18.51). *Pussa*.
A *pussaratha* is a chariot associated with a specific fruit called *puṣya*; or, it is a chariot made or prepared under the *puṣya* lunar mansion (*puṣyanakṣatra*).
A chariot covered or encased in tiger-skin is called *veyyaggha*; the skin that is a product of the tiger is *veyyaggha*.
No; the chariot is covered with tiger skin. No; in both cases there is an increase in the number of syllables.
According to the etymological definition, "those which go toward [or against] each other" are *paccayā* (conditions);

thus, they become conditions by being directed toward one another, just as various causal conditions exist by way of an instigator even when the action is performed by oneself. It is covered with the skin of a leopard.

A chariot is called *dīpa*; the leather (*camma*) is a transformation (*vikāra*) of the hide (*dīpin*), hence *dīpa*. By means of that [leather], the chariot is surrounded; thus it is *dīpa* with the suffix *ṇo*. 373.

Regarding the two types of vehicles drawn by men: *si* is used here. It is called a *sivikā* because it is resorted to (*sevīyati*) by those seeking comfort; the suffix *ṇvu* is applied, there is the augment *vā*, and the substitution of *it*.
For suffixes such as *kita* generally denote the object (*karman*) and so forth, while suffixes such as *kicca* can also denote the agent (*kartṛ*).

Just as in cases such as “the Vinaya, the Nissaya, the ascetic practices (tapanīyā dhammā),” etc., it should be understood that [the suffix] occurs even after the objects of an action (kamma) when they are the agents of the action due to the Great Authority (mahāpadesa).
Alternatively, it is a *sivikā* because it brings about welfare (*sivaṃ karoti*); here, *-ika* is the suffix.

It is a *yāpyayāna* because it is driven or conveyed by those who are lowly or contemptible (*yāpyehi adhamehi*). For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: “*Yāpya* means ‘water for drinking’ or ‘despicable.’”

Two [terms] for a cart (*sakaṭa*): *anitthī tu*. A word for gender (*liṅgapada*) ending in *-tu* is feminine. From the root *sak* (to be able), with the suffix *-aṭ*. From the root *an* (to breathe/live), used instrumentally;

or, "that which has no nose" (*nāsā*) is *anaṃ*; there is elision (*sālopa*) and shortening of the vowel. In the neuter, it is *anaṃ*; in the masculine, *sakaṭo*. "Not feminine" (*anitthī*)—thus says the *Amarakosa*, 18.52.
Two [terms] for a wheel (*cakra*): that by which one performs going is a wheel (*cakka*); with the suffix *-dvitta*, it becomes *cakkādi*. A part of a chariot is a chariot-part (*rathaṅga*).
The end within that wheel is the rim (*nemi*); it leads the wheel among women (*nāriyaṃ*), that is, among females (*itthiyaṃ*).
*Nemi* is derived from the root *nī* (to lead), with the suffix *mi* and the vowel change to *ī*. It is also used in the sense of a "foundation" (*padhi*). 374.
In the middle of that—meaning in the middle of the chariot or the wheel—is the hub (*piṇḍikā*) in the shape of a wheel, upon which all [the spokes] rest.

The wooden pieces are attached. The *nābhi* is feminine due to its association with *piṇḍikā*; when the suffix *īpa* is added, it becomes *nābhī*. It is called *piṇḍikā* because it "binds together all the wooden pieces" (*piṇḍeti*).

[Root] *piṇḍ* means "to collect"; the suffix *a* is used, and *ka* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). It is also *piṇḍī*. It is called *nābhi* because it is "like a navel" (*nābhi viyā*). That part of the chariot where the yoke-wood is attached is the *yugandhara*.

It is called *kubbara* because it "covers" (*vuṇoti*) or conceals the earth (*kuṃ pathaviṃ*); [root] *vu* means "to cover," with the suffixes *ra* and *ussa*, and the vowel lengthened. It is called *yugandhara* because it "supports the yoke" (*yugaṃ dhāreti*); the suffix *a* is used in the sense of a designation (*saññāyaṃ*), and the vowel is shortened according to the rule of expression.
"Akkho" means a cart, or a part thereof; thus the teacher Ajaya said:
"Akkho [is used] for the *vibhītaka* tree, the *nimba* tree, a cart, and in common usage;
it refers to a part of a chariot, the god Kaśyapa, a die, and also to a sense-faculty."
*Āṇī* is the wedge at the tip of a sword; it is feminine. Regarding *aṇī*, the commentator of the *Cintāmaṇi* (18.56) reads *ruddha* in two ways:

"In the case of the wedge at the tip of an axle and in the case of boundaries and dice, these two are *aṇī* and *āṇī*. And the *Nānatthasaṅgaha* also states: "*Aṇī* and *āṇī* are considered [the terms for] the wedge at the tip of an axle and for boundaries and dice.

*Assi* means the corner of a sword. The root *aṇ* means "to sound," with the suffix *ṇi*. In the former alternative (*pubbapakkhe*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening; *ana* means "breathing" or "life."
Or *ṇattaṃ*. A shield for a chariot (*varutho*) made for the purpose of protection against arrows, spears, and the like, which is known as "chariot-guard" (*rathagutti*).
From the root *vara* (to ward off), *varaṇa* here means warding off; thus it is called *rathagutti* because it protects the chariot and its occupants.
Regarding the word *gutti*: in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*, it is stated that "*gutti* refers to a prison, and in the sense of being on the ground, it means protection or restraint."

375. Regarding the word *dhura*: it is used for the front part of chariots and so forth, reckoned as the "mouth" (*mukha*). The root *dhṛ* means "to hold" or "to bear. Here, the "mouth of the vehicle" (*yānamukha*) is also intended.
The axle, the linchpin, and so forth are called the "limbs" (*aṅga*) of the chariot. The root *ak* means "to go";

thus, *akṣa* (axle) is a specific piece of wood situated between the two wheels of the chariot. It is called *upakkhara* because it is placed above; it is a specific piece of wood located above the axle. [Source: *Amarakośa*.
However, it is stated that the word *upakkhara* denotes all the components of a chariot, as in the *Amarakosa* (18.55):
"The component of a chariot is *upakkhara*. There is also a reading, *apakkhara*.

In every vehicle, such as an elephant and so forth, the triad beginning with "vehicle" (*yāna*) is used; in all cases, it is formed by the instrumental case (*karaṇasādhana*). It is to be connected [to the root] as that by which one is joined (*yujjati*).

*Yoggaṃ*, *ṇyo*. *Pattaṃ* and *dhoraṇaṃ* are used here. *Pata* is in the sense of going; *dhora* is in the sense of skillful movement. In these cases as well, the derivation is by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇasādhana*). 376. A set of four [terms] refers to a charioteer (*sārathi*).
One who moves by means of a chariot through his skill is a *rathacārī*. One who impels or drives is a *sūta*;

from the root *sū* (in the sense of impelling), with the suffix *to*. From *aja* (in the sense of going): one who drives is a *pājitā*, with the suffix *ritu*, beginning with a long vowel. From *sara* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *thi*: by means of a chariot... [is a *sarathi*].
Or, he is called a *sārathi* because he goes along with [the chariot]; this is derived from the root *i*, except as a conventional metaphor.
Herein, the terms *niyantā*, *yantā*, *khattā*, *sabyaṭṭho*, *dakkhiṇattho*, and *rathakuṭumbī* are also used.
It is said: "The driver, the winner, the controller, the charioteer, the charioteer, and the master."
“The left side and the right side—these are the names for the chariot and the charioteer.

Thus it was said. In terms of meaning, *sārathin* and *rathakuṭumbin* are synonyms. Regarding the leader of the chariot, however, he will later say: “*Rathāroha*, *rathika*, and *rathī*. The root *khud* means to press or crush; with the suffix *-tu*, the letter *d* becomes *t*, and with the addition of the prefix *us*, it becomes *khattā*.
These three terms refer to other warriors who excel at driving the chariot, who are here also called “leaders of the chariot” (*rathanāyakā*). One who mounts the chariot is... [the term *rathāroha*].

*Rathika* and *rathī*. One who yokes with a chariot (*ratha*) is a *rathika*, and [one who possesses a chariot] is a *rathī*. *Rathina* and *sandanāroha* also apply here. There are two terms for a warrior: *yodha*.
In the sense of combat (*yudha*), the suffix *ṇo* is applied. One who serves (*bhaṭati*) or yokes himself is a *bhaṭa*;

the suffix *a* is used. In some cases, *yoddha* is also used. 377–379. A set of four terms for a foot soldier: *padāti*. One who moves (*atati*) or goes (*ajati*) by means of feet (*pada*) is a *padāti*. The root *ata* is used in the sense of continuous movement; the suffix *i* is added. *Pada-*...

Regarding "gamane" (in going): it goes on foot, thus "patti"; the suffix *i* is added, and there is reduplication (*dvitta*). Alternatively, it gives with the foot, thus "patti"; here there is elision (*alopa*) of the *a*, and the *d* becomes *t*.

These two [meanings] are neuter; the two to be mentioned next are masculine. It goes by means of feet, thus "padago" or "padiko. "Pādātiko" is also used here. It moves by means of its feet, thus "padāji";
the suffix *ī* is added, and there is shortening (*rassa*), as in "padājin" (Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā 18.66).

*Chakkaṃ* means armor (*kavaca*). *Naha* has the sense of binding; with the suffix *ṇo* in the instrumental sense, it becomes *nahaṃ*. *Kaṅka* has the meaning of motion; with the suffix *aṭ*, it becomes *kaṅkaṭo*.

That which wards off (*varīyate*) the arrow is *vammaṃ*; *vara* has the sense of warding off, or *vara* has the sense of wishing; with the suffix *mo*, the *ra* becomes *ma*. *Kaca* has the sense of binding;

with the suffix *a*, there is the augment of the letter *va*, thus *kavacaṃ*. That by which the chest (*ura*) is covered is *uracchado*. The word *vā* combines the two [terms] as being both masculine and neuter. *Jala* has the sense of shining.
*Ṇvu*. *Tanuttaṃ*, *daṃsanaṃ*, and *jagarō* are also used here. Regarding the verse: “*Jagaro kaṅkaṭo yogo, sannāho ca uracchado*” (Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.64;
Byākhyāsudhā 2.8.64), Vopālita [explains it thus]. The triad refers to one who has put on armor.

One is *sannaddho* because he is properly bound (*sammā naddhavā*) with leather (*cammena*), [the suffix] *dho* [is applied]. *Sajju* means “in going,” [with the suffix] *a*. One who is bound with armor (*vammena naddhavā*) is a *vammiko*. *Daṃsito*, *uracchadiko*, *byūḷhakaṅkaṭo*, and *jagariko* are also used here.

The two [forms] *paridahite* and *vatthādo* [are derived as follows]: the root *muc*, preceded by *ā-pati*, is used in the sense of burning (*paridahane*); both forms end in *-to*, and belong to the *bhū*-class (the first class).

In the alternative view, according to the rule *“susapacasakato kkhakkā ce”* (Kacc 642), the suffix *ta* becomes *kkha* due to the presence of the letter *ca*, and there is elision of the final part of the root.
Thus we have *pinaddho*; *apinaddho* is also found here. In the former view, there is also the elision of the vowel *a*.
A set of four [terms] regarding the category of "going before" (*abhicāra*). *Puracaraṇasīla*: one whose nature is to go before. There is no elision (*alopa*) of the seventh vowel in either case.

From the prefix *pubba-* (or *pubbe*), with the suffix *ṇī*. *Pubbaṅgama*: one who goes before others; from *para-pakkha* (the other side) with *a*, or from *pubbaṃ* (before) or *pubbe* (in front), with the suffix *ṇī*, meaning "one who goes before.
There is an elision of the second vowel. *Puroga*, *aggesara*, *paṭṭha*, *aggatosara*, *purassara*, and *purogama* are also used here.

Two terms refer to one who does not move quickly. One who moves slowly by nature is *mandagāmī*; the suffix *ṇī* is used here. From the root *manth* (to churn/stir), which has multiple meanings including "to be defiled," one who becomes defiled is *manthara*;

the suffix *aro* is used here. Three terms refer to one who is swift. One who moves rapidly is *turita*; from the root *i* (motion) with the suffix *to*. *Turassi*, *pajavī*, and *java* are also used here. Two terms refer to the mere state of being fit for victory. From the root *ji* (to conquer), with the suffix *tabba*, we have *jetabba*; with the suffix *ṇya*, it becomes *jeyya*. (380) Three terms refer to a hero.
From the roots *sura*, *vīra*, and *vikkranta* (belonging to the *curādi* class of roots): one who acts with heroism (*surayati*) or displays valor (*vīrayati*) is a *sūra* or a *vīra*.
And: *a*, *dīghādi*, and *ka* [are used] after the root *kant* (to cut), as in *vikkanta*. The word *sahāya* has two meanings: "companion" and "going together.

One who goes together (*eti*) is a companion (*sahāya*); in all cases, the suffix *ca-a* is applied to the agent. The prefix *anu* has the sense of "afterward. *Samā*—these two have the same meaning. *Anuplapo* and *abhisaro* [also mean companion].
Words such as *sannaddha* and *pabhuti*, when following [the aforementioned], are used in the three genders.

"Pātheyya" (provisions for a journey) is mentioned here because it is commonly used by kings and others specifically for journeys; "pātheyya" means "beneficial for the path" (*pathe hita*), with the suffix *-eyya*.

"Sambala": in the *samba* group [of roots], there is the suffix *-ala*; or, it is "sambala" because one "allays" (*sameti*) the fatigue of the road, with the suffix *-ala* and the addition of the augment *bā*.

381. The group of four refers to the army. It is called "vāhinī" because it carries [the troops]; "dhajinī" because it possesses banners; and "senā" from the root *si*, meaning "to bind," with the suffix *-na*.
*Camū* means an army (*adana*). It is called *camū* because it devours (*camati*) those who are timid. Here, *putanā*, *anīkinī*, and *varūthinī* are also used.
In this context, *putanā*, *anīkinī*, *vāhinī*, and *camū* refer to types of armies. Rudra states: “*Putanā*, *anīkinī*, *camū*, *senā*, and also *senāntara*. And Rabhasa states:
“*Vāhinī* refers to a division of an army, to an army itself, and also to a flowing river. The group beginning with *cakkā* (wheel) etc., generally refers to an army.
And regarding *senāṅga*: in the case of Cāṇakya, however, a specific division of the army is called an *anīka*, as in the phrase “three triads are an *anīka*.
There is indeed an explanation for this in the *Kāmandakīya*, as follows:
“Those three men who would be the foot-soldiers of a horse...”
Thus, there are five parts for its trunk, which are to be controlled by the elephant; fifteen toes upon its feet;
this is the arrangement for the elephant, and fourfold is that of the chariot.
"Anīkaṃ" should be understood as "viññeyyaṃ"; thus there are nine verses and two feet.

That by which an analysis (viggaha) is performed is a *cakra*. [The root] *bala* is in the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *a*. [The root] *aṇa* is in the sense of sound, with the suffix *ika*.
The letter *vā* indicates the neuter gender. The arrangement and distribution of a fourfold army, well-equipped, for the purpose of battle in various regions is [the meaning of] *vinyāsa*.
*Ṭhapanaṃ* (deployment) is called *byūha* (array). Deployment is the arranging [of troops] after having divided them. Its divisions are four basic arrays:
the staff (*daṇḍa*), the snake (*bhoga*), the circle (*maṇḍala*), and the compact (*asaṃhata*). Among these, the transverse movement of the divisions is the staff array.

The following movement of the divisions in a straight line, or their movement from one side to another, is the snake array. The movement of the divisions in all directions while maintaining a circular formation is like the body of a serpent; this is the circle array.
The *maṇḍala* (circle) formation: when the ranks stand without striking one another, yet remain more closely knit together, their movement is broad and not compact.
As it was said by Kāmandaka:
"Movement across [the front] is called the *daṇḍa* (staff); the *bhoga* (serpent) is indeed a winding movement."
“The mandala moves in all directions; it moves extensively and is unassailable.

The rear of the formation (*byūha*) itself, being a single part of the formation, is the “rear of the formation” (*byūhapaṇhi*); it is the back of the formation, or simply the interior of the formation.
Where the king stands and receives the enemy army with his own, that place is at a distance of two hundred and eighty bow-lengths behind the army.
An army unit accompanied by its standing retinue is called a "receiving unit" (*paṭiggaha*).
382–383. A single elephant together with twelve men is called "one elephant";
by this definition, at the very least as the lower limit, three elephants constitute what is known as an "elephant corps. Likewise, a single horse together with three men [constitutes one horse].

One chariot accompanied by four men and one horse—by this definition, at the very minimum, three horses and three chariots constitute what is called a "chariot-army" (*rathānīka*). Therefore, he said, "three each of elephants and so forth.
Four men, armed with weapons such as swords in their hands, are called a "foot-soldier-army" (*pattānīka*). Here too, [the calculation] is according to the very minimum.
This is the section on divisions. In the *Amarakośa*, however, it is explained differently:
"The *ekaka*, *ebha*, and *ratha* of that [army]; the *patti* consists of five foot-soldiers;
by tripling the components of the *patti*, the designations are applied in successive order."
"Senāmukha, gumba, gaṇa, vāhinī, pūtana, camū, anīkinī—these, it is said, are the ten units, each ten times greater than the last, known as the 'unshakeable' (akṣobhinī). (Amara 18.80–1).
The meaning of this is: three horses, one elephant, one chariot, and five foot soldiers constitute what is called a *patti*, a unit of the army.

By means of all the components, beginning with the elephant and so forth, according to their qualities as previously stated, there arise in successive order the designations "division" (*senāmukha*) and so on.
By the expression "in successive order," the meaning "according to what was previously stated" is indicated; therefore, this was said: "Three *pattis* constitute a *senāmukha*.
Three *senāmukhas* constitute a *gumba*. Three *gumbas* constitute a *gaṇa*. Three *gaṇas* constitute a *vāhinī*."
Three *vāhinīs* make a *pūtana*; three *pūtanas* make a *camū*; three *camūs* make an *anīkinī*. Ten of those *anīkinīs* are an *akṣobhinī*.
In that regard, the number of chariots is twenty-one thousand eight hundred and seventy. The number of elephants is exactly the same.
And likewise: Fifty-six thousand, six hundred, and ten.
The number of those horses, indeed, without the chariot and the horse [itself],
was one hundred thousand men, nine thousand, three hundred,
and fifty foot soldiers— thus it is explained in the *Byākhyāsudhā* (2.8.80).
384. Having shown the army by way of its minimum extent, he said, "Sixty... they go," etc., in order to show it by way of its maximum extent.
"Yanti" means when there is an army acting as the agent that constructs a vehicle; while the dust is being raised, in what [objects] does it settle?
In bundles of sixty bamboo poles. Of what measure are they? Each having sixty spokes. This is the unshakeable army.

The name *senā* [is used here] in its highest sense. It is called *akkhobhinī* because it cannot be disturbed by anyone; [this applies to] rivers and the like. The root *khubha* means "to move. 385. The tetrad refers to prosperity (*sampatti*).

*Dhanukkaṃsa* is prosperity. The root *pada* means "to go"; [from this, one] develops [the form]. In the alternative view, according to the rule "for the feminine, *ati* or *yava*," the suffix *a* is applied.

*Lakkha* means "mark," "sight," or "number"; with the suffix *ī*, it becomes *lakkhī*. Both *lakkhī* and *sirī* were previously mentioned as deities, but here they are mentioned in the sense of the excellence of wealth.

This pair [of terms] is the opposite of success (*sampatti*). It is called *vipatti* because one attains what is unshapely (*virūpaṃ pajjati*); the suffix *-ti* is added after the root *pad*. Alternatively, *vipatti* is the attainment of the unshapely; this is the abstract noun (*bhāva*). Because it accompanies misfortune (*āpadā*), *vipatti* is feminine. The tetrad [of terms] refers to weapons.
They go to fight, taking up [these things], thus they are *āvudha*; the suffix *-a* is added to the root *vā*. Or else, it is *āyudha*. The root *hṛ* means "to carry away.

It is called *heti* because it carries away life; the suffix *-ti* is added, and the *r* is elided. Or it is established by way of the root *han*. The root *sas* means "to injure"; the suffix *-tha* is added.
There are eight [points] here. *Asu* means "to cast.

(386–387) He spoke thus in order to show the weapon in brief: "That which is released from the hand, that which is not released from the hand, that which is released by means of breath, and that which is released by means of a machine"—the entirety of that weapon is fourfold, because it does not exceed those many divisions.

He stated the specific nature of these four with the words beginning "that which is released from the hand" (*muttāmuttañca*). A *yaṭṭhi* is a particular type of blade, not a walking stick (*kattaradaṇḍa*).
“*Yaṭṭhi*, *hāralatā*, and *sattha* [are used] for the staffs of bows,” according to the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*. That which begins with that (the staff) is a weapon;

it is both "released" (*mutta*) and "unreleased" (*amutta*), hence *muttāmutta*, a *kammadhāraya* compound, like *katākata* (done and undone). A *churikā* is a small sword (*asiputti*); that which begins with that is "unreleased. From the root *yant* (to contract), *yanta*; [this refers to] the bow and so forth. 388–389. The group of five [terms] refers to the bow. *Usu*:
it pierces (*asati*) and is hurled (*khipati*), hence *usu* with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the object. From *dhana* (wealth/grain), [comes *dhanu*].

*u*, *hana* (in the sense of harming), or *u*; *has* becomes *dha*; thus, *dhanu*. “Even if a bamboo bow is pure, what will it accomplish if it lacks string?”—this is the usage in the masculine gender in the *Hitopadesa Kathāmukha* 23.
“*Sara*, *vāpa*, and *dhanu* are feminine; *tuṇatā* and *tiṇatā* as well,” according to *Tikaṇḍasesa* 2.8.51.
It is called *kodaṇḍa* because it punishes (*daṇḍayati*) by what name? [The root] *daṇḍ* is used in the sense of inflicting punishment.

It is called *kodaṇḍa* because it tames (*damayati*); from the root *dam*, the suffix *ḍa* is added. Or, it is called *kodaṇḍa* because it afflicts (*dunoti*); from the root *du* meaning "to torment," the suffix *ḍa* is applied.
Alternatively, it is *kodaṇḍa* because its staff (*daṇḍa*) is crooked (*kuṭila*) or contemptible (*kucchita*). From the root *cap* meaning "to torment," with the suffix *a*, we get *capa*;
this refers to a bamboo split, and its derivative is *cāpa*. The suffix *ṇa* is added. It is called *sarāsana* because it remembers (*sara-sati*) or hurls arrows (*sarati*).
*Kammukaṃ*. It is called *kammukaṃ* because it originates for the sake of action (*kamma*).

The group of three [suffixes] refers to a quality (*guṇa*). A *guṇa* is that by which an arrow goes; its suffix is *ṇo*, and there is *assu*. Alternatively, *gu* means "to sound," or it is a *guṇa* because one moves by means of it;

the suffix is *yu*, with the substitution of *ṇ*. *Jarā* means the decay of age; the suffix is *a*, with the substitution of *ji*. In another sense, there is the elision of the vowel *i*, resulting in *jayā*. It is also said: "And *jiyā*."

The reading is: "Then, [the suffix] *dvaya* occurs after a quality (*guṇa*). Here, *mubbī* and *siñjinī* are examples. *Mubbavikāra* (a transformation of *mubba*) is *mubbī*. *Siñja* means "inarticulate sound"; with the suffix *inī*, it becomes *siñjinī*. *Tipāda* refers to a section of the *Kaṇḍa*. *Sara* is used in the sense of "harming.

From the root *sarati* ("he harms"), with the suffix *ṇo* used for a masculine noun, we get *saro*. *Patta* means "wing" (*vāja*); because of its connection with that, *pattī* is formed with the suffix *ī*.

*Sā* is used in the sense of making thin (*tanukaraṇa*) or at the end of a word; it belongs to the *div-ādi* class. With the suffix *ṇvu*, there is elision of the *ya* sound. *Vaṇyate* means "it makes a sound by this"; thus [the word *vaṇī* is derived].
*Vāṇo*, *ṇo*, and *vaṇa* mean "sound. That by which one is sounded is *kaṇḍaṃ*; *kaṇa* means "sound," with the suffix *ḍo*, or it means "piercing" (*kaṇḍa-bhede*).

*Isa* means "to go," with the suffix *u*, making *issu*; or *usa* means "burning. *Khura* means "cutting," with the suffix *apo*; alternatively, it goes into the hole (*khe*)—thus it is *khuro*; with the suffix *assu*, that which protects it is *khurappo*.

*Tija* means "sharpening," with the suffix *yu*. *Asa* means "throwing"; with the suffix *yu* in the passive sense, [it becomes *āsuyya*]. *Visikho*, *ajimhago*, and *khago* [mean "straight-flying" or "bird"].
*Āsuga*, *kalambo*, *maggaṇo*, and *ropo* are also used here. Because it pierces while entering, it is called *visikho*. [The root] *kala* means to intoxicate;

*ambo* [is derived from this]. [The root] *magga* means to search; [the suffix] *yu* [is added]. [The root] *rupa* means to delude; it belongs to the *divādi* class; [the suffix] *a* [is added], and there is the substitution (*ropo*). According to the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.8.52):
"Also *thūlakheḍo*, *vipāṭo*, and *citrapuṅkho* are synonyms for an arrow."
The group of five [words] pertains to the *kalāpa* (bundle). The root *tūṇ* is in the sense of filling; it belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and the *nadādigaṇa*.

In the Amaramālā, in the section on masculine nouns, the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (18.88) states: “*Tūṇo*, *nisaṅgo*, *tūṇiro*, *upāsaṅgo*, and *vāṇadhi* [are synonyms for quiver]. In the section on feminine gender, it is also stated as "*tūṇā*. However, here [in this text], both "*tuṇī*" and "*tūṇo*" are used.
Because it is the locus for collections of similar things (*sarasa*), it is called a *kalāpa*. With the suffix *ira*, it becomes *tūṇiro*.

*Vāṇadhi*: that in which arrows (*vāṇa*) are placed (*dhīyante*) is a *vāṇadhi*. Regarding this, Amarasimha states: "A quiver is called *tūṇa*, *pasaṅga*, *tūṇira*, *nisaṅga*, or *vāṇadhi*; there are two [types].

(390) The next two terms refer to the arrow-feather (*vāja*), which is called *kaṇḍapatta*. From the root *pat* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *kho* (i.e., *ghan*), the form becomes *patta*;

or it is so called because it is made from a wing (*pakkha*). Or, it is a *vāja* because one goes (*vajati*) by means of it; the suffix is *ṇo*. *Visappī*: an arrow (*sara*) that spreads out unevenly is a *visappī*.
*Diddha* means smeared. *Disa* means to sprinkle;

here, the suffix *to* is applied. The root *lip* is also used here. In the triplet [of roots], it is to be pierced. That which is aimed at for the purpose of piercing is a *lakkhaṃ*. That which is to be pierced is *vejjhaṃ*;

the suffix *ṇya* is applied, *jha* becomes *jjha*, and *issa* is substituted. That in which the arrow (*sara*) flies—that is, goes—is *sarabyaṃ*; the vowel *a* is elided. There is constant repetition of the vowels.

Subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*) is the practice with arrows. Rudda states: “In the case of disease and in the case of worship, ‘worship’ (*upāsana*) also refers to the practice with arrows. Worship is the drawing and shooting of the arrow after having reached the target.
391. Regarding the five [qualities] of the sword: that whose tip is circular is the *maṇḍalagga*. A *nettiṃsa* is that which has emerged from thirty finger-breadths. *Asa*...

*Khepana* means throwing; *khippati* means to throw, hence *asi* (sword). *Khagga* is used in the sense of breaking into pieces. *Sāyaka* refers to an arrow. *Candahāsa*, *riṭṭhi*, *kakkhalaka*, and *karavāla* are also terms for this [sword].
Its sheath is called *kosi*, which is feminine. *Kusa* means to smear or adhere; *kosi* ends in a short vowel.
The word *tharu* refers to the hilt of a sword, a dagger, or similar weapon. *Thara* means the movement of a blade, with the suffix *-u*.

392. The triad [of terms] beginning with *khagga* refers to weapons such as swords; *phalaka* refers to a shield. *Kheṭa* is derived from the root *khi* (to eat), with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Phalaka* is derived from the root *phala* (to spread/bear fruit), with the suffix *ṇvu*; it means that which bears fruit (*phalati*), and is not feminine. *Phala* is also [a term for a shield].

It is derived from the roots *cara* (in the sense of moving or eating) or *camu* (to eat), with the suffix *mo*, or simply *a*. *Vaṇṭānihāra* (the hilt of a sword), *sakhaggākaṭi*, *hatthakuṇḍādi*, *illī*, and *ilī* refer to the same object. It is derived from the root *ila* (to move), belonging to the *nadādi* class. *Karapālikā* is so called because it protects the hand (*karaṃ pālayati*); it is formed with the suffix *ṇvu*. This pair of terms refers to the scabbard (*asiputtiyā*). *Churikā* is derived from the root *chura* (to cut), with the suffix *ṇvu*.

*Sasū* is derived from the root *sas* (to injure), with the suffix *ti*, belonging to the *nadādi* class. *Asidhenukā* is also a term for a small knife, meaning "the daughter of the sword" (*asino puttī*).

Two [terms] for the axes of carpenters: *muggara* and *dughaṇa*. The root *mura* means to swallow; with the suffix *ara*, it becomes *muggara*. Alternatively, *muggara* is derived from the root *muc* with the suffix *ara*. *Ghana* is also used. (393) Two [terms] for an arrow: *salla* and *sūla*. The root *sala* means swift motion; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *salla*.

Alternatively, from the root *sara* meaning to injure, with the suffix *lo*, the *ra* is replaced by *la*. *Saṅku* is derived from the root *saṅka* meaning doubt, with the suffix *u*. *Sūla* is also used; it is derived from the root *sūla* meaning to cause pain. Two [terms] for an adze: *vāsi* and *taccha*.
The root *vasa* means cutting, smearing, or taking away, with the suffix *ṇī*. *Taccha* is derived from the root *taca* meaning to make thin, with the suffix *yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* class.
There are two terms for an axe. That which has a wretched (*kucchita*) edge because it cuts is a *kudhārī*;
it is also called a *kudhāra*. It is an *pharasu* because it pierces (*parasati*) or harms another; [the suffix] *u* is added, *pha* becomes *pho*, and there is the elision of *sa*.

*Parasu* is also used; that word *parasu* is neuter. *Parasudha* is also used here. There are two terms for a stone-cutter’s chisel. *Ṭaṅka* means binding. *Dara* means cleaving. It is a *pāsāṇadāraṇa* because it cleaves stone; [the suffix] *yu* is added. *Pāsāṇadāraka* is also used.
394. "Dvayaṃ hatthappamāṇe kaṇaye kaṇḍe" (Cintāmaṇi-Ṭīkā). It is propelled by means of the *cakkapūraṇa* and other winds. [The root] *kaṇ* means sound; *ayo* is a suffix.
Because it has the nature of splitting (*bhindana-sīlatā*), it is *bhindī*. That which moves (*vāti*) or goes (*gacchati*) by means of that is *vālo*;
with the suffix *alo*, it becomes *bhindivālo*, and in its short form (*ḷatta*), it is *bhindivāḷo*. It is abbreviated (*rasso*).

The *cakra* and others are types of weapons. Among them, a specific type of weapon having the shape of a wheel is a *cakra*. The root *kant* means "to cut"; thus, *assu*, *kunto* (a spear) is that which has a long shaft. *Gadā* and *satti* are well-known [terms for mace and javelin]. *Tikaṃ* refers to the corner portion.

From the roots *kuṇa* in the sense of "sound" or "instrument," or *kuṇa* in the sense of "contraction," with the suffix *ṇo*: from *si* in the sense of "service," with the suffix *a*, there is shortening, resulting in *asso*.

From *kuṭa* in the sense of "crookedness," with the suffix *iṇa*. 395. These two lines concern the expedition of one desiring victory; in all cases, they are formed as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*). That which reaches [its goal] after setting out.

*Yāyate niyyānam*, *yu*. From the rule “*chadādīhi tatraṇa*,” the suffix *traṇa* [is applied] to form *taraṇa*. *Yātrā*, *ā*. Because *nada* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (classes defined by their form), there is an absence of the suffix *ī*.

*Ṭhā* in the sense of stopping movement; preceded by *pa*, it means "to set out. With the suffix *yu*, *patiṭṭhīyate* becomes *paṭṭhāna*; with the prefix *pa*, it means "one who goes before" (*purecārin*).
A pentad [of terms] for mere dust. And likewise, the *Amaramālā* states: "The word *paṃsu* is considered a masculine noun; *khoda*, *reṇu*, *cuṇṇa*, and *dhūli* may be feminine."
*Cuṇṇa* [is used] in the sense of powdering or crushing into powder. *Paṃsu* [is used] in the sense of scattering. *Raja* means passion;

it is also a neuter member of the *manogaṇa* group, and by association with that, *paṃsu* is also [neuter]. According to Rabhasa: "The neuter [*kliva*] is used in the sense of fault and dust. Alternatively, *paṃsu* is neuter by association with *cuṇṇa* and *raja*.
*Dhū* is used in the sense of shaking or trembling; it belongs to the *li*-class and the *nadādi* group. *Ri* is used in the sense of motion; with the suffix *ṇu*, it becomes *reṇu*.
396. One who composes praise of lineage (*vaṃsastuti*) like a bamboo-rod staff (*vaṃsakkamavedī*) is a *māgadha*. Regarding him, [the term] *madhuka* is stated.

He originates from the *khattiya* or *vessa* castes; he is called a *māgadha* because he stands firm upon the path of his lineage (*vaṃsamaggaṃ thavati*), where *tha* becomes *dha*. Because he runs along the path (*maggaṃ dhavati*), he is a *madhuka*, formed with the suffix *ṇvu*, with the elision of *g*.
He who recites the *Vīriyādithuti* by means of his virtue (*sīla*) is a *vandī*;

the suffix *ṇī* is applied after *sīla* and other such words. He who awakens by making manifest the end of the night is a *vetāḷika*; because he awakens by making manifest [the time] with the sound of a drum (*tāḷa*), he is a *vetāḷika*, with the suffix *ṇika*.

He who recites while wandering with a wheel, having been tormented by many [people], is a *cakkika*; in both cases, the suffix *ika* is used in the sense of "wandering. The root *ghaṇṭ* has the meaning of "speaking" and belongs to the *curādi* class.

397. The group of five begins with *dhaja*. From the root *kit* in the sense of dwelling (*nivāsa*) and removing disease (*rogāpanayana*), with the suffix *u*: it removes (*apaneti*) by this, thus *ketu*. From *dhaja* in the sense of moving (*gamana*), with the suffix *a*:
it flies up (*uppatati*), thus *paṭākā*; or from *paṭa* in the sense of movement (*gati*), thus *paṭākā*.

Or, that which is split (*dalīyate*) and torn apart (*vidārīyate*) by the wind (*kena vātena*), thus *kadalī*, belonging to the class beginning with *nada*; or, because its leaves (*dala*) are wretched (*kucchita*) due to being cut and broken, she possesses them, thus *kadalī*.
*Kadalī* and *paṭākā* [refer to] a woman by virtue of association with a companion. *Kadalī* also refers to a plantain tree. *Ketana* refers to a father.

And here, because of its association with a banner (*dhaja*), *ketu* is both masculine and neuter. As stated in the *Amarakośa* (18.99): "The *paṭākā*, the *vejayantī*, the *ketana*, and the *dhaja* are not feminine.
Regarding the term *aññamaññassa*: having regard for one, another; having regard for another, yet another. That which is egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and conceit (*abhimāna*).

The term *aham-mahamikā* refers to the act of thinking, "I am [first], I am [first]. It is the running forward of warriors against one another, each bypassing the others, with the thought, "I shall be first, I shall be first.
In that context, however, it is called *ahampubbikā*. The word *aham* is an indeclinable particle resembling a case ending;
when the suffix *-ka* is added in its own sense (*sakatthe*), there is no doubling of the word because the sense of repetition (*vicchā*) is already understood.

398. The group of four [words] relates to strength (*bala*). *Bala* means life-force; it is derived from the root *bal*, with the suffix *a*. *Dhā* is used in the sense of stopping motion; with the suffix *mo*, the *dh* becomes *th*. *Saha* means "with that" (*tena*), thus *sahaṃ*; *saha* also exists. *Saka* means power (*satti*). *Draviṇaṃ*, *taro*, *parakkamo*, and *pāṇo* also [denote strength]. Excessive courage is called *vikkama*.
When there is victory (*jaya*) or when it has been won (*jita*), the drink made on that occasion is *jayapāna*. However, in the *Amarakosa*, it says: "But *vīrapānaṃ*..."

Regarding the statement, “That drink which [is drunk] when battle has arisen or is about to arise” (Amarakosa 18.103), its meaning is as follows: that drink which warriors drink together with their kinsmen—
preceded by an invocation to the deities— for the purpose of generating courage when there is a risk to life in an impending battle,
