and which is drunk when battle has actually arisen for the purpose of displaying victory, is called *vīrapāna* (the hero’s drink).

399–400. *Sāḍḍhapajja* means battle (*yuddha*). *Saṅgāma* means battle; it belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in *a*. *Hara* means taking away (*harana*) and acting with violence (*pasayhakaraṇa*).

*Ara* means going (*gamana*), ending in *a*; thus, *samara*. *Raṇa* means sound (*sadda*); it is used in the neuter and feminine genders. *Aja* means going (*gamana*), with the suffix *ṇi*, forming *āji*, which ends in a short vowel.

Warriors are summoned (*āhuyyante*) therein, from the root *hu* meaning sound, ending in *a*. *Yudha* means conflict (*sampahāra*), ending in *to*. Because they fight there after having taken up [their weapons], it is called *āyodhana*.
*Yu*: from the root *yu* (in the sense of joining), there is *saṃyugaṃ* and *saṃyuttaṃ*. *Bhaṇḍa*: from the root *bhaṇḍ* (in the sense of reviling). *Viggaho*:
they clash (*viggayhanti*) and fight (*yujjhanti*) in this; thus it is a conflict (*viggaho*). *Kalaho*: they quarrel (*kalahanti*) in this; thus it is a quarrel (*kalaho*). *Medhā*:

from the root *medha* (in the senses of intelligence, non-violence, and assembly), with the suffix *ṇvu*, [we have]: *jaññaṃ*, *pavidāraṇaṃ*, *akkandanaṃ*, *saṅkhyaṃ*, *samīkaṃ*, *samparāyakaṃ*, *anīkaṃ*, *abhisampāto*, *kalisaṃ*, *phoṭo*.
*Atyāmadda*, *duccāda*, and others also refer to combat. However, some say that the pentad beginning with *bhaṇḍana* refers to quarreling (*kalahe*) and not to combat (*yuddhe*);

this should not be accepted because it is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "The word *bhaṇḍana* occurs in the sense of armor (*kavace*), in combat (*yuddhe*), and also in the sense of reproach (*khalikāre*).

Two terms refer to fainting (*mucchā*). *Muccha* is used in the senses of delusion (*moha*) and a heap (*samussaya*). *Muha* means mental confusion (*vecitte*). Three terms refer to forceful compulsion (*balakkāre*). *Pasahana* becomes *pasayha*; [it is derived] with the suffix *ṇya* in the sense of capability (*satti*). Forceful compulsion (*balakkāra*) is the act of one who is strong, or an act by means of strength. *Haṭha* is used in the sense of forceful compulsion, with the suffix *ṇa*. *Pasaṅga* is also used in this sense.

401. That which is the manifestation, the disclosure, the alteration, and the arising otherwise of a real entity, indicating and making manifest pleasant and unpleasant fruits—that is *uppāda* (arising).
It is called *uppāda* because it falls upon [the fruit] or goes toward it while disclosing pleasant and unpleasant results; thus it is also *uppādo*.
This particle *pi* takes on the gender of either the preceding word or the following word. "Ignorance and that which is a condition is 'ignorance-condition' (*avijjāpaccayo*)."

In compounds such as *viggahavākyaṃ* ("a sentence that is a conflict"), the gender of the preceding member (*pubbapada*) is adopted; however, here the word *uppāta* is expressed in the masculine gender.
The set of four (*catukkaṃ*) refers to synonyms for *uppāta*.
[The root] *i* means "to go," beginning with the long vowel. That which does not arise at all times is called *ajaññaṃ* ("not noble" or "unfit").
*Ajanna*: that which does not produce a fruit; for it merely makes the fruit of karma manifest, like smoke [makes fire manifest], but does not produce it—thus it is called *ajanna*.
*Upasagga*: that which, having approached (*upagantvā*), clings to or manifests; from the root *sajj*, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Upaddava*: that which, having approached, afflicts;
from the root *du* (to burn/afflict), with the suffix *a*. And here, terms such as *īti* (calamity) and others also apply to that which produces [the affliction].
Just as there are calamities such as old age [and so forth]. 402.
In wrestling (*mallayuddha*) and boxing (*bāhuyuddha*), they fight by performing a "nibbuddha" (grappling). Here, *nibbuddha* refers to fighting by means of binding the lower body;
or, O Venerable One, it is called *nibbuddha* because they pierce (*vedhenti*) one another here. Piercing (*vedha*).

In the sense of piercing, [the root *vidh*] takes the suffixes *-to*, *-essu*, and others by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Two [terms] refer to the act of conquering: *ji* in the sense of victory; with the suffix *-ṇo* added according to the rule "and in the sense of an abstract state" (*bhāve*), it becomes *jaya*.
Defeat (*parājaya*) is that which is breaking (*bhaṅga*) in battle (*raṇa*); the root *ji* preceded by the prefix *parā-* refers to breaking in battle.

Two [terms] refer to mere flight, but not specifically to fleeing from the field of combat itself: fleeing (*palāyana*) is going away (*ayana*) by avoiding (*parivajjetvā*); [it is also] departing (*apavajjetvā*).

*Gamanaṃ* means departure (*apakkamo*). *Padāvo*, *dāvo*, *sandāvo*, *viddavo*, and *davo* also mean retreat (*apayānaṃ*). 403. *Pajjaṃ* [is used] in the sense of killing (*māraṇe*). *Mara* [is used] in the sense of giving up life;
in all cases, it is a noun derived from the state (*bhāvasādhanaṃ*). *Mārīyate* [means] killing (*māraṇaṃ*); [the suffix] *yu* [is applied]. *Hana* [is used] in the sense of harming (*hiṃsāyaṃ*);

with the suffix *ṇam*, there is the substitution of *ghāta* for *hana* according to the rule "for *hana*, *ghāta*. *Nasa* [is used] in the sense of disappearance (*adassane*). *Sūda* [is used] in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇe*). *Hiṃsa*...
*Hiṃs* means injury. With the suffix *sara*, there is the feminine suffix *āp*; thus, *hiṃsā*. With the suffix *ṇam*, there is the substitution of *vadh* for *han*;

thus, *vadhanaṃ*. *Sas* means injury. With the suffix *yu*, there are the forms *ghāto*, *ghātanaṃ*, *nibarahaṇaṃ*, *nikāraṇaṃ*, *pavāsanaṃ*, *saññāpanaṃ*, *pamathanaṃ*, *kathanaṃ*, *ujjāsanaṃ*, *ārambho*, and *piñjo* also occur here.
*Varah* is used in the senses of affliction, reproaching others, injury, and taking.

*Kara* means to injure. *Vasa*, preceded by *pa*, has the sense of harming; it belongs to the root *vas* in the sense of dwelling. *Ñā* means killing, tormenting, observing, or perceiving; *pā* is its augment, signifying making known.
*Matha* means to agitate; *katha* has the sense of harming. *Jasu* means to injure, or *jasi* means to strike, belonging to the *cur*-class (the tenth class).

*Ā-rabhi* means killing. *Piñja* means injury, bestowing strength, or a dwelling. These are the verbal roots (*dhātus*) that have arrived in their respective order according to the [standard] enumeration.
404. *Pajjaṃ* means death. *Kāla* refers to the past and so forth; its activity is [death], for it is said in Jaṭa 1.2.190: “Time devours beings.
From the root *mṛ*, with the suffix *cu*, we have *maccu*; or alternatively, with the suffix *tyu* after *vaj* and others.

Thus, in two senses, it is similar to *maccu*. *Accaya* is the passing beyond. *Dhana* means wealth or grain. Because it is an activity of time, it is called *kāla*; it brings about the end of the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Or it is time; no. That which moves toward the end is *anta*. *Cu* means to fall away. 405. The triad refers to one who has died.
One who goes to or moves toward the other world is a *peta*, and also a *pareta*; [the suffix] *to* [is added], with the elision of *ra* from the prefix. One who dies is *mata*.

*Parāsu* (one whose vital breaths have departed) and *pattapañcatto* (one who has reached the state of five) are also used here. The dyad refers to the pile of firewood for cremating the dead, which is called *phullī*.
It is so called. That in which one is piled up is a *citaka* (funeral pyre); it is both *cita* and *to*. In the former case, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*).

*Citā*, *cityā*, and *citipi* are used here as well. Two terms refer to the cemetery: *āḷahanaṃ* is that where they come and burn [the body]. From the root *daha* (to burn, to reduce to ashes), the suffix *yu* is added, and *da* becomes *ḷa*.

*Āḷāhanaṃ* is also used. A *susānaṃ* is the place for the lying down (*sayana*) of a corpse (*chava*); *su* is substituted for *chava*, and *sāna* is substituted for *sayana*. Alternatively, it is so called because they lie (*senti*) there.

For them, O youth, there is a cemetery for their corpse. [The word] *chava* means a corpse; it also refers to a funeral pyre (*pituvana*). There are two meanings regarding a dead body: "a corpse" (*kuṇapa*) and "one possessing a putrid odor.
Or, it is called *kuṇapa* because it leads (*neti*) to what is contemptible (*kucchita*); from the root *ap*, with the suffix *-ṇa*. [The root] *chava* is in the sense of going; see Aṭṭhakathā 406.
Because it is headless, it is empty of a head (*sirosuñña*); because it is accompanied by actions such as dancing, the body (*deha*) is called *kāya*; [and] *kabandha*—in battle...

The definition of a *kabandha* is: "Among thousands of warriors who are heroes with heads, at that time, this one headless trunk (*kabandha*) alone was blinded by action. Thus, a *kabandha* is one that fulfills the number of thousands in battle.
Because it is said "it dances," the term is used metaphorically for that which is devoid of actions such as dancing.
A *kabandha* is blind because of a certain head that does not exist; [the word] has the letter *va* in its middle. Even though it does not exist...
For the state of being a cause is seen in the world, such as how a good harvest or a famine is brought about by rain;
as it is in the world, so it is in the Teaching, as in the case of the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and others.
A "charnel ground" (*sivathikā*) is said to be a cemetery full of raw, putrid, and undecayed dead bodies.

And here, by the designation of the primary meaning as "object" (*atthappadhāna*), the word [“sadda”] is designated; just as in the expression “mindful and clearly comprehending,” it is a phenomenon (*dhamma*) by the designation of the primary meaning as “person” (*puggalappadhāna*).
*Chavā* means a corpse; it is derived from the root *dhī* with the suffix *ṇvu*. The *cha* becomes *sa*, and there is the substitution of *tha* and *it*.

Thus, *chavathikā* (a cemetery) is also formed. 407. Two things are drawn together: the term for a human corpse and the term for a singer. One who salutes with the perception of release is a *vandī*. The root *vanda* is used in the senses of salutation and praise.
*Ī*, even when short, is a vowel. *Karamara* refers to one who must be killed by the hand of an enemy (*sattu*).

*Paggaha* and *upaggaha* are synonyms. There are two [meanings] for *jīvita*: life and breath. It is called *pāṇa* because one breathes (*pāṇati*) by means of it; the suffix is *ṇo*. That by which one comes into being is *asu*. From the root *asa* (to exist), with the suffix *u*; also from *āsu* (quickly) or from *asu* (to agitate).

*Bandhanāgāra*, *bandhanageha*, and *kārā* mean a prison. They are called *kārā* because they "do" (*karonti*) harm (*hiṃsanti*) therein; the root *kara* signifies "harm. It is also a place of confinement (*bandhanālaya*). *Kara* means "harm," while from the root *yata* (in the sense of "bestowing") come *kāraṇā* and *yatanā*.
Intense suffering is also found there. The commentary on the Chapter on Khattiyas is finished. 408. Regarding *dvipāda*:
a *brāhmaṇa* is one who is a kinsman of Brahmā (*brahmuno bandhu*), or one for whom Brahmā is a kinsman (*brahmā bandhu yassa*); this is by virtue of his family conduct and his state as a *brāhmaṇa*.

He is called *dvija* (twice-born) because he is born twice; however, the term is used figuratively for one who is born only once. He is *vapismā* (one who has shaved), [ending] in *-po*. He is *assi* (a master). He is *brahmā* (a descendant of Brahmā) and *brāhmaṇo* (a Brahmin);

here, there is the insertion of *n*, the substitution of *ṇ*, and the lengthening of the vowel. He speaks the words "bho bho" (O, O! by his nature for the purpose of addressing those with whom he is associated through learning;

[this is formed] with the suffix *ṇī*. There are two [types] regarding the teacher of the Vedas (*chandojjhetar*). One who studies the *Brahmasutta* is a *sottiyo* (Vedic scholar); [the rule] "that which is indicated by *na* is impermanent" applies here, ending in *kā*.

1.2.18. Because it is stated [in the *Paribhāsendusekhara* 97] that "what is not joined with *na* is impermanent," there is vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*). Alternatively, by means of *yadādi*, there is the substitution of *sottiya* for the word *chandas* according to *Pāṇini* 5.2.84.
One who studies the *Chanda* is called *chandaso*; this is masculine. It refers to two types of students (*sissa*).

They are called *sissā* because they desire to hear; from the root *su* (to hear), with the suffixes *so* and *ussi*. One whose habit is to dwell near or in the presence of the teacher: because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), there is elision of the locative case ending.
409. These four types of persons, beginning with the *brahmacārī*, are called "those who dwell in a hermitage" (*assama*). This word *assama* is both masculine and neuter.

Among them, one who is devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacariya*), wears a girdle of *muñja* grass and so forth, and studies the Vedas is a *brahmacārī*. [The term is derived from] "one who practices the life of celibacy, which is the study of the Vedas," using the suffix *ṇī*.
One who is established in virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and performs the five great sacrifices, is a householder (*gahaṭṭha*). [The term is derived from] *gaha*...
One who dwells there with a wife is a householder (*gahaṭṭha*). Beyond the householder is the third, the forest-dweller (*vānapastha*).

One who exists in a forest region, or in a remote forest, is a forest-dweller; his qualities consist of sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair and antelope skins, dwelling in the forest, eating what is obtained by begging, and so forth.
Having spent the third part of his life as a forest-dweller, one who has taken up the yellow robe and the staff is a monk (*bhikkhu*).
The bhikkhu is equal toward all beings, supreme in the sphere of meditation. He is equal in austerity and in exertion;

they settle there, not in non-doing, but through the perception of the agent. According to the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: “*Assama* occurs in the fourfold set beginning with ‘brahmacariya’ and also in the sense of a monastery. 410.
The three trainings, virtue and the rest, practicing together as one, are mutual companions (*sabrahmacārino*) to one another.

“Name”: those who practice together with fellow celibates (*brahmacārī*) are *sabrahmacārins*. By the word “mutually” (*mithu*), it is shown that the term *sabrahmacārī* is understood through its own inherent quality;
thus, the status of being a *sabrahmacārī* is established for the fellow celibates as well. There are two types of those who confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).
One is called an *upajjhāya* because, having approached with the mind, he contemplates (*jhāyati*) the faults and non-faults of his disciples.
And the preceptor (*upajjhā*). [The root] *jhi* means to think; with the suffix *ṇo*, preceded by *upa-*, it becomes *upajjhā*.

In the alternative sense, such as the royal lineage, one who teaches the *Veda* and so forth in another tradition is called “*upajjhāyo*, *upajjhā*,” because they are studied after approaching them. These two terms refer to the one who gives formal dependence (*nissaya*).

One who practices what is beneficial for disciples is an *ācariya*; [the suffix] *ṇyo*. One who gives dependence is [an *ācariya*]; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is applied in the sense of the object and so forth.
411. Having shown the teacher within his own dispensation (*sāsana*), he says "upanīya" and so forth in order to show him even in other systems (*parasamaya*).

Alternatively, whatever twice-born Brāhmaṇa, having brought some Brāhmaṇa near to himself—since it consists of six limbs beginning with *kalpa* and is thus "with limbs" (*sāṅga*) and "with secret portions" (*sarahasya*)—first of all (*pubbaṃ*) taught the Veda, which is the object of the action, even though it had not been previously taught by anyone; [that Brāhmaṇa...]

One who causes [others] to study and trains them is called an "ācariya" among the brahmins; he is called an *ācariya* because he leads [them] from the beginning and trains them—the suffix *-ṇya* being used here.
Others, as previously mentioned, are *upajjhāyas*. 412. *Pajjaddhaṃ* refers to the lineage of oral instruction.
"The others and the others" (*pare ca pare ca*) constitute the succession (*paramparā*), namely the former teachers (*pubbācariyā*). From that...
"Ābhataṃ pārampariyaṃ. The term *itiha* is a collection of indeclinables (*nipāta*). That which is to be spoken as "Thus it was said by the ancient teachers" is *etihya*;
[the suffix] *ṇya*. With the suffix *ṇa*, it becomes *etihaṃ*. That which is seen—that is, uttered—by approaching a teacher is *upadesa*;
[the root] *dis* in the sense of uttering, with the suffix *ṇa*.
The triad [of suffixes] occurs in the sense of sacrifice (*yañña*). The root *yaja* is used in the senses of worshipping deities, gathering, performing, giving, and religious duty (*dhamma*);

the act of sacrificing is *yāga*, with the suffix *ṇo*. It is called *katu* because it is performed by those seeking heaven; the suffix *tu* is added. When the suffix *ñña* is applied to this, it becomes *yañña*.

The ground prepared and consecrated for the purpose of sacrifice by means of mantras and so forth is called *vedi*; with the suffix *ī*, it is also *vedī*. It is called *vedi* because one finds (*vindati*) gain and honor upon it; from the root *vida* in the sense of finding, with the suffix *iṇa*.
413. The five sacrifices beginning with the horse-sacrifice are called the "great sacrifices" (*mahāyāga*).

It is said that in the time of the ancient kings, there were four bases of social integration—namely, the *sassamedha*, the *purisamedha*, the *sammāpāsa*, and the *vācāpeyya*—by which kings held the world together.
Among these, the taking of a tenth portion from the harvested crops was called the *sassamedha*; it refers to the wisdom (*medhā*) in the successful production of crops.
The sacrifice of grain (*sassamedha*) means wisdom regarding food.
The sacrifice of men (*purisamedha*) means the provision of six-monthly rations and wages for great warriors; its underlying meaning is wisdom in winning over men.
The sacrifice of wealth (*dhanamedha*) means taking a written pledge from poor people and providing them with two thousand pieces of wealth for three years without interest.
It is called *sammāpāsa*. For it causes people to look toward [the king] correctly and keeps them bound as if in their hearts; therefore, it is called "the correct throw" (*sammāpāsa*).
Furthermore, speaking with gentle words such as "Dear father," "Uncle," and so forth, is called *vācāpeyya*; the meaning is that one speaks words that are blameless and pleasing.
Thus, a kingdom held together by these four bases is prosperous, flourishing, abundant in food and drink, and secure.
Nirabbuda. People dwell there joyful and delighted, tossing their children about on their chests with the doors of their houses left wide open;
this is called "Niraggaḷa" (boltless) because of the absence of bolts on the house doors—this is the ancient tradition.
However, later, during the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins [considered] these four bases of sympathy and this prosperity of the kingdom...
Turning it upside down and making the root the top, they performed the five sacrifices known as the "Horse Sacrifice" (Aśvamedha) and so forth.
For this was said by the Blessed One in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta:
"They were perverted, having seen a tiny thing as large."
"Having composed mantras there, they approached Okkāka"—thus [it is said in] SuN 301, 304.
Now, in order to show the meaning established by them after they had turned it over, he spoke the passage beginning with "the horse sacrifice" (assamedha).
Therein, "horse sacrifice" (assamedha) means that they slaughter a horse here; "human sacrifice" (purisamedha) means that they slaughter a human being here.
It is called *sammāpāsa* because they cast and throw a stick here that must be properly inserted through a hole in the yoke.
Because they drink there the ghee and honey prepared with mantra-words, it is called *vājapeyya*.
It is called *niraggaḷa* because no bolt (*aggaḷa*) remains here, since all of one’s own property has been given away without concealment and without remainder. This...

The commentary on the meaning [of the sacrifices] follows the order in which they appear in the Canon (Pāḷi); however, here, the commentary on the meaning of the horse-sacrifice (assamedha), the human-sacrifice (purisamedha), the *niraggaḷa*, the *sammāpāsa*, and the *vājapeyya* should be written according to the order in which they occur here.

414. Regarding the triad concerning the sacrificer (*yājaka*): *Yajanasīlo* [becomes] *idi*, *yassi*, and *jassa* by means of the suffixes *do*. One who sacrifices is an *ijo*; [this is formed with] the suffix *a*. Alternatively, [it is derived from] a woman...
“Born when the season has arisen, thus ‘born of the woman’ (*itthitujo*). There is also the reading *nārītviyo*. There is also the reading *utujo yājako tathā*, which is excellent.
However, having disregarded other systems [of grammar], the teacher—perhaps thinking that the words *itidvija* and *iditvija* have the same meaning—may have said *idi tvijo*;
in this case, the word *yājaka* should be seen in the rule for the suffix *ṇvu* in verse 17.17 of the Amarakosa.”
The two [terms] refer to one who initiates a sacrifice or another assembly. One who is good in an assembly is a *sabhya*.

Those who enter (*samāvasanti*) a gathering (*samāja*)—a multitude of people—having come together to become part of it, are called *samājā*; one who becomes united with them is a *sāmājika* (the suffix *-ika* is added).
Here, *sabhāsada* and *sabhātāpa* are also used.

The group of five [terms] share a common meaning. A *parisā* is that in which one sits (*senti*) all around (*pari*); *si* is used in the sense of sitting. A *sabhā* is that in which they speak together (*saha bhāsanti*);

there is the elision of the suffix *-ha*, or alternatively, it is a *sabhā* because the virtuous (*sabbhi*) dwell (*bhāti*) therein. A *samajjā* is that in which people gather (*samajjanti*), come together (*saṅgacchanti*), or meet (*milanti*);

the root *aja* means "to go. A *samiti* is that in which they assemble (*samayanti*) or meet; the root *i* means "to go," and the feminine suffix *-ti* is applied. Meeting (*milana*) is the state of becoming one (*ekībhāva*).
In this [term], people sit down on all sides; thus it is *saṃsad* (an assembly). It refers to women and eunuchs. *Goṭṭhī* and *aṭṭhānī* are also used here. Cows (*gāvo*) stand (*tiṭṭhanti*) in this;
thus it is *goṭṭhī*. They come (*āgantvā*) and stand in this; thus it is *aṭṭhānī*, with the suffix *-yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* group, and having a short vowel as its initial.

415–416. These four, beginning with the *bhikkhu*, are called assemblies (*parisā*). One is a *bhikkhu* by virtue of the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīlatā*) and so forth. “With reference to... (*uddissa*)...
"The noble ones abide; this is the entreaty of the noble ones," so it is said (Jātaka 1.7.59). The root *bhikkha* means "to beg. With the suffix *yom*, we have *bhikkhu*.
With the suffix *inī*, we have *bhikkhunī*; the *y* is elided. Those who approach the Three Jewels and sit (*āsayanti*) there are *upāsakas*;

[the suffix] *ṇvu* is used, from the root *āsa* meaning "to sit. With the feminine suffix *itt*, we have *upāsikāyo*. And here, by virtue of the commonality of their renunciation (*pabbajjā*) and the commonality of their gender (*liṅga*), [they are included].
The novices are included among the monks, and the female novices and others are included among the nuns;
furthermore, all remaining beings, such as gods and humans, are divided into two classes according to gender and are included within the two [groups] by way of their commonality of sex.
However, although the Brahmās lack sexual organs, they are included among males because of their masculine form. Likewise...

It should be understood that among the eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), those with both sexual characteristics (*ubhatobyañjana*)—specifically, those with male characteristics on both sides—are included among men, while those with female characteristics on both sides are included among women.
Having thus shown the assembly by way of four categories, he said "Or else," etc., in order to show it by way of eight as well. Its meaning is as follows:
—Regarding the term "assembly" (*parisā*), there may be eight; by virtue of what are there eight?
By virtue of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the twice-born, the brahmins, the householders, the kṣatriyas, Māra, the householder, the recluses, the Cātumahārājika gods, and the Brahmās.
These eight assemblies have been stated here according to their manifest status and their preeminent status; therefore, it is not as it was previously.

All [the meters] are included; for those beginning with the *Tāvatiṃsa* are stated by way of their manifest forms, whereas the *samaṇa* meters are stated by way of their manifest forms and by way of their excellence.
417. That which is called *gāyattī* is that in which there are six syllables in each of its four feet.
Because it is not employed as a sequence for the *utthā* and so forth, it is the meter named *gāyattī-pamukha*. It is called *gāyattī* because it sings (*gāyati*).
*Ge sadde*, thus *aya*. That which covers over what is blameworthy (*vajja*) is *chanda*; [the root] *chad* means to cover (*saṃvaraṇe*).
For it was said by the monk Buddhagutta in the *Pajjaviveka*:
"The deathless is the beginning, the middle is the [noble] path, and the well-established is the foundation."
“Pādas are those that stand outside the application [of the rules], and they are not recited because of their incapacity.

Furthermore, that which possesses twenty-four syllables, which is the beginning of the Vedas, and which—unlike the *gāyattī* among the meters—is not four-paded but rather three-paded, is called the *Sāvittī*. The word *Sāvittī* is also a synonym for *Gāyattī*: “*Sāvittī*...”
Because it is stated in the *Majjhima Nikāya* (2.400) and the *Sutta Nipāta* (573) that "the mouth of the Veda is the Sāvittī," and also because it is said, "But they sing the Sāvittī.
However, here it is stated by way of its analysis, as in: "I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
This speech belongs to the seer Savitṛ, thus it is the Sāvittī; [this is the etymology].

418. *Habya* is food intended for the deities; when it has been cooked, the vessel such as a pot (*thālī*) that serves as its support is called *caru*. Because it is situated therein, by way of figurative designation (*upacāra*), the food itself is also called *caru*.
[The suffix] *-u* is added to the root *car* (to move); thus *caru* is masculine. Indeed, the *Amarakosa* (17.22) states:

*“In the sense of the cooking of sacrificial food, *caru* is masculine.”* Regarding the ladle (*kaṭacchu*) made for the purpose of lifting out the sacrificial food and so forth during the act of offering (*homa*): [it is used] for the sake of taking up the sacrificial food and other items for the ritual of oblation.
*Sujā*: A woman (*itthī*) is called *sujā* because she gives birth (*jāyati*) to sacrificial offerings (*havya*) and other things easily (*su-*).

*Dvayaṃ khīranne*: There are two [words] for milk-rice (*khīranna*). It is the supreme food (*paramaṃ annaṃ*) because it is divine (*deva*). It is *pāyāsa* because both states—being drinkable (*pātabba*) and being edible (*asitabba*)—are present in it;
[the suffix] *-āya-* is added to words ending in *-ā*. *Pāyasa* is also used here. *Dvayaṃ devanne*: There are two [words] for divine food. [The root] *hu* is used in the sense of giving (*dāne*).
In this [context], it is neuter. 419.
*Thūṇā* refers to a sacrificial post (*yaññathambha*). It is made of *beluva* or *khadira* wood.

It is a wooden pillar for tethering the animal to be sacrificed, or whatever wooden pole one erects at a complete sacrifice—that is a *yūpa*. … [a variety of wooden posts used for binding sacrificial animals] …
The word *thambha* (post) is [formed] with the suffix *ca* (*ka*) in the sense of being a mark of the completion of a sacrifice; it begins with a long vowel and ends in *ppati*.

The word *yu* is [formed] with the suffix *missana*; it begins with a long vowel and ends in *po*. The word *thu* is [formed] with the suffix *abhitthava*; it begins with a long vowel and ends in *ṇo*. That wood which is rubbed against another piece of wood for the purpose of producing fire is called *nimmanthyadāru*;
in that context, *araṇī* is derived from the root *ara* (to go) with the suffix *aṇi*, and with the addition of *īm*, it becomes *araṇī*.
The three fires beginning with the *gāhapacca*. That which is connected with a householder (*gahapati*) is the *gāhapacca* fire; [the suffix] *-ṇya* is used here.

That which is of that same origin as the *āhavanīya* fire, and which is worthy of receiving the oblation (*āhuti*), is the *āhavanīya*. The *dakkhiṇaggi*, however, is both of that origin and of another origin.

It is called *dakkhiṇaggi* because one relinquishes the gift (*dakkhiṇa*)—that is, the object to be given—as the "foremost" (*agga*) therein. *Agga* means giving; it is so called because the act of giving (*dāna*) is offered (*aggīyati*) or bestowed (*dīyati*) within it.
The *Aṅguttara-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* (3.9.20) states that the "summit of giving" (*dānagga*) refers to the "place of distribution" (*parivesanaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, in this context, the three—namely, the recipient (*gāha*), the foremost gift (*paccagga*), and so forth—are to be regarded as "summits" (*agga*) because they are the causes for the destruction of those who act wrongly. However, in the commentary on the *Sattaka-nipāta* of the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*, it says:

"Offering" (*āhuna*) means honor; those who are worthy of such offering are "those worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyyā*). [These are] mother and father; for mother and father [are the primary objects of honor] for their children...
Because they are of great assistance, they are worthy of offerings; yet sons who act wrongly toward them are reborn in the hells and other realms of misery.
Therefore, although parents do not themselves burn [the child], they serve as a condition for one who burns [them];

thus, in the sense of being that which is burned, they are called "fires worthy of offerings. He who is of great assistance to a woman by providing her with bedding, clothing, ornaments, and so forth—

A woman who transgresses against him is reborn in the hells and other such realms; therefore, for the reason of burning [the transgressor], he too is called a "householder-fire" (gahapataggi) in the same manner as the preceding ones.

Regarding the term "fire of those worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyyaggi): here, "offering" (dakkhiṇā) refers to the four requisites, and the Saṅgha of monks is the one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya).
He [the Saṅgha] is for householders in the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts...
It is of great benefit through the enjoining of such wholesome qualities as attending upon one’s mother and father, and attending upon righteous recluses and brahmins.
A householder who practices wrongly in this regard, having reviled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, is reborn in the hells and other such realms;
therefore, he too, by the same principle as before, is a "conflagration" in the sense of burning.
It is called “the fire worthy of offerings” (*dakkhiṇeyyaggī*). According to the *Aṭṭhanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* (3.7.46), ordinary fire produced from wood is called “wood-fire” (*kaṭṭhaggi*).

420. Verses on Giving (*Dāna*): *Hā* is used for relinquishing (*cāga*); *ṇo* [is used] for the two, three, four, and five syllables; *caja* is used in the sense of loss (*hāni*). *Saja* is used for letting go (*visagga*); letting go is giving (*dāna*). With the prefix *upa*, *saja* means to release (*visajje*);

with the prefix *va*, it is *vosaṅga*. *Disa* is used in the sense of bestowing (*atisajjana*); bestowing is giving. *Visaggo* = giving (*dāna*). *Upasaja* = to release (*visajje*). With the prefix *va*, *vosaṅga*. *Disa* = in the sense of bestowing (*atisajjana*). Bestowing is giving.

Giving (*dāna*), awakening (*pabodhana*), and seeking (*padesana*)—these are the meanings here. [The root] *dā* is in the sense of giving; *yu* is a suffix. *Tara* is in the sense of floating and crossing; here, "crossing" refers to the overcoming of the stream of stinginess (*macchera*).

[Hā]: In the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*), it belongs to the *cur*-class; the suffix *to* is added, and there is the elision of *yā*. Alternatively, in the *bhū*-class, by the rule "for those ending in long *ā*, [the suffix] *āya*," there is *āya*, and thus it means "that which has been left behind" (*vihāyita*).

[Vajja]: In the sense of avoiding (*vajjana*); in all cases, this is derived as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). Through specific prefixes, these express the meaning of giving. Touching (*phassana*) and establishing (*patipādana*) are also included here.
421. The "five great renunciations" (pañcamahāpariccāga) are described by way of the best wealth, sons, wives, kingdom, and limbs.
Therein, "best wealth" refers to treasures such as white elephants and the like. "Sons" refers to those born of the loins, or alternatively, both sons and daughters.
"Wife" refers to a devoted and beloved consort. "Kingdom" refers to natural sovereignty or the revenue arising therefrom. "Limbs" refers to the eyes and so forth.
"Great renunciation" (*mahāpariccāga*) means a renunciation performed by great, supreme persons; or, the renunciation of great persons is "great renunciation";

or, the renunciation performed for the sake of the great goal—the state of Buddhahood—is "great renunciation"; or, because it is difficult for base persons to perform, it is a great or excellent renunciation, hence "great renunciation."

422. Having shown the uncommon objects of giving by way of the three perfections beginning with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), he said, "Food, drink," and so forth, in order to show the common objects of giving.
Therein, "food" (*anna*) refers to anything such as solid food (*khādanīya*) and the like, excluding drink.
"Drink" (*pāna*) refers to that which is to be drunk, such as water and so forth. "Vehicles" (*yāna*) refers to elephants and the like, including even sandals.

The means of locomotion. A garland (*mālā*) is a wreath (*mālya*), as well as a flower (*puṣpa*). Anointment (*vilepana*) is that which colors the skin, or it is a refined fragrance (*vibhūta-sugandha*).
Fragrance (*gandha*) is any scent other than that. A bed (*seyyā*) refers to couches and so forth; by the mention of "bed," a seat (*āsana*) is also included here.
Lighting materials (*padīpeyya*) are whatever is suitable for a lamp, such as oil and the like. These ten are known as the objects of giving (*dānavatthu*). They are given.
That which goes forth is giving (*dāna*). Its basis (*vatthu*) is the cause; it is called the "basis of giving" because it arises at the time of that [giving's] arising.
Alternatively, giving is that which is to be given, such as food and so forth; that itself is the basis. These ten bases of giving have been explained according to the method of the Suttas.

However, they should also be explained according to the methods of the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma; for in the Abhidhamma, they are treated by way of the giving of the six objects of sense, beginning with visible form.
Six bases for giving have been recorded; in the Vinaya, four are recorded by way of robes, almsfood, medicine, and lodgings.
Regarding this, the teachers say: "The giving according to the Vinaya is more fruitful than the giving according to the method of the Suttas.

Why? Because, while permitting that anyone—even one who is immoral—may be given to merely on account of the gift of food and so forth, [the Vinaya] prescribes it through the appropriate terminology of almsfood and so on."
And it is because it has been authorized that [the gift] should be given only to those who possess virtue and so forth. For a specific gift is more fruitful than a general gift;

even more fruitful than that is a gift according to the method of the Abhidhamma. Why? Because by way of giving while focusing specifically on the ultimate reality (paramattha) regarding form and the other aggregates, it is an especially distinguished gift.
As for us, however, whether it be a gift according to the method of the Suttanta, or a gift according to the methods of the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma—
Or rather, we say that whatever is endowed with the threefold excellence of the field and so forth, that alone makes it highly fruitful.

423. On that day—the day of death—whatever gift of alms-food, handfuls of water, and so forth is given for the sake of the deceased, this gift is called *uddhadehika*, meaning "pertaining to the state beyond the body.
A gift of handfuls of water, gold, and so forth offered in honor of one's father is called *nivāpa* (the sowing). To sow [merit]...

In the continuity of the seed, no. That which is prescribed by the teachers—such as Rājamataṇḍavi and Sottara—according to the rules regarding the proper time and so forth, namely that very gift to one’s father, such as feeding ascetics and brahmins, is called *saddhā*.
[The analysis is: "he has faith (*saddhā*) in this gift" (*assa dānassa*), thus [the suffix] *ṇo*.
From the word *satthato*, the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), expressing the meaning of non-limitation (*avadhyattha*).

424. Regarding the group of four concerning those who have come to the house: *sātaccagamane*, *itthi*, *atithi*. According to the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.7.9), which states "atithi in two [meanings]," it is both a woman (*itthiyam*) and a guest (*atithi*).
One who comes is an *āgantu*. Food and so forth to be given to those who have come to the house is called *āhunam*;
one who is worthy of receiving that is a *pāhuno*. From the root *vis* in the sense of entering (*pavesane*), *āvesanam* becomes *āveso*.

One who causes intoxication is an *āvesika*; *atyāgata* is also used here. One who desires to go is a *gamika*, with the suffix *-ika*. The two [terms] refer to that which is strewn with honored flowers, grass, and so forth.

*Aggha* is used in the sense of honoring; with the suffix *-a*, it is *agghiya*, and also *agghaya*. Alternatively, from *aggha*, the suffix *-iya* is added in the sense of "that which belongs to it. 425.

In the sense of "for the feet," as in *pādaddha*, there is *pajja* when referring to water and so forth. That which is beneficial for the feet (*pada*) is *pajja*. The seven words beginning with *āgantvā* and ending with *pajja* occur in all three genders.

*Chakka* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). *Ci* is used in the sense of accumulation (*caya*). *Acca* is used in the sense of worship; [with the suffix] *yu*, it becomes *pūjā*. *Pūja* is used in the sense of worship; with the feminine suffix *ati*, it becomes *pūjā*.

*Hara* is used in the sense of taking away (*haraṇa*); preceded by *upa*, *hara* is used in the sense of worship; with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *upahāra*, in the masculine. *Bala* is used in the senses of life-force (*pāṇana*), worship (*pūjā*), and restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*);

with the suffix *i*, it becomes *bali*, in two genders. *Māna* is used in the sense of worship; with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *mānya*. *Namassa* is also used here; *namassa* is used in the sense of worship; with the feminine suffix *a*, it becomes *namassā*.
426. This is a tetrad concerning *namassati* (to revere). In the word *namassati*, *namas* means "reverence" (*vandane*), while *ss* is a suffix added after the prefix *pubba*.

Alternatively, *namu* means "bowing" (*namane*). *Namo-karaṇaṃ* is "the act of making homage"; here, *ṇo* is the suffix. In the term *namato*, there is the elision of the genitive case ending (*chaṭṭhī-lopa*). According to the rule “*lopañca tatrākāro*,” when the vowel *o* is elided, the vowel *a* is inserted as a substitute.
Alternatively, *namanaṃ* is *namo*; the act of that (*tassa karaṇaṃ*) is *namakkāro*. For the word *namosaddo* here is twofold, just like the word *raho*.

It occurs [as follows]: one [root] ending in *a* has its own gender (*saliṅga*), while the other, ending in *o*, is without gender (*aliṅga*). From the root *vanda* in the senses of salutation and praise, with the suffix *yu*, there is *vandanā*;
when the nasal (*n*) is elided and lengthening occurs, it becomes *abhivādanaṃ*.

The group of three [roots beginning with *pata*] is used in the sense of mere wishing. From *attha* in the sense of requesting, with the suffix *yu*, there is *patthanā*; *atthanā* is also [used]. From *ṭhā* in the sense of stopping movement.

The suffix *yu* is applied after the prefix *paṇi* to form *paṇidhi*, meaning "aspiration" (*patthanā*). Here, the vowel *i* is substituted for *a*, and *dha* is substituted for *ta*. This word *paṇidhi* is masculine (*pulliṅga*) when referring to a person. It also signifies "supplication" (*yācanā*) in this context. 427.

*Ajjhesanā* (entreaty) is a specific kind of aspiration consisting of the application of someone to a certain purpose, preceded by acts of honor (*sakkāra*), directed toward venerable persons (*garu*) and others who are worthy of being propitiated.

[The root] *isa* is used in the sense of seeking (*gavesana*); alternatively, *isa* is used in the senses of motion (*gati*), injury (*hiṃsā*), and cutting (*avadāna*). The suffix *yu* is added to form *ajjhesanā*, as in: "May the Blessed One teach."
"Teach the Dhamma, O Sugata! (Mahāva. 8.428). The group of four [terms] refers to recollection.

*Esa* means seeking; *yāgama* and *pariyesanā* mean searching. *Pariyeṭṭhi* occurs in the three [cases]. *Gavesa* means investigation. The triad [of terms] refers to that which is to be propitiated and to what is agreeable to the mind.
*Āsa* means sitting near; with the suffix *-yu*, it becomes *upāsana*. *Su* means hearing; the desire to hear is [the meaning of *sussūsā*].

*Sussūsā* (desire to hear) is formed with the suffix *sapaccaya* according to the rule “after *bhuj*, *ghas*, *saha*, *su*, etc., when the sixth case ending follows. It begins with *dvitta* (double consonant), and that woman is the one who desires to hear.
From the root *car* (to practice), the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), resulting in *pāricariyā* (service).

429. The triad [of terms] refers to silence. *Mona* is the action (*kamma*) of a sage (*muni*); the suffix *ṇo* is applied. From the root *tuha* (to eat), the suffix *ṇha* is applied and there is the elision of the *hal* (consonant), [resulting in *tunhī*].
"Tuṇhī" means "one for whom silence is the goal"; thus it is *tuṇhī*. The state of that is *tuṇhībhāva*. Alternatively, the becoming silent of one who was not silent is *tuṇhībhāva*.
Or else, he is *tuṇhī* because he devours (*tohati*); the root is *tuha* in the sense of eating, where "eating" means harming; with the suffix *-ṇi*, there is a change of vowel quality.
The state of one who is *tuṇhī* is *tuṇhībhāva*.

The group of five [is explained] in successive order (*anukkama*). *Paṭipāṭi* means falling in accordance with what is appropriate; from the root *pat* (to go), the suffix *ṭo* is applied in both cases.
That is feminine. *Anurūpa-kamo* or simply *kamo* itself is *anukkamo*. *Pari-ayana*—that is, proceeding without transgression—is *pariyāyo*. *Anupubbī* is that which conforms to what precedes it;
it belongs to the class beginning with *nada*. This [word] is not masculine. *Anupubbi* also exists. From the root *kam* (in the sense of desire and longing), the suffix *ṇo* is applied.
430. *Tikaṃ* (triad) refers to virtue (*sīla*). *Tapa* means to heat or torment. That which torments the defilements (*kilesa*) is *tapo*; [the suffix] *a*. *Yamu* means to cease;
cessation is refraining (*viramaṇa*), with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). *Si* means to bind; that by which the mind is bound is *sīla*, with the suffix *lo*.

Alternatively, *sīla* means to collect (*samādhāna*); collection is the state of being a foundation for wholesome states (*dhamma*). Or, *sīla* is in the sense of concentration (*samādhi*); here, concentration is the [foundation] of wholesome states.
It is an undertaking, except for the practice of virtue; or alternatively, it is called *tapa* because it "torments" (*tapati*) oneself and others in the hells and other realms of suffering.

Restraint (*saṃyama*) is the curbing or abstaining from unwholesome states; here, concentration occurs specifically by way of unwholesome states—this is the etymological explanation of the term, excluding virtue.
“*Vrata* is a restriction ordained by the Teacher. Rabhasa states: “*Niyama* [is used] in the sense of *mantana* (counsel), *paṭiññā* (promise), *nicchaya* (resolution), and *vata* (vow).
And that *vata*, characterized by fasting and so forth, is called merit (*puñña*). The *Amaramālā* states: “*Sīla*, *cāritta*, *vāritta*, and the merit of fasting and so forth [are synonyms].

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), [it includes] abstaining from pungent food, salt, and meals, as well as non-eating, non-consumption, and so on. And here, *tapa* and the others are mentioned according to their primary sense.
The term *sīla* (virtue) applies to wholesome conduct by way of common usage (*rūḷhī*), and it also applies to unwholesome conduct by way of common usage.

Terms such as *niyama* (restraint) apply primarily to unwholesome conduct, while they apply to wholesome conduct by way of common usage; this is the distinction between *sīla* and *vata*. The root *yam* means to restrain. The root *vat* means to proceed (*vattana*);
and here, "proceeding" means either practicing or maintaining concentration (*samādhāna*). The suffix *-vata* may also occur in the masculine gender.
The pair [refers to] transgression of a boundary (*mariyādātikkama*). *Kamu* means stepping; *vītikkama* is a distorted form of *atikkama*. Transgression of a boundary is misconduct (*ajjhācāra*).
Here, "seclusion" (*viveka*) refers to the three beginning with bodily seclusion. *Vica* is used in the sense of separating (*vivecana*) and also in the sense of being distinct (*puthabhāva*);

the suffix *-no* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), following the rule for doubling consonants and so forth. Those whose self (*atta*), body (*sarīra*), mind (*mano*), and nature (*sabhāva*) have become distinct and separate from the group and so forth—[these are the secluded ones].

*Puthugattā*: the state of being separate for them is *puthugattatā*. [In the variant reading] *puthagattatā*, there is the insertion of the letter *g* between the body (*kāya*) and separation (*viveka*), etc.
"This man is of such a nature, or we too are of such a nature"—this is the discernment of knowledge (*ñāṇaviveka*) through the differentiation of ordinary persons (*pakatipurisa*).
Others say: *atta* means intellect (*buddhi*); that which possesses a manifold state is *puthubhāva*, and the state of that is *puthugattatā*. From another source.
The state of being dissimilar is, according to others, the quality of being diverse or manifold.

431. The minor and lesser rules, the minor observances (*cūḷavatta*), the major observances (*mahāvatta*), or the practice of the observances (*vattapaṭipatti*) is called "pertaining to higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārika*).
This is because it exists within higher conduct—that is, within excellent conduct—and is thus termed *ābhisamācārika*. It is distinct from that which is minor and lesser.

Other forms of virtue, such as the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and so forth, are called "the beginning of the holy life" (*ādi-brahmacariya*) because they are to be practiced at the outset of the holy life—the Noble Path—for that purpose. 432.

One who has turned away from or is shielded against evil, unwholesome states is *upāvuta* (variant: *upāvuto*); one who is not shielded [by them] is *anāvuta*; and one who is free from all food, drink, enjoyments, and so forth is *vigata*.
That which is an abiding or dwelling together with virtues such as moral conduct (sīla) and the like, having become free from [defilements], is to be understood as "upavāsa.

[The root] *vas* means to dwell; it belongs to the *div-ādi* class. *Upavasanaṃ* is *upavāsa*, with the suffix *ṇo*. Alternatively, it is *upavāsa* because it is a dwelling (*vāsa*) that is "gone away from" (*vigata*) [impurities] and "endowed with" (*upeta*).

433. [The suffix] *-addha* occurs after *bhikkhu*. One who possesses the practice of austerity (*tapas*) is a *tapassī*; [the suffix] *sī* follows *tapa-* and so on, and there is doubling of the vowel.
A bhikkhu is one whose nature is to see fear (*bhayadassanasīlo*). A *samaṇa* is so called because he is "pacified" (*sameti*), from the root *yu*.

One who has "arisen" (*sañjātā*) the going-forth (*pabbajā*) is a "renunciant" (*pabbajito*); here the suffix *-ito* is used in the sense of "having arisen. Alternatively, he is a renunciant because he "goes toward" (*vaja-ti*) what is best; from the root *vaja* meaning "to go," with the suffix *-to*. One whose wealth is the practice of austerity (*tapas*) is a "wealthy in austerity" (*tapodhano*).
There are two [terms] for one who is restrained in silence. One who restrains speech is *vācaṃyama*; there is the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*) and the shortening of the vowel.
One who possesses silence (*mona*) is a *muni*; there is the shortening of the vowel and the suffix *-su*. There are two [terms] for one endowed with intense dwelling, the holy life, and so forth.

From the application of austerity (*tapas*), a *tāpasa* (ascetic); the suffix is *-saṇa*. From the root *isa* in the sense of seeking, *isi*; or from *isa* in the sense of going—so called because of going to the further shore (*pāra*) of knowledge or of saṃsāra, thus an *isi*.
i. *Pārikaṅkhī*: Here, "pārī" means that which has the further shore (*pāra*) as its object; it is sublime knowledge (*brahmajāṇa*). One who desires that is a *pārikaṅkhī*. 434.
Two [terms] refer to the group of those with conquered faculties. Those whose groups of faculties are restrained are called *yatino* and *vasino*.

They are *yatino* because constant restraint (*yataṃ*)—that is, the restraint of the faculties—is present in them. *Yati* is derived from the root *yat*, meaning to exert or restrain. *Vasino*... [derived from the root] *vas*, to dwell or master.
*Pāguṇye*: those who possess *vasu* (wealth/qualities) are *vasino*.
[End of] the triad concerning the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*). *Sārī* was the name of a brahmin woman; her son was Sāriputta.

They find satisfaction (*tussanti*) in him because of the accomplishment of their aims, thus he is *Tissa*, [the suffix] *so* being added to *tussi*. He is honored as Tissa Upatissa. Alternatively, he is simply called "Tissa."
“Phussa” or “Upatissa” are names taken at will by his parents during his childhood; “Sāriputta” is [derived] from the name of his mother;
but “Dhammasenāpati” is the name given by the Perfectly Enlightened One when he had attained the state of an Arahant.

Those for whom the armies of unwholesome states—such as sensual desire and the like—have been conquered by the weapons of wholesome states are the Dhammasenāpatis; they are numbered in the hundreds of thousands of many millions.
The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples; among them, he is the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) in the sense of being their leader and guide.
(435) Regarding the two [names] for Mahāmoggallāna, who stands on the Blessed One’s left side: he is born in the Kola family, thus he is Kolita; he is also Kolita.

He is the offspring of the Brahmin woman Moggallī, thus he is Moggallāna; this is the suffix -ṇa. Regarding the two [terms] for the noble state of a recluse (ariyasāmañña): the enemies are the defilements (kilesārayo).
It destroys, thus it is *arahā*; that very one is *ariya*. Or, in the sense of "going to the *ara*," he attains delight (*arati*) in the states of the path and fruit;
thus he is *ariya*, with the suffix *-ṇya*. "He has attained" means *adhigata*, with the suffix *-to*.
Because the *asekha* (one beyond training) is included, by the word "beginning with stream-enterers" (*sotāpannādika*), only the six types of persons are comprised therein; therefore—

It is established that there are seven types of trainees (*sekha*), beginning with those standing on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), and one type of non-trainee (*asekha*), which is the Arhat.

They are called "trainees" (*sekha*) because they are endowed with the three trainings; by the elision of the letter *ka*, the forms “*sekhā*” and “*asekhā*” also occur. These two [categories] have not yet attained [the goal].
A person who is separate from or distinct from the Noble Ones (*ariya*) is a worldling (*puthujjana*); or, he is a worldling because he generates various defilements (*kilesa*).

436. The two [factors] are in the fruit of the highest path (*agga-phala*). It is called "higher knowledge" (*aññā*) because one has known by not transgressing the limit of the Noble Ones (*ariya*) as seen through the first path and so forth;

or alternatively, it is "higher knowledge" because it slays (*māraṇa*) the five higher fetters (*pañca-uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), such as lust for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) and so on, by way of their total destruction (*odhi*).

Here, the suffix *-ā* has the sense of a limit (*maryādā*); for the root *ñā* is used in the senses of slaying, honoring, and investigation, and the feminine suffix *-ā* is applied. It is the state (*bhāva*) of an Arhat.

"Arahant-ship" (*arahatta*): the suffix *-tta* denotes "being" (*bhāva*). Here, "being" is the cause for the occurrence of both the verbal expression and the cognition. And that [cause] is twofold, by way of the cause for derivation (*byuppatti*) and the cause for occurrence (*pavatti*).
In this context, "derivation" (*byuppatti*) refers to that which arises from specific [elements] such as roots, stems, and suffixes;
it is the form of words such as *go*. The cause of that [form] is the "cause of derivation" (*byuppattinimitta*), namely, the roots, stems, suffixes, and so forth.

*Byuppatti-nimitta* (the etymological cause) is that which produces various forms of words, such as *go* ("cow") and so forth; it is precisely that [cause], namely the aforementioned action (*kriyā*) and the rest.
*Pavatti-nimitta* (the functional cause) is that which sets [a word] in motion and employs it for this or that meaning; it is the word *go* and so forth.

Its cause is the *pavatti-nimitta*, which consists of names based on genus (*jāti*), action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and substance (*davva*). Among these, the etymological cause (*byuppatti-nimitta*) pertains to the production of the form of the word.
The cause [of the word] is the reason for its application; however, the cause for the occurrence [of the word] is the reason for its usage.

This, in brief, is the distinction between their characteristics. Regarding the two [words], *cetiya*: *thu* is used in the sense of praise, beginning with a long vowel (*po*). *Cita* means "worship"; that which is to be worshipped (*cetitabba*) is a *cetiya*.
Here, the word *thūpa* applies even when the mouth [or opening] is present, whereas the word *cetiya* applies only when the mouth is absent.

“At the shrine, at the sacred precinct, at the image of the Buddha, and at the tree of the four directions”—thus [it is said]. This is from the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 12.7, the *Vyākhyāsudhā* 2.2.7, by Ruddo.
The pair [of terms] is in the sense of *ānanda* (joy). *Dhamma* is the teaching (*pariyatti*);

that itself is the "merchandise" (*bhaṇḍa*) or wealth because it bestows happiness. Its "storehouse" (*agāra*) is the place of storage, the house (*geha*). One who stands in the state of that is a "Dharma-treasurer" (*dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko*); the suffix *-ika* is used here. *Nanda* is in the sense of *samiddhi* (success/prosperity).
These two words are identical and have the same meaning. 437.

The pair [of names] refers to Visākhā, the daughter of a seṭṭhi. She is called Visākhā because she has various (vi-) and many (sa-) branches (sākha) consisting of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth. She is called Migāramātā because she stands in the place of a mother to the seṭṭhi Migāra.

The pair [of names] refers to the seṭṭhi Anāthapiṇḍika. He is called Sudatta because his self (attā) is beautiful (sundara); he is called Sudatta because his gift (datta) was beautiful (sundara). His giving was magnificent.
Or "Sudatta"—this is his name as it occurred during his youth. "He gives alms (piṇḍa) to those who are without a protector (anātha)"—thus he is called Anāthapiṇḍika;
this is his name derived from his activity. 438–439.
These five, beginning with the bhikkhu, are "fellow-practitioners" (sahadhammika). They are called fellow-practitioners because they practice the Dhamma together, that is, collectively.
The eight requisites beginning with the bowl are mentioned by way of the superior category;

however, by way of the intermediate category, ten requisites should be mentioned, including the walking stick and the oil tube; and by way of the inferior category, twelve requisites should be mentioned, including the sunshade and the sandals.

440. There are two [terms] for a novice (*sāmaṇera*). A novice is one who is subordinate to a monk (*samaṇa*). Because he possesses the characteristics and conduct of a monk, he is designated as "a monk," thus he is a *samaṇuddesa*.

The root *dis* means "to utter. The triad refers to the naked ascetic (*acelaka*). Space itself is his garment or cloth; he does not have a natural (woven) cloth, thus he is *digambara* ("clothed by the quarters"). The suffix *go* is applied here.
He has no cloth (*cela*) as his garment, hence at the end of the compound the suffix *ko* is used. Because he is bound by the four ties (*gantha*), he is a *nigaṇṭha* ("one without ties").

*Nisadda* means "binding. There are two [terms] for one who possesses matted hair (*jaṭā*). One who has *jaṭā* is a *jaṭila*; [the suffix] *-ila* is used here. One who wears *jaṭā* is a *jaṭādhara*. 441.
The thirty-four tenets beginning with *Kuṭisaka* should be understood from the scriptures of other systems (*parasamaya*);
likewise, the sixty-two views should be understood from the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. *Iti* signifies completion; *ete* signifies illustration. These are the ninety-six tenets.
They are called *pāsaṇḍa* because they cast and set in motion the snare of craving (*taṇhā*) and the snare of views (*diṭṭhi*).
There is also a reading: "Thus these ninety-six. 442. The triad [of suffixes] occurs after *su*.

From the root *pu*, meaning "to purify," with the suffix *to*; it undergoes doubling, etc. From *yata*, meaning "to strive," with the suffix *to*; it begins with a long vowel, etc. Two [suffixes] occur after *camma*. *Carita* is *tanti* (tradition); from the root *carati*, the suffix *mana* is added; or, from *camu*, meaning "to eat," the suffix *mana* is added. From *aja*, meaning "to go," the suffix *yu* is added, or *ino*.
Two terms for a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*). That by which one cleanses or purifies the teeth is *dantapona*; [the suffix] *yu* is used. *Dantapoṇa* is also correct.

A stick for the purpose of cleaning the teeth is *dantakaṭṭha*. Two terms for tree bark. *Vakka* means bark; [the root] *val* (to peel) with the suffix *ka*. *Tara* means crossing; from this, with the suffix *ita* and the pleonastic suffix *ko*.
443. Two terms for a vessel in general. That in which something falls is a *patto* (bowl); from the root *pata* (to go/fall), with the suffix *to*. *Pā* means to protect; with the suffix *ti*.

Two [meanings] for *kuṇḍikā*: the essence (*maṇḍa*) or clarity of water; it is called *kamaṇḍalu* because it takes that (*taṃ lāti*). [The root] *kuḍi* means "to protect," with the suffix *ka* used in its own sense. It is a support-stick for one who is old and infirm. 444.

That practice of the holy life (*brahmacariya-kamma*), beginning with "abstaining from taking life," which is constant throughout one's entire life as an indispensable requirement, depends upon bodily means—that is, it requires the body itself as the instrument and not an external instrument; this is called *yama*. [The root] *yamu* means "to cease."

“In the restraint consisting of constant action that requires the maintenance of the body, in the restraint toward King Yama, and in the twin [restraints], one should practice self-restraint (yama) threefold”— thus says the Amarakośa 17.38. [The word] *ruddo* [is explained as follows].
Furthermore, that action such as fasting which is restricted to a specific time by means of the bright fortnight (*sukkapakkha*) and so forth is "restriction" (*niyama*).
It is called *niyama* because it is to be restricted by way of time and other factors; the root *yam* means to cease. Rudra states:
"In the sense of counsel, in the sense of a promise, *niyama* [is used] in the sense of certainty and a vow."
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇavagga is finished. 445. *Dvayaṃ vesse*:
the root *vis* means "to enter," with the suffix *so*. With the *iyāna*-suffix, it becomes *vesiyāno*. *Ūrujo* (the thigh-born) and *ariyo* (the noble one) also apply here.

The pentad refers to livelihoods such as agriculture and the like. The root *jīv* means "to sustain life," with the suffix *yu*. In all cases, the suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*); some say it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*).
*Vatta-vattane*: these two [terms] refer to livelihood (*jīvikā*). He shows the various forms of the verbal roots *vṛt*. *Dvayaṃ kasikamme*:
there are two terms for agricultural work. Plowing is *kasi*; that itself is the work, hence *kasikamma*. From the root *kasa* (to scratch/plow), with the suffix *i*, we have *kasi*.
*Dvayaṃ vāṇijje*: there are two terms for trade. The work of merchants (*vaṇija*) is *vāṇijja* and *vaṇijjā*. *Dvayaṃ pasuposane*: there are two terms for the rearing of cattle. Of cows...

*Gorakkhā* means cattle-herding. The protection, nourishment, medical treatment, and so forth of livestock such as cows, buffaloes, and the like, is called "livestock-herding" (*pasupālana*) by its own nature;
and these aforementioned types of livelihoods constitute the three occupations for a *vessa*, consisting of the various forms of agricultural work and so on.

This triad pertains to the householder. One who stands in a *gaha*—that is, in a house—or in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) by way of existence, is a *gahaṭṭha*. One who dwells in an *agāra* (house) is an *agārika*; one who possesses a *gaha* is a *gihi*, [formed with] the suffix *-assi*, and the vowel is shortened.

447. Two [terms] regarding *kasibala*. One lives by means of a field (*khetta*). A *kassaka* (farmer) is so called because he plows (*kasati*); the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. Two [terms] regarding the field (*khette*). It is a *khetta* because seeds are sown (*khipanti*) therein;
from the root *khipa* in the sense of throwing, with the suffix *to*, it becomes *khitta*. Alternatively, it is a *khetta* because it protects (*tāyati*) what is sown (*khitta*);

or from the roots *khi* in the sense of dwelling and going, or *traṇa* in the sense of protection, it becomes *khetta* or *khetra*. From the root *klid* in the sense of becoming moist, with the elision of *la*, it is a *kedāra* because it is made to become moist (*kledīyati*).

Alternatively, it is *kedāra* because there is tearing (*vidāraṇa*) when there is water (*ke*); due to its being a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), there is no elision of the locative case ending. Here too, it is a place for sowing (*vāpa*);

or else, it is a *vāpa* because it is sown (*vappate*) therein—the suffix *ṇo* is applied. Both [terms] refer to a lump of clay. From the root *leḍḍ* (in the sense of "clinging together"), with the suffix *u*, we have *leḍḍu*. It is stated that *utta* is used in the masculine: "The *leḍḍavas* are in the masculine. Thus.
*Amara-kośa* 19.12: Two [terms] refer to a spade (*khaṇitti*). That by which one digs is a *khaṇitti*; the root *khanu* means "to dig," with the suffixes *ṇatta* and *ussi*.

That by which something is split is "splitting" (*avadāraṇa*); the root *dara* means "to split," with the suffix *yu*. (448) Three [terms] refer to a sickle (*dātta*). One cuts or reaps with it, thus it is a *dātta*;

the root *dā* means "to reap," with the suffix *to*. It is also called *dātra*. The root *lū* means "to cut"; the past participle is *lavitta*, with the suffix *asu* for the sense of casting away. *Asita* is used in all cases; the suffix is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

A triad for the whip-handle: *tud* in the sense of piercing, with the suffix *-na*, makes *patoda*. With the suffix *-ta*, it becomes *tutta*. *Aj* in the sense of driving away and going, with the suffix *-ana* (instrumental), makes *pājana*;

with a change of vowel (*vaṇṇavikāra*), it is *pācana*. *Todana* is also used here. A triad for the rope: *yuj* in the sense of joining, with the suffix *-ta*, makes *yotta*. *Rudh* in the sense of obstructing, with the suffix *-u*, gives *ussatta* and *rajju* through the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatta*). *Ras* in the sense of tasting, with the suffix *-i*, gives *rasi*; *ābandha* is also used here. A dyad for the plough:
that by which one ploughs (*phālayati*) or cleaves (*pāṭayati*) the earth is *phāla*, with the suffix *-a*. *Kas* in the sense of scratching, with the suffix *-aka*, makes *kasaka*.
“*Phālakasakā*” (plowshares and plows) refers to *ruddo*. *Nirīsaṃ*, *kūṭakaṃ*, and *halampi* [are synonyms]. *Nirīsaṃ* means that which has come out from the pole (*īsā*).
From the root *kuṭa* (to cut), with the suffix *ko* in the sense of identity, we have *kūṭakaṃ*; it begins with a long vowel. From *hala* (to scratch/plow). [This] triad refers to the plow.
It is called *naṅgalaṃ* because it cuts (*lunāti*) while making the limbs of the earth (*bhūmi-naṅga*) limbless (*amanaṅga*). From the root *sī* (to bind), with the suffix *ro*.
*Sīro*. In the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: “*Sīro* [is used] for a sharp-edged plough. A ploughshare (*godāraṇa*) is also included here. The pole of a plough is *īsā*;

*īsā* [is used] in the sense of sovereignty (*issariya*), and *īsā* [also means] a woman. According to the *Cintāmaṇiṭīkā*, *Vyākhyāsudhā*, and *Rabhasa*: “*Īso* [is used] for a lord, for a heap, and for the female pole of a plough.
(Cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.13–4; Vyākhyāsudhā 2.9.14; Rabhasa).

In the *Yugakīla* [lexicon], the word *sammā* means "right. That by which one is right is *sammā*; *samu* means "to calm" (*samane*). *Sītā* refers to the furrows of a plow; it is the track of the plow.
As stated in the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (3.3.191): "The furrow of the plow, the celestial Gaṅgā, and Jānakī are called *sītā*.
[The root] *sī* means "to lie down"; with the suffix *-ta*, *sītā* refers to a woman.

450–451. The term *aparanna* refers to specific types of grain such as mung beans (*mugga*). It means food that occurs after the *pubbanna* (the first harvest); it is "subsequent food" (*aparanna*) and also "other food.
The term *pubbanna* refers to rice and other primary grains; it means food that occurs before the *aparanna*; it is "first food" (*pubbanna*) and also "prior food.
Their status as prior and subsequent should be understood in terms of their occurrence or non-occurrence during the First Eon (*ādikappa*).
The seven grains beginning with *sāli*. *Dhāna* means nourishing; those things which are good for that [nourishing] are *dhaññāni*, with the suffix *ya* shortened.

*Kalamā* refers to varieties of fine grain such as red rice (*rattasāli*), great rice (*mahāsāli*), sixty-day rice (*saṭṭhikā*), and so forth; these are called *sāli*. It is called *saṭṭhika* because its ripening takes sixty days.
From the root *sāl* (to praise), with the suffix *i*, we have *sāli*. That which carries or promotes the life of beings is *vīhi*; from the root *vah* (to carry).

*pāpuṇe*, *brūha*, *vuḍḍhiyañca*, *i*, *assī*; in the case of *pakkhe*, there is elision of *ra*, as in *vīhi*. That which stains (*dūseti*) the blood (*koraṃ rudhiram*) is *kudrūsa*; [it is derived from] *go-vaḍḍhana*, with the suffix *a*.

There is a change of color (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*), and *ossa* is substituted for *u*. From the root *gudha* in the sense of piercing (*parivedhane*), with the suffix *uma*: *godhumo*. According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon:
"The wheat flower (*godhūma-sumana*), the foreigner (*milakkha*), food (*bhojana*), *pāvaṭo*, and barley (*yava*). From the root *vara* in the sense of choosing (*varaṇa*) and sharing (*sambhatti*).
*Ṇvu*, *varaka*. *Yu*, *missa*, *na*, *a*, *yava*. *Kaṅgu*: because it possesses a beautiful head (*sobhana-sīsa*), it attains a desirable state;
thus it is *kaṅgu*. *U*. “*Sāmā*, *piyaṅgu*, *kaṅgu*, [and] *dve*” (Rudda).

Their varieties—that is, the specific divisions of those grains—are called *nīvāra* and so forth. *Nīvārā* refers to grass-grains; by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), *sāmāka* and others are included.
Two [meanings] for *kaḷāya*: *caṇa* (to give), with the suffix *ṇvu*, thus *caṇaka*; it also refers to the chickpea (*harimantaka*). It is called *kaḷāya* because it takes (*lāti*) the wind (*kaṃ*);

the letter *ḷ* is substituted, thus also *kalāya*. Two [meanings] for the general term *sāsapa* (mustard): “*Sāsapo* is indeed *sarisapo*, *kaṭusneho*, and *tantubho*,” according to the *Tikaṇḍasesa* 2.8.3.

“In the masculine, *siddhattha* [refers to] the son of Suddhodana; in the neuter, to the white mustard,” according to the *Rabhasa*. [It is called *siddhattha*] because the goals (*atthā*) are accomplished (*siddhā*) within it.
*Siddhattha*: *Sāsa* means instruction; it is derived from the root *apa*. It is included here because the mustard seed (*sāsapa*) is a variety of rice. 452. Two [names] for *kaṅguya*:

it reaches (*aṅgati*) a state of being dear (*piya*), thus *piyaṅgu*. Two [names] for *atasi*: from the root *ava* (to protect), with the suffix *mo*, and the prefix *avassu*; the doubling of the consonant, and *ummā*. From the root *ata* (to go constantly), with the suffix *aso*, belonging to the *nadādi* class.

*Khumā* is also used here. Four [names] for a crop: from the root *kiṭa* (motion), with the suffix *ṭho*; or that which has been ploughed (*kasita*) or produced there is *kiṭṭha*; for a crop grown in a place where there was previously *kiṭṭha* (salt/sterile soil).
“Kiṭṭha” is said [to mean] a field by way of its location (*ṭhānūpacāra*); there is the elision of *ṭha*, and the suffix *assi*.

The root *sas* is used in the senses of going, harming, and reaching; it takes the suffix *so*. *Thambo* means a thicket; that which makes such a thing is *thambakari*. Grain (*dhañña*) is also included here.
For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: “*Dhañña* refers to rice among grains; *dhañña* is also used for one who possesses merit; *dhaññā* refers to *vātāmalakī* plants.”

453. There are two terms for the stalks of rice and other grains: *kaṇḍa*. From the root *kaṇ* (to sound), with the suffix *ḍo*, we have *kaṇḍa*. From the root *nal* (to bind), with the suffix *ṇo*, we have *nāla*; also *nāḷī*. When that very stalk of rice and so forth is without grain, it is called *palāla*. From the roots *pala* (to cut) and *pavana* (to blow), with the suffix *alo*, we have *palāla*.
There are two terms for worthless, empty grain: *bhusa*. From the root *bhas* (to reduce to ashes), with the suffix *assu*, we have *bhusa*;

it also means "excess. *Thusa* is also used. From the root *tus* (to throw up), [we derive *tuṣa*]. That which moves (*iṅgati*) by what wind (*kena vātena*) is called *kaliṅgara*; there is the substitution of *l* and the suffix *aro*. The bark or husk of grains themselves is called *taca*.

*Thusa*, *tusa*, and *tuṭṭhi* denote satisfaction; *tho* is its [suffix]; *thusa* is masculine. According to the *Amarakosa* (19.22): "In the sense of grain, *thusa* is masculine. 454. Two terms refer to a disease of rice.

It is called *setaṭṭikā* because it stands (*aṭati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*) by means of making the color white (*seta*); that very thing is *setaṭṭhikā*. Two terms refer to the husk of the grain (*taṇḍulakaṇa*).

From the root *kaṇ* in the sense of closing, or from *kaṇ* in the senses of closing, sound, and motion, with the suffix *a*: *kaṇo*. From the root *kuṇḍ* in the sense of burning... [the word *kuṇḍaka* is formed].
The suffix *ko* occurs after a word ending in *sakattha*. The two [terms] *dhana* and *maddana* occur in the sense of a threshing floor (*dhaññamaddanabhūmi*).

*Khala* occurs in the sense of purity (*soceyya*). A place where grains are prepared and threshed is called a *dhaññakaraṇa*. The words *thambo* and *gumbo* refer to the stalks or clusters of grasses and crops;
*thamba* occurs in the sense of deficiency or obstruction. *Guha* occurs in the sense of concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*); *bo* is substituted for *ha*, and *mo* is substituted for *ssa*.
455. Two [terms] for a pestle (*musala*): that which has iron at its tip is *ayogga*; from the root *musa* (to crush), with the suffix *-alo*. Two [terms] for a winnowing basket (*suppa*):

it cuts away or removes what is contemptible, thus *kullo*; from the root *supa* (to measure), with the suffix *-a*, or because one remembers by means of it, thus *suppaṃ*, with the suffix *-po* and the vowel change to *assu*.
*Papphoṭanaṃ* (shaking off) is also used here. Two [terms] for a hearth (*uddhana*): that upon which pots and such are placed is *uddhanaṃ*; also *uddhānaṃ*, with the suffix *-yu*. *Culla*...

In *hāvakaraṇe*, [the suffix] *i* or *īm* is used; thus, *cullī* (a hearth). *Adhisayanī* means a bed or seat; *antikā* is also used here. From the root *ati-adi* in the sense of binding (*bandhane*), that by which alms-food and so forth are bound is called *antikā*;
the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. Ajaya states: "The word *antikā* is used in the senses of proximity (*santike*), vicinity (*sannidhāne*), and also for a hearth (*uddhane*).
A basket (*kaṭa*) made of *kāsā* grass and other materials, by which a *marāva* (granary) is tied; and a *marāva* is a rice granary—"a *kusūla* and a rice granary," [it is said].

"and a thicket, and a desert," [says] Rabhasa. Some say that *marāva* itself is a mat (*kaṭa*); that is not so, because in the *Amaramālā*, in the section on synonyms for the foot [of a verse], they are read separately:
"A granary (*kusūla*) and a *marāva*, and a *kilañja*, and it would be a mat (*kaṭa*). *Kil* means to bind; a binding is a *kila*;
that which is produced for that purpose is a *kilañja* (with the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta*). *Kaṭ* means to go; [the suffix] *a*.

456. *Aṭṭhakaṃ* (the eightfold) [is derived from] *thāli* (a pot). It is called *kumbhī* because it is desired (*kāmīyati*). The root *kam* means "to desire. [The suffixes] *assu*, *ī*, and *ca* [are applied]. Alternatively, it is called *kumbhī* because it exists on the earth (*kuyā pathaviyā bhavati*).
Or, it is called *kumbhī* because it speaks by means of fire (*kena agginā bhaṇati*). The root *bhaṇ* means "sound"; there is the elision of *ṇ*.

Or, it is called *kumbhī* because it is filled (*umbhīyati*) with water (*kena jalena*). The roots *ubha*, *ubbha*, and *umbha* mean "to fill. In all cases, the *na*-class [suffixes] are applied. The root *piṭh* [is used] in the senses of harming and defilement.

*aro*: [The suffix] *aro* occurs after the root *kuṇḍ* in the sense of burning. *khalo*: [The suffix] *khalo* occurs after the root *soc* in the sense of being distressed. *ḷattaṃ*: [The suffix] *ḷattaṃ* occurs after the root *ukh*. *alo*: [The suffix] *alo* occurs after the roots beginning with *nad*. *Rassō*: [The vowel] becomes short before the suffix *apaccaya*.

*Ukhā*: [The word] *ukhā* [is formed from the root *ukh*]. *Thalā*: [The suffix] *i* occurs after the root *ṭhā*. *Thālī*: [The word] *thālī* [is formed] when the suffix *īm* follows. *Kolambo*: That by which one speaks with fire is called *kolambo*; [this is] the elision of the *niggahīta*, and the substitution of *ba* for *va*.
Alternatively, it is *kolambo* because it hangs (*olambati*) upon the fire (*ke aggimhi*). *Labi*: [The root] *labi* means to sink down.

*Tikaṃ* means "water-jar" (*maṇika*). *Mana* means "knowledge"; with the suffix *i*, there is the substitution of *ṇ*; thus, *maṇi* itself becomes *maṇika*. *Bhaṇa* means "sound"; with the suffix *ṇvu*, *araṃ* means "quickly"; that which has this speed is *arañjaro*.

457. *Dvipādaṃ* means "water-pot" (*ghaṭa*). *Ghaṭa* means "to move"; with the suffix *a*, in the group beginning with *nada*, it becomes *ghaṭī*. *Kuṭa* means "crookedness. That which shines or adheres by means of water is *kalasa*;
*lisa* means "to adhere," with the suffix *a* and the substitution of *i* for *s*; *kalasa* occurs in three genders. *Vara* means "prohibition" or "acquisition."
...ṇvu. Because it accompanies the *kalasa* (water-pot), the *vāraka* (jug) is also [included] among the three. "The *kalasa*, however, is among the three," according to the *Amarakośa* 19.31.
That which is to be eaten is "eating" (*bhuñjana*), such as food and so forth; its vessel or container—even one fashioned from gold, silver, and so on—is called *kaṃsa*.
"In another sense, *kaṃsa* means a measure; likewise, it may also mean brilliance (*tejas*)."

"In a drinking vessel (*pānapatta*) and in bronze (*kaṃsa*), in beauty and in fame. Because it is stated [here] as a general term, *kaṃsa* refers to a drinking vessel as well. The root *kan* is used in the senses of shining, going, and beauty;

from it comes *kaṃsa*. It is not feminine. This triad [of terms] refers to the commonality of a vessel. The root *am* is used in the sense of going; with the suffix *-atta*, it becomes *amatta*. The root *bhāj* is used in the sense of dividing; it belongs to the *cur*-class and takes the suffix *-yu*. 458.
This pair [of terms] refers to the receptacle for vessels and the like. That which approaches the vicinity (*anta*) of what is to be contained (*ādheyya*) is called *aṇḍupaka*.
*ntassaṇḍa*, and *ga* with *ko*. *Cumb* [is used] in the sense of contact between faces; *aṭo*, *assu*, and *ko* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). *Sarāva* has two [meanings]:
it is called *sarāva* because it "flows" (*sarati*), meaning it goes toward increase; [the suffix] *avo*. *Mall* in the sense of holding; [the suffix] *ṇvu*. *Vaḍḍhamānaka* is also here:
it is called *vaḍḍhamānaka* because it "increases," meaning it becomes broad; [the suffix] *ko* in the sense of identity.
Two [terms] refer to an implement used for stirring curd, condiments, and so forth. *Kaṭa* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *chu*, followed by *dvitta* and others.
