*Du* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *bo*, followed by *nadādi*; *dabbī*, and in the abbreviated form (*rasse*), *dabbi*. *Khajākā* also; from *khaja* (to churn), with the suffix *ako*;

*khajākā* is feminine. Two [terms] refer to a storehouse for grain and such. *Kusa* (in the sense of binding), with the suffix *ūlo*. *Kusa* (in the sense of reviling), with the suffix *ṭho*. Both are masculine and neuter.

459. *Sāka* (vegetable) is derived from the root *sāk*, meaning "to eat," with the suffixes *māsādi* and *sākamatta*, followed by the suffix *ṇvu*. *Ḍaṃsa* means "to eat," with the suffix *ṇvu*. There is elision of the initial *s*.

Thus, *siggu* (coriander) and *haritaka* (myrobalan) are also included. *Harita* (green) takes the suffix *ko* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (19.34), the *Rabhasa* lexicon states: "The masculine form [of *sāka*] refers to the measure of a vegetable; it also denotes coriander and the *sobhañjana* plant.
There are two types of *addaka* (potherb). That which is born from water (*āda*) is *addaka*; the vowel is shortened. Like a horn (*siṅga*), [it is so called].
That which has truth as its body is indeed *siṅgivera* (ginger).

When it is dried, it is then called *mahosadha* (great medicine), because of its pungent taste it is a "great medicine" (*mahantaṃ osadhaṃ*). It is also called *suṇṭhī*, *nāgaraṃ*, *visaṃ*, and even *visabhesajjaṃ* (antidote to poison). [The derivation is: from the root *suṭhi* meaning "to dry," with the suffix *i*, forming *suṇṭhi*;

with the feminine suffix *ī*, it becomes *suṇṭhī*. There are two names for *marīca* (black pepper): *marīca* and *kolaka*. From the root *mara* meaning "to abandon life" with the suffix *co*; and from *kula* meaning "to count" with the suffix *ṇvu*. Amarasīha states: "Marīca, kolaka, kaṇha, usana, and dhammapattana."
460. *Kañjika* (sour gruel) has three syllables. That which exists in the country of *Suvīra* is *sovīra*.
That which is brightened (*añjiya*) by what water would be *kañjiya*. That which is produced from the water of *āra*—that is, the water taken from the husks of rice growing in the earth—is *āranāḷa*.
For it is said: “*Āra* is in the word *sute’kkaja*; *nāra* is in the words for rice-water,” where the short *ra* becomes *ḷa*. Water produced from boiled rice is [called] *thusodaka*.
*Thusodaka* is either the water itself or that which is produced from *thusodaka*. Sourness produced from grain, such as rice, is *dhaññambilam*.
It is called *bilaṅka* because it "makes the wind *laṅkati*"—that is, it makes it inferior—or because it "specifically overcomes (*visesena laṅkatī*)" the wind; thus it is *bilaṅka*.
Included here also are *kummāsa*, *abhisutaṃ*, *avantisomaṃ*, *kuñjalaṃ*, *kañjikaṃ*, *maṇḍa*, *jeṭṭhambu*, and *khadikā*.
The word *dvayaṃ* [refers to] the two types of salt (*lavaṇa*). From the root *lū*, meaning "to cut," with the suffix *yu* and the substitution of *ossāna*, it becomes *loṇaṃ*.
461. These five, beginning with *sāmudda*, are the divisions or specific varieties of salt.
That which is obtained from the salty water situated on the ocean floor, which has dried up and become solidified, is *sāmuddalavaṇa* (sea salt). It is also called *akkhivaṃ* or *vasiraṃ*.
*Vasu-thambhe* means *iro*. That which originates in the region of Sindhu is *sindhava*, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Sitasivaṃ* is [equivalent to] *sītasivaṃ* (in the sense of being able to endure cold);
it is also *māṇimanthaṃ* and *sindhujaṃ*. *Sita* means white; *siva* means auspicious; this is a *kammadhāraya* compound.
Alternatively, *sitasiva* refers to a binding. *Maṇimantho* is a mountain; that which originates there has the suffix *ṇo*. *Kāḷaloṇa* is the name for *sovaccala* salt.
The salt that is black in the middle is one of the three types of salt—sweet, salty, and alkaline (Amarakośa, Mahesvara-ṭīkā).

Because it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (19.43) that "the *tilaka* is there in the dark-colored [salt]," and because it is stated in the *Byākhyāsudhā-ṭīkā* that "it exudes (*sandate*) intoxication (*mada*) or joy (*muda*), thus it is *visodarādi*," it is also called *tilaka*. That which is called *ubbhida* is *romaka* salt.
It is said that in the region of Sambhara there is a salt-mine called Ruma. Whatever wood enters there quickly dissolves and becomes salt;

the salt produced from that is *romalavaṇa*. It is also called *vasuka*. Because it is capable of breaking [substances] by causing wood and other materials to abandon their own inherent nature, it is called *ubbhida*;
the suffix *-us* is used here in the sense of capability (*sakyatthe*). That which is called *bilāla* is produced in a place near the shore of the ocean.
Salt produced by baking clay; that which is produced from salt-clay found in a place near the ocean shore, known as *bilāla*, *essitta*, or *lo*;
or alternatively, that which is called *ubbhida*, namely salt produced by baking clay that has emerged from the earth in any location whatsoever.
*Bilāla* refers to salt produced by splitting open a salt-bearing stratum of earth. [The prefix] *vi-* [is used here].
The root *dal* means to split. The suffix *lo* [is applied]. Alternatively, *ubbhida* refers to prepared salt. *Bilāla* refers to "feces-smell" (vaccagandha) or black salt.
462. The five beginning with *guḷa* are products of sugarcane. *Guḷ* means to protect; *guḷa* is the boiled juice. *Phāṇ* means to move;

with the suffix *to*, it becomes *phāṇita*, which is somewhat more solid than *guḷa*. *Khaṇḍ* means to crush; *khaṇḍa* is even more solid than *phāṇita*. [It is the product] of a specific variety of sugarcane.
That which arises in the form of a pellet during the cooking of the juice when it has reached the stage suitable for *khaṇḍa* (crystallized sugar) is *macchaṇḍī*, also known as *khaṇḍasālūka*.

According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: “*Macchaṇḍī* is *pupphaguḷā* (flower-sugar), while *thaddhapatta* (hardened leaf) is *phāṇita* (molasses)”; others, however, state that *phāṇita* is *khaṇḍakakka* (crude sugar).
The root *sar* means to injure; with the suffix *kharapaccaya*, it becomes *sakkharā* (gravel/sugar), which is also called *sitā* (white sugar), because it binds or restrains craving (*taṇhā*).
*Sitā*. In the term *sitasakkharā*, however, *sita* means white; or it is called *sakkharā* because its size and shape resemble those of sugar crystals.

Furthermore, these substances beginning with molasses (*guḷa*) become progressively more solid in their order. In this context, *macchaṇḍī* (treacle) is a derivative of *phāṇita* (unrefined syrup), and *khaṇḍa* (crystallized sugar) is a derivative of that.
There are two types of *guḷa*. It is called both *visa* (poison) and *kaṇṭaka* (thorn) because it causes destruction among those afflicted by diseases and the like.

463. *Bhaṭṭha* refers to parched grain. *Lāja* means parching; *bhajjana* is the same as *lāja*. *Akkhata* means not cut (*na khataṃ*). According to Rudda: “The third [form] is *pakati*; *akkhata* is used for three [meanings]: parched grain and the uninjured. The word *dhānā* may be used for parched barley (*bhaṭṭhayava*);

according to Rabhasa: “*Dhānā* is used in the plural for parched barley; it is feminine when meaning ‘newly risen’ or ‘the vulva’. From the root *dhā* (to hold), with the suffix *yu*. Two [words] refer to the powder of barley and so forth.
From *saca* (to assemble) or *saca* (to sprinkle), with the suffix *tu*. *Mantha* means stirring. These three [terms] are synonymous.

It is called *pūpa* because it "fills" (*pūreti*); *po* is the suffix. When joined with the vowel *a*, it becomes *apūpa*, as in the pair "lābu, alābū. A preparation made from flour of rice and so forth is called *piṭṭhaka*;
here, *ko* is the suffix used for a designation. 464.
Regarding the group of six [terms] related to a cook (*sūda*): one who prepares or has prepared, or will prepare, food and curry is a *bhattakāra* (cook) or a *sūpakāra* (cook).

*Ca*: [This particle is used] in the sense of "and. *Sūda*: [Derived from] *savati* (to flow) and *paggharati* (to drip). One who causes the essence (*rasa*) to flow or drip is a *sūda* (cook); [the suffix] *do*, beginning with a long vowel.

Alternatively, *sūda* is used in the sense of dripping; [the suffix] *a*. *Āḷāra* is a preparation such as soup (*sūpa*) and the like; one who makes that is an *āḷārika* (cook). One who cooks rice (*odana*) is an *odanika* (rice-cooker). One who prepares the essence is a *rasaka* (essence-maker). The pair refers to *sūpa* (soup/sauce).

Because it is to be drunk for the sake of pleasure, it is *sūpa*; [the suffix] *a*, beginning with a long vowel. That by which food (*bhatta*) is specifically anointed—that is, enters within—is *byañjana* (condiment/garnish); [from the root] *añja* (in the sense of going), [the suffix] *yu*.
465. [The suffix] *pañcaka* occurs after the root *tip* in the sense of "eating. After the root *ud*, [the suffix] *yu* occurs in the senses of "flowing" and "moistening.

The letter *vā* indicates that the word *odana* is neuter. [The word] *kura*: from the root *kura* in the sense of "sound," or from *kara* in the sense of "doing"; it is called *kura* because it makes a sound (*balati*). [The word] *assu*:

from *kira* in the sense of "scattering," or from *kirati* in the sense of "desiring to eat"; it is called *kura*. [The word] *issu*: from *kara* in the sense of "harming," or from *ku* in the sense of "sound."
The suffix *rap*. That by which one partakes, or that which is to be eaten, is *bhatta*; [here] *bhaja* means "to serve," with the suffix *to*. That which is to be eaten is *bhikkhā*;
[the root] *bhakkha* means "to eat," with the suffix *assi*, or *bhikkhā* means "to beg"; *bhikkhā* also refers to a woman. [The root] *ada* means "to eat," with the suffix *to*.
Due to the rule beginning with *bhid-ādi*, there is a substitution of *anna*, and the elision of *da*.
The group of four [roots] is for eating; *asa* is for consuming; *kamma* is for action. *Hara* is for taking away.

Because it brings (*āharati*) strength and life, it is called *āhāra*; the suffix *ṇo* is applied. From the root *bhuja*, the suffix *yu* is applied, making *bhojanaṃ*. *Ghasa* is for eating; the suffix *ṇo* is applied. *Andha* also occurs here; from the root *ad*, the substitution of *andha* for the suffix *tapa* is established by rule (*nipātanā*).

There are two [words] for rice gruel (*yāgu*). *Tara* is for floating and crossing over. Because it floats, crosses over, or becomes pervasive (*byāpībhavati*), it is called *taraṇaṃ*; the suffix *yu* is applied.

*Taralaṃ* and *taralāpi*. That which reaches (*pāpuṇe*), [ending in] *gu*; or in the sense of mixing (*missane*), [ending in] *gu*, with the suffix *ussā*. *Uṇhikā*, *sāṇā*, and *vilepī* are names for rice-gruel (*yāgu*).

In the sense of cooking (*pāke*), [ending in] *yu*, it is *sāṇā*. 466. *Khajja* and the others are four types of food (*asana*). From the root *khād* in the sense of eating (*bhakkhane*), with the suffix *to* in the passive sense (*kamme*), belonging to the *bhujādi* class. *Khajjaṃ* refers to meat and so forth.

*Bhojjaṃ* refers to food and the like. From the root *liha*, meaning "to taste," with the suffix *ṇya*, and the substitution of *ha* for *ya*, we have *leyyaṃ*, such as honey and the like. *Pātabbaṃ* means "that which is to be drunk," hence *peyyaṃ*; from the root *pā*, meaning "to drink," with the suffix *ṇya* and the substitution of *ā* for *e*, *peyyaṃ* refers to soup and the like. Both terms apply to rice-gruel (*bhattamaṇḍa*).

From the root *su*, meaning "to hear," with the suffix *ṇa* according to the rule beginning with "visarujapadādito," [we have *savanaṃ*]. From the root *camu*, meaning "to eat," preceded by the prefix *ā* in the sense of drinking, with the suffix *ṇa* in the passive sense, [we have *ācāmaṃ*].

No. Here, *māsa* means "measure" (*parimāṇe*), and *ara* is a suffix. In the word *ālopa*, there are two [roots]: *lup* in the sense of "cutting off" (*chedane*), preceded by *ā-* in the sense of "collecting together" (*sampiṇḍane*), and *ku* in the sense of "sound" (*sadde*).

Alternatively, *kavi* in the sense of "color" (*vaṇṇe*) with the suffix *alo*; the substitution of *ḷ* for *ra* occurs. Or, it is *kabaḷo* because its strength (*bala*) is provided by water (*toya*)—that is, by saliva. It is masculine; it also refers to a "mouthful" (*gāsa*). 467.

The word *maṇḍa* is used for the foremost taste among all tastes, all flavors (*rasānaṃ sabbarasānaṃ aggamhi rase*). *Maṇḍa* is used in the sense of "ornament" (*bhūsāyaṃ*). [As stated: "The crest of all flavors... (*sabbarasagge*)...

The lion among gods (amarasīha) [is called] *amaṇḍamanitthiya* (one who does not eat the scum). (19.49) There are two [terms] for what remains after eating (*bhuttato sese*). *Vighāsa* is vile food or leftover food. What remains after eating is *bhuttasesa*;
one who has that is a *bhuttasesaka*, with the suffix *-ka* used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

There are two [terms] for one who eats leftovers (*vighāsāde*). One who eats *vighāsa* is [called *vighāsāda*]; the suffix *-a* is applied to the root *damu* (to subdue), with the suffix *-ṇvu*. There are two [terms] for thirst (*pipāsāyaṃ*). The desire to drink is *pipāsā*; from the root *pā* (to drink), with the suffix *-sa*, doubling of the initial consonant, etc. *Tasa* is used in the sense of thirst; the suffix *-yu* is applied.
468. *Dvayaṃ* (pair) refers to the desire to eat. *Khudda* is hunger; there are two [meanings]. *Jighacchā* is the desire to consume;

*ghasa* means to eat, and *cho* is used in the sense of desiring, following the rule for double consonants (*dvittādi*). *Maṃsarasa-paṭicchādanīyaṃ* (meat-juice-covering) is so called. *Chanda* means desire. It is called *paṭicchādanīyaṃ* because it covers;
the suffix *-anīya* is used. Alternatively, *chada* means to conceal; it is called *paṭicchādanīyaṃ* because it is to be covered by meat.

*Dvaya* [is used] in the sense of vomiting (*uggāra*). *Deka* [is used] in the sense of making a sound (*sadda-ussāha*). *Udrekā* means that which strives to go upwards; from the root *dek*, with the substitution of *r* for one *d*. *Uddeka* is also [correct].
*Gir* [is used] in the sense of swallowing (*niggiraṇa*), as in *issā* (envy) and *uggāra* (vomiting). *Pāda* [is used] in the sense of satisfaction (*titti*).

One who is satisfied is *titta*; the state of being so is *sohiccaṃ*. *Tip* [is used] in the sense of satiating (*pīṇana*); it belongs to the *bhuj*-class and takes the suffix *-ya*, and with the suffix *-issa*, it means "to satisfy."

469. *Yathicchitaṃ* and *yathicchite*: these two function as adverbs (*kriyāvisesaṇa*) and are therefore neuter. For even though verbs and indeclinables (*abyaya*) possess unity [of number], their qualifiers (*tadvisesaṇa*) become neuter even when they themselves are singular.
This is because, since verbs and indeclinables have attained the state of being mere existence (*sattābhūta*), there is no assumption of distinctions of gender or number;
thus, the qualifiers of those [verbs and indeclinables] also possess the common gender of the neuter.
The singular number is appropriate for a generic term (*sāmaññasaṅkhyā*); for example: *muduṃ pacanti*, *sāduṃ pacanti* ("they cook soft [food]," "they cook delicious [food]").

Even when the verbal root has a plural ending, there is still only the singular number for its qualifier; the accusative case is used for the qualifiers of the action because every meaning of a verbal root is pervaded by the sense of "doing" (*karoti*).
Thus, *muduṃ pacanti* means "they perform the act of cooking softly"; therefore, [the accusative applies] to words such as *mudu*.

The status of being an action (*kammatta*) belongs to those very qualifications (*tabbisesanānaṃ*). However, another says: "All meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvatthā*) are followed by the meaning of 'becoming' (*bhavatyatthānugatā*);

the meaning is that the action of 'becoming' (*bhavatikriyā*) undergoes the state of being an action (*katvattha*). In the expression ‘Devadatto pacati’ (Devadatta cooks), the cooking associated with Devadatta becomes [the action];

‘gacchati’ (he goes) is the becoming of going; ‘paṭhati’ (he reads) is the becoming of reading. According to his opinion, the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) is used, as in "gentle cooking" (*mudupacanaṃ*).
The meaning is: "he cooks in such a way that it becomes [so]. *Ramaṇīyaṃ pāto* (pleasant in the morning), *vimalaṃ pāto* (spotless in the morning), *idam upakumbhaṃ* (this is near the jar).

From the root *kam* in the sense of desire, with the suffix *ṇo*, we have *kāmaṃ* (at will) and *nikāmaṃ* (excessively). From the root *is* in the sense of wishing, with the suffix *to*: by the rule "after *sad*, *i*, *san*, and *pucch*, etc., *ta* becomes *ṭha*," its *ta* becomes *ṭha*, resulting in *iṭṭhaṃ* (desired).

Preceded by *pari*, the root *āp* in the sense of reaching, with the suffix *to*: it belongs to the *bhujādi* class, the vowel is shortened, and there is the augment *y*. Thus, *paryāptaṃ* (sufficient).
And: “*Sattyaṃ* [is used] in the sense of prohibition; *tittiyaṃ* [means] sufficient; *pariyattaṃ* [means] according to what is desired,” says Rabhasa in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (19.57).
*Yathicchitaṃ* means not exceeding what is desired; it is an *abyayībhāva* compound in the sense of *yathā-atthaṃ*.
*Pakāmaṃ* is also used here. *Dvipādaṃ* refers to a merchant (*vaṇijaka*). One who lives by buying and selling is called an *ika*. *Satthaṃ* is a collective term for those who live by trade.

"Vahati" means he carries or causes to reach another place; [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied after "kamma" and other such words. A caravan leader (*satthavāha*) is a chief of merchants; because of his connection with that [leadership], he is called a *satthavāha*, with the suffix *ṇo*.

A marketplace (*āpaṇa*) is the business of buying and selling; because of his connection with that, one is called an *āpaṇika*, with the suffix *ṇika*. The root "vaṇ" means sound; [from it comes] *ijo*. A trader (*vedahaka*), a merchant (*negama*), one who lives by trade (*paṇyājīva*), and a merchant (*vaṇija*) are also used here.
470. *Vikkaya* means the giving away of one’s own wealth to another beforehand. The root *kī* is used in the sense of bartering goods; one engaged in that is a *vikkayika*.
One who sells is a *vikketā*; [the suffix] *itu* is applied. *Kaya* means the giving away of one’s own wealth after receiving the wealth of another.
One who lives by buying is a *kayika*. One who buys is a *kināti*; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is applied.

Two terms for one who employs wealth for interest: *dhanappayuttarī*. Regarding debt (*iṇa*), the word *uttama* becomes *uttamaṇṇo*; it is placed first in the compound due to its designation [as a term of respect], and it undergoes the changes of *issatta* and *dvitta*.
One who employs (*payojeti*) wealth for the purpose of increase is a *dhanika*. Two terms for one who takes up wealth: [the same two as above].

Regarding debt, the word *adhama* becomes *adhamaṇṇo*. One who takes up debt is an *iṇāyiko* (or *āyiko*). Alternatively, one who brings forth (*āyati*) or circulates debt is an *iṇāyako*, with the suffix *-ṇvu*.

471–472. *Dvayaṃ iṇe*. It is called *uddhāra* because it is raised up (*uddharīyate*) or seized (*gayhate*); the root *dharati* preceded by *upa-* is used in the sense of seizing, with the suffix *ṇo*.
It is called *iṇaṃ* because it goes toward increase (*eti vuḍḍhiṃ gacchati*); [the suffix] *yu* is added, and there is the change to the nasal *ṇa*.

*Pariyudañcanaṃ* also [means this], for it is surrounded and seized (*parito udañjhate gayhate*); [the suffix] *yu* is added. *Vuttaṃ* is a verb. Whatever wealth by which a profit is obtained, therein, in that principal capital, there are the two terms beginning with "root" (*mūla*).
It is established upon the root. It is the very first thing brought as a gift (*pābhata*). One should establish the pair.
"The declaration of truth" means that this must certainly be performed; or, "making true" (*saccāpana*) means the performance of truth, which is to say, the filling of the mind with truth.
The word *sacca* is a verbal form (*dhāturūpa*), with the suffix *yu*, and there is the elision of the letter *p* in the middle of the word *sacca*. Of truth...
Or, *āpuṇanaṃ* means the attainment of truth (*saccāpanaṃ*). [It is used] after the root *apadhātu*. Vopālita states in the *Thīkaṇḍa* of the *Tikaṇḍasesa*: “*Saccāpanā* and *saccākati*.
It performs truth, or the act of making truth is *saccakāra*; *saccaṅkāra* is also used. In the *Amarakosa*, verse 19.82, it says:
“In the neuter, *saccāpanaṃ*, *saccaṅkāro*, and *saccākatitthiya*. These two [terms] refer to a commodity that is to be sold.
*Vikkinitabbaṃ* means "to be sold," [formed with] the suffix *ṇya*. The root *paṇ* is used in the sense of trade; both [suffixes] occur in the three genders.

The pair [of terms] refers to the delivery and fulfillment of a deposit (*nyāsa*). The delivery of a deposit is its fulfillment (*sampanna*), which is its return. The verb *dadāti*, preceded by *pati-*, has the meaning of fulfilling a deposit; likewise, it occurs preceded by *pari-*. *Paridānaṃ* is also used here.

The pair [of terms] refers to a deposit (*nyāsa*). *Asu* is used in the sense of casting away. It is called *nyāsa* because it is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*), [formed with] the suffix *ṇa*. It is called *upanidhi* because it is placed near (*upanidhiyyati*), [with] the suffix *i*; *upanidhi* is masculine. "In the masculine, *upanidhi* and *nyāsa*"—thus it is stated in the Amarakosa (19.81).
473. Numerical terms beginning with *eka* (one) and ending with *aṭṭhārasa* (eighteen) denote the objects to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*) and function in all three genders.
When the object to be numbered is singular, they form a grammatical coreferential construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in "one brahmin" (*eko brāhmaṇo*) or "eighteen brahmins" (*aṭṭhārasa brāhmaṇā*);

however, they do not form a non-coreferential construction such as "if eleven [belong] to the brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānaṃ ekādasa*). By the word "in three," it is indicated that it is not only the word *eka* [that functions thus].
[The author] shows that it is indeed "with gender" (*saliṅgo*), and furthermore, "even having eighteen endings.

Therefore, the statement in some places that they are "without gender" (*aliṅgatā*) should be understood as referring to the absence of specific genders (*liṅgavisesābhāva*), and not to the absence of gender in general (*sāmaññaliṅgābhāva*).

By this same method, [the meaning] in such passages as "The dual number is 'excessive gender' (*atiliṅga'), and that is called a verb (*ākhyāta')" should also be understood. Thus, "a man... [is explained].
In such instances as “the man goes,” “the woman goes,” and “the mind goes,” the word *gacchati* (goes) should be understood as expressing those respective specific genders;
however, in cases such as simply “it goes,” it should be understood as expressing a general gender.

Numerical terms such as “twenty” and so forth apply both to the act of counting and to the thing counted, as in “twenty cows” or “a twenty of cows. But when these [terms] refer to the thing counted as a singular unit (*ekatta*), [they function as follows:]...
They establish that the state of being a group (*vaggatta*) is essentially distinguished by its unity.

At that time, even when the number is different, it always remains in the singular case within a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in "twenty cows" (*vīsati gāvo*). If [the number] is in the singular, how is this so?

There are such usages as "two twenties," "three twenties," "five hundreds," and so on; thus he says, "even when there is plurality due to a division of groups. [This applies] to "twenty" and the others.

When it is intended to express a division of groups (*vagga*), plural forms occur even when there is a plurality [of individuals] and even when the plural suffix is used. However, in the *Amarakośa* it is stated:
"In the sense of another number, words such as *vīsati* (twenty) and so on also become plural when they are in grammatical apposition with that [other number]" (*Amarakośa* 19.83–4).
Here, "another number" refers to a division of groups; therefore, even for two [groups], there is a difference merely in conventional designation.

It should not be seen as a diversity of meaning. By extending the term *navuti* [to include] the word *na*, those numbers beginning with twenty (*vīsati*) and so on, even when having different genders, are used in grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the feminine (*nāriyaṃ*, *itthiyaṃ*), such as "twenty pots" (*vīsati kuṇḍāni*). The numbers beginning with twenty are *vikata*-compounds and collective *dvanda*s.

Because gender is determined by worldly convention (*lokāsayattā*), the rule "the gender of a *dvanda* is that of a singular" applies, and thus they are neuter; according to the ultimate view (*paramatena*), the numbers beginning with twenty are unarisen (*abyuppanna*).
According to the opinion of Kaccāyana, however, they are "arisen" (byuppannā).
474–476. There are twenty-four numerical categories beginning with "hundred" (sata) and ending with "incalculable" (asaṅkhyeya).

Among these, the word *sata* is derived from the repetition of the word *dasa* ("ten"); likewise, the word *sahassa* is derived from the repetition of the words *sata* and *dasa*. [The root] *yuja* means "to join" (*yoge*).
*Niyuta* and *ayuta*. *Yu* means "to mix" (*missane*); with the suffix *to*, it becomes *yuto*. *Lakṣa* means "seeing" or "number";

*lakkhaṃ* is also a hundred thousand (*satasahassa*). *Kuṭa* means "cutting" (*chedane*); that which cuts tenfold is *koṭi*. By being distinguished by a prefix (*upasagga*), one specific number is called *pakoṭi*;
two [of those] mixed together are one *koṭipakoṭi*. *Naha* means "binding" (*bandhane*); with the suffix *to*, there is an augment (*āgama*). *Vida* means "attaining" (*lābhe*).

*u*: there is the elision of *niggahīta* (anusvāra). *Aba* is used in the sense of non-harming and in the sense of going; *do* are two augmentations. *Ahi* is used in the sense of going; *hap* is the suffix.

*Ava* is used in the sense of protecting; *vo* [is the suffix]. *Aṭa* is used in the sense of walking; *ṭo* [is the suffix]. *Sogandhika* is said to be a specific number by way of a particular name for a lotus;

likewise, each specific number is expressed by names such as *uppala* and so forth. *Katha* is used in the sense of a continuous discourse; *yu* [is the suffix]. Because it cannot be numbered, it is *asaṅkhyeyya* (incalculable).
[Objection: "If it is impossible to calculate [them], there ought to be only one; so how is it that the distinctions such as 'one incalculable' (*asaṅkhyeya*) and 'two incalculables' are stated?
[Response: This is not a fault, because they can exist even when distinguished by way of time, location, and so forth.
Among these numbers, in successive order, each is multiplied tenfold, reaching the limit of hundreds of thousands and so on.
It becomes [one] koṭi and so forth, ending with the asaṅkhyeyya, multiplied by one hundred thousand—that is, multiplied by one hundred thousand.
Therefore, one line accompanied by two zeros (śūnya) becomes one hundred; likewise, one accompanied by three zeros becomes one thousand;
one accompanied by four zeros becomes a niyuta; one line accompanied by five zeros becomes one lakh (lakh); and furthermore, one line accompanied by seven zeros—
A *koṭi*, and likewise a *pakoṭi* together with fourteen *suññas*; in this manner it should be carried on until the *asaṅkhyeyya*. This is the opinion of some teachers.
Alternatively, all [numbers] beginning with the hundred and ending with the *asaṅkhyeyya* should be multiplied by ten; this is the opinion of Kaccāyana, for which reason he states the rule:
"And from that point onward, multiplied by ten. Alternatively, [the sequence] from the hundred up to the *lakkha*...
Ten times ten makes one hundred; thus, one line accompanied by two dots becomes a hundred. Likewise, with four, five, and so on dots, it becomes a thousand and so forth.
However, one line accompanied by twelve dots is a *koṭi*, and likewise, with nineteen dots, it is a *pakoṭi*.
This calculation should be carried out up to the *asaṅkhyeyya* by adding seven dots to each successive unit; therefore—
In the specific calculation of the *asaṅkhyeya*, there are one hundred and forty-five points; this is our opinion. However, in the *Amarakośa* (19.84), it is stated:
“The *paṅkti* consists of a hundred thousand and so forth, each subsequent term being ten times greater. The meaning of this is as follows:
the number ten is called a *paṅkti*; starting from that, the sequence beginning with a hundred thousand and so on should be understood as increasing tenfold at each step.
It is as follows: ten times ten is a hundred; ten times a hundred is a thousand; ten times a thousand is ten thousand (*ayuta*); ten times ten thousand is a hundred thousand (*lakkha*);
ten times a hundred thousand is a million (*payuta*); ten times a million is ten million (*koṭi*).
In the same way, ten times ten million is an *abbuda*; ten times an *abbuda* is a *paduma*; ten times a *paduma* is a *khabba*. Ten times a *khabba*...

From *mahākatha* comes *mahāpaduma*, from that *saṅku*, from *saṅku* the ocean (*samudda*), from that the end (*antya*), from the end the middle (*majjha*), from the middle the further half (*paraddha*), from the further half the deathless (*amata*), from the deathless a number ten times greater, and the twentieth place is the "incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeya*);
beyond this is the "immeasurable" (*atulya*). For since the exposition is for the entire assembly, all the arguments of everyone are presented here.

477–478. By means of the expression *sādhika* (plus) with the word *pāda* (foot), it demonstrates this meaning of the words: "one and a half" (*aḍḍhena catuttho*) is *aḍḍhuḍḍha*; "two and a half" (*aḍḍhena tatiyo*) is *aḍḍhatiya*; and "three and a half" (*aḍḍhateyyo*) is likewise.
When the word *catuttha* and others are combined with the prefix *aḍḍha*, they undergo the substitutions *aḍḍhuḍḍha* and so forth.

By means of the expression *sādhika* with the word *pāda*, it demonstrates this meaning of the words: "one and a quarter" (*aḍḍhena dutiyo*) is *diyaḍḍha*; and "one and three-quarters" (*divaḍḍho*) is likewise.
It shows [this]. Here, the recurrence of the word *aḍḍha* (half) even for that which is hidden is intended because there is no other expression [for it];

it is thus in all cases. 479–480. That by which something is measured (*mīyate*) or delimited is *māna* (measure). And that, according to the influence of the balance (*tulā*), the cubit (*pattha*), and the finger (*aṅguli*), is threefold with respect to the object to be measured.
[The root] *tul* is in the sense of weighing; it belongs to the *cur*-class, and *tulā* is feminine. [The root] *pad* is in the sense of going; [the suffix] *tha*. *Aṅga*...
*Gamane*, *ulo*, *aṅgulaṃ*; there is also the reading *aṅgulī*, meaning a finger or a digit.
Four *vīhīs* (grains of rice) combined together have the same weight as one *guñjā*. Likewise, two *guñjās* have the same weight as one *māsaka*;
this principle is to be applied throughout. Two *māsakas* are called an *akkha*, also termed a *vibhītaka*, because their weight is equal to that of an *akkha* fruit.
Or *akkho*. Here too, there is *kari*; the root *kas* means "to scratch," with *a* as the suffix and *ri* in the middle; it is not feminine.

Five *akkhas* are called a *dharaṇa*, formed from the root *dhar* with the suffix *yu*. Eight *akkhas* are called a *suvaṇṇa*. Five *dharaṇas* are called a *nikkha*. Five of those *nikkhas* are called a *pāda*.
According to the opinion of some, that *pāda* applies to a fourth part [of a *nikkha*]. It is exactly as previously stated.
Four *vīhaya* are called a *guñjā*. Two *guñjā* are called a *māsaka*. Two *pañcamāsaka* (five-māsaka coins) are ten *māsaka*, which is called an *akkha*.
Eight *akkha* are called a *dharaṇa*. Five *dharaṇa* are called a *suvaṇṇa*. Five of those *suvaṇṇa* are, in our opinion, called a *nikkha*.
[The root] *kan* is used in the senses of appearance, movement, and beauty; with the prefix *ni-*, it becomes *nikkha*, as in the case of a gold ornament.
A fourth part of any given substance is a *pāda*. Ten *dharaṇas* are called a *pala*; it is used in the sense of weight (*pathe*) and in the sense of movement (*gatimhi*).
(481) A hundred *palas* of any given substance is a *tulā*. *Tula* is used in the sense of measuring (*ummāne*), as in "a woman (*tulā nārī*).
It is used for the wooden framework of houses, for a bench, and for a woman.
In the *Mānabhaṇḍa* and similar works, it is stated that twenty *tula*s among hundreds of *rāsi-pala*s are called a *bhāra*.

The root *bhar-* is used in the senses of bearing, supporting, and nourishing (*dhāraṇa-posanesu*). Furthermore, the *Ajaya-ṭīkā*, known as the *Vyākhyāsudhā*, explains: "A *bhāra* consists of two thousand *palas*, and it is also a measure for gold. *Vivadha* refers to a specific kind of load.
A *kahāpaṇa* is a unit of commercial value made from silver by means of a *karisa*; it is a piece of silver measured by the standard of a *karisa*.
*Paṇa*, *paṇiya*, and *dabbabheda* are synonyms for a coin; *kahāpaṇa* is a specific type. The substitution of *ri* occurs [for *ra*]. When the substitution of *aha* occurs, it becomes *karisāpaṇa*.
These two are modifications of form (*rūpavikāra*), except where they are used figuratively.
Thus, the measures of weight have been explained. 482. To show the measures of capacity, he says "a *kuḍuva*" and so forth. One *pasata* is called a *kuḍuva*. The root *sar* means "to go."
The elision of the *ra* suffix; *kaḍi* in the sense of breaking; *vo* [suffix]; *kaḍissa* becomes *kuḍu*; four *kuḍuvā* make one *pattha*. Four *patthas* make one *āḷhaka*.
Now, regarding the honorific suffix *ṇvu*, the measure of ten fingers or twelve fingers in height is also called an *āḷhaka*. Four *āḷhakas* are called a *doṇa*;
there is also a reading "four *āḷhakas*" (*caturāḷhaka*). The root *du* means "to go"; with the suffix *ṇo*, from *duṇa* meaning "going" and "harming."
Or, *doṇa*. By means of the particle *vā*, it is *doṇo*.
483. Four *doṇas* make a *mānikā*; *māna* [is used] in the sense of measuring (*pūjāyaṃ*), with the suffix *ko* added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

In the word *caturmānikaṃ*, the aggregate of four *mānikās* is called a *khārī*; *khara* [means] destruction (*vināse*), with the suffix *ṇo*, belonging to the *nada*-class. Ten *ambaṇas* amount to one hundred and ten *doṇas*.
*Kumbha* is shown as a specific type of measure by the name "pot"; there is also a reading, *ambaṇa*.
To show the synonyms available for these specific measures, he says: "āḷhaka," and so forth. *Tumba* [is derived from] the root *tumb*, meaning "to shake," with the suffix *a*.
The two [terms] refer to a *pattha*. This word *pattha* occurs in both its general sense and its specific divisions; however, here it denotes a specific measure.
This is intended [here]. In the *Nala-gaṇṭha*, it means debt. It is called *vāha* because it carries (*vahati*); from the root *vaha* in the sense of reaching, with the suffix *-ṇa*.

To show the measure of an *ambaṇa* or its synonyms, he said: "eleven *doṇas*" and so forth. From the root *amba* in the sense of moving, or *amba* in the sense of sound, with the suffix *-yu*; thus it is stated as that which is desired. However, the measure of a finger (*aṅgula*) was explained in the section on the earth (*bhūmi-vagga*) during the discussion of terms such as *aṇu*.

485. *Catukkaṃ* (a group of four) [is derived] from *bhaj*. *Visa* means entry; it begins with a long vowel. *Koṭṭhaṃ* refers to the body; one who lies therein is a *koṭṭhāsa* (portion). [The suffix] *āttaṃ*.

*Ana* means breathing, or *ama* means going; [the suffix] *so*. That which is divided and served is a *bhāga* (portion). [The suffix] *ṇo*. *Vaṇṭaka* is also used here. From *vaṭi* meaning division, [the suffix] *ṇvu*;
or, from a word ending in *ṇ*, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
*Vibhavantaṃ* means possessing wealth. *Dhana* refers to grain; the suffix *a* [is applied]. This is one's own (*attano ayaṃ*), hence *sassa*. *Duiva* means *dabba*, in the sense of essence;
*iva* is used in the sense of *iva*, hence *vo*. *Vida* means acquisition, hence *to*. One who is the master (*pati*) of that wealth is *sapati*; that which is good (*sādhu*) for him is *sāpateyyaṃ*;
it is to be understood by the suffix *ṇeyya*. *Vasa* means dwelling, hence *u*. *Ara* means going, hence *tho*. *Rassa* becomes *to*. That by which things arise or originate is *vibhava*.
a. Gold, as well as a treasury. 486.

Gold that has been worked or unworked, silver, mixed and combined (*milita*; *ka.*), or even individually combined (*pacceka*; *Amarakosa*, *Khīrasvāmī-ṭīkā*), is denoted by the two terms "treasury" (*kosa*) and so forth;
therein, that which is massed together, fashioned into ornaments, and brought into a state of craftsmanship.

Or it is made. "Unmade" refers to substances such as powders and the like that have not yet been fashioned. "Other than those" means other than gold and silver; "fiery substance" (*tejasa*) refers to copper.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), bell-metal, tin, lead, and so on are included, as well as non-fiery substances such as silk cloth, wood, and the like, which are of poor quality.
All of that is "movable property" (*kuppa*). [The root] *gup* means to protect; thus it is called *guppati*. The suffix *po* is added, and *ga* is substituted for *k*.

The pair consists of gold (*kañcana*) and silver (*rūpiya*). Silver refers to that which has been struck [into coin], such as the forms of excellent horses, boars, and men; it also refers to coins like *dīnāras* and the like, which are struck by a hammer. It is called "silver" (*rūpiya*) because it possesses forms (*rūpa*) that have not been struck [as mere raw metal].

The root *rūp* is used in the senses of striking and praising; the suffix *iya* is added. 487–488. The word ending in *hirañña* refers to gold. That which has a beautiful color (*vaṇṇa*) is "gold" (*suvaṇṇa*). The root *kan* means "splendor";

with the suffix *ṇvu*, we get *kana*. "Born" (*jāta*) means produced. "Jātarūpa" (gold) means that which is excellently born (*pakaṭṭha-jāta*). The suffix *rūpa* is applied in the sense of excellence, and the suffix *rūpa* is also applied in the sense of praise.
Thus, by the rule *subhū-pasaṃsāyaṃ rūpaṃ* (Pāṇini 5.3.66), it is "gold" (*jātarūpa*). Alternatively, it is *jātarūpa* because its form (*rūpa*) has been born (*jāta*).

[The root] *iṇ* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "shining" (*ditti*), due to its polysemous nature. It is called *suvaṇṇa* (gold) because it shines well (*suṭṭhu dippate*) or is endowed with luster (*dittiyā yujjate*). [In the derivation of *suvaṇṇa*:

from the prefix *su*, by the rule *vā paro asarūpā* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), there is elision (*ilopa*) of the suffix *-a*, followed by doubling (*dvitta*). [The root] *kañ* is used in the sense of shining (*ditti*), with the suffix *yu*. It is the color of the Teacher (*satthu vaṇṇo*).
That which has a color like that [of gold] is *hari*. It carries away the mind alone, thus it is *hari*. The suffix *i* is used in the sense of desire (*kamu*), according to Būṇa.

The mind moves beautifully therein, thus it is *cāru*; the suffix *ṇu* is used. The root *hi* is used in the sense of motion; the suffix *mo* is added. The root *haṭa* is used in the sense of splendor (*ditti*); the suffix *ṇvu* is added. That which deserves heating or burning is *tapaniya*; the suffix *iya* is added. The root *hara* is used in the sense of taking away;

the suffix *añña* is added, and the vowel *a* is substituted. The root *hā* is used in the sense of abandoning or in the sense of motion; the suffix *añña* is added, and the substitution of *hirā* occurs.
The four beginning with *cāmīkara* are specific varieties of that gold. *Cāmī* is a species of flower; because it produces [the color] from that, it is *cāmīkara*.
Alternatively, *cāmī* means fire. From the root *camu* (to eat), with the suffix *ṇī*, it is *cāmī*; because it produces [the color] from that, it is *cāmīkara*.
*Satakumbha* has the color of the filaments of the *paddha* flower; because it resembles that color, it is *sātakumbha*. [It is so called] because it is like a divine tree...
At the place where the great *jambu* tree is established is the river Jambunadī.
The gold produced from the seeds of fruits the size of great elephants or the size of water-jars that fall into it is called *jambunada*.

This gold, however, arises with a brilliance like fire and as an incomparable ornament for the gods. Regarding the term "analam" (fire-like), Amarasiṅha explains that it refers to the specific quality of this gold while retaining its general nature as gold.
He recites [the following]. *Siṅgī* is a species of fish, so called because of its color. Alternatively, it is *siṅgī* because it is produced from pieces of stone shaped like that [fish).
However, in the *Amarakośa*, gold and other metals are also listed under the general term for gold (*suvaṇṇa*), whereas *siṅgī* refers specifically to a particular kind.
For it is said there: "That which is gold for ornaments is known as *siṅgīkanaka*" (Amarakośa 19.96).
The meaning of this is as follows: the name for gold used as an ornament, such as bracelets and earrings, is "siṅgī.
"Siṅgīmaṇḍanasovaṇṇa" (gold for ornaments of siṅgī) is a treasury of gems. Because of its golden nature, siṅgī is called "kanaka.

489. The pentad [of terms] refers to silver. It is "rūpiya" because it possesses form (rūpa). From the root *rañj* (to color), hence [the suffix -iya]. From the root *sañj* (to adhere), with the suffix *jhu*, there is the elision of *ñ*.

*Sajjhu*: Because it is associated with form (*rūpa*), it is *rūpī*. In the word *sañja*, meaning "to cling," there is the suffix *jha*; the *ñ* is elided, resulting in *sajjhaṃ*. There is also a reading as *rūpiyajjha*;
in that case, it is established by the suffix *iyajjha*. It may be ill-colored, like a date palm, or even white.
Regarding gold and silver that have been refined: "Silver is considered *rūpiya*."
The word *khale* (in the threshing floor) is neuter; *khajjūra* (date palm) is [neuter] when it means "among trees";
*setā* (white) is [feminine] in the sense of "a wall" (*bhittikāyaṃ*), while *sajjha* (white) is neuter in the three genders.

The triad beginning with *vasu* occurs in the sense of "of our own kind" (*asmajātīyaṃ*) such as in *puppharāga* (ruby) and so forth, and in *muttāvajira* (diamond) and so forth. *Vasa* (to dwell), [ending in] *u*, [expresses] delight (*ratiṃ*).

It is called a *ratana* because it "spreads" (*tanoti*); the suffix *-no* is applied after roots such as *tan*, with the elision of the syllable *ti*. According to the *Amarakośa* (2.8.126), "a *ratna* [is used] for that which is best of its kind.

Thus, the best of elephants is the "elephant-jewel" (*gajaratana*), and the best of women is the "woman-jewel" (*itthiratana*). From the word *manas*, with the suffix *i* and the feminine suffix *ī*, we have *maṇī*.
The ruby (*puppharāga*) and others to be mentioned later are its varieties—that is, specific types of that gem. It is called a "gem" (*maṇi*) because it shines and delights (*rañjeti*).
The redness of the flower is the blossom of speech. 490.
These seven, beginning with gold, are called the jewels (*ratana*). The *maṇi* is the precious gem. 491.
To show the manner in which the seven jewels are obtained, he says "the ruby" (*lohitaṅga*), and so forth. This refers to the triad beginning with the ruby.
*Rattamaṇi* means a red gem. It is called *lohitaṅga* because it is marked with a red color; or, its body (*aṅga*)—its physical form—is red, thus it is a *lohitaṅga*.

Here, *paduma* refers to the *kokanada* (red lotus); a gem resembling its color is a *padumarāga*. It is also a *soṇaratana* (ruby), and here it is also *lohitaka* (red). There are two [types] of *veḷuriya* (beryl):
a bamboo (*vaṃsa*) has a pith-like core (*tacasāra*), and a gem of that color is *vaṃsavaṇṇa* (bamboo-colored). It is called *veḷuriya* because it appears like a bamboo.

In the word *ivatthe*, there is the substitution of *i* for *ya*, and the suffix *rāgama*. There are two [forms] for *pavāḷe*. From the root *vala* in the sense of "covering," with the suffix *ṇo* and the substitution of *ḷ* for *ra*, we have *pavāḷo*; by the rule of optionality (*vākārena*), *pavāḷo* is also valid.
From the root *du* in the sense of "going" or from *du* in the sense of "afflicting," with the suffix *mo*, we have *dvittaṃ*.
(492) There are two [names] for the *kabara* gem. That which is produced in *Masāragiri* is *masāragallaṃ*; here, *la* is substituted for *ra*. *Kabaro*...
*Sabala* means "mani. There are two [terms] for pearl: *muttā* and *muttika*. From the root *muc*, meaning "to release," with the suffix *tha*, we have *muttā*;
*muttika* is formed by adding the suffix *ika* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). Since adjectives (*satthikā*) may deviate from the gender and number of their base noun, it is here neuter.

Furthermore, the reason for mentioning the synonyms for jewels out of order is to indicate the absence of a sequence based on the order of their arising or their relative excellence among the seven treasures.
Two [terms] for brass: *rī* (in the sense of going) and *ri*. *Rīti* is also used. Rudda states: “*Rīti* is used in the senses of conduct, sand, iron dross, and copper.
That which has the dross (*kūṭa*) of iron itself is *rītikā*. The word *dabba* is also used here. Two [terms] for cloud: *ama* (in the sense of going), *alo*. *Abbha* means sky and cloud;
because it is designated by that [name], it is *abbhaka*, with the suffix *ka* added to form a designation. “It is also called *megha* and *ambara*; *gori*...”
For it is said: "The seed and the cloud. Here, *girija* refers to bitumen (*silājatu*).
493. The triad concerns metals. *Lū* means cutting; *ho*. *Aya* means going; it belongs to the *manoggaṇa* class and so forth. That which is black and is iron is *kāḷāyasa*.
*Satthaka*, *tikkhaṇa*, *piṇḍa*, *ayasa*, and *asmāsāra* are used here as well. In the phrase "the sword among weapons and metals," the word has multiple meanings.
“*Sāmudda-lavaṇa-ittakkaṃ, visa-lohājimukkake*” means quicksilver (*rabhaso*). *Paṇḍa* means going; *assa* is its essence. According to the *Tvamaramālā*, in the section on neuter nouns:
“*Kāḷāyasa-mayo loho, assasārañca satthakan*” (Iron is made of black metal, and steel is the essence of iron). Two [terms] refer to the fickle (*capale*). *Pāra* means capability;

with the suffix *-do*, it is *pārada*, meaning that which can transform all metals into gold. *Rasa* means sound; that which sounds when thrown into fire is *rasa*, and *rasa* also refers to the sweet and other tastes. The fickle one (*capalo*) and the alchemist (*sūto*) are also included here.
“In *cañcalādi* [the word] *capala* [is used];
in *sārathi*, *rasa*, and *pasūta*, [the word] *sūta* [is used]; in three senses;
*pārada* is called *rasendra*, and it is also termed *pārata*.”
Tārapāla states:
"Mercury (pārada), the perfected mineral (siddhadhātu), the excellent seed (varabīja), and the quicksilver (sūtaka). — *Tikaṇḍasesa* 2.9.34.
*Tikaṃ nāge* (The triad refers to the elephant). *Tipu* means "to press" (*pīḷane*), according to the *Uṇhīsadīpanī*.

Since the word *tipu* is also used for "white," it is specified by the word "black" (*kāḷa*) and thus called *kāḷatipu*. Therefore, some maintain that the word *tipu* denotes both [lead and tin], as stated in the *Amarakośa* (19.105):
"An elephant, lead, tin, silver, and tin are *piccaṭa*," and in the *Tikaṇḍasesa*, the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*, and other works: "*Tipu* refers to lead and tin."

Because it has already been stated [elsewhere], it need not be included here; therefore, there are only two designations for the object: *kāḷo* (black) and *tipu* (tin). It is called *kāḷo* because of its black color.

*Tipu* has the same meaning as previously explained. [Etymological derivation: From the root *tap*, meaning "to heat," with the suffix *u*, it becomes *tapa-u*. From *sī*, meaning "to lie down," or from *si*, meaning "to bind," with the suffix *so*, it becomes *sīso*.
According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "The best of elephants is *bhakadduja*; *kliva* refers to lead and tin. *Yogiṭṭha* is one name [for tin].
Regarding lead (*sīsa*): “It is called *vappa*, and it is merely lead,” says the *Amarakosa*.
“*Ārakūṭa*, *rīti*, lead (*sīsaka*), tin (*tipu*), *vaddhaka*;
*nāga*, *mahāmala*, and *yogiṭṭhaka* [are synonyms]. — [Amara-kosa 2.9.93]
Vyāḍi: “The head alone is full of impurities; even the back and the anus are so;
and even the *āluka* root, like gold and other [precious things], originates from vermilion.”
*Tantātantaraṃ*.
However, *raṅga* and *vaṅga* mean "to go" (*gati-attha*); as it is said:
"The *raṅga* [is] the elephant of the gods, the *mudaṅga*, the *kusumbha*, the village, and the saffron."
*Tikaṇḍasesa* 2.9.34: "Two [meanings] for *haritāla*.
*Haritāla* is so called because it is an ornament (*alaṃ*) of green color (*harita*); this is merely its etymological derivation. This word, however, is a conventional term (*rūḷhisadda*).
It leads to joy (*pīti*), thus it is *pītana*. Regarding this, Amarasīha states in the *Amarakośa*: 'Both *piñjara* and *pītana*, as well as *tālamāla*, refer to *haritāla*.'"

19.103. *Piñja* means color (*vaṇṇa*). *Ara* means a disease. *Ala* means an ornament (*bhūsana*); it is called *ala* because one adorns (*alanti*) with it, hence the suffix *-ṇo*. However, Mādhava says:

"Yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), *ala*, the color of the *tāla* tree, and the ornament of actors (*naṭabhūsana*). The *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.9.35) states: "But *kappūra* is yellow orpiment; *godanta* is the name for an actor. 494. There are two [names] for vermilion (*sindūra*).
It is called *piṭṭha* because it is produced from *piṭṭha-nāga* (a type of mineral). That which originates in the land of China is *cīnapiṭṭha*. Thus there are two.
There is an elision of the latter member in the first compound. *Sanda* means hearing; *ūro*, horse. “Sindūra is produced from elephants,” says Amarasīha (Amara-kośa 1.9.105).
Here it refers to spring powder (*vasantassava*), red dust, and red sand. *Tūla* has two [roots]: *tula* in the sense of rubbing down (*nikase*), with the suffix *a*;
and *picu* in the sense of crushing (*maddane*), with the suffix *u*. *Picu* and *tūla* together constitute its name. “*Tūla*, *picu*, *picutūla*, and *makkaṭisutta* [are synonyms].”
For "takkoṭī" is a term for a wasp. By the word *madhu*, a small creature is meant; "small" (*khudda*) is what is expressed. Small creatures include bees and the like.
Among them, honey made by bees is called *bhāmara*; that made by flies is called *makkhika* and is also termed *saragha*; and that made by wasps is called *vāraṭa*.

*Puttikā*: the suffix *ṇo* is applied in all these senses after the word *putta*. *Madhu*: from the root *und* (to moisten), with the suffix *u*. *Khuda*: from the root *khu* (sound), with the suffix *do*; or from *khud* (thirst). The two [terms] refer to a lump of honey-cakes. *Madhucchiṭṭhaṃ*:
that which is left over (*ucchiṭṭha*) and prepared (*sajjita*) by small bees (*madhūhi khuddajantūhi*). *Sajja*: in the senses of preparation, attachment, embracing, and formation (*nimmāna*).
*Formation* (*nimmāna*) means aggregation (*sampiṇḍīkaraṇa*). The suffix *to* is applied; there is the substitution of *ṭha* for *ja*, and *cha* for *sa*.
*dvittaṃ* and *ittaṃ*. The root *sic* means "to flow"; [the suffix] *tha* [is added]. *Sitthaṃ* itself is *sitthakaṃ*. *Madana* is also used here. 495. A triad for a cowherd (*gopāla*).
He protects (*pāleti*) the cows and he guards (*pāti*) them, thus he is a *gopālo*; [he is also] a *gopo*. The suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the object (*kammani*).

He counts (*saṅkhyāti*) the cows, thus he is a *gosaṅkhyo*; the prefix *sam-* is used with the root *khyā* in the sense of counting. *Goduho*, *ābhiro*, and *vallavo* are also used here. A dyad for a cow-owner (*gomiko*). Cows...

*Gomā*: one who has cows (*go*) is called *gomā*; [this is derived from] the root *mantu*. With the suffix *ika* and the augment *mā*, it becomes *gomiko*. *Dvipādaṃ balīvadde*: [The word *balīva* refers to] a bull.

From the root *usa* (to burn), with the suffix *abho*, [it becomes *usabho*]. One who increases strength (*bala*) is called *balībaddo*; this is due to irregular derivation (*nipātanā*). *Goṇo*: one who goes (*gacchati*) is called *goṇo*; [the suffix] *yu* is applied, the *m* is elided, and the vowel is lengthened (*asso*). [Alternatively,] from the root *gamu* (to go) with the suffix *ro*, it becomes *go*.
"Sagge kare ca vajire, balīvadde ca go pumā": The masculine noun *go* [is used] for heaven, a hand, a thunderbolt, and a bull.
"In *thī*, *sorabheyyi*, *nettam*, *bu*, *disā*, *vacana*, and *bhūmi*.

— This is the rule for *ru*. The root *vas* means "to dwell," and [the suffix] *abho* is applied. That which dwells is a *vasso*; from the root *vassa* meaning "to sprinkle," with the suffix *ṇo*, the vowel *a* is substituted, and there is the elision of the conjunct (*saṃyogalopa*).
Thus, *ukkho*, *bhaddo*, and *anavāho* are formed; *sorabheyyo* is also included here. From the root *ukkha* meaning "to sprinkle": that which carries a cart (*anaṃ*) is an *anavāho*.
No. *Surabhi* means a cow; its offspring is *sorabheyyo*, which is to be understood [as a bull].
496. That cow, when grown old, is called *jaraggavo*. A cow that has reached old age is *jaraggavo*; [the suffix] *-avo* is substituted for *-simhi* (the locative case ending).

When joined with the words *missa* or *bālya*, it refers to a calf that has reached some degree of youth but has not yet attained the state of a full-grown ox (*balībaddha*). "A calf that has grown... [is the meaning].
*Vacchataro* is a string of names. *Dammo* is one who deserves to be tamed; [the root] *dam* [is used] with the suffix *mo*. In the sense of dwelling, from the root *vas*, with the suffix *cho*;

the word *taro* is a substitution for *vaccha* itself, as in the case of a cow, according to Pāṇini 5.3.91—this sutta should be consulted. *Samā* and *eti* are two words of identical meaning. Both refer to a beast of burden.
One who bears the yoke by nature is *dhuravāhī*, formed with the suffix *ṇī*. One who is worthy of bearing the yoke is *dhorayho*, formed with the suffix *ṇo*, where *va* is replaced by *ya*.
Because he is preeminent among cattle and oxen, a person is called *govinda*; or, *govinda* means "lord of cattle" (*gavām indaḥ govindaḥ*), or "one who finds cattle" (*gavāṃ vindati govindaḥ*).
(497) By means of this, one carries: *vaha*. The root *kuk* in the sense of taking up, with the suffix *uda*, becomes *ussatta*; the *da* is replaced by *dha*, resulting in *kakuda* and *kakudha*.

These two refer to the hump on the shoulders. The root *vis* in the sense of entering, with the suffix *yu*. The root *sī* in the sense of lying down, with the prefix *go*, elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and shortening of the vowel. Because of its red color...

*Rohiṇī*: not [derived] from *nadādi*. 498. The triad [of terms] is for the general sense of "cow" (*gāvī*). It is also *gāvī* when masculine; then the suffix *ī* is applied to the stem *go*. Because it is possessed of horns, it is *siṅginī*; here the suffix *inī* follows a *taddhita* derivative.

Two [terms] refer to one who has no son. From the root *han*, the feminine form is *a*; the killing of one who kills is *vadha*; there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and the substitution of *dha* [for *ha*].
*Jho* means barren (*bandha*, in the sense of binding); *vañjhā*. *Vasa* is in the sense of desire; [the suffix] *a*.

A cow that has recently calved and whose milk is of high value is called a *dhenū*; *dhe* is in the sense of drinking, [with the suffix] *nu*. Both terms refer to one who desires her calf. She desires her calf, thus she is *vacchakāmā*. She takes her calf, thus she is *vacchalā*.

They say both of these refer even to one whose body is accompanied by a calf. 499. Two terms refer to a churning vessel. It emits the sound "gagga," thus it is *gaggarī*, belonging to the class beginning with *nada*. It churns...

*Manthanī*: from the root *manth*, meaning "to stir" (*viloḷane*), with the suffix *yu*; it belongs to the *nadādi* class; both forms are feminine. Where many [objects] are bound together in one place that is suitable for much binding, there are the two terms beginning with *sandāna*.
The prefix *sam-* combined with the root *dā* (in the sense of "giving") has the meaning of "restraining"; with the suffix *yu* in the instrumental sense, it becomes *saṃdāna*.
From the root *dā* (in the sense of "giving"), with the suffix *mo*, it becomes *dāma*.

Two [terms] for cow-dung: *govañca*. *Miha* means to sprinkle; the suffix *lo*. Cow-dung is *gomīḷha*. Born from a cow is *gomaya*; both are not feminine. Two [terms] for ghee: *sappi* and *ghata*. *Sappa* means to go; the suffix *i*; *sappi* is neuter. *Ghara* means to sprinkle; the suffix *to*. Here, it refers to clarified butter (*havīpya*). 500.

Butter produced from curd of that same day, or produced from milk, as well as fresh butter which is its natural state, is *ghata*. That which has been brought forth (*nīta*) from fresh curds and so on is *nonīta*;
the suffix is *vasso*. *Navanīta* (fresh butter) is also [included]. Two [terms] for the essence of curd: the scum (*maṇḍa*) or the essence of curd.
*Dadhimaṇḍa* (whey). [The following are] synonyms for whey: *mathu*, *maṭṭhu* (with *to* suffix), and *matthu* (in the neuter). Regarding the fourfold set for milk:

*khīra* (milk) is derived from the root *khī* (to perish), with the suffix *-īra*. *Duddhaṃ* (milk) is that which is milked; it is derived from the root *duha* (to fill/milk), with the suffix *-ta*. *Payaḥ* (milk) is that which is to be drunk; it is derived from the root *pā* (to drink), with the suffix *-ya*, and the vowel *ā* is elided. *Thaññaṃ* (breast-milk) is that which is produced from the breast (*thana*). There are two terms for buttermilk (*takka*): *takkaṃ* is that in which three parts of water exist;

it is derived from the root *taka* (to press), with the suffix *-a*, the insertion of the vowel *i* according to the rule "the vowel *i* is inserted according to tradition," and the doubling of the consonant. Furthermore, *matha* (to churn/stir) with the suffix *-ta*—wherein the vowel *i* is inserted as per the aforementioned rule—[also denotes buttermilk]. However, elsewhere:
“Half-filled with water, stirred up and churned;
mixed with one-third [of its volume] of buttermilk—this is called ‘churned’ (*mathita*), while ‘water-departed’ (*gatodaka*) is that from which the liquid has gone.
Thus, *takka-mathita* is mentioned as a distinct category, whereas *gatodaka* refers to that which is devoid of liquid.
“Freshly churned, unctuous buttermilk, or whey with a quarter part water;
diluted half with water, or equalized with water—let them drink this.
— *Ratanamālā*

501. There are five [products] beginning with milk, which possess flavors derived from cow’s milk: milk (*khīra*), fresh curd (*dadhi*) produced from milk—for it is said in the *Ratanamālā*, “The auspicious curd born of milk” (*khīrajaṃ dadhimaṅgalaṃ*)—butter (*ghataṃ*) produced from curd, as well as clarified butter (*nītaṃ*);

and buttermilk (*takkaṃ*), which is the remainder of all [the preceding], or rather, [buttermilk] produced from milk alone. [Note: *Dadhi*: from the root *dhā* (to hold), with the suffix *i*, doubling of the consonant, and a change by rule. *Ghataṃ*: from *dadhi* with the suffix *gha*; *nītaṃ* is not [produced] from that.]
A group of six is *eḷaka*. One who does not bleat even when being tormented is an *urabbha*; the root *ru* means "to sound," O friend. *Meṇḍa* is in the sense of crookedness; *ku* is a prefix.
*Mesa* is so called because it rubs (*misati*) against one another on the ground; "In rubbing, *mesa*; having rubbed, there is an elevation" is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*.

One who does not cry out is an *uraṇo*; the root *raṇa* means "to sound. *Avi* is derived from the root *ava* meaning "to protect," with the suffix *i*; "The *avi*, *sela*, and *mesakkha*"—thus says Amarasīha.
*Amara* 23.207: The reading *ajī* is also found. [The root] *ila* means "to go"; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *elū*. Here, *uṇṇāyu* is derived from the connection with *uṇṇā* (wool);
the suffix *yu* is added. Both *uloma* and *sasaddā* are stated by Rabhasa.

502: This triad refers to a goat (*aja*). [The root] *vasa* means "to dwell"; with the suffix *to*, it becomes *vasto*; *vatto* is also used. Others, however, state that *vasa* belongs to the *curādigaṇa* in the sense of "smelling" or "eating."

*Ajja*: "aja" means going; or, because it is not born (*na jāyati*), it is *aja*. *Chagalaka*: "it goes while cutting," thus *chagalaka*; from the root *cho* (to cut), *gamu* (to go), and the suffix *ṇo*;

the *m* of *massa* becomes *l*; the *o* is elided; the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*); *chakalaka* is also used. *Chāga* is also used here. Two terms refer to a young elephant (*karabha*).

*Vasa* means luster; with the suffix *to*, it becomes *vassa*; or from *usa* (to burn) with the suffix *otta*, etc., it becomes *oṭṭha*; it also refers to the lip (*dantacchada*). *Kara* means making (*karaṇe*).
Abho: Some read it as *kharabho*. It refers to a camel, a *maya*, and a large-limbed animal.
Two terms refer to the donkey (*gadrabha*). From the root *gad* (to cry out), *rabha* is derived; thus, *gadrabha*. Because its throat cavity (*kha*) is large, it is called *khara*;

this is the suffix *ra*. *Cakkavā*, *bāleyya*, and *rāsabha* also refer to it. From the connection with wheels (*cakra*), the suffix *vantu* is applied. Because it is joined with strength (*bala*), it is called *bāleyya*.
In the case of *rasa* and *sadda*, there is no [gender] distinction; these two are neuter (*aviyaṃ*). This [word] for *uraṇa* is *uraṇī*. This [word] for *avi* is *avī*.
The word *ajā* alone refers to a she-goat. However, others, having stated the reading "uraṇī, ajī, ajā," say that all three are synonyms for *uraṇī*;
according to their view, it should be understood that the words *ajī* and *ajā* are also synonyms for *uraṇī*. Alternatively, this is a triad.
*Ajā*. Since the term *uraṇī* can also be used as a synonym for *ajā*, it is stated: "The female goat (*uraṇī*) is indeed *ajī* or *ajā*.
For in the section on multiple meanings, the glossary verse (1124) states: "On the threshold, *eḷaka* means a goat (*aja*). Here, *eḷaka* is used as a synonym for *uraṇa*.
The commentary on the Vessavagga is concluded.

503. Regarding the triad on the *sudda*: *sad* means "to taste" (*assādane*); *do* is the suffix; *assu* is the prefix. *Anta-vaṇṇo* means "one of lowly appearance. *Vas* means "to sprinkle" (*secane*);

because he must be sprinkled with impurity, he is a *vasala*, [formed] with the suffix *alo*. Alternatively, he is a *vasala* because he sprinkles urine and excrement wherever it may be; here too the suffix *alo* applies even after a root ending in a consonant.
He is born from a lowly limb of Brahmā—namely, his foot—thus he is "born from a lowly place" (*jaghaññajo*).
The Māgadhas and others, ending with the Sūtas, are of mixed caste (*saṃkiṇṇajāti*) because their mothers and fathers belong to different castes;
this is the meaning, for "mixture" (*saṅkara*) is precisely the association of different castes. A son born to a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is a Māgadha.
This is a derivative based on the act of praising (*thuti*). A son born to a Kṣatriya through connection with a Śūdra woman is an Ugra; [the root] *ug* means "to assemble," with the suffix *-na*.
504. One born of a Kṣatriya man and a Brāhmaṇī woman is a Sūta; *su* means "to overcome," and it begins with a long vowel.
From a Vaiśya man and a Śūdra or a Vaiśya woman, one is a Karaṇa or an Ambaṣṭha. A Māhiṣya is born of a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya woman; a Kṣattṛ is born of a Kṣatriya man and a Kṣatriya woman;
and a Sūta is born of a Brāhmaṇī and a Kṣatriya man.
Among them, the Vedehaka belongs to the Vessas;
the Rathakāra, however, belongs to the Māhiṃsas,
from whom Karaṇya originated.
He who was born from a Brahmin woman and a man of the lowest caste (caṇḍāla) is called a Caṇḍāla. Among them,
Karana has the occupation of writing and engraving, while Ambaṭṭha has the occupation of divination.

*Dvayaṃ sippini*: One who performs or fashions paintings, plaster-work, and so forth is a *kāru* (artisan); [the suffix] *ṇu* is added. One who possesses a craft (*sippa*) is a *sippika* (craftsman). A collection of those artisans of the same class is called a *seṇī* (guild); [the root] *si* is used in the sense of serving, with the suffix *ṇi*. 505.
These five types of craftsmen, beginning with the carpenter, are known as *kārava* (workers) or *sippina* (artisans).
And it is said: “The carpenter, the weaver, the dyer, the barber;”
"And the fifth is the leather-worker; the artisan is considered a craftsman.
(506) This group of five concerns the carpenter (*tacchaka*). The root *taccha* means "to make thin. One who makes thin is a carpenter (*tacchaka*), from the suffix *-ṇvu*.

One who increases [the wood] by cutting it is a joiner (*vaddhakī*); the root *vaddha* means "cutting," belonging to the *curādigaṇa*. It is said: "And in the sense of cutting, there is also *vaddhana*."

*Ratnamālā*, suffix *ṇvu*. With the sense of agency (*sakatthe*), suffix *ī*: *vaddhakī* (carpenter), also *vaḍḍhakī*. He who cleaves or cuts by means of a plane (*palāda*) and a measuring tool is a *palagaṇḍo*.

The root *gaṇḍ* [is used] in the senses of cutting, plastering, accumulation, and a part of the face. A *palagaṇḍo* is also one who lives by plastering (*sudhājīvī*). The root *ṭhā* is used in the sense of stopping movement;
there is the addition of the letter *pa*. There is also the substitution of *tha* for *ṭha*. "He makes a chariot" (*rathaṃ karoti*); [this is] in the sense of the object (*kammani*).
No, O chariot-maker, [the suffix] *ṇo* is also used for a leather-worker (*cammakāra*). There are two [forms] for a goldsmith (*suvaṇṇakāra*). One is *nāḷidhamo*:
he blows through a tube (*nāḷi*), having placed it in his mouth, making the tube resound with breath from the mouth for the purpose of kindling the fire.

507. Furthermore, there is the name *pukkusaṃyāvapāda*. [The suffix] *ve* is used in the sense of weaving (*tantasantāna*); one who weaves cloth (*tanta*) is thus called a weaver (*vāyī*), by means of the suffix *ṇo*. *Pesa*... [text breaks off].

In the case of *peraṇa*, *payatta*, and *nagatī*: one who performs *pesana* (sending) is a *peso*; he who does that [is called] a *peṇo* by means of the suffix *ṇo*. A *kuvinda* is also included here; he who finds (*vindati*) what is base (*kucchita*) is a *kuvinda*.
From the application of the craft of garlands (*mālāsippa*), or from the application of weaving garlands (*mālāpana*), one is a *mālika* by means of the suffix *ika*.

One who sports with or desires (*lalati*) clay (*kuṃ*) is a *kulāla*; the root *lala* is used in the sense of desire, with the suffix *ṇo*. Both [terms] refer to one who lives by the craft of the needle (*sūcikamma*). The craft of the needle and the shuttle (*sūcivāna*).

"Sewing" (*sūcana*) is twofold: [the act of] piercing and [the act of] stitching. In this context, one who sews by means of the activity of a tailor (*tunnavāyakamma*)—which serves as the occasion for the designation—is a "tailor" (*tunnavāyo*);
one who employs the craft of needlework is a "needle-worker" (*sūciko*). 508.
One who makes leather—that is, brings it to a transformation—is so called; the suffix *ṇo* is used here in the sense of the object (*kammani*). The root *kapp* means "to cut."

*Ṇvu*. Regarding *naha-soceyye*: due to its derivation from the *div-ādi* group, there is the addition of the letter *pa* and other modifications. Alternatively, one who does not cause to be washed (*na hāpeti*) is called a *nahāpita*. The root *hā* means "to diminish" (*parihāne*).

The suffix *ṇāpe* is applied, followed by *to*, which functions as an affix (*essittaṃ*). Because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), the original form (*pakati*) is lost. *Khurī* and *muṇḍī* are also included here under the *div-ādi* group.

One who possesses a razor (*khura*) is a *khurī*; one who possesses a shaven head (*muṇḍa*) is a *muṇḍī*. The established usage includes *muṇḍo*, *muṇḍī*, and *muṇḍako*. *Divā* means "during the day. *Kitti* [is derived from] *kitteti*.
His occupation is *divākitti*. According to Rudda, "A *caṇḍāla* is a *divākitti*, and a *nahāpita* [is another].

That in which thread becomes dyed (*ratta*) is *raṅga*; it is the yellow orpiment, realgar, and so forth. One who makes a living from that is a *raṅgaja*; the suffix *-ṇa* is used here in the sense of the object.

One who plows (*kasati*) a heap (*puñja*) is a *pukkusa*; this is due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Alternatively, "pu" is a name for a man; one who removes (*apaneti*) him is a *pukkusa*. "Puppha" refers to excrement or a flower; one who discards (*chaḍḍeti*) that is a *pupphachaḍḍaka*; the suffix *-ṇvu* is used. The root *chaḍḍa* means "to remove."
509. The three terms *veṇa*, etc., are identical and have the same meaning. One who lives by means of bamboo is a *veṇa*; the *ṇ* is changed to *n*. *Veṇu* is also [a synonym].
*Vilīva* is a derivative product (*vikati*) of bamboo, rattan, and so forth; one who makes such things is a *vilīvakāra*. *Naḷa* is also a derivative product of bamboo, rattan, and so forth;
one who makes that is a *naḷakāra*, with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the object (*kammani*). Alternatively, one who makes a basket (*vilīva*) from reeds is a *naḷakāra*.

From here onwards, [the suffix] *soṇḍika* up to *pādena* [is explained]. *Cunda* is used in the senses of cutting (*chedana*) and urging (*sañcodana*). Alternatively, *cunda* is used in the sense of perceiving (*nisāmana*).
*Bhamu* is used in the sense of instability; one who performs that is a *bhamakāra*. *Kara* is used in the sense of making (*karaṇa*); thus, *māro*, *kammāro*.

With the suffix *ṇvu* added to the root *kam* (in the sense of action), there is *lohakārako*—a smith. One who heats iron and fashions it, whether it be fashioned from a mine (*ākaroṭṭhita*) or fashioned from a forest (*āṭavoṭṭhita*), is also called a *lohakārako*.
510. A dyer has two tasks: washing cloth and dyeing it. Therein, one who washes cloth is a *ninnejaka*:

from the root *niji* in the sense of cleansing (*suddhi*), or in the sense of purification and cleaning (*soceyya-socana*). One who dyes cloth is a *rajaka*. From the root *ranja* in the sense of coloring (*raṅga*), with the suffix *-ṇvu*.

One who leads (*neti*) is a *nettika*. With the suffix *-ko* in the sense of identity, he is a *nettika*; or alternatively, one who is engaged in a net (*nettiya*) by means of leading water is a *nettika*, [or] in a net (*nettiyā*).
One who leads with a net is called *nettika*; here, *-ika* is the suffix. One who carries water is an *udahāraka*. The suffix *-ka* is added to form a collective noun (*kalopa*).

Because of his habit of playing the lute, he is a *vīṇāvādi*. Because of his application to the craft of playing the lute, he is a *veṇika*. Regarding *usu*, one who works with arrows is an *asukāra* or a carpenter; specifically, an *usuvaḍḍhakī*.
By this, it is shown that the word *vaḍḍhakī* (carpenter) denotes all craftsmen; thus, a goldsmith is a *suvaṇṇavaḍḍhakī*.
The terms *tantavaḍḍhakī* (weaver) and others should also be applied accordingly.
511. One who blows into a flute (*veṇu*) or a bamboo pipe (*vaṃsa*) is a *veṇudhamo*. One whose craft involves the playing of the flute is a *veṇaviko*, with the suffix *-ika*.
One who produces sounds from drums and the like on another person’s body using his own hands is a *pāṇivādo*. One who strikes with the hand is a *pāṇigho*; *pāṇiho* is also correct.
A *pāṇiya* is one whose craft and application involve the selling of living beings (*pāṇi*).
A *pūpiya* is one who lives by means of *pūpa*; that is, one for whom *pūpa* (cakes) is a commodity (*paṇiya*) to be sold. A *suṇḍā* is a tavern; because of a craving for it, one is a *soṇḍā*.

One who sells that is a *soṇḍika*. [The suffix *-ika* is applied] according to Kaccāyana 1.2.18, *nenaniddiṭṭham aniccaṃ*, which prescribes the addition of the suffix *-ka* after a word ending in *-na*.
*Aniccaṃ*: from *paribhāsa*, it means growth (*vuddhi*). He sells liquor according to his nature. Here, there is also the term *maṇḍahāra*;
he carries away (*harati*) or extracts (*uddharati*) the *maṇḍa*, which is the head-portion related to the liquor; thus, he is a *maṇḍahāra*. 512.
Two [meanings] are found in the deceptive act called *indacālakhya*. Because he was employed by the Asura Maya to deceive (*vañcayituṃ*) and move (*calayituṃ*) the gods (*sure*).

This is his *māyā* (illusion); *māya* itself is *sambara*. This belongs to him, thus it is *sambarī*; [the suffix] *ṇī* is applied because it begins with *nadādi*. Both terms refer to a magician (*māyākāra*).

One who is engaged in *indajāla* (sorcery) is an *indajālika*. A miracle-worker (*pāṭihāraka*) is also included. It is called *pāṭihāraka* because one "dispels" (*paṭiharati*) [doubt] by means of this; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is applied. 513.

The commonality of the Noble Ones (*ariyasāmañña*) refers to the meaning of the four [occupations], beginning with the sheep-slaughterer (*orabbhika*). Those who live by killing sheep (*urabbha*) or rams (*eḷaka*) are so called.
Sheep-slaughterers live by killing sheep; pig-slaughterers live by killing pigs; likewise, hunters live by killing deer. Fowlers live by killing birds;
thus they exist according to their respective orders.
(514) Regarding the two types of net-catchers: *vāgurā* is a net for binding deer; one who operates with that is a *vāgurika*, as is a *vākarika*.

*Vaka* means "taking. *Aro*, *ā*, and *vākarā*: one who acts by means of that is a *vākarika*. In the first alternative (*pubbapakkhe*), there is *go* for *ka*, and *assu* [is added], making *vāgurika*.
Two terms refer to a porter: one who carries a burden is a *bhāravāha*; with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the object, it becomes *bhārika*. One who carries a burden is a *bhārika*.
Three terms refer to a servant who lives on wages: one who lives by wages is a *vetanika*. One who is supported by wages is a *bhata*; he is bought by means of wages.
Thus, *bhatako* means "one who is hired," or "one who is conscious" (*saññāyaṃ*). Or, one who consumes (*bhuñjati*) wages (*bhatiṃ*, i.e., remuneration) is a *bhatako*;

it refers to a servant (*ko*), specifically one in a position of authority (*issattaṃ*). One who performs work is a *kammakaro*; he is also called a *kammakāro*. These six terms refer to a slave (*dāse*). One who does something is a *kiṅkaro*, because of his requesting of duties to be performed for his master, thinking, "What shall I do today? (*aham ajja kiṃ karissāmi*).
Or *kiṅkaro*. [The root] *dās* means "to serve. One who serves him is a *dāsa*; the suffix *a* is applied. [The root] *ciṭ* means "to be sent. He is sent by his master, thus he is a *ceṭa*;

the suffix *ṇo* is applied, and the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*), making it *ceṭaka*. [The root] *pis* means "to send"; the suffix *ṇo* is applied, and there is doubling of the consonant *s*.

[The roots] *bhṛ* and *dhṛ* mean "to support" and "to nourish. He is supported, thus he is a *bhacca*. By the rule of splitting the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)—"after *ric*"—the suffix *ricca* is also applied after roots beginning with *bhṛ*, and for *ram*, there is *ranta*.
In the word *rādino*, there is the elision of the *ra* sound, and it becomes *bhacca*. One who serves a master is a *paricāriko*. Also included here are:
*dāsero*, *dāseyyo*, *goppako*, *niyojjo*, and *abhujisso*.

(515) Furthermore, those slaves (*dāsā*) may be of four kinds, according to whether they were born in the house and so forth. One born from the womb of a female slave within the household is an *antojāto*.

One who has been purchased for wealth is "bought with wealth" (*dhanakkīta*); one who has entered into servitude by giving wealth is likewise "bought with wealth. One who has entered into servitude of his own accord for the purpose of warding off fear and so forth is "one who has approached servitude" (*dāsabyopagata*);
and one who has been brought there in the capacity of a convict is "brought as a convict" (*karamarānīta*). Thus, it is established that these slaves are of four kinds. 516. *Dvayaṃ bhujisse*:

The root *bhuj* means "to protect" and "to consume"; *isa* is a suffix; the doubling [of the consonant] occurs. *Tikaṃ nīce*: "Low" (*nīca*) means "one who gathers what is inferior" (*nihīnaṃ cinoti*).
Low, no; the lengthening of a short vowel. In the root *jam* (to eat), [it becomes] *mo*. One who certainly goes to ruin is a *nihīnaka*;
from the root *hā* (in declining) and *i* (in going), with the suffixes *yu* and *ko* in the sense of agency.
“The low person is discolored, wicked, despicable, and a worldling (*puthujjana*).”
“Base, low-born, vulgar, insignificant, and the opposite of that.
(Amarakosa 20.16) One whose complexion has departed is "vivaṇṇa. Regarding the word *assama*: "The term *assama* refers to a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārin*) and so forth;

it applies both to a group of four and to a monastery (*maṭha*)," according to the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*. One who delights in evil is a *pāpara*. In its primary sense, it refers to the state of being as one was born.
Existence (*bhava*) exists, but activity (*byāpāra*) does not—this is established; no. A person who has become separate from the virtuous (*sajjana*) is a worldling (*puthujjana*).
One who sounds or goes away from the center is a marginal person (*apasada*). One who takes hunger is a glutton (*khulla*); for *lo* is the substitute for *da*, thus *khulla* itself is *khullaka*.
One who takes what is shaken or moved is "the other" (*itara*).

The pair [of terms] refers to one who is not indolent (*anālase*). Laziness (*kosajja*) is the state of being idle (*kusīta*); one who has no such thing is "free from laziness" (*nikkosajjo*). The root *las* means "to desire. One who desires little is "lazy" (*kilāsu*); the suffix *ṇu* is added. One who does not desire is "non-lazy" (*akilāsu*). The root *mand* means "to sleep"; the suffix *a* is added.

One who does not exert himself or play is "indolent" (*alaso*). 517. The group of four refers to the outcaste (*caṇḍāla*). One who cooks dogs is a "dog-cooker" (*sapāka*). *Caṇḍa* means "fierceness," with the suffix *ālo*. A descendant of Mataṅga is a "Mātaṅga. The root *cu* means "to fall away," with the suffix *ṇvu*, forming *cavaka*. There is also a reading "plavaka"; the root *plava* means "to move," with the suffix *ṇvu*.
