"The outcastes, the plavakas, the Mātaṅgas, the Divākittis, the Janaṅgamas;..."
“Nisādas, apacāntas, and those dwelling at the edge [of society], Caṇḍālas, and Pukkusas.”—thus in the Amarakośa, 20.19–20.
The Milakkha-jātis (outcaste tribes) and so forth, who dwell in the great forests, are sub-divisions of that Caṇḍāla; they are his specific types.
But he who eats the flesh of goats and speaks that which is outside the world—
this man is devoid of all proper conduct.
The "Milakkhajāti" (the race of the Milakkhas) refers to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 20.20.

[The term] *milakkha* is used in the sense of indistinct sound. They are called *milakkhā* because they speak indistinctly (*abyattaṃ bhāsanti*) at the end of their speech; their birth or origin (*jāti yoni*) is therefore *milakkhajāti*.
A Kirāta is one who wears peacock feathers and the like. The root *kira* means "to scatter"; thus, he is a *kirāta* because he scatters [his ornaments].
*Kirāta* means a hunter. A *savara* is one who wears leaves as clothing. An *aroha* is one who moves through all states of existence (*sabbagati*). By such terms as these, one refers to a *pulinda*.
The root *pula* has the sense of "greatness"; with the suffix *-da*, it becomes *pulinda*. Some say that a *pulinda* is one who speaks his own dialect but does not understand foreign languages;

*pulinda* is a synonym for *savara*. (518–519) This triad refers to those who are merely hunters. This too is a type of barbarian (*milakkha*), so called because they slaughter and kill deer, fish, and other creatures.
*Nesāda*: from the root *ludh* (to strike), with the suffix *do*; or from *lū* (to cut), with the suffix *do*; in both cases, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of the same meaning (*sakatthe*).

One who pierces is a *byādha*; this is a lengthening of the short vowel. Both terms refer to a deer-hunter (*migaludda*). One who kills deer is a *migava*, with the suffix *vo*. One who pierces deer is a *migabyādha*.

*Sunakha* means a dog. *Saramā* is heard; its offspring is *sārameyyo*, which is to be understood [as such]. His beautiful claw (*nakha*) is a *sunakha*; or else, it is the claw (*unakha*) of a dog (*suna*).

Or, *suna* is in the sense of "going" (*gati*). Thus, in all cases, the derivation of the form should be understood either by way of a derivative suffix (*pāṭipadika*) or by way of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
*Suna* is in the sense of "going," or the claw (*uno*) of a dog (*suna*). *Soṇa* is in the senses of color (*vaṇṇa*) and going (*gati*).
*Sun* in the sense of "going": *ṇo*, *ṇattaṃ*, *sunassa vā oṇo*. *Kuk* in the sense of "taking": *uro*, *kukkuro*. *Sun* in the sense of "going":
with the substitution of *ussa*, *svāno*; with the substitution of *uva*, *suvāno*. That which remembers (or kills) deer is *sāḷūro*: *ūro*, with the substitution of *ḷo* for *ra*.

In words beginning with a long vowel, *sūno*. With the suffix *ussātta*, *sāno*. When there is elision of *na* and the suffix *ussātta*, *sā*; this is masculine: *koleyyo*, *migadaṃsako*; *bhasako* is also used here.
One born in a family or household is *koleyya*. One who bites deer is a *migadaṃsaka*. One that barks or howls is a *bhasaka* (the root *bhas* meaning "to speak").
A dog that has become insane through the use of medicine and the like, or through natural disposition, is called an *aḷakka* or an *atisuna*.

[The derivation is: from the root *ala* in the sense of "obstructing," with the suffix *ṇvu* in the sense of an object; due to the doubling of the consonant and the shortening of the vowel, it becomes *aḷakka*. *Alakkha* is also used. An *atisuna* is a dog that has exceeded its normal nature.
520. *Sādibandhanaṃ* means a leash for dogs and the like, such as ropes; it is called *gaddūla*. [The root] *gad* means "to sound," with the suffixes *ula* and a long vowel.

There are two [derivations] for a lamp. From *dīpa* in the sense of "shining," with the suffix *ṇvu*; from *ciṭ* in the sense of "sending," one who is sent by a hunter is a *ceṭaka*, with the suffix *ṇo*, the pleonastic suffix *ko*, or established by the suffix *ṇvu*.
The triad refers to the snare (*pāsa*). *Bandh* means "to bind"; the suffix *yu* is used in the sense of the agent. *Ganth* means "to tie" or, alternatively, "to coil";
here, the *nth* becomes *ṇṭh*. *Pas* means "to press" or "to touch"; the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the agent. The dyad refers to the deer-cage (*vākarā*);

that which is made from hemp, bark, and so forth for the purpose of binding deer and other animals. *Vak* means "to take up"; with the suffix *aro*, and in the feminine, the suffix *ā* is added after *a*. It is called a "deer-tie" (*migaganthanī*) because it ties or binds the deer.
“*Migabandhanī*” is also a reading. 521.
There are two types of *kumīna*. That into which fish enter but do not emerge is a *kuveṇī*, such as a net (*nadādi*)—so called because it is a wretched braid (*kucchitā veṇī*).
A *kumīna* is that in which fish have reached a state of being condemned; or, from the root *kam* (to step) with the suffix *-īna*.
*Macchādhānī*: that in which fish are placed is *macchādhānī*; [the suffix] *yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* group. Two terms for a net:
it is called *ānayo* because they are brought (*ānīyante*) by means of it; [the suffix] *ṇo*, with *ī* changed to *e*. That which is placed in water is *jālaṃ*;
[the suffix] *ṇa*. Two terms for a place of execution: it is called *āghātanaṃ* because they come and kill there; [the suffix] *yu*, and *han* becomes *ghāta*. [The suffix] *va* is used for killing.

*Marana-ṭṭhānaṃ* means a place of execution, a place of killing. *Dvayaṃ* refers to two things: *adhikoṭṭane*. Because of constant pounding (*ākoṭṭanattā*), together with the prefix *sa-* (meaning "with") and the root *ūna-* ("deficient"), it is *sūnā*;

or, from the root *suna* meaning "to go," with the suffix *a*, and lengthening of the initial vowel, etc., it becomes *sūnā*. From the root *kuṭa* meaning "to cut," that in which they are pounded excessively is *adhikoṭṭanaṃ*.
522. *Dvipādaṃ* refers to a thief. One who does that is a *takkara*; or, one who suspects (*takkeyati*) for the purpose of theft is a *takkara*. *Takka-*...

In *vitakke*, [the suffix] *aro* [is applied]. In *mosa* and *theyya*, [the suffix] *ṇvu* [is applied]. In *cura* and *theyya*, [the suffix] *ṇo* [is applied]; or, one whose nature (*sīla*) is theft is a thief (*coro*), [formed with] *ṇo*.
In *thena* and *coriya*, [the suffix] *curādi-a* [is applied]. A single house, that is, a dwelling without a companion, is an "isolated house" (*ekāgāra*);

one for whom that is the purpose is an "isolated-house dweller" (*ekāgāriko*), [formed with] *iko*. For indeed, an isolated house is the purpose of one intent on theft (*mosatthi*). *Samā* has the sense of equality. *Dassu* is also used here.

*Daṃsa* (to bite) [is used here]; there is the elision of the *niggahīta*. This triad refers to the act of stealing. Stealing (*theyya*) is the action of a thief (*thena*); thievery (*corikā*) is the action of a robber (*cora*). Deceit (*moso*) is the act of lying (*musana*); the suffix *-no* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). *Ve* (to weave) [is used]; *vema* is not feminine. A loom for weaving (*vāyanadaṇḍaka*) has the sense of weaving; it is also called a *vāsaradaṇḍaka*. 523.
This triad refers to thread (*sutta*). *Suca* (to go) [is used]; the suffix *-to*. *Tanu* (to expand); the suffix *-tu*; *tantu* is masculine, because it serves as the basis for weaving.

*Tantaṃ*. In the sense of "plastering work" (*lepyādikamma*), the word *pottha* refers to the act of plastering and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), writing works such as booklets (*potthalika*) are included.

[The root] *pus* is used in the senses of "anointing," "pouring," and "filling"; the suffix *tha* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*). Alternatively, in the sense of "plastering work," where the work itself is the object (*kammakāraka*), the word *pottha* refers to that which is to be plastered;
in this case, *tha* is added in the sense of the object (*kammani*), resulting in *potthaṃ*.
The pair beginning with *pañcālikā* refers to cloth, tooth-sticks, horns, and stuffed dolls (*potthalikā*). It is called *pañcālikā* because it possesses five limbs (*pañca-aṅga*) while still alive;
the suffix *-ika* is added, with the letter *l* inserted in the middle. It is called *potthalikā* because it is adorned with cloth (*potta*);
from the root *ala* (to adorn), the suffix *-ṇvu* is applied. In the passage, "Four people took up the cloth (*potthaka*)," the word *potthaka* refers to cloth.
Indeed, the word *pottha* itself is called “*potthaka*” by means of the suffix *-ka* added in its own sense. There is also the reading “*puttalikā*”;
it is called a “doll” (*puttalikā*) because it is decorated like a son (*putta*), and here *puttikā* is also used.
524. That which is the drawing out or extraction of water from a well or a pit is called “*ugghāṭanaṃ*.”
It is also called "ghaṭīyantaṃ. It is "ugghāṭanaṃ" because water is drawn up (uddhaṃ ghaṭīyati udakaṃ); [the suffix] -yu is used. This word "ghaṭa" is the same as "ghaṭī";
it is "ghaṭīyantaṃ" because of its movement by way of going upwards and downwards; [the suffix] -anto or -to is used in the sense of reaching a state of motion.

There are two types of "mañjusā," that which is made of wood and that which is made of bamboo. "Mana" means knowledge; [the suffix] -so is used; "jumajjho" is the "jūka" of a wise man (from the ṇvādi group).

215) This should also be seen in the *Uṇādivutti* (4.77): *pela* in the sense of going (*gati*), or in the sense of protecting (*pālane*); with the suffix *lo*, there is the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*, resulting in *peḷā*. *Pala* in the sense of guarding (*rakkhaṇe*);

with the suffix *a* in the agentive sense (*kattari*), there is the substitution of *assa*, resulting in *peḷā*. A triad [of these] refers to a basket (*pacchiya*). *Piṭa* in the sense of collecting (*saṅghāte*); with the suffix *ṇvu*, *piṭaka*;
in the sense of growth (*vuddhimhi*), *peṭaka*. *Pasa* in the sense of protecting (*pālane*); with the suffix *chi*, *pacchi*, in the feminine (*itthiyaṃ*).
525. *Dvayaṃ kāje*. That in which various burdens (*bhāra*) are broken (*ābhañjanti*) or suspended is called *byābhaṅgī*. [The root] *kaj* means "to weave" (*byadhana*);
with the suffix *ṇo*, there is the elision of one *j*, and with *kaca* meaning "binding" (*bandhana*), or with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), *ca* becomes *ja*, thus *kājo*;

*kāco* also exists. Here, the suspension in the *kāja* is what is known as a *sikkā*, a contrivance made of cane and the like. [The root] *sak* means "power" (*sattiyaṃ*); with the suffix *ko* in the sense of agent (*kattari*), and with the penultimate vowel lengthened (*upāntassi*), it is *sikkā*; *kājo* also exists.
Regarding the word *upāhana*: it is called *upāhana* because one is bound (*upanayhati*) or fastened to it;

there is a reversal of the vowel quality (*vaṇṇavipariyāsa*), the short vowel becoming long, and [the form] *upāhanaṃ* is derived with the suffix *-ka*. That by which one walks is a *pādu*; the suffix *-u* is feminine, as in *pādu*.

According to the *Tikaṇḍasesa* (2.10.13): "The words *pannaddhī*, *pādukā*, *pāṇihitā*, and *padarathī* [are synonyms]. Its varieties (*tabbhedā*) are the specific types of that *upāhana*, namely *pādukā*.
In the sense of "going" (*gamana*), with the suffix *ṇuka*, there is *pādukā* (shoe/sandal);

it has many layers and is made of leather, though some say it is made of wood. [This concludes] the triad regarding the leather thong (*cammarajju*). The root *vara* is used in the sense of desire (*icchā*) or restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*);

from that, by means of the suffixes *cha* and others, we have *varattā*, *varattaṃ*, *varatrā*, and *varatram*. The root *vaddha* means "to increase"; with the suffix *ka* in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*), there is *vaddhikā*. It is called *nayha* because it is bound (*bandhīyate*).
*Yāya naddhī*: from the root *naha*, meaning "to bind," with the suffix *to*; it belongs to the *nadādi* group. *Dvayaṃ aggidīpane*: there are two [roots] for the kindling of fire.

From *bhasa*, in the sense of "shining" (*bhāsa-dittīsu*), that by which fire is blown is *bhastā*. With the suffix *to*, it is *bhastrā* in the sense of "a bellows. Because it belongs to the *nadādi* class, which is an open-ended group (*ākati-gaṇa*), there is no application of the suffix *ī*. *A cammamayaṃ pasibbakaṃ*: a bag made of leather is a *cammapasibbaka*; it is also called *cammapasibbakā*. *Tejase suvaṇṇādike āvatyate yatra*:
that in which gold and other such things are placed is called a crucible (*mūsā*), such as a crucible for gold and so forth. From *musa*, in the sense of "stealing" (*theyye*), with the suffix *a*.

*Mūsā*, beginning with *dīgha*. From *kala* onwards up to *pāda*, it is a name (*nāma*). *Kuṭa* in the sense of cutting; a noun formed by the instrumentive case (*karaṇasādhana*), *kūṭa*, beginning with *dīgha*;
by means of the vowel *vā*, it becomes *kūṭo*. A solid mass of iron, or made of iron, is *ayoghana*.
(527) The tools of smiths are *kammārabhaṇḍa*. It bites together (*saṅgamma ḍaṃsati*), thus *saṇḍāso*; [the suffix] *ṇo*, with the elision of the *niggahīta*.
*Saṇḍāsa*: that by which iron and so forth are grasped. *Dvayaṃ*: the two [terms] for the lower part, namely *ayoghana*.
*Muda*: in the sense of contact; *mudatthi*, *muṭṭhi*, *itthī*. *Adhikaraṇī*: that in which one performs work (*adhikaroti*), with the suffix *-ī*;
belonging to the *nada*-class. *Tabbhastā*: the bellows (*bhastā*) of those smiths used for kindling the fire, called *gaggarī*, which is also termed "a torch" (*ukkā*).

And that woman is called *gaggarī* because she makes the sound "gagga"; it also refers to a churning vessel. Both [terms] are in the Minor Collection (*Khuddaka-saṃhitā*). The root *sas* means to injure;
with the suffix *tha*, it becomes *pipphalaṃ*, as it splits even what is dear; the root *phal* means to split. 528. There are two [terms] for *nikasa*. The root *sā* means to make thin;
with the suffix *yu* and the lengthening of the vowel, it is *nikasa*; gold is tested or examined by it, thus it is *nikasa*.
*Kaso pi*. Regarding *sūcī*: *nāsāvijjhanam* (piercing with a needle); *ārā* means "going" (*ara gamane*); *ārā* also refers to the awl used by leather-workers for piercing hides.
Some say, "The triad [of *ārā*, *sūcī*, and *kaso*] refers to the needle.

Regarding the pair [of terms] for a coarse leaf: it is called *khara* because of its rough touch (*kharasamphassatāya*). It is called *kakaca* because it cuts or tears (*kacati pāṭayati*); it is not feminine.

“*Kakacaṃ* and *kharapattaṃ*” is found in the neuter section of the *Amaramālā*. In the treatises of Vacchāyana, the sixty-four arts such as singing and so forth are called “external arts” (*bāhirā kalā*), while the sixty-four internal arts such as embracing, kissing, and so forth are called by the term “arts” (*kalā*).
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), whatever manual labor (*kārukamma*) is mentioned therein is included; all that work, beginning with the arts, is “action” (*kriyā*).
*Sippa* means: *sī* in the sense of lying down (*saye*), *po* in the sense of moving (*gamane*), and *sappa* in the sense of approaching (*upāntassi*);

thus, *sippa*. 529–530. That which is made as a likeness (*paṭisadisa*) by means of stone and so forth, there is the tetrad beginning with *paṭimā*. From the root *mā* in the sense of measuring (*māne*), here the measuring consists of making something similar;
with the suffix *a* applied to the agent (*kattari*) or the instrument (*karaṇe*), we have *paṭimā*, as in "the statue" (*nārī*). From the root *vam* in the sense of vomiting (*uggiraṇe*).

*Bo*, *ittaṃ*, *paṭibimbaṃ*. [The root] *dhā* means "to hold"; with the suffix *i*, it becomes *paṭinidhi* (a counterpart). In two senses: *paṭimānaṃ*, *paṭiyātanā*, *paṭicchāyā*, and *paṭikatippatra*. *Pajjaṃ* is used in the sense of "similar.
In that context, *sama* and its derivatives function even when standing alone in the three genders (*tisu*), and they also occur in the sense of "similarity.

Furthermore, the three [suffixes] at the end—namely *-sannikāsa*, *-sama*, and *-sadisa*—function as subsequent members of a compound (*uttarapadībhūta*). For example: *tena samo’yaṃ* ("this is equal to that"), *taṃsamo’yaṃ* ("this is equal to that"), *taṃsamamidaṃ* ("this is equal to that").
In phrases such as *taṃsannikāso* (“resembling him”), these terms beginning with *nibha* and others are used only as final members of a compound;

they express similarity and follow the gender of the word they qualify (*vāccaliṅga*), as in: “a son resembling his father,” “a maiden resembling her mother,” and “a face resembling a god” (*devanibham-ānanam*).

(Byākhyāsudhā 2.10.37). *Sama* [is used] in the sense of *velamba*. That which partakes of a likeness is *paṭibhāga*; [the suffix] *ṇo* [is added]. [The root] *kāsa* means “splendor,” [with the suffix] *a*, [forming] *sannikāsa*.

He is called *sarikkhaka* because he is seen as if equal (*samānamiva naṃ dissati*). [The derivation is: from *samāna*, the suffix *ri*; for *sa*, there is *kkha*; the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). Thus, *sarikkhaka*.
Alternatively, *samāna* is derived from *sama* with the suffix *velambe* (i.e., *yu*), making it *samāna*; or, it is *samāna* because it possesses measure (*saha mānena*).

One who sees him by making him equal is called *sadisa*; this is from *samāna* with the suffix *sa*. It is measured (*sammita*) and delimited (*paricchinna*) by a similar determination (*tulyādhiṭṭhitāya*) which has the common property of delimitation (*paricchedasadhammā*).
*Tulya* means "equal" (*sammita*); *tulā* is also used in the sense of an affixless form. *Bhā* means "splendor"; *sannibha* and *nibha* [are derived from it].
*Bhūta* refers here to forms and so forth, as in *pitubhūto* ("like a father") and *māturūpo* ("like a mother").

This triad [of suffixes] is used in the sense of comparison (*upamāna*). That by which something is compared is *opamma*; *mana* preceded by *upa* means "to measure," and with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *upamāna*.

The term *itthiyamati* (the notion of "woman") is an *a*-affix. Furthermore, this [simile] occurs even when the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameyya*) possess the same characteristic;

as stated in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, verse 176: "A simile may exist when there is a common characteristic between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison. And Amarasimha says in the *Vyākhyāsudhā* 2.10.36:
"In those cases where that by which something is compared and that which is compared are present, there is also the threefold nature of the simile (*aupamya*)."

531. Regarding the group of four beginning with *vetana*: that by which one supports laborers is *bhṛti* (wages). [The root] *viṣ* means "to cause to go"; "causing to go" (*peraṇa*) is the directing toward movement and so forth;

the suffix *-ṇa* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), and there is also the form *nibbisa*, as well as *nivesa*. [The root] *vī* means "to go," and [the suffix] *-tana* is added. That which is connected with the capital (*mūla*) is *mūlya* (price);
or [it is derived from] *mūla* in the sense of "establishment," with the suffix *-ya* in the sense of the instrument.
“*Kammaññā*, *vidhā*, *bhaccā*, *bhattaya*, *bhamma-vetanaṃ*;
*bharaṇyaṃ*, *bharaṇaṃ*, *mūlyaṃ*, *nibbeso*, *paṇa-micca-pī*.
— Amarasīha, Amarakosa 20.38–9.

*Dvayaṃ jūte*: *Ju* in the senses of going and hastening; with the suffix *to*, and lengthening of the initial vowel, *jūtaṃ*; or *juta* in the sense of shining, with the suffix *a* in the instrumental sense.

*Ketavaṃ* is the work of a gambler (*kitava*) or a dealer (*jūtakāra*), with the suffix *ṇo*. *Akkhavatī* (the gambling hall) and *paṇo* (the stake) are also included here. Because the dice (*akkhā*)—meaning the gaming pieces—exist as its means (*upāyatthena*), [it is called] *akkhavatī*, with the suffix *vantu*;
this is feminine by its very nature. *Paṇo* is the wager (*aṭṭo*); because of its connection with that, it is called *paṇo*.

The group of five [suffixes] applies to the word *jūtaka* (“gambler”). *Dhāvantī* becomes *dhutti* by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātanā*); through connection with that, one is called *dhutta*. Alternatively, from the root *dhū* meaning “to shake,” with the suffix *to*, there is shortening, resulting in *dhutta*.
This term also applies to one who is addicted to all kinds of games. One who is addicted to dice is an *akkhadhutta*.

For one who transgresses the bounds of propriety and is addicted to games is called a “debaucher” (*dhutta*). One who desires gambling (*kitava*) is a *kitava*; this is by way of a grammatical irregularity. From the root *kita* meaning “to dwell.”
Or *avo*. One who plays with dice for sport is an *akkhadevī* (dice-player);

[the suffix] *ṇī*. 532. There are two [terms] for a guarantor (*pāṭibhoga*). One who stands as a surety (*paṭibhuñjati*) and protects is a *pāṭibhoga*; from the root *bhuja* in the sense of protecting, [the suffix] *ṇo*. One who stands as a counterpart (*paṭibhavati*) is a *paṭibhū*.
There are two [types of] twenty-four-sided dice (*pāsaka*), by which gamblers play; [the root] *aka* in the sense of crooked movement.

*Akho*, *akkho*. [The suffix] *ṇvu* is applied after the root *pasa* (to throw) when combined with the prefix *bādhanaphusana-*. *Devano* is also used here. It is called *devano* because one plays (*divyanti*) by means of it;

from the root *divu* (to play), [the suffix] *yu*. *Aṭṭhāpadaṃ* refers to the game-board (*sāraphalaka*). It is masculine or neuter; it is called *aṭṭhāpadaṃ* because it has eight squares (*aṭṭha-padāni*).

For in other regions, even the game of *pāsaka-jūta* (dice and board) is played on the same strip as *caturaṅga* (chess). [This is] a technical name (*saññā*), where the word *aṭṭha* occurs in the subsequent member of the compound.
The lengthening of a short vowel [occurs] according to Pāṇini 6.3.125. There is also the word *aṭṭhapada*. They move and turn back and forth upon the board;
thus they are *sārino*. Their board is a *sāriphalaka*; the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*).

The pair [of terms] refers to something marvelous (*abbhuta*), by means of which victory or defeat for the players and others occurs through the acquisition of hundreds and so forth. From the root *paṇ* in the sense of "transaction," with the suffix *a*, we have *paṇo*; *pano* is also used. From the root *abbha* in the sense of "going" or the prefix *abhi* in the sense of "sound," with the suffix *to*, there is *abbhato*; alternatively, due to the irregularity of vowel substitution (*asarūpadvitta*), there is also *abbhato*.

533. *Kiṇṇa* refers to liquor made from various substances that serve as the seeds of intoxication (*madirābīja*). It is so called because various substances are scattered (*kiranti*) and mixed therein.
In the case of honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*), the intoxicant made from *madhuka* flowers is considered "honey" (*madhu*).

The *madhuka* flower is honey; it is called "honey" because it is produced from that. Even when the intoxicant is made from *madhuka*, it is called "honey," such as *madhvāsava*, *mādhavaka*, and *mādhvika*; these are three names for the same thing.

*Surāntam majje*: *mada* (intoxication) and *ummāda* (insanity) [are the meanings]; *ira* is the suffix in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). A certain person named Varuṇa [first saw it], and because it was first seen by him, it is called *vāruṇī*;
or, from *vara* (in the sense of "longing for," *patthanāyaṃ*), with the suffix *yu* in the sense of the object (*kamme*), [forming] *assu*, [belonging to the class] beginning with *nada*.

That by which they intoxicate is *majjaṃ*; [the suffix] *ya* is used after *vajādi* [roots], and *jja* replaces *dy* [of *mad*]. *Su* (in the sense of "pressing," *abhisave*) and *ra*; or, *su* (in the sense of "excellent pressing," *suvane*), [forming] *surā*. [It is also called] *halippiyā*.
Hālā, Gandhottamā, Pasannā, Irā, and Kādambarī are also [names for this liquor]. It is "Halippiyā" because it is dear to Halin, that is, Balabhadra.
From the root *hala* (to plow) with the suffix *ṇo*, we have *hālā*. From *i* (to go) with the suffix *ro*, we have *irā*. First, regarding *kādambarī*:
it is that which exists in a *kadamba* hollow on Mount Gomandha; thus the scripture says: "Born in a *kadamba* hollow, therefore it is considered *kādambarī*."

*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 20.39: The pair [of intoxicants] arises from the juice of palm trees and so forth. It is called *āsava* because through it pride, human intoxication, and the like flow out (*āsavanti*). It is called *meraya* because it produces intoxication (*madaṃ janeti*); the suffix *-eya* is to be understood here, with the substitution of *ro* for *da*. *Sīdhu* is also included herein. They say these three terms are used even for specific types of *majja* (fermented liquor), and it is said:
"When the juice of sugarcane is fermented, it is *sīdhu*; when unfermented, it is *āsava*."
"Meraya is [fermented] from *dhātakī* flowers, sugar, grain, and sour gruel," according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (20.42) and the *Vyākhyāsudhā* (2.10.41).

534. Two terms for a drinking vessel: *saraka*. From the root *sṛ*, with the suffix *ṇvu*; or from *sṛ* in the sense of movement, injury, or thought. From *cas* in the sense of eating, with the suffix *ṇvu*;

both are neuter. *Sarako* also refers to *sīdhu* (a type of liquor). Two terms for a drinking circle (*āpāna*): *āpāna*. They drink together in this place; hence *āpāna*, with the suffix *yu*. A drinking circle is a storage area for drinks; thus, *pānamaṇḍala*.

535. By means of the inclusion of all genders (*samattaliṅgasaṅgaha*), one avoids incompleteness. Here, in this section, those masculine nouns—such as *yogika*, *sadda*, *aveṇika*, *māyākāra*, *cora*, *akkha*, *devī*, and so forth—which are spoken of or stated in the masculine gender because of their frequent usage and because they are seen to have abundant application in that single gender, [are included].

Due to their possessing those same properties (*taddhammattā*), by virtue of that connection (*taṃyogavasā*), and because they perform the same function (*ekakriyākārittā*), when there is a different grammatical behavior (*aññavutti*)—that is, when there is a behavior other than that [masculine] in the feminine and so on—[the same forms apply].

It is true that even when the gender is different, [the word] should be understood and applied even from the feminine gender; for example: "a female illusionist" (*māyākārī itthī*), "this family of illusionists" (*māyākāramidaṃ kulaṃ*), and so forth.

However, those such as the Māgadha, the Mālika, and the Kumbhakāra, who do not possess [the quality] as a defining characteristic, belong to two genders because they are words denoting a caste (*jāti*), just like the word *sudda* and others.
The commentary on the *Suddavagga* is concluded.
The commentary on the Catubbaṇṇavagga is completed.
5. Commentary on the Araññavagga 536.

The group of seven [verses] concerns the forest (*vana*). [The root] *ara* means "to go"; hence *arañña*. Why? Because it is not traversed by the water of passion; thus it is a forest (*kānana*) for living beings.
The root *dā* means to break or to cut. With the suffix *ṇa*, [it forms] *dāya*; by the rule "for roots ending in long *ā*, [the suffix] *āya*," it becomes *dāya*.

The root *day* means giving, going, or seizing; with the suffix *ṇa*, it becomes *deya*. The root *gah* means grasping, and *gāh* means stirring; with the suffix *yu* in the locative sense (adhikaraṇe), it becomes *gāhya*.

The root *vap* means sowing seeds; with the suffix *ina*, it becomes *vāpina*. The root *van* means to acquire or sound; with the suffix *a* in the agentive sense (kattari), it becomes *vanaṃ*. Since there are mountain ranges (*aṭā*) as parts (*avayava*) here, it is *aṭavi*; with the suffix *i* or *ī*, it becomes *aṭavī*.
The Mahāpadumalatā forest, the great wilderness (mahārañña), the rivers and so forth, and the boundless [spaces]—these are the forests (araññāni).
537. Not too far from the city, there is a grove of trees planted by virtuous people, a collection of trees such as the *pūga* and *panasa*;
that is called an "upavana" (park), and this is the Kittima Forest. That in which one finds delight is an "ārāma"; [the suffix] -ṇo [is added]. It is approached (upagataṃ).
A planted grove or park (upavana). 538.

That which is common to all, a shared enjoyment for all people in the world—the forest (arañña) belonging to kings and rulers—is called an "upavana" or "uyyāna. It is called *uyyāna* because people go there looking up [at it] (*ullokentā yanti etasmiṃ*); the prefix *yu-* is used here. Furthermore, the word *ākīḷā* (pleasure-ground) is also used here.

That very royal park (*rājopavana*) situated near the auxiliary buildings (*upakārikā*), or situated in front, is that which is filled with the inner apartments (*antepura*) and is known as the "Pamadavana" (the pleasure-grove of women).
Where the king dwells together with his harem, there is no entry for other people. A grove for wanton women is a *pamadavana*; [the word] is short. 539–540.

A row with intervals between is, for example, a *tarupanti* (row of trees) or a *pāsādapanti* (row of palaces); however, one without intervals is a *rājī* (line). In that context, the group of five [words] refers to a row (*paṅkti*).
The root *pan* is used in the sense of conventional usage and praise; thus, *paṅkti*. The root *vī* is used in the sense of going; with the suffix *thi*, it becomes *vīthi* (street/way).

*Vala* (in the sense of covering) takes *i*, forming *āvali*. From the root *āla* (to smear), *i* is added, forming *ālapi*. *Si* (in the sense of service) takes *ṇi*, forming *seṇi*. *Pā* (in the sense of protecting) takes *ḷi*, forming *pāḷi*, which is also used in the Sogata (Buddhist) tradition;
these two are identical. *Likha* (in the sense of writing) takes *a*, forming *lekha*. *Rāja* (in the sense of shining) takes *i*, forming *rājī*. A three-footed tree is called *rukkhamatta*.
That which drinks with its foot—that is, its root—is a *pādapa*; [the suffix] *ṇo* is added. From the connection with *viṭapa* (branch), it becomes *viṭapī*. [This refers to] a tree.
In *varaṇa* (obstructing), *a*; in *ruha* (to grow) or *janana* (producing), *kho*, [with] *hassa ko*. "It does not go" (*na gacchati*) is *ago*. In *sala* (going), *ṇo*;

or because of its essence (*sāra*), it is *sāra*; that itself is *sāla*, except through metaphorical usage. "It grows on the earth" (*mahiyam ruhati*), *a*. In *du* (going), *mo*. In *tara* (crossing over), *u*.
From which ground it is born is *kuja* (tree), also used for charcoal. Because of its connection with branches, it is *sākhī* (branching).
*Gamana* means going; *ṇo* is [the suffix] in the sense of "one who will go" or "in all seasons. A small tree that has not reached maturity is a *khuddapādapa*.
Those trees which bear fruit without flowers—such as the *assattha*, *udumbara*, *panasa*, and so forth—are called *vanappati*;
they are the lords (*pati*) of the forests (*vana*). However, those such as the mango and the date palm, whose fruit is produced from flowers, [are not].
“Vānappatayo. Those that exist in a forest-tree (*vanappati*) are *vānappatayo*. 541.

That which dies at the conclusion of the ripening of its fruit—such as the plantain, grain, and so forth—is called an *osadhi*. [Regarding the term *osadhi*: it is that in which one rests (*oso dhīyate yassam*);

*oso* is a synonym for *gloso*; it is here that splendor (*ditti*) is deposited, like clarified butter (*byākhyāsudhā*). That is an *osadhi*. Here, the word *osa-* is a substitute for the word *osadhi-*.
The feminine gender indicator [is as follows]:

*dvayaṃ* (both) [are used] even when arising from the seasons and when devoid of fruit. *Vana* means "requesting"; *vañjhā* [is derived thus]: she either bears (*vadhati*) or does not bear fruit (*na phalati*), hence *vañjhā*;
[the substitution of] *ya* for *ja* occurs, and the *jha* becomes *jha*, with the elision of the *niggahīta*. She whose fruit does not exist is *aphalā*; these two [forms].

In three [cases]. The triad [applies] to a tree, etc., when the fruit is present. From the root *phal* (to bear fruit), the suffixes *-ina*, *-vantu*, and *-ī* are added. 542. The tetrad [applies] to that which has blossomed.

From *phull* (in the sense of blossoming), the suffix *-ta* is added in the agentive sense, or the suffix *-ita* is added in the sense of "having arisen," or alternatively from *phal* (in the sense of spreading);

spreading is blossoming; thus *phulla*. From *kac* (in the sense of binding), preceded by the prefix *vi-* (in the sense of blossoming), the suffix *-a* is added in the agentive sense. It blossoms (*vikacate*).

It is called *vikaca* because it splits open (*vidalati*) or its petals become separated (*visiliṭṭhadala*). Here, the prefix *vi-* indicates separation (*visilesa*). The root *kas-* means "to go," with the suffix *-ta*.

Because the collection [of petals] has become separated from one another, it is called "opened" (*vikasita*). The word *phuṭa* also applies here; *phuṭa* means "to expand. The term *pāda* refers to the top of a tree.
According to the statement of Vopālita, "The words *nā*, *agga*, *sikhara*, and *sira* [are synonyms]," [the phrase] "the top of the head" (*sirassa agga*) is not [the intended meaning].
This is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). *Sira* means "head. *Aja* means "going"; *go* means "foremost" or "best" in three senses; *sī* means "to lie down," as in *kharasī* (a donkey);

or it refers to a crest or tuft (*cūḷā*), and because it is born like that, it is called *sikharo*. There are two meanings for *sākhā*: *sākha* means "to extend," with the suffix *a*. Regarding *latā*, it is said:

"The creeper (*vallī*) is fully described as *latā*; the branch (*sākhā*) is also [called] *sākhin*. Thus, *latā* has various meanings. *Lā* means "to take," with the suffix *to*, and the vowel is shortened.

543. *Chakkaṃ patte*. It is called *dala* because it splits (*dalati*) or expands; from the root *da*, with the suffix *a*. From *lasa* in the sense of shining, that which shines in a particular way is *palāsa*; with the suffix *ṇo*.
From *chada* in the sense of covering, that by which something is covered is *chadana*; with the suffix *yu*. It is called *paṇṇa* because it fills (*pūrayati*);

this is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or alternatively, from *pata* in the sense of going downwards: it falls before long, hence *paṇṇa*; and *patta* also, with the suffix *to*, in the masculine. In the sense of a designation, *chado* occurs with the suffix *ṇam*.

The pair [of terms] refers to the node on a branch possessing a cluster of leaves and so forth. From the root *palla* (to go), with the suffix *avo*. From the root *kisa* (to go), with the suffix *yo*, and the insertion of *l* in the middle. The pair [of terms] refers to a sprout. That which has just emerged or risen is *navubbhinna*.
From the root *aṅka* (to mark), with the suffix *uro*. 544. Up to the word *pakka* (ripe) is the name for the foot [of the plant].

The pair beginning with *makuḷa* refers to the opening of a bud that has awakened at the mouth. From the root *muca* (to release), with the suffix *ulo* and the prefix *ussa*, the *c* becomes *k*, forming *makuḷa*; or it is simply *makuḷa*. From the root *kuṭa* (to cut), with the suffix *malo* and the prefix *assu*, forming *kuṭumalo*.

*Kutumala* also [is formed as follows]: the two [suffixes] *khāra* and *ka* are applied to *jālapatta*, which is the natural state of both flower and fruit. *Khura* [is derived from the root] *khur* with the suffix *ṇvu* in the sense of destruction.

*Jala* [is derived from the root] *jal* with the suffix *ko* in its own sense (*sakatthe*), meaning grain; *jālakaṃ* is neuter. The two [terms refer to] the flower and the fruit when they have grown beyond the stage of the *jālaka*.
*Kala* [is derived from the root] *kal* with the suffix *ṇvu* in the sense of counting; *kura* [is derived from the root] *kur* with the suffix *ṇvu* in the sense of sound.
*Pupphādibandhanaṃ*: the binding of flowers and fruits is called the *vaṇṭa* (the stalk). That by which the stalk is bound is the *vajā* and so forth. 545. A triad concerning flowers (*puppha*).

The root *pasu*, meaning "to release the fetus from a living being," takes the suffix *ṇo*. In the language of the Khapaṇakas, even a tree is a *pāṇi*; [it is] among the *vuddha* and others. *Pasavo* (beasts) are derived from this.

*Kusa*, meaning "to revile," takes the suffix *umo*, with the vowel shortened. Or, from *kasa* meaning "to go," or *kāsa* meaning "splendor," [with] *umo* and a short vowel. *Puppha*, meaning "to blossom."
"It blooms" (*pupphati*), [thus] "flower. That which is born from a flower is called *rajo*, *pupphadhūlī*, or *parāgo*.

From the root *ranj* (to color), with the suffix *ṇo*. It is held that the sweet juice of a flower is called *makarando*. [It is called *makaranda*] because bees (*makkhikā*) delight (*ramanti*) in it;

[the suffix] *vajādi*. When covered with buds (*kalikābhi*), there are two [forms]: *ākiṇṇe* and *pariṇāyavati*. From the root *thu* (to praise), with the suffix *ṇvu*, [we get] *thavako*. From the root *gudh* (to pierce/perforate).
*ṇvu*, *dha* becomes *cha*: *gocchaka*. 546–547.
In the case of raw, unripe fruit, it is called *salāṭu*; *salāṭa* is used in the senses of "unripe" and "scolding. Because its state of being unripe exists, it is *salāṭu*.
However, ripe fruit is, in the primary sense, called simply "fruit" (*phala*); therefore, the designation "fruit" applies to the raw one as well.

It should be understood that [the term] occurs by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*). It refers to the production of fruit; and here, "production" means being well-ripened. However, when the fruit is dry, it is called *vāna*.
In that regard, *salāṭu* and *vāna* are used in three senses: as in *salāṭu jambū* (a raw jambu fruit), *salāṭavo māsā* (raw beans), *salāṭūni kumbhaṇḍāni* (raw cucumbers);
and *vānā harīṭakī* (a ripe hog-plum), *vāno muggo* (a ripe bean), *vānam ambaṃ* (a ripe mango).

In the case of *campakādi* (beginning with *campaka*), the suffix *ṇo* does not occur in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) or "part" (*avayava*)—as in *campakaṃ*, *karavīraṃ*, *kadambakaṃ*, *asokaṃ*, *kaṇṇikāraṃ*, or the flower of those beginning with *campaka*—because the flower has already emerged from that [source]. Thus, the names of flowers such as *campaka* and so forth function in the neuter gender.
As for *ambādi* (beginning with mango): *dāḷimaṃ*, *nāraṅgaṃ*, *āmalakaṃ*, *kuvalaṃ*, and *badaraṃ*.

The primary noun itself functions with respect to the fruit; for instance, in the case of the *āmalaki*, *kuvaliya*, and *badari* fruits, neither a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expressing a modification nor one expressing a part occurs in another sense, because the fruit has already emerged from that [primary noun]. Thus, names of fruits such as *amba* and others function in the neuter gender.

Likewise, words such as *mallikā* and others, though applied to flowers, retain their original gender through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference between the [flower] and its original gender.

In the case of common usage (*pavatti*), as for example: *mallikā* (jasmine) and *vanamallikā* (wild jasmine), etc. Even grains (*vīhi*) have the same gender as their fruit due to metaphorical transfer (*abhedopacāra*);

for example, the fruit of rice is called "rice" (*māsa*), the fruit of mung beans is called "mung bean" (*mugga*), and likewise for barley (*yava*), sesame (*tila*), linseed (*atasī*), millet (*kaṅgu*), and grain (*dhañña*).

The triad [of terms] refers to the fruit of the rose-apple tree (*jambū*). In that context, when the word is used for the fruit according to worldly convention, the term *jambu* is simply another primary noun (*pakatyanantara*).

It functions in the sense of fruit (*phale vattate*). When it does not function as a fruit, then [the suffix] *ano* is applied in the sense of modification or part (*vikāre avayave vā*). From the root *jam* meaning "to eat" (*adane*) and the suffix *ū*, we have *jambū*.
It functions in the sense of another primary form (*pakatyantare*) as a fruit. The fruit of the *jambu* tree is *jambuvaṃ*. And [it is also used as] *jambu*.

Even when functioning as a fruit, words such as *harīṭakī* and others are feminine by their very nature according to common usage (*lokato*), as stated in Amarakośa 14.18–20. The fruit of the *harīṭakī* tree is *harīṭakī*.
Likewise, for *kosātakī*, *sallakī*, *dakkhā*, *kaṇḍakārikā*, *sephālikā*, and so forth, there is an absence of suffixes in the sense of derivatives or parts, as in the previous cases.
Only the group of six beginning with *assattha* is formed with secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes;

when these refer to the fruits of the *assattha* and other trees, they may be neuter, with a change in form as follows: the fruit of the *assattha* is *assatthaṃ*; the fruit of the *veṇu* is *veṇavaṃ*.
The fruit of the *pilakkha* is called *pilakkha*; the fruit of the *nigrodha* is called *nigrodha*; the fruit of the *iṅgudi* is called *iṅguda*; the fruit of the *brahati* is called *brāhata*.
[The names] *vidārī*, *aṃsumatī*, *gambharī*, and so forth, apply to the root; they also possess their respective genders when referring to the flower.
However, the word *pāṭala*, by virtue of its natural property (*sabhāva*), is used for both the root and the flower when there is a desire to express non-differentiation.
The word *itthiliṅgo* [is used] in the sense of a feminine gender; [the suffix] *ṇam* occurs after the root *bhid* when expressing a modification or a part, as in *pāṭalam* (amarakośa 14.18–20).
The pair [of roots] *viṭ*—meaning "to pierce" (*vedhane*) or "to revile" (*akkose*)—and *apo*, *passa*, and *viṭabhi* [occur] in the sense of food, according to the *nadādi* group. 548.
Starting from the root—that is, beginning from the root—the portion of a tree extending up to the branches, ending at the branches, is called the trunk (*khandho*).
That which is also called “pakaṇḍa”: from the root *khanu* (to split), with the suffix *ava-dāraṇe*; *dho*, *khaṇḍho*; from *khāda* (in the sense of eating), or *ko*;
[in the phrase] “*khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā*,” there is the substitution of *khaṇḍha*; it is a cluster (*kalopa*).
*Koṭara* is the hollow or opening in a tree, the fissure of trees and such. From *kuṭa* (in the sense of cutting), with the suffix *aro*, *koṭara*; *nikkuha* is also used. Two.

*Samā*. [The suffix] *kā* is used in the sense of radiance (*ditti*). From the root *kas*, meaning "to shine," as in "a piece of wood (*kaṭṭha*) shines by means of fire"; thus, the suffix *to* is applied, and the *ṭṭha* is substituted for it, with the vowel shortened, resulting in *kaṭṭha*.
Alternatively, from the root *kas* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *to*, we have *kaṭṭha*.

From the root *dar* in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*), with the suffix *ṇu*. 549. A triad [of suffixes] occurs at the root. From the root *vu* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *do*; there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and from the root *budh* in the sense of "going" (*gamane*), with the suffix *a*, where *dh* is replaced by *d*.
In *mūlapatiṭṭhāyaṃ*, by the word *pāda*, all things in the sense of "foot" (*caraṇa*) that are synonyms for it are included;

it is called *pāda* because of its similarity to a foot, as in the portion of a tree trunk remaining on the ground when both [branches] have been cut off. In *saṅku*, [the suffix] *u* is added after the root *sañj* (in the sense of "doubt"), or after *sak* (in the sense of "power");

there is the elision of the final nasal (*niggahīta*). In *khāṇu*, [the suffix] *ṇu* is added to the root *khan* (in the sense of "digging or splitting"); it is also *dhruva*. It is *dhruva* because it is firm and enduring (*thirāyata*).
In the case of *dhū* and *gati*, there is the substitution of *theriy*.

There are two [meanings] for *kandādi* (beginning with *kanda*). It grows in the earth (*kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ*) thus it is *kuruhāṭa*; *aṭa* is used in the sense of calling (*avhāne*) and weeping (*rodane*). According to the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*:
"The word *karahāṭa* refers to the root of a lotus (*ambujakande*), and also to a flowering tree and a timid person. There are two [meanings].

*Kalīra* refers to the sprout of the *halā* (cassia fistula) and other such plants. From the root *kala*, meaning "to count," and the suffix *īra*. *Matthaka* means the head; it is so called because it is produced on the *masta* (the top), or on the *mattha* (the summit), or on the *sīsa* (the head).
[Verse 550] There are two kinds of *mañjarī*: that which has just emerged and is elongated and possessed of flowers, and that which is devoid of flowers.

*Vallarī*, however, is something else entirely, such as the *tālavallarī* (palm frond). From the roots *vala* and *valla*, meaning "to cover," with the suffix *ara*, belonging to the *nada*-class. It is called *mañjarī* due to its association with the *muñja* grass.
*Ro*, *nadādi*, and *ussatta*; both [refer to] a creeper (*nārī*). The pair [refers to] a creeper (*latā*). *Valla* means "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*), belonging to the *nadādi* group.
*Latā* has been explained by Halāyudha as: "*Latā*, *patāninī*, *vallī*, *matakī*, and *thā*.

That which lacks a trunk (*akkhandho*) or lacks a main branch (*appakkhaṇḍo*), such as those with many leaves, bark, and stalks; or that which has slender joints (*tanupakaṇḍo*), such as bamboo (*vaṃsa*) and reeds (*naḷa*), is [a creeper].
“Thambo” and “gumbo” are so called. [The root] *thaka* means to obstruct; with the suffix *-bo*, and changing *ka* to *mo*. [The root] *gup* means to protect;

with the suffix *-bo*, and changing *pa* to *mo*. A *patāna* is a mass of branches and leaves; the creepers such as *tambūlī*, *dhivusa*, *jīmūta*, and *gaḷojjhā* that are joined with that are called *vīru*.
It is called *vīru* because it grows (*ruhati*) in various ways (*vividhehi*); with the suffix *-kvi*, it becomes *vīru*, beginning with a long vowel, and thus also *gumbinī*.

551. [The word] *pajja* [is used] for the foot. In this context, the term “Bodhi tree” refers to that king of trees which was the site where the Blessed Buddha attained omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), except when used in a figurative sense. It is called *assattha* because omniscient knowledge dwells (*assati*) therein;
thus, the *ṭh* becomes *th*, and there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*) due to the victory over Māra and the attainment of omniscient knowledge.

He who comforts the Blessed One is called *assattha*; here the prefix *ā-* is used in the sense of instruction (*anusitthi*) and also in the sense of pleasing (*tosana*), with the root *sās* becoming *to* and shortening the vowel.
That in which omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is awakened is *bodhi*; from the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamana*), with the suffix *i*, it becomes *bodhi*.

It has two [synonyms]: *caladala* and *pippala*; it is also called *kuñjarāsana*. It has two [names] for its many branches. Because it obstructs the lower region (*adhobhāga*), it is called *nigrodha*.
*usso* and *gāgamo* [are added]. From the root *vaṭ* in the sense of piercing (*vedhane*), *vaṭati*, thus [with suffix] *a*.
Two [meanings] for *kabiṭṭha*: it stands upon a monkey (*kavi*), thus *kabiṭṭho*; generally, monkeys stand here, thus *kapittho* (*Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 14.21).
"In the sense of 'monkey' and 'wise man,' it is *kavī*"—thus Vopālita; likewise *kapittho*.

For *ṭha*, there is also *tha*. *Dadhittha* is also a sour fruit. There are two [names] for the *udumbara* tree: *yaññaṅga*—it is called *yaññaṅga* because it is a part (*aṅga*) of sacrificial rites (*yañña-kamma*) due to being a single constituent part—and *dubbī*.
In the sense of harming, [the root] *ara* undergoes the insertion of a *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and the elision of one *ba*. *Jantuphala* is also a name for *hemaduddha*. 552.
There are two [names] for the *koviḷāra* tree.
The *sukapadā* flower is pale yellow,
the *koviḷāra* is golden;
the first is white, the last is red.
"Both of these appear simultaneously," says the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.22).
Indeed, O Treasure Chest, even the lotus stalk is present here. Its leaf (*patta*) is twin (*yugam*), that is, paired (*yamakam*).

It tears apart with its three feet; it tears apart the wind, thus it is called "tearer" (*uddāla*). By way of its designation among the trees of the *siṅgāra* (erotic) and other [rasas], it is the king of trees.
*Rājarukkha* means a royal tree, or a tree that has become like a king in curing wind-diseases (*vātaroga*). *Katamāla* refers to one who has fashioned a garland with flowers;
it denotes one who displays elegance. *Indīvara* means "the lord of the wind" because it overcomes the wind, or "the sovereign";
alternatively, it is called *indīvara* because it is desired by *Indī*, the wife of Sakka. It is also known as *caturaṅgula*, *ārevata*, and *suvaṇṇaka*.
553. There are two [types] of *jambhīra*, that whose fruit is sour. Because it is sour (*ambilatta*), it is "sour-toothed" (*danta-saṭha*);

*saṭha* is used in the senses of deceit, fraud, and defilement. *Jamu* means eating; with the suffix *īra*, and with the addition of *bha* and *nta*, there is *jambha* (in the sense of opening the limbs), *jambhala*, and also *jambīra*.
There are two [types] of *varaṇa*. *Vara* is used in the sense of desire; with the suffix *yu*. *Kala* means counting; with the suffix *ira*.
*Naḍa* and others end in a short vowel. *Varuṇa* and *tittasāka* [also end in a short vowel]. There are two types of *phalahara*.
It is called *kiṃsuka* because its leaves and flowers give rise to the doubt, "What is this? Is it a *suka*? *Pāri* refers to the ocean;
that which is auspicious (*bhadra*) therein is *pāribhadda*, which is the same as *pāḷibhadda*. Because its leaves and flowers have the shape of a *koviḷāra* tree, [it is so named].

Pālibhadra. There are two types of *vidula*, which flowers during the rainy season (*abbhasamaya*). *Vaja* means "going," and *ulo*. *Vī* means "procreation," with the suffix *-asa*; it also ends in *-to*, preceded by *vi*.
Alternatively, *ata* meaning "perseverance" (*sātaccagamana*) is preceded by *vi*, with the suffix *-asa*. *Vānīra* is also [a name for this]. 554.
There are two types of *pītana*, whose leaves and fruits are sour, whose fruit is the size of a betel nut (*pūgaphala*), and which has the shape of the *sallakī* tree.

And that tree. In the word *amba*, [the suffix] *aṭ* is applied; *ko* is used in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*). In the sense of "to expand" (*tappana*) or "splendor" (*kantī*), [the suffix] *tano* is applied;

it expands joy (*pītiṃ*), thus it is *pītano*; *ko* is used in the sense of the base itself. Both refer to the *guḷapuppha* (sugar-flower) tree. In the sense of "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), [the suffix] *ko* is applied to *mana*, and there is the substitution of *madhu*.
A tree named after honey is *madhudduma*. Both refer to what is known as the *lambū* tree. Its fruit is sweet like sugar (*guḷa*), thus it is *guḷaphala*. *Pīla*...
On a pillar; thus, there are two [names] for *tikkhagandha*. It produces beauty (*sobha*), thus it is a *sobhañjana*;
or, that by which beauty is produced through its being the cause, is a *sobhañjana*. And it is said:
"It is infused with the juice of the *sirīsa* flower..."
"By this [ointment] made from a thousand-fold portion of white-named marīca,
along with katañjana, oil, and pādana, all poison-origins are pacified."

*Siggu* (the *sigru* tree) is so called because it is used for the purpose of destroying [diseases] by piercing; [it is derived from] *si*, *gu*, and *thī*. It captivates the mind (*cittahārī*), it is a destroyer (*pabhañjana*), and it is also a destroyer by piercing.
555. There are two names for the *visālataca* (the *saptaparṇa* tree): that which flowers in the autumn (*sarada*) is its flower.

Because it has seven leaves (*satta-panna*), it is *sattapaṇṇī* in the masculine. Its leaf is like an umbrella (*chatta*), thus it is *chattapaṇṇo*. It is also *visamacchado* because of its uneven covering (*visama-chada*), due to having seven leaves. There are two [names].
*Rathaddume*: That by which one spreads out a chariot is *tinisa*; thus, *iso*. It is called *atimuttaka* because one is completely released from burning and bile by means of it.

[This refers to] the *cittakimpi* plant. There are two names for *vātapotha*: it is *palāsa* because it cuts (*lunāti*) the wind; thus, *aso*. For Rudra says: "The *palāsa* is on the tree; *pīta* and *haritakī* are on the *suka*. It is also *vātapotha*, meaning the striking (*potha*) of the wind; *putha* is used in the sense of harming. There are two names for what is known as *putī*:
it is *ariṭṭha* because it possesses the quality of ariphala, which consists of the destruction of the delusion of living beings; [the form] *hanti* is due to grammatical elision (*nipātana*).

*Ar̥tha*: because it is desired by people who are enemies to disease, or because it is a fruit desired (*arita*) by those who seek it; *iṣu* means "to desire. *Phaṇa* means "to move," with the suffix *ilo*, [forming] *asse*.
556. The triad refers to the *siriphala* (the wood-apple tree). *Mala* means "to hold," with the suffix *ūro*, forming *mālūra*. *Bila* means "to split," with the suffix *ṇuvo*, forming *beluva*.

With the suffix *lap*, it becomes *billa*. *Saṇḍilya* and *selusa* are also [names for this]. As it is said: "In the various types of sages, *mālūra*; *saṇḍilya* among other trees; and *naṭa*, *billa*, and *selusa* [are synonyms]."
*The Cintāmaṇi-Ṭīkā*, 14.32, states that *rabhasa* [is the authority].
Regarding the word *tuṅga*: *punnāga* refers to a tree, a male-named nāga. As Amarasimha says in the *Amarakośa* (14.25): “The *punnāga* is a tall man, a *kesara*, and beloved by the gods.

Here, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule “in compounds where the first member is *puṃs*, such as gender (*liṅga*) and so forth. This is because it possesses an abundance of flowers and filaments (*kesara*).
*Kesara*: either from *kisa* (to emaciate), or *kesara* because of being joined with flower filaments (*kesa*), or *ro*.

The pair [of suffixes] *ava* and *lo* apply to the measure of *loddha*. *Sala* has the sense of going; with *avo*, it becomes *sāla*. It cuts (*lunāti*) the channels of blood, phlegm, and bile, thus it is *loddha*;
with *ddo*, it is *lodda*. *Tiriṭa* is also *sāvara*. As stated in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 14.33: "The word *sāvara* is said to mean offense, as well as *loddha* and evil."

*Tyajayo*. Two [words] for *dhanupaṭṭa* (bow-sling). *Pī* means drinking; *alo*, [the suffix] *īssa* undergoes the substitution *iyādeso*. *Sannakā* refers to ascetics (*tāpasā*); their tree is *sannakaddu*.
For it is said in another lexicon (*kosantare*) in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.35): "The *sannakaddu* is a bow-sling; the *varaṇa* tree is dear to ascetics. 557.
Two [words] for what is known as *mhanakū*. *Likuca* is the name of a wild mango tree (*ḍahurukkho*); because of its qualities, it is called *likocaka*. This is a technical designation (*saññā*).

*Ko*: the marking-nut tree (*aṅkola*). *Dvayaṃ* (the pair): both refer to the *kumbha* tree. *Garunā* (the heavy one): *guggulu*, the exudate of the *guggulu* tree, which removes disease; it is so called because it is "heavy" even for a physician, due to its medicinal potency.

[The form] is derived through irregular grammatical substitution (*nipātana*). *Kusa*: the *kusa* grass, used for cutting; derived with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Kumbho*: also refers to a heap or a mass. [It is used] in the sense of a specific heap, the frontal globe of an elephant, and a peak.
“*Kumbha* refers to the ears of *kaṇṇasu*, to a jar, to a lustful man, and to a female elephant;
however, *kumbha* is neuter in the sense of the *vaggulu* plant. — *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 14.34.
*Rabhaso*. In the sense of "going before," *puro* means "in front. *Ambe* consists of two [roots]:

*ama* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*), and *amba* in the sense of "sound" (*sadda*). *A* [is used] in the sense of "falling" (*cuti*), "sprinkling" (*āsecana*), and "protecting" (*rakkhaṇa*); or *cu* in the sense of "falling away" (*cavana*).
*To* [is a suffix]; it begins with a long vowel. *Rasāla* is also [derived thus]: because it "takes" (*lāti*) "flavor" (*rasa*), it is *rasāla*; [the vowel] is long. This mango is fragrant.
Being endowed with an extraordinary fragrance, it is called *saho* and *sahakāra*. It is *saho* because it possesses power (*satti*), or because it is able to make [the air] fragrant;
thus it is *saho*. It is *sahakāra* because it performs that endurance (*sahana*); or, *hā* signifies joy (*pamudā*), and because it exists together with that, it is *saho*;
or, because it produces joy (*saṃhā*) and abundance (*samuda*), it is *sahakāra*.

558. *Setambo* (the white mango) has two [components]. *Puṇḍa* means "to mark" (*puṇḍane*). Some say it means "to break" (*khaṇḍana*); with the suffix *ṇvu*, the feminine form *assī*, and the augment *ar*, [it becomes *puṇḍarīka*]. A mango tree that is white in color is a *setambo*.

*Bahuvāraka* (the watermelon) has two [components], referring to that whose fruits are very slimy. From the root *si* meaning "to bind" (*bandhane*), with the suffix *lu*; or from *sala* meaning "to go" (*gamana*), with the suffix *u* and the augment *asse*.
Because of its sliminess, there is much water (*vārī*) in it, hence it is called *bahuvāraka*; the suffix *ko* is applied for the sake of technical designation (*saññā*).

*Sīta*, *uddāla*, and *kaphala* [are synonyms]. There is a pair for *kāsmariya*. That which has leaves like those of the *sirīsa* tree is *sepaṇṇī*; it belongs to the *nada*-group, with the substitution of *se* for the word *siri*. Because it originates from the region of Kashmir, it is *kāsmarī*;
alternatively, *kāsa* means "splendor" (*ditti*), and *maro* belongs to the *nada*-group. It is also called *madhupaṇṇī* and *bhaddapaṇṇī*. There is a pair for the thorny tree that bears sour fruit.

It is called *kolī* because it brings (*lāti*) what is wretched (*kucchita*) due to its thorns (*sakaṇṭakatā*); it belongs to the class beginning with *nada*. [The suffix] *aro* is used after the word *vadara*, as in *nadādi*.
*Kuvalī* and *kakkandhū* are also [names for it]. 559. There are two [names] for the fruit of that *koli*: the fruit of the *koli* is *kola*. This part of the *badarī* is *badara*.
*Kuvala*, *phenila*, and *sovīra* are also [names for it]. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*: "But *sovīra* refers to eye-salve, sour gruel, and also to *badara*."
14.36 *Rabhaso*. There are two [meanings]: a tree grown upon a rock or other substrate within the *Assattha* (Ficus religiosa) family;

and a tree that "harasses" (*kasati*) another as its support, hence a *pilakkha* (the *kapi-athabbana* tree). [The root] *kasa* means "to scratch" or "to mark," with the suffixes *khatta* etc. applied according to grammatical rules.

A *pipphalī* is so called because it possesses fruit that is "unpleasant" (*virūpa*) due to being inedible; [the suffix] *ī* is added according to the *nadādi* group, and there is also the form *vissa*.

Two [names] for the *toyādivāpinī* (the plant that grows in water, etc.): its root is included among the "great five roots" (*mahāpañcamūla*). *Paṭa* means "to go"; with the suffix *-ala*, it forms *paṭala*, as in *nadādi*.
*Pāṭalī* and *pāṭalā* are also [names for this]. That which has a black flower-stalk is *kaṇhavaṇṭā*; this is also *kāsmariyā*.

*Alippiya* and *tambapupphi* are used here [for the same]. Two [names] for *gandhile*: because of its sweet fruit it is *sādu* (sweet), and because it is accompanied by a thorny stalk it is *kaṇṭa* (thorny).

And *ceti* [is derived from] *sādukaṇṭha*. Because it makes itself deformed by having thorns, it is called *vikaṅkata*; there is a doubling of the vowel (*dvitta*) and the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). 560. The group of four refers to the *tinduka* tree.

From the root *tanu* in the sense of expansion, with the suffix *uka* and the change to *da*. Or, from *ti* in the sense of harming, with the suffixes *u* and *ko* as a nominal suffix (*saññā*). That which has a black trunk and a dark bark is [called *tinduka*]. From *tima* in the sense of being wet, with the suffix *ūsa*, the suffix *ko* in its own sense, and the change to *va*. With the secondary suffix (*upaccaya*) *timbaru*.

Two [names] for the *tambaphala* tree: *Irāvatī*, because it was born on the bank of the river Irāvatī in ancient times; and *Erāvata*. *Nāraṅga*: "nāra" means water (*nīra*); that which goes to it is a *nāraṅga*. Two [names] for the *makkaṭatinduka* tree:

*Kula* (with the suffix *ṇvu*), and *Kākendu* or *Kākaluka*. 561. Three [names] for the *kadamba* tree: *Kadamba*, because it subdues (*dameti*) the wind (*kaṃ*); with the suffix *bo*. *Piyaka*, because it pleases (*pineti*);

with the suffix *ṇvu* and the substitution of *i* for *e*. *Nīpa*, because it leads joy (*mudaṃ*); with the suffix *po*. Two [names] for the *vidara* tree, whose resin is used to coat boxes and other objects: *Bhala*...

*Bhalla* is used in the senses of reviling, harming, and giving; *nadādi*, excluding *to*; *kaṇṭha* and *bhallātaka*—these three [mean the marking nut plant]. *Arūkara* and *aggimukha* are two names for what is known as *pāvusa*.

*Jhapa* (in the sense of burning) with the suffix *ṇvu*: see *vo*. *Paca* (in the sense of cooking) with the suffix *ulo*: these two refer to the *sirimaṭṭhi* tree, whose fruits are the size of black pepper and are sour. *Tila* (in the sense of moving) with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Khura* (in the sense of cutting) with the suffix *ṇvu*.
562. There are two [meanings] for *ambilikā*: the root *ci* in the sense of "accumulation" (*cayane*), and *co*, or *cica*, in the sense of "taking up" (*ādāna*) or "restraining" (*saṃvaraṇa*).

The root *tanu* means "to expand" (*vitthāre*); it is called *tintiṇī* because it expands (*tanoti*) a sour taste (*ambilarasa*). It has a double *t* and a nasal (*ṇat-taṃ*), and belongs to the *nadādi* group. There are two [meanings] for *ambilaṅkuraphala*: it refers to a certain tree and its fruit.

It is called *gaddabhaṇḍa* because its fruit is the size of a donkey's testicles (*gadrabhaṇḍa*); there is the elision of the *r*. The root *kapi* means "to move" (*calane*), followed by the suffix *tano*; the vowel is long.
[The word] *āgama* [ends in] *assa*. *Kandarāla* and *pilakkha* [are names for trees].
There is a triad regarding the *sāla* tree. [The root] *sal* means "to go"; with the suffix *ṇo*, it is *sāla*, or it is *sāla* because of its possession of pith (*sāra*).

Because its leaves resemble a horse's ear, it is called *assakaṇṇa*. [The roots] *sanj* (in the sense of) "clinging" and *sajj* (in the sense of) "eating," with the suffix *a*, [form *sajja*]. There are two [meanings] for *nadīsajja*. [The root] *ajj* (in the sense of) "driving," with the suffix *uno*, [forms *ajjuṇa*].
*Kakka* means "greedy" (*lolya*) and "upward" (*uddha*). *Vīrataru* and *indaduma* [are synonyms]. (563) The triad [of terms] refers to the *mucalinda*.
*Cula* means "submerging" (*nimujjana*). *Mucala* means "conjunction" (*saṅgāta*). *Indo* [is a synonym for the moon]. *Nīpa* and *kadamba* [are synonyms].

The triad [of terms] refers to the yellow *sāla* tree. *Piyaka* and *kadamba* [are synonyms]. *Asa* means "eating" (*bhakkhana*). The suffix *-yu* is applied. The yellow-flowered *sāla* tree is the *pītasāla*. *Bandhūkapuppha* and *jīvaka* [are synonyms].

Two [names] for *jhāṭali*: *golīsa* (from the root *lih*, with the suffix *so*); and *jhāṭala* (from *jhaṭa* "to gather," with the suffix *alo*). It is a tree with long fruit shaped like the *pāṭali* flower;

it is also called *pamokkha*. 564. Two [names] for the *rājāyatana* tree: *khīrikā* (due to its sap-filled nature); and *rājāyatana* (because it was the dwelling place of the King of Gods), which also applies to the *piyāla* tree.
Two [names] for the *kapphala* tree: *kumbha* (it is filled or covered by a wretched fruit).
She rejoices in what is loathsome, thus she is *kumudikā*; [the suffix] *ṇvu*.

There are two names for the *guvāka* tree, from whose fruit that which is called *tambūla* (betel) is produced. *Pūja* is used in the sense of worship; [the suffix] *ṇo*, [forming] *pūjā*, of which *go* is the [base].

*Kamu* is used in the sense of desire; [the suffix] *ṇvu* in the sense of the causal agent. *Khapura* is also [a name for it]. There are two names for *lohitalodda*. That which is designated as *paṭṭi*...
*Paṭṭi*. There is also a reading *paddhī*. Because it becomes red when lac is added to it, it is called *lākhāpasādano*.
It is also *kamuko*. 565. Two [names] refer to the *iṅgudī* tree; this thorny tree grows predominantly in the Middle Country. The root *iṅga* has the sense of "going";

from *ido*, with the suffix *issa*, belonging to the *nadādi* class. Because its fruit is used by ascetics (*tāpasa*), it is the "ascetic’s tree" (*tāpasataru*). Two [names] refer to what is commonly known as the *bhujapatta*.
*Sundaratace* means a tree whose bark they write magical syllables (*mantakkharāni*) upon. *Bhujo* is the hand; it is called *bhujapatta* because its leaves resemble hands.
It is called *ābhujī* because its bark is folded by those who write mantras. *Bhūjo* refers to leather; it also has a soft bark. Two [names] refer to the *simbali* tree.
It is *picchilā* because of its connection with *piccha* (slime); the suffix is *ilo*. *Samba* is used in the sense of a circle (*maṇḍala*), with the suffixes *ali* and *assi*. "Picchilā..."

*Pūraṇī*, *mocā*, *thirāyu*, *simbalī*, and *dvisū*—these are [names for the cotton tree] according to the *Amarakośa* (14.46). These two [terms] refer to a tree that has a slippery appearance and is covered in thorns.

[The root] *ruc* means "splendor"; with the suffix *yu* in the sense of the causal agent, it becomes *rocu*. [The root] *kuṭ* means "crookedness"; with the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of the agent, it becomes *koṭa*.
Although it is not actually a *simbalī* tree, because its appearance is seen to be similar to a *simbalī*, it is called *koṭasimbalī*; this is masculine. *Kasambala* is also [a name for it].
566. Two [names] for the thorny *karañja* bush, known as *kaṇṭakarañja*, which is called *kalina* in the world.

The root *kṛ* means "to injure"; from it comes *karin*, meaning "one who injures. The root *pū* means "to purify," with the suffixes *ika* and *tonta*. Thus, *pūtikaraja*, *kalimāraka*, and *kalina* [are synonyms].

Two [names] for the yellow-nosed tree (*pītanāsakarukkha*) that has the shape of a pomegranate flower (*dālimapuppha*). The root *ruh* means "to grow," with the suffix *ṇī*. Because of its red flowers, it is called *rohitaka*.
The word *eraṇḍa* has two meanings. The root *eraḍ* means "to injure. That which injures the wind (*vāta*) is an *eraṇḍa*; [the suffix] *ṇo* is added. The root *maṇḍ* means "to adorn.

*Āmaṇḍa* refers to the scum of slightly clarified oil; or, it is that which gives (*dāti*) the raw (*āma*) wind, hence *āmaṇḍa*. The root *dā* means "to cut" (*avakhaṇḍana*); the *dā* becomes *ḍa*. *Cittaka* and *cañcu* [also mean "firebrand"]. It is said: "Cittaka is a synonym for fire;
*cañcu* is masculine and refers to both the firebrand and the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*)."
“One who stands on the tip of a bird’s beak is dead. Two [names] for the *sivārukkha* tree.

It is called *sattuphalā* because its fruit is joined with *sattu* (parched grain). That which heals a boil (*gaṇḍa*) is *samī*; it belongs to the *a*-class and the *nadādi* group; it also refers to the *pāribhaddaka*. It is also *garudāru* and *pūtikaṭṭha*. 567. Two [names] for the *karañja* tree:
that which has a garland (*mālā*) of black-red flowers is [called] *nattamālā*. That which colors (*rañjayati*) the head (*kaṃ*) is *karañja*, with the suffix *-ṇo*. It is also *cillavilla*.

*Karaja* is also [a term for *khadira*]. There are two [meanings] for *khadira*: the root *khada* means "to injure" (*hiṃsā*) and "to destroy" (*theriya*). It is called *khadira* because by it the teeth (*danta*) are injured; *ira* is the suffix.
Because by it the teeth are cleansed (*dhāvanti*) so as to be free from disease, it is *dantadhāvana*; the suffix is *yu*, and the root *dhāva* means "movement" (*gati*) and "purity" (*suddhi*).

*Gāyattī* is also [a term for *khadira*], as is *bālatanaya*. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.49): "The feminine *gāyattī* refers to the *khadira* tree, and also to a meter (*chandas*) consisting of six syllables."
*Vyākhyāsudhā* 2.4.50: *Rabhasa*. One whose son is a delicate child known as a "leaf-child" (pattasaññita) is a "son-of-leaf" (*bālatanaya*).

Both [terms] refer to the *khadira* tree, which has yellow sap; however, the group beginning with *khadira* specifically refers to that which has yellow sap. Because of its white color, it resembles camphor (*kappūra*);
its bark is like that, thus it is "camphor-bark" (*somavakka*). Regarding the word *soma*: "Soma [is used] for Kuvera, for a paternal deity, for a type of *vasu*, and for a source of wealth."
“*Dibba*, *osadhi*, *soma*, *latā*, *samīraṇa*, *kappūra*, *nīra*, and *vānara*—this is the compendium of various meanings.
The root *īs* (to go) is small; its *dalam* is *kadara*. The letter *la* [is used] for *ro*. The two [roots] *piṇḍ* and *īṭ* [form] *piṇḍītaka*. *Sal* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *lo*.
*Mad* (in the sense of intoxication), with the suffix *yu*. “In the *Amarakośa*: ‘*Piṇḍītaka*, *maravaka*, *sasana*, and *karahāṭaka*’” (Amara 14.52).
568. *Tikaṃ indasāle*. *Indasāla* is the chief (*inda*), the king, of the *sāla* trees; this is merely a designation, like the word *Sirivaḍḍhaka* used for slaves and others.
It is also called *indasāla* because it is the *sāla* of *Inda*, that is, Sakka. [The suffix] *ṇvu* is added to *salla* (arrow), belonging to the *nada*-class, as in *sallakī*.
[The root] *khara* is used in the senses of cutting and destroying; [the suffix] *ṇvu* is added.
There are two [meanings] for *devadāru*: the wood of the gods; and because it is auspicious (*bhadda*), it is called *bhaddadāru*.

It is also the tree of Sakka, the *pāribhaddaka*, yellow wood, timber, and even rotten wood. There are two [meanings] for *hemapupphaka*: that which was born in the city of Campā in the first age is *campayya* (derived from *campā*);
with the suffix *-ka*, it becomes *campaka*.

569. *Panasa* has two [meanings]. *Pana* [is used] in the sense of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and in the sense of praise (*thuti*); thus it is *aso*. Its fruit is provided with thorns, hence it is *kaṇṭakiphala*. *Abhaya* has two [meanings].
Because when it is consumed, there exists no fear of disease (*roga-bhaya*) nor the affliction of disease (*roga-vyatha*), it is *abhaya*.

It removes (*harati*) or drives away (*apaneti*) the fear of disease, thus it is *harītakī*; [the suffix] *to* is added, and *ko* is added in the sense of the object itself (*sakatthe*), belonging to the *nadādi* group. *Harittakī* is also [correct]. *Abyathā*, [meaning "without affliction"].
Pūtana, Amātā, Hemavatī, Cetakī, and Sivāpi. Two [names] for the Karisaphala tree.
It is called *akkho* because it devours disease (*rogaṃ asati bhakkhati*); *kho* is a suffix. It makes disease disappear (*vibhūtaṃ karoti*), thus it is *vibhītako*, also *vibhīṭako*.
It is the abode of spirits (*bhūtāvāso*), and also *kaliddumo*, being the tree that is the haunt (*āsayabhūto*) of the *kali* spirit.
*Kalidduma*. There are two [names] for the *pussaphala* tree. Because there is no death (*mata*) through it, it is *amata* (the deathless). The root *mala* means "to hold";

with the suffix *ṇvu*, it belongs to the *nadādi* group, thus forming *āmalakī*. It is also *vayaṭṭhā*. Because one stands firm (*vayo tiṭṭhati*) and becomes stable by means of this, it is *vayaṭṭhā*.
570. There are two [names] for the *ḍahurukkha* tree. Because it grows on the mountain named *Labu*, it is *labuja*. Due to its smallness, it is *līna* (hidden) and not manifest.
The fruit of this tree is called *kuci*; it is a *likuca* because of its falling (*nipātana*). There are two types with yellow flowers.

It is called *kaṇikāra* because it makes itself small (*kaṇiṭṭha*) due to having odorless flowers; here, the suffix *-ṭṭha* is elided. It is a *dumuppala* because it is a tree whose flowers are the size of a lotus (*paduma*).

There are three [names] for asafoetida (*hiṅguniyyāsa*). From the root *nī* (to lead), with the suffixes *-bo* and *-monto*. It is called *ariṭṭha* because it stands (*tiṭṭhati*) in a state of hostility (*aribhāva*) due to its bitter taste (*tittarasattā*).

It is called *pucimanda* because it crushes (*maddati*) the *puci* [sap]; there is the substitution of *itta* and the addition of the vowel *i*. It is also called *dhammasena* and *mālaka*. It is called *mālaka* because it afflicts (*malate*) with disease;

the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. These two names refer to the red-flowered variety. From the root *kṛ* (to make), the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. From the root *dal* (to split), the suffix *mo* is applied and the vowel *i* is added.

It is also called *dāḷima*. 571. There are two names for the yellow tree (*pītadduma*). It is called *sarala* because it endures (*sarati*) for a long period of time; the suffix *alo* is applied. It is called *pūtikaṭṭha* because its wood is indeed putrid (*pūti*).

*Pūtimutta* means "rotten urine. Regarding *dvaya*: *piccha* is in the sense of being slippery; *kapi* is in the sense of moving, with the suffix *-ila*. *Sāsa* is in the sense of instruction, or *sisa* is in the sense of desire;
with the suffix *-apo* and the elision of the *niggahīta*, it becomes *siṃsapā*.

It is also [called] *aguru*. The triad refers to the *phalinī* plant. *Sā* is in the sense of making thin, with the suffix *-mo*. Because it goes to a state of being beloved, it is *piyaṅgu*; with the suffix *-u*, it signifies a desirable state.

It is called *kaṅgu* because it goes (*gacchati*); [the suffix] *u* is added by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). It is also known as *mahilāhvayā*, *latā*, *gundā*, *gandhaphalī*, and *kārambhā*. There are two names for the *sirīsa*:
it is called *sirīsa* because it moves toward (*sarati*) or destroys (*hiṃsati*) disease; [the suffixes] *īsa* and *assi* are applied.
From the root *bhaṇḍ* (in the sense of reviling), [with the suffix] *ilo*, we get *kapītana*. *Kapītana* also refers to the *ambāṭaka* and the *gaddabhaṇḍa*.

572. Two [names] for the *maṇḍūkaparṇa*: *suṇa* (to hear), with the suffix *ṇvu*, and with a long vowel; that which has a long fruit-stalk (*phalavaṇṭa*). *Naṭa* and *kuṭannaṭa* are also [names for it]. Two [names] for the *bakula*: *baka* (to take), with the suffix *ulo*; because its flowers are endowed with filaments (*kesara*), it is called *kesara*.
Two [names] for the *malapuppha*: *kākānam udumbaro* is *kākodumbara*; that same [tree] is *kākodumbarikā*, with the suffix *ika* used in the sense of the object itself.
*Phala* (to produce), with the suffix *gu*, and *la* becomes *ga*. Two [names] for the *nāgarukkha*: it does not move (*na gacchati*), thus it is *nāga*, beginning with a long vowel.
A garland of *nāgas* (serpents) is a *nāgamālikā*; it is that wherein such a garland has arisen. (573) There are two [names] for *asoka*.

That by which there is no sorrow (*soka*) is *asoka*. *Vaja* means going; [with the suffix] *ula*, it becomes *vajula*. There are two [names] for *jayā*. It is called *takkārī* because it effects the overcoming of various diseases and so forth;
[from the root] *kṛ* with the suffix *ṇī*. It especially conquers, thus it is *vejayantikā*; [with the suffix] *anta*, belonging to the *nadādi* group, and the suffix *ka* in its own sense. "Jayā..."
“*Jayantī* is *takkārī*, [and] *nādeyī* is *vejayantikā*” (Amarakośa 14.65).
The pair [of terms] refers to the tree named *tamāla*, which grows near the ocean and has dark-colored leaves (*sāmada-la*). It is called *tāpiñcha* because it is born from the *Tāpī* river;

the suffix *-cha* is applied in the sense of "born from" (*aññattha*), with the addition of the nasal (*bindu*). For it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: “*Tāpī*, however, is a particular river. [The word] *tamu* means doubt.
Alo. There are two [names] for *kuṭaja*. It is called *kuṭaja* because it "cuts disease" (*rogaṃ chindati*); thus, *jo*. *Girimallikā* is the jasmine (*mallikā*) grown on a mountain (*girimhi jātā*);

here, it is also a synonym for Sakka. 574. The fruit of that *kuṭaja* is *indayava*. *Indayava* is a specific grain (*dhaññavisesa*) belonging to Indra (Sakka), like a barley-corn (*yava*). It is also called *kaliṅga* and *kaddayava*.
“*Kaliṅga* refers to the *pūtikarañja* and *dhūmyāṭa* trees when denoting a distinction of place;
it is masculine. It is neuter for the fruit of the *kuṭaja* tree, but feminine for a woman. Thus says the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.67).
According to the *Rabhasa*, however, the reading in the *Amaramālā* under the section on feminines is: “*Kaliṅga* refers to *andayava* [a type of grain] and is masculine. Its meaning is: *kaliṅgā*.
*Itthī*, *indayava*, and *pumā*. Two [meanings] for *kaṇikārikā*. *Aggimantho*: fire is churned by means of this; [the suffix] *ṇo*.
When that is rubbed with pieces of wood, fire arises. From the root *kaṇ* in the sense of "going," [the suffix] *ṇvu*.
*Jayā* also occurs here: “In victory, he [crosses] difficult paths; *jayantī* is the *gaṇikārikā*. Thus, *jayā* has various meanings.
Two names for *nigguṇḍī*: because there is no *guṇḍa* (the binding of the womb) in this plant, it is called *nigguṇḍī*. [The root] *si* means "binding";
since it prevents the binding of the womb (*sindu*), it is *sinduvāra*. *Indānī* is also used here; [it occurs] in the sense of making one an *indānī*, as in the words *sinduvāra* and *indanāri*.
Two names for *mallikā*: because grasses (*tiṇa*) are its spikes (*sūla*), it is *tiṇasūla*; [the root] *sūl* means "to cause pain. Wherever that [plant] grows—

In this context, the meaning is that the grasses become diseased. Regarding the verse: “*Tiṇasūlaṃ mallikāyaṃ, paṇḍakaṃ ketakīphale*”: it is called *mallikā* because it is worn (*mallate*) or held by all;

from the root *malla* (to hold), with the suffix *i*, and the suffix *ka* added in the sense of the base word itself. It is also known as *bhūpadī* and *sītabhīru*. 575. There is a pair of names for the black-flowered *sephālikā*:
*sephālikā* is so called because its stalks (*siphā*) possess matted locks (*jaṭā*); [this is formed] with the suffix *ika*, with the letter *l* inserted in the middle.
