*Nīlikā* is so called because of its blue flowers. *Suvahā* and *nigguṇḍī* are also [names for it]. According to Rudda: "The *sinduvāra* is also *nigguṇḍī*, as is the blue *sephālikā*. Two terms refer to the *vanamallikā*.
From the root *phuṭ* (to blossom), with the prefix *ā* meaning "intensely," it blossoms intensely, thus it is *apphoṭā*; the initial vowel is shortened. Four terms refer to the red-flowered variety.
From *bandh* (to bind), with the suffix *u* and the pleonastic suffix *ka*: *bandhuka*. It is called *jayasumana* because it is a *sumana* (jasmine) that brings about victory.
*Bhaṇḍi* with the suffix *tisma* becomes *bhaṇḍika*. It lives, thus it is *jīvaka*; from the root *jīv* (to sustain life), with the suffix *ṇvu*.

Since the word *jīvaka* applies to yellow sal trees and so forth as well, it is stated here as "bandhu-jīvaka" (the kinsman-life) to specify it by means of the word *bandhu*, or else this is the name for a single entity formed by the combination [of both words]. This is because of the statement: "The word *bandhu* refers to the *bandhuka* flower, a kinsman, and a brother."
And according to the statement: “*Jīvaka*, *pītasāla*, *khepana*,
*vuddhijīvī*, *sevinī*, *pāṇaka*, *phāti*, *kuṇḍika*,
and *pādapantara*,” both names should be understood here for the term "*bandhujīvaka*."

576. *Pañcakaṃ sumanāyaṃ*. That which possesses a beautiful mind (*mano*) is [called] *sumana*. Because of its fragrance, it is known by the collective name *jātisumana*. [The root] *mala* means "to hold"; with the suffix *-to*, it belongs to the *nadādi* group. [The root] *jana* means "to produce"; [with the suffix *-i*, it becomes *janī*]. Because its flowers appear during the rainy season, it is called *vassikī*. With the suffix *-iko*, it belongs to the *nadādi* group.
Two terms refer to that which is known as "Campeyya": *yutha* means "to injure"; with the suffix *-i* and the pleonastic suffix *-ka* (in the sense of itself), it begins with a long vowel.

That which originates in Magadha is *māgadhī*; it is also [called] *gaṇikā* and *ambaṭṭhā*. Two terms refer to that which is known as "Devāli": *sundaraṃ dalam etissā* means "its petals are beautiful," thus it is *sattalā*.
*Dassa* means seven; that which has seven petals is *sattalā*. *Navā* means fresh; *navamallikā* is a fresh jasmine (*mallikā*). It is also called *navamālikā*.

(577) There are two names for the *puṇḍaka*, known as *laṃsvaṇa*. It blooms in spring, thus it is *vāsantī*. It extends great joy, thus it is *atimutta* (by way of grammatical derivation). It is also a creeper (*latā*). It blooms in the month of *Mādhava* (Citta) or in *Vesākha*, thus it is *mādhavī*. [Regarding the term *latā*: it refers to the *jotimatī*, the *pakka*, the *sākhā*, the *vallī*, and the *piyaṅgu*.]
"Latā refers to *katthūrikā*, and it also [refers] to *dubbā* and *mādhavī*.

*Latā* has many meanings. Two [terms] refer to the *karavīra*: because they cry out wretchedly (*kucchitaṃ ravanti*), they are *karavīra*; *īra* means to cry out. Because it kills horses, it is *assamāraka*. It is also a kind of perfume. Two [terms] refer to the *mātuluṅga*:
that by which one who is intoxicated (*matto*) is destroyed (*lujjati*) is *mātuluṅga*; *luja* means destruction. Because its seeds are full, it is *bījapūra*.
*Rucaka* also [is a name for the dhattūra plant]. *Ruc* means "splendor"; the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. Both [terms] refer to the dhattūra. That by which one becomes intoxicated (*ummatto*) is *ugra*;

*mada* means "intoxication. It is called *mātula* because it kills (*māreti*); the suffix *ulo* is applied, and the letter *r* is changed to *t*. The *Amarakośa* (14.77) states: "Intoxicated, a gambler, a rogue, dhattūra, and that which is called 'gold'—these are synonyms for *mātula*, *madana*."
578. Two [names] for the *kaṇhapākaphala* (the fruit that ripens black): *karamanda* and *karamadda*. It crushes (*maddati*) the hand (*kara*) with its thorn;

hence *karamanda*. Also *karamadda*. *Susena*: it binds (*sinoti*) well; from the root *si* (to bind), with the suffix *yu*. Two [names] for the *kunda* flower: *kuṇda* and *māghya*. From the root *kuṇa* (contraction), with the suffix *do*, and the doubling of the *n*;
or from *kuṇa* in the sense of sound and equipment. *Māghya*: existing in *māgha*; with the suffix *yo*. For at that time there is an abundance of flowers and so forth.
"It exists" (*bhavati*); thus, it is designated as "existent" (*tabbhava*).
"Devas" (*devatāsa*) is a dual form. They sit among the gods; therefore, they are "those who dwell among the gods. It is called *jīmūta* because it arises during the time of clouds;
it means "a cloud. "Two" refers to the well-known flowering shrub with that name. They have flowered and do not become withered; thus, it is "unwithering" (*amilāta*).
It endures even for a long time, thus it is *mahāsahā*. 579. The group of four refers to the general term *jhiṇḍi*.

That by which beauty (*sirī*) exists is *sereyyaka*, [also] *ṇeyyaka*. Because its name contains the word "servant" (*dāsa*), it is *dāsī*. In the sense of scattering (*kira vikkiraṇe*), with the suffix *ā* and the doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*).

In the sense of sound (*kura sadde*), with the suffix *ḍo* and the suffix *ko* in its own sense (*sakatthe*). The pair refers to white *paṇṇāsa* [grass] when distinguished by its throat-like [color] and its leaf. In the sense of going (*aja gamane*), with the suffix *uko*. White (*sito*) and dry (*sukkho*) *paṇṇāsa* is *sitapaṇṇāsa*. The pair refers to *paṇṇāsa* that has not yet produced leaves. In the sense of trembling (*īra kampane*), with the suffix *yu*. It conquers the snake (*phaṇiṃ jayati*), thus it is *phaṇijjaka*, [a form] where *ya* becomes *ja*.

580. Two [names] for the hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*): *japati* (she repeats/incants) by means of it is *japā*; or from the root *ju*, meaning "to move," with the suffix *po*, and the vowel lengthened (*ussatta*).

Two [names] for a specific tree that grows in the desert (*marudesaja*), is thorny (*kaṇṭakini*), and is dear to camels (*karabhappiya*): *karīra*, etc. From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *īra*. *Kaca* (to bind), with the suffix *dvitta*, becomes *kakaca*; it is also called *ganthila*.
Two [names] for a dissimilar sprout (*vijāti-pallava*) produced on top of a tree: *rukkhādanī*. It is called *rukkhādanī* because, being born on a tree, it eats—that is, destroys—that [tree].

*Adda* is for harming; *yu*, *nadādi*, and elision of *da*. *Vanda* is used in the senses of salutation and praise; with the suffix *a*, in the feminine, and with the suffix *ka* in the sense of identity, its vowel becomes long.
*Rukkharuhā* is also *jīvantikā*. Two [meanings] refer to the *cittaka* plant. *Citi* is used in the senses of harming and fragrance; with the suffix *ṇvu*.
"Named after fire" means having a name that is a synonym for fire. *Pāṭhī* is also [used here]; this [word] is masculine.
581. Two [names] for the *gaṇa* (the host of spirits): *akka*. It is called *akka* because its name is synonymous with *sūriya* (the sun).

It scatters (*vikirati*), thus it is *vikiraṇa*; [the suffix] *yu* [is added]. *Assi*, *akkavha*, *vasuka*, *apphoṭa*, *mandāra*, and *akkapaṇṇa* are also [names]. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.80):

"In the masculine, *akka*, *akkavha*, and *apphoṭa* [refer to] *vanamālya* and *parājita*. *Rudda* [is another name]. *Mandāra* refers to the *devaduma* (the divine tree) and also to the *pāribhaddaka*.
In that *akka* tree, that which has white flowers is the *alakkā*. Because it is sufficient (*alaṃ*) due to its whiteness, the *akka* is an *alakkā*;

the substitution of *ḷ* occurs in the sense of ornamenting (*ala* bhūsane). It is also [called] *patāpa*. This pair refers to the *chinnaruha* (the wound-healing plant). A creeper that has become putrid is a *pūtilatā*;
or, according to the rule "pū pavane," it is called *pūti* because it purifies away disease and impurity; such a creeper is a *pūtilatā*. The root *guḷ* means to protect.
Co, *nadādi*. *Gara* means "to sprinkle. *Amatā* is also [called] *madhupaṇṇī*. Because its leaves are like honey, it is *madhupaṇṇī*. There are two types in the *dhanuseniya* [group]:
that which resembles *vacā* in its leaves, and the one with a smooth bark used for bowstrings. Precisely because it is a modification of *mubbā*, the bowstring is called "mubbī";
from the root *mubba* (to bind), with the suffix *a*, it becomes *mubbā*. It is *madhurasā* because of its sweet nature. *Devī*.
Moraṭā also [is a name for this plant]. From the root *mura*, meaning "to tremble," and the suffix *-aṭa*, [it forms] *moraṭā*.
582. There are two names for *makkaṭiyā* (the itchy vine). Because it produces itch (*kacchu*) in monkeys (*kapīnaṃ*), that is, in apes (*vānarānaṃ*), it is called *kapikacchu*.
*Kapikaccu* is also [a form]. Because its touch is painful, it is *duphassa*. It is also *attaguttā*, *jaḍā*, *abyaṇḍā*, *kaṇḍūrā*, *pāvusāyinī*, and *sūkasimbī*.
“That which is avoided by people because it produces an itch through contact (*phassa*) is called *attaguttā*—that is, one who is guarded and protected by oneself.
It comes into being and is born in the rainy season (*pāvusa-utu*); the suffix *-inī* is applied. A gourd (*simbi*) covered with bristles (*sūka*) is a *sūkasimbi*;

the final vowel is shortened. There are two [words] for the leaf of a frog (*maṇḍūkaparṇiya*). *Maja* means purity (*suddhi*); the suffix *-ṭha* is applied. *Kāsa* means luster (*ditti*); the suffix *-a* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), and the vowel is shortened.”

*Samaṅgā* and *yojanavallī*. It is called *samaṅgā* because it possesses (*samaṅgati*) [qualities]; the suffix *a*. That creeper whose length is a *yojana* is *yojanavallī*. Both [terms] refer to the *vanatittikā* plant.

[The root] *amba* means "to sound"; with the suffix *ṭha*, [it becomes *ambā*]. Or, from *ava* meaning "to protect," there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). From *pā* meaning "to protect," with the suffix *ṭha*, [it becomes *pā*].

*Setā* and *pāpacelī* [are also names for this]. It is called *setā* because it is joined with white color; the suffix *a*. Both [terms] refer to the *kaṭukarohiṇī* plant. [The root] *kaṭa* means "to rain," "to cover," or "to go."

U, kaṭu, nārī. It is called *kaṭukarohiṇī* because it grows (*ruhati*) while having a pungent taste (*kaṭukarasa*); from the root *ruha* (to grow), with the suffix *yu*, belonging to the *nadādi* class.
"Kaṭukarohiṇī" is this name taken as a whole; it is also called *kaṭurohiṇī*. 583.
There is a pair [of names] for *kharamañjarī*, known as "cacasima. It is so called because one wipes (*apamajjanti*) clothes and such things with it.
*Apāmārga* (Achyranthes aspera) has a long prefix (*upasagga*). *Sikharaṇī* means "having a crest" (*sikhara + ini*). *Dhāmārgava* and *vimukhapuṣpī* [also refer to it].
"In the *Ghosaka* [lexicon], *dhāmārgava* is considered masculine in the sense of *kharamañjarī*. *Vimukhapuṣpī* means "one whose flower faces away. These two [names] refer to *kaṇā*.
That by which bile (*pitta*) ripens or becomes disturbed is *pipphalī*, according to the *nadādi* class. *Māgadhī* means "born in Magadha" or "belonging to the Magadhans."
Or it is *māgadhī* because it first arose there, or because it is produced there in abundance; thus it is designated by that conventional name. *Vedehī*, *kaṇā*, and *kolā* [are synonyms].
This belongs to the people of Videha, hence it is *vedehī*. *Kaṇā* has various meanings; and it is said: "The *kaṇā* is long pepper (*pipphalī*) and cumin (*jājī*).
The dyad refers to the *tikaṇṭaka* (three-thorned plant). A thorn for cows is a *gokaṇṭaka*; or, a thorn stuck in the earth is a *gokaṇṭaka*.
*Siṅgha-ghāyana* is *āṭo*. *Palaṅkasā* is also *sādukaṇṭho*. In the *Yuttarāsnāya*, *palaṅkasā* is used for *thiyaṃ*.
*Sādukaṇṭho* is also used for *vikaṅkata*. There are two [names] for *hatthipipphali*: *kolavalli*—it is a creeper (*vallī*) named after that [fruit], or it is short;
*ibhapipphalī* means the *pipphalī* of elephants (*ibha*), that is, of *hatthīs*. *Kapivallī* is also *vasiro*. *Vasiro* has various meanings.
Vasira, apāmārga, sāmuddalavaṇa, and hatthipipphali—this [group] is masculine (puma). 584.
There are two [plants] for the purpose of clearing foul odors, which is also called *uggagandhā*. *Golomī* is that which grows in the place where the hair of cows is shorn;
*vacā* is speech (*viyatti*), with the suffix *a* in the sense of instrument; it is also *satapabbikā*. *Vacā* is divided into white and red roots.

There are two types; among them, the white variety is called *hemavatī* in the *Amarakośa* (14.102–3). There are two names for *apphoṭā*: it is called *kaṇṇī* because its flowers have the shape of an ear (*kaṇṇa*).
Because it grows on a mountain (*giri*), it is *girikaṇṇī*. It is called *aparājitā* because it overcomes diseases and other afflictions. There are two names for *kalasī*:
it is called *sīhapucchi* because its clusters of blossoms have the form of a lion’s tail (*sīhapuccha*). *Pañhi* is said to mean "not thin" (*appatanu*).
*Paṇṇī*: that which has leaves (*paṇṇa*) is *paṇṇī*. *Puthupaṇṇī* (the broad-leaved): it is also a cave; it is *puthupaṇṇī* because its leaves are broad and not closely joined.
Regarding *guhā* (cave), there is the "lion's tail" [reading] and the "thiyaṃ chamātuke" [reading]; in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.93) it says so. There are two [types] regarding *sālapaṇṇī*.
It is *sālapaṇṇī* because of its spreading like the leaves of a *sāla* tree. Or, it is *sālapaṇṇī* because its leaves are beautiful (*sāla*) and well-joined (*paṇṇa*). *Thu*.
*Gatitheriyāsu*, *iro*, *thiro*. 585. Two [terms] refer to the *kaṇṭakārikā* plant.
It is called *nididdhikā* because it burns up (*niddahati*) a handful of thorns; [the suffix] *-ṇvu* is used here. Because she causes fear and is thus like a tigress, she is called *byagghī*;
[the terms] *brahatī* and *khuddā* also apply. Two [terms] refer to the *nīli* tree. [The root] *nīla* means "blue. Because of its blue color...
*Nīlī*, *nadādi*, *inī*, *nīlinī*, *kāḷā*, and also *tutthā*.
*Kāḷā* refers to the plant *kaṇhativutā*; *nīlī* refers to the *yojanavalli* creeper;
*tutthā* refers to *paṇḍa* and *rasañjana*; and [it is used] for *sukhumelā* and *nīliyā*—according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.94–5).
The word *guñjā* has two meanings. [Derivation: From the root *jañj* (to fight), with the suffix *uko*; from the root *assi* (to throw);
from the root *guj* (to sound), with the suffix *a* and the addition of the nasal *bindu*. Its synonyms are:
*dumē*, *sā*, *rattikā*, *rattadala*, *cūḷāmaṇī*, *kākaciñcī*, *tulābīja*, *kaṇhalā*, and *sikhaṇḍinī*.
*Dvaya* is *maheruya*. This very *maheru* is known as *kaṇṭakavatī*. That which has a hundred roots is *sata-mūlī*.
It is called *satāvarī* because it wards off (*āvarati*) a hundred diseases; the root *vara* is used in the senses of warding off (*āvaraṇa*) and desire (*icchā*).
Alternatively, "Satā" and "Āvarī" are two names for it. For it is said in the *Amarakośa* (14.100): "Satamūlī, Bahusutā, Bhīru, Indīvarī, Varī."

586. *Ativisa* is twofold: *mahāvīriya* and *osadha*. *Mahosadha* is garlic (*lasuṇa*). According to Rudda, it is also *suṇṭhī*. It is called *ativisa* because it spreads excessively in medicinal preparations; it is also *visa*, *aruṇa*, and *siṅgī*. Regarding *aruṇa*:

"The word *aruṇa* is used for the dawn, the color of twilight, the thighless one (the sun), the sound *niḥ*, the tawny color, leprosy, and as a substance; its gender depends on the word it qualifies."
“Aruṇā, ativisā, sāmā, mañjaṭṭhā, ativutā, usīrā, ativisā, siṅgī, maggura, vallabhā. These two [verses] concern *somarāji*. [The root] *vaka* means to take up.
Because it is made equal to *soma*, the creeper is called *somavallikā*; the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). It has black fruit, and its fruit is also putrid.

*Dvayaṃ dāruhaliddārukkhe*: There are two [names] for *dāruhaliddā* (wood-haliddi) and *arukkha* (tree). From the root *dar*, meaning "to split" (*vidāraṇe*), with the suffix *bo*; the short vowel becomes long (*rassa bo*), yielding *dābbī*, which begins with a long vowel and belongs to the *nadādi* class.

Because it has the color of *haliddā* (turmeric) wood, it is called *dāruhaliddā*; it is also simply *haliddā*. *Dvayaṃ biḷaṅge*: There are two [names] for *biḷaṅga* (ginger). The roots *aṅga*, *raṇga*, and *laṅga* belong to the *daṇḍaka* group of roots meaning "to go" (*gatyatthā*).
With the suffix *a* and the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*, it becomes *biḷaṅgaṃ*. That which has variegated grains (*taṇḍula*) is *taṇḍula*; it is also a type of insect (*kimisatta*).
587. There are two names for *samantaduddhāya*: *nuha* and *uggiraṇe*. It begins with the letter *na*, and its name is great.

*Sīhuṇḍo*, *vajiradumo*, and *guḷā* are also [names for it]. There are two names for *dakkhā*: *muddikā* because of its connection with soft qualities (*mudu-guṇa*), and *madhurasa* because of its sweet taste.

Therefore, it is stated in the medical treatises (*vejjagantha*) that "sweet, salty, bitter, sour, pungent, and astringent" are the tastes; due to that [sweetness], it is called *madhurasa*. *Gotthanī*...
It is also *dakkhā*. This is a triad concerning *yaṭṭhimadhukā*. It is called *madhuka* because of its sweet taste (*madhurasa*); the suffix *-ko* is used here in the sense of comparison.

Because it has the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*), it is a *yaṭṭhi*, and because it is sweet (*madhura*), it is a *madhukā*; thus, it is *yaṭṭhimadhukā*. It stands (*tiṭṭhati*) in a state of sweetness (*madhurasabhāva*), hence it is *madhulaṭṭhikā*;
the *lo* is substituted for the long vowel, and the suffix *-ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakattha*). There is also the reading “*madhuyaṭṭhikā*,” and it is said: “*madhukaṃ klītakaṃ*.”
*Yaṭṭhi*, *madhuka*, and *madhuyaṭṭhikā* [refer to the same plant]. (Amara 14.109.588). There are two names for the *vātiṅgaṇa* (eggplant).

It is called *vātiṅgaṇa* because it is counted among those that remove wind (*vāta-hara*). [The root] *bhaṇḍ* means to revile; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it belongs to the *nadādi* class. By the addition of the letter *ṭ*, it is also *bhaṇṭākī*;
this is also the name for the large variety. "The *vātiṅgaṇa* is the *vāttāku*."
Vāttāka, sākaveḷu, bhaṇḍākī, rājakumbhaṇḍa, vāttākī,
and duppahāsinī— thus [it is said] in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 14.114.

*Rabhaso*. There are two [names] for *brahatiyā*: it is called *vāttākī* because it makes one free from disease (*nirāmaya*); it also refers to the *vātiṅgaṇa* plant. *Brahā* is in the sense of "living" (*vutti*); the suffix *-to* is added according to the *nadādi* group.
There are two [names] for *gorakkhataṇḍula*; and it is stated in another treatise (*tantantare*): "The *gaṅgerukī*, the *nāgabalā*, and likewise the *gorakkhataṇḍulā*.

It is called *nāgabalā* because its strength is like the strength of a serpent (*nāga*) due to its quality of removing diseases; the root *jhasa* has the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsa*). There are two [names] for the *aggisikhā* plant.

*Lāṅgalī* because its root resembles a plow (*naṅgala*); *lo* is elided, and the vowel is lengthened. There is also a reading *naṅgalī*. It is *sāradī* because it grows during the autumn season (*sarada*).

589. This triad refers to the plantain tree (*kadali*). It is *rambhā* because people delight (*ramanti*) in it; *bho* [is the vocative particle]. *Kada* means "to kill"; with the suffix *alo*, it belongs to the *nada*-class.

*Muc* means "to release"; with the suffix *ṇo*, it forms *moca*. This dyad refers to the cotton plant (*kappāsi*). It is *kappāsī* because its fruit produces cotton (*kappāsa*) which is of benefit to the world.
*Karoti* means a snare, a river, and so forth. *Vada* refers to a nun, a sheep, and also one who lives at the edge of the ocean.
As for *samuddantā*, it refers to cotton (*kappāsī*), a scale, and the *durālabhā* plant.
If the cotton grows in a forest, it is called *bhāradvājī*.

Two [names] for *paṇṇalatā*: a creeper born in the world of the *nāgas* is a *nāgalatā*. It takes on a copper color (*tamba-vaṇṇaṃ*), thus it is *tambūlī*; [it belongs to the class beginning with] *assu* and *nadā*.

Or, that which belongs to the *tambūla* is *tambūlī*. It is also called *tambūlavallī* and *nāgavallī*. "Tambūla" is the name for the collection of mixtures consisting of fruit, leaf, powder, and so forth;
the creeper used for that purpose is *tambūlavallī*, the creeper of the *nāga*-world. Two [names] for *dhātaki*: this is *tambapupphī*.
Used as an intoxicant (*majja*). The fragrant flowers known as *dhātakī*. Because its flowers resemble a mass of fire, it is called *aggijālā*.
It causes an excessive duration [of life], thus it is *dhātakī*;

[it belongs to the class beginning with] *nada*. 590. This pair is *sukkativutā*. That which has three lines of bark (*tacarāji*) woven into it is *tivutā*. Three folds (*puṭa*) are the lines of bark.
*Tissā* has three layers. *Saralā*, *tibhaṇḍī*, *rocanī*, and *devanī* (according to Ka. are synonyms. These two refer to *kaṇhativutā*.
It is called *sāmā* because it makes the body thin; that is, by acting as a purgative, it causes the body and disease to subside (*sāyati*).
“*Sāmā* refers to the dark-colored, to an old child, to the green color, and to a river.”
“*Tikaṇha*, *tivutā*, *guṇḍā*, *sārivā*, *ayaminī*.”—*Rabhasa*: [the root] *kala* is used in the sense of counting;

*kara* or *kāra* in the sense of doing; *a* is a suffix. *Kāḷā* (black) is feminine; it refers to the plant *kaṇhativutā*, as well as to indigo (*nīlī*) and *yojanavallī*. It also refers to *masūravidalā*, *addhacandā*, and *kāḷamesikā*.
Two [names] refer to *kukkuṭasiṅgī*. It is called *siṅgī* because its flowers resemble horns; it is also known as *kuḷīrasiṅgī* and *vakkaṅgī*. Two [names] [refer to this].
Regarding the plant known as *reṇukā*, it is called *reṇukā* among merchants and others. Its fruit is like a peppercorn (*marīca*). [The root] *reṇu* is used in the senses of "going" and "sound";
[the suffixes] *ṇu* and *kap* have been stated [by grammarians]. It is also called *dvijā*, *hareṇū*, *kontī*, and *bhasmagandhanī*. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.120):
"The word *hareṇu* refers to the pea (*kalāya*) and also to the female *reṇukā*. [This is from the lexicon] *Rudda*.
591. Two [names] for the *phālaka* (castor-oil plant): it is called *hirivera* because it grew from the body of the goddess named Hirī;
it is called *vāra* because it wards off (*vāreti*), or because its name is *vāri*; on the stem it is *vāla*. *Udījha* is another name for *kesambu*;

it is *udījha* because it grows in the region of *udīcī*, and it is called *kesambu* because it possesses all the names of both *kesa* (hair) and *ambu* (water). Two [names] for the *bimbikā* (the bimba fruit tree).
Its ripe fruit is red. It is called *bimbikā* because its fruit resembles the color of lips; for it is with its fruit that the lip is compared.
[It is also] *tuṇḍikerī* and *pilupaṇṇī*. The pair refers to *seleyya*;
that which grows on rocks, possesses a fragrant juice, and is known as *selaja* (rock-born). [It is found] on stone.
*Pāsāṇa* is to be understood as *seleyya*. *Asma-puppha* refers to the flower of a stone (*asma*), or alternatively, it is the black cardamom (*kāḷānusāri*).

The pair [of terms] refers to *elā*, which is known as *phālā*. From the root *ila* (to go), with the suffixes *a* and *issa*, [it is formed]. It is called *bahulā* because it takes many meanings (*attha*), or because it cuts away (*lunāti*) many diseases (*roga*); it is also the moon’s halo (*candavālā*).

592. The pair [of terms] known as *kuṭṭha* refers to the fragrant grass. From the root *kuṭ* meaning "to cut," with the suffix *tha*. Alternatively, it is *kuṭṭha* because it stands (*tiṭṭhati*) upon the earth (*kuyaṃ*).
Because it is the name of a disease, it is a disease; likewise, the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.126) and *Rabhasa* state:
"The *kovera*, the *bhāsura*, the *kuṭṭha*, the *pāribhāvya*, and that which is called *gada*. It is also *pākala* and *uppalu*. This is the pair.
Regarding *kevattīmutthaka*:
It is said—“Light, floating, and wild, known by the name *kuṭannaṭa*;
it grows in the shape of a frog amidst a mass of water-moss.”
*Vāneyyaṃ* means "grown in the forest"; it is derived from *vane*. *Keṣattīmutthaka* and *paṇḍo* [are examples]. *Soṇakosa* and *kuṭannaṭo* [are also names].

The root *kuṭ* means "to cut," while *naṭ* means "to bind" or "to perish. *Kuṭannaṭa* is a collective name [for these plants]. There is the addition of the nasal *ṇiggahīta*. *Dāsapura* is also [an example].

Plants such as creepers that end with the ripening of fruit are called *osadhi* merely by way of their genus (*jāti*), but not [specifically] the three myrobalans (*tiphalaka*) or the *kakkola* and so forth. The suffix *i* is applied; however, the plural number [is used for the class].
Precisely because of its abundance of meanings, it is also seen with the singular ending (*osadhi*). It refers exclusively to the feminine gender.

*Osadha* (the neuter form) refers to everything that is not a genus (*ajātika*). Because it brings about the ripening of fruit, anything other than a genus that effects the removal of disease is called *osadha*.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sabba*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that even a substance related to a genus of medicine is denotable by the term *osadha*, since it possesses the desired quality of being a cause for the action of removing disease.
From the word *osadha*, the suffix *ṇo* is applied in the sense of genus (*jāti*). However, some, instead of reading the text as "only that which is of the genus of medicine is *osadha*;

everything else is non-genus" (*osadhijātimattamosadhaṃ sabbamajātiyan*), read it as "only that medicinal substance which is of the genus of medicine is *bhesajja*; everything else is non-genus" (*osadhijātimattaṃ bhesajjaṃ sabbamajātiyan*).

This [variant reading] should not be accepted here, because a distinction has been stated for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the two words *osadhi* and *osadha*, which are used with partial modification of their forms.
It is also stated in the *Amarakośa*: "The term *osadhi* applies to those things possessing a genus (*jāti*), while everything that lacks a genus is called *osadha*" (Amarakośa 2.4.135).
In this context, one *m*-sound has been inserted on the side of the proponent’s own position by way of traditional grammatical authority (*āgama*).

593. The ten kinds of potherbs (*sāka*) are considered to begin with roots; it is so called because one is able (*sakoti*) [to eat] by means of them. Among these, "root" refers to radishes and the like.
The leaf of the *bākucā* and others; the sprout of the bamboo and others; the tip of the rattan and others; the bulb of the blue lotus and others; the core of the palmyra palm and others;
the fruit of the *kumbhaṇḍa* and others; the rind of the citron and others; the flower of the *vaṅgasūsenā* and others;
the mushroom of the *ahichatta* and others.
594. *Dvayaṃ eḷagale*. It cleans away scabs by means of its hair (*pakārena*), thus it is a *papunnāṭa*. [The root] *pu* means "to purify" (*pavane*); it belongs to the *kiyādi* group;
the suffix *-aṭo* is applied, and there is the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta*. It shears off the scabs of the *eḷaga* (the uraṇa-deer), thus it is an *eḷagala*.

It is a *daddugha*, a *cakkamaddaka*, and also called an *uraṇa*. It destroys scabs, thus it is a *daddugha*; for the root *han* becomes *gha*. Because of its circular shape, it is a *cakka* (wheel); it crushes that *daddu* (scab), thus it is a *cakkamaddaka*.

The *cakkamaddaka* (wheel-crusher). The one called *uraṇa* is the one called *mesa* (ram). The *taṇḍuleyya*, which has small leaves and small seeds with leaves touching the ground, is also named *appamārisa*.

It is called *taṇḍuleyya* because it is born from rice (*taṇḍula*); [the suffix] *-eyya* is used here. Because its leaves are small, it is "small" (*appa*), and because it has the bitterness of the *mārisa* fruit, it is a *mārisa*; thus it is *appamārisa* (small-mārisa).
*Dvayaṃ jīvantiyaṃ*: this is the form *jīvantiya*, meaning "the end of one who lives," such as *nadādi*. From the other [side], it is *yu*, such as *nadādi*.
*Jīvā*, *jīvanīyā*, *madhupi*. “*Heṃ nu nve nī*”. *Dvayaṃ jīvake*: this is included within the eight groups (*aṭṭhavagga*).
He is well-known among merchants by this very name. Because of his sweet nature, he is *madhuraka*; he causes to live, thus he is *jīvaka*, with the suffix *ṇvu*.
“Jīvaka, Siṅgaka, Seka,
Dīghāyu, Kuccasīsaka;
Rassaṅga, Madhura, Sādu.”
“The long-lived insect.
This is also [stated] in the *Amarakośugghāṭaṇa-ṭīkā* and in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*. 595.
Two [names] for garlic: that whose root is white in color; it is called *mahākanda* (large bulb) because its bulb is larger than that of the onion (*palaṇḍu*).
Due to the deficiency of the *ambila* (sour) taste, there is the substitution of *la* for *ra*, shortening of vowels, and the change of *na* to *ṇ*.

Alternatively, from the root *lasa* meaning "to shine," with the suffixes *yu*, *assu*, and *ṇatta*, we have *lasuna*. It is also called *mahosadha*, *ariṭṭha*, and *rasona*. There are two types: red-rooted and green.
*Palaṇḍu* is so called because of its fragrance; it has a beautiful bulb, hence it is *sukandaka*. It is also known as *kraṇasvananī*.
Two [names] for *paṭola*: *paṭa* means "to go"; *paṭola* is so called because it takes (*lāti*) a sharp (*paṭu*) taste, or because it is a creeper (*ussā*).

It is bitter due to its bitter taste. The suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of the base itself. Two [names] for the plant known as *kesarāñjana*, which is called *bhiṅgarāja*: *bhiṅga* refers to a bee;
having made [the plant] the color of that [bee], it colors them, thus it is *bhiṅgarāja*. From the root *muc* in the sense of "releasing," with the suffixes *-ava* and *-ussa*, it becomes *mākkava*.
596. Furthermore, this is "renewed" (*punannava*); even though it is old, it becomes new again through that state of being joined (*yogitā*), thus it is "renewed.

It destroys swelling (*sotha*), hence *sothaghāta*; the root *han* becomes *ghāta*. In the two words *anūpaja* and *sāka*: the root *tud* means "to pain"; the suffix *to* is used in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*).

That which has lost its "pressure" (*tunna*) during chewing is *vitunna*. The root *sad* is used in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "concluding"; the suffix *to* is applied, there is a substitution of *anna*, and the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

The word *kāravella* has two meanings. It is called *kāravello* because it hangs down in a loathsome form due to its bitter taste (*tittarasatā*). [The suffix] *-illa* follows the roots *ussā* (to be red) and *ratta* (red), while *lavi* (to hang down) is preceded by *ku*.

*Sasu* means to injure; with the suffixes *avo* and *nadādi*, it becomes *assu*. From the root *he* (to eat) and *khā* (to eat), with the suffix *le-khyā*, we have *lābu*. This triad refers to the gourd (*lābuya*). *Tumba* means to eat.
Because it consumes (*tumbati*) bile (*pitta*), it is called *tumbī*; it belongs to the *nadādi* group. With the prefix *na-* (negation), from the root *lamb* (to hang down)...

In *avasaṃsane*, there is the elision of *u*; *nassa* becomes *attaṃ*. *Alābu*: according to the Pāṇinīyas, by *uṇādi* 1.87, the prefix *ā-* combined with *lamb* in the sense of "hanging down" forms *ālābu*.
According to the Kātantrikas and likewise the Chandas, for us [the Moggallānas], having made the vowel short, it is *alābu*. When the suffix is elided (*alope*), it is *lābu*.
By metaphorical treatment as non-different (*abhedopacārena*), all three fruits are feminine gender; the word *sā* indicates the meaning of the feminine gender.

597. Two [terms] for *sampuṣka*. It is *eḷāluka* because it takes (*lāti*) water (*iraṃ*, i.e., *vāriṃ*) due to its abundance thereof. For the *Nānātthasaṅgaha* states: “*Irā* is used for water, liquor, earth, and speech.
[The suffix] *u* is added after *thi* in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*), and *ko* follows.

From the root *kuk* (to take), with the suffixes *aro* and *nadādi*, and the prefix *ussa*, it is so called because it produces wind (*kaṃ*) and phlegm (*kapha*); thus it is *kakkarī*. Elsewhere, the vowel is elided, as in *kakaḷī*. Two [terms].

*Kumbhaṇḍa*. It is called *kumbhaṇḍa* because its fruit is the size of a jar (*kumbha*); the suffix *-ṇḍa* is used here in a different sense. Alternatively, it is *kumbhaṇḍa* because it "swells like a jar" (*kumbho viya ḍeti*), with the addition of the vowel *i*.

Or, from the root *kus*, meaning "to cut," with the suffix *-aṇḍa* and the addition of the vowel *i*. Or, it is *kumbhaṇḍa* because it "swells the wind" (*kaṃ vātaṃ umbheti*), with the suffix *-aṇḍa*.
From the root *vall*, meaning "to enclose," with the suffix *-ibha*; it shines among all species of creepers due to the greatness of its fruit.
Or, it is called *vallibha* because it flows (*dibbati*), like *kakkāru*.
The pair refers to the *kakkariya* plant used for cattle-herding. *Indavāruṇī* is the wine (*vāruṇī*) of Indra or Sakka.

It is called *visālā* because it specifically causes the discharge (*sarati*) or destroys phlegm, bile, and so forth; for it is said: "The *sarameha* plant cures leprosy; *visālā* destroys phlegm and bile."

Regarding *dabbaguṇe*: it is called *visālā* because by means of it one spreads out (*visarati*) or purges (*virecati*). There are two [roots] for the suffix *-asaka*. It is called *vatthu* because the quality of alkalinity (*khāraguṇa*) dwells (*vasati*) in it.
The root *vas* is used in the sense of dwelling (*nivāse*), while *ratthu* and *vasa* are used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsāyaṃ*); thus, phlegm, wind, and bile dwell in it, hence it is *vatthu*.

*Vatthuleyyaka* is its collective name. The root *laya* means to cause to dissolve; it causes all defects to dissolve, hence it is *leyyaka*, with the suffix *-ṇvu* added to the stem *assa*; and it is also *vatthu*.
*Leyyaka* refers to *vatthuleyyaka*. "Mauṃ-heṃ. 598.
Two [terms] refer to radish (*mūlaka*). In the suffix *ṇvu*, it is *mūlaka*. *Ca* is used in the senses of reproaching and threatening; [the suffixes] *u*, *assu*, and *muṃ* follow.

Two [terms] refer to the *kalambuka* plant. *Tamu* is used in the sense of doubt; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *banto*. Regarding *ke*: because it hangs (*lambati*) in the water (*jale*), it is called *kalambuka*; [the suffix] *ṇvu*.
It is tears. *Upodikā* is so called because its water has departed (*udakaṃ apagatā*).

*Kāsamadda*, *jhajjharī*, *maggava*, and others are varieties of potherbs (*sāka*), specific types of greens. It is called *kāsamadda* because it crushes cough (*kāsaṃ maddati*). *Kaca* [is a root meaning] to scold or threaten;
with the suffix *-aro*, belonging to the *nada*-group, it becomes *jhajjharī*. It is also *kanakalā*. It is called [so] because it takes in wind (*phaṃ vātaṃ gaṇhāti*).
"Phaggavo, laugh at you, Phaggavo, ‘pai-teṃ-khā’.
(599–600) Two [words] are difficult to understand. It is called *saddalo* because its beautiful leaf (*dala*) has attained the status of a recitation of auspicious verses;

or alternatively, it is *saddalo* because by means of it the Brahmins take up—that is, utter, speak, or recite—the sound, namely the sound of auspicious verses. The root *duvbī* is used in the sense of harming.

*Dubba*: it is called *dubba* because it wards off (*vāreti*) misfortune (*avamangala*) and ill-fortune (*dubbati*); or, etymologically (*nerutto*), it is *dubbā* because it wards off bad omens (*dunnimitta*) and the like.
It is also known as *satapabbikā*, *bhaggavī*, *anantā*, and *ruhā*. If that *dubbā* is green and white, it is named *golomī*; it is called *golomī* because it resembles a cow’s tail (*goloma*).
It is also known as *satavīriyā*, *gaṇḍālī*, and *sakulākkhaka*.

Two [terms] for *bhaddamutta* (urine). *Gu* means sound; *do*. *Muca* means to release; *to*. Because it removes disease (*rogaharaṇattā*), it is both auspicious (*bhadde*) and urine (*mutte*), hence *bhaddamutta*;
[formed with the suffix] *nvāmyeyejījī*. Two [terms] for sugarcane (*ucchumhi*). It takes (*lāti*) the juice (*rasaṃ*), thus *rasāla*;

[the vowel] is long. *Isu* means desire; *u*. Or, *usa* means to burn; *u*. The *s* becomes *ch*; the preceding *issu* remains; there is a dissimilar doubling (*asarūpadvittaṃ*); *ucchu*; [used] in the masculine (*pume*).

A set of four [terms] regarding the bamboo (*vaṃsa*). The root *vī* means "to go"; with the suffix *ḷu*, it becomes *tacova* (its essence). With the root *vī* meaning "to go," the suffix *u* is added, there is the augment *n*, and the substitution of *ṇ*;

thus, from *vanati* ("it grows" or "it accumulates"), we have *vaṃso*. From the root *vana* meaning "accumulation," with the suffix *so*, or from *vasa* meaning "dwelling," with the instrumental suffix *a* and the augment of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), we have *vaṃso*.

It has a hundred joints, bears barley-like fruit, and is called *makkaro*; it is also called *tejo*. It is called *makkaro* because one "cleanses" (*makkaroti*) by means of it; this is a technical designation (*saññā*).

a. *Tikaṃ pabbe*. *Pabba* [is derived from] *pūraṇe* (to fill), *pabbaṃ*. *Phala* [is derived from] *visaraṇe* (to scatter), with the suffix *u*, and the substitution of *ḷ* for *ra*. *Gantha* [is derived from] *ganthane* (to tie), with the suffix *i*;
with the modification of the vowel (*vaṇṇavikāre*), it becomes *gaṇṭhi*, which is masculine.

Those bamboos (*veṇū*) that are shaken by the wind (*aniladdhutā*) and sound because they have been perforated by insects and the like, they would be called *kīcakā*; [derived from] *cakī* [in the sense of] *āmasane* (to touch), with the suffix *ṇvu*, and the transposition of the preceding and following consonants, thus *kīcakā*.

601. *Dvayaṃ naḷe*. From the root *nī* (to lead), with the suffix *ala*; from *ḷattaṃ*; from *dham* (sound) and *aggi* (fire) in conjunction; from *yu*; and *poṭagalo* is also used here. *Dvayaṃ kāse*.
That which goes (*gacchati*) to mutual contact (*puṭaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṃsaggaṃ*) is *poṭagalo*; the *m* becomes *l*. From *kāsa* (in the sense of shining), with the suffix *a*;

this is not feminine. *Dvayaṃ sare*. From *tija* (sharpening), with the suffix *yu*. That by which they run (*saranti*) is *saro*. In the masculine, with the suffix *a* in the sense of a technical term (*saññā*). From *sara* (injury).

Or [the word] *vā*. *Gundu* is also used here. The root of *bīraṇa*, a specific kind of grass with white flowers, is called *usīra*. [The roots] *vasa*, *kantiya*, *usa*, and *dāha* take the suffix *īra*.
*Pubba*, *vassu*, *abhaya*, *nalada*, *sebya*, *jalāsaya*, *amaṇāla*, and *lāmajjaka* are also synonyms. *Haritakī*, *abhayā*, and *paṇḍu* refer to the *harītakī* fruit;
*usīra* and *nibbhaya* refer to the fragrant root (*usīra*) in three genders.
*Jalāsayo* means a reservoir or a place where water is held; *usīra*, however, refers to the fragrant root (vacha).

*Sebyā* means those who are worthy of service (*sevārahe*). 602. The triad refers to *kusa* grass. *Kusa* is used in the sense of cutting (*chedane*), while *varaha* is used in the senses of excellence (*pādhānye*), reviling (*paribhāsanahiṃ*), and taking (*sādānesu*). *Isa* is used in the sense of burning (*du paritāpe*). *Abbhō*, *dabbhō*, and *kutho* also mean a sacred grass (*pavitraṃ*).
The two [plants] known as *gandhakheḍa* are types of grass; for it is said: “Bhūtīna and *gandhakheḍa*, fragrant and fond of cow dung.
Now, what is the difference between this and *rāmakappūra*? *Rāmakappūra* has many joints and possesses the fragrance of camphor.
*Gandhakheḍa*, however, has leaves similar to those of the *ikaḍa* tree, possesses the nature of branches, and clings to the ground; for this very reason, it is called *bhūtinaka*.
*Tiṇa* and *bhūtinaka* mean grass clinging to the ground; [the suffix] *ko* is used in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*).

There are two terms for intoxicating grasses such as those of cattle: from the root *ghas* (to eat), with the suffix *ṇo*; and from *yu* (to mix), with the suffix *aso*. There are two terms for the *pūga* tree: from the root *pūja* (worship/adornment), with the suffix *ṇo*, forming *pūgo*; and from *kamu* (desire), with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Ghoṇṭā* is also used for it, according to Rudra:

"The *ghoṇṭā* is found among the *badara* and *pūga* trees. (603) There are two terms for the *tāla* tree: from the root *tala* (to stand firmly), belonging to the *curādi* class, with the suffix *a*; and because it splits the wind and so forth, it is called *vibhedikā*.
“Wind-dispelling, nourishing, and also a destroyer of skin eruptions here;
blood-and-bile-removing and sweet—the palmyra (tāla) is considered to possess these seven qualities.

This is the quality of the substance. It is also the king of grasses (*tiṇarāja*). The pair refers to the date-palm (*khajjūriya*). [The root] *khajj* is used in the sense of eating and piercing; [the suffix] *-ūra*, as in the class beginning with *nadā*. [The root] *sid* is used in the sense of releasing and lubricating, [with the suffix] *-i*; or [from] *sandi* in the sense of flowing, [with the suffix] *-i*, and the penultimate vowel becomes long. *Sindi*.

604. The seven [species] beginning with *hintāla* are called "grass-trees" (*tiṇapādapa*) because they are grasses due to their lack of solidity, and they are trees because of their commonality with trees in drinking water through their roots.
[The root] *tiṇa* means "to eat. A *hintāla* is inferior to a *tāla* in size; there is an inversion of word order, and it is short.
It is called *nāḷikera* because it grows like a tube (*nāḷi*). The suffix *-ira* is used in other senses, as in *konto* and *nāḷikera*. There is also *lāṅgalī*.
“*Lāṅgalī* and *nāḷikera* [are found]; *lāṅgalī* is in *sirapāṇi*”—thus says Rabhasa in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (14.168). Because of its shape resembling a palm fruit (*tāla*), it is called *tāḷī*;

the syllable *ḷ* [is substituted], with the suffix *ī* in the sense of comparison. Alternatively, from the root *taḷ* meaning "to strike," belonging to the *curādi*, *nadādi*, and *tāḷī* groups, we have *tāḷī*.
From the root *kit* meaning "to dwell" and "to remove disease," with the suffix *ṇvu* and the *ī* due to the *nadādi* group, we have *ketakī*; this refers to the plant. This is the feminine form.
The commentary on the Araññavagga is finished.
6. Commentary on the Araññādivagga 605.
There are nine names for a mountain (*pabbata*). *Pabba* is from the root *pūraṇa* (to fill). *Gira* is from the root *niggiraṇa* (to emit); it is that which emits medicinal herbs and so forth.
*Giri*: (1) A heap of stones is a *sela*; or, it is a *sela* because stones (*silā*) abound therein;

or, from the root *sel*, meaning "to go" or "to move. (2) From the root *add*, meaning "to go" or "to beg," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class; or, from the root *add*, meaning "to harm," belonging to the *curādi* class. That which does not go (*na gacchati*) is a *naga*. That which does not move (*na calati*) is an *acala*.

A mass of stones is a *siluccaya*, meaning a height or a mound (*thūpa*). Because it possesses a peak (*sikhara*), it is *sikhari*; the suffix *-ī* indicates that it has become a distinctive mark (*tilakībhūta*).
It is called *bhūdhara* because it supports the earth (*bhuṃ bhūmiṃ dharati*); or, it is called *bhūdhara* because it is supported by the earth (*bhuyā dharīyati*).

[The suffix] *-a* is used in the sense of abundance; thus, *bhūdhara*. It is *ahāriya*; it is also a clan name (*gotta*). Because it cannot be carried to another region, it is *ahāriya*. By supporting the earth for cattle (*gavaṃ*), it protects them;

thus, it is *gotto*. This group of five [terms] refers to a stone. [The root] *ama* is in the sense of motion, sir. *Vana* and *sana* are in the sense of acquisition. It is called *pāsāṇo* because it spreads out or extends (*pasanati byāpeti*).

*Nipātanā*: from *pas* (in the sense of binding) with the suffix *yu*. From *asu* (in the sense of casting away), with the suffix *mo*; this belongs to the *rājādi* group; or from *asu* (in the sense of pervading). From *pala* (in the sense of protecting), *upalo*;
or from *upa* (in the sense of placing upon), with the suffix *alapa* as an irregular formation (*nipāta*). From *sila* (in the sense of high), with the suffix *a*; *silā*, meaning a woman. 606.

Words such as *Gijjhakūṭa* ending in *tikūṭa* are included here under the category of "curved ones" (*vaṅkādi*) by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*); furthermore, *Malaya*, *Daddura*, and others are mountains or specific types of mountains.
Vultures (*gijjhā*) are a specific kind of bird that dwell on its peak; or, it is called *Gijjhakūṭa* because it possesses a peak resembling a vulture.

It shines forth pre-eminently, thus it is *Vebhāra*. The root *aru* means "to shine. From the root *pula* in the sense of "greatness," it swells forth pre-eminently, thus it is *Vepulla*. It swallows seers (*isayo*), thus it is *Isigili*.
It meditates (*jhāyati*) in opposition to the course of the sun (*ādiccagamana*), thus it is *Viñjha*. Due to its pale-white color (*paṇḍuvaṇṇatā*), it is *Paṇḍava*; [the root is] *paṇḍa*...

Or, in the sense of a course of existence (*gati*), it is *avo*. It is *vaṅka* because of its crookedness. Two terms refer to the mountain of sunrise (*udayagiri*). In relation to the western mountains (*aparasela*), it is the eastern mountain (*pubbasela*).
It is called *udaya* because from it the sun and other luminaries rise (*udayanti*); or it is *udaya* because of its connection with the rising of the sun and so forth.

Three terms refer to the mountain of sunset (*atthagiri*). It is *mandara* because the sun is slow (*mandayati*) upon it; or it is *mandara* because the light is dull (*manda-pabha*) upon it. It is *arati* because of the lack of delight (*arati*) upon it.

*Sūriyo* means *Mandara*; the meaning is that it causes the disappearance (or non-perception) of the planets and constellations. [This is] the end of the section on nouns, verbal roots, and suffixes (*nāmadhātukāritanta*).
The pair [of terms] refers to the Himavat mountain. It is called *Himavā* because of its abundance of snow (*himappacuratā*), or because it vomits forth snow (*himaṃ vamati*);
[the suffix] *kvip* is applied, and the final consonant is dropped according to the rule for *rāja* and others. A mountain (*acala*) associated with snow is *himācala*.
607. It is called *Gandhamādana* because it intoxicates (*madayati*) or gladdens (*modayati*) the world with the scents of the fragrant substances produced upon it;

[the suffix] *yu* is applied. It is called *Kelāsa*. It is called *Cittakūṭa* because it is endowed with variegated peaks. It is called *Sudassana* because its sight is pleasant, or because it is beautiful to behold.
It is called *Kāḷakūṭa* because its peaks are black in color. It is called *Tikūṭa* because it has three peaks. These six are also specific names for mountains.
The level ground at the base of the aforementioned mountain is called the *sānu*.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the base (*pattha*) and the ridge (*sānu*) both exist upon the level ground of that mountain. It is called *pattha* because one stands firmly upon it; the *ṭha* becomes *tha*. The root *san* means "to share" (*sambhatti*);
with the suffix *ṇu*, it becomes *sānu*, meaning that which is shared or frequented (*sevīyati*). This form occurs in both masculine and feminine genders.

608. *Siṅga* is a name for a horn. From the root *kuṭ* (to burn), with the suffix *ṇo*, there is also *kūṭa* by way of grammatical rule. It is called *sikhara* because it grows (*ruhati*) like a crest (*sikha*);

this is according to etymological derivation (*nerutto*). It is called *siṅga* because it goes (*gacchati*) toward the crest; the root *iṅga* has the sense of "going," and the suffix *khalopa* [is applied].

There are two names for the place where mountains and such things fall: *papāta* and *taṭa*. It is *papāta* because they fall (*papatanti*) from it, with the suffix *ṇo*; the root *pat* means "downward movement. It is *taṭa* from the root *taṭ* (to rise up), meaning a slope or precipice.
Two [terms] refer to a mountain slope (*pabbatanitambe*). *Nitamba* also means the hips; it is formed with the suffix *ṇvu* from the root *kaṭ*, meaning "to cover" or "to rain.

On a mountain, the production (*pasava*) or flowing forth (*pasavana*) of water—such as from rocks and so on—is called a waterfall (*nijjhara*); it is a "flowing out" (*nissaraṇa*). [The suffix] *jho* is added to *sassa*. This is an irregular doubling (*asarūpadvitta*). *Jhara* is also used.

(609) Two [terms] refer to a cave (*kandara*), whether artificial or natural, and whether containing water or waterless. From the root *dara*, meaning "to split," [the suffixes] *a* and *ī* are added, forming *darī*.
*Kaṃ* is an indeclinable (*abyaya*) signifying water; by what is it hollowed out? By *kandara*. *Ā*, *kandarā*: these three denote a cave dug by the gods. *Leṇaṃ*: they hide (*nilīyanti*) in this;

from the root *lī* (to adhere), with the suffix *yu*. *Gabbharaṃ*: it calls forth movement or it makes crooked; [the form is established] by irregular derivation (*nipātanā*). Or, from the root *gabbha* (to hold), with the suffix *ara*.
*Guha*: from the root *guh* (to conceal), with the suffix *a*; thus, *guhā*.
Two [terms] refer to a stone lotus pond (*silāmayapokkharaṇī*): *soḍi* and *gabbhe*. *Soṇa* occurs in the senses of color, movement, and collection; *ḍo* and *ī* [are the suffixes].

Two [terms] refer to a mountain cave (*gabbhara*)—that is, a hollow place in mountains and the like whose interior is covered by creepers, sprouts, grass, and so forth: *kuñja* and *nikuñja*. *Kuñja* is formed with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
*nikuñja* is preceded by the prefix *ni*. Both are not feminine. The mention of *nikuñja* is for the purpose of excluding *pakuñja* and others.

610. The upper region of Mount Sela is called *uddhiccaka*. The ground adjacent to the lower part of Mount Sela is called *upaccaka*. Here, by those sounds ending in *-ccaka*, the suffix *-ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.34 (*yadādinā*). The small mountains situated surrounding the edge of the main mountain are called *pādā*.

In that context, there are two types beginning with *pāda*. It is so called because it is "traversed" (*pajjate*) or "gone to" (*gamyateti*); hence the suffix *ṇo*. A mountain near (*upanto*) or in the vicinity of Mount Sela is an *upantaselo*.

The mineral substances such as red chalk (*gerika*), realgar (*manosilā*), yellow orpiment (*haritalaka*), and bitumen (*kaṭṭhinī*) are indeed modifications of stone (*silāvikāro*) and are thus called "elements" (*dhātū*). [The root] *dhṛ* means "to hold" (*dhara dhāraṇe*); from this, with the suffix *tu*, we have *dhātu*.
The commentary on the Sela-vagga is finished.

611. The triad concerning the lion (*sīha*). "Kesara" means a mane; because he possesses it, he is *kesarī* (the maned one). He harms deer, thus he is a *sīha*; [this form arises] through grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) and the alteration of phonemes.
Alternatively, he is a *sīha* because his striving (*īhā*) exists for the purpose of killing deer; or, he is a *sīha* because he endures (*sahati*). He has five claws; he is also called *harī*.
His feet are like his face, capable of splitting the frontal globes of elephants; thus, he has five faces. He seizes deer, hence he is a *hari*.
Specifically, this refers to a beast called a *taraccha*—the size of a large dog, dog-shaped, with a body marked by black stripes, capable of harming cattle and humans, and having a short snout.
It is called a "dog-tiger. [The root] *tara* means "to cross over"; *cho* is the suffix; it is one who gives [fear] to deer.
*Migādano* [is formed] with *yu* after *nanda*, etc. There are two types of tiger (*byaggha*).

It is called a tiger because it kills (*vinihanti*) and is full of malice (*āghāyati*); the root *ghā* is used in the sense of grasping (*upādāna*). *Byaggha* is also a term for a leopard. *Puṇḍarīka*: it splits (*dāleti*) that which expands (*pumāna*); from the root *dala* in the sense of cleaving, with the suffix *ṇvu*. *Da* becomes *ḍa*, *la* becomes *ra*, and there is *assī*; thus, *puṇḍarīka*. “*Puṇḍarīka* refers to the white lotus.”
"In the white umbrella and in medicine;
in the tiger within the treasury and the ant-hill;
he [is] the world-guardian, the elephant, and fire."

In the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: The tiger (*vaggha*) is also called *saddūla*. It is designated as *saddūla* because it roars (*sarati*), thus "one who roars" (*saddūla*); [the suffix] *ūla*, with *da* at the end. Alternatively, it is *saddūla* because it goes (*ulati*) by means of its roar (*saddena*). The "island" (*dīpa*) is its skin; due to that connection, it is a leopard (*dīpī*);

in that leopard (*dīpini*). 612. A pentad for the clear (*accha*). *Asu* in the sense of causing to flow away (*khepana*), with the suffix *cho*. *Ica* in the sense of praise (*thuti*), with the suffix *a*, making *ikka*. *Bhalluka* also: from *bhala*, *bhall* in the senses of reviling, harming, and giving, with the suffix *ṇvu*; *assu*; *īsa* in the senses of going, harming, and giving, with the suffix *so*; short vowel, etc.; without the suffix *ap*, it is *iso*.

There are two [names] for the *rohita* (red deer): it is called *rohisa* because of its red color, and it is also called *lohita*. In the former case, that [suffix] belongs to it. There are three [names] for the *gokaṇṇa* (the spotted deer):
one whose ears are like those of a cow is a *gokaṇṇa*. Because he is associated with a herd (*gaṇa*), he is a *gaṇī*;

and because his horns are like thorns (*kaṇṭaka*), he is a *kaṇṭaka*. Thus, he is a *gaṇikaṇṭaka*. They also state that this is a collective name. Furthermore, he is a *gaṇikaṇṭaka* because he is both a *gaṇī* and a *kaṇṭaka*.
Two names should also be understood; for that very reason, the plural designation “gaṇikaṇṭakā” was employed.

613–614. The tetrad concerns the rhinoceros (*khagga*). Its horn is called *khagga*; because of its connection with that [horn], it is a “rhinoceros. For the *Nānatthasaṅgahe* states in the *Byākhyāsudhā* (2.5.4):

“*Khagga* refers to the rhinoceros among the divisions of the *gaṇḍaka*, namely the rhinoceros, the *gaṇḍasiṅga*, and the *asivuddha*. Because its shape is like a sword (*khagga*), its horn is so named.

*Khaggavisāṇo*, no. Here, the word *khagga* is a synonym for a sword (*asi*). He eats the foliage (*palāsa*), thus he is a *palāsāda*. A *gaṇḍa* is a certain part of the face; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *gaṇḍaka*.

Every species of wild animal, such as the tiger and so forth, is called a "beast of prey" (*vāḷamiga*) or "carnivore" (*sāpada*). Because the tiger especially harms humans and others, its wickedness is well known;
therefore, it is mentioned as the foremost among them. From the root *val* (in the sense of covering or restraining), [it is derived as] that by which one restrains oneself.

A *vāḷa* is a beast; a beast that is also a wild animal is a *vāḷamiga*, meaning a "wicked beast. [The word] *sāpada* refers to that by which one is cursed, as in "May the tiger devour you" and so forth;
the root *sap* means to revile, with the suffix *-do*, beginning with a long vowel.
*Plavaṅga* refers to a monkey. A *plava* is a particular mode of movement; one who goes by means of that is a *plavaṅgama* or *plavaṅga*. *Mara*... [text fragment]

*Pāṇacāge*, *aṭo*, *ko*, *canto*, *makkaṭo*. Like a man is a "man-monkey" (*naravānaro*); the word *vāsa-* is used in the sense of "like" (*ivātthe*), and because the names are joined in meaning, it forms a compound.
A beast that dwells in branches is a "branch-beast" (*sākhāmigo*). Because the root has the sense of "going," it is used as a verb. From the root *kapi* (to move), with the suffix *i*, we get *kapi*.
One who has wrinkled, loose skin on the face is a "wrinkle-face" (*valīmukho*). *Kiso* means one who is emaciated, or one who is distressed by the forest (*vanokopi*) in a wretched manner.
*Seti* means "lying down"; *kisa* means "emaciated. *Vana-moka-māsayo* refers to its forest-dwelling.

If that monkey has a black snout (*kaṇha-tuṇḍo*) and a dark face (*kāḷa-mukho*), then it is known as a "gonaṅgala," so called because its plow-like [features] resemble those of oxen (*gonnaṃ naṅgala-sadisatāya*).
615. *Pajjaddhaṃ* is the name for a jackal. *Sara* [is used] in the senses of going, harming, and thinking; *alo* is a suffix. It possesses a horn (*siṅgo*) that goes (*sarati*). *Jamu*...

*Adane*: with the suffix *ṇvu*, *bo* [is formed]; it means "eating. *Kusa akkose*: with the suffixes *tu* or *thu*, [the word *kusitu* is formed]. *Bherava* is so called because it is connected with terror;

or, it is *bherava* because it makes a sound (*ravati*) as "bhe. *Samu upasame*: with the suffix *ivo*, *sivā*, *nārī*, or [the root] *si* in the sense of service (*sevāyaṃ*), [the suffix] *vo* [is applied].
*Migadhutto*: he is a rogue among deer; that is, a rogue among those living in the forest. One who deceives a brahmin is a *vañcaka*.

The triad refers to the *biḷāra* (mongoose). *Bila* means "breaking," with the suffix *aro* and the letter *ḷ*. *Babba* means "going," with the suffix *u*. *Maja* means "cleansing," with the suffix *āro* and the elision of the final *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
It is also called *otu*, and *ākhubhuja* ("mouse-eater") as well. The dyad refers to the *koka* (red deer). This is a tawny deer the size of a dog. *Kuka* and *vaka* mean "taking" (*ādāna*).
It is also called *īhāmiga* ("striving deer"), because it strives (*īhati*) or longs for (*kaṅkhati*) among deer; [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied in the sense of an object (*kammani*).
616. *Dvayaṃ mahiṃse*. One who lies (*seti*) on the earth (*mahi*) is a *mahiṃsa*; [the suffix] *assa* is short, and there is the elision of the *niggahīta*.

*Lala* means desire; that which desires water (*udaka*) is a *lulāya*; this is by way of a fixed rule (*nipātana*), with the suffix *aya* and the substitution of *a* for *u*. That which moves or is born like a cow (*go*) is a *gavaja*.
That which moves like a cow is a *gavaya*; these two compounds have the same meaning.

*Dvayaṃ salle*. *Salla* [is used] in the sense of a swift-moving creature (*āsugati*). With the suffix *a*, it becomes *sallo*; with the suffix *ka* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), it becomes *sallako*.

It is called *sallo* because it "pierces" (*salati*) or "injures" (*hiṃsati*) a dog with a dart produced from its own body; thus it is both *sallo* and *sallako*. This [creature] has the form of a boar and is also a *salākāpāya* (a type of insect).

From the hair of this *salla* comes *salala*, and *salañca* may also occur. [The roots] *pala*, *sala*, and *patha* are in the sense of going (*gati*); [with the suffix] *alo*, [they form their respective derivatives].
With *nad* and other [roots], *salalī*; in the absence of *thitta*, *salala*; in *amhi*, *sala*. 617.
A group of five [roots] refers to deer: *hariṇo* because they are carried away by this; from *hara* in the sense of "carrying," with the suffix *yu*. And [the suffix] *ṇat* is merely a marker.

From *mara* in the sense of "abandoning life," with the suffix *a*, the substitution of *go* for *ra*, and the addition of *itta*. It runs, goes, or flees with a dog (*sena*), thus it is a *sāraṅga*. [The suffix] *dīghādi* [applies].

*Mago* and *migo*: these two are both simply "deer. It is the source (*yoni*) of the skin being used; or, because it is the cause for the arising of the existing skin, it is the "source of the skin" (*ajinayoni*).
This too is simply "deer. *Kuraṅgo* and *vātāyu* as well. It is called *kuraṅgo* because it runs (*raṅgati*) upon the earth (*kuyaṃ*).
It is called *vātāyu* because it moves through the wind (*vātaṃ ayati*). [End of] commentary.
Regarding the two types of pork: it is called *sūkara* because it produces a beautiful fruit (*sundaraṃ phalaṃ karoti*).
And it is said concerning the qualities of substances: “Pork meat is moistening, nourishing, and strengthening;
likewise, it subdues wind-disorders. It is light when young, appetizing, and heating. (Dabbaguṇasaṅgaha 2.11–2)

It is called a *sūkara* because it makes (*karoti*) pleasure (*sukha*), or because its trunk (*kara*) is beautiful (*sundara*). It is called a *varāha* because it strikes (*āhanti*) what is excellent (*vara*); or, since it is excellent, it is to be struck (*āhantabba*), thus it is a *varāha*.
It is also known as *kola*, *thaddhaloma*, and *bhūdāra*. The pair [of terms] refers to the hare (*sasa*). In the sense of "going" (*gati*), from the root *pela*, the suffix *ṇvu* is applied.
The hare (*sasa*) leaps (*pluta*) in its movement; hence the suffix *a*.
618. *Dvayaṃ eṇīmige*: [The word] *eṇī* means a female deer (*migiyā*). Alternatively, that which is the offspring of an *eṇa* is *eṇeyya*;

this is explained by taking the etymological sense as "the skin and so forth belonging to an *eṇa* or an *eṇī*. A deer (*migo*) that is the son of an *eṇī* female is an *eṇīmigo*. [The root] *i* is in the sense of motion;
with the suffix *yu*, and being included in the *nada*-group, when not beginning with *na*, it becomes *eṇa*. In this way, these [words] have been derived. *Dvayaṃ pampaṭake*: [The word] *paṭa*...

In *gamana*, the suffix *ṇvu* is applied, and a nasal (*bindu*) is inserted at the end of the prefix. In *pabbagati*, the suffix *ṇvu* is applied, a nasal is inserted, and there is the elision of the *b*.

Both terms refer to a deer of the wind (*vātamiga*). A deer equal to the wind in its movement is a *vātamiga*. [The suffix] *yu* is applied due to its quality of moving, as it belongs to the *nada*-class. Three terms refer to a mouse (*mūsika*). In *musa* (meaning theft), the suffix *ṇvu* is applied and the vowel is changed to *i*. In *ā-khanu* (meaning digging), the suffix *u* is applied and the nasal is elided. In *unda* (meaning flowing or moistening), the suffix *ūro* is applied. 619.
The *camara* and others, as well as the *sarabha* and others, are specific types of wild animals (*migantara*). The *camara* is well-known in the northern regions.
That which has a tail like a chowrie (*cāmara*): from the root *cam*, meaning "to eat," and *ara*; thus, *camara*. The female is *camarī*. A spotted animal with white hair:
from *pasa*, meaning "to bind," and *ada*. It leaps in a pit, thus it is a *kuruṅga*; [another form is] *kuraṅga*, where *a* is for the sake of euphony.

Because she stands in the place of a mother to all deer, she is a *migamātukā*, using the suffix *ko* in the sense of comparison. From *ru*, meaning "sound"; thus, *ru*. She makes a sound, thus [she is a *ruṇatī*].
In *raṅku*, there is the elision of the letter *ṇ* and of *u* after it; thus, one who makes oneself low (*nīca*) is called *nīka*. From *sarati* with the suffix *-bha*, we get *sarabha*.
It has eight feet, upward-looking eyes, and is even a slayer of lions; furthermore, its four legs point upwards. 620.

There are three beginning with *piyakā*, and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those such as *kandalī*, *cīna*, and *samūru* are included; these are of leathern origin, and [the suffix] is applied to that which has become so.
Because they are the causes for the arising of leather, these various types of animal hair and so forth grow in places such as Kamboja and the Northern Regions (Uttarāpatha),
and are known by those very names in those regions. Just as the word *miga* (deer) applies to the general category of wild animals and specifically to the species called *kuraṅga*,

and just as the word *loha* (metal) applies to the general category of fiery substances such as gold and specifically to certain ones, so too do the words *cammayoni* (leather-born) and *ajinayoni* (skin-born).
The term *miga* is stated as such for both the general class of animals (*migasāmañña*) and specific types of animals (*migavisesa*).

In the sense of "drinking" (*pīta*) and "shining" (*kantī*), the suffix *ṇvu* is applied, followed by the substitution of *iy*. Because the thigh (*ūru*) is exceptionally covered with skin, it is called *camūru*; here, one of the two *m* sounds is elided. From the root *kadi* in the sense of "calling out" (*avhāna*), with the suffixes *alo* and *ī*, we have *kadalī*; because that animal is a *miga*, it is called *kadalīmiga*.

Lions and others, whether explicitly mentioned or not, all four-footed creatures are termed "wild animals" (*migā*) and "livestock" (*pasavo*). They are called *pasavo* because they procreate (*pasavanti*); this is derived from the root *su* in the sense of "flowing forth" (*abhisava*), or from *pasa* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhana*), with the suffix *u*.

621. A group of four concerning the spider (*lūtā*). From the root *lū* (to cut), with the suffix *-ta*, we have *lūtā*; with the suffix *-ika* in the sense of identity, *lūtikā*. These two refer to the female spider. The woolly hair on its body is like a thread;

it has wool on its navel, hence it is called *uṇṇanābhi* (wool-naveled), with the vowel shortened. It moves along its own threads upon its branches like a monkey, thus it is called *makkaṭaka* (monkey-like).
Two [terms] for a centipede: *gomayajavicchika*. From the root *viccha* (to move), with the suffix *ṇvu*, we get *vicchika*; it is also called *satapadī*.

Because its foot (*aṅgula*) is like a line (*āḷa*), it is called *āḷivicchika*. Two [terms] for a house-lizard: *gharagodhā*. From the root *sarati* (to move), with the suffix *ū*, we get *avo* ending in *c*. A lizard (*godhā*) residing in a house (*ghara*) is a *gharagoḷikā*;
here, *dha* becomes *ḷa*, and the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity.

622. Two [meanings] for *godhā*: *gudha* (to rise) + suffix *a*, *godhā*, meaning "woman. *Kuṇḍa* (to burn) + suffix *a*, *kuṇḍo*. Two [meanings] for *rattapā*: *kaṇṇassa jalūkā* (the leech of the ear), *rattapā*, *kaṇṇajalūkā*. That which has a hundred feet is *satapadī*; the word *pada* here means "foot. Two [meanings] for *kalandaka*:

from *kanda* (to call out or weep) + suffix *ṇvu*, *kandati* thus *kalandako*, meaning "cricket" (*lamajjho*). Because of its black color, it is *kāḷakā*, referring to a female. Two [meanings] for *nakula*:
there is no lineage (*kula*) among snakes for this one, thus *nakulo*; it is also a type of venomous snake (*arisappa*). *Nakka*...
*Nakula*: It destroys (*nāseti*) mongooses (*ulūka*) and snakes (*kalopa*) on its seat (*āsana*); thus it is a *nakula*. The root *maṅg* has the sense of "going";

it is a *daṇḍaka* root; the suffix is *usa*. 623. There are two [terms] for the *kakaṇṭaka* (scorpion): *kuccha-kaṇṭaka* ("bad thorn"); the suffix is *ussa*. It remembers (*sarati*) and runs (*dhāvati*), thus it is a *saraṭa*;

the suffix is *aṭa*. There are four [terms] for a worm (*kīṭa*): *kīṭa* is from the root *kīṭ* in the sense of "binding," with the suffix *a*; or from *kīṭ* in the sense of "going," beginning with a long vowel. From *pul* in the sense of "greatness," with the suffix *ava*; the change to *ḷ* occurs. It moves (*amati*) in a bad way (*kucchitaṃ*), thus it is a *kimi*; the suffix is *i*; the palatalization (*assittaṃ*) occurs. It goes (*anati*) in various ways (*pakārena*), thus it is a *pāṇaka*; the suffix is *ṇvu*; the change to *ṇ* occurs.
Two [names] for a hair-insect (*kaṇṭalomakīṭa*): it clings to a high place, thus it is *uccāliṅga*; a creature covered with much hair is a *lomasapāṇaka*.
624–625. Names for a bird (*sakuṇa*) by way of its flight: it goes in the sky (*viha*), thus it is *vihaṅga* and *vihaṅgama*;
here the word *viha* is a synonym for the sky, or it is a substitution (*vihādeso*) for *vehāsa*. It possesses wings, thus it is *pakkhī*.
*Khaga*: one who goes in the sky (*kha*), or one who goes in the sky; thus, *khaga*. Born from an egg (*aṇḍa*);

one capable of flying upwards is a *sakuṇa*, *sakunta*, and *sakuṇī*—from the root *saka* (to be able), with the suffixes *-uṇo*, *-unto*, and *-uṇī*. One that flies or moves by means of wings (*patta*) is a *pataṅga*;
elsewhere, there is elision of the *ta*. Born twice—from the mother’s womb and from an egg—is a *dvija*. [Regarding] flying upwards and so forth...
*Vakkaṅga*: its limbs, such as the neck and so forth, are curved (*vakka*); or, it moves with a curved gait, thus it is *vakkaṅga*.

*Pattayāna*: he goes by means of wings (*pattra*); or, that [wing] is his vehicle. *Patanta*: he is as if falling from the sky while flying. *Nīḷaja*: he is born in a nest (*nīḷa*), that is, in a bird’s burrow (*kulāvaka*).
*Vaṭṭakā* and others, as well as *pokkharasātaka* and others, are specific varieties of those birds. *Vaṭṭa* [is derived from the root] *vaṭṭ*, meaning to turn or roll.
*Ṇvu*: *vaṭṭakā*, a quail. A *jīvañjīva* bird, the size of a peacock, with variegated wings, is born in the Southern Land (*Dakkhiṇapatha*) and other regions;
it is called *jīvañjīva* because it makes the sound "jīva-jīva. It is also [spelled] *jīvajīva* without the nasal (*anunāsika*). The bird *cakora* is dear to the moon;

from the root *caka* (to reflect), we have *uro* and *usso*, and also *caṅkoro*. From the root *tari* (to cross), with the suffix *ira*, and with the doubling of the consonant, we have *tittiro* (a partridge).

626. *Sala* [is used] in the sense of going (*gati*): *ṇika*, *ḷatta*, *sāḷikā*, *nārī*. Because it cries out (*ravati*) at the right time (*kalaṃ*), it is a *karavīka*; [the suffix] *īka* is applied, and there is the elision of *la*.
That bird whose song is compared to the voice of the Blessed One is called a "karavīka. A swan that is similar to one crying with speed (*java*) is a *ravihaṃsa*.
From the root *kusa* in the sense of sound (*sadda*), [the suffix] *thaka* is applied; there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*), and the *sa* of *kusa* becomes *ta*: thus, *kukutthaka*.
*Karaṇḍa* means a vessel; *karaṇḍava* is an aquatic bird. *Bilu* means a pillar; there is a substitution of *av* for *a*, thus *bilava*.
It is known as the "Gaṇḍaplava," a red-winged great bird, the *pokkharasātaka*. Because it has the designation of a lotus (*pokkhara*), it is called *pokkharasātaka*;
the suffix *to* replaces *ñña*, and the vowel is long. Or else, that is simply its collective name. At that time...
*sāda* is derived from the root *sad* (to taste), with the suffix *ṇvu*; the *d* becomes *t*, as in *pokkharasātaka*.

627. Seven [terms] belong to the *pakkha* group. That by which they fly is *patatta*; the suffix *to* is applied according to the rule beginning with "yadādi," and the doubling of the consonant occurs. From the root *ukh* (motion), with the suffix *yu*, the form *usse* is obtained;

with the suffix *assu*, *pekhuṇaṃ* is formed, where the *ṇ* replaces the *t*. From the root *pat* (to go), with the suffix *to*, *pātato* is formed; or alternatively, that which protects (*tāyati*) is *pattaṃ*. From the root *pat*...

Regarding the word *pakkha*: in the sense of "going," what is its derivation? One who wishes to fly (*patituṃ*) with his tail-feathers (*piñcha*) is called a *pakkha*. [The root] *pata* is used in the sense of going;

there is elision of the suffix *cho*, the addition of the vowel *i*, and the suffix *assi*. Regarding *chada*: it is that by which something is covered (*chādyate*). Regarding *niggaṇha*: from the root *gira* in the sense of "swallowing" (*niggiraṇe*), with the suffix *u*, the form is *issattaṃ*.
Or, from the root *gamu* in the sense of going, with the suffix *u*, the letter *m* is replaced by *r*.
Regarding the seed of birds, it is known as *au*; it is also used for the eggs of turtles and other such creatures, according to the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*:

"The word *aṇḍa* refers to the egg and the shell of birds and so forth. The root *aḍi* has the sense of an egg; with the suffix *ṇo*, we have *pesi*. *Pisa* means a part; with the suffix *i*, we have *pesi*. According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (15.37) and *Rudda*:
"The word *pesi* refers to the embryo and a type of vessel; *kosa* is desired only in the masculine [gender]. Both terms refer to the nest of a bird.
In the sense of blue color, there is *a*, *ḷatta*, *nī*, and *naye* or *ilo*. That which cuts (*lunāti*) what is contemptible, such as eggs and so forth, is a *kulāvaka*;

the suffix *ṇvu* is applied. 628. There are two [terms] for the mother of the Garuḷas. Because birds (*pakkhino*) bow down (*namanti*) to her, she is *vinatā*. The pair of female and male is called a *mithuna*;
since a number depends upon that which is numbered, it is the woman and man themselves who constitute the pair. From the root *mith* (in the sense of union), the suffix *uno* is added.
*Chakka* means a pair (*yugaḷa*). From the root *yuja* (to join), with the suffix *a*, we have *yuga*; with the suffix *ala*, *yugaḷa*; and by the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*, *yugala*.

Also, from *ubha* (to fill), with the suffix *ṇa*, there is the substitution of *dvanda*, hence *dvanda*. From *yamu* (to cease), with the suffix *ṇvu* and the elision of *a*, we have *yamaka*; with the suffix *la*, *yamala*; and without a suffix, *yama*. 629–631. *Maṇḍala* and its derivatives denote a collection (*samūha*).
A "collection" (*samūha*) is that which is gathered together (*sammā ūhate*) or specifically heaped up; it is formed with the suffix *ṇa*.

It is called a *samūha* because it carries (*ūhati*) or stands together (*tiṭṭhati*) with its parts (*saha avayavena*). From the root *gaṇ* (in the sense of counting), it is a *gaṇa* because it is counted together with its parts.
It is a *saṅghāta* because it goes (*gacchati*) together with its parts; from the root *han* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *-ṇa*.

It is a *samudāya* because it arises (*udeti*) together with its parts; here there is the augment *-d-* and a long vowel in the middle. It is a *sañcaya* because it accumulates (*sañcinoti*) its parts; from the root *ci* (in the sense of piling up).
It is called *sandoha* because it milks [the object] along with its parts (*avayava*); the root *duh* means "to fill. It is called *nivaha* because it carries the parts completely;

it is called *ogha* because it flows (*gacchati*) having made the parts its vehicle; the word *ogha* is derived from the root *uc*, meaning "to assemble," and by grammatical exception (*nipātanā*), the suffix *-gha* is applied to it (according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 15.39).
It is called *visara* because the parts disperse (*visanti*) therein; the suffix is *-ara*. It is near to the parts.
It is called a *nikara* because it "makes" (*karoti*). Or, it is a *kāya* because in it the parts designated as "bones" (*ka*) come together (*āyanti*) when viewed individually;

or else, it is a *kāya* because it is the coming-together (*āya*) of the foul things such as hair and so forth. Just as that [body] is the place of origin for its parts, so too here the term *kāya* refers to a collection.
It is called a *khandha* because it "bears" (*dhāreti*) a part designated as a "trunk" (*khaṃ*) in the sense of being an end; or it "devours" (*khādati*) the parts.
Or the aggregate (*khandha*); in the sense of "without middle or long," it is the arising (*samudaya*).

The root *ghaṭ* means to join. Joining is the state of being a heap; they join their own parts, thus it is a "heap" (*ghaṭā*). It goes together with its parts, thus it is a "coming together" (*samiti*). It goes together with its parts, thus it is a "conglomeration" (*saṃhati*);
from the root *han* in the sense of "going," there is the elision of the nasal (*n*). The root *ras* means to taste; [the suffix] *iṇ*. The root *puñj* means to heap. Together with its parts...
It extends and proceeds, thus it is *samavāya* (conjunction). It is also used for a *pūga* (guild) and for betel. It produces and causes to enter its parts, thus it is *jātaṃ* (born);

the suffix *-to* is added. It gives itself (*kaṃ*), thus it is *kada*; the eye and so forth are parts of the body. Like *kada*, it is *kada*; it speaks of or takes up those parts, thus it is *kadambakaṃ*.
Parts are specifically pushed together in it, thus it is *vyūha* (array). It stretches out and enters its parts, thus it is *vitānaṃ* (canopy); the suffix *-ṇo* is added. *Gupa*...
*Rakkhaṇe* (in the sense of protecting), *bo*, *passa*, *mo*, *gumbo*, *gumbampi*. It is called a *kalāpa* because it protects (*pāti*) its parts (*kalaṃ avayavabhāvaṃ*).

For since it is said, “A *kalā* is the sixteenth part,” it is understood that the word *kalā* also has the meaning of "part. *Jala* is in the sense of shining. It shines by means of its parts, thus it is a *jāla*.
It adorns by means of its parts, thus it is a *maṇḍala*; [the root] *maṇḍ* is in the sense of ornamenting, with the suffix *alo*.

632. By means of the following section on "Saddha," the divisions of groups (*gaṇa*) are explained. Among those, a group (*gaṇa*) or class (*vagga*) refers to a collection of beings—whether animate or inanimate—that share common characteristics such as birth (*jāti*), and so forth;

for example, "the class of kinsmen" (*bandhuvaggo*), "the *k*-class" (*kavaggo*), and so on. [The term] *vajja* means "to exclude" (*vajjana*); it is called a *vagga* because it excludes (*vajjeti*) those who do not share the same birth and other such traits.

[The suffix] *-ṇo* is applied, whereby *jjassa* becomes *gg*. A group of living beings (*jantu*) who share the same species or those of different species is called a "community" (*saṅgha*) or a "caravan" (*sattha*).

It is so designated, as in the cases of "the community of monks" (*bhikkhusaṅgho*) or "a caravan of merchants" (*vāṇijasattho*), and so forth. It is called a *saṅgha* because its constituent parts are brought together (*saṃhaññante*) and known without distinction within it;
this is the opinion of Ro. It is called a *sattha* because its constituent parts move or proceed (*saranti vattanti*) therein; the suffix *-tho* becomes *-to* by shortening.

A group (*gaṇo*) consisting exclusively of beings of the same class—that is, of similar birth—is called a *kula*, such as "a clan of kṣatriyas" (*khattiyakula*) or "a herd of cows" (*gokula*), and so forth.

*Kula* [is derived from] *saṅkhyāna* (counting) and *bandhu* (kinship); thus, *kulaṃ*. A group (*gaṇa*) of beings who possess the same Dhamma, that is, those with identical qualities, is called a *nikāya*, such as "the community of monks" (*bhikkhunikāyo*).
From the root *ci* (to accumulate), with the suffix *ṇo*: it accumulates or arranges its parts without distinction, hence *nikāyo*.
A group of animals of the same species is called a *yūtha*; and that is not feminine, as in "an elephant herd" (*hatthiyūtho*).

“*Migayūtha*,” etc.; *yu* means mixing; with the suffix *tha*, it becomes *yūtha*, beginning with a long vowel. One should look at the verse in the *Amara-kośa* (15.42): “*Gaṇo pasūnaṃ samajo, samājo aññesaṃ uccate*” [“A herd of animals is called a *samaja*; for others, it is called a *samāja*”].
Here, one should also understand that the word is used even when not explicitly mentioned.
