633. The group of four refers to the *garuḷa*. Because its beautiful wings (*paṇṇa*) are radiant like gold, it is a *supaṇṇa*. [It is] without a belly (*vinabhāya*).
*Venateyyo* means "the offspring of the mother named Vinatā"; it is derived from *ṇeyya*. Because he slays the poison-bearing *gara* (serpent), he is called *garuḷo*;

this is formed with the suffix *ṇo*, with the substitution of *ḷ* for the *ra* and *anta* sounds, and the modification of the vowel (*vaṇṇavikāro*), resulting in *garuḷo*. He is also known as the bird-lion (*pakkhisīho*), the lord of birds (*uḷūtīso*), the diamond-beaked one (*vajiratuṇḍo*), the food-taker (*sudhāharo*), the golden-winged one (*suvaṇṇapakkho*), and the seat of the serpents (*bhujagāsano*). (Tikaṇḍasesa 1.1.42)

"Pikantaṃ" refers to the *kokila* (cuckoo). It is called "parapuṭṭho" because it is nourished (*posita*) by another, namely the crow (*kāka*), which is of a different species (*vijātiya*). The root *pusa* means "to nourish" (*posane*), with the suffix *-to*. It is called "parabhato" because it is supported (*bhata*) by another;

the root *bhara* means "to support" or "to nourish" (*dhāraṇaposanesu*), with the suffix *-to*. It is called "kokilo" because it makes the sound "ku-ku"; the roots *kuṇa* (in the sense of making sounds) and *alo* [are used], and the root *kuka* (or *vaka*) in the sense of "taking up" (*ādāne*), with the suffix *-ilo*.

It is called "piko" because it cries out (*kāyati*) while hidden (*apihita*); the root *api* means "to disappear" (*antaradhāne*), resulting in the loss of color or form (*vaṇṇanāsa*), and there is also the elision of the syllable *pi*.
634. *Aṭṭhakaṃ more*. [The root] *mura* means to cover; with the suffix *ṇo*, it becomes *mura*. [The root] *maya* means to go; with the suffix *ūra*, it becomes *mayūra*.

Alternatively, it is a *nirukta* (etymological) derivation based on the connection with the excellence of the meaning of the verbal root: "it cries (*ravati*) in the great (*mahī*)"—thus, a peacock (*mayūra*). A crest (*sikhaṇḍa*) is its "choice" (*vara*); because of that connection, it is called *varahī*.
That which has a blue neck (*nīlagrīva*) or throat is also called *bhujaṅgabhuja*.
The word *dvaya* (a pair) occurs in the sense of a peacock’s crest and its flame. *Sikhā* (crest) has been mentioned previously in the sense of a mass of flames.

635–636. The tetrad [of roots] pertains to a peacock’s plumage. *Sikhaṇḍin* means "this is his crest" (*sikhaṇḍo assa atthi*); *vara* is used in the sense of excellence, while *paribhāsana*, *hiṃsā*, and *dāna* are the meanings of [the root *var*].

The suffix *a* is used in the sense of the instrument. What peacock (*maya*) shines by means of which? That is the *kalāpa* (plumage); [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied, and *sa* becomes *pa*. *Pī* is used in the senses of drinking and beauty; [the suffix] *cho* is applied.
There is the insertion of *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and shortening [of the vowel]. Two [parts] are in the place of the peacock's feathers (*piñcha*) and in the shape of its eyes.
The root *cadi* means "to delight" and also "splendor"; with the suffix *ṇvu*, it becomes *mecaka*, which is also said to mean "black color.

*Aḷyanti* means "they wander" like bees; they have six feet. One who drinks honey (*madhu*) or eats it is a *madhubbata*; the root *vata* means "eating. The root *bhama* means "non-staying"; because it wanders over the tops of flowers (*puppha*), it is a *bhamara*; the suffix is *ara*. The root *ara* means "going"; with the suffix *i*, there is the substitution of *ḷ* for *r*.

The group of four concerns the domestic pigeon (*gehavanakapota*). It is called *pārāpata* because it flies across (*pārena*) with its wing (*sabala*); it is also [derived from] *pāravat*. The root *kapa* means "to cover" or "to move.

In *oto*, the suffix *para* has its initial syllable elided. The root *kuka* means "to take"; with the suffix *aṭo* and the vowel *u* being dropped, [it becomes *kapota*]. It is called *pārevaṭa* because it cries out (*ravati*) in various ways (*pakārena*);
the root *ru* means "to sound," with the suffix *aṭo*, the lengthening of the prefix, and the substitution of *assa* (for *a*), thus *pārevaṭa*; it is also *parevaṭa*.
The pigeon, the chejja, the kapota with red eyes,
and the pārāpata with its dark cry.
“*Pattī seno sasādano*” (The vulture is winged and has a nest)—thus says the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 15.14.
—Rabhasa. 637.
Two [forms] for the vulture (*gijjha*). [The root] *gidha* is used in the sense of longing; [the form] *jhassa jho* is an irregular doubling (*asarūpa-dvitta*), by means of the suffix *jha*.

Or it is established; likewise for *dhassa jo*. From *gidhati*, by *sma*, there is *a*; elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), the state of *issa*, and *gandho*. The triad [of suffixes] is common to *sena*.

One who cuts or severs the lineage (*kula*) of the *kukkuṭa* and others is a *kulala*; or, from *kula* in the sense of lineage, with the suffix *ala*. From *se* in the sense of going, with the suffix *no*.
Because of harming living beings (*sattānaṃ*), like a tiger (*byaggho*), she is a *byagghi*; she destroys living beings, thus she is a *nāso*. A *byagghi*.
Thus, "nāsa" is a collective name.

The three beginning with the hawk (*sakuṇagghi*) are its divisions, specific types of that bird. It is called a *sakuṇagghi* because it kills birds (*sakuṇa*); [the root] *gghā* (from *han*) means to kill. *Aṭa* means to go;
the suffix *ṇo* is applied, and the vowel is lengthened (*āṭo*). That bird whose beak (*tuṇḍa*) resembles a *dabbi* (a ladle) is a *dabbimukhadvija*. "The *dabbimukhadvija*... [and so on].
The term *āṭa* has the single meaning of "one who eats excessively"; thus, there are only two types of *sena* (birds). 638. Regarding the tetrad on the owl (*ulūka*):
it makes the sound "uhu," thus it is called *uhuṅkāra*. According to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), "one whose ears are raised" is *uddhaṃkaṇṇo*;
[alternatively], the owl is so called because it "burns" (*dahati*) with its eyes (*ulabhinetta*), or because of its upward-looking (*uddholokanā*). This is the etymology.
(Amarakośagghāṭaṇaṭīkā 15.15): It is derived from *u* meaning "to go" or "to meet," or by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) it refers to the hollow (*koṭara*). *Kusa* means "to revile";

he is called *Kosiya* because people revile him (*kosanti*) due to his unpleasant voice, or because he is to be reviled (*kositabbo*), or because he dwells in a hollow (*koṭare vasati*), according to etymological derivation (*nerutto*).
He is the enemy (*ari*) of crows (*vāyasa*, *kāka*), known by the name Sakka, blind by day, and having a nose like a vulva (*vakka*).
*Harinetta*, *divābhīta*, *kākabhīru*, and *ratticārī*. Regarding *vāyasa*:
it cries out (*kāyati*) the sound "kā," thus it is a *kāka*. *Riṭṭha* means a sign of death; he who has no such sign is *ariṭṭha*.
*Dhaṅka* refers to one with a terrible cry. *Bhata* means supported by a master. Regarding *vaya*: it means going; or simply, that which goes is *vāyasa*.

He is self-contented (*sakattha*), his offspring is born once (*sakiṃpaja*), he makes his own sound (*attaghosa*), he is supported by others (*parabharo*), he eats what is offered (*balibhujo*), and his mating is hidden (*guḷhamethuno*).
His offspring (*pajā*) is born (*pasūti*) only once (*sakiṃ*), that is, at one time. He proclaims himself as “crow” (*kāka*). He supports (*bharati*) a cuckoo (*kokila*) of a different species.
639. Because he moves (*ulati*) like a crow (*kāko*), he is a *kākoḷa*; this is the substitution of the letter *ḷ*. He is also called *doṇakāka* and *daddhakāka*. The pair [of sounds] is “*bī-lauṃ*.”
*Khyāta* means "renowned. *Lū* means "to cut," with the suffix *ṇo*; for *vas*, there is *lāpa*, and also *lāva*. Because it does not act like a clod (*leḍḍu*), it is a *laṭukikā* (also *leḍḍukikā*);

[the suffix] *ṇvu* is applied. This triad refers to the bird that has the characteristics of an elephant. It is called *vāraṇa* because it resembles an elephant (*vāraṇa*). That in which the trunk—the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) or indicator—of the elephant is found [is the *hatthiliṅgasakuṇa*].

*Vijjatīti* means "the elephant-sign" (*hatthiliṅgo*). That in which an elephant's trunk (*hatthisoṇḍa*) exists is called *hatthisoṇḍo*; together with *vihaṅgamo* (bird), it is *hatthisoṇḍavihaṅgamo*.

640. The pair [of suffixes] *ukka* and *usa*. It cries out loudly (*uccaṃ kosati*), thus it is *ukkuso*; from the root *kusa* meaning "to sound," with the suffix *a*. From the root *kura* meaning "to sound," with the suffix *aro*, in the feminine (*thiyaṃ*).

*Kurarī*. Regarding the bird known as *kolaṭṭhipakkhī* (the "swallower of *kolaṭṭhi*"), it is called *kukkuho*. The bird that swallows *kolaṭṭhi* is the *kolaṭṭhipakkhī*. It is called *kukkuho* because it makes the sound "kukku";
[the root] *hu* [is used], or [it is derived from] *kuka* in the sense of calling out (*avhāne*), with the suffix *uho*. This triad refers to birds. The root *su* means "to hear.
Because it hears even the sound of humans, it is a *suva* (bird); [the suffix] *a* is added, and there is a substitution of *u* for *v*. It makes the sound "kī."

*Kīra*: that which makes (*karoti*) is a *kīra*. Alternatively, it is a *kīra* because it makes the sound of humans. *A*, *assī*. *Suka*: from the root *suka* meaning "to go," it is a *suka* because it utters (*kāyati*) a beautiful or excellent human sound.
The pair [of terms] refers to the size of a cock. One whose crest (*cūḷā*) is copper-colored is [a *tamba-cūḷa*]. It is a *kukkuṭa* because it cries out (*kukkuṭati*).
Alternatively, from the roots *kuka* or *vaka* meaning "to take" (*ādāna*), with the suffix *aṭo*.
641. *Dvayaṃ nijjivhe*: "Nijjivha" means one who has no tongue; thus, it is a term for one without a tongue. *Dvayaṃ koñcāsakuṇe*: two [names] for the crane bird (*koñca*).

These are feminine gender names for pairs of birds. *Koñca* is used in the senses of crookedness and swelling; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *koñcā*. *Kanta* is used in the sense of cutting; with the suffix *yu*, it belongs to the *nadādi* group, forming *assu*.
*Kuṇḍanī* also [is a name], from *kuṇḍa* in the sense of burning.

The pair [of meanings] applies to *cakkavāka*. It is called *cakkavāka* by means of the word *cakkam*. [The suffix] *ṇo* [is added]. The root *vac* is used in the sense of speech (*viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ*). That which has *cakkam* as its name is [called] *cakkavāka*.
There is also [the meaning] "that which is named after a chariot part" (*rathaṅgāvhayanāmako*). A chariot part (*rathaṅga*) is a wheel (*cakka*).
Its name (*avhāyo*) is "chariot part," thus it is "named after a chariot part" (*rathaṅgāvhayanāmako*). By that, the name "chariot part" is said to be synonymous with "chariot wheel."

And herein, *lakkhitalakkhaṇā* (indication by means of what is indicated) is that where, through a word whose function is metaphorically transferred to its characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*), or through a primary or secondary function, another meaning is indicated by the meaning that has been indicated.
For example, in the phrase "one whose weapons are the parts of a chariot" (*rathāvayavāyudho*), by the word "parts of a chariot" (*rathāvayava*), the wheel is indicated;
it does not refer to a specific type of weapon having that shape or that name. In the phrase "a chariot with a fringe" (*pantiratho*)... [the word "fringe"] indicates the pole.
By the word *panti* (row), the ten-syllable meter is indicated, not the word *dasa* (ten) itself;
yet by those [words], the arrangement of the terms *āyudha* (weapon) and *ratha* (chariot)—namely, the specific deity "Cakkāvayavāyudho" and the specific king "Dasaratho"—are indicated.
Likewise here, by the term *rathaṅga* (wheel-component), a part of the chariot is indicated, and by the term *avhāyate* (is called), the act of addressing is indicated, and not...
By that [name] as well, the sound of speech is indicated. Furthermore, by those [qualities], the specific bird known as the *cakkavāka* is characterized through its mutual arrangement;
thus, this is a figurative application (*gaṇī vutti*) based on qualities such as whiteness and so forth.

Regarding the *cātaka* bird, there are two [meanings]: "this one drinks the water of the clouds"; and from the root *sar*, meaning "to injure," *sāra* means "refuge," and it goes to that, hence it is called *sāraṅga*.

“*Sāraṅga* refers to the *cātaka* bird, the deer, and the variegated [animal] (*sabala*); it is used in three senses,” according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (23.23) and the *Rabhasa*. From the root *cat* in the sense of “begging,” with the suffix *ṇvu*, we have *thokaka*;
one who possesses only a little (*thoka*) water (*kaṃ*) in the sense of striving for it is a *thokaka*.
642. Two [meanings] refer to the bird and the cat. From the root *tul* in the sense of “weighing,” with the suffix *iya*. A cat associated with wings is a *sū*.
Two [names] for the tree-worm-eater: *sata-patta* (having a hundred feathers) and *sārasa* (it remembers the worm); thus it is *sārasa*.

Two [names] for the white bird that dwells having made its nest together with crows: *sukka* (white), from the root *vaka* meaning "to take," with the suffix *a*; and because of its white color, it is *sukka*, and because it dwells together with crows (*kāka*) or because of its crow-like shape, it is *kāka*—thus it is *sukkakāka* (the white crow).

The word *visakaṇṭhikā* (the crane) has two [forms]. The suffix *ṇvu* is applied to the root *bal* (to live), with lengthening of the vowel and optionally the replacement of *a* by *ā*. A *visakaṇṭhikā* is one whose throat (*kaṇṭha*) is black, resembling poison (*visa*); she has no male (*pumā*) name. And it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"Just as in the species of the crane, a male is never found;
When the clouds thunder, they then conceive. — *Apadāna*, Thera-vagga 1.1.511.
643. There are two types of *kaṅka*. One whose back resembles iron is a *lohapiṭṭha*. *Kaṅka* means "greedy"; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *kaṅka*. There are two types of *pattakaṇṭha*.

Because it moves like one who is lame (*khañja*), it is a *khañjarīṭa*; [the suffix] *īṭa*. Because it produces happiness (*khaṃ*) for those who see it, it is a *khañjana*. Or, from the root *khañja* meaning "deficiency of movement," with the suffix *yu*.

There are two types of village sparrow (*gāmacāṭaka*), or simply a sparrow (*cāṭaka*). Because it cries out in quarrel (*kalahaṃ*), it is a *kalaviṅka*, beginning with the suffix *ya*. Or, because it cuts (*lunāti*) happiness (*kaṃ*), it is a *kalaviṅka*; [the suffix] *ika*, and there is the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*). From the root *caṭa* meaning "breaking," with the suffix *ṇvu*, it is a *cāṭaka*.

Two [types of birds] with feathers the color of beryl and variegated wings are known as *suvaṇṇacūḷa* (“golden-crested”). [The term is derived from] *dibba*, with the insertion of the nasal (*bindu*) and the doubling of the consonant. That which makes the sound “ki” is a *kikī*; [the suffix] *ṇī* is added, making it *kikī*.

A *cāsa* bird that flies in the sky is a *kikīdivi* (Amarakośa 15.16). Two [types of birds] resembling clouds are known as *ṭī-ṭau*. Because of its association with the *kadamba* tree, it is a *kādambo*. A black-colored swan is a *kāḷahaṃso*; it is also called *kālahaṃso*.
Two [types of birds] known as *ṅahe-ḍo* are called *sakuṇo*. It is said: “*Sakunto* refers to a species of bird, specifically the *bhāsa* bird among the winged creatures.”
In the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "A bird endowed with a beautiful form or wing is a *bhāsapakkhī*;
for it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: 'The *bhāsa* speaks in a beautiful form; speaking, she is the *bhāsapakkhinī*.

The pair [of terms] beginning with "nvā-mī-sve" is known as *nīlapakkhinī*. A *dhūmyāṭa* is so called because it moves through or endures smoke (*dhūma*); the suffix *-ṇa* is applied. It is a *bhiṅga* as well, because its characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is contemptible due to its black color.

There are two [types] of water-hen (*jalakukkuṭa*). Regarding *dātyūha*: from the root *dā* meaning "to cut" (*lavana*), *dāti* means "he cuts," "he plucks," or "he exerts himself"; thus it is a *dātyūha*. The sense of "cutting" (*khaṇḍita*) and "plucking" (*addhana*) is inherent. In the season when the crop is ripe, that which has a "throat" (*kaṇṭha*)—meaning a "plucking" (*kaṇḍaddhana*)—is a *kāḷakaṇṭhaka*; the suffix *-ka* is applied at the end of the compound. 645.

The group beginning with *khudda*, starting with *madhucchiṭṭhaka*, constitutes the category of "types of flies" (*makkhikābheda*). From the root *makkhi* meaning "to collect" (*saṅghāta*), with the suffix *-ṇvu*, we have *makkhikā*.
A "type of fly" (*makkhikābheda*) is the variety thereof. Among these, the one known as *mhaṇa* is the tawny fly (*piṅgalamakkhikā*).
Two [terms]: *ḍaṃsa* from the root *ḍaṃs* (to bite), *ḍaṃsa*; also *daṃsa*. Or, *ḍaṃsa* (to eat); it is the name for a tawny-colored fly.

The egg of a fly is called *āsāṭikā*. From the root *saṭ* (to be a part), with the suffix *ṇvu*. Two [terms] for what is known as "nhaṃ": *paṭaṅga*, because it moves (*paṭa*)—thus *paṭaṅga*; also *pataṅga*. It moves and harms, thus *salabha*; also *alabha*. Or from *sal* (to go). 646. Two [terms] for what is known as "cheṃ":
from *maka* (a living being), with the suffix *asa*, *makasa*. Two [terms] for the *varaṇaka* fly found in the heat of summer, among *nuhā* plants, and so forth.

It is called *cīrī* because it makes the sound "cīrī"; or [the root] *ciri* means to injure, belonging to the *nadādi* group and beginning with a long vowel. From the root *jhalla*, meaning sound, with the suffix *ṇvu*, we have *jhallikā*.

These two refer to a leather strip used for covering the gaps between palm leaves and so forth. Like lac (*jatu*), it is *jatukā*; the suffix *ko* is used in the sense of comparison. For the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (19.40) states:
"In the *Rabhasa* lexicon, *jatuka* is feminine when referring to asafoetida, leather strips, and lac. It is also *ajinaṃ*.
*Cammapattā*: one whose feathers (pattā) are made of leather (camma). *Dvayaṃ haṃsasāmaññe*: there are two [terms] common to the swan (*haṃsa*).

It travels the journey; thus it is a swan. One whose white wing-feathers (*chada-patta*) are so. Because it is stated that the etymology may be in any way whatsoever, even for one with non-white wings, there is *cakkaṅga* and *mānasoka*.
That which has the limbs (*aṅga*) of a wheel (*cakra*)—that is, of a ruddy goose (*cakkavāka*). That which has Lake Mānasa as its abode (*oka*).
647. Those distinguished by red and crimson feet and beaks, and white in body, are called *rājahaṃsa*; they are the kings (*rājāno*) of the swans (*haṃsānam*), thus "royal swans" (*rājahaṃsā*).
Those distinguished by soiled feet and beaks are called *mallika*. [The root] *mala* or *malla* means "to hold"; with the suffix *i*, it forms a noun.
According to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (15.24), Rudra states: "The word *mallika* refers to a species of swan and to a type of grass-spike. By the word *ākhyā*...
Bahubbīhi compound: those distinguished by dark (asita) and black (kaṇha) claws and beaks are the Dhataraṭṭhas; the descendants of the Dhataraṭṭhas are the Dhataraṭṭhas—this is not [the case here].
648. The triad refers to the animals (tiracchāne).
One that moves crosswise (tiriyaṃ) is "tiraccha"; for *tiriya*, it becomes *tiro*; for *añcati*, it becomes *ccha*.
The mother is an animal (*tiracchānī*); an animal itself is "gone to the animal state" (*tiracchānagata*). Alternatively, it is "gone to" or "attained" that state;
or it is "included within" them—thus it is "gone to the animal state. The word *siyā* ("might be") is a verb form independent of its root;
for the meaning of "becoming" (*bhavati*) or the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is sometimes independent of its root, but never independent of its suffix. Likewise...
Sometimes one regards both, but never without regarding both; this is the case everywhere. The Lion and Other Sections.
The Commentary on the Forest and Other Sections is finished.
7. The Commentary on the Abyss Section.

649–650. A set of four [terms] regarding the underworld (*pātāla*). *Adhara-bhuvana* (the lower world) is *adhobhuvana*. It is called *pātāla* because beings fall into it; the suffix *-āla* has a long vowel in its middle. It is the world of the *nāgas*. *Rasātala*:

from *rasā* (the earth) and *tala* (the base), thus "the base of the earth. *Sobbha* means a mere hole or pit. *Vivara*: from the root *raṇ* (in the sense of sound), with the suffix *-dha*, and the nasalization (*natta*), beginning with *ya*. *Vivara*:

from *vara* (in the sense of splendor), or from *vi-gata-vara*, meaning "that which has the warding off (*vāraṇa*) of splendor. *Chidda*: from the root *chid* (in the sense of splitting or making two). *Kuha*: from the root *kuh* (in the sense of wonder). *Susa*: from the root *sus* (in the sense of drying up), with the suffix *-ira*.

*Bheda* means breaking; *a*, *susata*, and *i* mean a hole (*susi*). That which one goes into after cutting is a fissure (*chiggala*), such as [the examples] beginning with that. A pit (*sobbha*) is that in which there is a well-filled void (*abbha*) or space.

Regarding the neuter term "hollow" (*susira*), which is a general designation for a cavity, it applies to all three genders when referring to a perforated or porous substance, as in: "a hollow tree," "a hollow mango tree," and "a hollow piece of wood."

Two [words] for a hole in the ground: *kāsa* (in the sense of digging) and *ava* (in the sense of protecting); with the suffix *-aṭ*, we have *āvāṭa* and also *avāṭa*. Two [names] for the queen of serpents:

*Vāsuki*, so called because he possesses (*vasu*) jewels (*ratana*). 651. Two [names] for the queen of *nāgas*: *Ananta*, so called because he was not found (*anupaladdha*) even by the gods; and *Śeṣa*, from the root *śis* (in the sense of harming), as they say he harms or fashions (*kappeti*) the world;

with the suffix *-a*. Two [names] for the boa constrictor: *Vāhasa*, from *vah* (to carry) with the suffix *-asa*; and *Ajagara*, from *aja* (goat) and *gil* (to swallow), meaning "he swallows a goat"; with the suffix *-ara*, the letter *i* becomes *ra*. Also *Sayī*, one whose nature is to lie down (*sayana-sīla*).

The pair *gonasa* and *sappa* are known as the "ṅā-cve" [snake]. It is called *gonasa* because its nose (*nāsā*) is like that of a cow (*go*); in this technical name, the word *nāsā* is replaced by *nasa* according to Pāṇini 5.4.119. *Tiliccha* means one who desires sesame (*tila*), or one who moves crosswise (*tiriyaṃ añcati*);

it belongs to the class beginning with *yad*. The pair refers to the *deḍḍubha*, which is called the "water-snake" (*jalasappa*). It is called *deḍḍubha* because it is covered (*ubhati*) by a line (*rāji*) of *deḍḍu* [spots]. Due to the presence of lines on its back, it is called *rājula*; the suffix *-ula* is used here.
These two names also apply to the deaf snake (*badhirasappa*). 652. The *kambala* and the *assatara*—these two families of *nāgas* dwell at the foot of Mount Meru.

Two [terms] for a snake living in a house: *vesmanivutthasappa*. There is also the reading *vammanī*. Because it is said, "a snake of the house that is not pure," it refers to one who possesses virtue (*sīla*), whose mind (*mano*) is such that he has not killed [the snake] due to its being free from venom;

[thus] *silutto*, with the elision of the vowel, etc. Two [terms] for a snake living on the tops of trees, etc.: *rukkhaggādinivutthasappa*. A snake that is blue or green is a *nīlasappa*. For Tārapāla says, "The word *nīla* [is used] for black and for green.

That which exists on a stone in the first instance is a *silābhu*. 653–654. *Visadharanta* means simply a snake. One whose venom (*visa*) is in his mouth (*āsī*) is an *āsīvisa*; *āsī* means the fang of a snake. *Bhuja*...
In the sense of crookedness (*koṭilya*): because it moves while being crooked, it is called *bhujaṅga*; likewise *bhujaga* and *bhujaṅgama*. In the root *ahi* meaning "to go":

because it crawls (*saranta*) and glides (*sappati*) as it goes, it is called *sarīsapo* (reptile); here there is elision of the conjunct (*saṃyogalopa*), and this is a compound without elision of the final vowel (*aluttasamāsa*).

*Bhujaṅga* and *bhujaṅgama* are also used. However, in the work of Sabbadhara, it is stated: "Because it glides (*sappati*) intensely (*bhusaṃ*) or repeatedly (*punappunaṃ*) in a crooked manner, it is called *sarīsapo*."
*Phaṇayogā*: one who possesses a hood (*phaṇa*) is a *phaṇī*. Because he moves with his body touching the ground, he is a *sappi*; the act of moving (*gati*) is *sappana*.

He goes swiftly (*araṃ*), that is, quickly; thus he is an *alagadda*. The substitution of *da* for *sa* and *la* for *ra* results in *alagadda*. This term also applies to water-snakes, as Amarasīha states in the *Amarakośa* (8.5):
"The *alagadda* is a water-snake (*jalavāḷo*). *Bhoga* refers to the hooded body; because of its connection with that, it is a *bhogī*. He goes by means of wisdom (*pannaṃ*); thus...
A *pannaga* is so called because it does not move with its feet (*pāda*). It has two tongues. Because it moves by means of its chest (*urasa*), it is an *uraga*.
It specifically seizes (*ālāti*) or grasps (*gaṇhāti*) or approaches (*āyuti*), thus it is a *vāḷa*; the *la* becomes *ḷa*, and *vā* refers to movement or *ālo*. It is long due to its elongated body.
That which has a long back—by rule of compound (*samāsa*), *ka* is substituted. That whose foot is the belly itself. It bears poison. A *cakkī*.

Kuṇḍalī, Gūḷhapāda, Cakkhussava, Kākodara, Dabbīkara, Bilesaya, Jimhaga, and Pavanāsana. He is Cakkī because of his connection with the wheel on his head. He is Kuṇḍalī because his body is like a coil (kuṇḍala). He is Cakkhussava because he hears with his eyes. His belly is like that of a crow (kāka). Because he moves by means of a forked stick (dabbī), his hood is the "fork" (dabbī); he makes it—that is, he spreads it—thus he is Dabbīkara. He is Bilesaya because he dwells in the hollows (bilesa). He is Jimhaga because he moves crookedly. He is Pavanāsana because he sits upon the wind. He is Cakkī due to the application of the wheel on his head. He is Kuṇḍalī because his body is like a coil. He is Cakkhussava because he hears with his eyes. His belly is like that of a crow. Because he moves by means of a forked stick, his hood is the "fork"; he makes it, he binds it. Thus he is Dabbīkara. He is Bilesaya because he dwells in the hollows. He is Jimhaga because he moves crookedly. He is Pavanāsana because he sits upon the wind. He is Cakkī due to the application of the wheel on his head. He is Kuṇḍalī because his body is like a coil. He is Cakkhussava because he hears with his eyes. His belly is like that of a crow. Because he moves by means of a forked stick, his hood is the "fork"; he makes it, he binds it. Thus he is Dabbīkara. He is Bilesaya because he dwells in the hollows. *Dabbīkaro*. Even in the *Sāmaññaniddesa*, it is precisely the black snake (*kaṇhasappa*) and others that are called *dabbīkara*. It moves crookedly (*jimha*) and tortuously (*kuṭila*). *Pavanāsana* means one who feeds on wind (*vātabhojī*).

The body (*tanu*) of the hooded snake (*phaṇin*) is called its "coil" (*bhoga*). It is called *bhoga* because it "enjoys" (*bhujati*); from the root *bhuja* in the sense of "crookedness," with the suffix *-no*.

655–656. There are two [terms] for a snake’s fang. That by which one is not (*asa*) is *asana*; that which exists in the mouth (*mukha*) is *āsī*. A snake’s fang (*sappassa dāṭhā*) is its supreme tooth.

There are two [terms] for a snake’s sloughed skin. Because it is shed (*nimuccate*), it is a snake (*sappa*); [the suffix] *ṇo* [is applied]. Because it resembles a garment (*kañcuka*), it is called a "slough" (*kañcuka*).
They are equal, having the same meaning.
There are two types of poison (*visa*). That which goes through the path of the hips and pervades the body is *visa*; [the root] *vis* means "to enter.
It swallows, thus it is *garaḷa*; [the suffix] *aḷa*. *Halāhala*, *kāḷakūṭa*, and so forth—these nine, including the *kākola* and other such beings, are the varieties of that poison.
And it is said: "In the masculine, *paṇḍa*, *kākola*, *kāḷakūṭa*, and *halāhala*..."
“Soraṭṭhika, Sukkikeyya, Brahmaputta, Padīpana, Dārada, and Vacchanābha—these are the nine varieties of *visa* (poison). (Amarakosa 8.10–11) In this context, *halāhala* is masculine;
by the use of the particle *vā*, it is also neuter, for in the *Tikaṇḍasesa* it is stated as “*hālāhala*. (Tikaṇḍasesa)
1.8.5 *Dīghādipi* (and so forth). The *halāhala* creeper is shaped like a palm leaf, has blue leaves, and its fruit resembles a cow’s udder (*gothaṇa*).
When it is near, trees and other plants are consumed by fire. It grows in the Himalayas, in Kiṅkhaḍā, in Koṅkaṇa, and in the southern ocean.

[The derivation is as follows: it is called *hala* because it "strikes" (*hanati*); with the suffix *a*, the *l* of *hana* is elided, resulting in *hala*. Since it is the *hala* even of *halāni*, it is *halāhala*; the vowel in the middle is long. [It is depicted] with a horizontal line.
That which is covered with double joints (*dvijapada*) and likewise pervaded by knots (*gaṇṭhi*) like dense drops (*bindu*), that is *kālakūṭa*.

And this is the resin of a tree resembling the *assattha* tree, which arose during the age of the Asuras in the battle between the Devas and Asuras from the very blood of the Asura named Puthumāli; it is found on mountains such as Ahicchattra, Malaya, Koṅkaṇa, and Siṅgavera.
It is called *kāḷakūṭa* because it is black in color and a "deceitful" (*kūṭa*) poison due to its resemblance to a forged iron mallet in its taking away the lives of beings.
However, according to the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā*: "The son of Brahmā is Kapila;
the one born on Mount Malaya is Khara; the burner is Padīpana; and the one with red color is Añjanaddija. (8.10–11)
That which grows in Darada is *dārada*, known by the name *suprabha* and well-known in that region. It resembles the *vacchanābha* (musk deer) and the leaf of the *sinduvāra* tree;
trees do not grow near it, and the wind touched by it causes decay. It is produced in the Vindhya and Kikkindā mountains.
Thus, the nature of other poisons (*visantarā*) should also be understood from traditional authority (*āgama*).

The pair [of terms] refers to those who catch snakes for the sake of wealth. One who has the habit of catching wild animals is a *vāḷagāhī*. One who plays with (*dibbati*) snakes with his mouth or snout (*tuṇḍa*) is an *ahituṇḍika*; the suffix *-ika* is applied. Thus, it is also stated in the *Amarakośa*, verse 8.11, in the *Amaramālā*:

“*Vāḷagāhī* and *ahituṇḍika*. 657. The triad [refers to] hell (*niraya*). Iron (*ayo*) is a desirable fruit; that from which this has departed is *niraya*. Alternatively, it is *niraya* because the movement (*raya*) there is censured (*nindita*). A corrupted state of existence is a miserable destination (*duggati*). It leads (*neti*) one toward demerit (*apuñña*), thus it is *naraka*; the suffix *-ka* is applied, and *narako* is also used.
Among those hells, that which is called the "Great Hell" (Mahāniraya) is eightfold; this he shows by the verse beginning with "Sañjīva.
It is called Sañjīva because even while dying, the beings there live again and again for the sake of experiencing the results of their karma.
In that hell, the bodies of the denizens are marked with black strings by carpenters and then planed with axes.
Thus it is called Kālasutta (Black Thread). Because they cry out with sounds of suffering intensely and repeatedly in this place, it is Roruva;

and because it is both great (*mahanta*) and a place of wailing (*roruva*), it is Mahāroruva. Again, by the term "Roruva," Cūḷaroruva (Little Wailing) is meant. Because beings fall into it intensely, it is Patāpana (Scorching);
because it is obstructed (*rudda*) by waves (*vīci*) and surges (*taraṅga*), or because there is not even a trace (*leso*) of a wave of happiness here, it is Avīci (Without Interval).
Regarding the phrase “*vīci sukhataraṅgesū*,” this refers to *Tikaṇḍasesa* 3.3.78. Therefore, because there is no wave (*vīci*) of happiness (*sukha*) here, it is called *Avīci*.
Because beings are struck (*haññanti*) here by mountains that have come from all sides, it is called *Saṅghāta*. Because they burn (*tapanti*) here, it is called *Tāpana*.
The word “iti” serves the purpose of concluding the list of the eight [great hells].

658. Among those, in the hells (*niraya*), there are these two hellish reservoirs and receptacles of water: *Vetaraṇī* and *Lohakumbhī*. *Taraṇī* means a boat; that which has no such [boat] is *Vetaraṇī*. A jar made of iron is *lohakumbhī*.

The pair refers to the hell-guardians (*nirayapāla*). *Kāraṇā* means torment (*yātanā*); it is intense sensation (*tibbavedanā*). One who inflicts this is a *kāraṇika*. One who casts beings who have gone to hell is a *nirayapa*.
The pair refers to the beings who have gone to hell. One who goes to hell is a *nerayika*. One who goes to *naraka* is a *nāraka*.
659. *Udadhi* is the name for the ocean that reaches to the horizon. It is called *aṇṇava* because water (*aṇṇa*) flows (*vāti*) or goes within it;

or alternatively, it is called *aṇṇava* because water (*aṇṇa*) exists within it—the suffix *-va* being used in the sense of existence (*assatthi*). It is called *sāgara* because it was dug by the princes (*sagarehi*) who were sons of kings;

or it is called *sāgara* because it is a mine (*ākara*) of those riches (*sānaṃ dhanānaṃ*); or from the root *kassa* (to desire) with the suffix *-go*, or from *sāga* (in the sense of restraint) with the suffix *-aro*. It is called *sindhu* because it flows (*sandate*).

*Sanda* means flowing; *savana* means flowing. *Ud* means moistening. Because the waters (*āpa*) are completely moistened (*sammā klidanti*) by this [moon] at its rising, it is called the *samuddo* (ocean).

The term *jalanidhi* (treasure-house of waters) and *udadhi* (water-holder) mean that the waters (*jalāni*) and liquids (*udakāni*) are stored (*nidhīyante*) or held (*dhīyante*) therein. In the word *udadhi*, there is a substitution of *uda* for *udaka*.

Of that ocean, there are the Milk Ocean (*khīraṇṇavo*), and so forth: the Salt Ocean (*lavaṇodo*), the Curd Ocean (*dadhyudo*), the Butter Ocean (*ghatodo*), the Sugarcane-juice Ocean (*ucchurasodo*), and the Wine Ocean (*madirodo*).
"Sweet-watered" (*sādūdaka*)—these are the seven specific types of great oceans (*mahānnavavisesa*). The ocean that has the color of milk is a "milk-ocean" (*khīraṇṇava*).

The shore-region of this sea, the region of the bank, is called the "tide-line" (*velā*); it is so called because in it the waters (*irā*) recede (*vigacchanti*). A whirlpool is called a "whirl" (*āvaṭṭa*), which is the revolving or turning of the waters like a wheel; it is a whirlpool because the waters revolve there.

The group of three [roots] ends with *bindu*. *Thu* is used in praise; *vo*, in increase. *Vidi* means "in a part," *u*, with the nasal dot (*bindu*). *Phusa* means "touching," *to*, [forming] *phusitaṃ*. A rampart, the protection of a house and so forth, and the outflow of water is called a *bhamo*;
*bhamu* means "unsteadiness. 661. *Siloko* refers to water. *Āpa* means "pervading"; it pervades everywhere, thus it is *āpo*. That which is to be drunk is *payo*;

from the root *pā* "to drink," with the suffix *ṇyo*. It is shortened, thus *payo*. *Jala* means "grain," with the suffix *a*. It wards off what is low and high, thus *vāri*; from the root *vara* "to restrain," with the suffix *ṇi*, it restrains.
They thirst for it, or they drink it; thus it is *pānīya* (drink), from the root *anī*. It flows, thus it is *salila*; [the root] *sala* means "to go," with the suffix *ilo*.
From the root *ud* meaning "moistening," with the suffix *ṇvu*, there is the elision of *u*; or alternatively, it is *daka* because it produces the cessation of thirst (*pipāsaccheda*).

For in the *Ekakkharakosa* verse 20, it says: "The roots *dā* mean 'giving' and 'cutting,' and [the vowel] is short. From the root *ana* meaning "sound," with the suffix *a*, there is doubling [of the consonant]; from the root *ara* meaning "going."

Or [the suffix] *to*, with *anna* as the substitute, and the nasalization (*ṇattaṃ*). From the root *nī* (to lead), [with the suffix] *īra*, we have *nīra*. From *vana* (in the sense of desiring), [with the suffix] *īya*: it is desired by one who thirsts, thus *vanaṃ* (water).

From *vā* (in the sense of moving), [with the suffix] *ala*, we have *vāla*. It protects and preserves, thus *toyaṃ*; from *tā* (to protect), belonging to the *curādi* group, [with the suffix] *ya*, and the change of the vowel *ā* to *u*.

From *amba* (in the sense of sound), [with the suffix] *u*, we have *ambu*. From *ud* (in the senses of flowing and moistening), [with the suffix] *ṇvu*, we have *udakaṃ*. From *kara* (in the sense of making), [with the suffix] *kvi*, we have *kaṃ*. [The word] *kamalaṃ*...

*Khīram* (milk): [derived from] *kamu* (to desire) with the suffixes *icchā* and *kantī*, and the suffix *alo*. *Khanu* (to injure) with the suffix *īro*, elision of *na*, or *khī* (to perish) with *īra*: thus *khīram*. 662. *Catukkaṃ* (a group of four), meaning a wave.
It is called a *taraṅga* because it moves crossing over (*taranto gacchati*) or because it goes toward the shore (*tīraṃ gacchati*).

This is an *aluttasamāsa* (compound without elision), with the substitution of *ī* for *a* in the subsequent member. *Bhaṅga* (breaking): it breaks by itself; [from root] *bhañja* with the suffix *a*. *Ūmi* (wave): [from root] *ūha* (to reflect/think) with the suffix *mi*, elision of *ha*, and the addition of *ara*.
In *gamane* (in going), *mi*, *assū*, and *ralopa*. That which collects (*cinoti*) diverse (*vicitta*) astonishment (*vimhaya*) is a *vīci*;

*i* [is the suffix], and there is lengthening of the prefix (*upasagga*). These two [terms] apply to both masculine and feminine. The pair *ullolo* and *kallolo* is said to refer to the great waves (*mahāvīcīsu*). In *ulla* [from] *ula* in the sense of "going," or *lola* in the sense of "madness" (*ummādane*): that which causes to surge (*ullolayati*) is *ullolo*; [the suffix] *ṇo*, and *dvitta* (doubling). In *kalla* in the sense of "sound" (*sadde*), with *olo*, it is *kallolo*.

663. *Sīlakaddhaṃ* [is derived] from *kaddama*. *Jala* means mud; the suffix *ṇo* is applied in the sense of an object (*kammani*), and the letter *m* is a modification of the phoneme (*vaṇṇavikāra*).

*Kala* in the sense of counting, with the suffix *alo*. *Paca* in the sense of speaking diffusely, with the suffix *ṇo*. *Cikkha* in the sense of speaking, with the suffix *alo*, and doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ*). *Kada* in the sense of striking, with the suffix *amo*, and doubling of the consonant.

*Chakkaṃ vālukāyaṃ*: [This group of six words refers to sand. *Pula* in the sense of greatness; with the suffix *ino*, it becomes *pulinaṃ*. *Vala* in the sense of covering; with the suffix *ṇvu* and the feminine marker *assu*, it becomes *vālukā*, feminine.
*Vaṇṇa* in the sense of sound; *vaṇṇo*. *Mara* in the sense of abandoning life; with the suffix *u*, it becomes *maru*; it also means a deity (*devo*). *Ara* in the sense of going;

with the suffix *u* and the feminine marker *assu*, it becomes *uru*; it also means great (*mahanto*). Thus: *vaṇṇo ca maru ca uru ca* = *vaṇṇamarūru*. *Sica* in the sense of trickling; with the suffix *to*, it becomes *sikatā*, feminine.
664. The ground situated in the midst of water, which serves as the basis for action, is called "antarīpa" (an island) or "dīpa" (an island).

It is "antarīpa" because it has entered between two bodies of water that have come together; the vowel *ā* is elided. Alternatively, there is the reading "antarīya"; in that case, the analysis (*viggaha*) is:

"that which exists in the interval (*antara*) between two bodies of water that have come together," with the vowel *ā* elided. This is because the two bodies of water that have come together serve as the cause for its existence therein.
*dīpo*. There is the elision of the *v* and *ā* vowels, and the substitution of *i*; thus, *dīpo*. By means of the vowel *v*, it also forms *dīvaṃ*. "Pañcaka" is a name for a shore (*tīra*).

In the sense of "success in action," *pāra* belongs to the *curādi* group; [suffix] *a*. In the sense of "obstructing," *kūla* takes the suffix *ṇo*. In the sense of "obstructing," *rudha* forms *rodhaṃ*. The term "patīra" is stated for the purpose of excluding other shores, etc. In the sense of "lying along," *taṭa* takes the suffix *a*; in the feminine, *taṭī*. 665.
The word *pāra* refers to the opposite shore; it is neuter. In the sense of "success in action," *pāra*... [belongs to the *curādi* group]. *Pāra*.
Or, it is "pāra" because it has the capacity (*sāmatthiya*) to cross over, meaning it is able to ward off waves and the like.
That which is called "apāra" is the near shore (*ora-tīra*). "Ora" means that which exists on this side of the shore; [the suffix] *ṇo* is added. "Apāra" is the other shore distinct from "pāra.
The group of five refers to a raft (*uḷumpa*). It is a "uḷupa" because it protects (*pāti*) from water (*uḷu*); by the addition of the nasal augment (*niggahītāgama*), it becomes "uḷumpa."
*Plava*: that by which one floats (*plavati*) or floats (*plavanti*), hence *plava*; from the root *plu*, meaning "to go," here specifically "going on water.

*Kulla*: from *kula*, meaning "lineage" (*santāna*); or, *ke* (water) + *ulati* (goes), hence *kulla* (a raft). This is a double consonant (*dvitta*). *Tara*: that by which they cross (*taranti*), hence *tara*; from the roots *tṛ* and *plu*, both meaning "to cross over. *Paccarī*:

that by which people repeatedly (*punaḥ-punaḥ*) move about (*aranti*) in the water through coming and going; hence *paccarī* (a ferry-boat), from the root *ar*. It refers to river-crossings and the like.

666. This is a triplet concerning the boat (*nāvā*). That by which one crosses is *taraṇī*; with the suffix *yu*, as in the class beginning with *nada*, it becomes *tari* when the suffix *ip* is applied, but with the suffix *īm*, it is *tarī*.

*Nu* is used in the sense of praise; with the suffix *a* and the substitution for the vowel *vuḍḍhi*, it becomes *nāvā*. Two [terms] refer to a pillar of the Laṅkā temple. From the root *kūpa* (in the sense of going), with the suffix *ṇvu*, it is *kūpaka*;

or else, with the suffix *ap*, the suffix *ko* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), thus *kūpaka*. From the root *kamu* (in the sense of desire), with the suffix *bho* and the suffix *ko* in the sense of identity, and with the addition of *assu*, it becomes *kumbhakaṃ*.
The two [terms] beginning with “*pe*” and ending with “*seṃ*” are well known. It is called *pacchābandho* because it is to be bound at the rear part of that [object].

That by which a *goṭaviso*, an *iso*, and an *avanto*—that is, a horse—proceeds toward a desired direction is a *goṭaviso*. The two [terms] beginning with “*pe*” and ending with “*tamā*” are well known.
Like the side of a boat, it is a large oar; because one propels the vehicle by means of it, it is so called, as it supports that [vehicle].
Not in the sense of *kammani* (the object). A boatman is one who is engaged with a boat. 667.

Two [terms] regarding the means of traveling by boat: *aritthaṃ* is that by which there is no pleasure (*arati*); it is derived from *chada* and other roots with the addition of the suffix *traṇ*, the insertion of the vowel *i*, and doubling of the consonant.

*Kenipāto* is that which is cast down into the water (*ke jale nipātiyate*); this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). Two [terms] regarding the helmsman: a ship is a vessel (*pavahanaṃ*); one who causes that to move is a ship-captain (*potavāho*). One who steers the ship is a helmsman (*niyāmako*); from the root *yamu* in the sense of "to cease," preceded by *ni* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *ṇvu*; thus *niyāmako*. Also in the sense of a helmsman.
Those merchants who carry out the business of trade by ship are called *saṃyattikā*. *Saṃyāna* means a voyage; it is the going to another island (*dīpantara-gamana*).

*Traṇa* (protection) is their purpose; thus they are *saṃyattikā*. [The suffix] *-ika* is added, with the elision of *ra* and the shortening of the vowel. Alternatively, it is established by the addition of the suffix *-tappaccaya*.
There are also sea-merchants (*potavāṇijā*); *pota* means a vessel, and they are the merchants of that.
668. *Laṅkārādayo* (ornaments, etc. and *phiādayo* (sails, etc. are the parts and components of a ship. *Lo* means "lord" (*indo*); the cause for that is *laṅkāro*.

*Vaṭo* is said to mean *sivaṭo* (a banyan tree); because it has that shape, it is *vaṭākāro*. For it is stated in the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*: "The word *vaṭo* [is used] for a wish-fulfilling tree and for a banyan tree.
*Phā* is in the sense of growth; with the suffix *-iyo*, it becomes *phiyo*.
Two [words] are known as "talaka. From the root *pū* (to purify), with the suffixes *to* and *vuḍḍhi*, it becomes *pavahanaṃ* because it carries away the controller.
*Vuttaṃ* is a verb. Two [words] refer to a wooden water-carrier: from *duṇa* (in the sense of moving or harming), with the suffix *a*, belonging to the *nada*-class, and *vuḍḍhi*, it becomes *doṇī*.
That by which one leads water (*ambu*) is *ambaṇaṃ*; there is the substitution of *ussa* and the change to *ṇa*. Alternatively, from *amba* (in the sense of sound), with the suffix *yu*.

669. Regarding the triad [of terms] beginning with *gambhīra*: the root *gam* means "to go"; with the suffix *īra*, there is the elision of *bha* and *ma*, resulting in *gabhīra*. However, when *mā* is elided, it becomes *gambhīra*.
Alternatively, it is called *gabhīra* because those who go (*gacchantā*) fear within it; it is also *gambhīra*. With the prefix *ni-*, the root *man* means "familiarity" (*abhyāsa*);

with the suffix *ṇa*, the *ma* becomes *na*, resulting in *nibbāna*. Its opposite, being the reverse of *gambhīra*, is called *uttāna*. It is *uttāna* because its measure (*tāna*) has risen up (*uggata*); it is not deep (*agambhīra*).

*Dvayaṃ agādhe*: "Gādha" refers to a footing or a desire for a firm foundation, as well as a knot. Where there is no footing, it is *agādha* (bottomless). Where one does not touch the lower surface, it is *atalamphassaṃ*.

The triad [of terms] refers to what is turbid (*appasanna*). Where there is no clarity, it is *anaccha*. *Kalusa* is also said to mean evil. *Vila* means to break; with the suffix *-ṇo*, it becomes *āvila*. Or, from the root *ava* meaning to protect, with the suffix *-ilo*, it is *āvila*. 670. The triad [of terms] refers to what is stainless (*nimmala*).
From the root *cho* meaning to cut: that which does not cut [the vision] is *accha*; with the suffix *-ṇo*, it is *accha*. *Saccha* is also used in this sense. *Sara*...

In the sense of "dispersing," there is the substitution of *anna*. That which has no impurity (*mala*) is *vimala*. The group beginning with *gambhīra* and ending with *vimala* applies to all three genders.

The group of five [words] refers to a fisherman. From the root *dhā*, meaning "to hold," comes *dhīvāra*. One who lives by killing fish is a *macchika*; here, the suffix *ika* is applied. [The word *maccha* means] fish.
One who binds with a net is a *macchabandha* (fisherman); or, one who kills fish is a *macchabandha*. There is the addition of the nasal stop (*niggahīta*).

*Kaṃ* means water; its *īlakkhī* (suffix) is *ī*. One who possesses a *vaṭṭa* (net) or the act of *vaṭṭana* (fishing) is a *kevaṭṭa*. *Kevaṭṭa* also [ends] in *-o*. One who is engaged in a net, or one who kills with a net, is a *jālika*;
here, *dāsa* (servant/slave) is also included. From the root *dāsa* in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), there is the suffix *-a*: "A *dāsa* [is used] in the sense of a fisherman and a servant."
*Cintāmaṇiṭīkā* 10.15, *Ruddo*, 671–672:
"Jhasāntaṃ" means fish. [The root] *mas* is for touching; it is established either by way of the verbal root *mar* (to die) or *mara* (giving up life), with the suffix *ino* and the elision of *ra*.
"Puthulomo" means one who has broad hairs in the region of the mouth. Because they are specifically types of fish such as the *pāṭhīna* and others—

Even for one who is hairless, this is the mode of livelihood. *Jhasa* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsa-ttha*), with the suffix *a*, thus *jhaso*. *Aṇḍaja* means "born from an egg. *Visāra*: by means of this, one moves about diversely (*vicitraṃ sarati*); [the suffix] *ṇo* is added.
Regarding rohit fish and others, the skin (*taco*) is the covering of the scales (*vakkalappāyo*); according to Ka., it is the covering of the fins (*battalappāyo*).
Because of its connection with that, the suffix *ī* is added, thus *sakalī*.

The various kinds of fish include the *rohitā* and so forth, as well as the *makara* and so forth. [The term] *rohita* is derived from the root *ruha* (to grow), with the suffix *-ta*; thus it is *rohita*. Because it is sweet in its digestion (*vipāka*), it is called *maggura*;

this is a modification of the color. Alternatively, it is *maggura* because it "intoxicates" (*majjati*). [The components are: *ūra*, *majja* (in the sense of purity), *jjassa* becomes *ggatta*, and there is a short vowel;

thus it is *maggura* [according to the rule] “ṅā khū. Because it possesses a horn (*siṅga*), it is *siṅgī*; [the suffix] *-ṇo* is applied according to the *nada*-class, and the *saṅgu* [element] is also included. It is called [such] because it moves through the wind (*vāta*).
Or *siṅgī*: [from] *hiṃsā* (to injure), *a*, *rassa go* (the substitution of *go* for *ra*), *assi*, elision of the *niggahīta*, [and the suffix] *nadādi*;
thus *siṅgī*. [By the rule] “*ṅa cve*. *Bala* in the sense of covering; *alo*, *lassa jo* (the substitution of *jo* for *la*); thus *balajo*. [By the rule] “*ṅa pā*. *Muñja* has the meaning of sound;
thus *muñjo*. *Pū* in the sense of purifying; *uso*, the substitutions of *vuddhi* and *āva*; thus *pāvuso*. *Mahāmukhamaccho*; [by the rule] “*ṅa ṭā*.”

*Sattavaṅka* means "crooked seven times" (*sattakkhattuṃ vaṅkatīti sattavaṅko*); [the suffix] *ṅa* is applied with the marker *se*. *Savaṅka* means "possessing a crook" (*saha vaṅkena*, or "that in which a crook is found");

[the suffix] *ṅa* is applied with the marker *mve*. *Naḷamīna* means "a fish shaped like a reed" (*naḷasaṇṭhāno mīno naḷamīno*); [the suffix] *ṅa* is applied with the markers *phau-ya*. *Gaṇḍaka* is derived from the root *kaḍi*, meaning "accumulation" or "parts of the body," with the suffix *ṇvu*;

[the suffix] *ṅa* is applied with the marker *mā*. *Susukā* is derived from the root *sas* (meaning "to injure"), with the suffix *u* and the augment *assu*; it is used in its own sense, and [the suffix] *ṅa* is applied with the markers *pau-ṭaye*.
It spreads from its resting place to its side, thus it is *sapharī*; [it refers to] a river and so forth. From the root *phara* (to spread), *sapharī* occurs in two genders; [the suffix] *ṅa-khū-mā*.
It scatters its mouth during the seizing of prey, thus it is *makara*;

[it refers to] a crocodile and so forth. 673. The seven great fish beginning with the *timi* are known as such. From the root *tima* (to be wet), *timati* thus it is *timi*; the suffix *i*, and *timi* also applies to the size of a fish.
*Gira* means "swallowing," [from the root] *ṇo*. *Lattaṃ* means "lordship. A *timi* with a "throat" (*gala*) is a *timiṅgala*; here there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
Because of its color, it resembles *piṅgala* and *timira*, thus it is *timirapiṅgala*. One who "rejoices intensely" (*ābhusaṃ nandati*) is *ānanda*;
[the root] *nanda* is used in the sense of prosperity. One who causes the *timi* fish to rejoice is *timinando*. There is also the reading *timindo*; [it means] the lord (*indo*) of the *timi* fish.
*Timinda*. That which has an additional growth (*adhika-āroha*) is an *ajjhāroha*.

A great *timi* fish is a *mahātimi*. (674) The pair [of terms] are known as *ṅa* and *phe*. A fish whose shape resembles a stone is a *pāsāṇamaccha*. Regarding the word *paṭhī*, it means distinctness in speech;
with the suffix *-ina*, the vowel is long in both cases, thus *pāṭhīna*; they also call it *ṅa-pau*. The pair [of terms] refer to a hook (*baḷisa*). It is called *vaṅkatī*.

*Vaṅko*: from the root *vaṅk*, meaning "to be crooked. *Balo*: from the root *bal*, meaning "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *iso*; the change to *ḷ* occurs. It also refers to a fish-hook; from the root *vidh*, meaning "to arrange" (*vidhāne*) and "to pierce" (*bhedane*), with the suffix *yu*, as it has multiple meanings.

*Tiko*: refers to the crocodile (*kumbhīla*). "Suṃsumāro" is a collective name. It is called *susu* because it "rushes" (*sasati*). *Susu* itself becomes *suṃsu*. It is called [suṃsumāra] because it "kills" (*māreti*).
*Māra* means *suṃsu*, and *māra* is indeed *suṃsumāra*. It is called *kumbha* because it swells (*ubhati*) or fills;

it is a reservoir of water. One who moves (*ulati*) or goes there is a *kumbhīla*. Alternatively, *kumbha* is a jar (*ghaṭa*); one who seizes (*lāti*) that is a *kumbhīla*. It is called *nakka* because it does not move (*na kamati*);
the suffix is *kvip*, and due to its being a nominal stem (*saññāsaddattā*), the original form of *na* is retained. Or, *nakka* is in the sense of "nose" (*nāsane*); it belongs to the *cur*-class.

The word *dvayaṃ* refers to two meanings for *kacchape*. A tortoise (*kummo*) is so called because its wave-like speed (*ūmi-vego*) is contemptible (*kucchito*). Regarding this, the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* (10.21) states:

"In the senses of speed, breaking, and appearance, *ūmi* is a masculine term for a wave"; and the *Nānātthasaṅgaha* states: "In the senses of speed, breaking, and appearance, *ūmi* is a feminine term for a wave and a ripple.

It is called a tortoise (*kacchapo*) because it drinks with its throat (*kacchena pibati*); the suffix *-ṇo* is applied here. *Kamaṭho* is also used in this sense; the root *kam-* means "desire," and *aṭho* is a suffix.

675. Two [meanings] for *kakkaṭa*: it is called *kakkaṭaka* because it "clings" (*kakatīti*). The suffix *-ko* is used in the sense of identity; or, from the root *kuk* (to seize) with the suffix *-aṭo*, there is the vowel lengthening (*ussattaṃ*).
From the root *kul* (in the sense of lineage and kinship) with the suffix *-īro*, or from *kuṃ* (the earth) and the root *lū* (to cut), one who cuts the earth is *kuḷīra*;

the suffix is *-īro*. Two [meanings] for *jalūkā*: *jalūkā* is a specific kind of leech (*ūkā*); or, it is called *jalūkā* because water (*jalaṃ*) is its dwelling place (*okaṃ gahaṃ*)—the suffix is *-ūsū*. From the root *uc* (to assemble).
No, it is *okaṃ*. One who drinks blood (*rudhira*) is a *rattapā* (blood-drinker).
The triad refers to the frog (*maṇḍūka*). From the root *maṇḍ* (to adorn), with the suffix *uka*, the vowel is long. From the root *dad* (to give), with the suffix *ura*, there is reduplication.

From the root *bhī* (fear), one who fears the serpent is a *bheko*; with the suffix *ika*, the vowel is long. *Vassābhū*, *sāluro*, and *plava* are also [names for it]. The pair refers to what is known as "tī. *Gaṇḍaṃ*...

One who produces an accumulation of pus is called *gaṇḍuppāda*. A creeper on the earth is a *mahīlatā*, which is also a *kiñculuka*. Why is it called *kiñculuka*? Because it swells (*culati*), thus it is *kiñculuka*; [it is] an *uka*-suffix. 676. There are two [words] for a pearl-oyster:
*sappa* [from the root] *gam* (to go), with the suffixes *i*, *assi*, *sippi*, and *thī*; and *sutti* [from the root] *su* (to flow/issue), with the suffix *tti*. There are two [words] for a conch:
*saṅkha* [from the root] *khanu* (to split/open), with the suffix *kvi*; and *saṅkha* [from the root] *samu* (to calm/settle), with the suffix *kho*. It blows the water (*kaṃ*).
It moves, thus it is *kumbu*; *u* is used for a female who is disliked.
The pair [of terms] belong to the class of small conch-shells (*khuddasaṅkhajātiya*). Like the claw (*nakha*) of a conch, it is a "conch-claw" (*saṅkhanakha*).

The pair [of terms] are known as "kharu. It flows in water, thus it is *jalasutti*; *su* is used in the sense of procreation. It goes together, thus it is *sambuko*; *u* and *ka* are suffixes, and *bonta* is also used; "sambuko..."
"Jalasuttīthī" (the woman at the water's edge)—thus [it is stated] in the *Cintāmaṇi-ṭīkā* 10.23, in the section on masculine nouns, by Vopālita.

677. Two [terms] for a reservoir (*jalāsaya*). A reservoir (*jalāsaya*) is a place where waters abide, a foundation for waters. Among those reservoirs, that which is deep and bottomless is called a lake (*rahada*). [The root] *hara*, meaning "to take," belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; with the suffix *do*, there is a change of letters (*vaṇṇavipariyaya*), resulting in *rahada*.

Two [terms] for a well (*udapāna*). In this, they drink water (*udakaṃ pivanti asmiṃ*); with the suffix *yu*, the *kalopa* [elision] occurs. In this, they drink (*pivanti asmiṃ*); it is a drinking-place (*pāna*), and that itself is a well (*kūpa*).
*Pāna-kūpa*: *ku* in the sense of sound; *po*; beginning with a long vowel; *kūpa*. Or, it is called *kūpa* because it is filled (*ubhati*) by what?

[The suffix] *po* replaces *bhassa*. *Andhu-pi*: *andha* in the sense of obstructing sight; *curādi* class; *u*. Both [terms] refer to a square pond. *Khanu* in the sense of digging; the suffix *to* in the sense of the object;
elision of *n*; beginning with a long vowel. *Pokkhara* means water; through its connection [with that], the suffix *ano*; *nadādi* class; thus *pokkharaṇī*.
678. Regarding the word *amara*, its suitability for designating a great lake with unfathomable waters, a place for lotuses, and a place devoid of lotuses should be seen in verse 10.28.
[The root] *taḷ* means to strike; or [the root] *tal* means to stand firm; *āko* is a suffix; on the other hand, there is the substitution of *ḷ*.
[The root] *sar* means to go; with the suffix *a*, it becomes *saro*. [The root] *vap* means to sow seeds; that by which they sow is a *vāpī* (pond), even one that is long and square.

A lake (*sarasī*) is that which possesses water (*sarati*); it is a term for a river or the like. The root *dah* means "to reduce to ashes"; alternatively, from the root *dhā*, meaning "to hold," with *dha* becoming *ha*.
A source (*ākara*) is the place of origin for lotuses (*ambuja*) or lilies (*paddha*).

A small lake is called a "pallala. Where there is abundant water during the rains, but only as much as the knee during the summer, or where it has simply dried up—derived from the root *palla*, meaning "to protect" (belonging to the *curādi* class), with the suffix *alo*—it is a *pallala*.
679–680. These seven great lakes are known as the *Anotatta* and so forth.

Among them, it is called *Anotatta* because the water there does not heat up due to being touched by the rays of the sun. It is called *Kaṇṇamuṇḍa* because of its proximity to the *Kaṇṇamuṇḍa* mountain.

It is called *Rathakāraka* because it "makes a chariot" (*rathaṃ karoti*); while this is the etymological derivation (*byuppatti*), the conventional designation (*saññā*) should be understood from common worldly usage alone.
Because he possesses six-colored tusks, he is the elephant king Chaddanta; because it is near the place where he dwells, the lake is called Chaddanta.
Because many *kuṇāla* birds are found there, it is *Kuṇāla*. *Mandākinī* is also said to refer to the celestial Ganges (*ākāsagaṅgā*).
Because many lions leap down into it, it is *Sīhappapāta*.

The pair [of terms] refers to a water reservoir constructed with embankments and the like near a well in a place abundant with water, intended for the drinking of livestock. It is called *āhāva* because livestock are summoned (*āhūyante*) here for drinking;
the suffix *ṇa* is used, and there is a substitution of *vuḍḍha*. It is called *nipāna* because they drink (*nipivanti*) therein; the suffix *yu* is used.

The pair [of terms] refers to a naturally excavated pool not made by humans, meaning it was created by the gods (*devanimmita*); others say it is derived from the root *soṇḍi*. According to the *Amara-kośa*: "An *akhāta* is a natural pool."
10.27. Indeed, *amaramālāyaṃ* [is] *puṃsakaṇḍaṃ*.
681. That which ends in *nadī* is *nadīyaṃ*. It flows, thus it is *anto*; beginning with *nada*, it is *savantī*. It goes to a low place, thus *ninnagā*, with the suffix *kvi*.
From the root *sand* (to flow), with the suffix *u*, there is vowel modification (*assittaṃ*), resulting in *sindhu*. From the root *sar* (to go), with the suffix *to*—
The augment *ik* is added, and it ends in a vowel (*sarit*). Water is its dwelling place; thus, "water" (*āpa*) and "ocean" (*samudda*), with the suffix *ṇo*, [form *āpanna*].
It goes to that [water], hence it is called *āpagā*. The root *nad* means "inarticulate sound"; it flows (*nadati*), hence *nadī*;

this belongs to the *nadādi* group, as waves are present here. These two [terms] refer to the Gaṅgā. According to worldly convention, she is called *Bhāgīrathī* because she was brought forth by King Bhagīratha; however, according to our own view:
"This is merely a name for that" is the definitive conclusion; thus it is in all cases. It "goes," therefore it is the Gaṅgā; it has been "gone to" (gamita), thus *go*.
Also, those who have gone to the three paths are "three-path-gone" (*tipathagatā*). A confluence, a meeting, or a junction of rivers (*sindhū*) is a "confluence" (*saṃbheda*).
In this [place], they break apart completely (*sammā bhijjanti*), thus it is a "confluence" (*saṃbheda*); the root *bhid* preceded by *sam* means "to meet," with the suffix *ṇo*.
682. These five rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, are called "great rivers" (mahānadī). Because she possesses swift movement that is not slow (*acira*), she is the *Aciravatī*.
[The root] *yam* means to cease; *Yamuṇā* is the sister of Yama, or *Yamunā*, where the suffix *-un* is used in the sense of "sister.

She is the *Sarabhū* because lakes (*sarāni*) exist by taking her as their boundary; or, the root *sar* means to move, to harm, or to think—the suffix *-ū* is added, and with the augment *abhot*, she is the *Sarabhū*.
In the word *mahāpūjāyaṃ*, [the suffix] *a* is applied;

it belongs to the class beginning with *nada*. The rivers such as the Candabhāgā and others are varieties of the five great rivers (*pañcamahānadī*). It is called *Candabhāgā* because it originates from a mountain named Candabhāga;

the suffix *-vantu* is added due to its connection with the root *sar* (to flow), with the letter *s* inserted in the middle, and it belongs to the class beginning with *nada*, thus forming *Sarasvatī*. The suffix *-vantu* is used here in the sense of excellence (*atisaya*).
683. *Niddosaṃ* means "faultless water"; thus it is the *Nerañjarā*. Alternatively, *nerañjarā* is a particular kind of musical instrument;
because its sound is equal to that [instrument], this river is named *Nerañjarā*. Because it is filled with various crocodiles (*nānā-gāha*), it has "wicked enemies" (*kucchita-vera*);

thus it is the *Kāverī*, beginning with "river. It gives happiness (*nammaṃ sukhaṃ dadāti*), thus it is the *Nammadā*; [the suffix] *ṇo* [is applied]. By the word "etcetera," [are included] the *Sarāvatī* and the *Vettavatī*.
The various types of rivers, such as the Kaṇṭakī and Kosikī, are included [herein].

The pair [of terms] refers to waterways found in places such as wells and temples. A "water-path" (vārimagga) is a passage for the exit of water. Regarding *nala*, the suffix *a* is applied; in the case of *nadādi*, there is the substitution of *ḷatta*; *panāḷi* is used in the feminine, while in the masculine it is *panāḷī*.

The triad [of terms] refers to a drain at the village gate, which is filled with impure, putrid mud. It is called *candanikā* because it causes the mind to burn (*dunoti*); this applies to the aforementioned examples.
684–685. *Jamu* (to eat), *alo*, *nadādi*, *bonto*, and *ḷattaṃ*: *jambāḷī*. That in which things stick is *oḷigallo*;
from *lagga* (to cling), *alo*, *ḷattaṃ*, *assi*, *galopo*, and the doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ*). This is a synonym for *paduma* (lotus) with its various suffixes.
It grows in a lake, thus it is *saroruhaṃ*; from *ruha* (to grow). It has a hundred petals; even though it is a specific type of lotus, it possesses the general quality of being a lotus (*padmatā*).

In particular, there is no difference [between the terms]. It finds (*vindati*) the enemy (*ara*), thus it is *aravinda*. The root *pada* means "to go"; the suffix *umo* is added. *Paduma* is not feminine. It grows in the mud (*paṅka*), thus it is *paṅkeruha*;
this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). The root *nala* means "to smell"; the suffix *ino* is added, and the vowel is changed to *ḷ*. The root *pusa* means "growth";

the suffix *kharo* is added, and the vowel is changed to *vuḍḍhi*. The *s* is changed to *ko*, thus it is *pokkhara*. Alternatively, it is *pokkhara* because it is born in the water (*pokkhara*). Even having emerged from the *muḷāla* [root],...

The *muḷāla* flower blooms. It is called *kamala* because it rests upon (*alayati*) and adorns (*bhūsati*) the water; the root *ala* means "to adorn. The *bhisapuppha* (lotus) is so called because it blooms after emerging from the stalk (*bhisat*).

It is called *kusesaya* because it lies or stays in the water (*kuse jale seti tiṭṭhati*); this is a compound with the elision of the intermediate vowel (*aluttasamāsa*). It is also called *tāmarasa*;

*tāmara* means water—as in another textual tradition which says, "If one [is] *tāmara*, he is a consumer of ghee"—it is called *tāmarasa* because it lies or stays therein (*tatra seti tiṭṭhati*); the suffix *ra* is added.
686. A white lotus is called a *puṇḍarīka*. [The root] *puḍ* means to break; some say it is *muḍi*. There is the suffix *ika*, and the augment *ara*;
*ma* becomes *pa*, and *i* becomes *ī*: thus, *puṇḍarīkaṃ*. A red lotus, however, is called a *kokanada* or a *kokāsaka*.
It is a *kokanada* because it makes a sound (*nādayati*) among the birds (*koke*); the suffix is *ṇa*. It is also a red water-lily (*rattuppala*). It is also called *kokanuda*.

*Pāṭha*. It is called *kokanada* because it "shines" (*kanati*) or "is beautiful" (*dibbati*); it belongs to the *bhū*-class (Dhātupātha 1025), with the suffix *do*. *Kana* [means] "to shine," "to be lovely," or "to go. It is called *kokāsaka* because it "shines" (*kāsatī*);
it has the suffix *ṇvu*, and *kāsa* [means] "to shine. Both terms refer to the filaments.
It is called *kiñjakkha* because it "is born in the *ki*"—referring to the *kamala* lotus and others—or because it "shines" (*jalati*) therein; it has the suffix *kho*.
*nassa* or *lassa*—what [is it]? There is the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). In the word *ke sarati*, there is the elision (*alopa*) of the locative case ending (*sattamiyā*).
"Two" refers to the neuter gender (*anitthī*). "Two" refers to the stalk of the lotus and so forth. It is called a *daṇḍa* because of its resemblance to a staff.

In the root *nala* meaning "to smell," there is the suffix *ṇo*. 687. "Two" refers to the lotus root (*muḷāla*). In the root *visa* meaning "to cause to go," there is the substitution of *bho* for *va*; thus, *bhisaṃ*. Alternatively, in the root *bhāsa* meaning "splendor," there is the substitution of the vowel *ā*.

It is called *muḷāla* because it is born from the root (*mūle jāyati*); here *alo* is used in another sense, with shortening of the vowel and the substitution of *ḷ*. Alternatively, *mūla* means "foundation," to which *alo* is added;
the remainder is as before. Both [forms] are not feminine. The two [terms] refer to the pericarp (*kaṇṇikā*).
A seed-receptacle, that is, a source for the seed, is a *bījakosa*. It is called *kaṇṇikā* because it is made upon the ear (*kaṇṇe karīyati*); it is an ornament for the ear.

It is called *kaṇṇikā* because of its similar shape. *Vana* means a dense thicket, such as a cluster of lotuses and the like. [The root] *saṇa* means to give; with the suffix *-ḍa*, it becomes *saṇḍa*. According to the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*:

"The word *saṇḍa* occurs in the sense of a collection of paths and the like, and in the masculine gender, it refers to a bull. (688) The pair [of terms] refers to the general category of the lotus, the water-lily, and so forth;
for indeed, the lotus (*padma*) is called both the great blue lotus (*mahoppala*) and the white lotus (*sitoppala*). [The term] *kuvalaya*...
For Vyāḍi says, "The blue lotus is the *nīla-indīvara*," and Bhāguri says, "The *kuvalaya* is the *utpala*, and it is considered the blue *indīvara*.
However, Vararuci says, "The *romo* and the *siti* are blue; the *kuvalaya* and the *indīvara* are the blue water-lily (*nīlambuja*).

Māladhi and Mādhava say, "O Paridhūsara, you possess a beauty resembling the petals of the *kuvalaya*. In that regard, the ancient tradition is followed here. If this is so, how [can it be used] with the word *utpala*?
Is it that the cognition [of the word *utpala*] applies only to the blue lotus (*nīluppalādi*) and not to the great lotus (*mahoppalādi*)? It is said:

Just as even within the general category of grain (*dhaññatta*), the word "grain" (*dhañña*) evokes the cognition of rice (*kāla*) and so forth, but not of mung beans (*mugga*) and so forth, so it is here as well.

The prefix *ut-* is used in the sense of drinking (*pāne*), and there is the suffix *-ala*. Because it floats (*plavati*) in water (*udake*), it is called *utpala*, and so forth. Like a ring (*valaya*) upon the earth (*kuyā*).

It is called *kuvalaya* because it brings beauty (*sobhā*). The term *nīluppala* consists of two parts. Regarding the blue color: *a* [is a suffix]; *nīla* means blue. *Indī* is derived from the root *ind*, meaning "to rule" (*indati*), belonging to the *nadādi* group; *indī* means Lakṣmī. *Indīvaram* is the best (*varam*) of that *indī*.

Alternatively, *inda* means supreme sovereignty (*paramissariye*), and *īra* is a suffix. In this blue lotus, the white variety is named *kumuda*. It is called *kumuda* because it rejoices in the water (*kuye modate*), with the suffix *ṇo*. Its bulb is like that of the *paduma* and other such lotuses.
*Sālūka* is explained as follows: *Kaṃ* means happiness; that which gives happiness is a *kanda*. Alternatively, the root *kanda* is used in the senses of calling out or weeping.
The root *sala* has the sense of going; with the suffix *uko*, it becomes long, thus *sālūkaṃ*.
(Verse 689) The triad [of terms] refers to the general state of being red, not-red, or dark-blue. It applies to a certain water-born flower other than the *kamala*, and not to the red one alone.
*Sogandhika* means "possessing fragrance" (*sugandha*). *Kallahāra* is so called because it beautifies like a necklace (*hāra*); there is the insertion of *l* and the doubling of the consonant.
*Dakasītalika* means that which makes the water cool.

The two [terms] refer to moss (*sevāla*). It is *sevāla* because it dwells in water (*udaka*); there is the insertion of *l* and the substitution of *i* for *e*. *Nīlikā* means that which turns blue (*nīlati*).
*Nīlā* means blue; or, because it is associated with the color blue, it is *nīlikā*, which also refers to moss.
Both [terms] refer to a place endowed with lotuses and to a cluster of lotuses. *Naḷinī*, *paṅkajinī*, *visinī*, *sarojinī*, and *padminī* are synonyms.

For Mādhava states in the *Ratnamālā*: “*Padmasaṇḍa* [is used] for its source. *Visa* means equal; by virtue of having that [suffix], it is *visinī*; [the suffix] *-in-* belongs to the *nadādi* class.
*Ambujinī* is so called because of its connection with lotuses (*ambuja*) or because it is a collection of lotuses.
(690) *Tilabīja* and the like are what is called *sevāla*. Among these, that which is the size of a sesame seed, situated in the water, and endowed with colors such as blue is called *tilabīja*.
That which is called a *saṅkha* is a particular kind of *sevāla* that has leaves, few stalks, is the size of a pot-lid or similar object, and possesses roots.
*Paṇaka* is the name of a particular kind of seaweed, blue in color and shaped like a bee; it is called *paṇa*, with the suffix *-ka*, thus *paṇaka*.
The commentary on the section on the underworld (*pātāla*) is finished.

Thus ends the commentary on the section on the earth (*bhūkaṇḍa*) in this *Abhidhānappadīpikā-vaṇṇanā*, composed by the wise Great Minister Sirimahācaturaṅgabala, a lion among the elephants of poets and a wanderer in the wisdom-grove of the entire great forest of grammar.
3. Sāmaññakaṇḍa. 1. Commentary on the Visesyādhīnavagga. 691.

Herein, in the Sāmaññakaṇḍa which is about to be explained, [the factors] are those dependent on the qualified (visesyādhīna), accompanied by both primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga) together with the pair of limbs and sub-limbs.
The groups are stated in their respective order according to the qualifiers— such as *sobhana* (beautiful) and so forth— which depend upon the qualified (*visesya*), which are mixed with one another,
possess various meanings such as substance, action, and quality, include indeclinables such as *samaya* and *vaṇṇa*, and also [words] like *cirassaṃ*;
and these are dependent on the preceding group, for indeed, [words] such as *sobhana* function as qualifiers among gods, humans, and so forth.

However, relations (*sambandhā*) and the like [are included] by virtue of being the substratum for that; *samaya* and the like, by virtue of being denoters; and *cirassaṃ* and the like, by virtue of being qualifiers of that action.
Precisely because of this commonality, this is the "General Section" (*Sāmaññakaṇḍa*). 692.
In this treatise, the determination of gender (*liṅgavinicchaya*) occurs through further variations of form; here too, in this section, it occurs through further variations of form.
In order to eliminate any misconception regarding grammatical deviation, he states the pervasive rule with the words beginning "the possessor of qualities" (*guṇin*), etc. Its meaning is as follows:

all words denoting qualities (*guṇa-śabda*), substance-words (*dravya-śabda*), and action-words (*kriyā-śabda*) that function as qualifiers are, by reason of their dependence upon the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), necessarily identical in gender with the qualifier;

they do not possess a different gender even when [the qualified object] is of another form. For example: *sobhanā itthī* (a beautiful woman), *sobhano puriso* (a beautiful man), *sobhanaṃ cittaṃ* (a beautiful mind).

693–696. *Subhantaṃ* means "beautiful. From the root *subha*, meaning "to beautify," the suffix *yu* is applied. From *ruca*, meaning "splendor," the suffix *iro* is applied. From *sādha*, meaning "accomplishment," the suffix *u* is applied.
That which satisfies the mind is *manuñña*. [The analysis is: from the root *ñā*, meaning "measure," "weigh," or "examine," the suffix *anta* with the vowel *u* is added;

or alternatively, it is *manuñña* because it greatly (*ā*) satisfies the mind (*manaṃ*), in which case the compound is analyzed as *mano-añña*, with the elision of the *ā*. From *cara*, meaning "motion" or "eating," the suffix *ṇvu* is applied.
It moves here, thus it is *cāru*. It is well split (*suṭṭhu darīyate*) and beautiful; the root *dara* means to split. The root *vaga* means to go;

with the suffix *u*, it becomes *vaggu*. The mind delights in this, thus it is *manoruha*; the root *kamu* means desire, with the suffix *to*. It carries the mind, thus it is *hārī*; the root *ṇī*. The root *mana* means to know; with the suffix *ju*, it is *mano*;

or that in which the mind speeds, thus it is *mañju*, with the elision of *na*. Because of its association with a pleasing character, it is *pesala*; for *piya*, there is the substitution of *pe*, and the change to *ī*.

*Bhadi* [is a root] in the sense of being auspicious (*kalyāṇe*), with the suffix *do*. *Vā* [is a root] in the sense of going (*gatiyaṃ*), with the suffix *mo*. *Kala* [is a root] in the sense of counting (*saṅkhyāne*), with the suffix *yāṇo*.

It is "agreeable" (*manāpaṃ*) because it applies (*appeti*) or increases the mind (*manaṃ*); or alternatively, it is agreeable because the mind reaches (*appoti*) it, where *āpa* means "to reach," preceded by *apa*.

It is "obtained" (*laddhaṃ*) because it is to be obtained (*labhitabbaṃ*), with the suffix *to*, and the suffix *ko* added for the sake of the word itself (*sakatthe*). It is "beautiful" (*subhaṃ*) because it shines well (*subhati*); or alternatively, it is beautiful because it exists (*bhavati*) with a beautiful intrinsic nature (*sabhāvena*).

*Puṅgava* means "bull"; *uttama* is derived from *ubbhuta*, meaning "excellent" (*aty-attha*), with *tama* added in the sense of superlative after the word *ubha* (both) or the sense of being pre-eminent;

or it is *uttama* because it has risen above (*uggata*). *Vara* is used in the sense of aspiration; *pavara*. In the sense of the suffix *iṭṭha*, there is a substitution of *ja* for *vuḍḍha*; thus, *jeṭṭha*.
*Pamukha* is one whose face (*mukha*) or undertaking (*ārambha*) is distinguished (*pakaṭṭha*). *Anuttara* is that which has no superior (*uttara*) or excellence (*uttama*).

*Pamukho* and *anuttaro* form a *dvanda* compound. In the case of words beginning with *apa*, the suffix *-vara* is applied. *Mukhya* means "like the mouth"; the suffix *-ya* is used in the sense of similarity (*ivatthe*). That which lays down the foot (*pada*) is *padhāna*; the suffix *-ana* is applied.
That which stands in the state of being foremost (*pamukha*) is *pāmokkha*; in both cases, the vowel is lengthened (*vuḍḍhi*). That which takes away (*rāti*) what is excellent (*para*) is *para*;
the suffix *-a* is applied. That which is to be known as "foremost" (*agga*) is *aggañña*; or, that which is to be measured as "foremost" is *aggañña*.

*Uttara* means "superior," being like the best (*uttama*). *Paṇīta* means "excellent" or "refined"; it is derived from the root *nī* (to lead) with the suffix *ṇo* in the sense of the object. *Parama* means "supreme," as it destroys (*māreti*) the supreme adversary;

or, it delights (*ramati*) in a state of excellence (*pakaṭṭha*), thus it is *parama*, with the suffix *ṇo*. Regarding those things that are desired, praised, or increased, the words *seyya* and *seṭṭha* are formed;
by the rule "in some cases when the vowel *a* is elided," the suffix *issa* is applied. One who leads (*neti*) a village is a *gāmaṇi*; [this applies] in the sense of one's character and so forth.

*ṇī* [in the sense of] "leading" (*netṛ*) becomes *ṇī*; when short, it is *gāmaṇi*. Because of being constant darkness, it is *santatamā*; [the compound] *santato tamo* (constant darkness) and *santassa ca so* (and that of the constant one).
