979. *Lañchana* means a mark or sign. *Paṭibimba* means a reflection or image. *Sīmā* means a boundary or limit. *Pakāra* means similar or like. 980.

*Mantana* refers to a four-cornered place and so forth. *Byasana* refers to misfortune, such as the ruin of wealth and so forth. *Vipatti* means failure or calamity. *Anattha* means harm or disadvantage.

981. *Raṃsibheda*: a particular kind of ray prior to the rising of the sun. *Abyattarāge*: when the redness is not yet fully manifest. *Lohite*: when it is red. *Pakatānivatte*: in the non-reversion from its natural state.

The meaning is also "in the natural state and in the non-reversion. *Nassanakkhare*: in the syllable of destruction (*nassa*). *Nassa* means "invisibility" (*adassana*) in the syllable. [As stated: "The *anubandha* is at the beginning of the root (*pakati*);
in the arising of a fault, it is the syllable of destruction (*vinassare*)."
It should also be seen in the verse from the *Amarakosa* (2.9.8): "In following the leader, and in conforming to what is natural."—From the *Nānatthasaṅgaha*.

982. *Avataraṇe*: in descending; *otaraṇe*: in entering. *Titthasmiṃ*: at a landing place for rivers and the like. *Vivare*: in an opening or manifestation. *Iṅgite*: in a gesture, such as the movement of the head and so forth.

983. A *khattā* is one born from a *khattiya*. A *sudiditthitanaya* is the son of a *sudiditthi*. *Tibba* means intense or excessive. *Ugga* means pre-eminent or best. *Dhiti* means fortitude or energy. 984.

*Pabhāta* means at dawn or early morning. *Niroga* means free from disease. *Sajja* means assembled, joined, or also a support. According to the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*: "The word *sajja* is used for one who is equipped and also for that which is joined. *Dakkha* means clever or skillful. *Kalla* is also used for one who is fit or ready. *Kūṭacariyā* means deceitful conduct or craftiness.
985. *Pakkhibhedo*: a bird the size of a pigeon (*pārāvata*), in whose house people create an object of meditation on the foul (*asubhanimitta*) when it has dropped its droppings.
*Pārāvate*: in the pigeon, which has a soft cry. *Saradabbhūte*: arisen in the autumn season. *Appagabbhe*: in timid speech. 986. *Kaṭhine*:
in that which is hard or harsh. *Sāhaso*: violence or forceful compulsion. *Appiye*: in that which is unpleasant or disagreeable. *Cīre*: in a rag; and "rag" also refers to flax.

987. *Migabheda* refers to deer the size of dogs. *Paṭākā* means a banner. *Moca* is well-known [as a plant]; *kadalī* ends in the vowel *ī*. *Dakkhiṇā* is the gift that should be given out of faith in the fruit of action (*kammaphala*).

988. *Uppāta* refers to a portent or a transformation of beings. *Vessānara* refers to fire. 989. *Potavāha* refers to one who carries a raft or a platform. *Niyantā* refers to a driver or a conqueror.
990. *Rodhana* means obstruction or covering. 991.
*Bhājana* refers to vessels made of lacquer and so forth. *Pariyatti* means mastery, thorough learning, or training; that which is to be mastered or trained in.
*Jarāsithilacammasmiṃ* means in the skin that has become flaccid due to old age, which is the cause of aging. *Udaraṅge* means on the lines of the skin of the belly.
992. In the three [terms] beginning with *vidārita*, the gender follows the word being expressed (*vāccaliṅgika*).

In the fourth means, namely *upajāpa* (instigation). 993. *Gāmasandohe* means a multitude of villages. *Paridhi* and *pariveso* refer to the halo around the sun and other luminaries. *Āgame* refers to the word of the Buddha. *Lekhe* refers to a written document that has been read. 994.
An iron-tipped piercing thorn is for piercing needles and the like. *Guṇukkaṃse* means an excellence of qualities. *Vibhave* means wealth. *Sampatti* and *sampadā* are two synonymous terms.

995. *Bhū* means earth (*pathavī*). Regarding the three meanings beginning with "suitable" (*yogya*), [the term *addha* applies] to these three: in the sense of "suitable" (*yogya*), it means what is appropriate (*anucchavika*); in the sense of "joined" (*yutta*), it means connected (*saṅgata*).

The word *addha* refers to a part (*bhāga*)—both an equal part (*samabhāga*) and an unequal part (*asamabhāga*). Among those, when it is an equal part, it is *addha*; otherwise, it is *addho* or *addham*.

On a road or a path (*pathe magge*), *addhā* is used in the masculine. *Addhā* is also used in the masculine for time (*kāla*). In the sense of "one side" (*ekaṃsa*) or "certainty" (*nicchaya*), *karīsa* is said to have four bases (*caturambana*).

996. *Usabha* means a bull, the leader of a hundred cattle, or the best among excellent things; it also refers to the sixty-second year [of the cycle]. *Taṃ* refers to the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*). *Paṅkti* means a row or a line. 997.

*Itthi* refers to the female sex organ, the physical mark of a woman. *Kilañja* refers to something made of reeds (*vilīva*). That word *kaṭa* has three meanings when used as a noun: "a mat" (*kaṭa*) refers to the act of weaving grass, [and also to a bedstead, etc.].
*Kilañja* is considered to mean "extraordinary" (*atisaya*),
"auspicious" (*siva*), "time" (*samaya*),
"the temple of an elephant" (*gajagaṇḍa*), and "a kind of grass" (*vippaliya*). — *Medinīkośa* 11.3.
Vopālita: “*Samaye ca kriyākāre, kilañje ca sare kaṭo*” (Tikaṇḍasesa 3.3.93). 998. *Mathita*: a specific kind of milk product. *Sūciphalā*:
the fruit of the *ambilapatta* tree. *Duddasa-itara*: not difficult to see; easy to behold. 999. *Antarīpa*:
dry land in the midst of water. *Pajjota*: a lamp. *Bandha*: connection. *Mihita*: a slight smile.

1000. *Thiyaṃ* means in the sense of "woman" (*itthisāmaññe*) or, alternatively, in the sense of "feminine gender" (*itthiliṅge*). *Dāre* means in the sense of "wife. *Sure* means in the sense of a "deity" (*devatā*) or a specific deity. *Vāsudeve* means in Nārāyaṇa. *Antake* means in Vasavatti (the Lord of the Vasus). *Asite* means in the black color (*kāḷavaṇṇe*). 1001. *Upaṭṭhāne* means in service (*pāricariyā*) and attendance (*sevane*).

*Aññaropane* means in the planting of another state—that is, in the planting of another nature upon something that does not possess that nature. *Sakko* refers to the word *sakka*. *Inde* means Sakka, the king of the gods (*devarāja*). *Janapade* means the people of Sakka (the Sakyans). *Sākiye* and *khame* [are used] in the three genders.
1002. There is a resolution regarding the three [terms] beginning with *vajjana*. There is also a resolution in the answering of the question. Regarding "dvija," it refers to a brahmin;

"ariya" also refers to a vessa. 1003. "Suṃsumāra" refers to a crocodile; "nakka" refers to a species of fierce fish. "Ulūpinī" refers to a female snake. "Uddāla" refers to the *selu* tree, whose fruits are extremely sticky.

1004. "Piyaka" refers to the yellow *sāla* tree. "Kaṇḍa" refers to an arrow. "Asana" refers to the act of throwing; [it is derived from] the root *asu*, meaning "to cause to throw. "Yuga" refers to the yoke of a chariot and so forth. "Vikāra" means transformation. "Antika" means near.
1005. *Lavitta* means given. *Ajjhesanā* is a request preceded by honor. 1006.

That which is called "cakkū" in the world regarding a *makaci* cloth—some say it is a "sāṇa" cloth—in books such as the *Saddasattha* and others; [it refers to] forms created by painters and the like in works such as painting.
1007. Regarding meritorious persons. In the work of plastering and whitewashing, it refers to the wooden handles of those applying lime.
1008. *Pāyite* means that which is to be drunk; there is also a reading as *vāyite*. In some places, it is seen as *dayite*. 1009.
It refers to specific colors such as red (*lohitādi*). In the sense of coloring, it appears in phrases such as *mukharāgo* (lip-color).

*Pavuddhadariyaṃ* means great fear. 1010. It refers to the fruit of the *kaseru* plant and the fruit of the thorny plant. It refers to a crossroads where paths meet. In the sense of abundance, it is known as *phālātī*. But in the sense of a fault, it is called *eḷa*.

1011. Regarding the *adhikaraṇa* (locative) case: *pattādhāro* means the receptacle for a bowl. *Ālavālake* refers to a hollow at the base of a tree, a pit serving as a reservoir for water used for watering the tree.
*Agabhedo* means the breaking of a tree; this was a tree that had been consumed by the Great Being during his time as Prince Temiya.
In that context, *kārā* means women. *Kāra* also means honor (*sakkāra*), in two senses [of the word]. However, in the sense of a prison, it is simply *kārā*.

1012. *Megha* means cloud; *pāsāṇa* means a solid stone. *Kuṇḍikā* refers to a water-pot; *bhiṅgāra* refers to a ceremonial vessel. *Padāti* refers to the fourth division of the army (the infantry). 1013.
The three designations *chidda*, etc., may apply to a hole, a flaw, and a fault, respectively. *Muccita* applies to that which has been released and to that which ought to be released.
1014. *Hatthiliṅga* refers to a male elephant and to a bird shaped like an elephant. *Mada* refers to the rut-fluid of an elephant.

1015. *Atthaṅgama* means destruction. *Nigama* refers to a place where a town has arisen, that is, a site where a town was established. *Āpaṇa* refers to one who lives by a shop—that is, one whose livelihood is through a shop—in the sense of the agent.
1016. *Harita* means having the color of a parrot’s wing.

*Paṇṇa* means merely a leaf. 1017. *Phala* refers to the fruit of trees and so forth; it denotes the mere fruit itself. That [term] expresses the state of being ripe. *Nāsamukha* means facing the nose and, in three senses, matured.
In *ājīvane*: in the means of livelihood. In *piṇḍane*: in the act of gathering or piling up. In *goḷake*: in that which is round or globular.

1018. In *paribbaye*: in wages or salary. In *kammādike*: in the cycle of action (*kamma-vaṭṭa*), the cycle of result (*vipāka-vaṭṭa*), and the cycle of defilements (*kilesa-vaṭṭa*). In *vaṭṭale*: in that which is spherical or bubble-shaped.
In *paccāhāre*: in a response or a reply. 1019. In *vikate*: in variety, or in being multiform.
1020. *Sabya* means left (*adakkhiṇa*). *Cāru* means lovely (*manuñña*). *Sarabya* refers to a target such as a wooden board to be pierced with an arrow. *Cihana* means a mark or sign. 1021.

*Seṇī* refers to a group of those who share the same craft (*samasippīnaṃ* = *samānasippīnaṃ*), specifically a female artisan. It also means a row or a line (*āvaḷiyaṃ* = *pantiyaṃ*). *Sudhā* means plaster. *Dhūli* means dust or pollen. *Vāsacuṇṇaka* means scented powder suitable for perfuming. 1022.

[The suffix] *jo* is used after *pasattha* (praised) to express "highly praised" (*atipasattha*), and after *vuḍḍha* (old) to express "very old" (*ativuḍḍha*). *Takka* refers to a specific kind of curdled milk. *Hoti* is the verb.
1023. *Paṇe* refers to the work of weavers and the like;
*kaṇhe* means black. 1024. *Sambhave* means white; *amejjhe* means impure or unholy. 1025.
*Ikke* refers to a black beast with much hair; *baḷise* refers to a fish-hook; *selabhede* refers to a mountain named Vaṅka.

1026. *Kuṇapa* refers to a dead body. When it has been divided into half-parts, he therefore said "in a man" (*purise*). And the repetition "in a man" is stated with reference to the most common usage; thus he said, "or a part, or the whole, in a male. 1027. At the mouth of the *saṃvarī* creeper at the beginning of the night.

1030. A specific class of deities is the *kumbhaṇḍa*, a type of *yakkha*. Among the species of creepers, there is one whose fruits are the size of a cooking pot (*ukkhalī*). In the fourth part—that is, in the fourth constituent portion. On the foot—meaning on the limb. On the bordering rock—meaning at the base of the mountain.
1031. *Loha* refers to copper; *setaloha* to silver. In the plural sense, it is used in the plural number. It denotes a type of artisan’s tool known as a *tū*.

*Khaṭaka* refers to one who holds a key in his hand. 1032. *Doṇi* refers to a wooden grain-measure. *Adhiṭṭhiti* means standing upon or being situated above. *Ṭhāna* means a place or merely a location. 1034.

*Vakka* and *hadaya* refer to specific divisions [of the body], etc. (Man. 1.110). *Vaṅka* means crookedness. The [three knowledges] consisting of the divine eye, the recollection of past lives, and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)...
By the term *tisso vijjā* (the three knowledges), eight types of knowledge (*vijjā*) are included.

In *buddhiyaṃ ñāṇe*, [it refers to] wisdom and knowledge. In *anākule*, it means free from confusion. In *siloke*, it refers to the *anuṭṭhubha* and other meters. In *addhe*, it means a portion. In *tīsu pajjo*, the word *pajja* [is used].

In *rukkhabhedasmiṃ udakappasādanaphale*, it refers to a species of tree that produces water-clearing fruit. In *kittime*, it refers to that which is produced by an instrument. In *vidheyye*, it refers to one who accepts speech. In *pubbamhi*, it means in the east. In *pūye*, it means in honor.

1037. In *laddhattharakkhaṇe*: in the guarding of wealth and other benefits already obtained. In *niyojane*: in the act of sending or directing. In *kāriye*: in the fruit of an action. 1038. In *assāsappatte*:

in one who has attained consolation. In *bodhidume*: in the Bodhi tree of our Blessed One. In *kurūre*: in one who acts with cruelty or harshness. In *nesādamhi*: in a hunter who snares deer, fish, and so forth.

1039. In *laggasmiṃ*: in attachment or clinging. In *majjhamhi*: in the middle or the belly. In *bhāge*: in a portion that is not overdone (*asamaddha*). In *dhanimhi*: in one possessing great wealth.
1040. In *gahane* and *saṅkare*. In *sasantāne*, [it refers to] one's own internal continuum (*niyakajjhattasantāne*). The distinction between *visaya* and *gocara* has been stated.
The commentary on the first half-verse is finished. 1041.

In *bhuvane*, [it refers to] the realm of desire (*kāmabhava*) and so forth. In *jane*, [it refers to] a living being (*pāṇi*). In *yase*, [it refers to] fame (*kittiyam*). In *pajje*, [it refers to] the *anuṭṭhubha* and other [metres]. In *rukkhe*, [it refers to] a tree and its varieties.

1042. *Vaṭo* means a banyan tree (*vaṭarukkha*). *Vāyase* refers to crows. *Bake* means white-leaved. *Avasaro* means an opportunity or space. *Ahaṃ* means a day. *Kuce* means in a non-womanly place. *Abbhe* means in a cloud (*megha*). 1043.
*Ucchaṅge* means on the upper part of a couch (*pallaṅka*). *Lakkhaṇe* means indicative.
*Diṭṭho* occurs in the senses of "in speech" and "in seeing," as well as in the sense of "appearance" (*obhāsa*).

1044. *Sūra* occurs in the words *sūraṃsu*, *sūriye*, and *kiraṇe*. *Dama* means self-control; *damana* means the act of taming. *Māna* refers to a specific type of pride. *Sānu* refers to a mountain ridge.
1045. *Tāpa* means the heat of the sun. *Sapaca* refers to a Caṇḍāla; he is called *sapaca* because he cooks a dog (*saṃ* + *sunakhaṃ pacati*).

*Pasu* means a four-footed animal. *Kuruṅga* is a species of deer with antlers. *Ulūka* is a bird that dwells in hollows. *Inda* is Sakka. [In the word] *Mahinde*, it refers to the *guggulu* resin, the owl, and the *palagga* plant.
*Kosiya* means "Amarasīha. *Māṇava* means "mortal.
*Attā* refers to the presiding deity of the body. *Sire* means "on the head," the highest limb. *Tipu* refers to black metal (lead).
*Bali* refers to that which is to be offered as a portion. *Hattha* means "hand. *Aṃsu* means "portion. *Danta* means "teeth. *Vippe* means "brāhmaṇas. *Aṇḍaje* means "born from an egg."

In "born from an egg" (*aṇḍasañjāte*). From "anu" onwards, [the following] are in the *anuṭṭhubhā* meter. "Face" (*ānana*) means the mouth. "Conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the eighty great precepts (*mahāvattā*) and so forth.

"Grain-limb" (*dhaññaṅge*) refers to split rice. "Subtle" (*sukhume*) means in the minute (*aṇumhi*). For Amarasīha has stated that "grain" (*kaṇa*) is a synonym for "subtle" in the phrase "lavalesakaṇāṇavo.
1048. "Pillar" (*thūṇā*) is the principal timber of houses and the like. "Dullness" (*jaḷattaṃ*) is the state of being bewildered. "Kummāsa" is a preparation of beans. "Sauce" (*byañjanaṃ*).
Then there is another term. A *phoṭo* is that which, when inverted, lacks painful sensation within the pus.
A *kapola* is the area between the cheeks and the temples. Regarding *mūlye*, it means in the original capital.
1049. *Bhāsapakkhī* and *pakkhī* are *bhāsapakkhina*; among them, [the word] "bird" (*sakunta*) applies both to the general category of birds and specifically to the *bhāsa* bird.
For Vopālita [explains] "vihaṅgame" as "speaking in a beautiful form," and "bhāsanto" as "the bird Bhāsa. There is also a reading: "sakunto bhāsapakkhinī.
[The word *bhāga* refers to] fortune (*bhāgye*), to action that brings about good or evil (*subhāsubhāvahe kammani*), and to an arrangement or instrument (*vidhāne karaṇe*). 1050.
That blue bird which, having flown up into the sky and then descended again, catches fish within the water, is the *nīlasakuṇo*.
*Cātaka* means a certain bird. *Eṇa* and *eṇī* refer to the deer known as the ena-deer. *Sara* means an arrow. *Seda* refers to sweating; *sida* means cooking. Cooking is the act of maturing.

[The word *seda*] occurs in the classification of monks in such phrases as "the one who completes the group" (*gaṇapūraka*). *Caya* means a heap or a collection. (Verse 1051) *Puñja* means a mass or a lump.

*Mesa* and so forth refers to the bull (*usabha*), copulation (*methuna*), the crab (*kakkaṭa*), the lion (*sīha*), the maiden (*kaññā*), the balance scale (*tulā*), the scorpion (*vicchika*), the bow (*dhanu*), the sea-monster (*makara*), the jar (*kumbha*), and the fish (*mīna*). *Loṇa* means salt, specifically the finest salt. *Saṃvaṭṭa* refers to the aeon of destruction (*vināsakappa*). *Kamuka* refers to the betel-nut tree.
1052. *Amata*: at the meal of the deities. *Lepe*: on a plaster made of pure sugar, lime powder, and so forth. *Satthe*: at a weapon; specifically, at a long-handled weapon. *Najjantare*:
among the five great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—at the fifth great river.
*Bhuvi*: on the earth. *Kriyā*: action arising from a woman’s state of passion (*siṅgāra-bhāva*). *Vilāsa*, however, arises from something other than that. *Atraje*: toward one's own son.
1053. *Kutha* is a rug for the back of an elephant. *Veṇī* is the mass of hair of women. For Vopālita says: “*Paveṇī*, *veṇī*, and *kutha* [are synonyms].
In some places, however, the reading is “*paveṇī* in the sense of lineage (*kula*) and braid (*veṇī*). *Vutti* means existence or livelihood. *Vutta* refers to what has been said or a report.
*Vetana* refers to that which is obtained through work; it also means maintenance, nourishment, and support.

1054. The word *mariyādā* has two meanings: existence (*satta*) and being present (*vijjamānatā*). *Samiddhi* means success (*sampatti*). *Soppe* means in sleep (*niddāyaṃ*). *Vutti* means the mode of livelihood (*jīvitavutti*). 1055. *Kuccha* means reproach (*garahā*).

*Apavāda* means censure (*avaṇṇavādo*), which includes speaking what is untrue (*abhūtākkhānaṃ*). *Dhañña* refers to a specific kind of grain, the head of which is the size of a thumb and is long. *Piyaṅgu* is a fragrant herb. *Mokkhe* means in Nibbāna. *Sive* means auspicious (*kalyāṇe*). 1056. *Rañjane* means in the act of dyeing, such as with saffron robes (*kāsāyādi*).
*Sūrate* means in sexual intercourse (*methune*). *Vāse* means in the act of dwelling (*vasanakriyāyaṃ*).
1057. In *pattha* it means a measure; in *mānatumbe*, a stalk of lotuses and the like; in *pipāsāyaṃ*, the desire to drink; *vutti* means existence. 1058.
In *pāṇyaṅge*, it refers to the navel of a conch; in *cakkante*, at the rim of a wheel. [The verse states:
“*Nābhi* occurs in the sense of a limb of the body, a field, the rim of a wheel, and a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*).”
“Nābhi is praised in the sense of exertion (*padhāna*), in *katthuri*, in meat (*maṃsa*), and in some cases,” says Vopālita.

(1059) *Antare* means between two things. “*Vīci* [is used] in the sense of intervals and waves,” says Vopālita. *Thiratte* means in steadiness, in the state of being firm. There is also a reading *dhīratte*, which has the same meaning. *Save* means in hearing.
1060. *Nissaya* means support or basis. 1061. *Vitta* means wealth. *Aṅka* means a mark or sign. *Buddhi* means knowledge. *Kha* means in the sky. 1062.

*Vata* means the conduct of non-Buddhist sectarians. *Āgu* means an offense. *Maṇi* here refers to a carved stone or a specific kind of gemstone designated as a "jewel. *Hāyana* means a year. *Vuṭṭhi* means raining.
1063. *Lipi* is a specific arrangement of the letters beginning with *a*. *Mokkho* is *nibbāna*. *Rate* means brave or courageous. 1064.

*Riṭṭhaṃ* refers to evil and the inauspicious. *Ariṭṭhaṃ* is used here as well; the vowel *a* is applied there to denote its state. *Aparādho* means fault or disadvantage. *Ketumhi* means on a banner or flag. *Cihane* means a mark or sign. Vopālita states: "The word *dhaja* [is used] for the lees of wine and for a banner or sign. 1065. It also means a mere gate or the area outside a gate.
From this point onward, those words that are said to have multiple meanings are called *vāccaliṅga* (words whose gender depends on their referent). *Phuṭe* means manifest or evident.
1066. *Ajjhakkhe* means overcome. *Jaḷe* means ignorant. *Lolupe* means excessively greedy. *Cale* means trembling. 1067. *Vikate* means deformed.
*Komalaṃ* means not hard. *Atikhiṇo* means blunt. 1068. *Site* means white. *Sūcako* means a slanderer. *Ahi* means a snake. *Sakke* means patient.
In the reading *satte*, however, the meaning is "one endowed with a spear. *Sambandhe* means connection. *Avippayoge* means non-separation. *Akhile* means entire.

1069. *Kevalaṃ* means unmixed (*asammissaṃ*). *Anto* means the end (*avasānaṃ*). *Adhamo* means base (*nihīno*). *Paṇato* means inclined toward the Buddha and others. *Ninno* is the opposite of level ground (*thalapaṭipakkho*). 1070.
*Suddhe* means unmixed with anything else (*aññena asammissite*). *Pūte* means pure (*mejje*). 1071. *Byāpe* means pervaded (*byāpite*).
*Bhāvini* refers to a future subject (*anāgate vatthumhi*). *There* means aged (*jiṇṇe*).
1072. Thinking that the word *bahu* occurs only in such instances as "it does not occur in one or in two," he says "tyādi" (and so forth).
However, because it is stated [in the grammatical treatises] that there are "singular and plural," the word *bahu* certainly applies to two as well.
Alternatively, the Teacher may have said "tyādi" while keeping in mind the statements of other systems; for in those [systems], it is threefold.
The word [vacana] refers to the singular, the dual, and the plural. For since grammar is intended for the entire assembly, the arguments of all [schools] are discussed in certain places.

*Dhī* means wisdom (*paññā*); he who possesses it is *dhīra*, meaning wise (*budha*). Alternatively, *dhī* is the act of holding; he who has that is *dhīra*, meaning possessed of steadfastness (*dhitimanta*). *Dhuta* means moved or shaken.
1073. *Yāna* refers to vehicles such as elephants and the like; *yogga*, however, means fit or suitable.
1074. *Vuḍḍha* means advanced in age; *kulaja* means of noble birth. *Vuddha* means aged or advanced in years. *Uru* means great in measure. 1075.
*Vutta* means spoken or to be spoken. *Uggata* means risen upward. *Āditta* means set ablaze by fire and so forth; *gabbhita* means conceived or brought into being.
1076. *Vigata* means free from passion (*vigatarāga*). *Vāyana* refers to a woven cloth (*vīta-paṭa*).

*Bhajjita* refers to grain and the like; *bhajja* means roasting or cooking. 1077. *Caya* means a heap or collection. *Sama* means equal. *Ari* means an enemy (*sattu*). There is also a reading of "samādisu. *Vīra* means one who is not timid, a hero. *Ravisūra* refers to the sun and the hero; here, "hero" (*sūra*) is used [to denote the sun]. *Kuddha* means possessed by anger. *Dūsita* means unpleasant. 1078.

*Diṭṭha* is seen in the sense of an enemy (*ari-sattu*) and also in the sense of being looked at (*ikkhita*). *Pota* means a child. *Vata* refers to a vow or a practice that is exclusively virtuous (*ekanta-sādhana*).

1079. *Salākā* refers to a tally used for counting. *Kusa* refers to grass. *Varahi* refers to a type of grass. *Khaye udayabbayānupassī* means one who contemplates arising and passing away in the face of destruction. *Vaya* also refers to a bird, as in such passages as: "For those birds that have left their nests and are without food, death shall come.

*Gabbha* means conceit or pride. 1080. *Biḷāla* means a cat. *Nakula* refers to the mongoose, the enemy of snakes. *Manthana* is the churning stick for churning milk. *Sattu* is a specific kind of parched grain or flour made from rice. *Assādilome* means the hair of horses and other animals.

*Ghāta* means death. *Rāsi* means a heap or pile. 1081. *Gopagāme* means in the village of cowherds. *Rava* means sound. *Sārathi* means a charioteer or driver. *Vandī* is a panegyrist or reciter of praises.
“In the charioteer, in the triple-god [Indra], in the one who has attained peace, and in the one who is known;
in the kṣatriya, in the brahmin, and in the one who recites; he is renowned among those who worship his feet. — Vopālita.

In the word *puppha* (flower), it is uncompounded with *sutta* (thread) and so forth. In *taddāme* (its garland), that is, in a flower-garland, it is compounded with *sutta* and so forth. In *sakaṭe* (chariot), it is *ana*. In *haye* (horse), it is *assa*.
1082. *Accana* means worship. *Bha* refers to a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). In the middle of the *Netta*, it is known as *sūla*. *Odhi* means a boundary or limit. 1083.
*Puṇṇatā* is fullness or completeness. *Avajja* is fault or defect. *Ābhoga* also refers to attention (*manasikāra*). The word *āḷi* denotes a woman. *Sakhī* is a female friend or companion.
*Setu* is a water-barrier (dam) and also the path across a river or similar body of water. *Satte* refers to those endowed with weapons; the meaning is "firm. "Firm" (*daḷha*)...
"Even one who is stout, well-fed, deeply immersed, and strong is considered dead," so said Upālita.

(1084) *Mokkha* refers to Nibbāna or the fruit of Arahantship. *Sāmin* refers to a husband. *Dhāraka*: one who supports (*dhāreti*) is a supporter (*dhāraka*); in that context, it also means a provider (*posaka*). (1085) *Sikhā* is a crest or tuft of hair. *Piñcha* is a tail-feather.
*Attani* is used in such expressions as "belonging to the Saṅgha" or "belonging to an individual. *Khepe* is used in the sense of reproach or censure.
1086. *Rūpe* means in color. *Karīse* means in dung. 1087.
*Khaṇḍe* means in pieces. *Sakale* means in the whole. *Paṇṇe* means in the leaves of trees and so forth. *Kaṇḍe* means in an arrow.

*Salākā* refers to a splinter used for medical purposes. *Sucittaṃ* is the state of being clean; in that. *Gate* refers to the action of going. For the root dictionary states: “*Dhāva* [is used] in the sense of movement and purification.”
*Hāva*: the graceful gestures arising from the amorous state of women. *Avijjā*: in ignorance; in lack of knowledge. *Mucchā*: in fainting;
in a state of unconsciousness. 1088. *Ghammajalaṃ*: sweat produced on the body by heat. *Pāka*: in cooking; in ripening. *Goḷa*:
a ball of clay known as *muyī*. *Ucchumaya*: produced from sugarcane juice. *Mitta*: a dear friend, or merely a friend. *Sahāya*: a companion.
*Atthacare*: one who acts for the welfare [of others]. *Pabhū*: a master; a lord (*adhipati*).
This is masculine. 1089. *Kurūre*: in cruel deeds. *Parasmiṃ*: in another place, or in the other world (*paraloka*). *Atra*: in this place, or in this world. *Aṅko*: a mark or sign.
*Aṅko* is also used for an act in a drama or for an offense. *Apavādo*: public reproach or censure. *Dese*: in a region or a specific locality.
“*Bhave*, *janapade*, *deso*, *jane*, and also *janapade*,” says Vopālita.
(1090) *Pajja* means a verse (*śloka*). *Vacībhede* means in articulate speech. *Anvaye* means in a lineage or continuum. *Sarūpasmiṃ* means in similarity or sameness. *Talaṃ* means the lower part.

(1091) *Vilagge* means in the middle of the body. *Vemajjhe* means in the common sense of the middle. *Kusumaṃ* means a flower or blossom. *Utu* means the female flower. *Subbate* means in a beautiful wind.

1092. *Kosa* means a bag for carrying sectarian marks (*liṅga*). *Gabbhara* means a cave. *Bila* refers to the dwelling place of ants and the like. *Gaṇḍaka* refers to a rhinoceros horn. *Kadamba* is known as the *thina* tree. *Duma* means a tree.

*Caya* means a heap or collection. 1093. *Bha* refers to a specific lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). *Dhenu* refers to a cow or a female animal with horns. *Yoni* refers to the female organ of women. *Sira* means the head. 1094.
The word *bhogī* refers to a person possessing enjoyments and to a serpent. *Siva* is the Great Lord (Śiva). *Bala* refers to strength and power.
In *tejasi*: Vopālita [states], "Vīriya (energy) occurs in the sense of semen (*sukka*) and radiance (*pabhāva*); *teja* (heat/luster) also occurs in the sense of power (*sāmatthiya*).
Furthermore, the word *teja* applies to those two aforementioned meanings as well as to brilliance (*ditti*).

1095. *Santati* means continuity. *Khaggaṅge* means in a part of a sword, specifically its sharp edge. *Sūte* means in a charioteer. *Paṭihāre* means in a messenger who conveys a message. *Vitti* is derived from the root-meaning of *vida* in the sense of "acquisition" (*lābha*). *Pīḷā* means affliction or distress.
1096. *Rava* means sound. *Palāsa* refers to rice from which the husk has been removed.
1097. *Rukkha* refers to a mango tree. However, in other systems (of grammar), there is an objection [to this usage].
*Adhika* means exceeding; *pema* means affection. 1098. *Ketu* means a banner. *Lekhya* refers to that which is to be written, i.e., a letter. But *lekhā* refers to a line.
1099. *Sattha* means a type of weapon; it means a living being (*pāṇi*) and a heap or collection (*caya*).
1100. *Āḷi* means a riverbank and the holding of water.
1101. *Saṃsad* means an assembly or hall. The word *ayana* occurs in the sense of going and on a path.
1102. *Rukkha* means among trees; *gaṇa* means a tree. *Sūra* means the sun. *Koṇa* means a corner or intermediate direction. *Haya* means a horse or steed. *Khandha* means the shoulder or upper arm.
The word *acci* refers to a flame, specifically the flame of fire. It also applies to its rays and the rays of other luminous bodies;
however, it is not used in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*).

1103. The word *abhāva* refers to the destruction of that which exists. The word *asatta* is used in the sense of non-existence. *Bhutti* is the act of eating. *Jīva* refers to life-force (*āyu*) in the context of living beings (*pāṇa*), and to the living being itself in the context of those possessing life-force (*jana*).
1104. *Chadana* refers to the covering of houses and the like. *Rāsi* means a heap, as well as a group of things belonging to the same category (*sahadhammīnaṃ gaṇo*).
“*Nikāya* [is used] in the sense of a dwelling, a characteristic, and a collection of things joined together.”
“May you dwell sharing in one place; this is said regarding the supreme self,” says Vopālita.
*Yajana* means the worship of deities. *Accana* means mere worship. *Dikkhā* refers to shaving the head, initiation, observances, vows, and ascetic practices. 1105. *Karaṇa* is *kāra*;

that itself is *kārikā*, meaning action (*kriyā*), with the suffix *-ika* used in its own sense. In the case of *pajja* as well, the meaning is the same. *Cihana* means a mark or characteristic. *Thīraja* refers to the menses of women. *Puppha* means a flower. *Vānara* means a monkey.
1106. *Adhare* means on the lower lip. *Kharabha* is known as "ka-la-au. *Luddha* refers to a greedy person. *Āvila* means turbid or not clear. 1107. *Caramhi* refers to a guard or watchman. 1108.

*Hāsa* (laughter) and *gandha* (fragrance) together form *hāsagandhā*; [the word refers] to those. Here, *gandha* means that which travels far. *Cāru* also means beautiful or excellent. *Khala*, in the sense of moving or accumulating, with the suffix *to*, becomes *khalita*.
1109. *Vakkala* means the bark of a tree. *Adhirohe* refers to the act of climbing. *Vatthantara* is a variegated cloth, which is produced in the country of China.
1110. *Paṭihāre* is known as *ḍagā*. *Mukhe* is the place of entry for food and so forth. *Pete* refers to one who has gone to the other world. *Aparaṇṇa* refers to beans (*muggā*) and the like.

*Kāla* is defined by a period of thirty days and nights. 1111. *Dose* means anger. *Ghāte* means killing. *Migādo* refers to four-footed animals. *Chagale* means a goat. *Arūpe* refers to contact (*phassa*) and so forth. *Avhaye* refers to perception (*saññā*). *Darathe* refers to the torment arising from body and mind. *Bhīti* is fear.

1112. *Bhāra* refers to a load, such as a burden of firewood and so forth. The word *sujā* denotes a ladle or a spoon; it also refers to Indrajāyā, the wife of Sakka. *Vihāyasa* means in the sky or the atmosphere. 1113. *Maṇika* refers to a large water vessel.

*Ratana* refers to a precious gem, a product of stone, or that which shares the common characteristics of a jewel. *Sela* refers to the Candana mountain. *Ārāma* refers to flower gardens and other such parks. Regarding this, Vopālita states:
"In the region of Malaya, between the Selanga mountains, and also for one who dwells in Malaya. *Aṅka* means a mark or sign.
1114. "In the pot of ghee, in that which is to be offered as oblation, and in other things;
in secrecy and in deliberation, 'seclusion' [is used]—so says Upālita. 1115. 'Flow' (pavāha) means the flow of water."

“*Vega* means speed and flow, and also the *mahākāla* fruit,” according to Vopālita in the *Medinīkośa* 3.24. *Khila* means a small particle (*aṇu*). *Kaṇa* means a little. 1116. *Apāṅga* means the corner of the eye;
“*Apāṅga* refers to one deficient in limbs, the corner of the eye, and also a mole (*tilaka*),” according to Vopālita in the *Medinīkośa* 3.28.
*Muktāguṇa* refers to a string of pearls, that is, a pearl bound by thread. *Gahaṇa* means grasping; in that [sense]. *Makuḷa* means unopened (as a flower). *Rasa* means the salty taste.

1117. *Ago* and *nago* are two designations that apply to rocks and trees respectively. *Svappe* means "very little"; the sense is "in a lesser degree. It is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in such phrases as "merely bowing" (*namanamatta*).

*Accana* refers to worship (*pūjā*). 1118. *Chidda* refers to a fault (*dosa*). *Otaraṇa* refers to a descent, such as a ford for water (*jalatittha*), etc. *Ayyaka* refers to a paternal grandfather (*pitupitā*).
1119. *Rukkha* refers to a sword-blade (*khaggaphala*). *Suna* refers to a dog (*sunakha*). *Gandha* refers to a fragrant scent (*adhivāsanagandha*).

1120. *Koṇe* means in a corner. *Savane* means in hearing. *Pantiyaṃ* means in a row. *Bhāgyaṃ* means merit (*puñña*). *Ekadeso* means a single part, such as a third portion and so forth. *Ajapālake* means in a lotus pond. Regarding *kuṭṭhaṃ*, Vopālita states: "It refers to a disease and to fragrance. 1121.

*Senāsane* means in a monastery (*vihāra*) and so forth. *Sene* means in a seat (*pīṭha*) and so forth. *Cundabhaṇḍamhi* means in the equipment belonging to the Cundas. Regarding *bhamo*, Vopālita states in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*:
"It refers to the flow of water, a vessel (*bhaṇḍi*), and a specific type of artisan (*sippiyantaka*) called a Cunda. The word *aṃsu* refers to cloth and so forth.
*Loma* means hair; *karaṇa-matta* means merely an instrument. *Abyaya* refers to indeclinables beginning with *pa*. 1122. *Kha* means within;

*sūkara-vacca-saṇṭhāna* means shaped like a pig's excrement; *dhañña-vikāra* means a derivative of grain. *Diś* means direction; *ripu* means enemy. *Pati* means husband; *ariya* means lord or master. 1123. *Rāga* means passion, such as that of the *kasāya* dyes.

“*Raṅgo* [is used] in the sense of giving (*dāne*), in the sense of a rogue (*khale*), and in the sense of tin (*tipumhi*) when it refers to dyeing (*tacche*); thus says Vopālita. *Peyya* [is used] in the sense of water and so forth. *Pītiyaṃ* [means] in the act of drinking (*pivanakriyāyaṃ*).

“*Pāna* [is used] in the sense of protecting (*rakkhaṇe*) and in the sense of drinking (*pītiyaṃ*); thus says Vopālita. *Uddhāro* [is used] in the sense of debt (*iṇe*) and in the sense of lifting up (*ukkhepane*).
*Ummāre* [means] at the door-post (*dvārummāre*). Since the word *eḷaka* denotes both a ram and a goat, it is said: “*Eḷako* [means] in a goat (*aje*).”

1124. *Pahāra* means a blow or striking; it is that wherein one strikes, thus *pahāra*. It also denotes a watch (*yāma*), a year (*hāyana*), or a season (*saṃvacchara*). In the sense of a water-pot, it is known as *kayā*. In the sense of a measure, it refers to four *pattha*s.

In the sense of husks, it refers to the outer skin of rice. 1125. *Kūpa* means a pit or well. *Caya* means a heap or collection. *Kāsu* means she, or the earth. *Upanisā* means cause, secrecy, or proximity. Vopālita says:

"In the sense of a phenomenon, *upanisā* refers to the Vedanta and also to secrecy. In the sense of a rhinoceros, it is known as *phokha*. In the sense of what is other than virtue, it refers to the non-virtuous.

1126. In the phrase "he adjudicates a legal case" (*aṭṭaṃ vinicchināti*) and so forth, it means a lawsuit. In the phrase "connected with gate-towers and watchtowers" (*gopuraṭṭehi saṃyutta*) and so forth, it means a watchtower.
In the phrase "makes a cry of distress" (*aṭṭassaraṃ karoti*) and so forth, it means being distressed. The root meaning of *aṭṭa* is "legal action," "transgression," and "violence.
In the sense of a forest, it means a grove. In the sense of arising, it means birth, and in the sense of movement through the air, it means flying.

1127. *Lāmaka* means base or inferior. *Khandha* refers to the aggregates (*rūpa*, etc.). *Mūla* means root capital. *Upadā* means a gift or present. *Dasā* has two meanings: it denotes a state or condition, and the hem of a cloth.

*Ghāta* means killing. 1128. *Gabbha* means the womb or the interior. *Ghaṭana* means the act of joining or cementing. *Rāsi* means a heap; in these senses, the word *ghaṭa* is used. *Abhihāra* means an offering or worship.

*Bandhana* (binding) is seen in such phrases as "a wall-enclosure" (*pākāracaya*). 1129. *Thoka* means small or little. *Cāga* means giving, as well as loss or abandonment. *Gīvā* and *gala* are two synonyms for debt. There is also a reading: "In the sense of debt, *gīvā* and also *gala*. *Gala* means the throat.

1130. *Daṇḍa* also means violence (*sāhasa*). *Paṭa* refers to a specific kind of cloth; for cloth made by mixing hemp (*sāṇa*) and other fibers is called "linen" (*bhaṅga*). *Chavaka* refers to the physical body (*kaḷevara*). 1131. *Anaṅga* refers to Māra.
*Duma* refers to the *karahāṭaka* tree. Vopālita states:
"Madana [means] Māra, the rogue, the spring season, the tree, and the seed. *Pamātari* refers to the mother of one's mother. *Veṭha* and *veṭhana* refer to a turban (*uṇhīsa*).
1132. *Taṇḍuleyya* refers to the sesame-fruit vegetable. *Ayye* means mistress or lady. *Mutti* means liberation or release. 1133.
*Aṅka* refers to a mark or characteristic. *Ākāra* refers to gestures such as shaking the head, etc. *Vappa* refers to seed fit for sowing. *Vappa* also means a bank or shore;
it further refers to the base of a wall, irrigation water, and heat. The term *sammuti* (convention) is used in the sense of permission and common usage. The word *akkhata*... [text ends]
In the sense of parched grain (*lājā*) and various preparations of rice (*dhaññavikati*), the word *napuṃsaka* is used [as a neuter noun].

(1134) *Satraṃ* is used in the sense of sacrifice (*yāga*), worship of the gods (*devapūjā*), and constant giving (*sadādāna*). *Sasu* is used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*). *Satraṃ* is also used in that sense. *Soma* refers to a medicinal herb (*osadhi*) and the moon (*canda*).
"Soma [is also used] for Kuvera and for the deity of the ancestors (*pitudevatā*)."
“In the Vasuppabheda and Vasudhākara [ponds],
in the divine medicinal Sāmalatā creeper,
in the breeze, in camphor-water, and in the monkey.”

Vopālita. Regarding the phrase *yugagehaṅga*: it refers to a structural component of a house that has become a yoke (*yuga*), placed upon pillars according to their east-west alignment. When the structural components of the house are placed according to their south-north alignment, it is called a *saṅghāṭa*.
The commentary on the verse quarters is finished.
The commentary on the *Anekatthavagga* (The Chapter on Multiple Meanings) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Section on Indeclinables (Abyayavagga) 1136–1137.

*Cirassa* and the other three are four [particles] having the sense of "long time. *Cirāya* and *cirā* occur here [as examples]. *Sahā* and the other three are four [particles] having the sense of "together with" (*saha*). *Punappunam* and the other four are five [particles] having the sense of "repeatedly. *Vinā* and the others are five [particles] having the sense of "without" (*vajjana*). 1138.
*Balavam*, *suṭṭhu*, *atīva*, *kimuta*, *su*, and *ati*—these six are used in the sense of "excess" (*atisaya*). Furthermore, *suṭṭhu* is also used in the sense of "praise" (*pasaṃsā*).
"Even in questions, how much more so?"—*āho*, *kiṃ*, *kimu*, *udāhu*, *kimuta*, and *uda*: these six are particles used for alternative options (*vikappa*) and deliberation (*vitakka*).

Among them, the word *āho* begins with a long vowel. For Bhāguri says: "The words *āho* and *udāhu* are used in the sense of alternative options (*vikappa*) and in making something manifest (*vibhāvana*).

As in: "Is this a tree stump, or is it a man? However, Rudda says it begins with a short vowel: "*Aho* is used for a lord (*issara*), for what is superior (*adhika*), for an alternative option (*vikappa*), and for wonder (*vimhaya*). As for the word *kimu*:

*Rassanto* (ending in a short vowel): *Kimāyaṃ khāṇu*, *kimu puriso*. The word *uda* begins with a short vowel (*ud-asaddo rassādi*). *Dhūmo ayam oda kāpotaṃ*; here the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of a collection (*samūhatthe*).
The word *kiñca* is also used in the sense of an alternative (*vikappe*). The word *kimuta* is stated to express excess (*atisaye*). 1139.

*Bho*, *are*, *ambho*, *hambho*, *re*, *je*, *aṅga*, *āvuso*, *he*, *hare*—these ten are terms of address (*avhāne*). The words *haṃ* and *ho* are also included here. *Kathaṃ*, *kiṃsu*, *nanu*, *kacci*, *nu*, *kiṃ*—these six are identical (*samā*) and possess the same meaning (*samānatthā*).

1140. *Adhunā*, *etarahi*, *idāni*, and *sampati*—these four [terms] signify "now. *Aññadatthu*, *taggha*, *sasakkaṃ*, *addhā*, *kāmaṃ*, *jātu*, *ve*, and *have*—these eight signify certainty (*ekaṃsa*) and the sense of certainty.
1141. The seven beginning with *yāvatā* express limitation (*pariccheda*). Among them, *yāvatā* and *yāva* denote indefinite limitation.
*Tāvatā*, *tāva*, and *ettāvatā* denote definite limitation. *Kittāvatā* and *kīva* denote the sense of inquiry regarding limitation.
1142–1143. *Yathā*, *tathā*, *yatheva*, *evaṃ*, *yathānāma*, *yathāhi*, *seyyathāpi*, *evamevaṃ*, *vā*, *tatheva*,

*yathāpi*, *evampi*, *seyyathāpi*, *nāma*, *yathariva*, *yathā*, *ca*, *viya*, *tathariva*— these seventeen [particles] occur in the sense of resemblance (*paṭibhāga*) and the sense of similarity (*sadisa*).

1144. *Saṃ*, *sāmaṃ*, and *sayam*—these three have the sense of "by oneself" (*sayam-eva*). *Āma*, *sāhu*, *lahu*, *opāyikaṃ*, *patirūpaṃ*, and *sādhu*—these seven have the sense of acceptance (*sampaṭicchanatthe*). *Āmantā* is also used here [in that sense]. 1145.

The six beginning with *yam* (i.e., *yam*, *tam*, *etam*, *enam*, *imam*, *kim*) are used in the sense of cause (*kāraṇatthe*). The two words *cana* and *ci* signify "not all" (*asākalye*), meaning "not in its entirety.

Examples of usage include *kadācanaṃ* and *kadācī*. The word *mudhā* means "fruitless," i.e., devoid of result; it also means "without purpose" (*nippayojana*). It is also used in the sense of "without root" (*amūle*).
1146. The word *jātu* is used in the sense of "in one respect" (*ekamse*). *Sabbato*, *samantato*, *parito*, and *samantā*—these four are synonymous. 1147.

*Na*, *a*, *no*, *mā*, *alaṃ*, and *nahi*—these six are particles of negation. *Ce*, *sace*, and *yadi*—these three are used in the sense of "if. The word *saddhaṃ* is used in the sense of "favorable. *Nattaṃ* and *doso* are used in the sense of "that which is provocative of passion.

The word *divā* is used in the sense of "day" or "days. 1148. *Īsaṃ*, *kiñci*, and *manaṃ*—these are used in the sense of "slightly. *Atakkite* and *avitakkite* mean "unexpectedly" or "without reflection. *Sāhasaṃ* is used in the sense of "forceful compulsion. *Aggato*, *purato*, and *pure*—these are used in the sense of "from the front" or "before. The words *pecca* and *amutra* refer to "another world" or "the next life."

1149. *Aho* and *ca hi* are used in the sense of wonder (*vimhaya*). *Aho* is also used in the sense of choice (*vikappa*) and in the sense of agreement (*sammoda*). The word *tuṇhī* signifies silence (*mone*) and non-speaking (*abhāsana*). *Āvi* and *pātu* signify the sense of being manifest (*pākaṭattha*). *Sajju* and *sapadi* signify "at that very moment" (*taṅkhaṇe*). 1150.

*Sudaṃ*, *kho*, *assu*, *yagghe*, *ve*, *hā*, and others beginning with the letter *ha* are particles used for the purpose of completing the metrical line (*padapūraṇe*). *Antarena*, *antarā*, and *anto* signify "within" (*abbhantare*). *Avassaṃ* and *nūna* signify certainty (*nicchayatthe*).

1151. *Saṃ* is a prefix with the sense of "seen" (*diṭṭha*) and "joy" (*ānanda*). *Samupajo* and *saṃpyatra* [are used] in the same sense. In the expression of desire (*kāmappavedana*), that is, in the declaration of a wish, as in: "Does your mother live? or "This is what I desire.
*Usūyopagame* means an approach preceded by envy (*usūyā*). Rudra states: "In the consent to desire (*kāmo*), and also in the approach with envy (*usūyopagame*)."
This meaning is also seen in the cases of *usūya*, *upagama*, and *anuññāna*.
1152–1153. "Yathāttha" means truth (*sacca*). "Yathātatha" is the non-transgression of that [truth]; here, the indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva*) is formed with the word *attha*.
This word *tatha* is a synonym for "become" (*bhūta*). The words *sadā*, *sanam*, and *sana* mean "eternal" (*nicca*). The word *sana* is also used here. "Pāyo,"...
*Bāhulyaṃ* means "abundance" and *samā* means "equal. *Pañcakaṃ* refers to the external [set]. *Saṇikaṃ* is a word meaning "not fast" (*asīgha*).
1154. *Sammā* and *suṭṭhu* are two synonyms for "well.
1155. *Sāyaṃ*, *sāye*, and *sāyanhe* mean "in the evening. *Atrāha* means "on this day"; here the word *ajja* (today) is used.
1156. *Yattha* and the other three [words] denote indefinite places and so forth; *tattha* and the others denote definite places and so forth.
1157. *Sammukhā*, *āvi*, and *pātu* are synonymous.
1158. The three beginning with *appeva* express doubt. The words *iti*, *itthaṃ*, and *evaṃ* are used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). The word *kathañci* expresses difficulty (*kiccha*).

1159. *Khedo* means weariness; *khinnatā* is the state of being weary. *Sacchi* is used in the sense of "before one's eyes" (*paccakkhe*). *Dhuvaṃ* is used in the sense of "firm" (*thire*) and as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). *Tiro* and *tiriyaṃ* are identical in meaning. *Duṭṭhu* and *kusa* are used in the sense of "badly" (*kucchāyaṃ*).

1160. *Suvatthi* is used in the sense of "blessing" (*āsiṭṭhatthamhi*). *Dhi* is used in the sense of "censure" (*nindāyaṃ*). The seven particles beginning with *kuhiñca* have the sense of asking about place and so forth (*ṭhānādipucchanatthā*).

1161. *Iha*, *idha*, *atra*, and *ettha*—these express meanings such as "place" (*okāsatthādi*). The pair beginning with *sabbatra* is used for all [three] times and so forth (*sabbasmiṃ kālādike*). *Kadā* is used for "at what time? (*kismiṃ kāle*). *Kudācanaṃ* is used for "at what time? (*kasmiṃ kāle*).

1162–1163. Having demonstrated the indeclinables (*abyaya*) that are counterfeits (*patirūpaka*) of case-endings, nouns, and verbs, he says “in the sense of the commencement of an action,” etc., in order to demonstrate those other types of indeclinables.
Among these, a counterfeit of a case-ending is, for example: “*cirassaṃ*, *ciraṃ*, *cirena*,” and so forth.
A counterfeit of a noun is, for example: “*āma*, *sāhu*, *lahu*, *opāyika*,” and so forth. A counterfeit of a verb is...
For example: "a" and so forth. A verbal-like form (*ākhyātapatirūpaka*) is, for example:

"atthi" and so forth. *Sambhava* means origin or source. *Udiṇṇe*, *pavuddhe*, and *vaḍḍhane* mean increased or grown. *Tisa* means satisfaction; [the suffix] *ti* means satiety. *Niyoge* and *niyojane* mean commissioning or directing.

*Agge* means foremost or supreme. *Tappare* and *tappadhāne* mean devoted or intent upon. *Saṅge* and *laggane* mean attachment or clinging. *Pakāre* means similar or of a kind, or else difference. *Antobhāve* means inclusion within.
In the sense of "thrown in"; in the sense of separation or being away; in the sense of a part or a portion;

in the sense of steadfastness, energy, or exertion—these four meanings are either connected with *dhātu* (element) or connected with *nāma* (name). However, regarding the meaning of the name-word *pā* when not so connected, it is stated in the *Ekakkharakosa*, verse 73:
"The word *po* may be used in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), or *pā* may occur in the sense of winds."
1164. *Vikkama* is exertion (*padhāna*). 1165–1167.

When placed in renunciation (*sanyāsa*), it is liberation (*mokkha*), which is *nibbāna*. A heap (*rāsi*) is a collection (*nikara*). A house (*geha*) is an abode (*nilaya*). Instruction (*ādesa*) is the act of explaining (*ācikkhana*).

A simile (*upamā*) is that which resembles. Transgression (*accaya*) is overstepping. Proximity (*sāmīpya*) is the state of being near. Cessation (*uparati*) is tranquility (*upasama*). Removal (*nīharaṇa*)...
Removal (*apanayana*). Obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), bringing forth (*āharaṇa*), grasping (*gahaṇa*).

1168. In the case of high work (*uddhakamma*) and in a park (*uyyāna*). In separation (*viyoga*) and when raised up (*uppāsite*). Attainment of purpose (*atthalābha*) is *uppatti*. In the sense of being powerful (*pabala*) and very thick (*mahābahala*). *Dakkhaggatā* means in the state of skill (*dakkhabhāva*) and in the state of preeminence (*aggabhāva*).

In power (*satti*) and in liberation (*mokkha*), which is *nibbāna*. 1169. And *du* [is used] in the sense of absence (*abhāva*): *dussīla*, *duppañña*. In the sense of lack of success (*asamiddhi*): *dubbhikkha*. Not rejoicing (*anandana*) and not delighting (*amodana*).

1170. *Samantattasamiddhīsū*: in the sense of "on all sides" (*samantabhāve*) and in the sense of "prosperity" (*samiddhiyaṃ*). *Saṅgate*: in the sense of being joined or united. *Vidhāne*: in the sense of an arrangement or performance. *Pabhavo*: origin or source. *Punappunakriyā*: repeated action; doing again and again. 1171–1172. *Atisayo*: here it means "excessive" (*adhimattaṃ*).

The word *bhusa* has the sense of intensity (*bhusattho*) and the sense of "all around" (*samantattho*); therefore, it should be understood that the word *bhusa* also possesses the meaning of "everywhere" (*samanta*) as a synonym.
*Issariyo*: lordship or power. *Accaye*: in the sense of passing by or transgression. *Kalahe*: in the sense of strife or dispute.
*Bhāse* means in speaking; there is also the reading *bhāsāya*. *Kuccha* means in censuring. *Vimukha* means in the sense of being turned away.
*Moha* means delusion. *Padhāna* means distinguished or preeminent. *Dakkhatā* means skillfulness or cleverness.

*Kheda* means exhaustion or fatigue. 1173. *Jānana* means in knowing or understanding. *Avaṃsira* means in the lower part. *Aniñcaya* means in non-ascertainment. *Avaññāta* means in contempt or disrespect.

*Deso*, *byāpanaṃ*, and *hāni* form a *dvanda* compound. In the sense of verbal action—that is, in the act of speaking. In the sense of theft—that is, in robbing. And in the sense of ignorance, as well as in the sense of acquisition and so forth. 1174. *Anu* is used in the sense of "behind" (*pacchātthe*) in the word *anucaro*.
In the sense of "intense" (*bhusatthe*) in *anuggato*. In the sense of "similar" (*sadise*) in *anurūpo*. In the sense of "following" (*anuvattiyaṃ*) in *anveti*.

In the sense of "inferior" (*hīne*) in *anu Sāriputtaṃ paññavanto* ("those wise ones inferior to Sāriputta"). In the sense of "third" (*tatiyatthe*) in *Bārāṇasī nadimanvavasitā* ("Bārāṇasī is situated along the river"). [It is also used] in the sense of place (*deśe*) and in the sense of characteristic (*lakkhaṇe*).

The particle *anu* is used [as a kamma-vacana suffix] in the sense of (1) shadow (*vicchāya*), (2) being in such a state (*itthambhūta*), and (3) a portion (*bhāga*), etc. (1) In the sense of a mark (*lakkhaṇa*): "The moon shines following the tree" (*rukkham-anu vijjotate cando*). In the sense of shadow:
"He stands following tree after tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkham-anu tiṭṭhati*). In the sense of being in such a state: "Devadatta is good toward his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaram-anu*).

In the sense of a portion: "Whatever may belong to me here" (*yad-etttha mam-anu siyā*). [The particle *pari* is used as follows: In the sense of embracing: "He embraces" (*parissajati*). In the sense of censuring: "Having censured" (*paribhāsetvā*). In the sense of wearing: "Having put on the garment" (*vatthaṃ paridahitvā*).
*Avañña*: contempt or insult. *Ādhāra*: support; *bhojana*: food; *soka*: sorrow; *byāpana*: pervasion. *Tatva*: reality or true nature. *Lakkhaṇa* and so forth:

characteristic, description, state of being thus, and portion. 1176. *Visiṭṭha*: distinguished; *abhidhamma*. *Uddhakamma*: superior work; *sāruppa*: suitable; *vuddhi*: growth; *pūjā*: honor; *adhika*: excessive. *Kula*: family; *abhijana*: lineage.

In the sense of falsehood (*asacca*), regarding the fourfold [categories] beginning with characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), [the prefix] *abhi-* is used according to Pāṇini 1.4.91: *abhirabhāge*, excluding the sense of "portion" (*bhāga*).
In the *Lakkhaṇa* and other works, the designation *kammappavacanīya* is stated (in the *Rūpasiddhi*, section on *kāraka*). 1177.

*Adhi* [is used] in the senses of superiority, lordship, reading, pronunciation, determination, attainment, certainty, the upper part, etc., hiring, devotion, and qualification. 1178–1179. Regarding the reading *vāmādāne*:
*vāme* means left or contrary; *ādāne* means taking or grasping. In the sense of "taking up speech," it is said: *paccassosi*. In the sense of a substitute (*paṭinidhi*)...

In the sense of "resembling the primary," [it refers to] the Buddha. In the sense of "obstructing" and "turning back. In the sense of "depending on" (*paṭicca*), regarding the meaning of the word *paṭicca*. In the fourfold [categories] beginning with "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*).
1180–1181. In the sense of "nearness," "commencement of action," "limit," "upward action," "desire," "binding," and "pervasion" (*abhividhi*).

And *ā*: in the sense of difficulty (*kiccha*), slight meaning (*īsattha*), returning (*nivatti*), lack of confidence (*appasāda*), blessing (*āsīsana*), refuge (*saraṇa*), and the refuge of speech (*vākyasaraṇa*); likewise when recollecting (*anussaraṃ*).
Also in the sense of support (*patiṭṭhāyaṃ*) and in cases such as wonder (*vimhaya*). 1182. *Atīta* [is used] in the sense of having become (*bhūtabhāve*).

1183. Even regarding honor (*sambhāvana*) and celestial sensual pleasures (*dibba-kāma*), he does not find delight therein. *Sambhāvana* means being honored; by way of words of high praise, it signifies non-obstruction even in the absence of actual power.

*Saṃvaraṇa* means covering or closing. 1184–1185. *Apagata* means gone away or departed. *Upekkhā* [is used] in the sense of arising or fitting together. *Upakhāriya* means an excess; *doṇa* [is used] in this sense.

*Buddhupakkama* refers to a former deed; it is the cutting off of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Paccupaṭṭhāna* refers to the manner of being grasped or appearing. *Uparitta* refers to the state of being above or superior.
1186. *Upapanno*: "Fasting while not eating. *Upadese*:

"In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat. *Vacanapaṭiggāhe*: "May it be so. *Idamatthe*: [this refers to] the meaning of the word *idaṃ*. 1187. *Samuccaye*: in the sense of conjunction;
*kevalasamuccaye*: in the sense of exclusive conjunction.
Robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings—these he gave to those who have become upright, with a mind full of serene confidence.

(2.22.551) In the compound *cakkhusota*, both "eye" (*cakkhu*) and "ear" (*sota*) are included. This is a cumulative compound (*anvācaya*), where one term is stated as the primary element and the other is added.
The expression [“samaṇabrāhmaṇā”] occurs because of the subordinate status [of the members]. “Guard your virtue and give gifts.

“Ascetics and brahmins” (samaṇabrāhmaṇā) refers to ascetics and brahmins respectively. In that regard, there is neither pure conjunction (kevalasamuccaya) nor subsequent conjunction (anvācaya) within a compound;
only the other two types exist within compounds.

1188. The letter *pa* [indicates] similarity and distinction. It is said that *go* [is used] when there is a reversal of the word-meaning (*padattha-vipallāsa*). In the sense of completing a desired word, it is called *samāpana*. 1189. *Pajjaṃ* is in the sense of the particle *vā*.

In this case of restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*), the subsequent [element] is dissimilar (*asarūpa*). The root *ṭhā*, preceded by *vi* and *ava*, is used in the sense of returning from a course;
[the suffix] *to* is added, *ṭhātissa* becomes *tho*, and there is doubling of the dissimilar [consonant]. "Restricted option" (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*) means an option that is fixed or determined.
The prefix *ava-* [in the verb] *saja* occurs in the senses of releasing, embracing, and creation;

it means "adornment" (*bhūsana*) in the sense of decoration (*alaṅkāra*), and "prohibition" (*vāraṇa*) in the sense of warding off (*nivāraṇa*). *Pariyatti* refers to mastery or thorough acquisition; *alaṃ* is also used in the sense of fitness. Furthermore, the word *atha* may occur in four senses: sequence (*anantara*), etc. (1190).

It occurs in three senses beginning with praise (*pasaṃsā*), in acceptance (*svīkāra*), and in acknowledgment (*paṭiññāna*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the word *nāma* signifies four senses: manifestation (*pakāsa*), purpose (*attha*), possibility (*sambhāva*), and anger (*kopa*), among others. Its specific function is restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). (1191)

1192. *Anuññā* means consent (*anumati*). *Santānaṃ* means inclination (*anunaya*). *Ālapanaṃ* means addressing (*sambodhanaṃ*). The word *vata* may signify: certainty (*ekaṃsa*), compassion (*dayā*), pity (*karuṇā*), laughter (*hāsa*), joy (*pahāsa*), distress (*kheda*), fatigue (*parissama*), addressing (*ālapana*), wonder (*vimhaya*), and marvel (*acchariya*).

1193. At the beginning of a sentence: “*Handa vadāmi te*” (Come, I shall tell you). *Visāda* means dejection (*kheda*). The words *yāva*, *tāva*, and *tūti*—as well as the compound *yāvatāva*—signify totality (*sākalya*) and entirety (*niravasesa*).

*Yāvadatthaṃ* means “as much as is taken. *Māna* means measure (*pamāṇa*). [The phrase] “*Yāva pamāṇamariyādā-vadhāraṇatthakaṃ*” signifies the sense of delimitation (*avadhāraṇatthaka*) regarding measure and boundary (*pamāṇamariyādā*).
“Mata” means “known,” according to Bhāguri. When a limit is delimited, [it is used].
The word *purattha* signifies the eastern direction; it also occurs in the sense of what is to come, in front, in abundance, as the first, and at the beginning.
It also refers to a continuous sequence, that is, a composition of sentences such as a narrative of the past.
*Cirantare* means in the past. *Nikaṭe* means in the proximate or present. *Āgāmike* means in the future.

(Verse 1195) The word *khalu* is used in the sense of prohibition, as a particle for the ornamentation of a sentence (*vākyālaṅkāre*), as a decorative element of speech (*vākyabhūsāyaṃ*), in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*) meaning "only," and in the sense of well-known fact (*pasiddhiyaṃ*).

The word *abhitō* is used in the senses of "near" (*āsanne*), "facing" (*abhimukhe*), and "on both sides" (*ubhayato*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādinā*), it is also used in the senses of "quickly" (*sīghē*) and "entirety" (*sākalye*).

It occurs in the sense of "at. *Abhitoyam* means "near" (as in *āsanne*). *Abhitova* means "facing" (*abhimukhe*). *Abhito* occurs in the sense of "on both sides" (*ubhayato*), as in *abhito maggassa*.
It occurs in the sense of "quickly," as in *abhito adhīyitvā*. It occurs in the sense of "entirety" (*sākalye*), as in *abhito vanaṃ daḍḍhaṃ*. 1196.

*Yadi* occurs in the sense of "even though" (*anuggahaṇa*) and in the sense of "reproach" (*garaha*). *Api* occurs in the sense of "certainly" (*ekamsattha*) and in the sense of "not otherwise" (*avitathattha*). Furthermore, the word *pana* may occur in the sense of "distinction" (*visesa*) and in the sense of "filling the verse" (*padapūraṇa*).

1197. The particle *hi* occurs in four senses: as a cause (*kāraṇa*), and so forth. The particle *tu*, however, occurs in three of those four senses, excluding the sense of cause. The particle *ku* signifies evil, slightness, reproach, and loathing. 1198.

The particle *nu* is used in the sense of doubt and in interrogation. The word *nānā* signifies multiplicity and exclusion. The word *kiṃ* is indeclinable; it is used in interrogation and in loathing.

It possesses all three genders, but when used in the sense of restriction (*niyama*), it is restricted to the three genders [as an adjective]. [The word *vāri*] means water. [The word *muddha*] means the head.
And *kaṃ* is used for happiness as well; and it is said in the *Nānatthasaṅgahe*:
"What [word] is common to Brahmā, the dark-blue, and all nouns;
and what is [used] for fire, a peacock, happiness, the head, and water?"—the answer being *kaṃ*.
1199. The word *amā* is used in the sense of "together with" (*sahattha*) and in the sense of "proximity" (*samīpattha*), as in *amāvāsī* (the new moon) and *amāgata* (come together).

The word *puna* is used in the sense of "division" (*bheda*) and "distinction" (*visesa*), as in *apaṭhame puna dadāti* ("he gives again [in a different case]"). The word *kira* is used in the sense of "report" (*anussava*), "gradual hearing," and "disapproval.
The word *uda* is used in the sense of "also" (*apyattha*), "question," "option" (*vikappana*), and "alternative" (*atthantarassa vikappana*).

1200. *Paccha* refers to the western direction and to the final, future time. *Sāmi*, however, means "portion" (*addha*) and "part" (*bhāga*), as well as "loathing" (*jigucchana*) and "censure" (*nindā*).
Regarding "portion" and "part," *sāmi* is so stated; it is the same for "loathing" as well.

*Pātu* means "manifestly" (*pakāsa*), "that which is to be manifested" (*pakāsanīya*), "possible" (*sambhava*), and "arising" (*uppatti*). *Mitho* means "one another" (*aññoñña*) and "in secret" (*raho*).
1201. The word *hāsa* is used in the senses of exhaustion, sorrow, and suffering. The word *ahaha* is used in the senses of exhaustion, wonder, and the marvelous.

The word *dhi* is used in the sense of causing injury and in censure. The words *tiriyaṃ* and *tiros* function in the sense of concealment; as in *tiriyaṃ katvā kaṇḍaṅgato* (having concealed from the arrow-shaft) or *tirokatvā*. 1202–1203.
Regarding the established usage of indeclinables (*abyaya*) classified as prefixes (*upasagga*) or particles (*nipāta*), which possess both enumerated and unenumerated meanings:
Having shown some [examples] in the extensive application (*pacurappayoga*), he says "tun" and so forth in order to show others as well by way of summary.
And here, by the words beginning with *tu* and ending with *jj*, only those [suffixes] ending in them are taken;

for it is not possible for these alone to function as indeclinables (*abyaya*). Its meaning is as follows: [the suffixes] ending in the *tu-na* suffix, and likewise *tvāna*, *tave*, *tvā*, *tuṃ*, *dhā*, *so*, *thā*, *kkhattuṃ*.
The suffixes *to*, *tha*, *tra*, *hiṃ*, *canaṃ*, *hiṃ*, *haṃ*, *dhi*, *ha*, and those ending in *yakāra* (the letter *y*), as well as *hiṃdha*, *dhunā*, *rahi*, and *dāni*;
furthermore, *kiṃsmā*, *vo*, *dācanaṃ*, *dājjathaṃ*, and *thattaṃ*; and those ending in the suffixes *jjha* and *jjhu*; and *abyayībhāva* compounds;
and those ending in the substitution of *yā* for *tuṇādi*—these are called indeclinables (*abyaya*). An example of usage is: *kātuna*, *katvāna*, *kātave*, *katvā*, *kātuṃ*, *sabbadhā*.
Examples include: *sabbaso*, *sabbathā*, *catukkhattuṃ*, *sabbato*, *sabbattha*, *sabbatra*, *kuhiñcanaṃ*, *kuhiṃ*, *kuhaṃ*,
*sabbadhi*, *iha*, *yahiṃ*, *idha*, *adhunā*, *etarahi*, *idāni*, *kva*, *kudācanaṃ*, *kadā*, *ajja*,
*kathaṃ*, *aññathattaṃ*, *ekajjhaṃ*, *sajju*, *upanagaraṃ*, *antopāsādaṃ*, and *abhivandiya*.
This, however, is the concise definition of all indeclinables (abyaya):
"That which remains the same across the three genders,
all case endings, and all numbers, and does not undergo change— that is an indeclinable."
The commentary on the section on indeclinables (*abyayavagga*) is finished.

Thus ends the commentary on the General Section (*sāmaññakaṇḍa*) within this *Abhidhānappadīpikā-vaṇṇanā*, composed by the wise Great Minister Sirimaḥācaturaṅgabala, who wanders with the knowledge of the great forest of all grammar and is a lion among the elephants of poets.
Commentary on the Conclusion (*nigamanavaṇṇanā*).
1. By the passage beginning with “*Saggakaṇḍo*,” the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* illustrates her possession of three stalks that resemble a skull, oil, and a wick. 2.
By the *toṭaka* verse beginning with “*Tidive*,” its purpose is explained. Its meaning is as follows:
the person who is the agent [in the world] of the thirty-three gods (*tidiva*), in the Brahma-world, on earth in the human world, and in the abode of the serpents in the Naga-world—
In this *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, which illuminates and makes manifest the designation that is the common name for all things denoted that are present in these three locations,
a person who is skillful and clever through hearing, memorizing, and so forth, [becomes proficient] in the word of the Great Sage,
the Perfectly Enlightened One— namely, that which is reckoned as the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya.
One who is skillful in speech is clever; by that very skillfulness, one is called wise. 3–9.

Now, having shown the name, qualities, residence, manner of composition, and the virtues and name of the monastery in which this book was composed, seven verses were spoken to show the author’s own name and qualities.
Among them, the second is called *bhujaṅgappayāta*. This is the commentary on the meaning of their connection and intent: he—
The king named Parakkamabhuja caused [it] to be built; this is connected with the word "protected" (*rakkhesi*). What qualities did that king possess?

He was adorned with virtues (*guṇabhūsana*), wearing the ornaments of virtues such as faith (*saddhā*) and the rest. He was radiant (*tejassī*), endowed with splendor. He was victorious (*jayī*), possessed of victory over his enemies.
He had the prowess of a lion (*kesarivikkama*), being endowed with heroic qualities like the lion (*kesara*), and he was full of valor (*vīriyavā*). Where did that king reside? That king...

He was one whose habit was to dwell on the island named Laṅkā. For a long time, for a long duration, he righteously—by means of proper methods and causes—brought into harmony the threefold division of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha that had been split into three distinct Nikāyas;
thus, being one who "causes to be made" (karoti), he is a "maker" (kammika). Likewise, he was always diligent toward his own person as if it were his very body.

Having sacrificed for a long time with costly requisites, he protected that Tipiṭaka. Likewise, just as by the king— by means of his own reputation, consisting of his faith and other virtues, which served as the instrument— the island of Laṅkā,
which was his own dwelling place, became his field of action, was made crowded, congested, and devoid of space, so too [was it filled] with monasteries.
Lanka has been crowded with villages, monasteries, fields, and ponds. Thus,
because I obtained the favor of that king— who was unique among others and who granted all desires—
and reached the state of being a composer of books within the domain of the wise, [I dwell] in the palace adorned with gate-towers and other structures built by that same king.
In the section on heaven (*saggakaṇḍa*), which resembles a section on the divine world (*devaloka*), within a collection of lakes possessing pure water and endowed with reservoirs of excellent water,
reflected like a mirror-image of the Great Monastery of Jetavana— the dwelling place of the Blessed One— it is considered excellent, esteemed as an excellent abode, or approved by the virtuous;
it is a cluster of villages accompanied by a multitude of villages joined by water-reservoirs for alms-round.
This *Abhidhānappadīpikā* was composed by the wise Elder Moggallāna— who dwelt in the monastery known as Mahājetavana, living there with peaceful conduct and tranquil behavior,
desiring the endurance of the True Dhamma, and endowed with preeminent knowledge—
after the name of the venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the possessor of psychic powers who was the second chief disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Concluding Statement:
If a fault here has the possibility of being established by means of valid cognition,
it likewise penetrates even into those possessed of virtues.
Just as water, food, or even a living creature—
whether four-footed or footless, or even a blade of grass—
is spoken of for the purpose of making it known without causing it to tremble.
Virtue and fault always alternate;
therefore, O Wise One, may you be impartial toward me.
May you forgive my faults or lead me toward virtue.
He who was Sīhasūra, the lord of white elephants,
the king of kings in Tambadvīpa,
the ruler of men who conquered the elephant Dubbāra and others.
Endowed with qualities such as beauty and fearlessness,
bearing that very name and born from the lineage of that [lineage],
he was possessed of faith and other virtues, and was one who had shattered the four armies.
Nāgādithāma is exceedingly difficult to overcome;
he is of lofty wisdom, steadfast, and renowned.
Therefore, I have been most graciously favored by him.
By means of a compendium not shared by others,
I have briefly composed this commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*,
for the benefit of those who hear it and for easy understanding.
May the king protect his subjects as a snake protects its eggs;
may the people also practice the Dhamma;
and may they fulfill their well-considered goals.
"May the god also rain in due season.
The Commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā is finished.
